The lawyer of Junaid Hafeez, a Fullbright scholar imprisoned for 13 years in a Pakistani jail, tells DW he is hopeful for his release
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:59:00 UTC
22:59:00 KST

Will Pakistan scholar facing death for blasphemy be freed?
September 30, 2026
Junaid Hafeez, a former university lecturer and Fullbright scholar was thrown in prison 13 years ago under Pakistan's strict blasphemy laws for comments he allegedly made on Facebook. After a trial that spanned years, a court in 2019 sentenced him to death.
Last week, a high court in Lahore began hearing Hafeez's appeal, raising hopes his conviction could be overturned.
"I want to see my son free and back home. We are fighting a very difficult battle," Junaid Hafeez's father, Hafeez-un-Naseer, told DW.
Naseer said he met with his son in prison last Thursday through a glass window, speaking to him by phone.
"This case has taken everything from us," he said.
Saif-ul-Malook, a lawyer representing Hafeez, said the academic has read around thousands of books during his years in prison.
"He is an intellectual. His health is fine, but he is frustrated inside the jail," Malook told DW. "I am hopeful that under this bench, he will be released."
Who is Junaid Hafeez?
Before his arrest, Hafeez was a Fulbright scholar and had studied in the United States. He later returned to Pakistan and began working as a lecturer in English literature at Bahauddin Zakariya University in the city of Multan.
Human rights groups say that shortly after he began working there as a graduate student in 2011, he found himself targeted by an Islamist student group who took issue with what they considered Hafeez's "liberal" teaching.
Hafeez was arrested on March 13, 2013, accused of using a fake Facebook profile to insult the Prophet Muhammad in a closed group called "So-Called Liberals of Pakistan."
His father has said he was set up by the Islamists on campus, who wanted to get one of their own into an open position at the university.
What are the details of the blasphemy case?
His trial began in 2014. Because of security concerns, legal proceedings were later moved to Multan Central Jail, and were repeatedly delayed until he was sentenced to death by a trial court in Multan. Hafeez challenged the verdict in 2020, and his appeal has yet to be decided.
The Lahore High Court heard Hafeez's appeal on September 22 before a two-member bench. The judges issued notices to the prosecution and the complainant and asked for arguments on the electronic evidence being relied upon in the case. This includes Facebook material attributed to Hafeez.
"Lahore High Court judges have generally been reluctant to hear blasphemy appeals. This time, Justice Sadiq Mahmud Khurram is on the bench. Let's see how he approaches the case. In my experience, there is prejudice against the accused at every stage," Malook said.
Pakistan's blasphemy laws in focus
Hafiz Ehtisham Ahmed, an Islamabad-based Islamic activist, told DW he thinks the court should uphold the blasphemy conviction, arguing abolishing the laws could "encourage disrespect for religion."
"There is international pressure on Pakistan to change these laws. If Hafeez is acquitted, it would raise serious questions about the justice system," Ahmed said.
Strict blasphemy laws in Muslim-majority Pakistan have been widely condemned internationally for their arbitrary applicaiton and the potential for abuse of power.
Pakistani policy analyst Raza Rumi said that judges are under intense pressure when handling blasphemy cases.
"Acquittals or even procedural decisions can trigger threats and public backlash, contributing to delays and caution in handling such cases," Rumi told DW.
Security has been a major issue throughout the proceedings.
"Human rights groups have documented threats against judges, lawyers, and prosecutors in blasphemy cases. Concerns over their safety can affect both the pace of proceedings and judicial independence," Rumi added.
At least seven judges were transferred during the trial. Hafeez's first lawyer, Rashid Rehman, was shot dead in his Multan office in May 2014. He had reportedly received threats in connection with the case.
What are the chances for Hafeez's appeal?
Hafeez can still be released if the Lahore High Court overturns his conviction. But that will depend on the judges' assessment of the evidence and the arguments made during the appeal. A death sentence imposed by a trial court does not become final without scrutiny by the high court.
For Hafeez, the question now is how quickly the Lahore High Court can hear and decide his appeal after years of delays. The next hearing is due on October 10, but it is unclear how long it will take the court to decide.
"We wish that one night we could go to sleep and wake up to find our son free and back home," said father Naseer.
"I still remember the pain we have endured over all these years since my son was falsely accused. Thirteen years have taken so much from our family, but we have never stopped hoping that one day Junaid will walk free," Naseer added.
Human Rights Watch (HRW) has called for the blasphemy conviction to be overturned. In a February press statement, HRW called for Hafeez's release, adding he has been kept in solitary confinement since June 2014.
"If his appeal is rejected, Junaid's mother will not survive it. His father can barely walk. The whole family has been destroyed. If released, I believe Junaid will become an internationally recognized intellectual, lecturing at leading universities," said lawyer Malook.
"We hope that Hafeez's remaining life will not be wasted in the prison on the death row ands case will be finally concluded and he will be acquitted," he added.

====================================================================================================

Everything Netanyahu does is to stay out of jail: The Bibi Files’ director
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:58:14 UTC
22:58:14 KST

- ‘It’s sort of almost like a monkey on his back, and people forget that he’s motivated to stay out of jail, and everything he does comes back to that,’ Alexis Bloom tells Anadolu
- Bloom says film struggled to secure mainstream US distribution despite Academy Award shortlist, international screenings
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s every political move is shaped by his ongoing corruption trial and his desire to avoid jail, according to Alexis Bloom, director of the documentary The Bibi Files.
“The main message of the documentary is that this man who is leading Israel to the bottom of the sea has a very serious legal case,” Bloom told Anadolu ahead of a screening of the film at the European Parliament in Brussels.
“It’s sort of almost like a monkey on his back, and people forget that he’s motivated to stay out of jail, and everything he does comes back to that,” she said.
Netanyahu was indicted in 2019 on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate cases. He has denied wrongdoing and pleaded not guilty. His trial, which began in 2020, remains ongoing.
Bloom said she wants audiences to look beyond the rapidly changing daily news cycle and consider Netanyahu’s legal troubles as part of the broader context surrounding his political decisions.
“I would just say, in the daily reporting of deaths and riots and settlements and all the very intense news that happens day to day, take a breath and step back and remember the big picture,” she said.
The Bibi Files is built around leaked footage of police interrogations of Netanyahu, his wife Sara, his son Yair and people in their political and personal circles.
Producer Alex Gibney received more than 1,000 hours of leaked interrogation material before approaching Bloom to direct the documentary, which also involved interviews with insiders willing to speak about Netanyahu.
For Bloom, the film, which premiered in 2024, is an example of how cinema can turn complex political and legal issues into a story that audiences can experience on a more immediate and personal level.
Difficult journey to audiences
The film itself has faced obstacles reaching audiences.
The day before its screening at the Toronto International Film Festival, lawyers representing Netanyahu sought an injunction from an Israeli court to prevent publication of the interrogation footage.
The court rejected the request and the screening went ahead.
The film has also faced restrictions in Israel because of privacy laws, while it has been distributed and screened internationally.
However, Bloom said the difficulties continued beyond Israel, particularly in the United States.
"It was very difficult to release this film in America, and some newspapers didn't even want to review it," she explained.
"We did not get mainstream distribution, even though we were shortlisted for an Academy Award, and it broadcast all over Europe. An American mainstream streamer didn't want to take us on, so it was difficult to get it out there," the director added.
The film has received strong critical attention internationally. Rotten Tomatoes currently lists it with a 95% critics’ score.
‘People are moved by art’
For Bloom, the documentary also illustrates the ability of art to engage audiences with political and social questions in ways conventional political discourse often cannot.
“I think that people are moved by art, and it’s very important for art to engage them,” Bloom said.
“I think art is political. That’s my instinct.”
Political issues, she said, are frequently presented through legal documents, official statements, speeches and daily news reports, but cinema can create a different form of engagement.
The ability of art to move audiences is not separate from its political significance, she added.
"If we want to make political changes, we have to engage people not just with dry old literature, or slogans or kind of bureaucratic means. It has to be through art. It has to be through music. It has to be through everything," she said.
'You cannot stop thousands of cinemas'
Despite distribution hurdles, the film is finding another route to audiences through cinemas.
The documentary is preparing for a major theatrical release in Italy, with screenings planned in around 130 cinemas, accompanied by a live event.
"People want to see what's happening in Israel and want to know what are the corruption allegations against Netanyahu," Italian distributor and journalist Giulia Innocenzi told Anadolu.
She said some screenings had already sold out and expressed hope that the response would encourage more cinemas to show the documentary.
"But not all of them want to screen this movie because, of course, Netanyahu is very powerful, and it's a political issue," Innocenzi said.
She also recalled attempts to block the film’s screening.
"Bibi Files was not screened in Israel because of violation of privacy policy, but also Netanyahu tried to block this movie before the Toronto Film Festival," Innocenzi noted.
She argued that cinema can offer political expression more room than traditional media because attempts to restrict one outlet do not necessarily prevent audiences from accessing a film elsewhere.
“You can try to stop one media stream. You can try to stop a TV channel, but you cannot stop thousands of cinemas,” she said.

Spain orders probe after rights group alleges troops abused migrants in Ceuta
MADRID, Sept 29 - Spain's Defence Ministry said on Wednesday it had alerted prosecutors to an Amnesty International report alleging the military tortured or mistreated migrants in Ceuta, and ordered an internal probe into whether any personnel were to blame.
The rights group accused members of Spain's armed forces of torture and other cruel, inhumane or degrading treatment of migrants stranded in the North African enclave after over 72,000 crossed the border from Morocco in late July.
Though most of the migrants later went back, at least 10,000 remain in the tiny Spanish enclave in North Africa, straining local resources and fuelling tensions.
Amnesty International Spain Director Esteban Beltran told Reuters the group had documented 22 cases of torture and abuse by military personnel. In what he said appeared to be a pattern, troops had pursued, beaten and humiliated migrants, including women and unaccompanied children, in nighttime operations.
Amnesty said photographs and videos it reviewed were consistent with allegations of excessive force, including images of hooded personnel striking migrants and spraying their faces with irritants before pushing them across the border.
"In view of the report made public by Amnesty International, it has been agreed to send the report to the prosecutor's office and the duty court in Ceuta, and to instruct the Operations Command to investigate and clarify any possible individual responsibilities," the Defence Ministry said.
Amnesty's Beltran welcomed the move but said it should have come sooner, calling for an exhaustive investigation and the suspension of any military personnel implicated.
"These individuals cannot remain in their duties for a single minute longer, at least as a precautionary measure, until responsibilities are determined," he said.
Amnesty also called for improved humanitarian assistance for migrants still sleeping rough in Ceuta.
"This situation has worried us greatly. They are living in deplorable conditions," Beltran said. REUTERS

Sweden should apologise for injustices against Sami people, commission says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:57:48 UTC
22:57:48 KST

Sweden should apologise for injustices against Sami people, commission says
STOCKHOLM, Sept 30 - The Swedish government should apologise to the indigenous Sami people for past injustices and Sami interests should be given stronger consideration against mining and wind power projects, a government-appointed commission said on Wednesday.
An estimated 80,000 to 100,000 Sami live in the northern lands of Sweden, Finland, Norway and Russia, where reindeer herding over vast areas has been the cornerstone of their culture and livelihood.
The government-appointed Truth Commission said that the Swedish state had unilaterally taken ownership of large parts of Sami land, especially during the 18th and 19th centuries.
"The indigenous Sami people today face major challenges in preserving and developing their culture as a direct consequence of the Swedish state's past and present policies," the Truth Commission wrote in the report published on the government webpage.
The commission's findings add Sweden to a list of Nordic countries confronting their treatment of the Sami. Norway, which is home to around 50,000 Sami people, officially apologised in 2024, and a Finnish commission called for redress in 2025.
The report said Sami communities had been forcibly displaced as far back as the 17th century. The commission urged the government to "acknowledge the historical wrongs, abuses, and violations ... and the harm this has caused the Sami people".
The Swedish parliament recognised the Sami as an indigenous people in 1977, but relations with the state have often been contentious. In recent years, they have clashed with authorities over mining and wind power projects the Sami feel impact their reindeer herding.
The commission said the government should strengthen the land use rights status for reindeer herding. The Sami reindeer herding areas cover around a third of Sweden, bigger than the total area of England. REUTERS

LIVERPOOL, England — Nigel Farage will use a speech in a Brexit-backing Labour heartland to start the fightback after Andy Burnham reignited Britain’s EU debate.
The Reform UK leader — a key architect of Brexit — will make a “major speech” in Doncaster on Thursday to rail against the Labour prime minister opening the door to a possible return to the bloc, a senior Reform official told POLITICO.
Burnham used his first Labour conference as leader, in Liverpool on Tuesday, to snip three political livewires in British politics, including proposing a change to the “triple lock” protecting the state pension and electoral reform.
Advertisement
Farage is spoiling to address all these fault-lines on Thursday.
“He will talk about Burnham wanting to take us into the Euro, return us to freedom of movement with 500 million people and losing the ability to nationalize key industries,” said the Reform official, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss the pending speech in Doncaster.
The Yorkshire city voted 69% in favor of leaving the EU in the 2016 referendum, making it one of the most pro-Brexit areas in the U.K. One of its MPs is Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.
Burnham has reopened the debate in Labour and beyond by saying he will canvass opinion on several options for Britain’s future arrangement with Brussels and set them out around the time of a EU-U.K. summit later this year.
Those options, he has said, could include rejoining the single market, the customs union, or “go all the way,” which Reform is interpreting as scrapping the Pound in favor of the Euro. Burnham has not made that specific pledge, and Labour resisted Britain joining the single currency when it was introduced.
Farage is meanwhile planning to argue that EU re-entry would curb the ability of British governments to nationalize key industries — a play by the Reform leader that upends the traditional left-right debate in British politics. Burnham has put emphasis on bringing back “public control” of privatized utilities rather than public ownership, but Farage has changed tack from his Thatcherite credentials to express support for nationalization in some sectors.
Advertisement
So far most of Farage’s criticism of Burnham’s speech has centered on accusing Labour of “going after pensioners” on the triple lock.
But his stance on the PM announcing a commission to investigate overhauling Britain’s first-past-the-post electoral system will be one to watch.
The current voting system makes it incredibly hard for insurgent parties, like Reform, to get a foothold in Parliament. But after a certain polling threshold is crossed it rewards parties with vast numbers of seats on proportionally little of the vote.
Farage has long been in favor of changing this system — but his party has recently attacked Labour’s reversion to a more proportional voting system in mayoral races as being an “establishment stitch-up.”

“We are here during an attack on the plane. We just subdued the terrorists and are preparing to land,” the man said in Hebrew.
“Anyone who can hear me, we need help. We are about to land in Tabuk, apparently in Saudi Arabia. An unknown area. All the passengers are safe and well, except for the pilot. We need help.”
A key piece of information from the FlyDubai flight is that someone in the cockpit transmitted emergency codes.
Pilots use four-digit ‘squawk codes’ to broadcast their position for air traffic control. These are used for routine flight but also in emergency situations.
Aircraft trackers at Flight Radar say the FlyDubai plane transmitted both emergency and hijack signals.
The plane transmitted a 7700 squawk code that means emergency. It also transmitted a 7500 squawk code, which can mean a hijacking.
These codes have to be manually entered from the cockpit.
Passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon said the plane was “pretty much out of control” when the alleged stabbing took place over Jordan on the flight’s path from Dubai to Tel Aviv.
“The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane,” she told reporters by speakerphone held up by her mother who was waiting at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv.
“It was really on the way to crashing and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralised him,” she said.
“There was also a doctor who gave first aid and people who treated both of them. Other than the pilot, there were no injuries but the bigger fear was really a crash, which is exactly what he was trying to do.”
Her mother, Yasmin Abukasis, said her daughter was on the flight to attend a service for her brother killed in the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack.
Her daughter “thought they were going to die”, Abukasis told AFP, adding that one woman “went to the [cockpit] and saw a lot of blood”.
She said that two other pilots were on the plane and took charge, diverting it to Saudi Arabia.
A commercial plane travelling from Dubai in the United Arab Emirates to Israel has been forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, after an apparent brawl between its pilots prompted distress signals that briefly raised fears of an attempted hijacking.
The flydubai flight was over Jordan when it diverted to Saudi Arabia, transmitting three emergency signals, one of which indicated a possible unlawful interference.
The plane dipped dramatically during the reported fight, descending about 16,000ft in just two minutes.
Israeli officials scrambled fighter jets, fearful of a possible hijacking attempt on a plane containing dozens of Israelis, and the plane landed at Tabuk airport in north-western Saudi Arabia.
A passenger told the Jerusalem Post that one pilot stabbed another and tried to force him out of the cockpit, prompting other Israelis to rush into the cockpit and subdue the attacker as the plane began to plunge.
It was not immediately possible to verify those reports. Pictures of a passenger with blood on their shirt were published by Israeli media.
A spokesperson for the Israeli prime minister’s office initially said that the flight diversion was not because of a hijack attempt; authorities later said they were investigating.
The FlyDubai flight FZ 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia this morning after transmitting emergency signals.
According to Israeli media, a fight had broken out between the plane’s two pilots. Passengers described one of the pilots being seriously injured in an alleged stabbing.
The Boeing 737 plane, which Israeli officials said had between 160 and 180 passengers on board, transmitted a general emergency signal about two and a half hours after departing from Dubai, according to flight-tracking website Flightradar24.
It diverted to Saudi Arabia as it flew over Jordanian airspace, transmitting another emergency signal that indicated what is known as a possible unlawful interference.
The plane again transmitted the initial general emergency signal before later landing at Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk airport.
The aircraft’s data appeared to show that it had suddenly and rapidly descended by nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds before the first emergency signal. It was not immediately clear who transmitted the emergency signals.
Tabuk airport said the plane landed at 9.45am local time and that both pilots were taken to hospital after sustaining injuries.
The Israeli prime minister’s office said the situation was “under control” and that steps were being taken to bring the passengers to Israel.
Israeli minister claims 'terrorist' attempted to crash plane bound for Tel Aviv
An Israeli minister has decried what he described as a “terrorist” incident to kill Israelis after a flight was forced to land in Saudi Arabia when a physical altercation between the pilot and co-pilot prompted initial fears of a hijacking.
A Boeing 737 Max 8 with up to 180 passengers on board made an emergency landing at Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk airport this morning after transmitting three emergency signals, one of which indicated what is known as a possible unlawful interference. Türkiye’s premier aviation, space and technology festival TEKNOFEST opened its doors to visitors Wednesday in the southeastern province of Sanliurfa.
TEKNOFEST Southeast, a leg of the event held in southeastern Türkiye, brings together tech enthusiasts, young investors and thousands of visitors for various shows, exhibitions and the finals of technology competitions across 14 categories from Wednesday through Oct. 4.
Describing Sanliurfa as “the zero point of history,” Bayraktar said it was among the lands where humanity transitioned to settled life, developed agriculture and laid the foundations of civilization.
‘More than 1.6 million young people applied’
Holding its 15th festival since its launch in 2018, Bayraktar said the TEKNOFEST “seedling we planted in 2018 has today turned into a major technology movement.”
He said young people from all 81 provinces of Türkiye and 97 countries were participating in the festival, adding that more than 730,000 teams and over 1.6 million young people had applied to technology competitions in 62 categories.
“These are not just numbers. They are Türkiye’s changing story,” Bayraktar said.
He highlighted the participation of young people from southeastern Türkiye, saying children in the region were learning artificial intelligence and robotics at DENEYAP Technology Workshops.
Referring to the region’s hot climate, Bayraktar said: “When we came to Urfa, we understood something else. If a system works smoothly at noon in the Urfa heat, it will work anywhere in the world, and even in space.”
‘National Technology Initiative is not only in the sky’
Bayraktar said confidence strengthens production, production strengthens technology, and technology creates the foundation for independence.
“That is why the National Technology Initiative exists,” he said.
“The National Technology Initiative is not only in the sky. It is in the fields, factories, laboratories, hospitals, workshops and universities.”
He said the initiative aims to turn ideas into economic value, dreams into production, projects into employment and technology into prosperity for Türkiye.
“Our goal is high technology, domestic production and value-added exports,” Bayraktar said.
“We want to build an entrepreneurship ecosystem that will strengthen our country’s full independence, led by the TEKNOFEST generation.”
- Agricultural technologies in focus
Bayraktar also highlighted the strategic importance of agricultural production, saying food had become a more critical issue than ever.
“We can no longer view agriculture simply as a traditional sector. Agriculture must become one of the high-technology fields of the future,” he said.
He pointed to next-generation national agricultural technologies, AI-supported solutions, genetic science, efficiency and sustainable production as areas of focus.
“As the solutions developed by young people meet these fertile lands, our future will become stronger and more prosperous,” he said.
- Bringing science together with conscience
Bayraktar also addressed the rapid transformation driven by artificial intelligence, saying the technology could accelerate learning and research but should be viewed as a tool that expands human potential rather than a guide that replaces human judgment.
“Technology is a tool. It is the human who determines its direction and must make the final decision,” he said.
“Our aim is not merely to develop technology, but to determine what kind of spirit and direction we will give it,” Bayraktar said.
“We want to use technology for the benefit of humanity. We want to bring science together with conscience, intelligence with morality, and power with justice.”

KAZAN, September 30. /TASS/. Russia is deploying a mechanism to recover illicitly obtained assets that were moved abroad, Prosecutor General Alexander Gutsan said at the 36th meeting of the Coordinating Council of Prosecutors General of the CIS member states.
The session focused entirely on "Modern challenges and new solutions in asset recovery from abroad."
Gutsan thanked his CIS counterparts for prioritizing Russian requests for mutual legal assistance.
"This year, cooperation enabled the freezing of assets held by individuals accused of grand embezzlement and tax crimes in Kazakhstan and Tajikistan, as well as in Mongolia, Bulgaria, Hungary, and Spain," he reported.

"A unified asset recovery mechanism is currently in operation. It ensures seamless coordination among justice, foreign affairs, financial intelligence, and preliminary investigation agencies, as well as other bodies, to trace property abroad and execute asset seizures," the Prosecutor General said.
He noted that asset recovery and the expansion of international cooperation have been integrated into Russia’s national anti-money laundering (AML) framework and designated as a strategic priority by President Vladimir Putin. Consequently, the regulatory framework and law enforcement practices are being upgraded to dismantle the channels used to siphon criminal proceeds out of the country.
The Prosecutor General's Office plays a leading role in spearheading these recovery efforts. Since 2020, it has hosted an interagency task force combining the resources of 17 authorities and organizations. Its mandate involves resolving bottlenecks in specific cases, developing methodological guidelines, and drafting proposals to refine legal frameworks and international cooperation.
"At the same time, it must be acknowledged that executing existing procedures faces various complexities in most jurisdictions," the head of the supervisory agency concluded.

Children Are Back in School. Measles Is, Too
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:50:07 UTC
22:50:07 KST

This fall in the U.S., as kids settle into a new school year, measles is spreading at a level not seen in 35 years. Children have died. And in just the past month, 10 children have been infected in an outbreak linked to a single daycare in Georgia. Far too many students are entering classrooms vulnerable to a highly contagious and dangerous virus.
Yet there has been relative silence from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the agency where I once served as a senior leader, about measles. CDC’s back-to-school messages on X have advised families about sleep, physical activity, healthy lunches, and bullying. All are important. But one message emphasized in prior years at the start of school is noticeably absent and can now be found only in CDC’s online archives: Get your child up to date on routine vaccinations. During the country’s largest measles resurgence in decades, that should be the nation’s most urgent back-to-school message.
CDC’s reticence extends beyond social media. Four measles-associated deaths reported by Pennsylvania were initially absent from the agency’s national dashboard. In late August, CDC posted two of the Pennsylvania deaths, then added an asterisk and language that it was reviewing additional information. The deaths were later removed without a clear explanation. Now two deaths are reported on CDC’s dashboard as of September 28 without identifying the states. This is not transparency; it is silence at a moment when families need clear, accurate information to protect their children.
Why are these deaths being left off the official tally? There’s a disagreement between federal and state officials over how to count measles deaths—even though Pennsylvania investigated each death and reported them to CDC through the established nationally notifiable disease surveillance system that has been used by state and local health departments across the country for years. In late August, when officials from Pennsylvania announced the first two deaths there, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS), even questioned if the deaths were fabricated. But Pennsylvania’s definition of a measles-associated death ensures that deaths unrelated to underlying measles infection are not counted.
Leaders at HHS and CDC have said they are working to clearly define measles deaths and that it will update its counts as reviews are complete. But the agency has not explained which deaths they are currently counting, how these decisions are being made, why the data reporting system used by states was changed, and how they will account for the secondary infections and other complications caused by measles.Two former leaders of the National Center for Health Statistics have called this out publicly, writing in STAT that these changes will delay reporting and add to public confusion about the severity of measles.
An important question to ask is whether shifting explanations and new disease-classification systems are clarifying the outbreak or miring it in confusion and making it easier to minimize. A single measles case can expose dozens of classmates, teachers, and siblings, as well as infants too young to be vaccinated. Federal officials should be using their platforms to prevent the next case and not debating the numbers.
Meanwhile, the big picture is being missed: We know how to prevent this.
After the last significant measles surge in the late 1980s, the CDC Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommended that all kids receive a second dose of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine at age four to six. One dose is approximately 93% effective against measles; two doses are approximately 97% effective. But national MMR coverage among kindergartners fell again during the 2025-2026 school year, and approximately 280,000 kindergartners attended school without documentation that they had completed the MMR series. Vaccine exemptions in 24 states exceeded 5%, meaning these communities no longer have the 95% adequate protection to keep measles from spreading.
The impact extends beyond the child who becomes sick. When an unvaccinated student is exposed to measles, they will often be required to stay at home for at least 21 days. That means missed academics, missed social interactions, and missed work for parents. In addition to the impact on a child and their family, each case of measles costs the public-health system on average $58,600 to respond to, including the cost of contact tracing and quarantines. And measles isn’t over when the rash goes away. It can result in “immune amnesia,” meaning kids are more likely to get other infections over the next two to three years, and approximately one in 10,000 people who recovered from measles will die years later from the rare brain disease subacute sclerosing panencephalitis.
Amid the recent deadly outbreaks of measles, our federal health leaders have too often paired a lukewarm recommendation to vaccinate with insinuations and incorrect information about vaccine ingredients, fetal tissue, or waning immunity. The same week families needed clarity about a growing outbreak, Kennedy addressed a conference hosted by Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine organization he once led.
In response to the outbreak, Pennsylvania has opened up nearly 150 pop-up vaccination clinics in homes and community centers, engaged health systems and local clinics across the state, requested federal support for additional vaccinations, developed a dashboard showing community transmission by county, and worked with coroners to investigate deaths. This is boots-on-the-ground public health.
Our federal health leaders should reinforce that work rather than cast doubt on it, giving parents and schools clear guidance and reporting cases consistently and transparently. Data and definitions matter, but we cannot lose sight of the people who are behind each of these data points. Each case number represents someone who became sick, and behind each death is a grieving family and a life that deserves to be counted. Now that children are back in school, our responsibility is both simple and urgent: to use the tools we know work to keep this preventable disease out of the classroom.

Kremlin dismisses Atlantic US-Russia swap claim
The Kremlin has categorically denied that Moscow and Washington discussed a plan whereby sanctions targeting Russia could be eased in return for the release of US nationals imprisoned in Russia.
Presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Wednesday responded to a question about an article in the Atlantic citing anonymous sources that claimed the administration of US President Donald Trump was considering relaxing some economic restrictions if Moscow would release individuals Washington considers unjustly imprisoned.
“The issue was not discussed in those terms and could not have been, because we categorically reject the notion that there are any political prisoners in Russia and consider framing the issue in this way entirely inappropriate,” Peskov told journalists.
Russian and US special services continue regular contacts concerning various prisoner exchanges, he added.
According to The Atlantic, the proposal was advanced by White House envoy John Coale and approved by Trump for exploration several months ago. The initiative, the outlet's sources speculate, could have reportedly allowed Washington to broaden its engagement with Moscow beyond negotiations over Ukraine and pursue deals involving Russian oil, diesel, rare earth minerals and other commodities.
Trump’s envoys have been exploring ways to revive economic ties with Russia but have so far viewed at least a partial ceasefire in Ukraine as a prerequisite, the outlet wrote on Tuesday.
Washington and Moscow have separately discussed potential economic cooperation. Following talks between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow earlier this month, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said the sides had discussed possible “major, mutually beneficial Russian-American projects.”
The Atlantic also claimed that Washington is seeking to arrange lower-level talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine as early as next month, could focus on a limited ceasefire covering energy infrastructure, potentially in the UAE.
Moscow has repeatedly said it opposes a temporary truce that would allow Ukraine to regroup and rearm, insisting that hostilities can end only through a comprehensive settlement that addresses the root causes of the conflict. Peskov was not asked to respond to the claim.
Speaking at the UN Security Council last week, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Moscow would not agree to pause military operation because such a step could be used by Ukraine’s European backers to supply Kiev with more weapons.
The prospect of renewing US-Russian business ties before the Ukraine conflict is resolved has been sharply criticized by Vladimir Zelensky, who told The Atlantic he would try to “block” any sanctions relief for Moscow before hostilities end.

Royal Run 2027 sells out more than 100,000 spots in under three hours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:48:40 UTC
22:48:40 KST

Eight Danish municipalities did not meet the required staffing ratio in kindergartens in 2025, according to figures published Monday by Statistics Denmark.
The municipalities are Ringsted, Odder, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Struer, Brønderslev, Rebild and Thisted.
Under the political requirement, there must be at least one pedagogical staff member for every six children in kindergartens. In 2024, 14 municipalities failed to meet the requirement.
The trade union BUPL, which represents pedagogues working in Danish children’s institutions, noted that more municipalities now meet the requirement than before.
“Staffing ratios have improved, and that is an important first step to ensure the quality in our daycare institutions,” BUPL chairperson Elisa Rimpler said.
“But we are not at the finish line at all when it comes to giving children the quality they are entitled to.”
Since 2024, there has also been a requirement of at least one employee for every three children in nurseries.
Five municipalities failed to meet that requirement last year: Bornholm, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Thisted and Rebild.
Rimpler said the figures were not good enough and called on municipalities to increase their efforts.
“There is a need to build on top of this, because in many places the staffing ratios on paper are experienced as very far from reality,” she said.
“Both because managers, long-term sick employees, and pedagogues employed to support individual children are counted, and because many of the extra employees do not have the necessary professional qualifications.”
According to BUPL, the law does not require the employees counted in the staffing ratios to have professional training.
The union said the share of pedagogues among staff was 57% in 2019, compared with 50.6% last year.
Children, Elderly and Housing Minister Jacob Mark of the Socialist People’s Party, SF, said it was serious when municipalities failed to meet the legal requirement.
He said the minimum staffing ratios were working because more nurseries and kindergartens were getting more staff around children and nationwide cuts to staffing had stopped.
“But, as I also see, there are eight municipalities that do not meet the minimum staffing ratios. That is completely unacceptable. I am going to intervene against that,” the minister said.
Mark also criticized the practice of counting managers and long-term sick employees in the staffing figures. He said managers are not with children all the time, while long-term sick employees are not with them at all.
According to Mark, municipalities “just” need to hire more pedagogical staff.
The minister said he will send a letter to the eight municipalities that do not meet the requirements. The same municipalities will also face scrutiny from Ankestyrelsen, Denmark’s public authority for supervising municipalities and other public bodies.
Ankestyrelsen can impose a range of sanctions after assessing why a municipality is not complying with the law, including advisory opinions and fines.
“Now they have had four years. Now they must reach the finish line with those minimum staffing ratios,” Mark said.

Egypt, UN envoy discuss Libya's political roadmap, elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:48:00 UTC
22:48:00 KST

Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and UN envoy to Libya Hanna Tetteh have discussed the latest political and security developments in Libya and efforts to advance the political process and hold elections.
Abdelatty received Tetteh in Cairo to discuss developments in Libya and efforts to advance the political process within the framework of the UN roadmap, the Egyptian foreign ministry said in a statement on Wednesday.
Abdelatty expressed Egypt's support for UN efforts to reach a "comprehensive Libyan-Libyan political settlement," stressing that the political process should remain "Libyan-owned and led."
He emphasised the importance of pushing for presidential and parliamentary elections to be held simultaneously, ending transitional periods and unifying Libya's state institutions.
The Egyptian minister also stressed the need to respect Libya's unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Resolving Libya’s political crisis
Egypt is one of the parties to the Tripartite Mechanism of Libya's Neighbouring States, which also includes Tunisia and Algeria.
The Tripartite Consultation Mechanism on Libya was launched in 2017 and suspended in 2019 before resuming in May 2025, when the foreign ministers of the three countries held a consultative meeting in Cairo. The mechanism aims to contribute to resolving the political crisis in neighbouring Libya.
For her part, Tetteh briefed Abdelatty on developments in implementing the roadmap in Libya, according to the statement.
She also reviewed ongoing steps to address outstanding issues related to the constitutional and legal framework governing elections, it added.
Libya has faced political division between two governments since 2022: the internationally recognised administration of Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibeh in Tripoli and a government led by Osama Hammad based in Benghazi and supported by the eastern-based parliament.
UN-led efforts to hold national elections remain stalled, prolonging the oil-rich country's decade-long conflict and instability.

====================================================================================================

Palestinian archaeologists race against time to save Gaza’s heritage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:45:56 UTC
22:45:56 KST

Palestinian archaeologists race against time to save Gaza’s heritage
A Palestinian team rescued Gaza’s artefacts. The question now is where to store them.
Alongside Israel’s genocide in Gaza, there has been an apparent attempt to erase the Palestinian enclave’s cultural heritage.
At least 164 cultural sites in Gaza have been damaged since Israeli military operations began in October 2023 and March 2026, according to UNESCO.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Federal US judge faces complaint over staunch pro-Israel advocacy
- list 2 of 4How a Swedish Palestinian minister raised controversy with Star of David
- list 3 of 4Judge nixes Trump lawsuit alleging Harvard did not protect Jewish students
- list 4 of 4Palestinians in occupied West Bank hold firm on Indigenous Peoples’ Day
Among the ancient landmarks affected in waves of Israeli bombing are the Great Omari Mosque and Hamam al-Sammara, Qasr al-Basha in Gaza’s Old City, and the al-Qarara Cultural Museum near Khan Younis.
Among the rubble are precious artefacts and antiquities, which tell a story of Gaza’s rich cultural history, being at the crossroads of multiple empires and peoples over centuries.
Amid the destruction and disorder of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which has killed at least 74,022 Palestinians, valuable relics of Palestine’s history are being lost.
The Mayasem Association for Culture and Arts’ “Guardians of Heritage” team is racing against time to recover these items at risk of deteriorating or being stolen.
Shaimaa Mohammad al-Natour, assistant coordinator of the programme, told Al Jazeera that her team has so far rescued more than 1,700 historical pieces from four museum collections since their work began.
The team is working hard to recover the remaining lost artefacts of Gaza’s 5,000-year-old history. But they face huge challenges, including continued displacement, a shortage of specialised restoration equipment and Israeli military restrictions.
There is also the dangerous task of rescuing items near the so-called “Yellow Line”, a dividing zone in Gaza where Israel has complete military control. As of April, 196 Palestinians have been killed in this area since a ceasefire came into effect in October 2025.
“The nature of the areas used to be manageable, but their current locations are completely inaccessible,” al-Natour told Al Jazeera.
“The main difficulty in continuing our work with these collections is their location behind the ‘Yellow Line,’ which poses a grave risk to the team. One of our core principles is: human life comes first.”
With 84 percent of all structures in Gaza damaged or destroyed since Israel’s war on Gaza began, the team currently works from a tent in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis. What began as a self-initiated effort has turned into a field operation with the huge burden of ensuring that Gaza’s heritage is not lost.
The team conducts extensive field surveys across southern and central areas of Gaza to document the damage inflicted on both private and public museum collections during Israel’s nearly three-year assault on the enclave.
It is the first organised local effort to address the impact of the war on the region’s historical landmarks. The team works closely with locals and displaced residents who find artefacts among the debris which carpets Gaza.
“We handle notifications by first filling out a comprehensive survey containing the informant’s details, the artefact’s location, and its condition,” al-Natour said.
“The team then heads to the site to rescue the items, after which the processing stages begin: cleaning, archiving and photography.”
The team follows a strict protocol to ensure the historical and spatial value of each retrieved piece is preserved, starting from recording the circumstances of its discovery to giving it an independent digital identity.
“After rescuing the pieces from their locations, the documentation and archiving process begins. We try as much as possible not to bring any artefact into storage without a record and basic information to help us identify its origin,” said al-Natour.
“We start by logging the location and it from multiple angles and link the images to a unique number or code for the artefact to prevent any mix-up.”
The team is committed to preserving the information, image, unique code and origin of every artefact they find, despite encountering significant challenges.
Certain archaeological items, particularly pottery and glassware, are subject to immense physical stress caused by explosions and collapsed building debris, resulting in fractures. These need the utmost care when being handled, with the team operating a policy of minimal intervention and stabilisation through conservation first aid. They know that permanent restoration could cause irreversible damage or alter original features.
They begin by inspecting each piece, documenting its condition, and photographing damage to the item. But they are limited by the technical gear at hand: mobile phones for high-resolution photography and parallel paper records to safeguard against any possible data loss from the Excel sheets that document the items.
Identification tags with a unique number record each artefact, while basic packaging materials and wooden crates store the items. Soft brushes are used to gently remove surface dust from pottery without compromising original markings.
While these tools provide a short-term solution to the problem of conservation, more professional methods remain contingent on securing essential equipment and resources, which they currently lack. Securing these tools is difficult in a war zone.
“In times of war, sometimes the greatest achievement is simply halting the deterioration of an artefact and keeping it intact as much as possible until suitable conditions for specialised treatment become available,” she said.
Operating from a tent in a coastal region exposes the recovered materials to volatile weather conditions, as well as insects and rodents. Destructive environmental factors such as humidity, mould and vibrations also threaten both the artefacts and the wooden boxes they are stored in.
“The wooden crates themselves require continuous monitoring because humidity and temperature fluctuations can rot the wood or foster mould growth, which in turn damages the contents inside,” al-Natour said.
“Furthermore, constant movement and transporting crates from one spot to another expose the items to shocks and vibration, particularly fragile or broken pieces … Working in an area housing vast numbers of displaced people makes daily movement and transport much harder, while storage space remains extremely limited.”
The solution would be to establish a stable storage environment where temperature, humidity, ventilation, and lighting can be controlled. Specialised packaging and preservation materials suitable for each archaeological item are also needed, along with devices to monitor environmental conditions within the storage space.
“Our greatest need is to transition from emergency rescue to long-term professional conservation,” al-Natour said.
“Furthermore, we need specialised training in preventive conservation, emergency collection management, handling damaged artefacts, damage assessment and database management.”
The team is now looking at the next stage of operations – shifting items from tents to more secure locations. But this will be a lengthy process that will require reviewing records and databases, cross-referencing item numbers with crate contents, photographing their condition before and after transfer, and reorganising them to ensure easy access and tracking.
The impact of the initiative extends beyond saving stone artefacts and ancient vessels to building community awareness that makes residents and displaced individuals the guardians of their own culture, oral history and heritage.
“Through our activities with children, youth, women and displaced residents, we organise simplified educational and field activities, workshops, and programmes linked to antiquities, traditional crafts and oral history. We encourage participants to ask questions and document stories tied to places and artefacts,” said al-Natour.
Still, despite the challenges, there are lessons learned in saving Gaza’s cultural heritage.
“The rescue process itself has become an educational tool – when people see a team working under these conditions to extract a historical piece from beneath the rubble, they begin to view heritage as something worth protecting rather than something dispensable in times of crisis,” said al-Natour. “We firmly believe that community awareness is one of the most vital lines of defence.”

"US envoy warns EU’s ‘Buy European’ defense push could fragment transatlantic defense industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:43:51 UTC
22:43:51 KST

Melike Pala
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
US Ambassador to the European Union Andrew Puzder warned Wednesday that the bloc’s efforts to prioritize European-made weapons could fragment the transatlantic defense industrial base.
Speaking at Euronews’ Defense and Space Summit in Brussels, Puzder said military capability and availability should take precedence over the geographic origin of defense equipment.
“Only our enemies benefit when we lose focus on making sure we have the most effective weapons, supporting our mutual defense,” he said.
“One attack by a powerful adversary on a member state, and we’ll all be glad that we focused on weapon superiority rather than regional economics,” Puzder added.
The ambassador stressed that “when lives are at stake, capability and availability should determine the solution, not geography.”
The European Commission and EU member states have been advancing proposals aimed at strengthening the bloc’s defense industry and reducing reliance on US-made weapons.
The EU initiative has divided member states, with some governments cautioning against protectionist measures and stressing the importance of access to US defense capabilities.
Puzder said the European Commission had indicated it had no intention of preventing EU member states from using national funds to purchase US weapons systems.
He said the goal should be “an alliance which faces our adversaries with unity and strength rather than division and self-interest.”

UNICEF warns conflict deepens deprivation among children in Lebanon
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:43:10 CST
22:43:10 KST

BEIRUT, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Four in five households in Lebanon are struggling to afford basic necessities as the Israel-Hezbollah conflict compounds the country's prolonged economic crisis, leaving more children facing hunger, interrupted education and limited access to health care, the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) said Wednesday.
According to a new UNICEF assessment, 22 percent of surveyed households said their children had gone to bed hungry, while only 10 percent of households with children under five were able to provide an adequately nutritious diet.
Financial hardship has also restricted access to health services, with 31 percent of households reporting that children had gone without needed medical care, mainly because families could not afford it.
The assessment found that 14 percent of households had at least one child working, more than twice the rate recorded in January 2025.
"Children and young people in Lebanon are being asked to bear a burden no child should have to carry," said Marcoluigi Corsi, UNICEF representative in Lebanon.
The conflict has also taken a heavy toll on children. Since March 2, at least 261 children have been killed and 1,056 injured, with UNICEF estimating that about 12 percent of injured children are now living with disabilities.
Education has been severely disrupted, with 436 schools damaged or destroyed, putting around 100,000 children at risk of being without classrooms. Some 86 teachers have also been killed or injured.
The psychological impact has been widespread. UNICEF estimates that around 770,000 children have experienced psychological distress over the past six months. More than half of households reported a deterioration in their children's emotional well-being, while 63 percent said their children were anxious or nervous.
UNICEF said it has intensified its humanitarian response since January, including treating injured children, delivering supplies to shelters and medical facilities, and assisting displaced families.
"Without urgent and sustained action, an entire generation of children and young people risks carrying the scars of this crisis into adulthood," Corsi said. ■

Asian Games | Day 11 roundup: China secures historic 100th diving gold; Nagoya mayor apologizes for Games issues
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:43:01 CST
22:43:01 KST

by sportswriter Li Jia
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Following mounting complaints about transportation and accommodation disruptions at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, the mayor of Nagoya apologized Wednesday for the inconveniences experienced by athletes. Meanwhile, China dominated the diving competition, sweeping all 10 gold medals on offer and securing the nation's milestone 100th Asian Games diving gold.
Addressing the situation, Nagoya Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa formally apologized to athletes for the "inconveniences" at the Games following a series of complaints. The Asiad has faced logistical problems, including a shortage of beds and transportation failures, prompting criticism of the organizers' handling of the Games.
"We must offer our apologies to the athletes and others affected by these inconveniences," said Hirosawa, who also serves as deputy president of the local organizing committee.
"We must sincerely reflect on the mishandling that occurred," he added. "There were human errors and a lack of communication with the national teams. We are responding based on what has happened."
Led by their all-conquering divers, China extended its lead atop the medal table with 150 gold, 66 silver and 59 bronze medals. Japan was second with 50 gold, 76 silver and 73 bronze, followed by South Korea with 24 gold, 30 silver and 48 bronze.
Olympic champions Chen Yiwen and Lian Junjie each won gold in the final two diving events of the day, completing China's 14th consecutive clean sweep of gold medals at the Asian Games.
China has won every diving gold medal since its first Asiad appearance in 1974, with Lian's victory in the men's 10m platform bringing up the 100th consecutive Games gold medal for his nation in the sport.
However, the milestone victory was not an easy one for Lian, who finished only 4.05 points ahead of silver medalist Rikuto Tamai of Japan in a tight battle for the top spot. Meanwhile, China's 15-year-old Zhao Renjie took bronze in his Asiad debut.
"The men's platform is an extremely difficult event, and I had prepared myself for all kinds of circumstances. I am very happy to win China's 100th Asian Games diving gold. It means a great deal to me," Lian said.
"This milestone was made possible by the efforts of our predecessors, built up little by little over generations. Their work has given us the sense of mission and responsibility that we carry today," he added.
Earlier in the day, Chen Yiwen retained her title in the women's 3m springboard. Chen Jia took silver, while Japan's Sayaka Mikami finished with bronze.
Meanwhile, in water polo, China's men thrashed Thailand 26-4 to set up a semifinal clash with Kazakhstan while defending champion Japan will take on Iran in the other semifinal.
On the football pitch, China took an early lead but ultimately lost 2-1 to South Korea in the men's semifinal, missing out on a place in the final.
At the velodrome, China set new Asian records in both the women's and men's team pursuits to win three gold medals in track cycling. In the women's team pursuit final, the Chinese quartet won in 4:08.818, lowering the previous Asian record of 4:09.438. In the men's final, China clocked 3:47.621 to break the previous Asian record of 3:48.127. The women's keirin title also went to China as Yuan Liying produced a powerful late surge to overtake her rivals and claim gold.
Over in canoe slalom, Hu Zhaoshan won the men's kayak single title, while Huang Juan claimed the women's canoe single gold medal.
In archery, China finished with silver in both the men's and women's compound team finals, with India securing the two golds.
In the sport climbing men's boulder event, China missed the podium as Pan Yufei took fourth and Hu Junzhe came sixth. Japan's Sorato Anraku won the title.
In women's hockey, China reached the final after beating Japan 4-2 in a shootout in the semifinals.
On the tennis courts, China will have two players in the women's singles semifinals after Wang Xiyu and Zhang Shuai knocked out both of the host nation's quarterfinalists at the Higashiyama Park Tennis Center.
Elsewhere, the judo competition kicked off with China taking three bronzes in the men's 66kg, women's 52kg, and men's 60kg categories. ■

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Japanese siblings Mitsuki and Hayato Kondo won gold within half an hour of each other as judo began at the 2026 Asian Games on Wednesday, while China collected three bronze medals.
Mitsuki, 21, set the family celebration in motion with an ippon victory over Kazakhstan's Abiba Abuzhakynova in the women's 48kg final.
Her elder brother followed in the men's 60kg final against Kazakhstan's Yeldos Smetov, the 2024 Paris Olympic champion. Hayato scored a yuko midway through the contest and added another in the closing minutes before surviving Smetov's late attack to secure Japan's second judo title of the day.
"Mitsuki is a strong player so I expected her to win. When I actually saw her accomplish that right in front of me, it really pressed a switch in me and got me fired-up. I was like 'All right, let's go.'" Hayato said.
The Kondo siblings claimed two of the four golds on offer at the Aichi International Arena. Mongolia's Yolk Kazirbyek won the men's 66kg title, his country's first judo gold of the Games, while Uzbekistan's Sita Kadamboeva was crowned in the women's 52kg.
China's Ma Yulin, beaten by Hayato Kondo in the quarterfinals, returned to face defending champion Yang Yung-wei of Chinese Taipei for the bronze.
Neither scored in regulation time. After a lengthy golden score contest, Ma countered Yang's attack for a waza-ari, ending the bout after 12 minutes and 49 seconds.
China collected two more bronzes. Xue Ziyang beat Kazakhstan's Gusman Kyrgyzbayev in the bronze medal match of the men's 66kg division, while Xu Aoyu defeated Mongolia's Uranzaya Bayanmunkh in the women's 52kg category.
"I'm pretty satisfied with the third place finish," Xu said. "It's my first Asian Games, The first major international competition I've participated in. I want to keep working and keep getting better results."
Five more individual titles will be decided on Thursday. ■

China to accelerate modern water network development during 2026-2030
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:42:54 CST
22:42:54 KST

The State Council Information Office (SCIO) holds a press conference on accelerating the construction of a modernized water network in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Jin Liwang)
BEIJING, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- China will step up efforts to build a modern water network during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), with the national water network expected to cover 82 percent of the country's territory by 2030, Minister of Water Resources Li Guoying said Wednesday.
As part of this effort, China will strengthen flood control by improving a system comprising reservoirs, rivers, levees and flood storage and detention areas, and by upgrading monitoring and forecasting based on satellites, radar, rainfall stations and hydrological stations, Li told a press conference.
By the end of 2030, the country aims to add 15 billion cubic meters of reservoir storage capacity and bring 91 percent of key levees up to standard, he said.
China will accelerate efforts to build a system for the optimal allocation of water resources and water supply, and coordinate the development of the national backbone water network with provincial, municipal and county-level water networks.
It will speed up the modernization and upgrading of irrigation districts and promote standardized rural water supply and management. By 2030, the country aims to add 40 million mu (about 2.67 million hectares) of irrigated farmland and raise the rural tap water coverage rate to 98 percent.
The country will strengthen the protection and restoration of aquatic ecosystems, including restoring rivers and lakes and tackling groundwater over-extraction and soil erosion. By the end of 2030, it aims to treat an additional 310,000 square km of land that has been affected by soil erosion.
The country aims to establish a national water network dispatch center, a big data center and basin-level sub-centers, enabling comprehensive monitoring and sensing, intelligent analysis and forecasting, and forward-looking decision support to improve the coordinated management of flood control, water supply and ecological protection, said Li.
Building a modern water network is of particular importance for China, where water resources are unevenly distributed across regions and seasons and floods and droughts occur frequently, with intensifying impacts of global climate change and frequent extreme flood and drought events.
The water network is one of the "six networks" prioritized during China's 15th Five-Year Plan period, alongside new-type power grids, computing power networks, next-generation communication networks, urban underground pipeline networks and logistics networks.
During the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), China completed 5.68 trillion yuan (about 843 billion U.S. dollars) in water conservancy investment, started construction of 181 major water conservancy projects and put 94 major projects into operation, with the national water network covering 80.3 percent of the country's territory by the end of 2025. ■

Italy's main opposition PD boycotts antisemitism bill vote amid split on left
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:42:52 UTC

Italy's main opposition PD boycotts antisemitism bill vote amid split on left
ROME, Sept 30 - Italy's Democratic Party did not take part in a parliamentary committee vote on Wednesday on a highly contested bill against antisemitism, highlighting divisions on the left over a law seen as potentially curbing criticism of Israel.
A PD source said the party considered the definition of antisemitism included in the bill was "divisive" and urged the right-wing ruling coalition backing it to change its formulation, but this call is likely to fall on deaf ears.
The bill would write into law the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition of antisemitism, which lists certain criticisms of Israel as examples of antisemitism.
Critics say this definition could restrict freedom of expression, censoring legitimate activism for Palestinian rights and contributing to conflating Jews with the state of Israel.
The dispute reflects broader differences on the Italian left over the war in Gaza. The PD has condemned the violence, but has adopted a more cautious tone than its allies, the Five Star Movement and the Green Left Alliance (AVS), which have accused Israel of genocide, which Israel denies.
APPEAL TO CHANGE
Most PD lawmakers abstained when the bill passed the Senate earlier this year, but a small group voted in favour, exposing divisions within the party. The bill is now due to obtain final approval at the lower house Chamber.
"We call on the majority to heed our appeal to change that divisive definition and make it clear that those who criticise the actions of the Israeli government cannot be accused of antisemitism," PD lower house leader Chiara Braga said last week.
Party member Emanuele Fiano, the son of an Auschwitz survivor who supports the bill, criticised the PD's decision not to back it, saying: "I will not accept the fight against antisemitism being portrayed as an obstacle to criticism of (Benjamin) Netanyahu's government, the Israeli military or violence by settlers."
The AVS and Five Star voted against the proposal.
"There is no doubt that on an issue such as antisemitism it would be desirable to have a unanimous vote, but there is equally no doubt that this bill needs to be changed because it is fundamentally flawed," AVS co-leader Nicola Fratoianni said.
Supporters of the bill say stronger safeguards are needed following a rise in antisemitic incidents after Hamas-led attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, and the ensuing Gaza war. Italy's Antisemitism Observatory recorded 963 cases in 2025, more than double the number reported in 2022. REUTERS

Chinese icebreakers Xuelong, Xuelong 2 return after fruitful Arctic expedition
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:42:37 CST
22:42:37 KST

SHANGHAI, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- China's research icebreakers Xuelong, or "Snow Dragon," and Xuelong 2 returned to Shanghai in east China on Wednesday after nearly three months of the country's 16th Arctic Ocean expedition.
The expedition successfully completed key tasks, including comprehensive investigation and monitoring, cutting-edge scientific research, and international cooperation. According to the expedition team, both the scale of the expedition and the total number of tasks reached new highs.
It achieved fruitful results in new scientific discoveries, theoretical breakthroughs, technological tests, and equipment applications, providing strong support for a deeper understanding of and effective response to global climate change and promoting sustainable development in the Arctic, said Wang Jinhui, the leader of the expedition team.
A series of new discoveries and breakthroughs made during the expedition have refreshed China's understanding of the marine environment and geophysics of the Arctic Ocean. For example, researchers found that the subsurface water in some areas of the Arctic Ocean exhibited a warming phenomenon.
During the expedition, Chinese researchers also captured some juvenile polar cod in a densely ice-covered area in the high Arctic, a discovery that may deepen scientists' understanding of the species and its habitat's ecosystem.
Through the dual-vessel operation of the Xuelong and Xuelong 2, 19 ice station operations and 95 sets of ice-based buoy deployment tasks were completed in the high-latitude waters of the Arctic Ocean in a coordinated manner, establishing a local unmanned observation array. Both the number of stations and the number of ice-based buoys deployed reached a record high, according to He Jianfeng, the chief scientist of the expedition team.
"The relevant work can not only deepen China's understanding of the rapid changes in the Arctic Ocean, improve the accuracy and level of our prediction of sea ice and ocean changes in the Arctic Ocean, but also provide valuable cross-seasonal first-hand observational data for the international governance of the Arctic Ocean's ecology," He added.
Significant breakthroughs have been achieved in the application of high-latitude communication technology. During ice station operations, the Xuelong icebreaker achieved video call and data transmission with the Qinling Station in Antarctica via its shipborne satellite internet communication equipment.
The expedition team has carried out various forms of scientific research cooperation, with seven scientists from Russia, Germany, Thailand and China's Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.
Organized by the Ministry of Natural Resources, the 16th Arctic Ocean expedition was carried out by four vessels: Xuelong, Xuelong 2, Jidi and Tansuo-3.
Jidi and Tansuo-3 are still on their research missions and are expected to return in mid-October. ■

ATHENS, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis on Wednesday announced a new package of measures aimed at easing pressure on households and businesses from rising fuel and operating costs.

Combined with discounts offered by refiners, the total reduction will be 20 euro cents (23 U.S. cents) per liter.

BEIJING, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday called on the nation to forge ahead with firm confidence and take solid steps to achieve the great national rejuvenation.
Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks at a reception held at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing to celebrate the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China.
China's National Day falls on Oct. 1.

The International Register of Damage has opened all 43 categories of claims for submission
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:41:09 EEST
22:41:09 KST

The International Register of Damage has opened all 43 categories of claims for submission
Kyiv • UNN
The Register has opened all 43 categories of claims for damage caused by Russia's aggression. 195,000 claims have already been submitted, with more than 65,000 entered into the Register.
The International Register of Damage for Ukraine has opened all 43 categories of claims for compensation for losses, damage or harm caused by russia’s full-scale aggression against Ukraine. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi reported this, according to UNN.
Details
As of today, the International Register of Damage has opened all 43 categories for claim submission. Now available are 21 categories for individuals, 11 for legal entities, and 11 for the state—the last three of which were opened today
According to him, the Register covers a wide range of losses and damage caused by Russian aggression—personal losses, damage to housing and property, business losses, the destruction of infrastructure, damage to cultural heritage and the environment, as well as losses incurred by the state. A total of 195,000 claims have already been submitted, more than 65,000 of which have been entered into the Register.
Additional information
Olena Shuliak, Chair of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on State Building, Local Governance, Regional and Urban Development, noted that the opening of the final category marked the completion of the phased launch of the claims submission system, which began on April 2, 2024.
The last categories to be opened included three categories for the state of Ukraine: B1.6 (other property losses), B3.1 (environmental damage), and B3.2 (plundering and/or appropriation of natural resources). Claims in these categories may be submitted by Ukraine, its central, regional and local authorities, as well as state and municipal institutions and organizations.
Of the 43 categories, four concern physical harm—bodily injuries, sexual violence, torture, forced labor or service. Another 29 categories concern material damage: damage to or destruction of housing, businesses and infrastructure, as well as economic losses. Ten categories cover moral harm: forced displacement, the death or disappearance of relatives, deprivation of liberty, the forced deportation of children and adults, and loss of access to healthcare and education
Shuliak added that the submitted claims are processed by the Secretariat of the Register and will subsequently be transferred to the International Claims Commission, whose convention of establishment was adopted on December 16, 2025, at a Diplomatic Conference in The Hague. The Commission will consider the claims on their merits, determine the amount of compensation in each specific case, and adopt the relevant decisions.
Reminder
A claim to the International Register of Damage via "Diia" can still be submitted under four more categories related to access to healthcare and economic losses.

A faster-than-expected inflation jump across the eurozone’s biggest economies raises the odds that the European Central Bank will hike interest rates again this year to bring price growth down to target.
The move would add to economic headwinds and sovereign borrowing costs at a time when governments are already grappling with the highest yields since the 2012 sovereign debt crisis.
Wednesday’s preliminary data showed inflation in Germany jumped to 3.3% in September, from 2.9% in August. In France, inflation jumped to 3.4% from 2.6%, and in Italy to 4.1% from 3.2 percent. Spain reported inflation of 5% on Tuesday, up from 4.6%.
Advertisement
The numbers all came in above forecasts and hit multi-year highs.
The increases were driven in large part by energy prices as the Middle East conflict continues to disrupt oil and gas markets. The ECB has raised rates twice this year, bringing its deposit rate to 2.5% in September.
The next step is considered more challenging as it could push rates from the upper end of neutral into restrictive territory, where they begin to slow economic activity.
Higher rates are also lifting government borrowing costs. Sovereign yields have reached their highest levels since the 2012 debt crisis, adding pressure to public finances.
France has seen the steepest increase in its borrowing cost among eurozone member states as investors demand an additional premium for holding its debt, given massive fiscal and political uncertainty in the run-up to French presidential elections.
The level could still rise should investors be disappointed by the hotly awaited budget announcement in Paris on Thursday.
Eurostat will release inflation numbers for the 21-nation euro zone as a whole on Friday.
