The share of non-cash payments in Latvia reaches a historical high  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:05:24 UTC
22:05:24 KST

The most recent (autumn 2026) "Payment radar" published by Latvijas Banka suggests that the ratio of non-cash to cash payments in Latvia was 81% to 19% in August 2026. The share of non-cash payments has reached a historical high. In February 2026, the share of non-cash payments reached 79%, compared to 78% in February 2025.
The latest information on the money usage habits of Latvia's population is outlined in the "Payment radar" based on the results of a public survey conducted by the market and social research agency SIA Latvijas Fakti. The "Payment radar" is published semi-annually and is available on Latvijas Banka's website. The development of the ratio of non-cash to cash payments and their interaction (as at August 2026) is the central measurement of the overview, supplemented by more detailed numerical information and expert commentaries.
Ratio of non-cash to cash payments
The ratio of non-cash to cash payments was first measured in February 2017, with non-cash payments accounting for 58% and cash payments for 42%. Since then, the share of non-cash payments has gradually increased and, in recent years, has stabilised at close to 80%. That threshold has now been crossed.
In August 2026, the average number of payments per capita in a week was 16.1 (compared to 15.1 and 17.9 in February 2026 and August 2025 respectively), including 13 non-cash payments and 3.1 cash payments. Following a deeper analysis of these data, SIA Latvijas Fakti concludes that, on average, one adult in Latvia makes 8.2 card payments, 4.8 online payments, and 3.1 cash payments per week.
Modern payment technologies
Data from the "Payment radar" suggest that people are increasingly choosing to make payments by smartphone – as many as 34% of Latvia's population already use this option, marking another record high. Smartphone payments are particularly popular among younger people, with most respondents aged 34 or younger using them.
The use of instant payments has remained stable at the 40% mark (41% in August 2026, compared to 42% in February 2026). Among those who use instant payments, more than one in five use the option of making a payment by providing only the payee's phone number (21% in August 2026, compared to 19% in February 2026).
The survey shows no impact of the August 2026 storm, as most respondents completed the survey before the storm occurred. However, concerns about access to cash have increased. In August 2026, 75% of respondents were satisfied with access to cash from their bank accounts (79% in February 2026), while 14% were dissatisfied (11% in February 2026).
The lessons from the August storm will also be taken into account regarding cash
Ilze Posuma, Member of the Council of Latvijas Banka, analyses the lessons from the August storm in the commentary section of the "Payment radar".
During the August storm, electricity and communications were disrupted simultaneously, also affecting the operations of retailers and shopping centres. As a result, critical financial services infrastructure was able to provide support and perform its functions only to a limited extent. The most extensive damage occurred early in the night, and following disruptions to the electricity network, communications towers continued operating for only a few hours using autonomous power supply solutions. By morning, their power sources had been exhausted, leaving some areas without either electricity or communications.
"This is the key lesson from the crisis at the national level: without electricity and communications, other solutions cannot function either. If retailers cannot operate, critical financial services are also unavailable. How can this be addressed? This requires a national-level solution, with priority potentially given to ensuring the operation of critical communications towers and retailers rather than critical ATMs," emphasises Ilze Posuma.
The information collected by Latvijas Banka suggests that several hundred offline payments were made in shops during the crisis. Most critical ATMs (77 out of 94) remained operational during the crisis, although they were mainly located in areas where no power outages occurred or where outages were resolved quickly. Only a few critical ATMs experienced an outage lasting longer than permitted under the applicable regulations. The main problems were identified with ATMs located in shopping centres, which could not be opened due to power outages and were therefore inaccessible to the public. Banks are assessing each such situation individually. At the same time, it is clear that action is needed to take the lessons from this storm into account.
Latvijas Banka has already drawn the attention of the responsible authorities to issues concerning ATM availability and proposed additional solutions. One such solution could involve essential services centres, where people could buy essential goods in one place, including by making offline card payments, as well as access cash. These centres could, for example, be set up at retail outlets or petrol stations.
They would operate alongside the resilience hubs proposed by the head of the Crisis Management Centre, where people would have access to information, first aid, communications, and other essential services. These hubs would be particularly important in situations where, for whatever reason, the nearest crisis shop would be inaccessible or people would be unable to reach it.
"The lessons learned from the storm will help strengthen the country's overall resilience to crises in the coming months. At the same time, Latvijas Banka encourages everyone to continue to act sensibly and plan ahead, including by keeping some money in cash or building up savings specifically for crisis situations. Such an emergency cash reserve should be held in small-denomination banknotes and should be sufficient to cover a family's needs for one week," recommends the Member of the Council of Latvijas Banka.
It is also advisable to identify the ATMs closest to one's home, including critical ATMs, in advance on the website of Latvijas Banka (the map is available here: https://www.bank.lv/en/services/map-of-atms-in-latvia). Information on offline payments, in turn, is available here: https://www.bank.lv/en/news-and-events/news-and-articles/news/17790-offline-card-purchases-have-been-introduced-by-10-retailers. It is important to bear in mind that this solution can only be used by physically inserting the payment card into a card terminal and entering the card's PIN.
For more information on critical financial services, see the website of Latvijas Banka: https://www.bank.lv/en/operational-areas/customer-protection/critical-financial-services.
The contours of the digital euro are becoming increasingly clear
Zita Zariņa, Member of the Council of Latvijas Banka, provides an update on the digital euro project in the "Payment radar". It has regained momentum, with European legislators finally reaching agreement on a number of widely debated aspects. The next step is the reconciliation of positions in the so-called trilogue procedure – in July, negotiations officially began between the European Parliament, the Council of the European Union (EU), and the European Commission with a view to completing the legislative process for a common regulatory framework for the introduction of the digital euro.
It is hoped that the political negotiations and adoption of the digital euro regulation will be completed later this year, allowing the Governing Council of the European Central Bank (ECB) to take a formal decision by the end of the year and launch pilot projects, with the actual introduction of the digital euro planned for 2029.
Zita Zariņa highlights a number of important aspects of the digital euro that will help the public better understand the digital euro project and its impact on our everyday lives.
- The digital euro will complement rather than replace cash
The digital euro will be a complementary alternative to existing solutions and a new way of making payments digitally. Just as cash (banknotes and coins), the digital euro will be central bank money. Cash will continue to exist and remain available to people as it is today. Moreover, EU legislators and the ECB are working to strengthen the use and availability of cash.
- Europe will have its own public, pan-European payment solution
The introduction of the digital euro will provide Europe with a payment infrastructure based on central bank money and European rules. This will reduce Europe's dependence on payment solutions managed outside Europe and provide an additional solution for people's everyday digital payments. The distribution and use of the digital euro will be supported by European payment service providers, through which everyone will be able to open a digital euro account and make payments.
- The digital euro will be intended primarily for everyday payments, not for saving
The digital euro will be a means of payment that can be used in shops, online, and for payments to other people. To prevent it from becoming an alternative to bank deposits and having negative effects on the functioning of banks, a limit will be set on the amount of digital euro that can be held in each customer's account. However, everyone will be able to link their digital euro account to their commercial bank account, enabling them to make payments even when the amount of the desired purchase exceeds the balance in their digital euro account (the shortfall will automatically be taken from the commercial bank account and transferred to the payee).
- The digital euro will also be usable without an internet connection
The digital euro is designed to enable offline payments, allowing people to pay each other and make payments to merchants even without an internet or mobile network connection at a particular moment. This will be particularly important in places with poor connectivity and in situations where digital communications are disrupted.
In Latvia, critical financial services, including offline payments, have already been introduced, but such solutions are not widespread elsewhere in Europe, and the digital euro will reduce this vulnerability. In Latvia, it will serve as a backup solution providing greater security.
- The digital euro will be designed with particular attention to privacy
When making online payments with the digital euro, the Eurosystem (comprising the ECB and the national central banks of the euro area) itself will not be able to identify the individual user and their payments. The payment service provider, in turn, will have access to the information necessary to process the payment and comply with regulatory requirements. This is similar to how bank accounts operate today.
Meanwhile, offline payments will provide a level of privacy similar to that of cash – only the payer and the payee will know about the specific payment.
- The digital euro will also be able to provide an additional payment option in the event of technical disruptions or crises
The digital euro is being developed with the aim of ensuring continuity of payments even in challenging circumstances. Its offline functionality will enable payments to be made even without an internet or mobile network connection. Moreover, the architecture of the digital euro system provides solutions for situations where a particular payment service provider experiences a disruption and is unavailable to process a digital euro payment.
When can we expect the new euro banknotes in our wallets?
Jānis Blūms, Head of the Cash Department of Latvijas Banka, outlines the next stages in the development and issuance of the new third series of euro banknotes in the "Payment radar".
He thanks each and every one of the 37 137 people in Latvia who took part in the public survey on the design of the next generation of euro banknotes. Overall, almost 10 million people participated in the survey. People throughout Europe were invited to share their views on which of the proposed designs under two themes – "European culture" and "Rivers and birds" – should be used for future euro banknotes.
The Governing Council of the ECB, which also includes Mārtiņš Kazāks, Governor of Latvijas Banka, is expected to select one of the design proposals by the end of this year. Work will then begin on adapting the selected design for use on banknotes, incorporating complex, high-tech security features as well as various tactile and colour elements needed both to protect the banknotes against counterfeiting and to assist blind and partially sighted persons.
"The development of banknotes is an ongoing race between central banks and counterfeiters, and this is one of the reasons why banknotes are regularly updated and enhanced. The new banknotes are expected to incorporate various modern technological solutions that will make life more difficult for counterfeiters," notes Jānis Blūms. The existing euro banknotes are already relatively well protected against counterfeiting: across the euro area, 14 counterfeit banknotes were detected per million genuine banknotes in 2025, compared with 18 counterfeit banknotes per million genuine banknotes in 2024.
Designing attractive and secure euro banknotes is only one step in the process. It is important that, when they are issued, they can be used without restrictions: cashiers need to be familiar with the new banknotes, vending machines need to accept them, and the counterfeit-detection equipment used in shops needs to recognise them. Achieving this will require significant work, both to inform professional cash handlers and to reprogramme various equipment. Surely, the introduction of new banknotes into circulation is a national-level event, and it will be preceded by a wide-ranging information campaign.
The new euro banknotes will also follow the "feel, look, tilt" principle (https://www.ecb.europa.eu/euro/banknotes/current/security/html/index.en.html#feel). This will allow anyone to check whether a banknote is genuine. Euro banknotes contain dozens of different features that are difficult to counterfeit, and even if a counterfeiter manages to reproduce one of them, it is very rare to find counterfeit banknotes that successfully replicate several anti-counterfeiting features.
"No decisions have yet been taken on the timing or technical arrangements for introducing the new euro banknotes. However, previous experience with the first and second series of euro banknotes allows us to confidently expect that the process will be gradual and carefully planned.
It is also important to remember that, when a new euro banknote design is introduced, people and businesses do not need to exchange their existing banknotes for new ones. The old banknotes retain their status as legal tender indefinitely and are gradually replaced by new-design banknotes as they return to the central bank," reminds the Head of the Cash Department of Latvijas Banka.
He also looks back at how the first and second series of euro banknotes were introduced.
"Latvijas Banka is ready for the practical introduction of the new euro banknotes. We will draw on the experience gained during the introduction of the euro in 2012–2014. Particular attention will be paid to communication with professional cash handlers and particularly vulnerable groups in society, as well as to informing the public at large," states Jānis Blūms. "Cash is more than a means of payment and a store of value – it is also one of the elements of society's security. We will develop and issue banknotes and coins for as long as demand for them exists in society. Cash has a future!"
For the sociological survey data and detailed information, see the autumn 2026 "Payment radar" of Latvijas Banka.

Grenfell fire police investigators hand files on 20 firms and 54 people to CPS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:05:24 UTC
22:05:24 KST

Police investigating the 2017 Grenfell Tower fire have handed over files of evidence relating to 20 companies and 54 individuals to prosecutors.
The Metropolitan police described the move as a “milestone” moment that paved the way for what it said would be “the very best possible evidence for charging decisions”.
Potential offences include corporate manslaughter, gross negligence manslaughter, health and safety offences, fraud and fraud-related offences and misconduct in public office.
The Guardian has learned that a leading prosecutor has been appointed to head any possible court cases.
The fire on 14 June 2017 – which was found by a public inquiry to have been avoidable – led to the deaths of 72 people in North Kensington, west London. It was the result of “decades of failure” by central government to stop the spread of combustible cladding combined with the “systematic dishonesty” of multimillion-pound companies whose products spread the fire, a public inquiry found in 2024.
The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) has said charging decisions will be made before the 10th anniversary of the disaster, which falls on 14 June 2027.
Kevin Southworth, a deputy assistant commissioner at the Met, said: “This is a milestone moment in the police investigation into this devastating tragedy which took the lives of 72 people.
“We appreciate, of course, it has taken nine years to get to this point. As we have said before, this is one of the most complex investigations ever undertaken by any UK law enforcement agency – the scale is truly enormous.
“While we know this has had a significant impact on those waiting for answers, it has necessarily taken this long to ensure our investigation is meticulous and presents the very best possible evidence to the CPS for charging decisions.”
Investigators have looked at the role of more than 15,000 people and 700 organisations as part of the inquiry, and have submitted 12,600 pages of evidence to the CPS.
A total of 14,700 statements have been taken and more than 27,000 exhibits, including cladding, insulation, doors, windows and other parts of the building, down to screws, nuts and bolts, are stored in a secure warehouse.
Scale replica parts of the tower are being built at a cost of £2m in anticipation of potential court proceedings.
Frank Ferguson, the head of the CPS’s special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “Today marks an important step in the Grenfell Tower investigation, and we understand the enduring impact this tragedy continues to have on bereaved families, survivors and all those affected.”
He added that the CPS remained confident that it would complete the process and make charging decisions before the 10th anniversary of the fire next year.
Grenfell United, which represents some bereaved families and survivors, said: “We expect the Met and the CPS to do everything in their power to make sure this case moves forward without further unnecessary delay. Our families have waited long enough.
“We want those responsible to face justice. If people are found guilty of crimes that cost our loved ones their lives, we want to see them behind bars. Only then will people see that there are real consequences for what happened at Grenfell.”
Survivors and politicians called for justice to be achieved rapidly before the 10th anniversary of the disaster.
The Labour MP for Kensington and Bayswater, Joe Powell, said: “We must do everything in our power to ensure that justice is delivered as swiftly as possible.”
Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, thanked investigators for “painstakingly” examining thousands of pieces of evidence, while the Labour MP David Lammy expressed disappointment it had taken so long.
Lammy said: “I said the morning after Grenfell that it was an act of corporate manslaughter. I’m pleased that this has happened but disappointed it has been so slow.”

M-Fly, a Kyiv-based company that builds stabilized cameras and laser guidance systems for military drones, has raised a new funding round led by MITS Capital to expand production as orders from Ukraine and NATO countries grow.
Existing investors MITS Capital and Freedom Fund backed the round, joined by Norwegian defense-focused venture firm Gardar and a new investor the company did not name. M-Fly announced the round on Sept. 30 but did not disclose how much it raised or what the company is now worth.
Before this round, the company had raised $1.4 million by mid-2026 through a friends-and-family round, grants from Brave1, the Ukrainian government’s defense technology cluster, and venture funding from MITS Capital, Freedom Fund, Resist.ua and Ukrainian entrepreneur Borys Shestopalov, co-founder of HD-group.
M-Fly’s main products are gimbals, the gyro-stabilized mounts that keep a drone’s camera steady and pointed at a target while the aircraft moves. The company says it has tested its stabilization system in combat in Ukraine at speeds of up to 350 km/h (217 mph).
Its lineup covers several sizes. The RB-220 is a heavy-duty gimbal for large drones, crewed aircraft, helicopters and naval drones that can also serve as a ground station for air defense. The RB-150GD pairs thermal and daylight cameras for medium-sized drones, and a weather-resistant version for boats, the RB-150 Marine, is in development. M-Fly also sells laser guidance systems, including the RB-150CW and Seeker, and plans to release the RB-100, its smallest gimbal for light drones, in the first quarter of 2027.
“Over the past 12 months, we have doubled our team and increased revenue severalfold,” said Vladyslav Myhovych, founder and CEO of M-Fly.
Myhovych said demand from Ukrainian customers and NATO allies has risen sharply since the start of 2026, driven by Ukraine’s growing use of interceptor drones and the resulting need for cheaper reconnaissance drones carrying good cameras. He said a gimbal can make up around a third of the cost of a reconnaissance drone, and that some imported gimbals cost several times more than the aircraft they are mounted on.
“What matters even more than performance is that the company has cracked the unit economics, allowing it to price its products significantly below those of its closest competitors,” said Denys Gurak, co-founder and chief operating officer of MITS Capital.
M-Fly says it keeps prices down by building nearly everything itself, from motors and camera lenses to cameras and software. The company says that lets it price its systems close to Chinese products while keeping Chinese components below 6% of each unit, an important point for Ukrainian and European buyers wary of relying on China for drone parts.
This year the company also moved its image processing onto a platform built around a graphics processing unit, which it says makes its systems less tied to specific chips and memory components and lets engineers switch parts quickly when supplies run short. Myhovych described the change as making the company “almost hardware-agnostic” amid a global shortage of memory chips.
M-Fly was founded in late 2023 out of its founders’ earlier volunteer project supplying the military, and later went through the MITS Capital accelerator. Myhovych said the new money will go toward expanding production facilities and speeding up how quickly the company adapts its products.

Ülle Madise has broad public backing as Estonia's next president
Nearly two-thirds of Estonia's residents support electing Ülle Madise as Estonia's president, a new Emor survey shows.
Almost one-third (31 percent) of respondents fully support her, and the same share (32 percent) somewhat support her.
21 percent do not support electing Madise: 11 percent do not support it at all and ten percent somewhat do not support it. 17 percent were undecided.
There is considerable support in society for Ülle Madise as Estonia's next president, Emor research director Aivar Voog said.
She has been visible to the public for years as chancellor of justice and is therefore familiar to most residents. The result shows that broad political support in the Riigikogu is accompanied by fairly strong public support.
Support for electing Madise is somewhat higher among people age thirty-five and older. Among residents of other nationalities, a significant share (35 percent compared with 13 percent among Estonians) are unable to give an assessment.
Looking at support by party preference, the new president is strongly backed by supporters of the Social Democratic Party (86 percent), Reform Party (83 percent), Eesti 200 (83 percent), Parempoolsed (80 percent) and Isamaa (68 percent).
Supporters of the Estonian Center Party are more hesitant (23 percent undecided and 34 percent supportive), while opposition dominates among EKRE supporters (67 percent do not support).
The Riigikogu elected Ülle Madise as Estonia's next president on September 2 with 71 votes in favor.
The data is based on Emor's nationwide representative online survey conducted September 17–24, 2026. A total of 1,114 Estonian residents age sixteen and older were interviewed.

Generators, wells, and mobile boiler houses: how Kyiv hospitals are preparing for winter
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:03:07 EEST
22:03:07 KST

Generators, wells, and mobile boiler houses: how Kyiv hospitals are preparing for winter
Kyiv • UNN
More than 65% of the capable network of healthcare facilities in Kyiv are already autonomous; they are expected to prepare all 100% by the end of October, but whether they will make it in time - remains an open question.
During a large-scale power outage, a hospital cannot simply stop operating until the electricity comes back on. Surgeries, resuscitation, ventilation, childbirth and intensive care must continue. Therefore, even after an attack on a facility’s energy infrastructure, electricity, water, heat and the ability to protect patients from a repeat attack are all needed simultaneously. Is Kyiv’s authorities’ capable network of medical facilities preparing for the winter that was dubbed the “most frightening” even before it arrived? Read the UNN article.
The capital’s capable network includes 21 medical facilities, including clinical and children’s hospitals, psychiatric and oncology dispensaries, a phthisiopulmonology hospital, the Perinatal Center, as well as the City Center for Reproductive and Perinatal Medicine.
In Kyiv’s Comprehensive Resilience Plan, strengthening the autonomy of healthcare facilities is identified as one of the priorities. City authorities’ representatives have stated that autonomy means not only backup electricity supply, but also reserve sources of water and heat. This should guarantee the uninterrupted provision of medical care.
"The resilience of the healthcare system today means hospitals’ ability to operate continuously under any conditions. We are consistently creating the necessary reserves for this — from autonomous power supply to alternative sources of water and heat. This is an investment in patient safety, the stable work of medical personnel and the capital’s readiness to respond to any challenges," emphasized Tetiana Mostepan, Director of the Kyiv City State Administration’s Department of Health.
On September 11, the Kyiv City State Administration’s Department of Health reported that more than 65% of the facilities in the capable network were already fully autonomous. Readiness is planned to reach 100% by the end of October.
Power supply sources
The main focus is evidently on diesel generators and comprehensive energy storage systems. The city allocated almost UAH 49.6 million for these needs.
Separately, the capital’s medical facilities received 132 diesel generators as humanitarian/charitable aid or purchased them with their own funds.
Medical facilities also use alternative power sources. For example, Kyiv City Clinical Hospital No. 12 installed a 100 kW solar power plant. The hospital also installed 10 battery storage units with a total capacity of 51.2 kWh and two 50 kW inverters.
Particular attention is being paid to facilities that receive patients with polytrauma and injuries. According to the Department of Health, they are already equipped not only with primary but also with additional generators in case the main equipment fails. Evidently, the decision to provide additional generators was made after an incident that occurred at Kyiv City Emergency Hospital in January 2026. After an energy infrastructure facility was hit, the hospital was left without a centralized power supply. A 400 kW generator had been installed at the facility, but it failed to start. Doctors receiving those injured in the enemy attack on the capital had to work with flashlights and portable lighting for some time. Eventually, small mobile generators were connected to the main nodes; later, the State Emergency Service brought in an additional generator, and the main generator was also successfully started. However, this incident demonstrated that the system has vulnerabilities, and when lives are at stake and every minute — or even every second — counts, this can come at an extremely high cost.
Backup water supply
In January 2026, 13 medical facilities in the capable network had wells to ensure an autonomous water supply. One such facility is the City Perinatal Center, which has its own well; in addition, it launched its own pellet boiler house even before the full-scale war began.
To ensure an uninterrupted water supply for the remaining facilities, the city allocated UAH 87 million in May this year.
At the same time, an examination of procurements for well-development works by specific institutions raises doubts as to whether all hospitals will be provided with autonomous water sources by the end of October. For example, Kyiv City Clinical Hospital No. 6 only announced a tender for the purchase of the relevant works on September 17. According to the tender conditions, the works must be completed by December 31 of this year. It should be noted, however, that most institutions announced their tenders significantly earlier.
Heat supply
At the beginning of 2026, the city authorities reported that eight of the capital's healthcare facilities were equipped with autonomous boiler houses, while another 13 facilities could be promptly connected to mobile boiler units.
In the summer of this year, the Kyiv City State Administration reported on a much more extensive backup heat-supply system: at 23 municipal healthcare facilities at 37 addresses, heat-supply systems were reconstructed so that they could be connected to mobile diesel boiler units. Separately, together with the WHO, as part of the Heal Ukraine project, the city worked on installing modular solid-fuel boiler houses for eight healthcare facilities at nine addresses.
After the Russian attack on November 25, 2025, some hospitals lost centralized heating. Kyiv deployed nine mobile boiler units for six healthcare facilities. The boiler units supplied them with heat for approximately one day—until regular heat supply was restored. Earlier, in October, mobile boiler units had supplied five healthcare facilities. Once again, mobile boiler units had to be deployed at the end of December 2025 to heat six hospitals.
At the beginning of 2026, Kyiv reported that the city had a fleet of 69 mobile boiler units that could be promptly connected to hospitals, social institutions, and other critical facilities if the main heating network was damaged. More generally, the city began modernizing the heating systems of institutions, including ensuring the possibility of connecting them to mobile boiler units, in 2022–2023.
Winter will show
The capital's hospitals are entering the new heating season with a greater margin of safety than before: the city is expanding backup generation, equipping wells, and increasing backup heat-supply capacity. Part of this system already had to be tested last winter, when healthcare facilities lost centralized heating and electricity supplies following Russian attacks.
At the same time, preparations are not yet complete. As of September, some hospitals were only carrying out procurements or works necessary for autonomous water and electricity supplies. Against this backdrop, the city authorities aim to bring all facilities in the capable network to full autonomy by the end of October.
Thus, the final readiness of the capital's healthcare system for winter will be determined not by the number of generators, wells, or boiler houses procured. The main test lies ahead—whether, after another attack, every hospital will be able to continue performing operations, maintain the functioning of intensive care and ventilators, deliver babies, and provide patients with water and heat even when external networks are out of operation for an extended period.

While Russia Pounds Kyiv, Most Russians Support ‘Global Cooperation’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:02:00 UTC
22:02:00 KST

On Sept. 28, a Russian drone reportedly struck a National Academy of Sciences building in central Kyiv, setting it on fire. Three days earlier, Vladimir Putin had accused the Baltic states of violating Russian speakers’ rights and presented Moscow’s response as consistent with international law.
While a new UN Foundation survey found that 62% of Russian respondents believed countries should solve problems together rather than prioritize national interests at cooperation’s expense, a separate August polling by the Levada Center showed that 76% approved of Putin and 68% supported Russian military actions in Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
How can support for international cooperation coexist with approval of a government invading its neighbor?
The surveys may be reaching different Russians
GeoPoll’s September survey for the UN Foundation questioned 250 people in each of 20 countries. Russian participants answered online, with recruitment guided by quotas for age, gender, and geography.
The methodological annex describes the sample as nonprobability-based and warns against treating each country’s results as nationally representative.
In practical terms, that means researchers cannot assume the people who participated accurately reflect the wider Russian population.
An uneven balance of ages or locations could contribute to that problem, even though the researchers used demographic quotas to limit such imbalances. The more difficult issue is that matching basic characteristics does not necessarily produce a politically representative sample.
Russian Airlines See 7% Drop in Passengers Amid Airport Disruptions From Ukrainian Drone Attacks
For example, an online survey could meet its age quotas while disproportionately reaching people comfortable using digital technology. Their views might differ from those who rarely go online or decline surveys.
Meanwhile, Levada’s August survey used a different approach: face-to-face interviews with 1,600 adults across urban and rural communities in 50 Russian regions, with results weighted to population characteristics.
The two surveys therefore provide a broad comparison of attitudes, though still largely contradictory.
People may give the answer they consider safe
Who agrees to participate is only one issue – what people feel able to say is another.
Daniil Chebykin, a Russian opposition activist and founder of the Omsk Civic Association, previously told Kyiv Post that political interviews at respondents’ homes can create pressure to conceal dissent.
“The respondent understands that the people asking the questions have his home address and other information,” he said.
Chebykin argued that critics may refuse an interview altogether or give an answer they consider safe. As a result, some opinions never enter the sample, while others enter it inaccurately.
His comments concerned state-linked Russian polling and should not be read as evidence that reportedly non-Kremlin affiliated Levada manipulates as results. Yet, they do identify a broader concern about political questioning under repression, without establishing how much it affects any particular rating.
The risks of dissent are concrete. Opposition politician Lev Shlosberg received an 11-year-and-one-month prison sentence in August in cases involving an anti-war debate and a reposted newspaper cover, as Kyiv Post reported.
Expressing support for countries working together is considerably less politically confrontational than telling an interviewer that Putin is wrong.
Different questions can therefore produce different levels of candor, even before differences in sampling are considered.
Some respondents may see no contradiction
A person who accepts the Kremlin’s claim that Russia is defending itself may also sincerely favor peace and international cooperation. From that perspective, responsibility for ending the confrontation rests elsewhere.
Chebykin’s work with Russians seeking to leave military service offers examples of how that understanding can change.
In an earlier interview with Kyiv Post, he described soldiers who initially accepted official explanations but became disillusioned after experiencing the front and their commanders’ treatment.
“They increasingly understand that they are not fighting Nazis and that they are not defending Russia from NATO,” he said.
Other respondents may interpret cooperation more narrowly. They could favor countries working together on trade, climate, or health while endorsing military action they consider justified. The UN Foundation question did not ask them to apply their answer specifically to Russia’s invasion.
The apparent contradiction may thus involve different understandings of the war and of cooperation itself, rather than a conscious decision to endorse incompatible principles.
Wanting negotiations is not the same as rejecting the war
Levada’s war polling provides a closer comparison within one respondent pool: 68% supported Russian military actions, while 59% favored negotiations.
Those majorities necessarily overlap. Some respondents supported the campaign while also wanting talks.
That could reflect fatigue, concern about casualties, or hopes for a settlement favorable to Russia. The question did not establish which territories respondents thought Russia should retain or what concessions they would accept.
Accordingly, a preference for negotiations does not automatically mean rejecting the invasion. People can want fighting to stop while believing their own side should keep what it has seized.
The UN Foundation survey also found Russian respondents relatively hopeful: 46% described themselves as hopeful about the world and 44% as worried. The pooled figures were 34% and 57%, respectively.
What that means practically isn’t fully known: The survey also cannot tell us whether Russian respondents’ hopefulness reflected expectations of peace, confidence in their government, or concerns unrelated to Ukraine.
The government’s double standard is clearer
The uncertainty surrounding individual attitudes does not obscure the contradiction in Moscow’s own conduct.
At his Sept. 25 press conference, Putin accused the Baltic states of violating Russian speakers’ rights and said Moscow was responding “within the framework of international law,” according to Ukrainska Pravda.
Yet Russia has also been condemned of illegal war of aggression and continued it despite the International Court of Justice’s March 2022 order to suspend military operations.
The Kremlin often invokes international protections while threatening neighboring countries and disregarding constraints on its own actions.
As Kyiv Post reported, Moscow’s claims to protect Russian speakers also recall arguments used to justify aggression against Ukraine. Meanwhile, Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev warned that Lithuania could “disappear from the map of the world” in a conflict linked to its potential hosting of nuclear weapons.
The polling does not show how many Russians recognize or approve of that double standard. It leaves several explanations open: different groups answering the surveys, concealed dissent, acceptance of official narratives, or support for cooperation that stops short of accepting concessions by Russia.
Distinguishing among them would require asking the same respondents more specific questions. Would they support withdrawing Russian troops, complying with an international ruling, or accepting Ukraine’s independent security choices?
For Ukrainians, those answers would reveal considerably more than a general preference for countries solving problems together.

British firm set to clear space junk passes security audit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:01:20 UTC
22:01:20 KST

- Astroscale UK has achieved ISO/IEC 27001:2022 information security certification after a 20-month company-wide program and an independent audit.
- The company is preparing ELSA-M, a planned debris removal mission launching on an ISAR Aerospace Spectrum rocket, and the UK Ministry of Defence's Orpheus program.
Astroscale UK, the British arm of the Japanese company building spacecraft to clear junk from orbit, has earned an international information security certification as it prepares a planned debris removal mission and a defense program for the UK Ministry of Defence.
The company said on Sept. 30 that it achieved ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification after an independent audit and a 20-month, company-wide effort to put new security policies, processes and oversight in place. The standard sets out how an organization identifies and manages risks to its information, and Astroscale UK says its version also covers newer risks tied to artificial intelligence and outside suppliers.
Astroscale UK says the certification is meant to give customers, government partners and suppliers confidence in how it handles sensitive information on ELSA-M, which the company says will be the world’s first active debris removal mission, meaning a spacecraft sent to capture and remove a dead object from orbit. ELSA-M is set to launch on a Spectrum rocket from German launch company ISAR Aerospace, though Astroscale has not given a date.
The company is also working on Orpheus, a UK Ministry of Defence program that Astroscale says is developing a sovereign British defense capability for servicing satellites in orbit. It gave no further details on what Orpheus will do or when.
“Our missions combine frontier robotics and autonomous rendezvous with exacting operational discipline,” said Nick Shave, managing director of Astroscale UK.
Both programs rely on rendezvous and proximity operations: flying one spacecraft close to another, inspecting it and working with it without a collision. The same skills that let a spacecraft grab a piece of debris could let it inspect or service another satellite, which is why the work draws interest from militaries as well as satellite operators.
Astroscale first tested those skills on ELSA-d, launched in 2021, which demonstrated long- and short-range rendezvous and the magnetic capture of a client spacecraft. In 2024, the company’s ADRAS-J mission approached a discarded Japanese upper-stage rocket body to within 15 meters (49 feet) and inspected it, even though the rocket body was not built to be approached. Astroscale UK built the ground systems for that mission and led its flight dynamics, including planning the close approach maneuvers and handling collision warnings.
Astroscale, founded in 2013 and headquartered in Japan, has also won work with Japan’s space agency JAXA, the U.S. Space Force, the European Space Agency, the UK Space Agency and satellite operator Eutelsat.
“Achieving ISO 27001 is tangible evidence that we are building the secure, resilient organisation needed to deliver complex space missions in the UK,” Shave said.

China fails to create US and Taiwanese skepticism despite best efforts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:01:05 UTC
22:01:05 KST

The recent summit in Washington between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping concluded with a heavily publicized trade truce that saw Beijing walk away with a reprieve on electric vehicle tariffs, while Washington secured expanded purchase agreements for US coal.
Yet, beneath the veneer of transactional diplomacy, the summit exposed a sophisticated, multi-layered arena of geopolitical posturing, psychological warfare and state-sponsored disinformation centered entirely on the future of Taiwan.
A primary point of public friction leading up to the summit was the temporary hold on a NT$450 billion (US$14 billion) arms sale package to Taipei, which includes critical air-defense assets and anti-drone systems. While immediate commentary characterized the delay as a symptom of a transactional foreign policy, seasoned analysts recognized it as standard Washington posturing.
Historically, modern US administrations — including those of George W Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden — have paused or delayed arms packages to Taiwan at least four times to evaluate domestic defense supply chains, balance regional allocations and maximize diplomatic leverage during high-level bilateral encounters.
Trump’s historical record supports this strategic interpretation. During his first administration, he authorized the largest cumulative arms sales for Taiwan in history, greenlighting paradigm-shifting capabilities such as F-16V fighter jets, M1A2 tanks and critical technology for Taiwan’s domestic submarine program.
This trajectory continued into his second term with a NT$350 billion single-year defense package in December 2025. Once the pending NT$450 billion package is signed, Trump’s aggregate arms approvals will approach NT$1.28 trillion, effectively doubling the totals approved during the entire eight years of the Obama administration.
Strategic hesitation
By withholding final approval until after the summit, Washington effectively retained a major geopolitical counterweight, keeping Beijing off-balance. This strategic hesitation successfully neutralized behind-the-doors lobbying by the Chinese delegation.
Xi reportedly pressed Trump to shift traditional US terminology from “does not support” Taiwan independence to an explicit commitment to “oppose” it. The White House successfully resisted this rhetorical upgrade, scrubbing all mentions of Taiwan from the official readout to preserve long-standing strategic ambiguity.
When questioned, Trump deflected, noting only that “Xi understands very much how I feel,” leaving Beijing to calculate the exact boundaries of US resolve.
Failing to secure concrete policy concessions in the meeting rooms, the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) propaganda apparatus and the United Front Work Department launched a coordinated cognitive warfare campaign. This information operation relied on manufacturing domestic panic and manipulating public skepticism on both sides of the Pacific.
The campaign received an artificial boost just days before the summit when an article by analyst Jennifer Kavanagh went viral. Published by Defense Priorities, a Washington think tank funded significantly by the Charles Koch foundation, the piece advocated for the complete retrenchment of US forces in Asia to the Second Island Chain, effectively suggesting the abandonment of Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines in favor of a consolidated footprint in Guam.
While the article represented a fringe academic viewpoint within Washington, CCP state media and covert influence networks weaponized it instantly. In the US, United Front-linked accounts signal-boosted the piece to exploit isolationist, “America First” skepticism, framing security support for a fellow democracy as an unnecessary economic and military liability.
Economic tripwire
Concurrently, in Taipei, the same text was used to validate the narrative of “US skepticism.” Coordinated online networks circulated rumors that the White House was actively preparing a retreat strategy, trying to break Taiwanese public morale by painting Washington as an unreliable ally ready to discard its partners for commercial concessions.
The US countered this psychological pressure with explicit displays of military capability and symbolic pageantry. As Xi arrived at Joint Base Andrews, the conclusion of the US National Anthem was synchronized with a low-altitude flyover of two nuclear-capable B-1B Lancer supersonic bombers. The display served as an unambiguous, physical reminder of the US military-industrial complex.
Furthermore, Taiwan’s modern “silicon shield” — the global economy’s absolute reliance on TSMC’s advanced semiconductor fabrication — ensures that any contemporary attempt by Beijing to establish a blockade or force cross-strait aggression would instantly collapse global markets, including China’s own economy. It remains a high-tech economic tripwire that makes unilateral aggression a self-defeating trap, reinforcing why the strategic alliance remains bulletproof despite Beijing’s digital rumor mill.
Despite the choreographed optics, the post-summit fallout exposed significant rhetorical friction. The most glaring gaffe emerged when US Ambassador to China David Perdue revealed on Fox News on Sunday that Trump had casually asked Xi if China would like to purchase US weapons.
Though the State Department and a visibly defensive Trump scrambled to walk back the comments by claiming Perdue had likely confused “China with Taiwan,” the leak exposed a hilarious subversion of expectations. Xi spent years demanding an end to US arms sales, only to enter Washington and receive an impromptu sales pitch for American military hardware.
History lesson
Simultaneously, a battle over historical memory erupted. During a state dinner toast, Xi lauded how the US and China “fought side by side as allies to win World War II.” The White House subsequently repeated this framing in its official fact sheet.
Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council immediately issued a sharp rebuke, noting that the current ruling regime in Beijing did not exist during World War II, having only seized power in 1949. The heroic ally that fought alongside the US against militarism was the Republic of China — modern-day Taiwan. Taiwan’s officials directly called out Beijing for attempting to plagiarize Taiwan’s military history to gain favor in Washington.
The summit’s peak of diplomatic theater occurred during that very same White House state dinner. As US and Chinese dignitaries entered the dining room, a harpist performed “The Moon Represents My Heart,” a classic timed to honor the Mid-Autumn Festival.
While Western observers viewed it as a polite nod to Chinese culture, the track choice operated as a biting, high-level diplomatic subtweet. The song was popularized globally by the late, legendary Taiwanese singer Teresa Teng (鄧麗君).
Teng was an unyielding cultural icon of democratic resistance who famously refused to ever perform in China while it remained under CCP rule. At the height of the Cold War, her broadcast concerts were played through massive military loudspeakers across the Taiwan Strait to counter communist programming.
By utilizing Teng’s signature melody to welcome the Chinese delegation, the event served as a subtle but unmistakable assertion of Taiwanese cultural primacy and democratic endurance, directly undercutting Beijing’s attempts to erase Taiwan’s identity from the international stage.
Ultimately, the summit demonstrated that while great powers continue to negotiate over raw commodities like coal and electric vehicles, the strategic autonomy of Taiwan remains protected by a robust blend of US defense commitments, historical military resilience, deep global economic integration and a cultural legacy that continues to outmaneuver Beijing’s finest propaganda efforts.

EU-backed scheme helps rural Swedish households on lower incomes go electric

A Swedish government scheme, part-funded by the EU's Social Climate Fund, is offering rural, lower-income drivers financial support to switch from petrol and diesel to electric vehicles.
"I couldn't understand why people bought electric cars, because it didn't look like it was trustworthy," says project manager Olivia Almquist, who replaced her unreliable 30-year-old petrol car with an electric one. "And now I can't understand why not everyone is buying an electric car."
Sweden's electric car premium gives eligible drivers up to 120 euros a month towards leasing costs, plus a one-off 1,600 euro bonus for the lowest earners. To qualify, applicants must earn under 80% of the national average wage, live in a rural area, and buy a car costing between 6,000 and 40,000 euros.
For social worker Daniel Caldeman, who drives 65,000 kilometres a year, the savings have been dramatic: his monthly fuel bill has dropped from around 800 euros to just 150 euros for charging. "I like being eco-friendly and I think about not polluting the environment," he says, "so yeah, it was a factor, but I think that the main factor was economics for me."
Backed by 400 million euros from the EU's Social Climate Fund, itself financed by carbon taxes raised through Europe's Emissions Trading System, the scheme has drawn over 20,000 applicants since it launched in March. According to the Swedish Environmental Protection Agency, nearly 90% of purchases are second-hand vehicles, with officials aiming to eventually help 115,000 households move away from fossil fuels.

Common diseases decline in Helsinki as health gaps persist
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:00:57 EEST
22:00:57 KST

The prevalence of common diseases in Helsinki fell by 10 per cent between 2019 and 2025, with residents recording lower levels of illness than Finland as a whole, according to data published by the City of Helsinki. Differences between parts of the capital remain substantial despite the overall decline.
The reduction was driven in particular by declines in hypertension and coronary heart disease, the city said in a research review based on data from the Social Insurance Institution of Finland, Kela, and Statistics Finland.
In 2025, the prevalence of the most common diseases in Helsinki stood 21 per cent below the national level.
Researchers examined seven common diseases. Psychotic disorders were the only category with a slightly higher prevalence in Helsinki than across Finland. Coronary heart disease and hypertension showed the largest relative differences in Helsinki’s favour.
A separate morbidity index also recorded a decline. The measure combines data on disability, mortality and eligibility for medicine reimbursements. Disability recorded the largest decrease among those three components.
Helsinki scored 84 on the age-standardised morbidity index in 2025, compared with a national reference value of 100. Age standardisation allows comparisons between areas with different age profiles.
The city-level figures mask differences between Helsinki neighbourhoods.
Morbidity remained below the Helsinki average in the inner city and the northernmost parts of the capital. Nine of the city’s basic districts recorded levels substantially above the city average, even after researchers accounted for differences in residents’ ages.
The gap between areas also increased slightly. Changes in disability between 2023 and 2025 played a central role in the widening geographical differences, according to the review.
The City of Helsinki linked much of the variation to differences in the demographic and socioeconomic composition of neighbourhoods. Disease prevalence tends to be higher in areas where residents have lower incomes, connecting geographical health differences with disparities between population groups.
The findings point to differences in demand for health and social services across the capital. The city said services should be directed towards areas with greater needs alongside measures addressing health differences between population groups.

====================================================================================================

BNN IN FOCUS | Political party review: United List – is the “Kulbergs effect” working?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:00:42 UTC
22:00:42 KST

Author: Ilona Bērziņa
Just a few months ago, the United List (AS) was one of the opposition forces in the 14th Saeima, associated more with heated parliamentary disputes, the Rail Baltica parliamentary inquiry and criticism of Evika Siliņa’s government. Now the situation is completely different. AS representative Andris Kulbergs heads the Cabinet, while the United List is the clear leader in the polls.
In the latest SKDS poll, conducted from the 4th to the 16th of September among 2,035 Latvian citizens, 14.4% of all respondents said they were ready to vote for the United List. This was the highest result among the parties. Sovereign Power/Young Latvians ranked second with 9.4%, while Latvia First was third with 9.2%.
Compared with August, support for AS has declined slightly, but the party has retained first place. The September poll by Latvijas Fakti paints a similar picture. AS received the support of 15.9% of all respondents, compared with 15.6% in August. Among voters who had already made their choice, support for AS reached 23.8%.
This strongly resembles the position New Unity found itself in before the 14th Saeima election. In the final SKDS poll before that election, New Unity had around 20–23% support among respondents who had named a specific choice. The Factum Interactive poll conducted from the 15th to the 20th of September showed a very similar level of support – around 21–24%.
There is another similarity:
both political alliances largely have their prime ministers to thank for their strong voter support.
In New Unity’s case, it was Krišjānis Kariņš, who took on the task of forming his first government under highly complicated circumstances and successfully steered it through the waves of the pandemic. In the case of AS, it is Andris Kulbergs, who was not afraid to take the helm of the government for a very short period – just four months – and whose sharp rhetoric appears to resonate with voters.
SKDS polls showed a sharp increase in support for the United List following the formation of Kulbergs’ government: from 6.8% in April and May to 9.8% in June. In the pre-election period, this makes it possible to speak of a clearly visible “Kulbergs effect”. Whether this story will end in a similar way to the “Kariņš effect” remains to be seen.
A look at the alliance’s history
Officially, the political alliance consists of the Latvian Green Party, the Latvian Association of Regions and the Liepāja Party.
The alliance was also formed with the participation of non-partisan professionals brought together by Uldis Pīlēns in the United List of Latvia association, which was later renamed Latvia’s Restart and is now headed by Andris Kulbergs.
One of AS’s distinctive features is that it brings together people and organisations with very different political backgrounds: the Green Party, which left ZZS because of its cooperation with Aivars Lembergs’ For Latvia and Ventspils, representatives of regional politics, members of Liepāja’s political elite, people from the business community and non-partisan professionals.
In the 2022 election to the 14th Saeima, AS received 11.01% of the vote and 15 seats, becoming the third most popular electoral list. Its strongest support came from Liepāja and South Kurzeme. The parliamentary group later shrank to 12 MPs.
Uldis Pīlēns, without whom AS would most likely not be what it is today, has been both the alliance’s candidate for prime minister and its candidate for President of Latvia. He now publicly acknowledges that he has relatively little involvement with the United List, while stressing that he has not severed ties with the alliance and believes AS is a political force capable of surviving in the long term.
Pīlēns, however, is not among the candidates on the AS electoral lists.
Electoral list leaders and their track records
AS is running under number seven, and each of the five electoral districts is headed by a politician already well known to the public.
In Riga, the list is headed by Andris Kulbergs, the current Prime Minister and AS candidate for the post after the election. Before entering politics, he was known as a representative of the automotive industry. In the Saeima, he became particularly prominent as chairman of the parliamentary inquiry into the problems surrounding Rail Baltica and later a commission investigating costs at Rīgas siltums.
In Vidzeme, the list is headed by Edvards Smiltēns, chairman of the Latvian Association of Regions, former Speaker of the Saeima, current Justice Minister and one of the two co-chairmen of the AS board.
In Latgale, the number one candidate is Juris Viļums, an MP in the 11th, 12th and 14th Saeima and head of the AS parliamentary group, with longstanding ties to Latgale. He founded Latgolys Saeima and is a member and one of the founders of the Latgolys Studentu centrs association, now known as Volūda. Former President Raimonds Vējonis is number two on the Latgale list.
In Kurzeme, the list is headed by Māris Kučinskis, a former Prime Minister who also served as Interior Minister during the 14th Saeima and is one of AS’s most experienced politicians.
In Zemgale, the number one candidate is Edgars Tavars, chairman of the Latvian Green Party, co-chairman of the AS board and current Minister for Smart Administration and Regional Development.
The second and third positions on the electoral lists also include a number of familiar names, among them Raimonds Bergmanis, Ingmārs Līdaka, Linda Matisone, Inga Priede, Edgars Putra, Aiva Vīksna and doctor Andris Skride.
What does AS promise?
The United List’s election programme is relatively broad, but economic policy, security and public administration clearly dominate.
On security, the alliance promises to expand the State Defence Service, strengthen the capabilities of the National Guard, complete the eastern border defence line, develop drone and counter-drone technologies, establish a network of shelters, and strengthen the police, Border Guard and State Fire and Rescue Service.
In public finances, the goal is to achieve a balanced base budget within four years. AS also promises to establish a Latvian Development Fund to manage state assets and to review the Rail Baltica project, reducing it to the “minimum viable” scope.
On the economy, AS promises a more stable tax system, a 10% micro-enterprise tax rate for individuals, a reduction in personal income tax on capital gains to 17%, retention of the current corporate income tax regime, less bureaucracy and a state-guaranteed housing construction programme in the regions.
In healthcare, the alliance proposes a state health insurance model under which funding would follow the patient even if they chose a certified private healthcare provider. It also proposes a unified appointment system, transforming the National Health Service into a fund and gradually reducing co-payments for children, seniors and patients with chronic illnesses.
For the regions, AS promises a new municipal financing model, road funding from vehicle taxes, development of ports and special economic zones, and equal EU area-based payments for farmers. Families would be offered housing grants and guarantees, while returning emigrants would receive a special tax regime for four years.
On energy, AS wants to review the implementation of the European Green Deal, examine the use of small modular nuclear reactors and simultaneously develop renewable energy. In foreign policy, the programme declares clear support for NATO, the EU and Ukraine.
Four months at the helm of government
Kulbergs formed his government as a short-term “government of action”. Even while the coalition was being formed, its partners stressed that they would focus primarily on tasks that could still be completed during the remaining term of the 14th Saeima.
AS also secured a highly influential set of positions: the prime minister’s office, the Finance Ministry under Māris Kučinskis, the Justice Ministry under Edvards Smiltēns and the Ministry of Smart Administration and Regional Development under Edgars Tavars.
One of the most visible changes in governance was an attempt to divide ministers’ work into specific tasks that could be reviewed on a regular basis.
However, creating a “short list” did not go particularly smoothly, and it eventually evolved into a government action plan containing 150 measures, with another 35 tasks to be implemented if additional funding could be found without negatively affecting the budget.
Of the 150 measures, 37 relate to budget stabilisation and spending efficiency, 34 to security and foreign affairs, and 21 to reducing bureaucracy and improving the efficiency of public administration.
By mid-August, seven of the ministers’ priority tasks had been fully completed, while results had been achieved on 26 priority measures overall. The remaining measures had been launched and were still being implemented.
A government with a short “shelf life”
Kulbergs’ government was formed only a few months before the 15th Saeima election, and during the debate on approving his Cabinet, Kulbergs himself said that the election result would provide the true assessment of the government’s performance. Judging by the polling figures at the end of September, voters appear satisfied so far.
Unlike Krišjānis Kariņš’ second government or Evika Siliņa’s government, the Kulbergs Cabinet has not had several years before the election to build up a record of achievements.
Four months is enough to demonstrate a leadership style, priorities and initial decisions, as well as to appeal to the public with sharp rhetoric and tough criticism, but it is too short a period to reliably assess the long-term results of many reforms.
What could strengthen AS’s pre-election position…
The first factor is the prime minister’s office. Following the formation of the Kulbergs government, the party’s polling numbers rose significantly. His advantage in pre-election communication is that he can speak not only about what AS would like to do, but also about what the government is currently doing.
The second factor is the alliance’s regional infrastructure. AS is not simply a project of Riga-based politicians. The Latvian Association of Regions, the Green Party and the Liepāja Party have municipal politicians across many regions, while a large proportion of the candidates are connected with municipalities, regional institutions, agriculture and local businesses.
The third factor is the concentration of experienced politicians. Kučinskis is a former prime minister, Vējonis a former President and defence minister, Smiltēns a former Speaker of the Saeima, and Bergmanis a former defence minister.
This allows AS to project an image of experienced professionals with considerable experience in government. In other words, here is the new “adult in the room”.
…and what could make things more difficult
AS is not a single ideologically homogeneous party, but rather a combination of three parties and non-partisan figures. The Latvian Green Party, the Latvian Association of Regions, the Liepāja Party and the Latvia’s Restart group of professionals all have different political histories and their own regional interests.
During the current Saeima term, the alliance has also lost several MPs, with its parliamentary group shrinking from its original 15 seats to 12. Putting together a joint electoral list is one thing; keeping a unified political organisation together for four years is another.
Another factor is the short lifespan of the Kulbergs government. As AS itself stresses in its programme, four months is not enough to resolve problems that have accumulated over many years.
The party therefore has the prime minister’s office, but still has relatively few results of its own government work on which to base a longer-term assessment.
Who is the AS voter?
The latest publicly available September polling data do not provide a full socio-demographic breakdown that would make it possible to say precisely that the typical AS voter belongs to a particular age, income or education group. However, previous election results, the party’s structure, its candidates and its programme point to several potential segments of the AS electorate.
The first is regional voters. AS already enjoyed particularly strong support in Liepāja and South Kurzeme in 2022, while the municipal networks of the Latvian Association of Regions and the Green Party provide the alliance with recognisable figures in Vidzeme and Zemgale as well.
The second group consists of centrist or moderately conservative voters who want neither distinctly left-wing nor radically populist politics and who prioritise security, business, efficient public administration and regional interests.
The third group is interested in improving the business and economic environment. Since the days of Pīlēns, AS rhetoric has prominently featured the language of “professionals”, “crisis management”, productivity, investment, reducing bureaucracy and making public administration more efficient. The economic proposals are also among the most detailed sections of the party’s programme for the 15th Saeima election.
A fourth potential group consists of people who previously voted for ZZS, New Unity or regional lists but who, for one reason or another, are now looking for an economically pragmatic and simultaneously Euro-Atlantic alternative.

MI5 issues spy alert to UK universities over Chinese front company stealing research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:00:41 UTC
22:00:41 KST

China’s intelligence service used a front company to pay grants to British universities and steal crucial research about technology projects, MI5 said on Wednesday in a rare public espionage warning.
Britain’s domestic security service said researchers and academics should cease work with the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI), sometimes also known as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT). MI5 believes it poses a “significant threat”.
The Chinese organisation has given money to 100 or more academics at a string of universities across the UK, in return getting access to the research, which it is alleged found its way back to China’s intelligence service.
MI5 is now prepared to say publicly that the CGTRI is a front for Chinese intelligence, namely the Chinese ministry of state security (MSS). It said continued collaboration could be prosecuted under the National Security Act 2023.
Areas of research targeted include AI, cybersecurity, covert communications, and the embedding of data in pictures online called steganography. MI5 believes it has clear evidence of sensitive information being passed back to Chinese intelligence. The Guardian understands that as well as research money, some British-based academics were given awards, as in honours, by the Chinese.
Successive British governments have courted Chinese investment and encouraged cooperation.
In the alert issued on Wednesday, the Security Service said: “MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage.”
It said that the CGTRI had “very strong ties to the … MSS, China’s civilian intelligence and security service”.
It added: “Many academic institutions and individuals will to date have engaged with CGTRI in good faith given CGTRI’s obfuscated links to MSS.
“UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions. Further, academics are advised to establish the ultimate funding source when conducting any research collaboration with Chinese institutions, to ensure CGTRI is not involved.”
The alert warns of “potential criminal consequences”, in a section issued after consultation with the Crown Prosecution Service, which authorises criminal prosecutions in England and Wales.
“Through this espionage alert, MI5 has placed the fact that CGTRI has very strong ties to MSS in the public domain,” it states. “Going forward, academic institutions, staff and researchers should ensure they are aware of the National Security Act 2023, particularly offences under section 3 (assisting a foreign intelligence service) and section 17 (obtaining a material benefit from a foreign intelligence service).
“Under section 3, an offence is committed if the person a) engages in conduct that is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out UK-related activities, and b) knows, or having regard to other matters known to them ought reasonably to know, that their conduct is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out UK-related activities.”
Such is the scale of Chinese state espionage targeting the UK that MI5 has decided on a deterrence strategy via a public alert such as this, rather than pursuing every single case. It hopes universities will heed the warning and immediately cease their work with the CGTRI.
The Guardian understands MI5 believes Chinese intelligence gained access to cutting-edge British research on scraping social media (searching and retaining useful information from social media sites).
The National Security and Investment Act 2021 could prevent a state such as China, assessed as having hostile intent towards the UK, from buying access to the technology on a commercial basis.
The security minister, Dan Jarvis, demanded universities end ties to the CGTRI. He said: “This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security and that of our allies.
“I have written to all university vice-chancellors to ensure they support their staff to end all arrangements with this company, preventing further benefit to the Chinese intelligence services and ensuring compliance with the National Security Act.”
He added: “International partnerships are vital to ensure our universities and research institutes continue to thrive, but we will take robust action to defend against the threats we face. That means supporting our police and intelligence services to expose and disrupt harmful activity, using the full force of the law.”
Responding to the MI5 alert, Vivienne Stern, the chief executive of Universities UK, which represents 142 institutions across the UK, said universities took their responsibilities around research security and national security extremely seriously.
“The sector has made significant investments in recent years to strengthen due diligence, risk assessment and research security processes, while continuing to support the international collaboration that is essential to world-leading research and innovation,” she said.
“Close engagement between government and the higher education sector is vital to ensuring that universities and the country continue to benefit from international collaboration while effectively managing national security risks.”
Libby Hackett, the chief executive of the Russell Group of research-intensive universities, said: “All our universities take national security responsibilities very seriously. Working closely with government departments and the security services enables universities to take swift action to protect UK interests – and we will continue to do so in the face of new and emerging threats”.
The Chinese embassy has been approached for comment.
