Ukraine Identifies 23 Companies Making Missiles for Russia’s Pantsir—One-Third Remain Unsanctioned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:36:00 UTC
19:36:00 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Identifies 23 Companies Making Missiles for Russia’s Pantsir—One-Third Remain Unsanctioned
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) has identified 23 Russian companies involved in producing 95Ya6 guided missiles for Russia’s Pantsir air defense systems, the agency said on September 30.
The information was published on HUR’s War&Sanctions portal and details companies participating in the production chain for the 95Ya6, the primary medium-range missile used by various modifications of the Pantsir system.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Pantsir is a family of Russian short-range self-propelled surface-to-air missile and gun systems designed to protect military, industrial, and other strategic facilities. Russia also uses the systems to strengthen air defenses at low and extremely low altitudes and counter large-scale aerial attacks.
According to HUR, the Shipunov Instrument Design Bureau plays a central role in the production chain as the primary developer and manufacturer of the 95Ya6 missile. The company is also involved in producing weapons for Russia’s Orion unmanned systems, Krasnopol guided artillery shells, and cannons for Sukhoi fighter jets.
Among the newly identified companies are the Komponent plant, which produces proximity target sensors for the missiles; the Sergo Ordzhonikidze Saratov Electrical Instrument-Making Plant, which supplies radiation and power units; and the Tambov Elektropribor plant, which manufactures control equipment for the 95Ya6.
HUR said approximately one-third of the 23 companies disclosed in the latest update are not currently sanctioned by any country participating in the international sanctions coalition.
The latest disclosure follows HUR’s earlier publication of information on more than 50 companies involved in manufacturing the 72V6 combat vehicle used in the Pantsir-S1 system.
Russia has deployed Pantsir systems to protect strategically important sites, including placing them on rooftops in Moscow since 2023. According to HUR, a newer Pantsir-SMD-E variant has also been observed in the Russian capital this year. Unlike previous versions, the system uses small TKB-1055 Gvozd missiles instead of automatic cannons.
“Air defense systems, including Pantsir systems, provide protection for Russian facilities producing cruise and ballistic missiles, while also shielding Russian military formations during offensive and defensive operations in Ukraine, as well as other strategically important sites in Russia,” the agency added.
The disclosure comes after Ukrainian forces destroyed two Russian Pantsir-S1 systems in separate strikes in temporarily occupied Crimea and Russia’s Krasnodar region in late August.
One system was destroyed near occupied Kerch on August 29, while another was struck near a military airfield in Yeysk, Krasnodar region, the following day, according to the open-source channel Dossier Shpiona, which published images of the destroyed systems.

“If People Are in a Bunker, Business Stops”: Missile Alerts Cost Ukraine $45 Million an Hour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:35:54 UTC
19:35:54 KST

- Category
- Life in Ukraine
“If People Are in a Bunker, Business Stops”: Missile Alerts Cost Ukraine $45 Million an Hour
Ukraine is losing an estimated $45 million for every hour that missile alerts force businesses to suspend operations, as intensified Russian aerial attacks increasingly disrupt economic activity across the country, The Guardian reported on September 30.
Ukraine’s Economy and Environment Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko said Russian forces have increasingly targeted infrastructure critical to the economy, including industrial facilities, warehouses, logistics hubs, and data centers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Kravchenko, the expanding use of jet-powered drones has added to the pressure on businesses, with Russian forces deploying the weapons against a growing range of targets.
“What we had not fully anticipated was how quickly Russia would develop these jet-powered drones and use them to target everything,” Kravchenko told The Guardian.
The attacks have repeatedly brought economic activity to a halt as employees are required to move to shelters during air raid alerts, which can last for up to 10 hours a day.
“If people are in a bunker, business stops,” Kravchenko said.
In an effort to limit the economic impact of prolonged alerts, the Ukrainian government recently introduced a two-tier warning system intended to allow businesses to continue operating when the threat level permits.
Under the system, a “red” alert signals a missile threat and requires people to seek shelter, while a “yellow” warning indicates a drone threat and allows many businesses to remain open.
According to the outlet, Kravchenko said more than half of businesses continue operating during yellow alerts, allowing economic activity to continue despite the ongoing threat of Russian aerial attacks.
The economic disruption comes as Russia continues to target Ukraine’s commercial and logistics infrastructure. Russian attacks have damaged around 500,000 square meters of warehouse space, while Ukraine could lose more than $2 billion in export revenue in the second half of 2026.
The ministry said Russian forces carried out more than 25 strikes on warehouse facilities during the first half of the year alone. Russia has also targeted Ukraine’s broader logistics network, launching more than 1,000 attacks on railway infrastructure and repeatedly striking ports in the Greater Odesa area.
Overall, Russia launched 3,177 jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles against Ukraine in September, up from 2,850 recorded in August.

Russia posts highest crude export earnings since 2022 – Bloomberg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:35:25 UTC
19:35:25 KST

Russia posts highest crude export earnings since 2022 – Bloomberg
Russia’s earnings from seaborne crude exports have surged to their highest weekly level since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, Bloomberg has reported. Rising oil prices and stronger shipment volumes have boosted Moscow’s revenues despite Western sanctions.
The gross value of Russian crude exports reached $2.75 billion in the week through September 27, the outlet reported on Tuesday. On a four-week basis, shipments averaged 3.71 million barrels per day, their highest since early August, while their value climbed to $2.39 billion a week.
According to the outlet, the increase has been driven by both higher crude prices and growing export volumes. Global oil prices have risen sharply during the US-Israeli war on Iran amid the disruption of shipping via the Strait of Hormuz, boosting earnings for major producers outside the Persian Gulf, including Russia.
The surge comes despite Western efforts to curb Moscow’s energy earnings. The G7, EU and Australia introduced a $60-per-barrel price cap on Russian crude in December 2022 alongside an EU embargo on seaborne imports, followed by restrictions on Russian petroleum products in February 2023.
The measures were designed to reduce Russia’s revenues while keeping its crude flowing to global markets and avoiding a supply shock. Moscow responded by redirecting much of its oil trade away from Europe toward China, India and other markets, which now account for the bulk of Russian seaborne crude purchases. According to Bloomberg, shipments to Asian customers, including cargoes whose final destination was not yet known, rose to 3.61 million barrels per day in the four weeks through September 27.
Russia’s latest crude windfall has, however, been partly offset by falling exports of refined fuels. Moscow has restricted diesel shipments to protect domestic supplies after an unprecedented wave of Ukrainian drone strikes damaged refineries across the country, while lower processing rates have left more crude available for export.
Russia has consequently raised its crude-export forecast for 2026 by about 150,000 barrels per day while cutting its forecast for refined-product shipments by roughly 500,000 barrels per day, according to Bloomberg.
Western governments are meanwhile continuing to pressure European states that still rely on Russian energy. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul urged Slovakia on Tuesday to phase out Russian oil and gas and increase pressure on Moscow, days after meeting Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in New York.
Slovakia has resisted a rapid cutoff, with Russian supplies accounting for more than 80% of its oil and over half of its gas imports in 2025, according to the European Commission. Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanar said the country had built its energy infrastructure around Russian supplies and warned that abandoning them immediately would create “enormous problems,” arguing that alternative routes currently lack sufficient capacity.

Unknown

Vladimir Putin has bestowed state honors on 51 employees of Russia’s state-run Pervy Kanal (Channel One), the result of a decree dated Sept. 29. Among the honorees are propagandists whose reports The Insider has previously debunked as false.
Correspondent Ivan Blagoy received the Order of Friendship. He authored a widely known 2016 report about “Lisa,” a girl in Germany who was allegedly abducted and sexually assaulted by immigrants. German police later established that she had neither been abducted nor raped.
Kirill Brainin received the Order of Honor. The Insider has also repeatedly debunked his reports, including stories about the Skripal poisoning case and a claim that Lithuanian President Dalia Grybauskaite had cooperated with the KGB.
Putin also awarded the Order of Friendship to Dimitri Simes, host of the program The Great Game. Simes is under sanctions imposed by Canada and Ukraine. He also faces criminal charges in the United States, where the Justice Department alleges that he continued working for Channel One after American sanctions were imposed on the network — receiving more than $1 million, a chauffeured car, and money for housing in Moscow. He is charged with violating sanctions and money laundering.
Also on the list was Yekaterina Berezovskaya, an anchor of the flagship news program Vremya. In March 2022, she presented a group of people who had traveled to Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory as Western journalists who were prepared to “look the truth in the eye.” The Insider later found that the group included a pro-Kremlin activist, an anti-vaccine conspiracy theorist, and a person linked to entities associated with Wagner Group co-founder and “troll farm” operator Yevgeny Prigozhin. Berezovsky is under Ukrainian sanctions.
In all, Putin’s decree granted state awards to 51 Channel One employees:
- Order “For Merit to the Fatherland,” 4th Class: Channel One Deputy Director General Tatyana Garanina and host Yury Simonov.
- Order of Honor: commentator Kirill Brainin.
- Order of Friendship: Sergei Andreyev, Ivan Blagoy, Alexei Kaskov, Dmitry Simes, Maxim Sharafutdinov, and Pyotr Shepin.
- Medal of the Order “For Merit to the Fatherland,” 1st Class: Yekaterina Berezovskaya, Roman Budnikov, Konstantin Vavilov, Maria Vasilyeva, Yelena Demidova, Grigory Yemelyanov, Svetlana Zeynalova, Yulia Zimina, Valeria Korablyova, Larisa Krymova, Yelena Lapshina, Olga Masliy, Yekaterina Mtsituridze, Anton Nenashev, Dmitry Orlov, Tatyana Pirogova, Timur Solovyov, Rustam Suleimankhil, Sergei Tugushev, Andrei Ukharev, Yulia Fatyukhina and Olga Chernosvitova.
- Medal of the Order “For Merit to the Fatherland,” 2nd Class: Sergei Arkhipov, Sergei Babayev, Ilya Bulavinov, Anton Volsky, Olga Vorontsova, Alyona Germanova, Roman Gutzeit, Alexander Dudkin, Alexei Zotov, Denis Kazansky, Alexander Kosygin, Olesya Loseva, Irina Muromtseva, Dmitry Popkov, Denis Ratov, Pavel Rudakov, Alexander Smola, Andrei Stolyarov, Valery Shein, and Yelena Shtokolova.
It was the second mass award ceremony for Channel One employees this month. Under a Sept. 3 decree, Putin honored another 28 of the network’s employees, including Deputy Director General Natalya Nikonova, department heads Sergei Sokolov and Svetlana Kolosova, sports commentators Vladimir Gomelsky and Viktor Gusev, host Arina Sharapova, and chief producer of music and entertainment programming Yury Aksyuta.

Missile alerts cost Ukraine $45 million for every hour businesses stop, economy minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:33:52 UTC
19:33:52 KST

Missile alerts cost Ukraine $45 million for every hour businesses stop, economy minister says
Missile alerts cost Ukraine an estimated $45 million for every hour they force businesses to stop operating, Economy and Environment Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko told the Guardian in an interview published on Sept. 30.
"If people are in a bunker, business stops," Kravchenko told the Guardian.
Kravchenko said prolonged missile alerts can bring large parts of the economy to a standstill as workers move into shelters, with some alerts lasting for hours.
Ukraine introduced a two-tier air raid warning system on Sept. 2 to reduce the economic disruption caused by prolonged alerts. Red alerts are issued when there is a missile threat and require businesses to halt operations and people to seek shelter. Yellow alerts warn primarily of drone threats and allow many businesses to continue operating.
Russia has intensified its aerial campaign against Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure. Kravchenko said more than half of businesses continue operating during yellow alerts, but those warnings do not mean there is no danger.
On Sept. 28, a Russian jet-powered drone struck the National Academy of Sciences building in central Kyiv during a yellow alert while employees were still inside. The attack killed an aide to former National Security and Defense Council Secretary Volodymyr Horbulin and injured others.
"What we had not fully anticipated was how quickly Russia would develop these jet-powered drones and use them to target everything," Kravchenko said.
Russian attacks have caused an estimated $10 billion in damage to fixed assets in Ukraine this year alone, according to Kravchenko. Steel plants, warehouses, logistics hubs, and data centers have all been hit as Moscow increasingly targets infrastructure supporting the country's economy.
Russia has also stepped up attacks on Ukraine's Black Sea ports and maritime export infrastructure, adding pressure on one of the country's main trade routes.
The government is now discussing ways to allow more private companies to purchase Ukrainian air-defense systems to better protect their facilities, Kravchenko said, while acknowledging that businesses cannot fully shield themselves from Russian missiles and drones.
The continuous damage is compounding pressure on Ukraine's state finances. Kravchenko said the government had reduced an estimated $27 billion budget shortfall this year to around $20 billion through spending cuts and additional domestic resources.
Kyiv seeks further support from the EU, Japan, Canada, and the U.K., including potentially bringing forward financing originally planned for next year.
"The cost of war is simply increasing," Kravchenko said, pointing to growing spending requirements for air defense and interceptor drones capable of countering Russia's newer jet-powered weapons.
Ukraine's external financing needs for 2027 are estimated at $52.6 billion, of which around $20 billion have been secured so far, according to the minister.

Testing ground to study facade systems effectiveness in Arctic opened in Murmansk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:33:32 UTC
19:33:32 KST

MURMANSK, September 30. /TASS/. Murmansk hosted the Northern Facade Summit, where was opened the first Arctic testing ground to study facade systems effectiveness in the Far North, the regional Ministry of Construction said.
"We have opened a testing ground on the Kola Bay shore to study facade systems effectiveness in the Far North," the ministry said. "We have been building new houses in the Murmansk Region using modern technologies that necessarily take into account snow and wind loads."
The testing ground, opened in the territory of the Murmansk Arctic University, has four models of houses with facade solutions common in Russia, the ministry continued. The basements and roofs have been re-insulated to minimize heat loss. The test facilities are equipped with a system for keeping automatically temperature at 21 degrees Celsius and indoor humidity at 50-60%, and special sensors record how much electricity is spent to maintain the set parameters depending on weather changes.
"The Murmansk Region is once again a testing ground for new technologies," the Murmansk Region's Deputy Governor Olga Vovk said. "This is due to the climatic specifics: high humidity, strong winds and temperature fluctuations. It is not so easy to build and operate houses in the Far North. To date, there are no studies confirming that structural wear in the Murmansk Region is higher than in other regions."
"Results of studies conducted at this testing ground, in particular, will help us explain at the federal level why our facilities more often need major repairs, and also will help resolve the long-standing dispute over which facade system is more efficient and durable in our climatic conditions," she added.
Earlier, similar testing grounds were opened in Azerbaijan, Uzbekistan and Yakutia. Each climate zone has its own specific features: heat, wind, and cold affect structures in their own way. "The climatic conditions of the Far North allow for research within a shorter period of time: while in other locations it takes 5-10 years, you may see the result of exploitation within 2-3 years," Chair of the Association for Polymer Efficient Technologies Development Olga Zauzelkova said. "We are confident that it is results of research at the Murmansk testing ground that will help us adjust regulatory documents so that we could live more comfortably in our houses."

National Coalition sets out €9bn spending cut plan
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:33:28 EEST
19:33:28 KST

Finland’s National Coalition Party (Kokoomus) has proposed €9 billion in public spending reductions for the next parliamentary term, with the largest savings aimed at healthcare and pensions. The party says €1 billion of the total would fund selected investments and reforms, leaving a net fiscal adjustment of €8 billion.
Prime Minister and party leader Petteri Orpo presented the programme on Wednesday with members of the party leadership.
Kokoomus described the package as its debt-brake programme ahead of Finland’s next parliamentary election.
The party plans to deliver the adjustment through spending cuts rather than tax increases.
“Finland’s problem is not taxes that are too low, but spending that is too high,” Orpo said at the press conference.
The programme allocates €2 billion in savings to social and healthcare services and another €2 billion to the pension system. It also targets €1.5 billion from index-linked spending, €700 million from state administration, €500 million from social security, €600 million from business subsidies and €1.7 billion from other expenditure.
Kokoomus has not set out all measures needed to secure the pension savings. The party wants employers, employees and the state to negotiate changes through Finland’s tripartite system.
Orpo said the party does not seek cuts to pensions already being paid. He raised pension accrual during periods of unemployment and study as areas for examination. Vice-chair Karoliina Partanen said longer working lives should form part of pension reform.
The proposed healthcare savings include changes to the funding model for wellbeing services counties, limits on treatments judged to provide little health benefit and measures aimed at reducing administrative costs.
Kokoomus also wants to reduce the number of wellbeing services counties from 21 towards a 5+1 structure. Party secretary Maggie Keskinen said the party also supports voluntary municipal mergers and tighter rules for municipalities facing financial problems.
The social security package includes plans to shorten earnings-related unemployment benefit to 300 days, with the possibility of shifting more support towards the start of an unemployment period. The party also proposes restrictions on housing support and new conditions for some benefits received by immigrants.
Other proposed cuts include €300 million from development cooperation and €300 million from transport network spending. State grants to organisations, municipalities and wellbeing services counties would fall by €200 million.
Kokoomus also proposes a €120 million reduction in funding for public broadcaster Yle.
The party plans to redirect €150 million in public research, development and innovation spending towards defence-related purposes. It also proposes charges for a second higher education degree, savings in the prison system and the abolition of Parliament’s annual discretionary “Christmas money” allocations.
Defence spending would remain outside the planned index restraints. Orpo said security and defence were areas where the party would not reduce commitments.
Kokoomus has also ruled out tax increases in the programme. Orpo later clarified that his statement about not taking money from people’s wallets referred to taxation rather than reductions in benefits.
Under Finland’s cross-party debt-brake agreement, the adjustment requirement for the next parliamentary term is expected to reach about €8 billion to €11 billion. Kokoomus parliamentary group leader Jukka Kopra said other parties should now publish their own plans before the election.

Estonia lowers apartment building renovation support share
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:33:00 UTC
19:33:00 KST

Estonia lowers apartment building renovation support share
While government support for apartment building renovations has so far covered 30 to 50 percent of renovation costs, in the coming years the government will cover just 20 percent.
In previous years, apartment building renovations have been supported mainly with European Union funding. As one EU budget period is coming to an end and another is only beginning, a gap has emerged in EU funding.
Infrastructure Minister Kuldar Leis said the government decided during budget talks to cover that gap from the state budget, allocating a total of €160 million for renovations over the next four years. The first €80 million application round is expected to take place as early as next year.
However, the use of state funding comes with stricter conditions. Previously, for example, renovation grants covered a higher share of costs in rural areas than in Tallinn or Tartu.
Those differences will now disappear. Regardless of whether an apartment building is located in Kehtna, Valga or Tallinn, the grant will cover 20 percent of costs.
Leis explained that at this level, the grant is budget-neutral because the money returns to the state budget through taxes.
"In the future, the trend will be toward lower grant percentages. There are currently so many apartment associations that want to renovate and it has become so popular that as a country we can no longer continue with grants covering 50 percent or more of the cost. It simply isn't possible," Leis said.
Asked whether poorer municipalities or rural areas could fall behind wealthier areas in renovations with the grant set at this level, Leis said a great deal still depends on local initiative — in other words, whether people are interested in renovating or not.
"Current experience shows that the most successful places have actually been smaller towns, not major cities. In smaller towns, it is easier to reach an agreement and they have also had very strong local leaders who have driven apartment building renovations. In some towns — take Põlva, where I live — more than 80 percent of apartment buildings have already been renovated," he said.
The situation is not as rosy everywhere, however. Kohtla-Järve finance chief Aivar Kamal said, for example, that not a single building in the city has yet been fully renovated. That is despite the fact that four-fifths of the city's residents live in prefabricated apartment buildings.
On the one hand, apartment values in the Ida-Viru County city are low, making loans financially unviable; on the other, Kamal said older residents simply do not see a need for renovation.
"If the grant rate falls this low, interest here will probably be close to zero. No one is going to prepare a grant application and apply to the state for support for that amount of money," Kamal said.
Kamal said he believed Kohtla-Järve residents would only be interested in renovation if the state covered around 90 percent of the cost.
Andres Jaadla, head of the Estonian Union of Co-operative Housing Associations, said the government's decision has both positive and negative aspects. He said it was positive that the government was allocating at least some money for renovations. According to Jaadla, the last apartment building renovation grant round took place in fall 2025 when nearly 350 apartment associations missed out on funding because there was simply not enough money available.
"Apartment associations will certainly now have to consider whether, with grant amounts changed to this extent, they can reach agreements within their buildings and move forward with renovations. This reduction in the grant percentage is certainly something that will require serious discussion," Jaadla said.
Apartment associations also betting on EU money
Jaadla said that, based on interest from apartment associations, the amount of funding could have been several times higher — somewhere around €400 million to €500 million.
"That might cover the current demand from associations that have already completed their preparations for renovation. From our perspective, this amount is certainly not sufficient," Jaadla said.
Kuldar Leis said, however, that the €160 million in state budget funding will not be the only support available.
This fall, for example, the government agreed that €288 million from the European Union's next budget period, covering 2028 to 2034, could be directed toward apartment building renovations, or about €40 million a year.
That could be supplemented by another €186 million from the European Union's Social Climate Fund, provided Estonia joins the ETS2 emissions trading system. The government has been critical of ETS2, however, and wants it either scrapped or at least postponed.
By comparison, around €330 million was earmarked for renovation grants in the previous European Union budget period, covering 2021 to 2027.

Russia Launches Winter Energy Campaign, Ukrainian PM Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:32:57 UTC
19:32:57 KST

[UPDATED: Sept. 30, 2:00 pm
                            , Kyiv time. Updated with information about the damage to the Trypilska Power Plant.]
                        
                                        Russia has launched a renewed campaign of mass assaults against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of the winter, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said on Wednesday, Sept. 30.
“Russia has switched to massive strikes on energy infrastructure,” Koretskyi wrote, reporting that Russian missiles and drones had attacked energy facilities in Kyiv, the surrounding region and elsewhere in Ukraine overnight.
“Since the summer, there has effectively not been a single day when the enemy did not attack energy infrastructure. But such a massive and combined attack took place for the first time since the end of the previous heating season,” he said.
The strikes damaged and destroyed energy equipment, although Koretskyi did not disclose which facilities were hit or the extent of the damage. He said he was awaiting a detailed report on the condition of the equipment and the expected timeframe for repairs.
Five killed as Russia attacks 11 regions
Eleven Ukrainian regions came under Russian attacks that started on Tuesday evening, according to the prime minister.
In addition to energy facilities, Russian forces hit residential buildings, social infrastructure, civilian businesses and railway facilities.
Koretskyi said five people had been killed across the country, including a child, while 14 others were wounded. The casualty figures covered the wider nationwide assault which were not limited to attacks on energy facilities.
“All those affected are receiving the necessary assistance. Emergency recovery work and efforts to eliminate the consequences of the attack are ongoing,” Koretskyi said.
The threat of further strikes was feared in several regions.
Utility worker killed in Kyiv
In Kyiv, a Kyivteploenergo driver was killed when a Russian attack hit a warehouse in the Solomianskyi district.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the driver had been working at the site alongside other utility specialists. A Kyiv Post correspondent reported that the attack hit the warehouse’s freezer rooms and set a truck on fire.
The Kyiv City Military Administration reported that another person was injured at the site.
Klitschko also said debris from the overnight attack was found on the grounds of a Western embassy in the Shevchenkivskyi district, without identifying the diplomatic mission.
DTEK said its workers had restored electricity to 8,000 households after energy infrastructure was damaged.
“We continue to work 24/7 to ensure reliable electricity supply for Kyiv residents,” the company said.
These latest incidents followed initial reports from the capital, where two women were killed and five people wounded, as Kyiv Post previously reported.
Fires and damage were recorded at residential buildings, warehouses, a store and other sites in the Sviatoshynskyi, Holosiivskyi, Obolonskyi, Podilskyi and Solomianskyi districts.
Authorities ordered to check backup power
Koretskyi instructed local authorities to inspect backup power systems serving critical infrastructure in their communities.
He said officials must complete the installation and connection of any remaining emergency power equipment as quickly as possible.
Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraine’s power system during the full-scale invasion, with the most intensive campaigns traditionally taking place during the colder months, when damage to electricity, heating and water infrastructure creates the greatest pressure on civilians.
Trypilska power plant equipment damaged
Russia’s attack damaged generating equipment at the Trypilska Thermal Power Plant in the Kyiv region, state-owned energy company Centrenergo said.
“Our immediate priority is to assess the condition of the equipment and determine the scope of the necessary work,” Centrenergo CEO Serhii Isachenko said.
“As soon as the security situation allows, our specialists will begin repairs. The team knows what to do and continues working,” he added.
The company declined to disclose further details about the damage for security reasons. Centrenergo said Russia was deliberately targeting Ukraine’s energy system ahead of the heating season in an effort to deprive residents of electricity and heat.

Access Opera, a partner agency of the American rapper Kanye West, has officially confirmed — via Instagram — that the musician’s purportedly scheduled concerts in Russia will not take place. It recommended that all ticket refund requests be directed to the Say agency.
Say itself said it would release information about the concerts on Wednesday, Sept. 30. “No earlier and no later — be patient,” the agency wrote on its Telegram channel. St. Petersburg’s Gazprom Arena, where West’s concerts had been scheduled for Oct. 10 and 11, last commented on the shows on Sept. 4. At the time, stadium representatives said no concerts by foreign artists were planned at the arena in October.

Zakharova also said the organizers had not filed an application for the event with Russia’s Culture Ministry, adding that they were “either simply unprofessional or this is some kind of provocation.”
According to the Kremlin-aligned publication RBC, West’s concerts in Russia had the backing of “several Kremlin officials,” but they did not coordinate the event with local authorities in St. Petersburg or personally with governor Alexander Beglov. City officials then sought clarification from Moscow, and by then questions had arisen among Kremlin officials regarding the musician’s verbal support for Hitler.
Tickets had been expected to cost from 9,000 rubles (just over $100) to 160,000 rubles (close to $1,900). In August, the concert received support from Elena Drapeko, first deputy chair of the State Duma’s Culture Committee. At the time, she said she hoped Kanye had “changed his mind and changed his attitude toward both Hitler and Russia.”
Ye began drawing widespread criticism and condemnation in recent years after he began making antisemitic remarks and voicing admiration for Adolf Hitler. In early 2025, in a series of posts on X, Ye openly called himself a Nazi. He later released a song titled “Heil Hitler” (along with a companion title, “WW3,” which similarly glorified Hitler) and also offered a $20 white T-shirt printed with a swastika and the code "HH-01" for sale on his website (which he also advertised at Super Bowl LIX).
Several of Ye’s European performances were canceled in 2026, including those scheduled in the UK and Poland. Britain blocked West from traveling to the country in April (when he was scheduled to headline London’s Wireless Festival) due to his antisemitic comments and celebration of Nazism. Several weeks later, the Swiss football club Basel also refused to host his concert at its stadium, St. Jakob-Park, saying the event was incompatible with the organization’s values.
West has issued apologies to the Jewish community on several occasions, most recently taking out a full-page advertisement in the Wall Street Journal in January 2026. In the ad, he said he had “lost touch with reality” and attributed his behavior to an undiagnosed brain injury from a 2002 car accident, along with untreated bipolar disorder
"I regret and am deeply mortified by my actions in that state, and am committed to accountability, treatment, and meaningful change. It does not excuse what I did, though. I am not a Nazi or an antisemite. I love Jewish people," he added.

Most drone interceptors ram or explode. This Ukrainian one just throws a net—six shots to a module
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:31:17 UTC
19:31:17 KST

A Ukrainian defense company has shown a new way to knock FPV drones out of the sky, unveiling a net-firing interceptor at the IT Arena tech conference in Lviv, dev.ua reported. The system, called Mangal and developed by Phantom Defense, is still a prototype—the company says the first production units could reach the market in a few months.
Ukraine's counter-drone work has turned into a crowded contest, with firms racing to field jammers, interceptor drones, and net-throwers that can blunt Russia's growing use of cheap FPVs.
What Mangal does
Phantom Defense designed the modular launcher to defend positions, vehicles, and other targets against enemy drones. It fires a special net weighted with sinkers. The net opens the moment it fires, tangling the drone and dragging it down. One module holds six charges. Two cameras give the crew a clearer view, and the system can detect targets on its own, which speeds up how fast an operator spots a threat. Crews can fix Mangal in place to guard checkpoints, trenches, or infrastructure, or bolt it onto a vehicle.
Why a net
FPV drones—aircraft a pilot flies straight into a target—have become a routine danger along the front. A small, fast drone is hard to hit with a single round. A net spreads as it travels, so it is more forgiving to aim. Neither Phantom Defense nor the outlets covering the launch have said how far Mangal's net can reach.
Ukraine’s newest interceptor doesn’t ram its target. It nets it for $27, then flies home to catch another
Other net-based counters
Other developers are turning to nets too. The WINFLY Spider is an interceptor drone that snares a target in a net and returns to its launch point intact, at about $27 a shot. That lets one aircraft make repeated intercepts instead of being spent on a single kill. Scan Horizon comes from Postup Solutions, a firm registered in Wrocław, Poland, and pairs a net launcher from Ukrainian company Ptashka Drones. Its net reaches about 30 meters. Contra Drone, meanwhile, has shown interceptor missiles that can reportedly carry net warheads alongside other options.

Hundreds of illegal Israeli settlers stormed into the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound in occupied East Jerusalem on Wednesday morning to mark the Jewish holiday of Sukkot, a Jerusalem Islamic Waqf official said.
The official, who requested anonymity, told Anadolu that hundreds of illegal Israeli settlers entered the mosque compound under Israeli police protection.
The incursions included the performance of Talmudic rituals, prayers, dancing and singing, in violation of the status quo at the mosque, the official said.
The historical status quo predating Israel’s occupation of East Jerusalem in 1967 stipulates that the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf, affiliated with Jordan’s Ministry of Endowments, has exclusive responsibility for administering the affairs of the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, which covers 144 dunams (about 14.4 hectares), as a place of worship exclusively for Muslims.
Far-righ Israeli groups had called for large-scale incursions into Al-Aqsa during Sukkot, which began on Saturday and runs through Friday.
The Jerusalem Islamic Waqf said earlier that more than 1,500 illegal Israeli settlers entered the mosque compound on Sunday, more than 1,700 on Monday and over 1,400 on Tuesday.
Incursions into Al-Aqsa have intensified since the start of the Jewish holidays, amid a heightened presence of Israeli forces and increased restrictions in Jerusalem.
The holidays began with the Jewish New Year on September 12 and 13, followed by Yom Kippur on September 21 and 22. Sukkot runs from September 26 to October 2, followed by Simchat Torah on October 3.
Since 2003, Israeli police have unilaterally allowed illegal settlers to enter Al-Aqsa through the Mughrabi Gate in the Al-Buraq Wall (Western Wall), accompanied by police officers.
The Jerusalem Islamic Waqf has repeatedly called for an end to the incursions, but Israeli authorities have not responded to the calls.
Palestinians say Israel has intensified for decades measures aimed at Judaising occupied East Jerusalem, including the Al-Aqsa Mosque, and erasing its Arab and Islamic identity.
Palestinians regard East Jerusalem, where Al-Aqsa is located, as the capital of a future Palestinian state, based on international resolutions that do not recognise Israel’s occupation of the city in 1967.

Black Twitter Is Thriving—on Threads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Last week, after a Mississippi grand jury declined to bring criminal charges in the death of Nolan Wells, the 18-year-old Black college student who disappeared on Horn Island while traveling with a group of white friends and was later found dead, Black users on Threads demanded justice.
“Just so it’s abundantly clear: The state of Mississippi is covering up the murder of Nolan Wells,” user @_taexoxo posted two days after the September 21 decision. The case has incited racial tensions nationwide.
“This year a grand jury handed down an indictment for a pool of water turning green, but didn’t indict when a black kid was found floating face down in water!” commented comedian D.L. Hughley.
Black Americans have never shied away from calling out America’s racial hypocrisies—Twitter served as an indispensable tool as the Black Lives Matter movement swelled in the 2020s—but the chatter on Threads was uniquely charged for Wells. It was the latest bit of evidence showing that the platform has emerged as a vital artery of the Black social media ecosystem, at times even rivaling the influence Black Twitter once embodied.
In 2021, when I first explored the cultural expansiveness of Black Twitter, I wrote that it was “all the things: news and analysis, call and response, judge and jury—a comedy showcase, therapy session, and family cookout all in one.” Five years later, Threads is proving to be its spiritual successor, a robust digital universe where no conversation, no matter how ugly or awkward, is off limits.
As with Black Twitter, on Threads you are just as likely to come across conversations around the ageism double standard that Black women face as you are off-the-cuff TV commentary. Speaking of HBO Max’s new superhero thriller, Lanterns, one user recently commented that it’s the first sci-fi show “with a black Chosen One and a white Magical Negro.”
“The heyday of Twitter was during the Obama era. Now we’re living through the second Trump administration. Having a place to laugh to keep from crying is just as important as it ever was,” Jamilah Lemieux, a cultural critic and author who has 208,000 followers on the Meta-run platform, tells WIRED.
Lemieux was active on Twitter for over a decade, where she discussed motherhood and women’s rights, but started to pull back because the level of harassment and vitriol she was getting started to outweigh her positive interactions.
Twitter underwent a noticeable vibe shift in 2022 after Elon Musk bought the platform and renamed it X. For day-one users, the app was less functional: It was harder to see the content you wanted, hate speech and propaganda accounts surged, and moderation seemed to disappear overnight. “I’m not surprised that that happened. It was a very deliberate shift away from the progressive Black voices that had defined the platform for its earlier history,” says Lemieux, who describes the current experience of posting on X as “screaming into the void.”
Lemieux has since decamped to Threads, where she has become a power user of sorts, riffing on everything from singer Chris Brown to public versus private education. “I wanted a social media home again, but I just wasn't really sure where I fit. I have always preferred text to video in terms of the creation. And Threads offered what I loved about Twitter, which is that I could reach people with my words without having to curate visuals.”
Today, some of the biggest cultural voices on X have migrated to Threads—including author Roxane Gay, activist Brittany Packnett Cunningham, and journalist Nikole Hannah-Jones, whose recent New York Times Magazine essay about her decision to enroll her daughter in low-performing, predominantly Black public schools sparked an intense debate online around using your child to fight systemic failures.
“omg the threads convo about that article is better because NHJ is on there replying to ppl, god all the employed ppl really did go to threads,” TV writer @theashleyray posted on X, telling another user, “black twitter is there.”
Bluesky, which launched as invite-only in 2023 before opening up to the wider public a year later, initially announced itself as one of the first serious alternatives to X. But it wasn’t until Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential win that millions of users, seemingly in need of a public sphere free of the MAGA-fueled rhetoric that had overtaken X, flocked to Bluesky. They were eager to recapture the spirit of social media’s earliest days.
Emboldened by its decentralized format and the promise of improved user safety mechanisms, Rudy Fraser, a developer with a background in community organizing, created Blacksky, a custom feed and moderation service that quickly became a central meeting ground for many Black users on the platform. It has proven to be a more secure social ecosystem for Black users, but it hasn’t exactly swayed public discourse in the way Black Twitter did with #OscarsSoWhite or #IfTheyGunnedMeDown.
Part of that is a numbers game, says Rianna Walcott, an assistant professor of communication at the University of Maryland who founded the Black Digital Migration Project, a research initiative examining how Black social media users respond to changing platform conditions.
“The problems of platform fatigue and reaching a globally Black audience are probably limiting Blacksky’s visibility, as it lacks the initial buy-in that comes from an already connected platform ecosystem like Meta’s,” Walcott says. In the beginning, Bluesky’s biggest user base was concentrated among progressives, particularly journalists, academics, activists, and writers. A 2025 Pew Research Center survey found that 69 percent of respondents who were left-leaning news influencers joined the platform during its first year. And while Blacksky was fundamental to the platform’s nascent growth, Black engagement has stalled for a number of reasons; several colleagues and friends of mine stopped using it after the first few months, seemingly disheartened by its low-key atmosphere, on top of having to rebuild their social media presence in a new corner of the internet.
Threads, meanwhile, prioritizes engagement and allows users to easily join communities like Black Threads, Black British Threads, or Black LGBTQ Threads that are tailor-fit to their interests. According to a Meta blog post from December, there are over 200 groups, which include everything from TV and fitness to the NBA.
“I think it matters more to Black users where they can find each other at volume rather than the overall politics of the platform,” says Walcott.
While Spill, the image-forward social media network launched by Alphonzo Terrell, a former Twitter employee, has been successful in directly appealing to Black people, Threads has a unique advantage when it comes to onboarding new members because of its tight integration with Facebook and Instagram, platforms that have over 6 billion users combined. Threads has more than 500 million monthly active users and, in terms of sheer capacity, is on track to surpass X’s 557 million monthly active users, according to a Statista report from March.
Lemieux appreciates how seamless the platform is compared to X. “We often joke that Threads will drop you off anywhere,” she says. “A lot of the laughter and humor, it’s not just Black people coming up with hashtags like it was before, sometimes it’s just a middle-aged white woman’s Facebook post, who has cross-posted to Threads without realizing it.”
Though many of the same people and conversations that defined Black Twitter have moved to Threads, “Black Threads doesn’t feel like an exact replica of Black Twitter to me,” says Phil Lewis, an editor at HuffPost and news aggregator. He says that Black Twitter especially “shined” when users live-tweeted events, like award shows and sports events. “I haven’t seen that yet. But you can feel when a cultural moment is happening on Threads in the same way.”
Even so, the platform has been able to move the needle in surprising ways. In August, when the majority-Black city of Gary, Indiana, lost power for two weeks, causing a food shortage, among a long list of other safety concerns, Lewis says it was users on TikTok and Threads who first raised awareness about the historic blackout, which had received very little national media coverage until that point. “Then news outlets started paying attention.”
One of the most striking things Walcott has noticed about Threads as the spiritual successor to Black Twitter is how users are deliberately building and maintaining a narrative of its history. “People talk about events in Threads history like they did and do with Black Twitter,” she says. “When something happens that calls for comment, people turn to Threads for that discourse, just as they once turned to Twitter as the center of a hypernarrative web.”
User @missglowdigger certainly agrees. “Threads is single handedly thee best thing to happen to black social media,” she posted in September.
To which she was swiftly reminded: “Yes it is and I love the community BUT let us not get too comfortable … this is still a White Mans app.”

IN BRIEF: What we know about Flydubai plane emergency en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

MOSCOW, September 30. /TASS/. The Flydubai plane that transmitted a distress signal indicating a possible hijacking while in flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier on Wednesday has landed at Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk Airport, a source in a Middle Eastern air traffic control service told TASS.
The plane activated an emergency signal and was diverted to Saudi Arabia after a violent incident between the pilots, Israel’s Channel 12 reported.
TASS has compiled the key details about the emergency.
Circumstances behind the incident
- A Flydubai passenger plane en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv signaled an emergency on Wednesday morning, according to Channel 12.
- The pilots first transmitted code 7700, signaling a general emergency, before code 7500 was activated, indicating a possible hijacking, the TV channel said.
- Afterwards, contact with the flight was lost.
- There were approximately 180 passengers on board the plane, Channel 12 said. It was denied permission to land in Israel and was diverted to Saudi Arabia near the airspace of Jordan.
- Fighter jets were scrambled after the distress signal, the TV channel continued.
- The plane had reached the border of Jordan before it was diverted to Tabuk Airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia without actually entering Jordanian airspace, data from Flightradar24 indicated. No further updates about the flight were available afterwards.
- The plane landed at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia, a source in a Middle Eastern air traffic control service told TASS.
- Later, Flydubai confirmed to TASS that the flight had safely landed at Saudi Tabuk Airport.
- All passengers are safe, the airline told TASS.
- The possibility of a hijacking is now ruled out, even as the circumstances behind the incident have yet to be clarified, the TV channel said.
Response
- Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu convened an emergency meeting with Defense Minister Israel Katz and Transport Minister Miri Regev in the wake of the emergency, Channel 12 said.
- The situation is under control, and measures will be taken to return the Israeli passengers on board the flight home, Netanyahu’s office said.
- Flydubai has informed Israeli authorities that a backup plane will soon be sent from the UAE to bring the Israeli passengers home from the kingdom following the incident en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv, Ynet reported.
- Flydubai is cooperating with the relevant authorities after the incident, the airline told TASS.

Latvia's pro-Ukraine prime minister leads in poll ahead of Saturday election

Unknown Publisher

Latvia's pro-Ukraine prime minister leads in poll ahead of Saturday election
RIGA, Sept 30 - Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' centrist United List is expected to win the largest share of seats in Saturday's parliamentary election but is unlikely to secure an outright majority and will need to cobble together a coalition.
Security concerns and cost of living issues have dominated the election agenda in Latvia, a NATO and European Union member state which borders Russia and is home to a significant Russian-speaking minority.
The latest SKDS/LSM opinion poll indicates that seven of the 14 parties contesting the election have a chance of winning more than 5% of votes cast and thus enter the 100-seat parliament.
Kulbergs presides over a broad coalition with New Unity, National Alliance and the Greens and Farmers' Union, formed after Evika Silina's government collapsed over its handling of Ukrainian military drones entering Latvia's airspace, a consequence of the war between Russia and Ukraine.
But in a sign of public disenchantment with politics, one third of those polled said they were either undecided or did not intend to vote, making the final outcome uncertain.
A high proportion of non-voters and of ballots cast for parties that fail to clear the 5% threshold means the parties that do enter parliament will ultimately receive a larger share of seats than the poll figures imply.
The following parties are seen as having the best chance of winning seats in the October 3 election, according to a September 4 to 16 poll by SKDS/LSM:
UNITED LIST (14.4%)
The centrist grouping of smaller parties was an also-ran in the 2022 election, and a junior coalition partner in 2022-2023. Its popularity soared in polls after backbencher Kulbergs was appointed prime minister in May this year.
A former racing driver with a hawkish stance towards Russia and a strong supporter of Ukraine, Kulbergs has a good chance of staying in power, polls show.
SOVEREIGN POWER & ALLIANCE OF YOUNG LATVIANS (9.4%)
This centre-left group was established in 2022 by politicians who were expelled from another party for refusing to condemn Russia's invasion of Ukraine. It seeks to attract the ethnic Russian minority vote.
LATVIA FIRST (9.2%)
The founder and leader of the centre-right Latvia First, veteran populist tycoon Ainars Slesers, has had business ties with Russian oligarchs. He is courting Russian-speaking voters by recruiting ethnic Russian politicians to his party and promising a more conciliatory approach toward the largest minority.
PROGRESSIVES (6.2%)
This left-leaning party is backed largely by young, socially progressive voters, founded in 2017. It was part of the government coalition until May after winning seats in 2022.
NATIONAL ALLIANCE (5.6%)
A nationalist party founded in 2010, it campaigns on a promise to protect family and traditional values. It was part of the ruling coalitions from 2019 to 2023 and joined Kulbergs' coalition this year. It promotes a hardline approach towards Russia and Latvia's Russian minority.
GREENS AND FARMERS' UNION (4.8%)
A coalition of conservative groups, it has been part of the current governing coalition since 2023.
NEW UNITY (4.3%)
The centre-right party won the election in 2022 and held the prime minister's post until May 2026, when Silina's government collapsed. It is at risk of winning no seats. REUTERS

Taiwan’s Chief Telecom partners with Google to mitigate subsea cable damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:28:14 UTC
19:28:14 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s Chief Telecom has partnered with Google Cloud to launch a service designed to mitigate the impact of subsea cable damage by providing alternative international data transmission routes for financial institutions, government agencies, and other critical industries.
Chief Telecom said Wednesday that its Multi-Route Protection Service combines its international submarine cable network with Google Cloud’s Cross-Site Interconnect (CSI) technology. The company said the system can automatically reroute data within milliseconds if a cable fails and offers a service-level agreement guaranteeing 99.95% availability.
Chief Telecom Chair Shao Hung-chia (邵泓嘉) said frequent cable disruptions in waters around Taiwan have highlighted the risks of relying on a single communications route. Chief Telecom President Liu Yao-yuan (劉耀元) said the service supports financial cybersecurity requirements, including network redundancy, business continuity plan testing, zero-trust security, supply-chain risk management, and AI data security.
Financial institutions can use the service to maintain transaction processing, accounting systems, and cross-border clearing networks during cable outages. Government agencies can also use it to maintain international communications and back up critical public databases across multiple locations.
Google Cloud Taiwan Deputy General Manager Chang Yu-chang (張裕昌) said growing demand for AI computing and large-scale data transfers, combined with the risk of cable disruptions, has increased the need for resilient communications infrastructure. He said Google Cloud’s global private network backbone will support secure, high-speed international data transmission.
Chief Telecom plans to expand the service to high-tech manufacturers and multinational health care providers while increasing bandwidth capacity. The company also plans to deepen cooperation with Google Cloud in international dedicated connections, multicloud connectivity, zero-trust security, and edge computing.
The launch comes amid broader concerns over subsea cable security, with a report identifying three undersea cable systems being built to connect Taiwan with the US as particularly vulnerable to potential Chinese gray-zone operations. Taiwan has experienced an average of seven to eight undersea cable disruptions per year in its surrounding waters over the past four years, with anchor dragging accounting for roughly 38% of incidents.

British police ask prosecutors to consider manslaughter charges over 2017 Grenfell fire

British police ask prosecutors to consider manslaughter charges over 2017 Grenfell fire
LONDON – British police said on Sept 30 they had asked prosecutors to consider charges including corporate manslaughter and gross negligence manslaughter against dozens of people over the 2017 Grenfell Tower fire which killed 72 people.
The Metropolitan Police said they had submitted their full case files to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) for charging decisions, which the CPS had committed to making before the 10th anniversary of the disaster in June 2027.
The force said it had also asked the CPS to consider health and safety offences, fraud and fraud-related offences and misconduct in public office as part of its investigation into Britain's deadliest fire since World War II.
Case files relating to 54 people and 20 companies and organisations have been sent, after investigators examined the role of more than 15,000 people and 700 organisations.
Police said they had gathered 165 million electronic files, taken 14,700 statements and collected more than 27,000 exhibits during what they described as one of the most complex criminal investigations ever undertaken in Britain.
A 2024 public inquiry concluded the disaster was the result of decades of failures by government, regulators and companies involved in Grenfell Tower's refurbishment. REUTERS

The Swiss economy is likely to grow faster than expected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:26:00 UTC
19:26:00 KST

The Swiss economy is likely to grow faster than expected
Economists at the KOF Institute at ETH Zurich have significantly raised their growth forecast for the Swiss economy for 2026. They are also more optimistic about the coming year. However, uncertainty remains high.
Gross domestic product (GDP) is expected to rise by 1.9% this year, excluding international sporting events, as economists announced on Wednesday. Back in the summer, they had initially expected growth of just 0.8%. The KOF Institute now forecasts growth of 1.7% for 2027 (previously 1.5%) and 1.7% for 2028 as well.
“Despite the pressures caused by US tariff policy and higher energy prices, the global economy has so far proved resilient,” the report states. The Swiss economy, too, performed significantly more robustly than expected in the first half of 2026. The strong second quarter was a particular surprise.
At the same time, the national accounts have been revised upwards, according to the data, and thus paint a “significantly more favourable picture” of recent developments. Nevertheless, uncertainties remain high due to the situation in the Middle East, US tariff policy and rising bond yields.
Rising employment expected
The labour market presents a mixed picture. A more positive assessment emerges from the revised data and the surprisingly strong second quarter. Consequently, the KOF Institute now expects job growth of 1.5% in 2026, having previously forecast just 0.5% in the summer.
On the other hand, however, unemployment remains high. According to the economists, part of the recent rise in unemployment could therefore be “structural in nature”. One factor is the increased use of AI. According to the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO definition), the annual average unemployment rate is expected to be 3.1% cent in both 2026 and 2027.

Ex-Pakistan SSG commando, highly trained LeT terrorist, Pahalgam mastermind: Who was Hashim Moosa; killed in J&amp;K encounter

Hashim Moosa (right) killed in an encounter in Jammu and Kashmir’s Budgam district
NEW DELHI: Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) terrorist Mohammad Asif alias Hashim Moosa, wanted for his alleged role in the 2025 Pahalgam terror attack, was killed in an encounter with security forces in Jammu and Kashmir's Budgam district on Wednesday.Moosa was killed during a joint operation by the Indian Army, Jammu and Kashmir Police and the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) in the Korag area of Yousmarg. His body was later recovered from the general area of Palmaidan along with war-like stores, according to the Army's Chinar Corps.Moosa's killing has brought renewed focus on the background of the LeT terrorist, who security agencies had identified as one of the key suspects in the Pahalgam attack and linked to other terror attacks in Jammu and Kashmir.
Who was Hashim Moosa?
Moosa was a Pakistani LeT terrorist wanted in connection with the April 22, 2025 Pahalgam terror attack, in which 26 people were killed.Former Jammu and Kashmir DGP S.P. Vaid on Wednesday described Moosa as a highly trained terrorist and alleged that his footprints had surfaced in several attacks in Jammu and Kashmir, including attacks in the Poonch region and the Pahalgam attack.Vaid said Moosa was considered the mastermind of the Pahalgam attack and described him as a Pakistani national and a commando-trained terrorist specialising in jungle warfare and guerrilla operations.
Is Hashim Moosa an ex-SSG commando?
One of the key aspects of Moosa's background now being examined is his alleged connection with Pakistan's military.News agency ANI also quotes security agency sources stating that Moosa had served as a para-commando in Pakistan's Special Service Group (SSG) where he held the rank of Havildar. Following his retirement from the SSG in 2023, he joined the terrorist outfit Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) and infiltrated into India.Vaid described Moosa as a highly trained commando specialising in ambushes and guerrilla-style attacks. He alleged that Moosa's footprints had been seen in attacks in Poonch, DKG, Bhimber Gali, the Gulmarg attack and the Reasi attack on pilgrims.The alleged SSG connection could shed further light on Moosa's training and his role within the LeT network, but the military background remains a matter of investigation.ALSO READ: 'Save Democracy March' announced: INDIA bloc projects unity amid SIR row, targets PM Modi, Amit Shah
What attacks is Moosa linked to?
The Pahalgam attack took place on April 22, 2025, when terrorists targeted tourists at Baisaran Valley. Twenty-six people were killed in the attack.According to the ANI report, Moosa was named as one of the key suspects in the attack and had been wanted by Jammu and Kashmir Police.The National Investigation Agency later chargesheeted seven accused in the case, including Pakistan-based LeT and The Resistance Front (TRF), which it charged as a legal entity for allegedly planning, facilitating and executing the attack.The NIA's 1,597-page chargesheet also named Pakistani handler Sajid Jatt as an accused.The agency had said its investigation detailed the Pakistan-based conspiracy and the roles of those accused in the attack.
How was Moosa killed?
Security forces launched Operation Korag in the Yousmarg area of Budgam following specific intelligence inputs about terrorist movement.During the joint search operation, troops observed suspicious activity and challenged the terrorists. The terrorists opened fire, triggering an encounter in which Moosa was killed.The operation involved the Indian Army, Jammu and Kashmir Police and the CRPF.The search operation continued after the encounter, with security personnel checking the surrounding area for any additional terrorist presence. During the search, Moosa's body was recovered from Palmaidan along with war-like stores, according to the Chinar Corps.
Pahalgam victim's daughter calls it ‘one chapter’ closed
The killing also drew a reaction from Asavari Jagdale, daughter of Pahalgam attack victim Santosh Jagdale.Speaking to ANI, Jagdale thanked the Army and intelligence agencies for the operation and recalled the April 22 attack in which 26 people were killed.She described the killing as a step towards justice but said the legal process must continue until the case reaches its final verdict.“I would say that one chapter of the case has ended,” she said.
Jagdale also urged security agencies to continue operations against terrorists and said the 26 families would consider the case fully closed only after completion of the legal proceedings.

European police forces drop Russian software firm following POLITICO probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:23:59 UTC
19:23:59 KST

European police forces drop Russian software firm following POLITICO probe
Authorities in at least three countries are suspending their use of Oxygen Forensics after allegations emerged about the company’s secret Russian owners.
BRUSSELS —Multiple European law-enforcement agencies will stop using Oxygen Forensics, a digital surveillance company accused of concealing its Russian ownership, after POLITICO revealed its spying services had been sold to police forces across the continent.
Romania's National Anticorruption Directorate (DNA) told POLITICO it has initiated procedures to terminate its contract with Oxygen Forensic’s "detective" software used to extract and analyze data from mobile phones in criminal investigations.
The agency's most recent annual license was purchased through a Romanian distributor on Aug. 27 for €13,000.
Advertisement
"In light of information recently made public about the company that produces this software, the National Anticorruption Directorate has initiated the necessary procedures to terminate the contractual obligations regarding this product," DNA said.
The agency added that its checks had found no evidence that data extracted or processed using Oxygen had been compromised.
Elsewhere, Latvia's State Police has suspended its use of the software while it assesses whether to continue using the technology. The police explained that officers had previously relied on it to extract and analyze electronic data, but stressed that its use "was under strict control," meaning it was isolated from employees' working computers.
In Britain, London's Metropolitan Police has paused its use of Oxygen and launched a full review. The National Police Chiefs' Council has also encouraged forces using the technology to conduct their own assessments.
Concealing control
The moves follow POLITICO reporting this week that the Virginia-based Oxygen, which the U.S. Justice Department has accused of being secretly owned and operated from Russia, participated in EU-backed digital-evidence projects and later supplied technology to European law enforcement agencies.
Other European countries that had purchased the services of Oxygen Forensics include Germany, Spain, Italy, Poland and Hungary. Police agencies from those countries have not responded to POLITICO's request for comment.
Advertisement
U.S. prosecutors allege that Oxygen's Russian owners concealed their control of the company after Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and that its technology continued to be developed and managed in Russia. The Justice Department does not allege that the software contained malicious code or was used to access customers' systems or data without authorization.
Following the revelations, political pressure is mounting. Belgian Green MEP Saskia Bricmont is calling on European governments to immediately stop using Oxygen and investigate whether sensitive information could have been exposed to Russia.
"It is particularly ironic to see that the EU has an extremely security-driven agenda while handing over the keys of its security to American and Russian companies," said Bricmont, the Greens' coordinator on Parliament's PEGA spyware inquiry.
She also criticized the European Commission for failing to act on earlier warnings from civil society about Oxygen's alleged Russian links.
A Commission spokesperson had noted earlier this week that the company was not a member of either EU-backed consortium, EVIDENCE and INSPECTr, and received no European Union funding. Still, Oxygen currently remains listed on the websites of both projects. On its own now-defunct website, Oxygen Forensics had also listed the European Commission as a client.

Minecraft hotel to open near London as gaming-themed travel goes up a level
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:22:01 UTC
19:22:01 KST

A new 69-room Minecraft hotel is coming to the UK, joining a growing crop of properties designed to let fans step inside their favourite games.
Minecraft is no longer just a game you can play – soon, it’ll be somewhere you can actually stay.
A new Minecraft World Hotel is set to open near London in 2027, giving fans the chance to sleep inside the world of the best-selling video game of all time.
The 69-room hotel will form part of Chessington World of Adventures’ new Minecraft-themed area, complete with a Nether-inspired roller coaster, immersive dining and plenty of pixelated details.
The announcement comes just as the trend for gaming-themed travel is at its peak.
Gaming-themed travel is becoming more than just a trip to a theme park or a visit to a gaming convention. Now more than ever, the hospitality industry is increasingly turning familiar game worlds into places travellers can actually stay, sleep and explore.
In Japan, MIMARU operates Pokémon-themed rooms across 10 hotels in Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka, with interiors packed with Pokémon characters and details including themed bathrooms and kitchens.
This month, the concept went a step further, as a Poké Ball-shaped hotel has opened in Hokkaido as part of a Pokémon Sleep collaboration. The three-metre-wide pod sits beside a lake and is designed to recreate the experience of sleeping inside a real Poké Ball.
Closer to home, Spain's Magic World Resort in Oropesa del Mar has a dedicated Magic Games Hotel, with gaming-themed rooms, consoles, VR and AR areas, tournaments and a video game museum.
Now, the UK is getting involved. Located within Chessington World of Adventures’ new Minecraft World-themed area, the new hotel with 69 themed rooms – 20 upscale rooms and 49 standard options – will open its doors on an as-yet-unannounced date next year.
The hotel will also feature an immersive restaurant and potion bar, and interactive elements, and iconic creatures, colours and biomes – or regions – from the game will come to life, offering guests a chance to experience living inside the magical world.
Cube-like trees and animals will bring the Overworld to life in the reception area, while lifts inspired by Nether portals and corridors that look like mine shafts will draw guests in.
The rooms themselves will house the blocks, objects, creatures, textures, and colours characteristic of Minecraft in the real world.
Fans of Minecraft will also be able to head next door to the theme park to try out Escape the Nether, the world's first Minecraft roller coaster, which will boast both indoor and outdoor sections.
The ride will be located in Minecraft World, which will further bring the game to life, offering family attractions, dining areas and themed shops, as well as immersive Minecraft experiences.
“We’ve thought about every detail, from the scale of the blocks to how to bring the creatures and biomes to life in the real world,” said Filip Keatly Thoms, Creative Director of Minecraft Parks and Experiences at Mojang Studios, which is behind the project.
“Our goal is to create an authentic Minecraft experience and allow visitors to experience the game in a completely new way.”

Chinese-run Brussels networking club raises intelligence concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:21:06 UTC
19:21:06 KST

The Global CEOs Dinner Club brings business leaders and political figures together at high-level events in Brussels and is now seeking to expand into France.
A Chinese-run networking club targeting business and political elites in Brussels bears the hallmarks of an influence and intelligence-gathering operation, a Western intelligence source has told Euronews.
The Global CEOs Dinner Club, which is now expanding to France, operates in a manner associated with China’s United Front, a Communist Party network used to promote Beijing’s interests abroad, according to the source.
The assessment comes as Belgium has recently been at the centre of several espionage probes launched by its Federal Prosecutor’s Office, including investigations into a former Chinese-Belgian researcher in the semiconductor industry and a Canadian national of Chinese origin working at NATO in Mons.
Yifei Yang, who runs the Global CEOs Dinner Club, studied in China and at a private European institute in Nice, France, before launching the organisation in Brussels last March.
French media outlet La Lettre reported last week that her activities had put at least one Western intelligence service on alert.
Asked by Euronews, one intelligence source would not confirm whether their service was investigating the case. However, after Yang’s activities were described to them, the source said they matched the modus operandi of China’s United Front.
The United Front is a decades-old Communist Party network known for promoting China’s interests through organisations and individuals abroad, while some of its activities have also been linked to the gathering of information for Chinese intelligence services.
Contacted by Euronews, Yang denied that China was behind the club, insisting that “we are neutral” and adding that its objective was to have an “impact on society” and “build sustainable business”.
Approached through Linkedin
Since last March, the Global CEOs Dinner Club has brought together business figures as well as people connected to Belgian and EU politics at events covering topics ranging from sustainability and diversity to technology and artificial intelligence.
On Wednesday evening, it was due to host a dinner entitled “China–EU EV Futures: Competition, Collaboration, and the Road Ahead” at a luxury Brussels hotel, bringing together business leaders, policymakers, technology executives and investors.
Guests included Hui Zhang, vice-president of Chinese electric vehicle maker NIO; Melanie Schuttenberg, a board member of Danish car components company TAJCO; and Ole Gerkensmeyer, CSO of Netherlands-based chipmaker Nexperia.
Yang said the organisation currently has 20 members from countries including France, Belgium, Denmark, Japan, China and Singapore. Annual membership costs €2,400 for individuals and €5,000 for companies.
“It is not all about business,” Yang told Euronews, describing the organisation as “value-driven”. She said 10% of its revenue goes to NGOs and charities.
The club’s website shows that speakers in recent months have included representatives from Belgian semiconductor research centre imec and Le Refuge, a shelter for LGBTQIA+ young adults.
Belgian senator Marie-Claire Mvumbi, who spoke at one of the club’s events on diversity, told Euronews that Yang had approached her through LinkedIn.
Mvumbi said between 30 and 50 people attended the event, which included discussions about diversity in business recruitment. “The event gave a good impression,” she said.
Yang says she hopes to expand the organisation into France and recently sent invitations for an event for female executives scheduled to take place in November at the luxury Le Meurice hotel in Paris.
