How will Burnham’s national care service work – and how will it be funded?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:17:03 UTC
19:17:03 KST

The prime minister said he wanted to create a care system that would give people ‘peace of mind’. Photograph: Sean Prior/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe prime minister said he wanted to create a care system that would give people ‘peace of mind’. Photograph: Sean Prior/AlamyExplainerHow will Burnham’s national care service work – and how will it be funded?PM has revealed more details about a proposed shake-up of adult social care – including a broad timetableAndy Burnham’s Labour conference speech gave a little more detail on how he intends to take forward what he said at the start of his premiership would be his signature social policy ambition: an overhaul of adult social care.What will Labour’s social care overhaul look like?Burnham was clear about the ambitious scale of his care vision – this was not simply change, it was about creating a whole new service: a “landmark policy, as significant as the creation of the NHS itself”. It would be a national care service, operating on NHS principles: free at the point of use and “where everyone contributes and everyone is covered”.It was more emphatic than his last social care speech in June, when he said a national care service “could be fully fledged [NHS-style] or lesser options or something in between”. After the speech, however, the prime minister’s aides clarified the new service would not resemble what most people would think of as an NHS-style system; it would be based on the Scottish adult social care approach: free personal care, with individuals paying for accommodation (“bed and board”) costs.Are we any clearer as to how it will be paid for?Experts say an NHS-style care system would be expensive – possibly the most expensive option – costing about £18bn a year. A Scotland-style system would cost an extra £7.5bn a year, according to the Health Foundation. Assessing the costs depends what services are included in the offer and how the cost is divided between individuals and the state. Burnham said it would be fully funded from within the public spending envelope. He said savings from scrapping the state pension triple lock, starting in the next parliament, would be funnelled into the care service.On its own this would not be enough to fully fund a universal NHS-style care service, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies. It seems probable that raising taxes will be part of the mix. Burnham said a care service would lead to NHS savings by reducing pressures on hospitals. This may free up £2bn a year in the long term, according to the King’s Fund thinktank. But it added that such figures should be treated with caution.Will individuals have to contribute to the cost of care?Under a Scottish-style system, yes. Burnham said a future care system would give people “peace of mind” that it would protect their “homes and their savings” if they needed care in later life.13:38Burnham’s triple lock gamble | Politics WeeklyThis clearly suggests people who do not qualify for state care support will not have their assets wiped out if they require expensive long-term care – though the prime minister did not spell out how this risk would be nullified. It seems probable, however, that individual’s assets would be better protected from care costs under a national care service, rather than being entirely insulated. Even the Danish care system – one of the world’s most generous according to the Nuffield Trust thinktank – expects individuals to pay for care home accommodation costs.Who will provide the care?Burnham was careful in his speech to thank care workers, recognising them as underpaid and undervalued. He apologised to them, saying politicians had let them down for too long. This was not just burnishing his pro-worker credentials but recognising that without a better paid, upskilled work force, providing a high-quality national care service is impossible.It also paves the way for a government U-turn on overseas care worker visas. He said care services would be “for people, not profit” which may be tricky given that the bulk of adult social care provision is privately provided, although it may signal a crackdown on “obscene” care profits.When will a national care service happen?Burnham set out a broad schedule. Louise Casey will produce her independent report on social care in 2027, setting out what a national care service could look like and how it could be paid for.A national care service would be in the next Labour manifesto, and were the party elected it would be introduced in the next parliament. It is a more urgent timetable than his predecessor, Keir Starmer, had envisaged, but some in the creaking care sector will worry it is not soon enough.How much of a political risk is there?Burnham admitted in his speech that he “may pay a political price” on social care but said he was prepared to do so in order to do what he thought was right. It seems unlikely that the Conservatives or Reform UK would support a national care service.But Burnham clearly believes he has the time to “lay the ground” and win over a public that typically has little understanding of the care system or the sometimes catastrophic risks to their family finances under the current system. A Budapest appeals court reduced the jail term on Wednesday for a German non-binary anti-fascist activist's sentence for participating in anti-Nazi violence from eight to seven years.
Maja T., 25, was found guilty in February of involvement in assaults in 2023 ahead of the annual "Day of Honour" in Budapest commemorating Nazi soldiers.
Prosecutors said the activist was part of a multinational far-left group that attacked nine people on the streets, including German and Polish citizens, whom they identified as far-right extremists.
The Budapest-Capital Regional Court of Appeal reclassified Maja T.'s role from co-perpetrator to accomplice, shortening the sentence by one year, the presiding judge said.
The ruling is final and not subject to further appeal.
The defendant entered the court led by guards on a leash amid faint cheers of "Maja" from the audience.
Ahead of the ruling, supporters put up banners near the court entrance demanding the release of the activist, amid a heavy police presence on surrounding streets.
Campaigners, including some German politicians, had questioned whether Maja T. would receive a fair trial, as the groups linked to the attacks were designated terrorist organisations last year by the former nationalist government of Viktor Orbán.
Multiple people accused of participating in the 2023 attacks have been put on trial in Hungary and Germany, with one receiving a five-year prison sentence in Germany.
Italy and France have refused to surrender two suspects to Hungary with courts in both countries citing the risk of "inhumane treatment" in prison.
In 2024, the German Constitutional Court found that Maja T. ran the risk of discriminatory treatment in Hungary as a non-binary person and should not be extradited.
But the ruling came hours too late to stop the handover.
Last year, Maja T. staged a 40-day hunger strike to protest the "unlawful handover" and "inhumane" prison conditions, an allegation denied by Hungary's prison service.

PARIS, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- France's consumer price index (CPI) is expected to surge 3.0 percent year on year in September, up from 2.4 percent in August, according to preliminary data released on Wednesday by the National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (INSEE).
In its provisional estimate, INSEE said the rise in inflation was mainly driven by higher energy prices, particularly petroleum products and gas.
Service price inflation was expected to edge up, partly because the seasonal declines in accommodation and transport service prices would be less pronounced than in September 2025. Food prices were also projected to accelerate, particularly fresh produce, while the year-on-year decline in manufactured goods prices was expected to ease. Tobacco prices were projected to increase at the same pace as in August.
On a monthly basis, consumer prices were expected to fall 0.3 percent in September, following a 0.7 percent increase in August. The decline was mainly attributed to the seasonal decrease in service prices after the summer period, particularly transport and accommodation services.
The decline was expected to be offset by rising energy prices, mainly petroleum products and gas. Food prices were projected to increase for the third consecutive month, while tobacco prices were expected to remain stable from August.
The Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices, used for comparisons across the eurozone, was expected to climb 3.4 percent year on year in September, up from 2.6 percent in August. ■

China's express delivery volume exceeds 150 bln packages by late September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:13:12 CST
19:13:12 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- China's 2026 express delivery volume had surpassed 150 billion packages as of Sept. 29, hitting the mark 12 days earlier than in 2025, the State Post Bureau (SPB) said on Wednesday.
The accelerated pace of parcel flows underscores the resilience and dynamism of China's economy, analysts noted.
China's express delivery sector has grown at a double-digit pace for several years, consistently setting new records. In 2025, the country handled 198.95 billion packages, up 13.6 percent year on year.
This momentum has carried into 2026. Given a steady economy shifting toward higher-quality growth, more consumer demand has been unleashed, providing a solid foundation for the expansion of the express delivery market.
China remains the world's second-largest consumer market and it continues to grow. In the first eight months of this year, total retail sales of goods and services, a major indicator of the country's consumption strength, rose 2.5 percent year on year, with online retail sales of goods and services reaching nearly 13.48 trillion yuan (about 2 trillion U.S. dollars), up 4.6 percent.
Fu Linghui, a spokesperson for the National Bureau of Statistics, said the consumer market is not only growing in scale but is also undergoing transformation, which is mainly reflected in the gradual shift of consumption structure and consumption patterns.
Smart and green products have emerged as bright spots, with wearables and high energy-efficiency home appliances among the fastest-growing categories. Meanwhile, livestream e-commerce and on-demand retail are playing an increasingly prominent role in driving the market's transformation.
The steady growth in express delivery this year also reflects a deeper shift in how China's logistics networks operate. Courier companies are no longer just delivering packages, but embedding themselves into the production lines of manufacturers to boost goods flows via industrial supply chains.
In Ningbo, east China's Zhejiang Province, courier companies have taken over spare parts warehouse operations for manufacturers including Geely Auto, linking directly into their production systems. Notably, the city has developed 282 such collaborative projects between logistics firms and manufacturers, with related business accounting for almost half of Ningbo's total express delivery volume.
Express delivery embedded deep in production chains is becoming a new engine for industrial upgrading, analysts said.
Moreover, China has expanded delivery networks into remote areas to improve public services and unlock consumer spending in the countryside.
Villagers in Changwangchuan, Fangxian County, central China's Hubei Province, once rode electric bikes more than 10 kilometers just to collect parcels, a trek made necessary by the county's mountainous terrain. A new pilot program is changing this, with authorities this year having moved to extend doorstep delivery services to rural communities in central and western China.
This program had covered nearly 3,000 villages including Changwangchuan by the end of August. For residents there, the change has made daily life markedly easier and given local express delivery volumes a measurable boost.
The express delivery industry serves as both a vital artery for the broader economy and an essential lifeline for everyday life, the SPB said, noting that as pro-consumption policies take hold and new growth drivers emerge, the sector is poised to play an even greater role in bolstering high-quality economic development. ■

An open letter to the honorable people of the United States of America
TEHRAN=The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has issued a letter addressed to the American people, outlining its views on recent developments and Iran-U.S. relations. The full text of the letter follows:
In the Name of God,
the All-Merciful, the Ever-Merciful 
   
 An Open Letter to the Honorable People of the United States of America
Indeed, God does not alter the affairs of a people until they alter their own affairs.
—The Holy Qur’an 13:11
To the honorable people of the United States of America—the scholars, the students, and the members of the media,
We begin this letter by saluting the noble souls of God’s greatest prophets—Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad, may His peace and blessings be upon them all.
Seven months ago, the U.S. military, launched a war, in violation of international law, against Iran by attacking an elementary school in Minab, murdering 168 innocent schoolchildren along with their teachers. Simultaneously, they attacked the offices of the Supreme Leader of the Islamic Republic of Iran, Imam Sayyid Ali Khamenei, martyring His Eminence and several members of his family, including his 14-month-old granddaughter.
To date, the war has claimed the lives of more than 3600 Iranians, the vast majority of them civilians, including 400 children. Eight universities, three hospitals, and eight schools have been bombed. Yet, despite the unprecedented acts of cruelty and violence suffered by the Iranian nation during this war, the United States and Israel have suffered a crushing defeat, while the Islamic Republic of Iran has achieved a decisive victory.
As the first casualty of the endless wars waged by the U.S. government has without exception been the truth, with the American people perpetually receiving the greatest harm as the result of the U.S. government’s campaign of deception, we wish to highlight some of the facts that are being withheld from the American public. After all, it is the American taxpayers who will have to bear the cost of America’s unjust wars, and so they deserve to know the truth.
Let’s start by considering a few questions. Why has Iran prevailed in its conflict with the U.S., whose military enjoys an annual budget one hundred times that of Iran’s armed forces and possesses a stockpile of weapons and munitions that dwarfs what is available to the Iranian military by an enormously lopsided ratio?
Why do Iranians chant, “Death to America”? Are they hostile to the American people?
The U.S. government claims that the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC) is a terrorist organization. Is this true?
Why have the vast and extensive efforts of the U.S. government over the past nearly five decades to restore its domination over the Iranian people continually failed?
Why is the U.S., if the present course continues, rapidly heading toward decline?
How will the present war between Iran and the U.S. unfold and end? How can the American people protect themselves from the consequences of their government’s unjust aggression and shield themselves against the worst harms of the impending collapse?
These are the questions we wish to consider in this letter. We will be candid and forthright. Should you doubt the honesty in the answers we provide to the foregoing questions, you can make a short trip to any part of Iran you wish—possibly even the Strait of Hormuz—and personally ascertain for yourselves the verity of our assertions.
Why Is Iran the Victor?
Why has Iran won the war despite having a defense budget only one percent that of the United States? Perhaps, the first reaction you may have to this question is credulity: “On what grounds do you claim that Iran is the victor?” To determine which side has won the war, we need to see which side has achieved its objectives. American and Israeli officials initially stated that the objectives of their assault on Iran were regime change and partition of Iran. However, after failing to achieve either objective, they started blurting out a changing list of objectives, announcing a new objective with every passing week, and this betrayed the absence of a coherent strategy in prosecuting the war.
The U.S. President has expressed thirteen different targets for the war once the failure of the first two objectives was clear: Iran’s unconditional surrender; seizing Kharg Island and taking control of Iran’s oil; a ground invasion and occupation of Iranian territory; the destruction of all industrial infrastructure; the destruction of all energy infrastructure and returning Iran to the Stone Age; the destruction of Iranian civilization; launching Operation Freedom and taking control of the Strait of Hormuz; debilitating Iran’s economy by preventing all exports and imports; destroying Iran’s nuclear industry; destroying Iran’s missile and drone capabilities; annexing the Strait of Hormuz to U.S. territory and imposing a 20 percent toll; destroying Iran’s air defenses and taking control of Iranian airspace; and ending Iran’s support for Islamic resistance groups in the region.
The United States and Israel expended thousands of bombs and missiles, striking government and residential buildings, dozens of less-advanced and lower-tier weapons-manufacturing facilities, and a number of decommissioned military installations. Yet, aside from damaging several buildings tied to Iran’s nuclear industry and a limited number of air-defense sites, they failed to achieve any of their declared objectives.
Now, nearly seven months into this unjust war, the U.S. military—the largest and costliest military in the history of the world—has scored no wins, and that is all the more humiliating when we consider that it fought the war in collaboration with the Israeli military, which claims to be the
Concrete Evidence of Iran’s Victory
Iran’s victory is not limited to thwarting the enemy in achieving its objectives. The armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran decimated American bases located in the Persian Gulf region. Iranian strikes neutralized a significant number of advanced American military assets—including more than 200 expensive strategic drones, 12 tanker and transport aircraft, 30 fighter jets, at least one AWACS aircraft, dozens of helicopters, and dozens of high-value radar and air-defense batteries—and substantially degraded the infrastructure at U.S. bases in the region, destroying more than 350 primary facilities and structures, while the operational capability of 18 U.S. bases was reduced to nearly zero. Arguably, however, the greatest consequence of this war has been the damage it has done to America’s reputation as the world’s sole superpower and the irreparable and gaping cracks it has created in the edifice of U.S. global hegemony. The U.S. can no longer boast of its status as the world’s hegemon. The points we will cover below make this truth sufficiently clear.
More important than all of these, however, are Iran’s remarkable strategic wins.
- The gains the US government had made in its decades-long cognitive and cultural warfare in weakening Iran’s national and religious values and alienating Iranian youth from their cultural heritage were largely neutralized. America’s heinous attack on the Minab Elementary School and its grave miscalculation in aligning itself with the deeply unpopular Israeli regime and martyring the Supreme Leader made the criminal nature of America’s ruling class tangible to the younger generations of Iranians. By strengthening the determination of the Iranian youth to resist and oppose the tyranny of global hegemony, the American-Israeli war reinvigorated the Islamic Republic and ensured that it will thrive for at least several decades to come.
- The media campaign by the U.S. government designed to mislead the American public by stoking hatred against Iran has considerably weakened. Contrary to the best efforts of the U.S. government, Iran’s standing in American public opinion is actually improving, while Americans’ awareness of—and hostility toward—the principal force behind the war, Israel, is visibly increasing.

- Not only did Iran retain its missile and drone stockpiles largely intact; it ramped up production of weapons and munitions and, amazingly, developed more advanced iterations even as the war raged on.
- With each passing day of the war, Iran’s air-defense capabilities became more mature and powerful. Iran successfully shot down the most advanced American and Israeli aircraft, including some equipped with the latest stealth technology.
- At the beginning of the war, people in the streets of Manama and Doha witnessed American military personnel fleeing their bases. They were reportedly running around in their underwear, looking for places to hide. In the following days and weeks, official U.S. military statements announced the withdrawal of successively larger numbers of American forces from the region. American bases have come to resemble ghost towns, and there is now serious discussion in the corridors of American power about the dissolution of these bases.

- Trump did not and could not destroy the Iranian civilization, which now, thanks to the war, shines brighter than ever before. Iran has gained a far higher standing in the eyes of people around the world. The cultural influence and standing of Iranian civilization are far greater than they were before the war. To verify this, you can travel to a few countries and pose as an Iranian, and the admiring welcome you will receive from people of different faith and nationalities will speak volumes.

This will in time serve as a powerful source of change, leading to seismic transformation in how people exercise their will to self-determination and stand up to oppression and injustice.
- The illegal move by the U.S. military to halt the free movement of ships in the Indian Ocean—which the Trump administration misleadingly calls “a naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz”—has in fact led to greater growth in Iran’s domestic production and a sharp boost in its economic engagement with its neighbors.
- The martyrdom of Imam Sayyid Ali Khamenei has shone a spotlight on the concept of wilayat al-faqih (“the rule of the jurisprudent”) in the global arena, introducing the reality of this religiopolitical office to the world and debunking the lies that try to falsely portray wilayat al-faqih as a form of dictatorship. The historic funeral procession of the martyred Supreme Leader, which saw the participation of over 40 million mourners in Iran and Iraq, served as a globally reverberating vindication of the superior moral and political legitimacy of the system of governance at the heart of the Islamic Republic of Iran. Though painful, the martyrdom of Iran’s Supreme Leader did not lead, as American and Israeli politicians had hoped, to the disintegration of the Islamic Republic, and this was a testament to the resilience of a political system rooted in the will of the people.
The martyrdom of Imam Khamenei demonstrated to the whole world that wilayat al-faqih is not an ordinary political office but is one founded on mutual affection and trust between a leader and his people. Wilayat al-faqih is the embodiment of all godly virtues in the political sphere. It was wilayat al-faqih that empowered Iran to stand firm against diabolical powers with incomparably greater firepower by enabling the country’s armed forces to fight successfully using only domestically
produced weapons and munitions; that succeeded in winning the hearts of people around the world despite overwhelming hostility from thousands of media outlets with virtually limitless resources affiliated with the world’s superpower; that ensured that not a single store shelf has been left empty in spite of 47 years of “crippling” sanctions; that facilitated the fastest rate of scientific progress in the world in the face of the most severe scientific and technological constraints; and that makes a leader who is capable of ruling for 37 years while maintaining a lifestyle resembling that of the lower echelons of the society and refraining from allocating any special privileges to himself or his loved ones.
The Main Factors Underpinning Iran’s Victory
The main factor behind Iran’s victory is not drones and missiles. The United States and Israel possess more powerful and more advanced missiles and drones, plus a variety of other forms of weaponry that Iran lacks. The principal reason for Iran’s victory is threefold:
- The Quran’s superior doctrine and worldview
- The Iranian nation’s faith in and unity around the tenets of the Quran
- The competent and righteous leadership of a man of God
- The Quran’s Superior Doctrine and Worldview
Iran is the birthplace of the most controversial and, at the same time, the most misunderstood political revolution in the modern era—a revolution founded on the Quran and the teachings of the most noble of divine guides. In a word, the underlying foundation of the Islamic Revolution of Iran is the Quran’s divinely revealed doctrine and worldview.
Honesty, liberty, equality, social equity, respect for the rights of others, political discernment, compassion, and the priority of human values over personal desires are among the basic social principles that stem from this Quranic doctrine.
The Quran proclaims all human beings brothers and sisters and servants of God. No race, color, ethnicity, or nation is given pride of place in Islam. Humanity is of one cloth, and an assault on a single human being is an assault on all of humanity.
The political philosophy upon which the intellectual foundations of the Islamic Republic are founded is informed by the central elements of the divine mandate of God’s prophets, especially an unqualified trust in God and an uncompromising struggle for justice. The Quran teaches us to neither oppress nor succumb to oppression.
In this light, one of the principal missions pursued by the leadership of the Islamic Republic has been a tireless effort to strengthen Iran, empowering it to protect and promote the Quranic values enshrined in Iran’s constitution and safeguard the integrity and autonomy of the nation against the unrelenting attacks of the forces of evil. Iran’s leaders feel personally obligated to fight ignorance and injustice and defend truth, justice, and freedom.
To surrender to the enemies of truth and justice would mean nothing less than resigning ourselves to the evisceration of the sacred values of the Quran and is therefore out of the question. It is this resolute determination to fight for truth and justice that constitutes the inexhaustible source of the
power that fuels the Iranian nation in its decades-long refusal to surrender, despite the persistent hostility of the world’s mightiest powers.
- The Iranian Nation’s Faith in and Unity around the Tenets of the Quran
The incredible spirit of resistance and struggle that permeates the nation of Iran stems from a deep faith in the Quran. The Iranian psyche is fundamentally shaped by real historical role models who personified the tenets of the Quran—towering figures of godliness who are revered in Iran as legends worthy of devotion and imitation. Any nation that looks up to these role models will undoubtedly be invincible.
Therefore, if you want to know the secret to Iran’s invincibility, you must read about the tragedy of Karbala and come to know Imam Husayn (peace be upon him), the archetypal exemplification of standing up for justice and welcoming death with open arms in defense of the truth. He bravely fought a fierce battle despite his thirst, continuing to fight even after witnessing all his men slain before his eyes, and never succumbing to the forces of evil.
If you want to understand why the Iranians are not intimidated by the extreme brutality of the American war machine after witnessing the mass killing of the children of Minab Elementary School and the assassination of their leader, you must read the tragedy of Karbala. Read how Imam Husayn’s adolescent nephew, Abdullah, rushed to protect his uncle with his bare hands and died in his uncle’s arms. Read how Imam Husayn’s infant son, Ali al-Asghar, had his throat rent by an enemy arrow, dying in his father’s embrace.
You wonder why Iranians—the people and the leadership alike—do not yield to the alluring promises the U.S. government dangles before them? Find the secret in the story of Hazrat Abbas, Imam Husayn’s devoted and loyal brother who, the day before Ashura, rebuffed a proposal by an enemy commander to give him amnesty if he agreed to leave his brother and who on the Day of Ashura lost both arms and then his life attempting to deliver some water to the parched children of his brother’s camp.
You wish to know how, against all odds, the Iranian nation has successfully withstood 47 years of severe economic hardship and endless plots and is not only surviving but is thriving? UK-France ‘one in one out’ deal to expire on Thursday, say sources
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:09:48 UTC
19:09:48 KST

The UK government’s “one in one out” deal with France, which was supposed to help deter small boat arrivals, is expected to expire on Thursday, government sources have said.
Negotiations to extend the deal have stalled over French demands for a Europe-wide deal instead, and a reluctance to scale up the numbers of people exchanged between the two countries.
Flights that remove people who have been already detained under the scheme will continue, but they are expected to end within weeks.
A UK government source confirmed that the expectation was that the deal would be formally drawn to a close on Thursday.
“We would like to see the deal continue. But it’s not the end of the world if it doesn’t because it never got to the scale where it would have been a proper deterrent to people coming to the UK in small boats,” the source said.
The French interior ministry told French media on Wednesday: “We are discussing with the British the terms of exiting the agreement.”
Negotiations in Paris over how best to tie up the deal are continuing between Home Office staff and their French counterparts.
More than 1,400 people who have arrived in the UK via small boats have been sent back to France under the deal. As of the end of June 2026, 1,117 people with links to the UK had been sent to the UK from France.
The deal had been set to expire in April but was extended to 1 October to help counter the anticipated increase in attempted crossings during the summer.
The scheme was announced by Keir Starmer and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, in July 2025 and the first flights took off in September that year.
At the time, Starmer described the deal as “groundbreaking” because it would help to deter the number of people crossing the Channel illegally.
“There is no silver bullet here, but with a united effort, new tactics and a new level of intent, we can finally turn the tables,” he said.
Many of the detainees deported to France under the deal have become homeless in the French capital.
Others have returned to the camps around Calais and Dunkirk, and some have made the Channel crossing back to the UK.
In June, France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, lauded the scheme as a potential deterrent but said France was not prepared to go it alone with Britain.
“According to information from the UN high commissioner for refugees, word of the scheme is beginning to spread, which is prompting a number of migrants to abandon their plans to make the crossing,” Nuñez told a parliamentary commission.
“The value of this scheme is therefore clear. Nevertheless, we consider that France should not bear the burden alone and that it would be better to incorporate it into an agreement between the EU and the UK.
“I have therefore already made it clear to my counterpart that this pilot agreement, which we signed in August 2025, was not intended to be extended beyond 1 October 2026.”
An EU-wide returns deal known as the Dublin agreement existed before the UK left the EU. Attempts to continue the returns deal post-Brexit have been rejected by EU leaders.
Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, disclosed to MPs this month that the deal cost about £56,000 for every person sent back to France.
She dismissed suggestions that an EU-wide system would be a “silver bullet” for the Channel crisis. She said: “It is a real mistake to think that that pact is the future. And if we were in that, this problem would go away, because I promise you it would not.”
She added that the government’s scheme had struggled to scale up to larger numbers of returns and it had been “operationally difficult” to increase removals because of constraints such as detention space.
“It’s not been without its challenges. Obviously, the numbers are still relatively small,” she said.
Between January and 27 September, 19,135 people crossed the Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 42% on the same period the previous year.

Talks to break the deadlock over the controversial Drumcree parade will continue with the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, on Wednesday as nationalist protesters declare the prospect of mediation with unionists “dead in the water”.
The nationalist Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition has at the same time launched a fresh legal challenge to reimpose the almost 30-year ban on the Orange Order marching down their road, mounting fresh arguments that the Parades Commission has “materially misdirected itself”.
Breandán Mac Cionnaith, the leader of the group, said his goal was “no parade, just no parade, that is what our community wants, that’s what nearly 4,000 people living in our community wants … that’s our mandate”.
After his meeting with Bryant on Tuesday he told residents at the local pastoral centre that mediation was “dead in the water”.
Members of the Portadown Orange Order left Drumcree church, the start point for the parade, overnight on Tuesday for the first time since the dispute over their march erupted on Sunday morning.
They made a further attempt to walk the route down the nationalist Garvaghy Road just after 10pm on Tuesday night, accompanied by the DUP MP Carla Lockhart, and returned to the church on Wednesday morning having vowed to remain there until the police allowed them to complete the march.
The Orange Order Portadown district master, Nigel Dawson, said he had “constructive” talks after his meeting with the Northern Ireland secretary over the possibility of a mediator on Tuesday night. “We look forward to the law being applied to the parade,” he added.
The two groups will have further talks with Bryant on Wednesday and the Garvaghy Road court hearing is scheduled for Friday, but there is little sign of a breakthrough.
The high court at a special sitting on Saturday heard that the documentation around the decision to allow the parade showed past risk assessments of disorder in relation to parade requests but none looking to the future.
Under a heading on a form listing any risk of public disorder or damage to property, the commission’s information was “directed to the past”, their barrister, Denise Kiley KC, told the judge. “Nowhere do we see any assessment of future risk,” she said adding that it was “not clear who had provided this template” to the Parades Commission.
Efforts to end the dispute, which has heightened sectarian divisions in Northern Ireland, were also brought to Dublin where Sinn Féin’s leader, Mary Lou McDonald, and the Northern Ireland first minister, Michelle O’Neill, met Micheál Martin and Simon Harris, the leader and deputy leader of the Irish government.
Martin has described the Parades Commission decision to allow the parade march down Garvaghy Road for the first time in almost 30 years as “incomprehensible and wrong”.
McDonald said people were “gobsmacked” by the decision as it had “the potential to drag that community and society back to a very bad and very bleak days”.
O’Neill has faced criticism from unionists after she and senior colleagues were among a large crowd that blockaded the road in the predominantly nationalist Garvaghy Road area on Sunday to prevent the parade from passing the route.
Under parading laws in Northern Ireland, protests must be notified to, and approved by, the Parades Commission adjudication body and the gathering at the head of Garvaghy Road, that continues on Wednesday, has not yet been notified. However, police have not tried to break up the protest, fearing it could trigger violence.
Bertie Ahern, the former taoiseach and co-architect of the 1998 peace deal that led to republicans and loyalists laying down their arms after 30 years of violence, warned of the dangers of returning to the “tribal past”.

Morocco appoints first female prime minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:05:30 UTC
19:05:30 KST

Morocco appoints first female prime minister
Moroccan King Mohammed VI has appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as the North African nation’s first female prime minister following her party’s victory in last week’s parliamentary elections, the royal palace has announced.
The monarch tasked the 50-year-old lawyer, who served as housing minister and mayor of Marrakech, with forming a new government, according to a statement released on Tuesday.
Mansouri’s liberal-centrist Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) won 97 of the lower house’s 395 seats in the September 23 vote and must form a coalition to secure a governing majority. She becomes the second woman to serve as prime minister in an Arab country, after Tunisia’s Najla Bouden, who held the post from 2021 to 2023.
PAM overtook outgoing Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch’s National Rally of Independents, which won 66 seats, followed by Istiqlal with 65, according to results published by the Interior Ministry on September 25. Turnout fell to about 38%, compared with around 50% in 2021, official figures showed.
PAM was part of Akhannouch’s outgoing coalition government alongside his National Rally of Independents and Istiqlal. During the campaign, PAM ruled out renewing the alliance with Akhannouch’s party, but Mansouri later said she had no “red lines” for coalition talks.
The appointment comes amid an investigation into suspected electoral fraud in the northern port city of Tangier. Prosecutors said a polling-station deputy allegedly removed ballots with the station head’s help before returning them to two polling stations in coordination with other suspects. Investigators found that ink on the seized ballots differed from that used at the polling stations.
Tangier Mayor Mounir Limouri, a PAM official, was placed in police custody on Monday as part of the investigation, multiple outlets reported, citing judicial sources. Five other suspects were held in pretrial detention. Limouri denied any connection to the alleged tampering.
PAM said it would take disciplinary action against members if investigators established their involvement.
Founded in 2008 by Fouad Ali El Himma, a close adviser and childhood friend of the king, PAM emerged as a secular-leaning rival to the Islamist Justice and Development Party.
The constitution requires the king to appoint the premier from the party that wins the most parliamentary seats but the monarch retains sweeping powers over defense and foreign policy.
The new government will oversee Morocco’s preparations to co-host the 2030 FIFA World Cup with Spain and Portugal. Spending on the tournament partly fueled deadly youth-led protests last year, with demonstrators demanding jobs and better healthcare and education. During the election campaign, parties offered jobs and affordable housing to attract young voters after July’s mass border crossing into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Reuters reported.
Mansouri has pledged a program offering “concrete and realistic solutions to citizens’ concerns,” acknowledging high expectations, particularly among young people.

Israel's Lobby: How pro-Israel groups influence US politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:03:53 UTC
19:03:53 KST

Breadcrumb
Who shapes America's Israel policy? Eli Clifton and Ian Lustick examine the power of Israel's Lobby
In late August, Jonathan Pollard, a former US Navy intelligence analyst convicted of spying for Israel in the mid-1980s and subsequently jailed for 30 years, announced that he would run in Israel's forthcoming October election as a member of the new right-wing Israel First party.
Pollard's return to public life follows his release from parole restrictions in November 2020. A month later, the US-born former spy left Newark Airport for Tel Aviv aboard a Boeing 737 owned by Israeli-American billionaire Miriam Adelson, who is said to be worth $33.9 billion and has donated more than $200 million to the Republican Party.
On arrival at Ben Gurion Airport, Pollard received a hero's welcome and was greeted by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Israel's Lobby, published in mid-August, opens with this episode. Written by two Jewish Americans — investigative journalist Eli Clifton and political scientist Ian Lustick — the book uses Pollard's return to Israel as an entry point into a much broader examination of the networks of money, politics and influence that shape US policy towards Israel.
The authors note that Pollard has since used his celebrity status to promote and champion one of Israel's most controversial politicians, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
"Pollard is a great entry point to begin a conversation about the influence of Israel's lobby in the United States," Clifton tells The New Arab.
"A spy being lifted out of the country on a billionaire's private jet sounds like a scene from a John le Carré novel. But this took place with open transparency, in the full glare of the world’s media."
So how does Israel — a country with a population of just 10 million and a landmass that is roughly the same size as the state of New Jersey — exercise so much influence in Washington?
This question is addressed several times in Israel's Lobby. Both authors define the lobby as "a loose coalition of individuals and organisations that actively work to shape US foreign policy in a pro-Israel direction."
They also stress the lobby's historical ties to Christian evangelicals and other streams within American politics, including US trade unions and the neoconservative movement.
"The Israel lobby has access to our campaign finance system here in America," Clifton, also a cofounder of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, explains.
"Other countries do not have that. Israel's lobby, by contrast, has an enormous influence over our politicians. This has serious implications for both our national security and our elections in the United States," he adds.
"Money is a major source of the lobby's influence and power,” Lustick tells The New Arab.
He recently experienced the lobby's censoring tactics firsthand while promoting his co-authored book in a church in suburban Philadelphia to a group called The Jewish Justice Collective.
"The church was subjected to demands from lobby representatives requesting the event be cancelled," Lustick explains.
"The lobby is constantly trying to prevent truthful views about Israel from being discussed in public."
A wave of repression
Both authors say the lobby's ascendancy in recent years has produced "a wave of repression and a constriction in the free-speech rights of Americans, unmatched since the anti-communist hysteria of the McCarthy period" in the 1950s.
They speak about some of the lobby's most powerful organisations, including the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).
In the 2022 tax year, AIPAC's primary fundraising vehicle, the American Israel Education Foundation (AIEF), had revenues of approximately $69.9 million and held assets worth over $186 million.
Today, most of AIPAC's resources are directed to influencing the voting patterns of US senators and members of Congress on matters pertaining to Israel.
The topics vary. In July 2023, for instance, Congress passed a resolution pledging continuing aid for Israel and declaring that the country was "neither racist nor an apartheid state."
"AIPAC is unquestionably the most successful foreign policy lobby in the United States," says Lustick, who served as the State Department's expert on Israel-Palestine affairs during the Carter administration (1977 to 1981).
The Anti-Defamation League (ADL) is another powerful group within Israel’s Lobby.
The organisation was founded in New York more than a century ago to combat anti-semitism and other forms of racism and bigotry.
Today, however, the ADL has redefined definitions of anti-semitism, say Clifton and Lustick. Presently, any criticism of the Israeli military or the Israeli government is being documented by the ADL as "anti-semitic incidents."
Both authors cite numerous examples of this information being used to shape public discourse about Israel across the United States.
In May 2023, the Biden White House issued the US National Strategy to Counter Antisemitism. This relied almost solely on data produced in the ADL annual audits, both authors explain.
In September 2025, the Trump administration did the same. On the latter occasion, the State Department organised a briefing for journalists on anti-semitism in America that relied entirely on the ADL's 2024 audit.
Clifton and Lustick claim these numbers were manipulated to dramatise a torrent of anti-semitism. The session opened with ADL statistics showing 9,354 antisemitic incidents in 2024, "the highest on record."
Citing ADL sources, the journalists were told that Jews "account for 2 percent of the US population but were the target of nearly 70 percent of religiously motivated hate crimes in 2024."
"The ADL is presently measuring things that were not previously defined as anti-semitism, such as protests against Israel," says Lustick.
"This is a shameless way to promote the false idea that a tsunami of anti-semitism has erupted in the United States because of October 7."
An anti-semitism witch hunt
Both authors describe this manipulation of statistics as "an anti-semitism witch hunt."
They say Israel's lobby uses "false, hoax-like, strange accusations of anti-semitism to try to suppress all serious debate about Israel."
Clifton and Lustick cite The Adam and Gila Milstein Family Foundation as a "prime example of the anti-semitism witch-hunt that Israel's lobby is presently engaged in."
In August 2025, the Milstein Family Foundation widely distributed an article originally published by Adam Milstein in The Jerusalem Post that attacked Zohran Mamdani, then a leading candidate in New York City's mayoral election.
The article referred to Mamdani as an "Islamo-leftist" who "refuses to acknowledge Israel's right to exist as a Jewish state," and as aligned with "anti-semitic incitement and terror."
Lustick describes The Milstein Family Foundation as "aggressive and far right."
He tells The New Arab, "They try to smear all critics of Israeli policy in American politics as anti-semites. They also find ways to suppress free discussion on university campuses across the United States about American policy in the Middle East."
Clifton and Lustick claim "the overwhelming majority of Jewish Americans do not prioritise Israel's well-being or interests."
And yet, Israel's lobby is consistently attempting to tell another story.
"The day-to-day messaging coming out from the social media channels of organisations like AIPAC and ADL essentially endorses the anti-semitic trope that all Jewish Americans, and all Jews, hold dual loyalties to Israel," Clifton explains. "But it's simply not true."
Lustick claims there has been a noticeable change at the "grassroots level" of Jewish institutions across the United States whenever the topic of Israel is raised, especially inside synagogues in recent years.
"Previously, it was to be expected that on major Jewish holidays there were lots of social, educational and cultural events that celebrated Israel," the political scientist explains.
"But now, in most non-Orthodox American synagogues, talking about Israel has become a very delicate and controversial issue. The rabbis avoid the topic. It's just too hot to handle, and there are now too many divisions within the Jewish community."
JP O’Malley is a cultural critic, journalist and writer. He writes regularly about books, geopolitics, history, film, arts and culture for various publications, including the Sunday Independent, The Irish Examiner, The New World, The Age and New Eastern Europe

‘He is, in simple terms, a man who destroys everything.’
In this entertaining short documentary from the Czech filmmaker Maja Penčič, truth and myth collide in the figure of Zoran, a former resident of a block of flats in Belgrade, Serbia, whose larger-than-life personality and convoluted biography have left behind accounts that can’t be reconciled. Throughout, a rotating cast of acquaintances characterise him as everything from ‘warm’, ‘intelligent’ and ‘exceptional’ to someone who ‘never feels shame’ to, quite simply, ‘a dick’. The home-video aesthetic lends the proceedings an intimacy and a faintly surreal quality that evokes the imperfections of memory. The film never settles on a single version of events, instead watching the details rearrange themselves around a few fixed points, until what is left is less a man than a cautionary tale.

Insects play critical role in ecosystems beyond just providing food, new research shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:00:24 UTC
19:00:24 KST

For many vertebrates, insects are more than a food source. As “little things that run the world”, insects provide critical functions such as protection, sanitation and shelter across ecosystems, according to a new study.
The study, published in Nature Reviews Biodiversity on Wednesday, sheds light on the various ways insects support vertebrates, ranging from birds and bats to reptiles, amphibians and mammals.
Nearly three-quarters of terrestrial and freshwater vertebrates eat invertebrates, according to the paper, with insects frequently making up a large portion of their diets.
However, their relationship goes beyond predator and prey.
The paper, led by Eliza Grames, an assistant professor of biological sciences at Binghamton University, State University of New York, documents dozens of less obvious ways vertebrates depend on the estimated 14m to 30m species of insects found around the world.
Chimpanzees, for example, have been recorded applying insects to treat open wounds, while more than 200 bird species use ants to remove parasites or maintain feathers. Other birds build nests near wasps or other stinging insects, in a likely effort to gain protection from predators.
Insects also provide shelter, the study notes. Birds, reptiles and mammals use termite mounds and ant nests, which can offer stable temperatures and humidity. White-throated round-eared bats, for instance, excavate cavities in termite mounds and use them as roosts.
Other insects act as sanitation workers. Dung beetles remove animal waste and can make dung drier and more aerated, in turn reducing parasite survival, according to the study. Meanwhile, moths living in some bird nests consume feces, feathers and other debris. The review notes that insects have performed similar functions for millions of years, citing evidence of beetles feeding on feathers in dinosaur nests during the Cretaceous period, which lasted from around 145m to 66m years ago.
Other insect-vertebrate relationships include beetles removing ectoparasites from rodents and snakes feeding on firefly larvae to obtain defensive toxins, as well as antbirds using live crickets during courtship.
Mutually beneficial relationships also occur across the insect-vertebrate realm, with sloths relying on moths to deposit nitrogen in their fur and spur algal growth, which the sloths then eat. Sloths then descend from trees once a month to defecate on the ground, providing substrate in which moths lay eggs.
According to the study, such overlooked relationships could become increasingly important as insect communities evolve. Although the extent of insect declines varies across habitats and regions, the review says that “widespread and considerable disruption” of insect communities is “inevitable” as land use changes.
Grames called the study a “wake-up call for anyone concerned about the biodiversity crisis”.
“We need to pay attention to insects and make their conservation a top priority, because conserving insects will benefit all the other species that rely on them. Insects are so much more than just food for vertebrates like birds and bats – they create and maintain habitat, provide protection to other species, help with reducing diseases and removing waste, and so many other ecosystem services that we, and other species, rely on. They really are the unsung heroes of the natural world,” she added.
Grames also pointed to the critical role insects play in addressing the climate crisis, saying: “About 12% of the global carbon forest stock is leaf litter and dead wood, and insects are responsible for decomposing about 30% of it. So even though insects are small, their activities influence global carbon cycles. Insects also help with forest regeneration by dispersing seeds into areas where other large-seed dispersers have disappeared. Pollination and seed dispersal, both of which are done by insects, are two of the biggest limitations in forest regeneration.”
The consequences for vertebrates remain difficult to predict due to the lack of studies on insect-vertebrate relationships. The study notes that “the lack of systematic descriptions of trophic and non-trophic interactions, hampered by an ongoing decline of natural history research”, makes it difficult to understand how changes in insect biodiversity affect other species.
For co-author Chris Elphick, a professor of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Connecticut, understanding the diverse roles that insects play across vertebrates’ lives is essential for designing effective conservation strategies.
“If you want to have vertebrates, then you’ve got to be thinking about insect conservation, and we don’t do that nearly enough,” Elphick said.

From mass raids to quiet crackdown: a timeline of Trump’s strategic ICE pivot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:00:24 UTC
19:00:24 KST

ICE agents take custody of a man at the Ventura county government center in California on 27 July 2026. Photograph: Blake Fagan/AFP/Getty Images
From mass raids to quiet crackdown: a timeline of Trump’s strategic ICE pivot
After switching tactics, federal agents are detaining and deporting record numbers of people from the US
When federal agents fatally shot the US citizen protesters Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minneapolis in January during the nation’s largest immigration-enforcement operation ever, it marked a turning point for the second Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign.
Donald Trump in his second term had sparked outrage and huge protests with federal immigration officers descending en masse on one Democratic-run city after another in what some leaders called militarized “invasions”. Los Angeles, Chicago, Charlotte, New Orleans, then Minneapolis saw lines of masked and armored officers swaggering into town to conduct street arrests, ambushes of day workers waiting in Home Depot car parks for hire, and neighborhood sweeps. Adults and kids were whisked off to detention and protests met with aggressive deployment of chemical spray, teargas, fists and batons. The killings in Minneapolis were the culmination of what appeared to many to be a federal shock force increasingly out of control while being defended by federal leaders – and public opinion broadly turned against this violence.
There was a change of personnel and the administration flagged a switch to a “quieter” approach to immigration enforcement. But while large-scale theatrics on the streets waned, less visible enforcement is no less aggressive on the ground today and continues to ramp up in multiple ways. Here’s a timeline of how the administration’s anti-immigration campaign has evolved in recent months as Trump races to remove millions of people from the US.
2026
26 JanuaryMinneapolis madness leads to a changing of the guard
Greg Bovino and other federal agents in Minneapolis on 13 January 2026, a week after the fatal shooting of Renee Good by an ICE agent. Photograph: Seth Herald/Reuters
Two days after Pretti was killed by Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers and 19 days after Good had been shot dead by an ICE agent, the US president announces that his “border czar”, Tom Homan, an immigration-enforcement veteran, will deploy to Minnesota, while Gregory Bovino, the border patrol’s confrontational commander-at-large, suddenly stands aside. Bovino was the face and voice on the street of federal aggression; Good, Pretti and ICE watchers were the symbols of the resistance; and Liam Ramos was the image of collateral harm.
The then secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, Kristi Noem, at a press conference in New York on 8 January 2026. Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPA
Kristi Noem becomes the first cabinet secretary fired during the second Trump administration when she loses her leading role at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Noem was tainted with scandals over her close relationship with senior adviser Cory Lewandowski and a $220m advertising campaign starring herself and using a firm with connections to her former staffer. She had also repeated a false narrative that Pretti “brandished” a gun at federal agents and called Renee Good a domestic terrorist. Weeks later, Bovino retires and tells the New York Times: “I wish I’d caught even more illegal aliens.”
Markwayne Mullin at a confirmation hearing for the position of secretary of homeland security in Washington DC on 18 March 2026. Photograph: Will Oliver/EPA
Markwayne Mullin, formerly a first-term senator from Oklahoma with “mixed martial arts fighter” on his résumé, is confirmed by the US Senate as the new DHS secretary. At his confirmation hearing, he says about immigration-enforcement officials: “My goal in six months is that we’re not in the lead story every single day.”
Oklahoma police shackle a man at the McIntosh county criminal justice center during an operation with ICE on 3 September 2026. Photograph: Nick Oxford for the Washington Post via Getty Images
The DHS, in its own words, has “supercharged” efforts to work with local and state law enforcement via so-called 287(g) agreements. From January 2025 these deals mushroomed nationwide, from 142 to 2,315, with most modeled as a “taskforce”. They deputize local and state officials to actively enforce immigration laws during regular police work – normally under federal jurisdiction. By spring, this collaboration acts as a force multiplier for arrests, while allowing federal agents to avoid the spotlight as local cops take on more frontline duties. It also makes immigration enforcement harder to spot for protesters.
A family leaves after an immigration court hearing at the Jacob K Javits federal building on 31 July 2026 in New York City. Photograph: Michael M Santiago/Getty Images
Attorneys and researchers start noticing immigration court dates being scheduled for unusually large groups of people with little to no notice, in what they say is a tactic to increase the number of deportation orders without ever giving someone an individualized hearing. These mass court dates balloon in June, affecting many thousands of people. Many more applicants struggle to find attorneys and prepare their now-rushed cases. Children are a particular target, too, being rushed through hearings as due process is undermined.
After the longest DHS shutdown ever, congressional Republicans use a partisan process to provide the department with an additional $70bn, funding it for the rest of Trump’s second term in a move that critics say undermines accountability. All told, the DHS has received roughly a quarter of a trillion dollars in funding since Trump retook the White House.
Demonstrators rally as the supreme court prepares to hear oral arguments in Mullin v Doe on 29 April 2026. Photograph: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty Images
The US supreme court rules in favor of the Trump administration’s bid to strip temporary protected status (TPS) from hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians who were legally in the US and protected from deportation. When Trump took office, 17 countries had active TPS designations, which allowed roughly 1.3 million people who were already in the US to live and work legally while it was unsafe for them to return home. But under his second administration, more than a million people who are generally law-abiding and often contribute economically to essential industries with significant labor shortages have already lost their TPS permissions. Now they face imminent risk of deportation to countries as dangerous as Afghanistan, Haiti and South Sudan if they do not qualify or cannot afford to apply for another immigration status. “We’re going after them right now,” Mullin has said of Haitians. “These individuals can either self-deport or we’ll arrest you and send you back. It’s that simple.”
Federal agents patrol the John F Kennedy international airport in New York on 23 March 2026. Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPA
ICE significantly increases its collaboration with the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) to detain immigrants with expired visas – many of whom have pending applications for green cards, asylum, employment-based visas, etc – at airports, sometimes near public spaces such as ticket counters or gates. However, the vast majority of arrests continue to occur where they are far less easy to detect and record on camera, such as in people’s homes and cars.
ICE agents detain an individual exiting his immigration court hearing at the Jacob K Javits federal building on 16 July 2026 in New York City. Photograph: Michael M Santiago/Getty Images
The DHS reports 49,571 immigration arrests, which sets a new monthly record for the second Trump administration, after previously doing so in June. A majority of the people arrested in July have no criminal history. Detentions also increase, with about 66,000 people in custody by the end of the month. Preliminary reports suggest immigration arrests in August have kept pace with July.
A memorial for Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who was fatally shot by ICE agents, on 14 July 2026 in Biddeford, Maine. Photograph: Ryan Murphy/Getty Images
An ICE officer kills Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, 26, in Biddeford, Maine, during a vehicle stop in which Durán was not the intended target, making him the 11th person fatally shot by federal immigration officials both on and off duty during Trump’s second term. The shooting comes days after federal agents similarly killed another immigrant father, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, in Houston while he was driving his building crew to their job. The DHS briefly pauses most ICE traffic stops until Trump intervenes, posting online: “We CANNOT give up one of I.C.E.’s most important and effective Crime Fighting tools, THE TRAFFIC STOP!” In one 24-hour period, 13 to 14 July, three people die in ICE-involved incidents.
AugustEven more local cops do ICE’s bidding
Federal officials reach the milestone of 1,000 new287(g) agreements since 26 January, expanding collaborations with local law enforcement agencies at an even faster clip than during the second Trump administration’s first year in office.
AugustVisa applications
All visas for people applying to immigrate to the US are paused for an unknown amount of time while officials undergo training around the new “public charge” policies.
Markwayne Mullin announces the success of Operation Rotten Apple, in New York on 1 September 2026. Photograph: David Dee Delgado/Reuters
Mullin retroactively announces Operation Rotten Apple, which from 27 July to 29 August quietly rounded up nearly 2,200 immigrants across New York state. The operation is a case study in how aggressive immigration enforcement continues, including in Democratic-led “sanctuary” cities, without the previous theatrics.
A migrant child seeking asylum waits to be processed by the US border patrol in Yuma, Arizona, on 3 May 2022. Photograph: Nicolo Filippo Rosso/Bloomberg via Getty Images
On August 1 the federal government ends its contract providing more than 20,000 unaccompanied immigrant children with legal representation. At the same time, attorneys report that immigration judges are taking a “deport at all costs” approach to their young clients, who suddenly are not receiving the time they need for their pending applications to be adjudicated by other agencies before they are ordered removed from the US. Many of these kids qualify for a green card or other immigration status because they have been abused, abandoned, neglected, trafficked or otherwise severely mistreated, but their applications are often subject to backlogs and quotas that cause delays. In September, the Guardian reveals that Stephen Miller, White House deputy chief of staff, has been leading an unprecedented drive across several government departments to accelerate the removal of undocumented immigrant children from the US, using tactics that critics say are cruel and racist, and, in some cases, flout federal law.
Taken together, these policy changes are less showy but they have ramped up arrests, detentions and the number of people forced to leave the United States – and put millions more at immediate risk of the same. Many of these people have legal status or ongoing cases for winning or upgrading their legal status, or years of crime-free, honorable life in the US, but are being rounded up, often with little access to due process or attorneys who can help. This latest iteration of Trump’s mass deportation campaign is no longer defined by federal agents patrolling cities with smoke canisters in hand. It’s much more insidious but also more ruthless and effective – and it’s happening everywhere.

Bill Gates predicts AI will kill a billion people – but saying he’s been wrong before is quite the understatement | Arwa Mahdawi

The Bill Gates rehabilitation tour is in full swing. After having his carefully cultivated image tarnished by the revelation of his connection to Jeffrey Epstein, Gates lay low for a while. Now, however, the Microsoft co-founder is once again thrusting himself into the public consciousness, this time with a dire warning about AI. If left unchecked, AI could cause “a billion deaths”, Gates declared in an interview with NBC on Sunday.
Perhaps I should be terrified by this announcement from a man who, for all his sins, knows a thing or two about technology. But I’m sick of hearing about the hypothetical dangers of AI when the technology is being used to kill people today. Gates may not be directly involved in Microsoft any more, but, rather than making prophecies about the future, I’d love to hear what he thinks about the company’s role in the AI-enabled destruction of Gaza.
Another thing I’d like to hear Gates explain is why he reckons anyone should trust his judgment about anything, considering he met with Epstein on several occasions after being introduced to him in 2011. To be clear: that’s three years after the financier pleaded guilty to charges including solicitation of prostitution from a minor. Gates, who has not been accused of involvement in Epstein’s crimes, has said he recalled “being aware that Epstein had faced prior legal issues”, but didn’t understand the extent of them. Two minutes of Googling (or Binging) could have made it clear the man was bad news.
The oversight is particularly strange because Gates is obsessed with his public image. His team have a custom-size mannequin on which they test his outfits. The goal, per the Wall Street Journal, is “to depict someone calm and approachable, like Mister Rogers”. Not someone who cavorts with a sex offender.
Ignorance isn’t Gates’ only excuse. He has also said that Epstein “knew a lot of very rich people and [claimed he] could get them to give money to global health”. It seems the 17th richest man in the world didn’t know any wealthy people he could hit up for donations himself and, for the sake of the world’s health, had to lean on a dodgy financier whose funds were obtained in mysterious ways.
I’m not accusing Gates of anything nefarious. But, if we are to take his Epstein excuses at face value, I’m accusing him of being a fool. If we can’t trust his judgment about a man like Epstein, I’m not sure we should trust his proclamations about the future of humanity.
Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

‘Beyond priceless’: how a halt to dredging saved the seas of Scotland’s Summer Isles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:00:22 UTC
19:00:22 KST

Inside a bothy overlooking the Summer Isles, in the north-west of Scotland, the lilting tones of a traditional Gaelic duo fill a room full of musicians, storytellers, artists, local people and revellers, hung with fish-shaped lanterns and “Happy Birthday” signs.
It’s no ordinary birthday. The people in the small cabin have come together, on a windy night in Achiltibuie, a string of coastal hamlets and villages north of Ullapool, to celebrate an important milestone in the community’s history: a hard-won battle to protect their waters from the ravages of scallop dredging.
The coastline here, a metallic grey seen through the bothy’s windows, is dotted with beds of one of the UK’s most biodiverse and carbon-rich habitats, a 9,000-year-old pink seaweed called maerl, two of which are a mile long. This rare, fragile and threatened seaweed produces hard, chalky, coral-like skeletons that provide nurseries for scallops and fish.
Now, 10 years after local people, divers, activists and creel fishers ran a successful campaign to have scallop dredging banned by law in a 600 sq km (150,000 acre) zone now designated a marine protected area (MPA), they say they have already witnessed a dramatic revival of marine life. The transformation of a seabed damaged by decades of dredging has allowed the recovery of scallop populations and ended the fractious territorial battles between the industrial dredge fishing boats and the smaller, more sustainable creel boats, local people say.
The community rowing club and nearby tour operators report increased sightings of whales, porpoises and dolphins. A large spawning ground for herring, once plentiful here but since overfished, has been spotted nearby and in prawn and lobster creels, or pots, which are laid on the seabed.
Diyanne Ross, 65, the local artist who made the lanterns, is part of the Blue Hope Alliance (BHA), a coalition of groups using citizen science to protect marine ecosystems in the north-west Highlands. She says the community’s achievements in protecting underwater habitats was the “most amazing thing to happen to the Summer Isles. It is an archipelago that is made in heaven for breeding fish.”
As a child, Ross remembers going out to sea for “boxes” of haddock, ling, pollack and cod – before populations declined. But she has seen recent signs of recovery. “There is more variety of fish being caught here than before,” she says. – anglers are catching haddock and cod.”
Outside on the pier, a hardy angler on holiday from Glasgow who has braved the wind to catch what he can, is rewarded by three fresh mackerel.
The recovery of scallop stocks, says Alasdair Hughson, a scallop diver, Scottish Creel Fishermen’s Federation (SCFF) chair and one of the BHA’s founders, has been “massive” and the seabed transformation like “night to day”. A decade ago, a boat supplying hand-dived scallops to his company, Keltic Seafare, would spend just two weeks in the Summer Isles.
Hughson, whose firm supplies shellfish to UK restaurants, admits his business stands to gain from the dredge ban, but says hand-diving is more sustainable, a claim backed up by research from Open Seas. The marine conservation organisation found low-impact fishing methods, such as diving and creeling, are not only more sustainable than dredging or trawling but that more of the revenue generated stays in the local economy.
Now, the Donna Marie creel boat, skippered by Ullapool-based Gary Lewis, runs to the Summer Isles almost all year. Lewis, who used to have to travel farther, to Skye and the Western Isles, before the dredge ban, says: “It’s not just the catch that’s improved, but the general health of the seabed.”
Central to the weekend-long Maerl-Herring festival celebrations, which includes storytelling, artworks and film, is the public launch of a BHA report spanning a decade of citizen science studies.
Jason Hall-Spencer, a professor of marine biology at Cyprus University of Technology, who wrote the report, says it shows the dredge ban in Wester Ross’s MPA, set up to protect the slow-growing maerl habitats and other marine features, has done its job. It has “protected the maerl to a massive extent” he says.
Author of the Conservation Status of Maerl Habitats in north-west Scotland, partly funded by NatureScot, Hall-Spencer has carbon dated the maerl in the bay as 9,000 years old.
“If scallop dredgers had spent the last 10 years going up and down here, the habitat would be obliterated,” he says. A single pass of heavy towed gear such as that used by scallop dredgers can crush or bury up to 70% of maerl. “The seabed is now incredibly rich. Maerl is a very important habitat, chock full of bivalves which provide food for skates and rays.”
Peter Drake, 73, a retired prawn fisherman from Polbain, a hamlet that is part of Achiltibuie, was part of Sea Change Wester Ross, a campaign group supported by SCFF, which grew into BHA. “It’s good to remember what we have achieved here” says Drake. “There’s already an improvement in fish populations, but it will take time.”
Orfhlaith McDevitt, 25, who has lived here for two-and-a-half years and runs Coigach Community rowing club, says: “People from the club say they see more minke whales, dolphins and porpoises than they did 10 years ago.”
Years before Ocean, David Attenborough’s documentary, sparked outrage by showing footage of scallop dredgers bulldozing the seabed, causing damage that could be seen from space, Sea Change and the SCFF compiled a body of evidence of the devastation scallop dredgers were doing to fishing grounds and seabeds in Wester Ross.
The dossier was presented to Scottish ministers in parliament. In 2016, despite fierce opposition by the dredging lobby, scallop dredging was forbidden by law in the Wester Ross MPA, now the biggest protected area in the world for maerl. Prawn trawling is permitted in designated areas, while hand-diving for scallops and creel fishing by local boats under 150 gross tons, is also permitted.
The maerl’s three-dimensional structure allows high levels of oxygen, essential to scallops, and emits a chemical that attracts them.
But threats to the ecosystem remain: the BHA surveys, also highlighted damaged maerl in some locations – from illegal dredgers and from invasive algal growth that scientists believe could be caused by nutrients from salmon farms.
“We know that salmon farms put more nutrients into the water,” says Sara Nason, a journalist and documentary maker who founded Sea Change, which later became the BHA and organised the Maerl-Herring festival.
The BHA has now launched a three-year project with more than £153,000 of support from the National Lottery Heritage Fund and additional funding from members of the North & West District Salmon Fishery Board, to continue its work.
Elsehere, the battle for Scotland’s sea rages on. The Scottish government, which was criticised in June by the independent watchdog Environmental Standards Scotland for not fulfilling its legal duty to restore and protect the seabed, has launched a public consultation on improving protections for marine habitats and species inside and outside the MPA network.
Theresa Ross, who runs Achiltibuie Stores for the community of about 250 people living along this stretch of coastline, says the MPA is “fully supported” by local people as it “ensures fishing is more sustainable”.
But for a rural coastal community, where the sea supports livelihoods and few jobs exist, there are competing concerns, she says.
“There are more people working on the fish farm here than fishermen,” says Ross, whose husband is one of about six fishers in the village, while her son is one of 10 working on the farms.
“I support the status quo. But the fish farms are full-time jobs, guaranteed employment and well paid,” she says. “They are not weather dependent, like fishing.”
Nevertheless, Nason is one of many who are delighted that the end to dredging has been such a success, describing the protection of the maerl beds as “beyond priceless … We’ve achieved recovery of the whole ecosystem.”
