Prosecco pratfalls and coffee catastrophes: Neets are missing out on formative first-job experiences | Isabel Brooks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:00:23 UTC
18:00:23 KST

Everyone remembers their first job. More often than not, it’s in the service industry. I started at 14, pouring drinks, serving food and standing with an ice-cream tray. This is where I learned how to handle mistakes, such as dropping an entire tray of prosecco glasses, or spraying hot coffee all over a bridesmaid because I plunged the cafetiere with too much gusto. I learned how to talk to angry strangers, and what it means to have a bad manager. I learned that the customer is always right, except when you’re talking to chefs, who will throw ham at your head if you tell them that. All in all, I did 10 years of restaurant, bar, pub and cafe work, from the age of 14 to 24, and I largely attribute the formation of my character to that decade of work.
But this kind of character-building experience is under threat. Job postings for temporary work in hospitality in the UK were down by 25% year-on-year between 2024 and 2025, with 22,369 fewer unique postings. Hospitality leaders have blamed rising wage and tax costs for their inability to hire new starters, and young people are bearing the brunt: nearly 1 million young people are not in education, employment or training (Neet), despite 84% of these seeking work. The Recruitment and Employment Confederation has explicitly warned that the industry relies heavily on 16- to 24-year-olds, so the impact will be on teenagers seeking their first job. In Manchester, Nell’s Pizza advertised 10 part-time roles for people between the ages of 14 and 18, and received about 2,000 applications.
But it’s not just the career prospects and the financial setbacks that are at stake here – young people will miss out on a more fundamental process of maturing. For many British teenagers, myself included, those summer jobs pulling pints are an apprenticeship in adulthood.
Working in hospitality as a teenager was how I grew up. If I hadn’t managed to get these jobs, I would never have had to apologise to an irate customer for the large snail that was crawling on the rim of their bowl (“our salad is just really fresh, sorry”), nor peel paralytic pensioners off the floor and deposit them into taxis. These may not immediately seem like transferable skills, but learning how to conduct myself in difficult encounters with people, in person, regardless of how random the specific instance, is a skill I am grateful to have – especially when people only a little younger than me are being served social, life and job opportunities that are increasingly remote and online.
I also think I would have less character, whatever “character” is, without this experience. In fact, the word comes from the Greek verb to scratch, cut or engrave, only becoming the term for “a sum of qualities that define a person” in the 1600s. Both still apply; the scratches we get along the way define us, or, in the words of Friedrich Nietzsche and Kelly Clarkson: what doesn’t kill you makes you stronger.
Could Britain’s Neet problem partly be one of young people losing access to the kind of first jobs that used to get them on to the career ladder? Of today’s 24-year-old Neets, 45% have never had a job, which suggests the salient issue is getting a foot in the door. The Neet crisis should be renamed the “teenagers can’t get bar work” crisis, because which 16-year-old or university student is getting a job that isn’t in hospitality?
It’s a mistake not to prioritise this industry, which, given the encroachment of AI, holds Britain’s future job prospects – more so than manufacturing or high-productivity service sectors. We need to stop seeing these jobs as merely stepping stones to better-paying, more prestigious jobs, but instead as a crucial part of the economy and, importantly, our lives. I am struck by how the rhetoric around Neets relies heavily on the word “cost”: the “cost” to that person later in life “will be up to £300,000” in lost earnings. The “cost” to the economy and the taxpayer is £125bn every year – “more than we spend on education”. What a bleak way to talk and think about people.
And what will happen to all these young people who miss out? There is strong evidence that a part-time job while at school leads to higher self-efficacy and greater confidence. So, without this training ground to experiment in adulthood, the scratches formed when young people finally join the workforce may be more painful. This forecasted damage has been given a name: “long-term scarring”.
As a young graduate, I was very lucky to get a job in a busy London restaurant. It was during the summer of 2020, prime pandemic time, and I had applied for 100 other jobs without hearing back. But employers since have never been interested in this part of my CV. How ironic, because that was the hardest job I’ve ever had, and it set the bar for the type of employee, colleague, friend and overall person I am now.
- 
  Isabel Brooks is a freelance writer

Super-rich UK energy and food magnates’ wealth skyrockets amid global crises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:00:21 UTC
18:00:21 KST

François Perrodo is what is known in motorsport as a gentleman driver. In June, he raced at Le Mans, earning a podium place. At the end of August he was back behind the wheel at the Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps. This time he won.
Gentleman drivers are wealthy individuals who fund their own participation. The FIA governing body caps costs to keep racing accessible to such enthusiasts. But for self-confessed petrolhead Perrodo, it is well within his means.
Perrodo is in charge of his family’s company, Perenco, one of Europe’s largest privately held oil and gas companies. Between this summer’s two big races, he was in the Democratic Republic of the Congo presenting a multibillion dollar oil investment plan to the president. In the past four years, his family’s wealth has increased by about £3bn. He is one of a number of UK-linked billionaires whose wealth has soared since 2022, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine kicked off a global cost of living crisis.
An analysis has found that families whose fortunes came from energy grew their wealth four times faster than their super-rich peers since 2022. Families whose fortunes came from food production increased their wealth three times faster.
The Perrodo clan take the first place in a list of 15 super-rich UK-linked families who have seen their wealth soar from doing business in energy or food production. In all cases, the analysis found, increases in wealth came alongside increases in profit margins at businesses they owned.
The rises in energy and food prices, caused by climate shocks, wars and geopolitical tensions, have driven a multiyear cost of living crisis. Energy prices have fallen back from their peaks, but in August 2026 gas prices were 31% higher than in January 2020, while electricity prices were 17% higher. Petrol is more volatile, but is currently about twice as expensive as 2020. UK food prices rose by a total of 38.6% between November 2020 and November 2025.
The research, commissioned by the antipoverty charity War on Want, found that households on the Sunday Times Rich List whose fortunes came primarily from energy saw their wealth increase by 20% between 2022 and 2026 – four times the list average. Households whose fortunes came primarily from food production enjoyed a wealth increase of 15%.
Ben Tippet, an academic who researches wealth inequality at Kings College London, did the analysis based on his previous research categorising the sources of the wealth of households in the Rich List. He compiled a sub-list of 15 families who had made the most money from doing business in energy or food.
The list includes household names such as the Warburton family, who have increased their wealth by £185m as the cost of bread has risen, and Iceland supermarket founder Malcolm Walker, whose fortune grew by £106m.
Top of the list for food is Ranjit Singh Boparan, for whom the past decade has seen a stunning turnaround in his fortunes. In 2018, the “chicken king” was forced to step down as chief executive of his family company, 2 Sisters Food Group (2SFG), after a food safety scandal. The analysis found that he and his wife, whose companies are said to produce a third of all poultry products eaten in the UK, had tripled their wealth since 2022, taking it to over £2bn.
Perenco, which specialises in eking out the last drops from ageing oil wells, has been embroiled in a number of scandals. Four years ago, it sued the Peruvian government to try to block an Indigenous people’s reserve. Three years ago, there was an oil spill in Dorset – an accident that earned it a £6m fine. And two years ago documents revealed it was failing to plug its old North Sea wells.
Perenco said it was a “recognised expert in the optimisation of mature fields” and that it takes human rights and environmental law obligations “very seriously”. It noted that it had withdrawn its claim against the Peruvian government after the country’s ministry of culture determined there were uncontacted Indigenous people in the area.
Regarding the Dorset oil spill, Perenco said “very specific conditions in this pipeline” led to a spill of 200 barrels of reservoir fluid, which was about one-eighth crude oil and seven-eighths production fluid, including biocides. “Perenco UK have made changes to their processes and conducted extensive checks to confirm that these conditions are not present elsewhere,” the company said. And it added that it is “fully compliant with all relevant deadlines” for its North Sea wells “and strongly refutes any suggestion that it is not fulfilling its decommissioning obligations, or is in any way putting the integrity of assets at risk”.
Boparan has committed to higher welfare and cuts to emissions at 2SFG’s farms. But chicken factory farming nonetheless places a heavy load on the environment: farming is the UK’s largest cause of river pollution, and chicken farms in particular have been accused of causing severe pollution in the rivers Wye and Severn.
Boparan and 2SFG declined to comment. But the British Poultry Council insisted “chicken farms are not harming rivers”.
“All manure is managed and accounted for with designated routes of use, and all under government-regulated environmental permitting schemes,” said Richard Griffiths, the council’s chief executive. “Chicken consumption is growing and we have a responsibility to produce it sustainably ... Chicken is not the only way forward, but it is the one that can deliver today, tomorrow, and the next day.”
The research comes as Labour members and politicians meet in Liverpool for the party’s annual conference with the cost of living crisis a priority for Andy Burnham’s government. War on Want says that can only work if the government also takes steps to limit extreme wealth. It is calling for the government to establish £10m as the upper acceptable limit for wealth; to introduce an annual wealth tax on all assets over £10m; and to work with foreign governments to support extreme wealth taxation globally, including through the emerging UN Tax Convention.
“The super-rich are profiting from the food and energy industries that fuel both the climate and cost-of-living crises,” said Nuri Syed Corser, a campaigner at War on Want.
“Working-class people face soaring prices and worsening climate impacts – and the billionaires who own food and energy companies are profiting from this hardship. We need to tax the super-rich and use their extreme wealth to tackle the climate and cost-of-living crises.”

4-winged fossil found in Liaoning challenges single origin of dinosaur flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:00:06 UTC
18:00:06 KST

4-winged fossil found in Liaoning challenges single origin of dinosaur flight
While both birds and some winged dinosaurs could fly, they built their ‘flying kit’ in a different order
The newly discovered species, named Norellraptor barsboldi, is a four-winged predatory dinosaur measuring 57cm (22 inches) long.
Belonging to the microraptorines – small dinosaurs with feathers and wings closely related to birds – the creature offers fresh evidence that flight evolved independently in different dinosaur lineages rather than from a single common origin.
“These results dismiss a shared developmental pattern driving the evolution of the flying dinosaurs and support multiple and independent selective regimes at the origin of the winged taxa in Paraves,” the researchers wrote, referring to the group that includes birds and microraptorines.
The team of scientists from institutions in China, Italy and Slovakia published their findings in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Communications on Tuesday.

Teknofest opens doors with firsts in southeast edition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:59:37 UTC
17:59:37 KST

The southeastern leg of Teknofest launched on Sept. 30 in the southeastern province of Şanlıurfa. (AA Photo)
The southeastern leg of Teknofest, Türkiye’s top aerospace and technology event, launched on Sept. 30 in the southeastern province of Şanlıurfa, seamlessly linking Neolithic heritage with groundbreaking advancements in defense and agriculture.
Held at Şanlıurfa GAP Airport across 191,000 square meters, the event is organized by the Industry and Technology Ministry, the T3 Foundation, and STM Defense Technologies, with state-run Anadolu Agency serving as its global communication partner.
The debut Göbeklitepe Experience Area surrounds an obelisk with 360-degree screens at the zero point in history to explore where it all began, connecting ancient defense milestones to the festival generation. Alongside Erdemir, the 2027 Multifunctional Advanced Materials and Systems Competition was introduced for university entrants to produce and test metal, composite and ceramic prototypes. Nearby, the 450-square-meter “Journey of Material” space maps material evolution across three rooms via symbolic objects and audiovisual media on past and future routes.
Area 26 - Experience Exhibition draws on Neolithic memory from Şanlıurfa and Taş Tepeler, tracing production from obsidian to weaving, script, astrolabes, sensors and AI via mechanics and digital art to reveal humanity’s shared story. In the Hezarfen Experience Area, Hezarfen Ahmed Çelebi’s flight dream meets modern aviation via holographic screens, multi-layered projections, live stage performances, light and sound. The HÜRKUŞ Mini Flight Area provides pedal planes on a track with a giant inflatable gate for children aged 3 to 8, while the “All Happy Families Resemble One Another” exhibition uses interactive applications to explore emotional and environmental domestic ties.
Introduced in 2025, the 3,200-square-meter TÜME Area unites agriculture, livestock and food technologies with tech firms, academics, investors, students and local growers within a single ecosystem. The zone presents AI-backed autonomous farm systems, milking robots, smart barns, imaging, sensors, herd tracking, genetics, drones and water tools, alongside competition finals, virtual reality setups, entrepreneur-investor meetings, career desks and Dost Stage interviews.
First held in Istanbul in 2018, Teknofest has grown into a major aerospace event, rotating across Anatolia annually to advance homegrown engineering and technological self-reliance.

Belgian Defence Minister Theo Francken told the Euronews Defence Summit in Brussels that Europe faces a “dark winter” of Russian hybrid attacks and urgently needs stronger air defences, describing Russia as the biggest threat to Belgium’s security.
Belgian Defence Minister Theo Francken warned on Wednesday that Europe must prepare for further Russian hybrid attacks in the coming months, saying the continent faces a “dark winter”.
Speaking to Euronews journalist Angela Skujins at the Euronews Defence Summit in Brussels, Francken described Russia as the biggest threat to Belgium's security. The country has experienced several drone incidents this year, some of which disrupted air traffic.
"Russia, air attack, air attack, air attack. This is the biggest threat. So we need air defence, air defence, air defence," Francken said. He added that Europe needs Ukrainian technology to counter Russian jet-powered drones.
"We need to have more stocks, more production, scale up production, and a large industrial base. Everything has to go faster. There will be more hybrid threat actions in the next few months. It will be a dark winter for Europe," he said.
The minister said Russia has 50 years of expertise in hybrid attacks and that Belgium must keep pace with technological trends.
"I don't want to have 200,000 drones somewhere in a stock, and in two months you cannot even use them because they're outdated. So we have to adapt," he said.
'Worst pupil in NATO'
Francken said Belgium had long underinvested in defence, but that the country is now stepping up spending.
"We were like the worst pupil of the NATO class. We had 1 per cent of GDP in defence spending," he said, adding that spending has already doubled.
"But I cannot do in 18 months what has been neglected for 40 years."
Francken noted that Belgium currently has the EU’s highest debt and one of its most challenging budgetary positions, but said the government remains committed to increasing defence spending.
He added, however, that allocating 5% of GDP to defence would not be realistic for Belgium in the near term.

Nearly 40% of global population exposed to harmful ozone levels in 2026: EU climate agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:58:55 UTC
17:58:55 KST

Nearly 40 percent of the world's population has been exposed to harmful levels of ground-level ozone in 2026, according to a new analysis by the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS).
The analysis, published on Wednesday, shows how extreme heat and air pollution combined to drive ozone pollution across large parts of the world during the first eight months of the year.
According to CAMS, only 5 percent of the global population was exposed to ozone levels classified as "good" under the analysis, while Asia was the world's most affected region, followed by Europe and North America.
Some 60 percent of Asia's population was exposed to "extremely poor" ozone levels in 2026, rising to 90 percent when populations exposed to "poor" and "very poor" levels were included.
In Europe, 50 percent of the population experienced "poor," "very poor" or "extremely poor" ozone exposure, with repeated heat waves between June and August contributing to elevated ozone concentrations.
‘Ozone-climate penalty’
In North America, more than two-thirds of the population experienced "poor," "very poor" or "extremely poor" ozone exposure, with emissions from major wildfires contributing to elevated ozone concentrations.
CAMS said Oceania remained the region with the lowest ozone exposure, with its entire population experiencing "good" or "fair" ozone levels.
In South America, 81 percent of the population experienced "good" or "fair" ozone exposure, while the figure for Africa was 56 percent.
The analysis also highlighted the increasing importance of transboundary air pollution, with wildfire smoke, desert dust and other pollutants travelling thousands of kilometres across national borders and oceans.
CAMS said the findings underline the relationship between climate change and air quality.
Ozone itself is a greenhouse gas, while higher temperatures can create conditions that favour ozone formation, creating what scientists describe as an "ozone-climate penalty."
"Air pollution does not respect national borders," Laurence Rouil, director of CAMS, said. "Wildfire smoke, ozone and dust can travel thousands of kilometres, affecting communities far from their source."
Rouil said the findings highlight the need for global action on air quality alongside climate measures.

Hackers’ cyberattacks on Ukrainians have focused on four areas - what to beware of
Kyiv • UNN
In the first half of 2026, malware caused 33% of cyber incidents, while social engineering accounted for 31%. Attackers are impersonating government agencies’ resources.
In the first half of 2026, more than 88% of all cyber incidents in Ukraine were related to malware, social engineering, infection, and system compromise. Attackers are increasingly exploiting deception and users’ trust. The State Service of Special Communications and Information Protection reported this on September 30, UNN reports.
Details
The largest share of cyber incidents involved the distribution of malware — 33%. Another 31% accounted for social engineering. System infections made up 15%, while system compromises accounted for 4.5%.
"Attackers are increasingly relying not so much on technical complexity as on deception and users’ trust," says the report "Cyber Threats: Ukraine" for the first half of 2026, prepared by CERT-UA specialists.
According to the available information, one of the most widespread tactics has been the use of plausible cover stories.
"The groups create fake web pages that imitate the resources of the CERT-UA team itself, the document management system of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine, or the Brave1 platform. Users are prompted to download a supposed "security update" or "service module," which is actually a tool for remotely accessing the device," the post says.
We remind you
Russian special services create fake resources of government bodies and media outlets to spread disinformation and steal Ukrainians’ data. The SBU urges people to remain vigilant.

TIMELINE - US ends military presence in Iraq after 23 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:56:38 UTC
17:56:38 KST

Iraq on Wednesday announced the end of the US-led international coalition’s mission, marking a transition toward bilateral security relations with coalition member states, the prime minister’s security adviser said.
The announcement comes as the US completes its military withdrawal from Iraq ahead of a Sept. 30 deadline, concluding a 12-year deployment launched to support the fight against ISIS (Daesh).
The departure terminates the multinational mission launched in 2014 rather than representing the first American exit from the country. US Central Command (CENTCOM) reaffirmed the broader timeline to Anadolu while declining to elaborate on final movements.
Here is how the US military presence evolved from invasion and occupation to counterterrorism operations and the final withdrawal.
The long-term American military presence started on Oct. 16, 2002, when the US Congress passed the Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq Resolution.
It empowered the executive branch to deploy armed forces against Saddam Hussein's government over allegations of weapons of mass destruction and ties to terrorism.
On March 19, 2003, US President George W. Bush announced Operation Iraqi Freedom to "disarm Iraq, to free its people and to defend the world from grave danger."
Coalition forces entered Baghdad in April 2003, causing the collapse of the government.
US troop levels crossed 145,600 personnel that month and remained above 100,000 for several years, according to Government Accountability Office data.
American troops captured Saddam Hussein near Tikrit on Dec. 13, 2003, leading to his trial by an Iraqi tribunal and execution on Dec. 30, 2006.
Faced with escalating sectarian strife, Bush announced a strategic reinforcement known as the "surge" on Jan. 10, 2007, deploying additional brigades that raised troop levels from 131,500 in late 2006 to a wartime peak of 169,000 personnel by August 2007.
On Nov. 17, 2008, US and Iraq signed a Strategic Framework Agreement alongside a bilateral Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA), establishing a mandate for foreign units to exit.
On Dec. 14, 2008, during a joint press conference, Iraqi Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki praised the ratification, while Bush called the agreement "a major achievement" during a press conference where an Iraqi journalist threw shoes at him.
Operation Iraqi Freedom formally concluded on Aug. 31, 2010, transitioning into Operation New Dawn with a reduced number of troops tasked with advising domestic forces.
On Dec. 12, 2011, US President Barack Obama and Maliki marked the conclusion of the campaign.
US Forces-Iraq cased their organizational colors in Baghdad on Dec. 15, 2011.
While the bilateral security treaty established Dec. 31, 2011, as the legal deadline for departure, the final operational convoy of 500 soldiers and more than 100 vehicles crossed the border into Kuwait nearly two weeks early on Dec. 18, 2011.
The security environment deteriorated rapidly when ISIS swept through northern and western Iraq, seizing the major metropolis of Mosul on June 10, 2014, and capturing approximately one-third of the Iraqi territory.
Following an official request for assistance from Baghdad, Obama deployed initial assessment personnel on June 16, 2014, authorizing targeted airstrikes and humanitarian airdrops on Aug. 7-8 to blunt attacks against Erbil and protect trapped civilians on Mount Sinjar.
On Sept. 10, 2014, Washington established a global coalition that expanded to dozens of member states, formalizing Combined Joint Task Force - Operation Inherent Resolve (CJTF-OIR) on Oct. 17, 2014, to conduct counterterrorism air operations and assist Iraqi ground units.
Following extensive urban fighting, Iraqi forces liberated Mosul in July 2017.
Iraqi Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi formally declared the territorial defeat of ISIS on Dec. 9, 2017, after regaining control along the border with Syria.
Regional tensions escalated sharply on Dec. 27, 2019, when a rocket strike on a Kirkuk military facility killed an American contractor, triggering US airstrikes against five Kata'ib Hezbollah installations.
Protesters breached the outer perimeter of the US Embassy compound in Baghdad on Dec. 31, 2019.
On Jan. 3, 2020, a US strike outside Baghdad International Airport killed Iranian Quds Force Commander Qasem Soleimani and Iraqi militia leader Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis. Two days later, Iraq's Council of Representatives passed a non-binding resolution demanding the expulsion of all foreign military forces.
On July 26, 2021, then-US President Joe Biden and Iraqi Prime Minister Mustafa al-Kadhimi agreed to terminate combat operations by the year's end.
The coalition formally ended its combat role on Dec. 9, 2021, shifting approximately 2,500 remaining American troops exclusively into training, advising, and intelligence-sharing functions.
Bilateral security dialogue restarted in August 2023, establishing the Higher Military Commission in January 2024 to assess the persistent ISIS threat and evaluate domestic defensive capabilities.
On Sept. 17, 2024, Iraqi Prime Minister Mohammed Shia al-Sudani said that the mission's rationale had concluded.
"Today, Iraq in 2024 is not the same as Iraq of 2014…We moved from a period of wars to a period of stability."
On Sept. 27, 2024, Washington and Baghdad finalized a roadmap: Phase 1 concluded the coalition's military tasks across Iraq by September 2025, while Phase 2 permitted foreign personnel to facilitate anti-ISIS missions in Syria from designated Iraqi facilities until September 2026.
On Sept. 30, 2025, the Pentagon announced it, along with coalition partners, would reduce the military mission.
On Jan. 18, 2026, the commission announced that coalition advisers had fully vacated federal military installations, including Ain al-Asad Air Base and the Joint Operations Command headquarters, transferring authority to domestic security personnel.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi visited Washington on July 14, 2026, where he met with US President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Trump affirmed that Washington would no longer require a military garrison inside the country, while Zaidi said that after Sept. 30, “there will be no need for any armed factions, and our security forces are capable of protecting our territory."
Baghdad reaffirmed Sept. 30, 2026, as the "fixed and final date" for the mission's conclusion following discussions on Aug. 12 between Zaidi and CENTCOM Commander Gen. Brad Cooper.
On Sept. 27, 2026, an Iraqi official said that foreign forces had completely evacuated, though the US did not confirm this on their side.
Casualty figures demonstrate the contrasting physical intensity between the original occupation and the subsequent counterterrorism mission.
During the 2003–2011 campaign under Operation Iraqi Freedom, approximately 1.5 million American service members served in theater.
According to the Pentagon's Defense Casualty Analysis System, 4,418 US military personnel were killed and 31,994 were wounded in action.
Financially, the US Congressional Budget Office reported on April 26, 2011, that military operations had cost taxpayers roughly $752 billion.
During the 2014–2026 campaign under Operation Inherent Resolve, Pentagon casualty registries recorded 123 total deaths and 499 service members wounded in action.
Civilian losses during the operations were extensive.
Across both phases from 2003 through 2024, the tracking initiative Iraq Body Count reported more than 200,000 conflict-related civilian deaths.
According to Every Casualty Counts, more than 300,000, including civilians and combatants, were recorded as killed during the period.

US completes Iraq withdrawal after 12-year ISIS mission as Iran-backed militias remain armed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:55:13 UTC
17:55:13 KST

The U.S. military announced Wednesday that it had completed the withdrawal of its troops from Iraq, bringing an end to the 12-year mission launched to fight ISIS after the terror group swept across large parts of the country in 2014.
The final U.S. troops and equipment left the last air base where American forces had remained in northern Iraq under an agreement between Baghdad and Washington. The withdrawal also closes a chapter that Iran-backed militias had long cited as justification for retaining their weapons, though the Iraqi government has now postponed their disarmament until at least June 2027.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said U.S. troops and equipment had completed an “orderly departure” from the air base in Irbil, in Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region.
“This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region,” he said. “It also marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship.”
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi presided over the handover ceremony and described the withdrawal as the beginning of “a new phase, one defined by Iraq’s sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, the unity of its decision-making, and balanced partnerships with its friends.”
The withdrawal comes amid the ongoing war between the United States and Iran, which has at times spilled into Iraq. Iran-backed groups welcomed the U.S. departure, while officials in the Kurdish region voiced concern, particularly over the removal of American air defense systems.
U.S. forces first invaded Iraq in 2003 and withdrew in 2011. Three years later, Baghdad invited a smaller U.S.-led force back after ISIS seized large swaths of northern and western Iraq. With the terror group later reduced largely to scattered sleeper cells, Washington and Baghdad agreed in 2024 to wind down the coalition mission.
U.S. troops withdrew from bases across most of Iraq last year, leaving a smaller contingent of several hundred soldiers in the Kurdish region. Those bases have repeatedly come under attack since the U.S.-Iran war began on Feb. 28.
The Sept. 30 withdrawal deadline had initially also been tied to a commitment to disarm armed groups operating outside state control. While several smaller militias agreed to surrender their weapons, powerful Iran-backed factions rejected disarmament or imposed conditions Baghdad was unlikely to meet.
Al-Zaidi has since pushed the deadline for militia disarmament to June 2027.
Qassem al-Araji, national security adviser to the Iraqi prime minister, hailed the end of the coalition mission as a major milestone.
“Following the negotiations and understandings that began on July 22, 2021, we arrive today at an important milestone: the end of the international coalition’s mission and the presence of its forces,” he wrote on X. “We are moving toward bilateral relations with coalition member states, a transition that strengthens sovereignty and serves the national interests and aspirations of the Iraqi people.”
Al-Araji said the end of the coalition mission did not mean the end of security ties with its members. Security and intelligence cooperation, exchanges of expertise and efforts to build Iraqi capabilities would continue through bilateral relationships, he said.
A ‘new political phase’
Iraqi forces said the coalition had completed its withdrawal from the Kurdistan region and that U.S. forces had returned home or moved to bases in neighboring countries.
They also stressed that the end of the coalition mission removed one of the principal arguments used by militias for keeping their weapons.
“It is essential that weapons be concentrated in the hands of the state. There is no justification for weapons remaining outside state institutions,” Iraqi forces said. “We respected the position of the militias that conditioned the surrender of their weapons on the withdrawal of coalition forces.”
The Qatari newspaper Al-Araby Al-Jadeed described Wednesday as the beginning of a “new security and political phase” for Iraq, marking the end of the U.S. combat military presence that began with the 2003 invasion, despite the eight-year interruption between the 2011 withdrawal and the return of American forces in 2014.
An Iraqi military source told the newspaper that the U.S. military had transferred its remaining equipment out of the country, including material used for housing and troop welfare, to Kuwait, Turkey and Jordan.
But the effects of the withdrawal are unlikely to be felt equally across Iraq. Officials in the Kurdish region have expressed particular concern over the removal of U.S. air defense capabilities at a time of heightened regional conflict.
The Kurdish regional government’s Peshmerga Ministry said the region had faced more than 1,000 drone and ballistic missile attacks during the recent U.S.-Iran conflict.
“The departure of the United States from the Kurdistan Region under these complex regional circumstances, without the provision of a defense system, is a matter of concern,” the ministry said.
‘The occupation is not over’
Iran-backed factions, by contrast, celebrated the withdrawal while making clear they do not view it as the end of their confrontation with Washington.
Abu Mujahid al-Assaf, a security official with the powerful Kataib Hezbollah militia, called the departure of U.S. forces “the beginning of full sovereignty.”
“The expulsion of the occupation forces, defeated, from the land of Iraq is the beginning of full sovereignty,” he said.
He also warned al-Zaidi’s government against implementing what he described as American plans.
“Any government that does not work for the benefit of the people will be overthrown by all means,” he said.
Al-Assaf has also threatened action if restrictions on Iranian flights remain in place after Oct. 1, saying Iran-aligned factions could move to close access routes to countries participating in what he called a blockade of Iran. He said the “Islamic Resistance” would monitor Iraqi airspace, issue warnings to aircraft it deemed hostile and then seek to shoot them down.
Other opponents of the United States in Iraq argue that the military withdrawal does not end American influence over the country.
The Hezbollah-affiliated Lebanese newspaper Al-Akhbar highlighted that argument Wednesday under the headline “Iraq: The day of incomplete sovereignty,” quoting an analyst who claimed that Washington still exercised influence over Iraqi political, economic and security decision-making.
Sources close to the militias told the newspaper that their definition of sovereignty goes beyond the departure of American troops and includes ending all foreign military deployments in Iraq, including Turkey’s presence, as well as rejecting outside influence over the country’s economic decisions.

"The orderly departure of Coalition forces and equipment from Erbil Air Base marks the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated ISIS in Iraq," Department of Defense spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement. "This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region. It also marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship."
The U.S. military launched Operation Inherent Resolve in 2014 to confront ISIS, the terrorist group that grew out of the remnants of al-Qaeda in Iraq and seized vast portions of Iraq and neighboring Syria in the years immediately preceding the U.S.-led operation.
Roughly 2,000 Americans were present in Iraq as of February, officials said at the time. By comparison, more than 160,000 U.S. service members were in the country at the peak of the late 2000s "surge" under Operation Iraqi Freedom — a prior mission to topple Iraqi President Saddam Hussein and grapple with a years-long civil war.
As part of the anti-ISIS mission, U.S. troops have served in both Iraq and Syria. The roughly 1,500 troops that had been in Syria for a number of years withdrew earlier this year.
The end of the mission was agreed upon several years ago between the U.S. and Iraq in a plan that prescribed a transition to a more bilateral relationship between the two countries. In the 2024 joint agreement, Iraq and the U.S. announced the end of the multi-country coalition to defeat ISIS by 2025, and the expected end of the Inherent Resolve mission by the end of 2026.
The mission has pushed ISIS from controlling any significant territory, but it doesn't mean ISIS ceases to exist. In December 2025, two U.S. soldiers and a translator were killed in an ISIS attack, according to the U.S. military's Central Command. The U.S. retaliated with airstrikes.
American troops have been targeted by Iran-backed militias inside Iraq in recent years, a threat that has grown more pronounced since the U.S. and Israel jointly launched the ongoing war against Iran. According to the Pentagon, militias affiliated with Iran launched more than 600 attacks against U.S. citizens and facilities between February and April 2026.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth addressed the attacks in a July meeting at the Pentagon with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, according to a Pentagon readout. They discussed the transition from the Global Coalition to Defeat ISIS to a bilateral relationship, and Hegseth, according to the readout, committed to ending Inherent Resolve by Sept. 30.
Al-Zaidi has promised to disarm the Iran-backed militias in Iraq. He told The New York Times this week the groups are expected to be disbanded by June 2027, after initially setting a September 2026 deadline.
"We expect the Iraqi Security Forces, including the Peshmerga [Kurdish forces] and other security forces in the Iraqi Kurdistan Region, to lead the continuing effort to secure Iraq and keep ISIS remnants suppressed," Parnell said in his Wednesday morning statement, adding that the U.S. military would "continue to provide targeted training and intelligence support to our Iraqi partners."
"The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq's remaining security challenges, including ISIS remnants and Iran-aligned militias that undermine Iraqi sovereignty and regional stability, now rests with the Government of Iraq," he said. "The United States remains committed to counterterrorism and will continue to work with Iraq and our partners to ensure ISIS can never reconstitute from Iraqi territory."
Can Iraq control Iran's proxies?
The formal end of the U.S. military deployment in Iraq that began with the 2003 invasion was celebrated by the government in Baghdad, which declared Sept. 30, "Sovereignty Day." This year, it will begin a three-day national holiday, and the government has called for nationwide celebrations.
Videos circulated widely on social media Wednesday showed military convoys transporting U.S. equipment out of the Erbil base.
Speaking to the national Iraqi News Agency, Sabah al-Numan, a spokesperson for the prime minister, insisted that the nation's security forces were fully capable of maintaining peace and stability across the country.
But the long-planned U.S. withdrawal comes at a highly volatile moment for Iraq and the region. With the U.S.-Iran war at a critical juncture as President Trump warns of possible new strikes despite furtive diplomacy, many Iraqis remain deeply concerned about a potential resurgence of extremist groups in the country, as well as the expanding influence of the Iran-backed militias that have long held significant power in parts of Iraq.
Despite the government's public optimism, several religious and ethnic minority groups harbor serious doubt about the central government's ability to keep those forces in check on its own.
"The majority of Iraqis doubt the ability of the security and military apparatus to maintain security in the country, whether regarding the prevention of external aggressions and attacks or internal movements by armed groups operating outside state control of the government," journalist and regional political analyst Saman Noah told CBS News on Wednesday.
That is "especially true given that experience has proven the government's inability to subject these [Iran-backed] groups to state decision-making, control their behavior or hold their members accountable," he said.
Noah said some of the concern stemmed from the Iraqi government's lack of adequate air defenses "to protect the country's airspace, as well as the reliance on American weaponry — whose maintenance, and consequently operation, could cease in the event of any dispute."
Those concerns have only been heightened by the government's failure to meet its own initial deadline to disarm the Iran-backed factions, and concern that such groups could draw Iraq into the broader regional conflict in support of Tehran.
The Kurds in Iraq and their Peshmerga forces have been close allies of the United States since the first Gulf War in 1991, partnering on numerous occasions over the past 35 years. They joined the U.S.-led international coalition to depose Saddam Hussein's regime in 2003, and more than a decade later they fought with coalition forces to deprive ISIS of its massive foothold in the region.
They have become increasingly concerned about Iraq's future and the prospect of Iran-allied militias seeking to expand their influence.
"We fought side by side with our American allies to bring peace and stability to the region," said Noreldin Waisy, a senior adviser to the Kurdistan Regional Government's prime minister. "To eliminate any doubt among the Kurdish people, we believe the Kurdistan Region must remain an essential part of the bilateral Memorandum of Understanding between the two countries."

Eiffel Tower chief to quit over exclusion of female staff
September 30, 2026
The head of the company that operates the Eiffel Tower is set to step down at the end of the year after female staff were excluded during a visit by a Hindu religious group in September.
An independent investigation found a series of failures surrounding the incident, which prompted Eiffel Tower staff to strike and drew criticism from French politicians.
What happened at the Eiffel Tower?
Patrick Branco Ruivo, director general of the Societe d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), will leave the position he has held since late 2018.
The company said an independent investigation into the September 5 visit had uncovered a series of operational failures that resulted in female employees being excluded.
It described the situation as "unacceptable."
Management had instructed female employees not to come into contact with a delegation from Bochasanwasi Shri Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS), a Hindu religious organization.
The company initially acknowledged that withdrawing female staff from the tower's third floor during the group's visit had been a mistake.
What has the Hindu group said?
BAPS denied asking for female employees to be removed or hidden during the visit.
"The religious practices of our monks were explained to the Eiffel Tower's management in advance. These are personal spiritual commitments, which our monks observe without seeking to impose them on others. They do not require women to be excluded from the places they visit," BAPS said.
BAPS is an international religious and civic organization within the Swaminarayan tradition of Hinduism. The delegation was in the region for celebrations connected with the inauguration of a traditional Hindu stone temple.
What happens now?
The incident led Eiffel Tower employees to strike on September 7, forcing the landmark to close for a day.
SETE chair Ariel Weil said the company would introduce measures and training programs aimed at promoting gender equality.
The German account also says a separate protocol department will be established following the investigation.
The 330-meter (1,083-foot) Eiffel Tower attracts around 7 million visitors annually.

A powerful Mediterranean storm brought torrential rainfall to southern France on Wednesday, prompting authorities to place the Herault and Gard departments under the highest-level red alert for rain and flooding, according to BFMTV.
Meteo-France issued the red alerts at 8 am local time (0600GMT), while the Bouches-du-Rhone, Lozere and Ardeche departments were placed under orange alert for severe weather.
The Herault River rose rapidly.

Authorities said the river had risen by more than 2 metres in just two hours overnight as heavy rainfall affected the Cevennes region.
Nearly 140 millimetres of rain was recorded in Moules-et-Baucels in the Herault department, equivalent to almost two months of average rainfall.
Other rivers and waterways also rose rapidly following the heavy rainfall early on Wednesday.
The Herault prefecture ordered schools to close for the day in eight sectors, including Montpellier, Mauguio, Lunel, Sommieres, Ganges, Sete, Clermont-l’Herault and Lodeve.
The prefecture also said public transportation was suspended across the department.
Authorities urged residents to remain at home, avoid unnecessary travel and refrain from using their vehicles.

Prosecutors did not indict Chou on coercion or alleged violations of the Physicians Act. After investigating the allegations, prosecutors concluded that the evidence was insufficient to establish those offenses and issued a non-prosecution ruling.
National Taiwan Normal University dismissed Chou in July 2025 and barred her from being rehired as a teacher for four years. The university's faculty evaluation committee cited sustained bullying and a power imbalance between Chou and students in its decision.
The case was investigated for about a year, with prosecutors interviewing current and former players and reviewing research-project records and the flow of research funds. Chou was released on NT$700,000 bail and barred from leaving Taiwan following questioning, per CNA.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Environmental Protection and Development Foundation (EPDF) and the Japan Environment Association signed the Taiwan-Japan mutual recognition agreement on environmental labels on Wednesday.

The EPDF said that in the future, Taiwanese products entering Japan, and vice versa, will need to obtain certification from only one country, eliminating the need to send products overseas for additional testing.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:48:56 UTC
17:48:56 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Kinmen National Park Headquarters released 200 native climbing perch into Lingshuihu Lake on Wednesday in an effort to help re-establish the declining population in the wild.
The fish were released in conjunction with local elementary schools, Lieyu Township elected representatives, and conservation group Aquatic Renewal Workshop, per CNA. It said climbing perch, once widely seen in Lieyu’s ponds and waterways, are now threatened by fragmented habitats and extreme weather.
The national park said it will continue promoting field investigations, habitat creation, conservation, and education efforts for climbing perch. It added that protecting Lake, a vital wetland, continues to rely on partnerships between the public and private sectors.
Aquatic Renewal Workshop head Chen Kuang-yao (陳光耀) said climbing perch were once a common sight in Kinmen, adding that their ferocity outmatches that of paradise fish, per UDN. He previously traveled to Hainan to observe the fish crawling on land, noting that a cut inflicted by the fish's operculum, or bony gill cover, left him a lasting impression.
Chen encountered a population of climbing perch in Lingshuihu Lake while investigating the area, per Liberty Times. He pointed out the fish can exchange air through a lung-like organ in its head, allowing them to remain out of water for extended periods as long as they stay moist.
Chen emphasized that while the fish appear to move with their fins on land, they actually use the protruding spines on their operculum to crawl. He added that although climbing perch are rumored to be able to climb trees, he doubts the claim because he has never witnessed the phenomenon.
Chen said Kinmen could be the only climbing perch habitat in Taiwan, per China Times.

Ukrainian Defense Tech L7 Simulators Standardized Across NATO Logistics Network
Ukrainian defense tech company L7 Simulators has secured NATO codification for its full line of military training systems. The decision covers equipment ranging from individual marksmanship tools to complex collective unit training platforms.
The company announced the milestone directly, noting that each simulator in its catalogue has received an official NATO Stock Number (NSN), as reported by Militarnyi on September 29.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
This unique 13-digit identifier allows defense logistics networks across NATO member states to identify and register the equipment. The listing simplifies inventory tracking, procurement procedures, and catalog searches across allied militaries.
The company also gained the clearance to codify future hardware additions directly into the supply database. While NATO codification integrates equipment into the shared alliance logistics architecture, it operates as a standardized inventory tool rather than a full technical certification of the hardware, according to Militarnyi.
L7 Simulators registered as an official manufacturer within the NATO codification system in December 2024. That initial entry followed the codification of its UNITS platform, an integrated training framework previously authorized for use by the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine.
The manufacturer now produces more than 50 distinct training models. The line includes simulators for infantry weapons, anti-tank hardware, air defense systems, and unmanned aerial vehicles, all linked through the central UNITS framework.
Among the systems modeled by the company are simulators for the Browning M2 heavy machine gun, Stinger surface-to-air missile, NLAW, Carl Gustaf recoilless rifle, RPG-7, and SPG-9.
On May 18, 2026, Ukrainian defense technology firm SKIFTECH unveiled a virtual reality trainer named "Reflex—Minus Drone," which was designed to prepare soldiers to shoot down Russian FPV strike drones using lessons drawn from frontline combat experience.
Built using actual battlefield data, the mobile platform simulated realistic drone behavior, flight speeds, and shotgun ballistics while incorporating a spatial audio component that allowed trainees to detect approaching threats by sound before visually spotting them.

Greggs to close four UK factories with potential for 740 job losses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:46:29 UTC
17:46:29 KST

Greggs has announced plans to close four of its factories, in a move that could result in 740 job losses over the next two and a half years.
The bakery chain said it was consulting on the closures, which would initially cost £60m when including disruption costs and redundancy payments but then could create £20m of savings each year by 2028.
The proposed cuts come as Greggs reported stronger sales growth in its most recent quarter at 7.7%, up from 7.2% in the first half of the year. The company said the closures, “while difficult, are necessary” to ensure it can grow in the “most cost-efficient manner”.
It said: “Our immediate priority is to minimise the impact on our people where possible. We will enter into a consultation period shortly to work with trade unions and employee representatives of those affected to refine and develop these proposals.”
The closures could affect factories in Enfield, north London, Penrith in Cumbria, Kelso in Roxburghshire, Scotland, and Seaham in County Durham. It will continue to run distribution operations from Enfield. The proposals could also affect manufacturing operations at its Treforest site in Wales, but this will continue as a distribution centre for business.
Greggs has grown to become Britain’s biggest fast-food business thanks to the popularity of its low-cost pastries, cakes and hot drinks. It has expanded rapidly this year, with 57 net new openings, as part of its plan to open between 100 and 110 shops by the end of 2026.
Iced matcha lattes and a bigger range of salads and chicken rolls also helped to boost sales over the summer, the company said. However, Greggs told investors on Wednesday that while stronger sales had “modestly improved” its outlook for this year, “there are signs of greater inflationary pressures in 2027”.
Alex Pugh, an analyst at the investment broker Freetrade, said that while the bakery chain “has survived a heatwave and a cost of living crisis … a £1.50 sausage roll could be a real test of loyalty”.
Earlier this year the company raised the cost of its bestseller sausage roll by 5p, taking it to £1.35 in most shops. It also increased the price of a latte by 10p, taking it to £2.25, as it looked for ways to combat rising wage, energy and packaging costs.
Shares in Greggs rose by 7.3% in early trading on Wednesday morning, making it the best performer across the mid-cap FTSE 250 index and taking its year-to-date rise to 17%. Greggs, which is headquartered in Newcastle, employs more than 33,000 people around the UK.

17:45:48 KST

In Hasselt (Limburg Province), on Tuesday, a nest containing around 2,000 Asian hornets was removed from the playground of a primary school. Given the location, pest control operator Nicky Torbeyns had to take extra care. An aerial platform and a special vacuum cleaner were used.
The nest was hanging in a tall tree on the playground. The school itself had requested the removal of the nest. Treating it with poison was not an option. “If we spray the nest with a biocide, the hornets will fall to the ground,” explains Torbeyns. “As the playground isn’t paved, it would be difficult to clear the insects away, and they can still sting for up to two days after they die.”
So, the pest controllers climbed the tree using a cherry picker and a vacuum cleaner. Torbeyns and his colleague donned protective suits. They sucked up the hornets with a vacuum cleaner, cut the nest out of the tree and brought it down. The school was given the nest as educational material.
Removing a nest like this is not without risk. “The moment you start cutting away the branches to get to the nest, the nest is alerted and the hornets go on the attack,” says Torbeyns.
The people on the ground also had to protect themselves. The headteacher, who wanted to take photos, was stung. The man operating the aerial platform had to stay in the cab with the doors closed.
Torbeyns’ colleague was wearing safety goggles but still got venom in his eye. “It’s not the case that a hornet sprays venom as it flies past; usually it stings,” explains Torbeyns. “But because we’re wearing suits with a kind of mesh at the front, their aggression causes them to fly straight into it. They get stuck and try to sting.”
“In doing so, the hornet can pierce the visor of the mask, after which the venom is forced into the eye under pressure,” Torbeyns continues. “That can cause a burning sensation. Fortunately, my colleague’s injury turned out to be not too serious in the end.”
Torbeyns is currently pretty busy dealing with hornet nests. “We’re pretty fully booked every day,” he says. He adds it was even busier last year, when he was sometimes fully booked three days in advance. In some local authorities, where he has been the regular exterminator for years, the numbers this year are slightly lower than last year.
The season isn’t over yet, Torbeyns emphasises. Once the leaves have fallen from the trees, he expects things to get even busier, as the nests will then become more visible.

Apple leads China smartphone sales after launch of iPhone 18 Pro. Can the momentum last?
Sales in the first three days were 12 per cent higher than the previous generation’s entire first week
Apple has claimed the top spot in China’s smartphone market following the release of its iPhone 18 Pro series, giving a potential boost to a sluggish handset market weighed down by weak consumer demand and soaring component costs.
Sales of the new Pro models in their first three days after launching on September 18 were 12 per cent higher than sales of the iPhone 17 Pro line-up during its entire first week last year, according to a report published on Wednesday by Counterpoint Research.
That strong start catapulted Apple to the No 1 position by smartphone sales for the week of September 14 to 20, with the company capturing 33 per cent of the market.
“The delayed launch of the base iPhone 18 may have driven some consumers to trade up to the Pro series,” said Ivan Lam, a senior analyst at Counterpoint Research. “Price hikes of over US$200 on many Chinese flagship models may have raised the price anchor, strengthening the iPhone’s relative value proposition.”

Indian among 5 crew members killed by pirates aboard hijacked oil tanker now under Somali forces’ control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:44:30 UTC
17:44:30 KST

Five crew members, including an Indian sailor, were killed by Somali pirates aboard a fuel tanker that was hijacked months ago off the coast of Somalia.Security forces have now regained control of the vessel.According to the Puntland Maritime Police Force (PMPF), the victims also included three Pakistani nationals and one Myanmar national."PMPF carried out a maritime operation off the coast of Dharin-baar, Bandar Beyla District, successfully rescuing the MT Honour 25 oil tanker, which had been hijacked by pirates," it said in a social media post on Tuesday.Puntland is a semi-autonomous region of Somalia.According to the PMPF, the pirates had initially offered to surrender while concealing the deaths of the crew members. It further stated that the ship was now safe and under Puntland government control. Sixteen suspected pirates were apprehended during the operation, while efforts to locate the remaining hijackers were continuing.
Vessel was hijacked in April
According to the European Union’s naval force Eunavfor, the MT Honour 25 oil tanker was hijacked in April while sailing towards Somalia’s capital, Mogadishu. It was carrying around 17 crew members, most of them Pakistani nationals, along with a cargo of oil products.
BBC Somali reported that the crew comprised 10 Pakistanis, four Indonesians, one Indian, one Sri Lankan and one Myanmar national.The commercial vessel, carrying 18,500 barrels of fuel bound for Mogadishu was hijacked on April 21.In a separate development, Somali pirates on Tuesday released a Togo-flagged tanker after holding it off Puntland’s Karkaar region.
Nearly 30 armed pirates disembarked from the vessel and handed over all 12 crew members—eight Egyptians and four Indians—unharmed to the local community. The pirates reportedly damaged the vessel, MT Eureka, and set parts of it on fire before fleeing.The tanker had been hijacked on May 2 off Yemen’s Port of Qana while carrying 20,400 barrels of fuel. A substantial amount of its cargo was siphoned off and sold at sea during the months it was held captive. The crew members are now in the care of local residents in the Hul-Aanood area.(With PTI inputs)

Ayse Bocuoglu Bodur and Emir Yildirim

Türkiye’s prime aviation, space and technology festival TEKNOFEST opened its doors to visitors on Wednesday, this time in the nation’s southeastern province of Sanliurfa.
TEKNOFEST Southeast, a leg of the event held in the southeastern part of the country, brings together tech enthusiasts, young investors and thousands of visitors for various shows, exhibitions and the finals of tech competitions across 14 categories from Wednesday through Oct. 4.
The event will host air shows by the aviation and defense industries, as well as demonstrations by the aerobatic teams SoloTurk and the Turkish Stars and other fighter jets.
Turkish Aerospace Industries’ (TAI) Atak, Hurkus and Anka helicopters, as well as Baykar’s Bayraktar TB2, TB3 and Akinci drones, will be on display alongside land and sea vehicles.
Visitors will experience a wide range of activities at the event, including concerts, various stage performances, exhibitions, educational workshops, simulation zones, a planetarium, science shows, the TEKNOFEST Time Tunnel, trade show events, an exhibition of homegrown naval, land and air vehicles, and special first-flight activities for students.
The first day of the event will feature a parachute jump, a flight demonstration with Baykar’s Bayraktar Akinci drone, a paramotor flight demonstration and a science show.
The program will also involve a TAI Atak helicopter flyover, a demonstration flight by the Turkish Gendarmerie’s Steel Wings aerobatic team, a demonstration by the Baykar Bayraktar TB3 and more.
TEKNOFEST Southeast admission is free, but visitors must register online before entering.
Visitors may enter and exit the event area between 9 am and 7 pm local time.
Free public transport to the event will be provided.

Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir cancels planned visit to the US amid rising IDF alert level
A senior IDF official explained the decision: "You can’t put the army on high alert and fly abroad"
The Chief of Staff, Lieutenant General Eyal Zamir, canceled his planned visit to the United States on Wednesday. This comes against the backdrop of increased alertness in the IDF and a sensitive security situation, as reported by i24NEWS military analyst Yossi Yehoshua.
The decision to cancel the trip was made by the military's top echelon even before Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's statements yesterday regarding threats to Israel. One senior IDF official made it unequivocally clear what prompted the move, saying, "You can't put the military on alert and fly abroad."
As part of the official visit to Washington, Zamir was scheduled to hold a series of strategic meetings with the American Chief of Staff and with the commander of the United States Central Command (CENTCOM).
The talks were intended to deal with joint security coordination and preparations for developments in the region. Nevertheless, the state of high alert declared in the operational units of the IDF, alongside the need for close management of readiness on the ground, determined that at this time the Chief of Staff must remain in Israel.
Suggested articles
- 'We identify a threat, but that does not mean that tomorrow morning we will be at war' | i24NEWS
- 'Israel’s security and IDF bases are not props for election videos,' Lapid says after security briefing | LIVE BLOG | i24NEWS
- Iran executes two men over January Mashhad unrest, sentences confirmed by Supreme Court | i24NEWS
The decision in the army comes against the backdrop of increasing security and political tensions in the past 24 hours, after Netanyahu claimed yesterday during a visit to the Tel Nof base that "there are indications that ahead of the elections our enemies will try to attack us," and sent a message stating that "our long arm will reach you anywhere and anytime."
The statement led to a late-night security update meeting between Netanyahu and opposition leader Yair Lapid, who claimed afterwards that "the IDF, Shin Bet, and the police are prepared for elections, and there is no reason to cause public panic." While the political arena saw confrontation between the sides over the timing of the warnings, the military command translated the situation assessment into an actual state of heightened alert, which led to the cancellation of the Chief of Staff's trip.

EU to offer single-market access to candidate countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:39:52 UTC
17:39:52 KST

EU to offer single-market access to candidate countries
Economic benefits would be conditional and can be taken away if non-members backslide on democracy or share sensitive tech with unfriendly governments, the plan says.
BRUSSELS — The European Union will open its vast economy to countries waiting to join its ranks, provided they agree to stand with the bloc against hostile states and industrial rivals, according to a draft European Commission proposal obtained by POLITICO.
Candidate countries — some of which have been waiting decades to become EU members — will be offered unprecedented "gradual integration" into the single market, including frictionless trade and access to research programs, while their applications are being worked on, according to the draft plan.
"The single market is the first priority for economic convergence," reads a review of the "pre-enlargement" benefits to be offered to candidate countries.
Advertisement
"Earlier integration would open opportunities for Union businesses, strengthen European value chains and reduce strategic dependencies. The Commission will identify where verified regulatory alignment and enforcement capacity allow deeper participation in research, innovation and industrial cooperation, and wider market access. Priority should go to opportunities that advance accession preparations and meet shared economic and strategic needs."
The review, overseen by top von der Leyen advisor Alexandre Adam — a former aide to French President Emmanuel Macron — would radically overhaul the EU's approach to countries in its neighborhood. At present, almost all economic benefits of closer cooperation are reserved for members, but no new state has joined since Croatia in 2013.
As part of Adam's package of measures, Ukraine, Moldova, Albania and Montenegro will be offered "road maps" designed to speed up the process of joining in the coming years. Others, like North Macedonia, Kosovo, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia and Turkey, have seen the process drag on — with fears growing that they will become disengaged or gravitate closer to Russia or China.
Under the Commission's plan, economic benefits offered to candidate countries will depend on their support for the EU's foreign policy objectives, with single market access hinging on them not sharing key technologies with hostile states and trade rivals.
"As industrial and market integration deepens, participation in sensitive sectors must be accompanied by cooperation on investment screening, export controls, sanctions implementation and the protection of sensitive technologies," the review document reads.
"Assessments of access should consider strategic alignment, critical dependencies and the capacity to manage risks to infrastructure and supply chains. Where those conditions are not met, the scope of participation should be adjusted under the applicable instrument."
Advertisement
Among the areas being considered for closer cooperation are semiconductors, quantum technologies, biotechnology, artificial intelligence and space.
In the waiting room
Von der Leyen touches down in Albania for talks on Wednesday as part of her tour of the Western Balkans. She'll also visit Kosovo and North Macedonia, which will miss out on an expedited pathway to join the EU under the new plan, and will use her visit to demand economic benefits of closer alignment.
"Gradual integration should be tangible for our citizens and businesses," Kosovo's prime minister, Albin Kurti, told POLITICO. "We want greater access to the EU single market, European funding and financial schemes, and joint programs in areas such as energy, digitalization, research, education and infrastructure."
"We support gradual integration, but it must be a pathway to full EU membership, not a parallel process or a substitute for it. Kosova is ready to do its part," Kurti added.
According to the review, the ultimate goal of candidate countries should be becoming full EU members. "Accession, however, takes time: candidate countries must complete a rigorous, merit-based process and deliver far-reaching and lasting reforms," it reads. "That time should be put to full strategic use to both prepare the Union for a larger membership and deepen gradual integration in areas of mutual interest."
However, the benefits will depend on the countries doing their part: "Where these obligations are not fulfilled, participation must remain reversible. Access should be suspended or withdrawn where warranted," the proposal warns.
Advertisement
Internal changes
Current EU members have expressed concern about the prospect of admitting new countries to the bloc that could then renege on their commitments and upend key policies. Under its former prime minister, Viktor Orbán, Hungary used its veto to block sanctions on Russia and support for Ukraine.
Adam's review — due to be presented to top officials on Oct. 6 when von der Leyen returns from the Western Balkans — will propose new conditions on those that join the bloc to ensure they don't backslide on democracy and the rule of law.
"The accession process must establish more than legal alignment," it reads. "Institutions must work in practice and reforms must endure. Monitoring, incentives and enforcement should therefore form a continuous framework extending beyond accession."
But the EU will also change to accommodate a broader membership, going far beyond the club of wealthy Western European democracies it was initially conceived as. The bloc can change its rules to be less vulnerable to individual members' whims, the review concludes, without having to reopen fundamental articles of EU law and potentially triggering national referendums across the bloc.
"The Commission supports Treaty change where necessary, but it considers that measures already available under the Treaties should be taken forward now," it concludes. Among the options being considered is a move to ensure more decisions can be made with a qualified majority of member countries on board.
"Qualified-majority voting is already the general rule under the Treaties, but unanimity remains in several strategically important areas. As membership grows, the risk of delay or blockage will likely increase," it reads.
Advertisement
So-called passerelle clauses, which allow decisions to be taken by majority vote rather than unanimously, could be used to smooth the passage of sanctions, responses to human rights crises and the deployment of civilian missions to conflict zones, the review says. However, these clauses require unanimous support of member countries to be activated in the first place.
Leaders from across the EU will be asked to weigh in on the discussion about how to bring new members into the bloc — and what to offer those still waiting — at a two-day summit in Brussels from Oct. 15.
Von der Leyen's enlargement commissioner, Marta Kos, has said that the new proposals, combined with support from capitals to accelerate the process, offer the chance for an “autumn of enlargement” in which unprecedented changes can be made.

German Social Democratic Party revives push for AfD ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:39:28 UTC
17:39:28 KST

German coalition party pushes to ban AfD
Germany’s Social Democratic Party (SPD) has called for a formal review that could pave the way for a ban on Alternative for Germany (AfD), as the right-wing party leads national polls following major regional election victories.
The push follows the AfD’s sweeping victories in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania earlier this month, where it secured 43.8% and 38.2%, respectively. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) suffered heavy losses, including failing to clear the 5% threshold in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
On Tuesday, SPD parliamentary leaders from the Bundestag, Germany’s state legislatures and the European Parliament wrapped up a two-day summit in Bremen by again labeling the AfD a “right-wing extremist party.” They accused it of threatening democracy “from within” and “normalizing racism.”
The AfD has rejected accusations of extremism. Responding to a parallel push for a potential ban in Hamburg this week, AfD parliamentary leader Dirk Nockemann called it an “attack on democracy and the will of the voters” and dismissed the proposed working group as “desperate.”
The Eurosceptic party advocates tougher immigration controls and opposes Berlin’s support for Ukraine and sanctions against Russia.
At the federal level, the AfD remains classified by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency as a suspected right-wing extremist organization.
In February, a Cologne court blocked an attempt by the agency to upgrade the AfD to confirmed right-wing extremist status, pending the outcome of the main proceedings. Several AfD state branches carry the stronger classification.
The SPD wants federal and state governments to set up a joint working group by year-end to examine whether legal grounds exist to seek a ban. Launching the review “is a legal necessity” and a “democratic duty,” it said.
Merz himself has expressed skepticism about pursuing a ban. Earlier this month, the chancellor said the legal hurdle was “very high” and argued that outlawing the AfD would not solve the problems its voters believe they face.
Under German law, only the Federal Constitutional Court can outlaw a party. A ban requires more than anti-constitutional views: a party must actively seek to undermine the democratic order and have the potential to achieve its aims.
The push comes as the AfD has opened up a record polling lead over Merz’s CDU/CSU bloc. An INSA survey put the AfD at 29.5%, compared with 19% for the CDU/CSU and just 14.5% for the SPD. The two governing parties together stood at 33.5%, only four points ahead of the AfD alone.
AfD co-leader Alice Weidel reacted to the poll by accusing the CDU of “clinging to the undemocratic firewall,” saying the policy was ultimately “destroying Germany.” The ‘firewall’ refers to the refusal by other major German parties to cooperate with the AfD.

The Delhi government this week unveiled a plan to battle the recurring toxic smog that blankets the Indian capital in the winter months.
The measures are set to be enforced from November, with some curbs to remain in place until February.
Here’s what the plan entails:
- a ban on dust-generating demolition activities and outdoor civil construction work from November 1 to January 31
- construction and demolition activities will see a complete ban in the peak winter phase, from December 10 to January 20
- use of private vehicles will discouraged with parking fees in authorized parking areas being doubled from November 1 to February 28

The INDIA bloc has announced a "Save Democracy " march as leaders of the opposition alliance met on Wednesday to mull a joint strategy over the issue of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls.
India bloc leaders will hold nationwide protest marches from October 2 to 8 at the district level, while all opposition MPs will march to the Election Commission on October 6, Congress party President Mallikarjun Kharge told a press briefing after the meeting.

The bloc's leaders also announced a major rally in the Indian capital on November 1, where they would raise issues related to alleged "vote theft".
Gandhi earlier posted on X, accusing Modi of using India's poll body chief Kumar "to steal elections".
The INDIA bloc on Wednesday also demanded that all cases linked to the SIR that are in the Supreme Court should be resolved "as soon as possible".
Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has accused the opposition of "misleading" the public on the SIR and of an "attack" India's constitutional bodies.

Apple on Wednesday introduced its payment service in India as it taps into the lucrative digital payments market in the world’s most populous nation.
Apple Pay is now available for Indian users across iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch, a statement from the US multinational corporation said, adding that support for Mac computers was coming soon.
