Europe’s energy security has a Black Sea opportunity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

Last Friday, 25 September, a vessel carrying 90,000 tonnes of Libyan El Sharara crude oil arrived at the port of Kulevi on the Black Sea coast in Georgia. It was the second Libyan delivery for the Kulevi Oil Refinery in less than a month, following the first cargo in August.
Black Sea Petroleum (BSP), a privately owned company based in Georgia, owns and operates the Kulevi Oil Refinery. Operations began in October 2025, and today the refinery processes exclusively non-Russian crude oil. The Libyan deliveries form part of a long-term supply agreement.
BSP’s existing production already offers a basis for supplying European markets with straight-run products, while EURO 5 fuel production is planned by 2029.
Kriti Legend at Kulevi with BSP’s first shipment of Libyan crude oil, 30 August 2026. / via Black Sea Petroleum
Europe’s need for diverse fuel supplies
Europe continues to import fuels used in transport and industry. According to Eurostat, EU net imports in 2024 amounted to 15.7 million tonnes of oil equivalent for gasoil and diesel and 11 million for jet fuel. Both are included in the Kulevi Oil Refinery’s expansion plans.
For Kulevi, the opportunity is to supply EU markets alongside Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan, drawing on non-Russian crude and the Black Sea’s shipping connections.
Following the Oil Coordination Group meeting on September 8, 2026, the European Commission reported that higher EU refinery production and alternative international supplies were helping meet demand for diesel and jet fuel. Stocks remained sufficient, but developments in the Middle East and seasonal demand could tighten markets in the weeks and months ahead.
Additional refining capacity connected to maritime trade could give Europe more sources of these fuels. For Kulevi, the opportunity is to supply EU markets alongside Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan, drawing on non-Russian crude and the Black Sea’s shipping connections. This would add another route through which international crude supplies can reach Europe as refined products.
An operating refinery connected to the sea
Four pipelines run for three kilometres between the Kulevi Oil Refinery and the nearby port and terminal. They carry crude oil, naphtha, gasoil and fuel oil. The port and terminal are separate facilities owned and operated by SOCAR.
Pipelines connecting the Kulevi Oil Refinery with the nearby SOCAR-owned port and terminal. / via Black Sea Petroleum
Crude arriving by sea or rail can reach the refinery through the terminal. Refined products can move in the other direction for shipment. The two Libyan cargoes show this infrastructure in use, bringing North African crude to the Black Sea for processing.
Black Sea Petroleum has invested €200 million in the Kulevi Oil Refinery to date. A further €650 million is planned by 2029 to expand refining capacity and introduce new fuel production units.
Supply contracts, certificates of origin and shipping records document the crude’s origin and its movement from the supplier to the refinery in Georgia.
The pipeline connection allows the refinery to use the terminal for both incoming crude and outgoing products. Expansion can therefore build on an established route to international markets. Greater refining capacity would increase the volumes handled through that route, while new production units would broaden the types of fuel available.
Investment already under way
Black Sea Petroleum has invested €200 million in the Kulevi Oil Refinery to date. A further €650 million is planned by 2029 to expand refining capacity and introduce new fuel production units.
Processing units and storage tanks at the Kulevi Oil Refinery. / via Black Sea Petroleum
The company plans to raise annual refining capacity from 1.2–1.5 million tonnes to 4.5–5 million tonnes by 2028. Plans also include bringing EURO 5 fuel production units into operation by 2029. The planned product range includes petrol, diesel, jet fuel, liquefied petroleum gas, marine fuel and bitumen.
These products would serve road transport, aviation, shipping and construction. Diesel and jet fuel would also place the expanded refinery in markets where the EU is a net importer. The investment programme is intended to support those exports while also meeting demand in neighbouring countries.
Honeywell refining technology and licensed processes will support the planned expansion, alongside automation and modular processing units. Engineering and construction for the next stages have continued since the first phase opened in October 2025.
BSP has completed 40,000 cubic metres of new storage capacity, with another 40,000 cubic metres nearing completion. This storage will support larger volumes of crude and products as production grows.
Building lasting European relationships
Led by co-founder and chief executive David Potskhveria, Black Sea Petroleum is establishing a Belgian company and plans to open its Brussels office in mid-October. The office will give EU institutions and European business partners a permanent point of contact for discussions about the refinery and its investment plans.
BSP’s European Advisory Council and strategic advisers bring experience in European and international affairs to its work with EU institutions, national authorities and businesses across Member States. They support direct relationships between the company’s team in Georgia and its European counterparts.
BSP welcomes interested partners to visit the Kulevi Oil Refinery, see production first-hand and meet the people responsible for its operations and development.
Last week’s second Libyan delivery provides a concrete starting point for those conversations. The refinery is operating, non-Russian supplies are arriving and investment is continuing. Its development could give Europe an additional source of fuels through an existing Black Sea route, with a company seeking lasting European partnerships.

FlyDubai flight diverts to Saudi Arabia after reported fight between pilots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:59:24 UTC
16:59:24 KST

Dubai to Israel flight makes emergency landing, passenger says "co-pilot tried to murder the pilot" and crash jet
A FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Israel was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia Wednesday after a violent attempt by one of the pilots to seize control of the aircraft and crash it, passengers and Israeli officials said.
"As they were approaching Israel, one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot and apparently attempted to crash the plane with everyone on board," Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a video statement, lauding passengers and other crew members who intervened. The prime minister said he said he had instructed Israel's "security establishment to prepare for potential additional threats."
An Israeli security official told CBS News that authorities were investigating the possibility that the incident could have been an attempted Sept. 11-style terror attack, and whether the attacker was working alone.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz called it "an attempted jihadist terror attack, which was thwarted only thanks to the heroism of several Israeli passengers who broke into the cockpit, overpowered the terrorist, and with their own hands returned control of the aircraft to an additional flight crew that was present," according to a statement.
The plane diverted to make an emergency landing in Tabuk, where there is a civilian airport adjacent to a Saudi military base. No passengers were injured in the incident, but the pilot attacked by his fellow crewmember reportedly sustained stab wounds, and Saudi authorities said two crew members were hospitalized with unspecified injuries.
According to Netanyahu, the pilot who carried out the stabbing was placed under arrest and was "being questioned by the Saudi authorities."
Passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon said the plane was "pretty much out of control" when the stabbing took place over Jordan.
"The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane," she told reporters by speakerphone held up by her mother, who was waiting at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv. "It was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralized him."
"There was also a doctor who gave first aid, and people who treated both of them. Other than the pilot, there were no injuries, but the bigger fear was really a crash, which is exactly what he was trying to do," Ohayon said.
Another passenger told the Jerusalem Post that intervening passengers shouted at two off-duty pilots at the back of the plane "to run and take control" of it, and one of them did so after the passengers managed to remove the attacker from the cockpit.
Israeli sources told the Post the would-be hijacker was an Omani national. There was no immediate confirmation of the details from Israeli or Saudi officials.
The crew of FlyDubai flight 1073, a Boeing 737 Max 8 aircraft, transmitted an emergency alert shortly after takeoff on Wednesday, according to publicly available flight tracking information. CBS News' British partner network BBC News said flight tracking data showed the aircraft plummeted more than 17,000 feet in two minutes around 8:21 a.m. local time.
A statement from FlyDubai said only that "an altercation occurred in the flight deck" and that the aircraft "was successfully secured by on-duty flydubai crew traveling on the flight, who diverted and landed the aircraft safely" in Saudi Arabia.
The airline confirmed said "all passengers and crew are safe and accounted for," and it confirmed that two replacement aircraft had been deployed to Tabuk to "relieve the passengers and crew," though many Israeli passengers told media outlets they would not reboard a FlyDubai plane.
"At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation," the airline said in its statement, urging "all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts."
The Associated Press cited an official as saying Israel scrambled warplanes during the incident, fearing a possible hijacking of the plane carrying dozens of Israeli citizens.
Netanyahu had warned in recent days of unspecified, escalating security threats to Israel and its interests amid its ongoing operations against Iran-allied Hamas in the Gaza Strip and Hezbollah in Lebanon.
FlyDubai is the lower-cost sister carrier of the United Arab Emirates state-owned flagship carrier Emirates airlines. The UAE has become a popular vacation destination for Israeli tourists since the two nations normalized ties in 2020.
Israel has not experienced a plane hijacking in decades, but it maintains some of the strictest airport security in the world.
Israel's far-right national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, in a social media post on Wednesday, said "the naive notion that our enemies value life and that we should have mercy on them received another reminder this morning in the form of a terrorist who planned to crash a plane and murder the 180 Israelis on board."
Israeli politician Benny Gantz, who is running in upcoming Israeli elections but polling badly, wrote on X: "It's still too early to know what the sequence of events was in this morning's Flydubai flight to Israel, but it's already clear that Israelis are a rare breed."
"The resourcefulness and courage displayed by the passengers on this flight, in the face of clear mortal danger, are exactly the stuff our people are made of," he said.
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee also posted about the incident Wednesday, saying: "Well this had everyone in the Middle East (esp Israel) on FULL ALERT this morning."
"Glad it wasn't more serious," he added, "but having pilots inflight detouring to 'fist city' not your ordinary experience."

Taiwan's GlobalWafers August profit rises 145% as wafer market outlook improves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:59:07 UTC
16:59:07 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — GlobalWafers Co.’s August profit more than doubled, with the silicon wafer industry expected to strengthen as AI and memory chipmakers expand production.
The company reported August revenue of NT$4.76 billion (US$149.6 million), up 7.63% from the same month a year earlier. Profit reached NT$704 million, a 144.98% year-on-year increase, according to CTEE and MoneyDJ.
AI and memory chipmakers are ramping up production, supporting orders for 12-inch products. A new round of price increases under long-term contracts for 2027 is gradually taking shape, further improving the outlook for wafer suppliers.
GlobalWafers' August revenue remained relatively subdued, partly due to a fire at its Novara plant in Italy in July and the traditional summer holiday period in Europe, which typically slows industrial activity. The company said the Novara facility is recovering faster than originally planned after the fire affected part of its back-end production of 8-inch wafers.
Key plant systems have been restored, while the epitaxial wafer process, which was not directly affected by the fire, has resumed. The first batch produced after the fire has already been shipped.
Full production has yet to resume, however, as back-end processes directly affected by the fire are still being rebuilt. Other GlobalWafers providing support are operating at full capacity.
On pricing, GlobalWafers has been negotiating with customers over adjustments for the second half of the year to reflect higher energy, raw material, logistics and overseas manufacturing costs. The size of the adjustments varies by product specifications and customer.
Meanwhile, market prices for 6-inch, 8-inch and 12-inch silicon wafers have been rising, with prices for some 12-inch products already adjusted. GlobalWafers is expected to benefit from high utilization rates at its existing facilities, the gradual recovery of its Novara plant, and higher wafer prices.
The market outlook is supported by a structural supply gap for silicon wafers, the base material used to manufacture semiconductor chips. Made from high-purity silicon, wafers provide the surface on which circuits are formed during chip manufacturing, according to Pocket Securities.
Twelve-inch wafers are widely used for AI servers, high-performance computing and advanced chips. Global monthly demand has reached about 11 million 12-inch wafers, while effective supply remains below 10 million.

Poundland’s management team are in “advanced talks” to lead a bid for the ailing cut-price retailer that could save up to 11,000 jobs.
The former Asda boss Andy Bond, who ran Poundland for a number of years from 2016 then stepped up to its former parent Pepco before leaving in 2025, is understood to be part of the negotiations to take on the business.
The management buyout team, which includes the current boss, Barry Williams, is understood to be negotiating with an unnamed financial backer.
Poundland’s current owners, Gordon Brothers, last month hired the advisory company Alvarez & Marsal to oversee a sale of the business at a reported price of £30m. The process has fuelled fears that the restructuring specialist is set on breaking up the retailer despite improved trading.
Interested parties are thought to include the US company Fortress, which owns Poundstretcher, and Modella Capital, the UK-based private equity owner of Hobbycraft and TG Jones that this year put the UK arm of Claire’s and The Original Factory Shop into administration. Neither of these players are involved with Bond’s team.
Sources said these financial companies were among those placing a first round of bids at the start of this week that are to be considered as early as Wednesday.
One source said very few bids were expected to include the entire business and it was a “great shame” if an offer to keep the business trading was not considered.
The discount chain, which employs 11,000 people and has 600 stores, said last week that it had returned to growth of 3.3% at established stores in the latest three-month period. “Profitability is on a strongly improving trajectory with expected pre-tax earnings around £80m better than last year.”
The company registered an £85m pre-tax loss in the year to the end of September 2025 but said it had a cash pile of more than £30m and several sources of borrowings.
Gordon Brothers had put in place a £95m lending facility, of which only £50m had been used, Poundland said.
The restructuring specialist, which bought Poundland from for £1 from Pepco Group in June 2025, agreed to pump £80m into the company as part of a rescue deal last year.
About 149 Poundland stores shut with the loss of 2,200 jobs under the rescue shake-up launched after challenging trading conditions and unpopular clothing ranges sent the retailer into the red.
It has since refocused on £1 items and relaunched its Pep & Co clothing brand after a switch to ranges supplied by its former parent group hit sales
However, the uncertainty about Poundland’s future has reportedly prompted an insurer to some of Poundland’s suppliers to pull credit. The move could cause problems with its supply of goods.

Chair of Russian opposition party Yabloko charged with “hooliganism” for spoiling his election ballot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:57:41 UTC
16:57:41 KST

A citation for petty hooliganism was filed against Russian opposition politician Nikolai Rybakov, chair of the Yabloko party, after he wrote slogans on four ballots during elections in St. Petersburg. The Insider identified at least 13 similar cases since 2022 in which a message or drawing on a ballot served as grounds for administrative prosecution. Rybakov became at least the 14th such voter.
Yabloko’s press service reported the petty hooliganism charges against Rybakov on Sept. 29. His case is being heard by the Vyborgsky District Court of St. Petersburg.
On Sept. 20, Rybakov voted at polling station No. 360 in St. Petersburg. None of the four ballots he was given included Yabloko or its candidates. The politician invalidated the ballots by writing “For peace,” “For freedom,” “For a ceasefire agreement,” and “For a life without fear.”
Rybakov had already done something similar in the September 2022 elections. At the time, according to photos published by the party, he wrote “I vote for peace” on his ballot before placing it in the box.
At least five such cases emerged in 2022
Some of the first known cases initiated over writing on ballots emerged during regional elections in September 2022.
In Moscow, Lev Karmanov drew a peace dove and wrote “No to war” on his ballot. Election commission members would not let him put the sheet into the electronic ballot scanner and offered him a new ballot instead while leaving the first one on the administrators’ table. Police detained Karmanov after he left the polling station, and the Chertanovsky District Court ultimately fined him 50,000 rubles ($600) for “discrediting the armed forces” — a ruling later upheld by the Moscow City Court.
The court found the message to be public, since the ballot is handed to commission members and later counted. In the ruling, it was thus stated that Karmanov “publicly displayed” a ballot with the message “No to war.”
That same day, in Veliky Novgorod, police filed a “discrediting” report against Anton Bochanov, who also wrote an antiwar phrase on his ballot before dropping it into a transparent ballot box. According to police, the message ended up facing outward and was visible to commission members and other voters.
In Kirov, a similar citation was filed against Natalia Ryabova, whose ballot bore the messages “Glory to Ukraine” and “Russia will be free,” along with an obscene phrase about Vladimir Putin. Additionally, media outlets reported on another administrative case concerning Moscow polling station No. 1936 in Orekhovo-Borisovo, where a voter left an anti-war slogan on their ballot.
Another case arose in 2022 in Aramil, Sverdlovsk Region, where art teacher Darya Sergeyeva wrote “No to war,” “Glory to Ukraine,” “Put Putin on trial,” and other phrases on her ballot while also drawing a peace dove and the Ukrainian flag. Commission members contacted the police. In November, Sergeyeva was fined 15,000 rubles ($180) for “discrediting the armed forces.”
The Insider found at least five episodes of administrative prosecutions over writing and drawings on ballots in 2022 alone.
Another six cases in 2024
The practice continued in the presidential election in March 2024. St. Petersburg resident Alexandra Chiriatyeva wrote “No to war” in red marker on the back of her ballot, and the Dzerzhinsky District Court charged her with two offenses at once: petty hooliganism and “discrediting the army.” Chiriatyeva was sentenced to eight days of arrest and fined 40,000 rubles ($480). A statement from St. Petersburg’s joint court press service claimed that by writing on the ballot, Chiriatyeva had “damaged state property.”
Another case emerged in Simferopol, where a woman wrote “No to war,” “Against human deaths,” and “Ukraine will win” on her ballot. The Central District Court of Simferopol fined her 40,000 rubles ($480) under the article on “discrediting” the army.
In Podolsk, near Moscow, Maria Alekseyeva was detained over writing on her ballot and charged with the same offense, after which the Podolsk City Court fined her 30,000 rubles ($360).
In Bratsk, Alexander Shokhirev wrote “No to war” and “Glory to Ukraine” on his ballot, photographed it, and then dropped it into a transparent ballot box. The Bratsk City Court found him guilty both of “discrediting” the army and of displaying banned symbols. He was sentenced to 12 days of administrative arrest.
A man from Dubna, Moscow Region, made a social media post featuring a photo of his ballot, which had been spoiled with the caption “No to war.” The Dubna City Court fined him 30,000 rubles ($360) for “discrediting” the army. In his case, the grounds for the charge were not just the message itself but also the posting of the ballot photo online.
Another case occurred during St. Petersburg’s regional elections in September 2024. Election observer Marina Popova dropped a ballot marked “No to war” into the box and was cited under two articles: petty hooliganism and “discrediting” the army. The Kuibyshevsky District Court sentenced Popova to five days of arrest and a 30,000-ruble ($360) fine.
The judge initially sent the citations back to police for revision, noting that the law does not provide for standalone liability for damaging a ballot. The following day, a different judge found Popova guilty after members of the election commission argued at the hearing that the ballot was state property and had been damaged.
In total, The Insider found at least six such episodes in 2024.
In 2026, ballot cases have already led to arrests
Besides Rybakov’s case, at least two more incidents are known from the September 2026 elections.
Stanislav Morozov, a blogger from Penza, posted a video of himself filling out ballots: on one, he wrote an obscene phrase about Vladimir Putin, and on another he crossed out the name United Russia and added a separate obscene message. The Pervomaisky District Court of Penza sentenced him to 14 days of arrest for petty hooliganism — the same article of the administrative code applied to Rybakov. The court’s published materials did not specify which of Morozov’s actions was deemed petty hooliganism.
In Vladimir, Alexander Stepanov wrote on his ballot: “No to war! For peace!” The slogan was noticed after the ballot ended up in a transparent ballot box. The Frunzensky District Court of Vladimir fined Stepanov 30,000 rubles ($360) for “discrediting” the army.
The Insider’s count of 14 such cases since 2022 excludes incidents in which people were only detained but no record of citation could be found, as well as detentions in which the report was filed solely over other actions, such as resisting police.
In at least three previous cases — those of Chiriatyeva, Popova, and Morozov — law enforcement used the same Part 1 of Article 20.1 of the Code of Administrative Offenses on petty hooliganism that is now being applied against Rybakov. The maximum penalty under this article is 15 days of administrative arrest.
Yabloko’s federal party list was removed from the State Duma race on Aug. 10 after internal polling appeared to show support for the anti-war party growing rapidly. Party leaders then urged supporters to invalidate their ballots by marking more than one box. By the start of voting, courts had also removed nearly 30% of Yabloko’s single-mandate candidates, The Insider calculated.

The EU sanctioned Russia’s Starlink rival but not the company that builds it. Experts call that the gap that matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:56:58 UTC
16:56:58 KST

The company that actually assembles Russia's homegrown answer to Starlink has been left off every Western sanctions list, a US research group and a Ukrainian anti-corruption watchdog separately told Euromaidan Press this month.
Both landed on the same gap—the manufacturer, Bureau 1440, and its leaders remain untouched by the West, even though Kyiv has already placed the firm on Ukraine's own sanctions list. They differ on how much a Western designation would achieve, not on where the opening is.
The company no Western government has sanctioned
Rassvet is Russia's low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation, built by the private firm Bureau 1440 to give Moscow's troops communications independent of SpaceX. Bureau 1440 launched its first 16 satellites in March 2026, building the network after SpaceX cut off the Russian units' unauthorized Starlink access. C4ADS, a US-based research organization, confirmed to Euromaidan Press that Bureau 1440 and its leadership sit outside every Western sanctions regime, and called designating the manufacturer the single most visible and effective step available.
Viktoriia Vyshnivska, a senior analyst at the Independent Anti-Corruption Commission (NAKO), a Ukrainian watchdog, was more measured. "We shouldn't expect a magical effect," she said, but sanctions would make the Western boards and components Bureau 1440 depends on harder and costlier to source. Many of those goods are already banned under EU export controls, she noted—yet the manufacturer itself remains off the lists.
The EU named the network but not the firm
The EU has already moved once. Its 21st sanctions package, adopted on 23 July, targeted the Rassvet network but stopped short of the manufacturer, leaving Bureau 1440 and its chief executive off the lists. On 28 August, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Kyiv had sent a formal note to the UN's telecom agency requesting that Ukraine be excluded from Rassvet's coverage. Days later, he urged EU ministers to sanction the project. Ukraine gave partners a list of nine entities tied to it, Militarnyi reported, citing sources.
For years Ukraine could find, jam, or knock out the communication links Russian forces leaned on. Rassvet may be the first it cannot. Vyshnivska put the useful window to slow it at about a year. Russia, by Ukrainian calculations, needs five to eight years to see it through.
Euromaidan Press examined how Russia built Rassvet, and how far it still has to go.

Pentagon selected Boeing for a new stealth fighter to replace the F/A-18
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:55:22 EEST
16:55:22 KST

Pentagon selected Boeing for a new stealth fighter to replace the F/A-18
Kyiv • UNN
Boeing defeated Northrop in the competition to develop the $20 billion F/A-XX. The first production aircraft are expected in the 2030s.
Boeing has been selected to develop a new-generation stealth fighter for the U.S. Navy, the Pentagon said on September 29. This is the company's second consecutive major victory in the fighter aircraft sector and concludes several months of delay for a program that is central to the U.S. strategy for countering China in the Pacific. UNN reports this with reference to Reuters.
Details
Boeing beat its competitor, Northrop Grumman Corp., in the competition for a $20 billion development contract to produce prototypes. The program could grow to hundreds of billions of dollars over its lifetime as production ramps up and, potentially, as international customers place orders.
In March last year, Boeing was also selected to develop the new F-47 stealth fighter for the U.S. Air Force, securing two major sixth-generation fighter development contracts in a row.
Boeing was viewed as a strong contender throughout the competition because of its decades-long history of developing carrier-based fighters for the U.S. Navy, including the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet, which the new fighter is intended to replace. This experience helped dispel concerns expressed by defense officials about whether Boeing would be able to provide enough engineers and suppliers simultaneously to carry out the F-47 and U.S. Navy fighter development programs—concerns that, it appears, were resolved in the company's favor, the publication writes.
Boeing shares rose 2.25% in after-hours trading on Tuesday, while Northrop shares fell 3.5%.
The new aircraft, currently designated "F/A-XX," will become the centerpiece of the U.S. Navy's next-generation family of Air Dominance systems.
The aircraft "is America's most important, non-negotiable investment in national security and long-term air combat capabilities," Michael Duffy, the Pentagon's chief weapons buyer, said in a statement.
The new aircraft is expected to have advanced stealth capabilities, improved range and endurance, as well as the ability to integrate with unmanned combat aircraft and naval carrier-based air defense systems.
The U.S. Navy still plans to acquire more than 270 Lockheed Martin F-35C aircraft for its carrier fleet, which will fly alongside the F/A-XX after it enters service. The first production F/A-XX aircraft are expected in the 2030s, while the Super Hornet fleet, which has been in service since the 1990s, is expected to continue flying into the 2040s.

South Korea calls for apology from North Korea after mine injures three soldiers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:53:24 UTC
16:53:24 KST

South Korea has demanded an apology from North Korea over a landmine blast that injured three soldiers, saying they were hurt by North Korean mines on the southern side of the border.
Kang Hyun-woo, the director of operations at South Korea’s joint chiefs of staff, demanded an apology and “responsible measures” from Pyongyang over the blast, which occurred on 21 September during a search operation south of the border.
He also called for an immediate halt to North Korea’s mine-laying and border fortification, which he said violated the armistice and the spirit of inter-Korean agreements. North Korea would bear “all responsibility” for any future developments, he said.
The incident echoes a 2015 mine blast in the demilitarised zone between the countries that seriously injured two South Korean soldiers and prompted Seoul to resume propaganda broadcasts over loudspeakers. North Korea responded to the move with artillery fire across the border before expressing regret during high-level talks.
The US-led UN command (UNC), which oversees the 1953 armistice that halted but did not end the Korean war, said on Wednesday that a joint investigation with South Korea’s military had identified a live North Korean anti-personnel mine on the southern side of the military demarcation line (MDL), the de facto border.
The UNC said an armistice violation had occurred and that it was addressing the issue through “established armistice mechanisms”.
The explosions occurred about 10 metres south of the MDL on the western front, as troops searched an area where North Korea was suspected of laying mines.
Two blasts went off about a minute apart, seriously injuring a battalion commander, whose foot was reportedly severed at the ankle, and an engineer. A third officer was present and has minor injuries from the explosion.
On Monday, South Korea’s military said interim findings showed the blasts were “highly likely” to have been caused by North Korean mines
North Korea has denied involvement. In a statement carried by state media on Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong, the sister of leader Kim Jong-un, called the incident “an obvious self-staged farce”.
“Our soldiers have never once crossed the border,” she said, warning that if South Korean troops fired directly at North Korean soldiers, border units would carry out “immediate and merciless retaliation”.
Chris Green, a senior consultant at the International Crisis Group, said the investigation findings would not settle the matter politically because the North would always have “guaranteed plausible deniability”.
There are no working communication channels between the two Koreas. Pyongyang severed ties in 2024, declared South Korea a hostile state and has since laid mines and built fortifications along the border. “Accidental escalation on the Korean peninsula is always just a few steps away and it’s fewer steps now than it was in 2015,” Green said.
The blast presents a challenge for South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, who has sought to revive diplomacy with Pyongyang. Last week, he told the UN general assembly that Seoul would be a “pacemaker” for peace, and urged Washington to ease sanctions in exchange for a freeze on North Korea’s weapons programmes.
The incident has also fuelled political tensions at home. Opposition politicians questioned whether the investigation had been delayed to avoid overshadowing Lee’s UN speech, a suggestion the presidential office denied.
The conservative People Power party has also called for the return of the propaganda loudspeakers, which were switched off and dismantled under Lee last year.
The mine blast adds to other diplomatic difficulties facing Lee. On Monday, Seoul demanded an apology from Ukraine after its president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, disclosed the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.
Seoul said the two sides had agreed to keep the transfer secret, citing the men’s safety and diplomatic and security considerations. Some critics said the secrecy was about not upsetting Pyongyang.

Independents Meelis Kiili and Leo Kunnas to run on Center Party ticket in March elections

Independents Meelis Kiili and Leo Kunnas to run on Center Party ticket in March elections
Meelis Kiili said shared views on security and societal development played an important role in the decision.
"I will start cooperating with the Center Party, but I will not join the party," Kiili told ERR's Russian-language portal on Wednesday morning.
Kiili and Leo Kunnas were jointly offered the opportunity to support the Center Party on security issues.
"These are times when standing aside would be unreasonable. I assessed my abilities, potential, the work I have done and my health and realized that I am in excellent shape and have a lot to offer. I made my final decision after I was able to present my program and vision to the Center Party leadership. It was a series of substantive discussions and I felt that I was understood," Kiili said.
Discussing the main points of his program, Kiili emphasized the need to unite society on national defense issues.
"We must not divide society, but rather strengthen it. Defense is not just military defense; it is also public security. It means the economy, it means social ties," Kiili said.
Kiili left open the question of whether he would head the Center Party's candidate list in Ida-Viru County.
"I am from there and I live there. But we have not yet agreed where I will run," Kiili said.
Offers from other parties
He said he had also received offers of cooperation from other parties but had not held negotiations with them.
Kiili confirmed that Leo Kunnas will also run on the Center Party's list. Kiili said the two had consulted closely with each other, having also found considerable common ground in the current Riigikogu while serving on the National Defense Committee.
"Although we represented different parliamentary groups, we have a great deal in common. We were able to draw up a national defense report that crossed party lines. We share common views and understandings," Kiili said.
In an interview with "Aktuaalne kaamera," Kunnas said he had not been asked to formally join the Center Party. His role is expected to be to assist the party with his knowledge and expertise.
"I have a long-standing tradition of remaining outside political parties," he said. Kunnas confirmed, however, that he had agreed to run on the Center Party's candidate list.
On Wednesday morning, the Center Party sent the media an invitation to Toompea, where it said it would "introduce Riigikogu MPs who will begin cooperating with the Center Party parliamentary group and will run for parliament on the Center Party's list."
Center Party Chairman Mihhail Kõlvart said at a press conference that both Kunnas and Kiili bring expertise to the party. "The Center Party's broader goal today is to strengthen its expertise in every field," he added.
Kõlvart explained that security is currently the priority and that the Center Party's new members have a vision for how the defense sector should develop. "They have leadership experience and a conceptual proposal for the Center Party on what our election platform should contain," he said.
Kiili went on to say that shortcomings in Estonia's security became apparent while the national defense report was being prepared. "But the report is one thing and the other is something the public is not yet very aware of. In parallel, we began developing a conceptual program to address those shortcomings," he said.
Kiili prepared to become defense minister
In an interview with "Aktuaalne kaamera," Kiili said he would also be prepared to serve as Estonia's defense minister.
Kunnas, meanwhile, said he had been ready to draw a line under his political activities. "When I left active service in 2007, I did so because the institution of the commander of the defense forces was removed from the Constitution of the Republic of Estonia, after which the status of both the commander and the Defense Forces itself gradually weakened and the Defense Forces was stripped of several key functions necessary for conducting combat operations," he explained.
He now believes the institution of the commander of the defense forces could be strengthened again and that the Defense Forces could regain its core functions.
Kunnas considers it necessary to address all the shortcomings identified in the national defense report. He also sees strategic problems in how the country is governed. "Number one, we don't manage resources; number two, we don't manage people," he said.

AI generated
JOHANNESBURG – Violence against women in South Africa is a national shame, President Cyril Ramaphosa said, after another woman’s corpse was found dumped over the weekend.
Eleven women’s bodies have been found in Ekurhuleni, a municipality east of Johannesburg, since July, reigniting public anger and fear after repeated government pledges have failed to curb gender-based violence.
The victims are mostly aged in their 20s or 30s, and some have been found stripped and showing signs of sexual violence.
“There are women lying tonight in government mortuaries waiting to be identified, waiting for someone to claim them, waiting to be taken home and laid to rest. How can our hearts not be broken? How can we not be angry?” Ramaphosa said in a televised address late on Sept 29.
“The violence inflicted upon the women of South Africa is a source of profound pain and national shame. The nation is angry. The women of South Africa are angry.”
Ramaphosa said police had not found evidence that a serial killer was behind the 11 women’s deaths but said all possibilities were still under investigation.
He said arrests had been made in connection with three of the killings and reiterated that investigations into all of the deaths would not be allowed to go cold.
South Africa has one of the highest per-capita murder rates in the world, but policing is weakened by corruption and a lack of resources. Only about one in 10 murders is solved. REUTERS

Nearly 40% of world population exposed to harmful ozone pollution in 2026: EU climate agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:51:31 UTC
16:51:31 KST

Melike Pala
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Nearly 40% of the world's population has been exposed to harmful levels of ground-level ozone in 2026, according to a new analysis by the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS).
The analysis, published Wednesday, shows how extreme heat and human-caused air pollution combined to drive ozone pollution across large parts of the world during the first eight months of the year.
According to CAMS, only 5% of the global population was exposed to ozone levels classified as "good" under the analysis, while Asia was the world's most affected region, followed by Europe and North America.
Some 60% of Asia's population was exposed to "extremely poor" ozone levels in 2026, rising to 90% when populations exposed to "poor" and "very poor" levels were included.
In Europe, 50% of the population experienced "poor," "very poor" or "extremely poor" ozone exposure, with repeated heat waves between June and August contributing to elevated ozone concentrations.
In North America, more than two-thirds of the population experienced "poor," "very poor" or "extremely poor" ozone exposure, with emissions from major wildfires contributing to elevated ozone concentrations.
CAMS said Oceania remained the region with the lowest ozone exposure, with its entire population experiencing "good" or "fair" ozone levels.
In South America, 81% of the population experienced "good" or "fair" ozone exposure, while the figure for Africa was 56%.
The analysis also highlighted the increasing importance of transboundary air pollution, with wildfire smoke, desert dust and other pollutants traveling thousands of kilometers across national borders and oceans.
CAMS said the findings underline the relationship between climate change and air quality.
Ozone itself is a greenhouse gas, while higher temperatures can create conditions that favor ozone formation, creating what scientists describe as an "ozone-climate penalty."
"Air pollution does not respect national borders," Laurence Rouil, director of CAMS, said. "Wildfire smoke, ozone and dust can travel thousands of kilometers, affecting communities far from their source."
Rouil said the findings highlight the need for global action on air quality alongside climate measures.

- The sole-source award runs through September 2030, with a third of the work in Louisville, Kentucky.
Raytheon has won a $247.1 million contract to build, upgrade and overhaul Phalanx close-in weapon systems for the U.S. Navy and U.S. Army, covering the shipboard gun, its land-based counterpart and the missile-armed SeaRAM, the U.S. Department of War announced.
Naval Air Systems Command awarded the firm-fixed-price contract to the RTX business without competition. It covers production, upgrades, conversions and overhauls of MK 15 Close-In Weapon Systems, along with hardware, equipment and spare parts, and runs through September 2030. The notice does not say how many new systems will be built or how many existing ones will be refurbished.
Phalanx is a radar-guided, computer-controlled 20 mm Gatling gun that fires between 3,000 and 4,500 rounds per minute. It is designed to shoot down anti-ship missiles and other threats that get past a ship’s longer-range defenses, and Raytheon says it is installed on every U.S. Navy surface combatant class and on ships from 24 allied nations.
The gun proved its value in combat on Jan. 30, 2024, when the destroyer USS Gravely (DDG 107) used its Phalanx to destroy a Houthi anti-ship cruise missile in the Red Sea. The missile had come within about 1.6 km (1 mile) of the ship, a matter of seconds from impact, and it was the first time a U.S. warship had needed the system during the Red Sea campaign.
The U.S. Army’s share of the contract goes to the Land-based Phalanx Weapon System, the core of its Counter Rocket, Artillery and Mortar defense, known as C-RAM. The land version, fielded since 2005, uses the same gun and radar to shoot down incoming rockets, artillery shells and mortar rounds over bases. The contract also covers SeaRAM, which pairs Phalanx’s sensors with a launcher for RIM-116 Rolling Airframe Missiles to engage threats at longer range than the gun.
The funding split shows how much of the work is for the U.S. Army. Of the roughly $240.6 million obligated at award, all of it fiscal 2026 money, about $104.2 million comes from U.S. Army procurement and operations and maintenance accounts. The remaining $136.4 million comes from four U.S. Navy accounts: procurement, operations and maintenance, shipbuilding, and weapons procurement.
A third of the work will take place in Louisville, Kentucky, the main center for Phalanx production and overhauls, and 7% in Tucson, Arizona. The rest is spread across 16 other named sites in the United States, plus Ottobrunn, Germany, at 4%, and various U.S. locations accounting for 23%.
The award follows a $205 million U.S. Navy contract Raytheon received in September 2025 for similar Phalanx production, upgrade and overhaul work running through 2029. In June 2025, the U.S. Army separately awarded Raytheon $279.2 million for management support of its Land-based Phalanx fleet through 2030.

Major banks raise interest rates after RBA lifts cash rate to highest since 2011
Australia's major banks will lift variable home loan rates by 0.25 per cent from next month, after the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) lifted the cash rate to its highest level in more than a decade.
This week's RBA decision took the country's cash rate to 4.6 per cent, an increase of 0.25 per cent, and the fourth hike this year.
The cash rate is the highest it has been since November 2011.
Commonwealth Bank, NAB, Westpac and ANZ announced increases to home loan variable interest rates by 0.25 per cent per annum, effective October 9.
CBA's group executive retail banking, Angus Sullivan, said the RBA's decision came during persistent inflation and ongoing global uncertainty, which were adding to economic pressures.
Most banks acknowledged many mortgage holders may struggle with the increased payments.
NAB group executive personal banking, Ana Marinkovic, said concerned customers should contact the bank early about their finances.
Westpac chief executive, consumer, Carolyn McCann, acknowledged the increase would impact households' cost-of-living pressures.
ANZ said it was reviewing its other interest rates.
Macquarie Bank also announced it would make changes to interest rates across its variable home loan and deposit products from October 15.
Its variable interest rates on transaction and savings accounts will increase by 0.25 per cent per annum, along with its variable home loan reference rates.

US sanctions target growing influence of Russia’s transnational economy — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:45:42 UTC
16:45:42 KST

ISTRA /Moscow Region/, September 30. /TASS/. The United States is using sanctions and economic pressure to counter the growing influence of Russia’s transnational economy, corresponding member of the Russian Academy of Sciences and director of the Primakov Institute of World Economy and International Relations (IMEMO) Fyodor Voitolovsky said at a session of the 23rd Annual Meeting of the Valdai International Discussion Club.
He noted that today "investment by Indian companies that are becoming transnational is growing, while many Russian companies have also become transnational."
"This is what the United States and its allies are primarily fighting against by creating this system of sanctions, restrictions, and economic pressure," Voitolovsky said. "They are fighting to prevent Russia from becoming one of the leading players in the global economy, with a vast transnational economy built around Russian companies."
According to the expert, over the past several decades the world has seen "the interests of big business and transnational corporations become increasingly intertwined with the interests of the state."
"With technological development, with advances in modern information and communications technologies, energy technologies, and many other areas, it is becoming clear that without state involvement, without strategic government investment in infrastructure and major long-term projects, and without cooperation between states and large transnational private businesses, neither countries nor transnational corporations, which are no longer exclusively Western, will become more competitive," he said.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said recurring incidents against the Muslim community in the country may not be isolated cases but could be part of orchestrated campaigns.
"The recurrence of incidents – both alleged and real – over a relatively short period of time leads me to believe that these are not random outbursts of emotion, but campaigns for which orchestrators should be sought," Nausėda told LNK television on Wednesday.
In mid-September, a Quran was allegedly burned publicly in Vilnius, with a pre-trial investigation into hooliganism launched over the incident.
Meanwhile, during Muslim prayers outside a mosque in Kaunas, bikers staged a protest, which included displaying a pig’s head. An investigation into incitement against a group of people and disruption of religious ceremonies has been launched over the incident.
Nausėda said Lithuania should remain a country where different religions and cultures coexist peacefully. He also said the migration issue is relevant, but it must be addressed directly, rather than through actions such as displaying pig's heads.
Previously, Nausėda proposed legalising a new model of fixed-term work permits for foreign nationals, which would speed up the processing of immigrants' applications and require them to leave Lithuania for at least six months after their two-year work permit expires.
In mid-July, parliament approved the president's proposals after deliberation. If parliament approves Nausėda's proposed amendments, they will come into force next year.
According to Nausėda, migration issues should not be addressed by focusing on separating Christian and non-Christian countries.
"Yes, there are issues related to additional tensions because people come from a completely [different] cultural environment, but they are not automatically bad people in themselves or people who wish ill upon Lithuania," the president said. "We should not fight against nationalities or countries; we should fight against the overall influx of migration."
He stressed that Lithuania should take action as soon as possible so that increasing immigration does not become a major challenge for the country.

U.S. Navy pays Boeing to plan Super Hornet line shutdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:41:37 UTC
16:41:37 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Boeing a $16.7 million order to plan the shutdown of the Super Hornet and Growler production lines, with work running to November 2030.
- Boeing will inventory government-owned tooling in St. Louis, El Segundo and Bethpage and recommend what to keep, store or dispose of.
The U.S. Navy has paid Boeing $16.7 million to plan the shutdown of the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and EA-18G Growler production lines, including a full inventory of the government-owned tools and equipment used to build the jets.
The firm-fixed-price order, placed by Naval Air Systems Command against an existing Boeing ordering agreement, covers planning, analysis, engineering and program management for closing the lines. Boeing will catalog and assess the tooling and production equipment, recommend what should be kept, stored or disposed of, and deliver a master property inventory and disposition plan. The work runs until November 2030.
The U.S. Navy announced the order on Sept. 29, the same day it picked Boeing to develop the F/A-XX, the sixth-generation carrier fighter meant to eventually replace both the Super Hornet and the Growler. The shutdown order was not competed and is funded entirely with fiscal 2024 Navy aircraft procurement money.
About 60% of the work will take place in St. Louis, where Boeing assembles the Super Hornet. Another 37% is set for El Segundo, California, where Northrop Grumman has long built the center and aft fuselage sections for the F/A-18E/F and EA-18G, and 3% for Bethpage, New York, where Northrop Grumman integrated the Growler’s electronic attack systems.
New Super Hornet production is already close to its end. The U.S. Navy placed its last order, for 17 Block III jets, in 2024 after Congress funded the aircraft, pushing the planned closure of the St. Louis line from 2025 to 2027. Final deliveries are expected by spring 2027.
Northrop Grumman finished the last fuselage sections and vertical tails for those jets last year, and Boeing confirmed it no longer builds the Growler, The War Zone reported in January. Growler production ended after the U.S. Navy and Australian orders were completed in the late 2010s, with the U.S. Navy buying 160 of the electronic warfare jets.
Both aircraft will stay in service for years after the lines close. Boeing’s Service Life Modification program, which adds Block III upgrades and 4,000 flight hours to older Super Hornets, is projected to continue into the mid-2030s, though Boeing is moving that work out of St. Louis to San Antonio and Fleet Readiness Center Southwest by 2027. The U.S. Navy plans to keep the Growler flying until 2046.
The F/A-XX will not arrive quickly enough to replace either jet soon. The Pentagon said the new fighter will begin to augment and eventually replace Super Hornets and Growlers in the 2030s.
The contract notice does not say how much tooling the U.S. Navy owns across the three sites, or whether any of it will be kept to produce spare parts for the fleet after the last new jet is delivered.

Andy Burnham: UK could ‘go all the way’ by rejoining EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:41:26 UTC
16:41:26 KST

Andy Burnham has opened the door to the UK rejoining the EU, saying Britain could “go all the way”, as he prepares to reconsider Labour’s post-Brexit red lines.
The prime minister used a series of interviews after his emotional Labour conference speech to spell out how wide-ranging his consideration of Britain’s future with Brussels could be because Brexit had caused “more harm than good”.
Burnham said the government could keep the current arrangements, seek a customs union, return to the single market or “go all the way” in what would be full EU membership. Speaking to the BBC, he said ministers would examine “what is doable” and the “pros and cons” of each option.
Asked whether he wanted the UK to rejoin the bloc, the prime minister told Radio 4’s Today programme he wanted to “look at the options”. He added: “We could stay as we are. That’s definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay. We could look at what George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said at their conference about the single market or we could go all the way.”
It is a significant shift from the position Labour fought the 2024 election on. Its manifesto explicitly ruled out returning to the EU single market or customs union, as well as restoring freedom of movement.
A customs union would bring Britain much closer to the EU on trade in goods. The UK and EU would apply the same tariffs to imports from elsewhere, removing trade barriers businesses have faced after Brexit. But it would not on its own put Britain back inside the wider single market or remove every border check.
If Britain were to rejoin the single market, it would be a significant step with the country having to accept closer alignment with EU rules.
“There are clearly options that need to be considered, and we have to look at what is doable and what would be the pros and cons of each,” Burnham told the BBC.
Although Burnham has not set out any timetables or specifics, to “go all the way” would mean considering EU membership. He went further in his interviews on Wednesday than his conference speech in which he told delegates Britain could not keep avoiding a decision about its long-term relationship with its largest trading partner.
The prime minister has vowed to set out different choices facing the country around the time of the UK-EU summit in November. “We’ve been in a rut. The country hasn’t been working for people as it should,” he told BBC Breakfast. The summit was originally supposed to take place in July under Keir Starmer but was postponed after his resignation.
While Britain will take part in the Erasmus + scheme again in 2027, the EU has authorised talks at the summit on closer electricity-market links, with negotiations on food trade and youth mobility still under way.
Burnham argued in his conference speech that leaving the EU had weakened Britain’s cooperation with EU countries on migration and said the summit would assess how the two parties could work more closely. “We will not give Britain the clear path we need into the rest of the century until we decide on a long-term relationship with what is still our largest market,” Burnham said in his speech on Tuesday in Liverpool.
“I cannot say to you that where we are is good enough. Brexit has done more harm than good. So I will take the opportunity around the [UK-EU] summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe are the different options for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners. And there are different options.”
The prime minister was more cautious when pressed on help households could receive in the budget given the looming winter and rising energy and fuel costs. Burnham said he was considering “everything that might help people” including whether to scrap panned fuel duty increases.
“The question I’ve got is: ‘How many can I afford?’” he told BBC Breakfast. The chancellor, John Healey, has said “fiscal discipline” will be at the heart of his budget despite facing calls to offer people more help with the cost of living.

Israel-Bound Flydubai Flight Diverts to Saudi Arabia After Pilots Fight

A flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv diverted to Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after a violent incident involving the pilots triggered emergency signals and prompted Israel to scramble fighter aircraft.
Flight FZ1073, carrying around 180 passengers, was flying toward Israel when it transmitted the international emergency code 7700 before briefly switching to code 7500, which indicates possible unlawful interference or a hijacking, according to flight-tracking data reported by The Times of Israel.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Boeing 737 then turned toward Saudi Arabia and landed safely at Tabuk Airport in the country’s northwest.
The aircraft had also undergone a sharp descent during the incident. Flightradar24 data cited by Reuters showed the plane dropping nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds before the first emergency signal.
Flydubai confirmed that the aircraft had experienced an “incident” while en route to Tel Aviv and landed safely in Tabuk. The airline said all passengers were safe and accounted for and that it was working with the relevant authorities, but did not provide details about what happened aboard the plane.
The initial fear of a hijacking was later ruled out. An Israeli official told Reuters that the pilots had transmitted the emergency signals after getting into a physical altercation with each other. It was not immediately clear whether either pilot had intentionally transmitted the signals.
Russia’s Su-75: Can Putin’s F-35 Rival Ever Get Off the Ground?
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu held consultations over the incident, while military chief Eyal Zamir conducted a situational assessment with senior air force and military officials.
Passengers describe chaos in cockpit
Later reports suggested the confrontation may have been more serious than a simple fight.
Passengers told Israeli media they heard screams coming from the cockpit and saw blood after the cockpit door was opened. One passenger account cited by The Times of Israel described a pilot apparently being stabbed with a pocketknife.
Reuters separately reported that a passenger’s family member said she was told that a man had taken a knife and forced a pilot onto the floor, with blood visible in the cockpit. Reuters said it could not immediately verify a photograph reportedly showing a bloodied shirt from inside the aircraft.
Israeli passengers and other crew members reportedly helped restrain the person involved.
Israeli officials have since said there are indications that one of the pilots may have attempted to take control of the aircraft and crash it. The Times of Israel described the claim as an indication under investigation rather than an established finding.
Second pair of pilots reportedly helped
The Times of Israel later reported, citing Channel 12, that a second team of pilots was traveling aboard the aircraft as passengers, dressed in civilian clothes.
According to the report, those pilots helped prevent one of the flight’s pilots from taking control of the aircraft. A senior Israeli official told Channel 12 that without their intervention, the incident could have ended in a major disaster.
The Times of Israel explicitly said the account had not been confirmed.
The same report, citing Israel’s Walla news outlet, said the pilot under investigation is an Omani citizen. That detail has also not been independently confirmed by flydubai, Saudi authorities or the UAE.
Earlier Israeli media reports said one pilot was of Russian origin and the other was Ukrainian, but those reports did not establish their citizenship.
Israeli fighters scrambled
The emergency signals initially prompted fears that the aircraft had been hijacked. Israeli fighters were reportedly scrambled as authorities tried to establish what was happening aboard the plane.
The flight was traveling over the region between Jordan and Saudi Arabia when it changed course toward Tabuk. The 7500 signal, which is associated with unlawful interference, was followed by another general emergency signal before the aircraft landed.
Netanyahu’s office said the situation was under control and that measures were being taken to return the Israeli passengers safely to Israel.
The Israeli military said Zamir held an assessment with Air Force chief Maj. Gen. Omer Tischler, Operations Directorate chief Maj. Gen. Itzik Cohen and Intelligence Directorate chief Maj. Gen. Shlomi Binder.
Investigation continues
The exact circumstances of the cockpit incident remain under investigation. Flydubai has so far described the event only as an “incident” and has not publicly confirmed reports of a fight, stabbing, attempted hijacking or the nationalities of the pilots.
The aircraft landed safely in Tabuk, and all passengers were accounted for. Flydubai said its teams were working with the relevant authorities and that further updates would be issued as confirmed information became available.
Flydubai operates daily flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv. Saudi Arabia and Israel do not have official diplomatic relations, although Saudi airspace has been open to Israeli commercial flights since 2022.

‘Dire situation’: Lebanese prisoners on hunger strike for 18 days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:40:07 UTC
16:40:07 KST

‘Dire situation’: Lebanese prisoners on hunger strike for 18 days
The medical condition of dozens of prisoners has deteriorated as inmates protest against suspension of amnesty law.
The medical condition of dozens of inmates on a hunger strike for more than two weeks inside Lebanon’s largest prison has become “dire”, and prisoners are refusing medication, according to a legal campaigner and a detainee.
Jassem Saad el-Din, who has been held in prison for about 10 years, spoke to Al Jazeera from the Roumieh prison about the protest against the suspension of a general Amnesty law that could have allowed the release of prisoners.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Syria and Lebanon make ‘significant progress’ at talks on joint interests
- list 2 of 3Lebanon and Syria reshape ties amid Israeli attacks and regional shifts
- list 3 of 3Lebanon passes long-sought amnesty law, a day after death penalty repeal
“We have been on a hunger strike for 18 days now – no medication, no medical care, nothing,” said Jassem, who is among hundreds of inmates on hunger strike.
“It’s actually been 10 and a half years that I have been detained without … being sentenced,” said Jassem, who was arrested after being accused of smuggling weapons and medicine to Syria during the war. “I mean, there isn’t a single country in the entire world that would keep a prisoner detained for this long without a sentence.”
Mohammed Sablouh, a Lebanese lawyer, earlier told Al Jazeera that about 400 prisoners are on a hunger strike. “Ambulances enter daily to take [dozens of] them away because their condition is dire,” he said.
“The prisoners are refusing medication, food and water,” Sablouh, who is also the director of the Prisoners’ Rights Center at the Tripoli Bar Association, said on Wednesday.
The inmates at Roumieh prison went on a hunger strike on September 12 in protest against the suspension of the amnesty law, which could have benefitted convicted prisoners and undertrials.
Protests have also been staged in Lebanon’s Tripoli, a Sunni-majority city, against the suspension of the law.
‘A political opportunity’
Most of the prisoners on hunger strike are Sunnis who were arrested for their solidarity with the Syrian revolution against President Bashar al-Assad, who was toppled in December 2024 after more than 10 years of bloody war.
The Free Patriotic Movement (FPM), one of the country’s largest parties, filed an appeal before the Constitutional Council over concerns that some of the inmates were charged with “terrorism”, including attacking the Lebanese army and planning bombings.
Hezbollah, one of the most powerful political groups, initially backed the law in the hope of getting amnesty for prisoners from the Shia community. But the group’s political arm did not vote for the bill due to its opposition to the release of Sunni prisoners, many of whom were jailed for their links to the Syrian war.
The Iran-aligned Hezbollah was a backer of al-Assad during the war, and sent thousands of its fighters to Syria to defend the Syrian regime.
The Constitutional Council is expected to issue its verdict next month.
Jassem said Hezbollah and FPM were behind challenging the amnesty law. “They are treating this as a political opportunity; they want to capitalise on this issue – or perhaps gain something from it, though God only knows exactly what,” he said.
“Our support for the Syrian Revolution is a primary reason why some of our young men – indeed, the majority of us – were imprisoned,” he told Al Jazeera.
Overcrowded prisons
Lebanese prisons are notorious for being overcrowded and thousands of inmates spend years behind bars without trial. Lebanon’s current prison population stands at more than 6,200.
The law passed on August 12 aimed to address overcrowded prison conditions in the country.
“Prison overcrowding exceeds 330 percent of the facilities’ actual capacity,” Sablouh said.
“The situation in Lebanon’s prisons is truly tragic, it can no longer withstand any … shock or any overturning of the amnesty law.”
More than 40 prisoners died in 2025. “Some died due to medical neglect, others under torture. Some died by suicide due to prolonged trials and repeated postponements,” Sablouh said.
The Lebanese lawyer blamed judicial delays for the large number of inmates, many of them arrested for petty crimes.
He pointed out the failure of the judiciary “to adhere to Article 108 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which sets a limit for pre-trial detention: two months for misdemeanours, renewable for an equal period, and six months for felonies, renewable for an equal period [up to a maximum of one year].”

Bruges cracks down on illegal holiday accommodation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:38:13 UTC
16:38:13 KST

The city of Bruges, capital of West Flanders, is continuing its crackdown on illegal holiday accommodation. Last year, more than 200 properties used for illegal holiday accommodation were discovered; this year, the figure has already reached 60. Officials hunt for illegal holiday homes by checking online listings. However, an increasing number of complaints are also being received from residents who notice unusual activity or are bothered by noise.
Councillor Raf Reuse asked the responsible alderman, Mathijs Goderis for an update on the situation. “In 2025, the city of Bruges opened a record number of 208 dossiers on illegal holiday homes and guest rooms. This year, another 60 have been added up to and including August,” replied the alderman.
Complaints help with detection
The city’s town planning inspectors track down illegal holiday homes and guest rooms, both offline and online. “But interestingly, we are also receiving an increasing number of complaints from members of the public,” says Goderis. “These come from residents of blocks of flats who notice that flats are being let to tourists, resulting in noise and other forms of nuisance, and even prostitution.”
Lengthy proceedings
According to the alderman, many offenders act in good faith. They rectify the situation after receiving a letter from the city. However, there are also cases where the city has to go through the full enforcement procedure.
“Some operators take their cases all the way to the Court of Cassation, Belgium’s highest court for procedural disputes. Such proceedings cost the city a great deal of time and money – up to 130 working hours and 14,000 euros in legal fees,” says Goderis. The city does, however, attempt to recover these costs from the party concerned.
Enforcement remains necessary
Bruges intends to maintain its stop on new holiday homes in the city centre in coming years. Goderis highlights the importance of the historic city centre as a place of residence for the people of Bruges: “We want our historic city centre to remain a vibrant place where the people of Bruges can still find a place to live.”

Xi pays tribute to national heroes on Martyrs' Day
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:38:02 CST
16:38:02 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping straightens the ribbon on a flower basket during a ceremony to present flower baskets to fallen national heroes at Tian'anmen Square in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 30, 2026. Xi Jinping and other leaders of the Communist Party of China and the state including Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang, Li Xi and Han Zheng attended the ceremony on Wednesday. The event was held to mark Martyrs' Day. Observed on Sept. 30, one day before National Day, the day commemorates those who gave their lives for national independence and prosperity. (Xinhua/Xie Huanchi)
BEIJING, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping and other Party and state leaders attended a ceremony to present flower baskets to fallen national heroes at Tian'anmen Square in central Beijing on Wednesday morning.
The event was held to mark Martyrs' Day. Observed on Sept. 30, one day before National Day, the day commemorates those who gave their lives for national independence and prosperity.
Since Martyrs' Day was established in 2014, Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, has maintained the tradition of paying homage to fallen heroes on the day.
The other leaders who attended the ceremony on Wednesday included Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang, Li Xi and Han Zheng. They were joined by representatives from all walks of life.
At 10 a.m., all attendees sang the national anthem, followed by a moment of silence in tribute to the heroes who sacrificed their lives for the liberation of the Chinese people and the development of the People's Republic of China.
Nine large flower baskets were placed in front of the Monument to the People's Heroes.
Xi and other leaders walked up to the foot of the monument, where he straightened the ribbons on the baskets. Then, they walked around the monument to pay their tributes.
The baskets, with ribbons reading "Eternal Glory to the People's Heroes," were presented in the name of the CPC Central Committee; the National People's Congress Standing Committee; the State Council; the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference; the Central Military Commission; non-Communist parties, the All-China Federation of Industry and Commerce, and patriots without party affiliations; people's organizations and people from all walks of life; veterans, retired senior officials and the relatives of martyrs; and Chinese Young Pioneers.
Yin Li, a member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and secretary of the CPC Beijing Municipal Committee, presided over the ceremony.
This year marks the 105th founding anniversary of the CPC and the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, which lasted from 1934 to 1936. The arduous journey helped lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution. ■

Xinhua Commentary: China's sci-tech self-reliance matters at home and beyond
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:37:59 CST
16:37:59 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Science and Technology said on Tuesday that the country is rapidly moving from being a participant and contributor in global science and technology to a pioneer and leader, emerging as one of the countries with the fastest-growing innovation capacity.
The message is clear: China is determined to achieve greater self-reliance and strength in science and technology, a national imperative firmly embedded in its modernization drive.
For decades, China's growth was powered by low-value-added manufacturing, energy-intensive heavy industry and a booming property sector. That model has run its course. As the world's largest manufacturing nation pivots toward high-quality development, it must foster new growth drivers through innovation.
Science and technology lie at the heart of that transition. The 15th Five-Year Plan, China's development roadmap for 2026-2030, positions sci-tech self-reliance as a strategic underpinning, aimed at cultivating new quality productive forces -- growth driven by innovation and rising productivity rather than by traditional inputs.
This shift is backed by hard numbers. In 2025, China's total R&D spending exceeded 3.92 trillion yuan (about 584.5 billion U.S. dollars), accounting for 2.8 percent of GDP. The country now has the world's largest cohort of science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) graduates, a vast digital consumer market that fuels innovation, and leading positions in 5G, quantum communication and drones. In 2025, the added value of high-tech manufacturing above designated size grew by 9.4 percent, far outpacing overall GDP growth of 5 percent.
Behind these figures lies a deeper transformation. China is reshaping its industrial landscape -- moving from isolated technological breakthroughs to coordinated progress across entire industrial chains, and from original innovation in key core technologies to large-scale application and industrial upgrading. It also aims to deliver tangible benefits for its people: better products and services, stronger agriculture, cleaner air and water, safer food, and healthier lives.
This drive is fueled by domestic economic needs, while remaining gaps in critical technologies underscore its urgency.
Despite remarkable progress, China still relies on imports for some of the most vital technologies. Advanced semiconductors, high-end manufacturing equipment and certain key materials remain vulnerable to external supply disruptions. Recent years of export controls and technology restrictions have made one lesson clear: core technologies must be developed through its own efforts.
This is why China is placing heavy emphasis on original innovation and breakthroughs in frontier fields such as artificial intelligence (AI), quantum technology, 6G and ultra-large-scale intelligent computing clusters. It is also prioritizing the localization of semiconductors and key materials, aiming to raise yields and capacity in advanced processes.
Yet China's sci-tech drive is often misread as both threatening and inward-looking. In reality, the country continues to create new opportunities for global development.
It expands the global supply of innovation. China's open-source AI models are increasingly adopted by developers, alongside U.S. models, while its advances in batteries and clean energy have made it indispensable in the global climate effort. Deeply embedded in global supply chains and capital markets, its tech-driven growth also serves as an anchor in a world facing fragmentation: expanding high-tech manufacturing creates demand for components, materials and services worldwide.
It widens the global frontiers of knowledge. China's achievements in quantum computing, AI and space science are expanding humanity's shared scientific base. A development plan recently released by the Chinese Academy of Sciences also pledges to step up AI-enabled scientific research -- a move that could accelerate discovery and benefit the world.
It embraces shared progress. China's development brings opportunities, not threats. It has established sci-tech cooperation with more than 160 countries and regions, and will continue to pursue an open, inclusive and mutually beneficial approach.
A more innovative China, deeply woven into the global technology ecosystem, is not a zero-sum challenge but a shared opportunity. China's technological innovation will not only shape its own growth trajectory, but also influence the global economy for decades to come. ■

“When the enemy jams communications and GPS, a drone loses its orientation and may fail to complete its mission.
