EU Approves 5 Defense Projects Worth $369M, Ukraine Takes Part in 4 of Them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:15:08 UTC
16:15:08 KST

The European Commission has approved the first five European Defence Projects of Common Interest (EDPCI) worth $369 million, with Ukraine included in four of them.
The projects will strengthen Europe’s defense capabilities by developing key military systems together. Following today’s decision, the defense projects can now move towards funding.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
EDPCI is a funding track within the European Defence Industry Programme (EDIP), a $1.7 billion EU-wide initiative to strengthen and modernize Europe’s defense industry. The Commission allocated €325 million ($368.6 million) to support the creation and deployment of EDPCI, a program of large-scale industrial projects that lays the groundwork for member states to collaborate on major defense initiatives.
“The proposal concerns an area of shared competence, in particular the industrial dimension of the Union’s defence readiness. The objectives pursued by the proposal cannot be sufficiently achieved by Member States acting alone”, the European Commission wrote in the document.
The industrial projects focus on five priority areas: drones and counter-drone systems, maritime and seabed defense, space, air and missile defense, and strengthening security along the EU’s Eastern Flank, wrote the European Commission on its website. Ukraine is participating in all areas except space.
Project Details
The industrial projects focus on the following key initiatives:
Russia Hits Kyiv With Ballistic Missiles, Killing 2 Women as Child Dies in Wider Region
- Drone and Counter-Drone European Resolve (DECODER): Aims to enable the coordinated development, scaling, and deployment of European unmanned and counter-unmanned systems to address critical capability gaps across member states. The estimated budget is $3.97 billion to $5.68 billion by 2033.
- Integrated Maritime and Seabed Defence (IMSD): Seeks to establish a federated and interoperable European maritime and seabed defense architecture. It is designed to strengthen the EU’s ability to prevent, detect, deter, and respond to threats across the maritime domain. The estimated budget is $48.9 billion to $81.8 billion by 2045.
- EU Federated Integrated Air and Missile Defence (EU-FIAMD): Designed to provide member states with a collective and effective integrated air and missile defense system, including early warning information and command-and-control capabilities. The estimated budget is $62.5 billion to $90.9 billion by 2040.
- Eastern Flank Watch (EFW): A comprehensive multi-domain effort to enhance the security of the EU’s eastern border, ensuring the protection of the entire union and strengthening its defense readiness. The estimated budget is $68.2 billion to $113.6 billion by 2036.
- Space: While Ukraine will not participate in this specific initiative, the project aims to create new market opportunities and reduce the EU’s structural dependence in the space sector. The estimated budget is up to $27.3 billion by 2034.

Groups raise concerns over Taiwan’s Maanshan nuclear plant restart review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:13:30 UTC
16:13:30 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Civic groups have called for greater scrutiny and transparency in reviewing the plan to restart the Maanshan Nuclear Power Plant following the Nuclear Safety Commission’s approval of an initial proposal.
The commission said Thursday that it had completed its review of an initial plan to restart the plant in Pingtung, which ceased operations after its operating license expired in May. It added Taiwan Power Company (Taipower) must carry out additional work, including safety inspections, before submitting another report for review.
Thirty-four environmental groups issued a joint statement Tuesday saying the proposal did not contain all the information necessary to determine whether the plant should be restarted. Even if the plant is restored to an operable condition, that would not by itself guarantee the safety of its operations, per CNA.
The decision on whether to restart the plant should not be based solely on its technical feasibility, it should also take into account factors including geology, climate, and natural disasters, the groups said.
The groups called for a broader range of experts to be involved in the review, beyond nuclear specialists, as well as meaningful participation from residents living near the plant. They also asked that the names of the members of the review committee and experts be made public.
The groups include Citizens of the Earth, the Pingtung Environmental Protection Union, and the Green Citizens’ Action Alliance.
At a public hearing on Aug. 1, Li Ken-cheng (李根政), chair of Citizens of the Earth, criticized the lack of public participation in the review process, demanding that the project undergo environmental assessment.
Lin Cheng-yuan (林正原), a researcher at the Green Citizens’ Action Alliance, said at the hearing that the Maanshan plant has been operating for 40 years, increasing the risks associated with aging equipment, and many of its components can no longer be replaced.
The plan submitted for review focuses on whether the plant can return to the condition it was in before its shutdown and does not address whether it would meet current safety standards after being restarted, he added.
In March, Taipower submitted an application to renew the Maanshan plant’s operating license after lawmakers amended the Nuclear Reactor Facilities Regulation Act in May to allow nuclear power plant operators to apply for 20-year license extensions beyond the existing 40-year limit.
Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) has said the plant could resume operations as early as 2028.

Mack’s hybrid tractor aims to replace U.S. Army’s M915 trucks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:13:12 UTC
16:13:12 KST

- Mack Defense will display its hybrid-electric Common Tactical Truck line haul tractor prototype at AUSA 2026 in Washington, D.C., Oct. 12-14.
- The U.S. Army program aims to eventually replace about 35,000 heavy tactical vehicles, including platforms such as the M915 Line Haul Tractor.
Mack Defense will display a hybrid-electric heavy tractor it built for the U.S. Army’s Common Tactical Truck program at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C., Oct. 12-14.
The truck is Mack’s on-road entry for the program and is designed to replace older highway haulers such as the M915 Line Haul Tractor. The Allentown, Pennsylvania, company said on Sept. 28 that the tractor will be on show at booth No. 7501 at the Walter E. Washington Convention Center.
According to Mack Defense, the Common Tactical Truck effort supports the planned modernization and eventual replacement of about 35,000 vehicles the U.S. Army uses for combat logistics, support and service-support missions.
The line haul tractor is based on Mack’s commercial Granite truck in a 6×4 configuration, meaning three axles with two of them driven. Mack says it is set up for moving heavy loads over long distances on highways and secondary roads. It shares its underlying design with Mack’s other prototypes to keep parts common across the family, which the company says simplifies maintenance and lowers lifetime costs.
All three of Mack’s Common Tactical Truck prototypes use high-voltage hybrid-electric systems. The company says they cut fuel use, allow extended “silent watch” operation with the engine off, and can export electrical power to equipment outside the truck. Mack pitches those features for situations where refueling may be limited and soldiers depend on onboard radios, electronics and possibly small field power grids.
Mack Defense began building the hybrid approach into its entry in late 2023, when it partnered with BAE Systems to integrate BAE’s Gen3 propulsion and accessory power management systems into its prototype.
The tractor also uses drive-by-wire controls, which replace mechanical links with electronic ones. Mack says that setup supports driver-assistance features including collision avoidance, blind-spot detection, driver alerts, anti-lock brakes, traction control and rollover mitigation, and leaves room for autonomous driving later. Other features include a new suspension for rough terrain, predictive maintenance technology meant to reduce unplanned breakdowns, cybersecurity measures, and an open systems architecture intended to make future upgrades easier.
“Our team used its experience in designing and integrating advanced vehicle technologies to build these next-generation trucks,” said David Hartzell, president of Mack Defense. “These upgrades will help provide the Army with safe, innovative, cost-effective, fuel-efficient and next generation tactical vehicles.”
Mack built three prototypes for the program: an on-road tractor, an off-road tractor and a load-handling system truck. The company also submitted designs for a cargo truck with a material handling crane, a wrecker/recovery truck and a tanker.
The company received its prototype agreement on Jan. 27, 2023, when the U.S. Army awarded Other Transaction Authority deals worth $24.25 million combined to four teams: Mack Defense, Navistar Defense, Oshkosh Defense, and a partnership of American Rheinmetall Vehicles and GM Defense. Each team’s prototypes represented its offering for the M915 Line Haul Tractor and M1088 Medium Tractor, the Palletized Load System, and the Heavy Expanded Mobility Tactical Truck, and the service ran an operational demonstration of the designs in August and September 2024.
When the prototype contracts were awarded, Mack Defense said an initial production contract could cover more than 7,000 trucks valued at over $5.1 billion.
The route to that production contract shifted in January, when the U.S. Army said in a Jan. 21 notice, reported by Janes, that it was re-evaluating its truck replacement plan after reviewing industry responses to requests for information issued in the fall of 2025. Before that pause, the service had planned testing to support a single-vendor award.
On March 19, 2026, the U.S. Army published a commercial solutions opening for the program, moving its acquisition strategy toward readily available commercial products, Inside Defense reported. The solicitation covered six vehicle variants meant to replace the Palletized Load System, the Heavy Expanded Mobility Tactical Truck and the M915 Line Haul Tractor, and said the Army would not rule out firms that specialize in only one or two variants.
Mack’s announcement does not say whether the company responded to that solicitation, and it gives no production timeline, quantity or contract value.
The company’s booth will also feature three products from its parent, Volvo Group. They include a Prevost H3-45 motorcoach with 56 seats and a Volvo D13 engine, and a Volvo Construction Equipment L120 wheel loader adapted for military use with a fording kit for water up to 1.5 meters (4.9 feet) deep, a split cab to reduce height for transport, and lifting and tie-down points for air freight. A Volvo Penta D16, a 16.1-liter inline six-cylinder off-road diesel engine, completes the display.

Taiwan forum highlights health benefits of regular exercise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:13:04 UTC
16:13:04 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan should make regular exercise part of everyday life to promote the health of citizens and to save medical costs, officials said Tuesday (Sept. 22) at an international symposium in Taipei.
During his opening remarks at the symposium, Sports for All Agency Director-General Fang Jui-wen (房瑞文) asked how many people in the audience had exercised that morning. Many in the 500-seat conference room raised their hands.
Fang said the show of hands appeared roughly consistent with Taiwan’s national average but emphasized the need to encourage more people to exercise regularly. According to a survey conducted by his agency, 35.6% of people in Taiwan were classified as regular exercisers.
Taiwan defines regular exercise as exercising at least three times a week for 30 minutes each time, with a heart rate of at least 130 beats per minute or enough exertion to cause sweating and shortness of breath.
Fang said the government hopes to increase the proportion of regular exercisers because physical activity offers a range of health benefits, including a lower risk of chronic diseases such as diabetes and hypertension. He also pointed to evidence linking physical activity to a lower risk of dementia and other health problems.
“We want people to ask, ‘Have you exercised today?’ instead of the common phrase, ‘Have you eaten today?’” Fang said.
He said the symposium was designed to help Taiwan learn from international experience, particularly from Japan and South Korea, where governments have developed programs encouraging people to incorporate physical activity into their daily routines.
The event adopted the phrase “From Now On...” as its theme, encouraging people to begin exercising immediately rather than waiting. Speaking to local media after his remarks, Fang said he hoped the symposium could become an annual event and provide a platform for experts from Taiwan and other countries to exchange ideas on exercise and public health.
Health Promotion Administration Deputy Director-General Lin Li-ru (林莉茹) also emphasized the importance of exercise as Taiwan deals with rapid population aging. Lin said regular physical activity could help people prevent or manage chronic diseases and maintain their health as they age.
“Exercise can prevent illness, and the data shows that it is very important for citizens to exercise,” Lin said. “If everyone gets in the habit of daily exercise, they can learn that exercise is a very important part of good health.”
South Korea’s experience
The symposium’s first speaker was Wook Song, a professor in the Department of Physical Education at Seoul National University. His research interests include exercise physiology, aging, chronic diseases, sarcopenia, and exercise interventions for older adults.
Song said research has increasingly demonstrated the relationship between physical activity and better health outcomes. He cited research indicating that physical activity is associated with a lower risk of death from all causes, as well as benefits related to conditions including diabetes and dementia.
One large study found that people who engaged in moderate-to-vigorous activity had a 31% lower risk of death from all causes than inactive people.
“Physical activity is great medicine, and we do not need to exercise like athletes,” Song said.
He also highlighted the potential benefits of combining aerobic and resistance exercise. Song said resistance training was particularly important as people age because muscle strength and function decline over time.
He discussed sarcopenia, an age-related condition involving the loss of muscle mass and strength or physical function. The WHO included sarcopenia in the International Classification of Diseases in 2016, while South Korea added it to its national disease classification in 2021.
Song said muscle strength generally peaks in early adulthood before declining with age, raising the question of how much of that decline can be prevented or slowed through regular exercise, particularly resistance training.
Governments face an “implementation gap” because although the health benefits of physical activity are widely recognized, many people still do not exercise regularly, Song said. He suggested governments could use incentives, fitness programs, and national campaigns to encourage participation.
South Korea’s National Fitness 100 program, for example, provides physical fitness assessments, exercise counseling, and nationally recognized certificates based on participants’ fitness levels. The program is available to children, adults, and older people through fitness certification centers.
Song also highlighted Seoul’s Wrist Doctor 9988 program, which uses smartphones and wearable devices to encourage residents to increase their physical activity.
The program awards points for activities such as walking, with accumulated points convertible into Seoul Pay credits that can be used at participating businesses. It had 2.55 million participants as of 2025, equivalent to about one-quarter of Seoul’s population. Song said such programs demonstrate how governments can use technology and incentives to make exercise easier to incorporate into everyday life.
The symposium’s broader message was that exercise should not be viewed solely as a recreational activity or something reserved for athletes. Instead, officials and researchers said physical activity can form part of a broader public health strategy aimed at helping people remain healthy and independent as they age.

Taiwan Army seeks NT$11 billion to boost Stinger missile stockpile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:13:02 UTC
16:13:02 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s Army has proposed allocating NT$11.03 billion (US$345 million) to replenish its Stinger missile stockpile, shortening the procurement schedule by a year.
According to the Ministry of National Defense’s proposed 2027 budget submitted to the Legislative Yuan, the procurement covers additional ammunition for existing Stinger missile systems, per Liberty Times. The project is separate from a previously budgeted military investment program to acquire man-portable Stinger missiles.
The latest budget classifies the purchase under logistics and maintenance spending for general ammunition procurement and maintenance, rather than as a new weapons acquisition program. The funding is intended to cover missiles purchased from the US, excluding launch systems and vehicle platforms.
The additional missiles are intended to replenish stocks for Taiwan’s existing Avenger mobile air defense systems, Dual Mount Stinger air defense systems, and Apache attack helicopters equipped with air-launched Stinger missiles, Liberty Times reported. The replenishment would strengthen the military’s ability to sustain air defense operations during a potential conflict across the Taiwan Strait.
The procurement was originally scheduled to run from 2026 through 2031, spreading payments over six years. The latest budget moves the completion date up by one year to 2030, shortening the project from six years to five while keeping total funding unchanged.
The proposed budget allocates NT$1 billion each for 2026 and 2027, with the remaining NT$9.03 billion scheduled for 2028 through 2030, according to Liberty Times. That translates to average annual spending of about NT$3.01 billion over the final three years, roughly three times the annual allocations in the initial phase.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The US is Taiwan’s most important ally, Deputy Foreign Minister Francois Wu (吳志中) said in an interview with Austrian newspaper Die Presse.
Wu said Washington has not stopped selling weapons to Taipei and the two countries continue to maintain close contact based on shared interests, according to the foreign ministry. Taiwan also enjoys bipartisan support in the US Congress, he said. Helping Taiwan strengthen its defense capabilities serves US interests as well, he added.
Responding to China’s claim that Taiwan is promoting “separatism,” Wu reiterated that Taiwan does not need to declare independence because it is already an independent and sovereign country. Taiwan has a democratically elected government, its own currency, foreign policy, legal system, and territory, he said.
The deputy foreign minister said the threat of a Chinese invasion or blockade is real but not imminent. Any action would disrupt global semiconductor supply chains and severely affect the global economy, he said.
Wu added that Taiwan is taking a pragmatic approach to foreign relations based on mutual concerns in the face of China’s influence within the UN system. The UN needs Taiwan’s democracy, expertise and experience, he said.
Taiwan continues to hold important advantages in advanced semiconductors, Wu said. He expressed confidence in the “Silicon Shield” and said Taiwan will continue working with the US and other like-minded partners to deter China from attempting to change the status quo by force.

Advanced British warship nears return to fleet
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:12:46 BST
16:12:46 KST

HMS Daring has taken on fuel for the first time in years, in the clearest sign yet that the destroyer is close to going back to sea after nearly a decade tied up alongside, according to the ship.
The ship’s own account posted the moment on Tuesday evening, noting she “hasn’t heard this over main broadcast for quite some time” before giving the pipe: “Do you hear there. No smoking, no naked lights, fuelling Ship.” A photograph with it shows a bunkering tanker secured alongside, hoses run across to the destroyer, and a rating on the upper deck watching it happen.
The pipe warns the ship’s company that fuel is going aboard and that ignition sources are banned while it does. Warships take on fuel because they are going somewhere.
Daring has been out of service since April 2017, and we reported last year when she passed 3,000 days alongside. She is now at roughly 3,470 days, or nine years and six months.
The vessel underwent the Power Improvement Project, the replacement of the diesel generators that had left the Type 45 class at risk of losing all power at sea, along with a wider package of refit work. She came back to Portsmouth in early 2023 and has not moved since.
Crewing began ahead of trials, with shakedown expected from around the turn of this year. That would be her first time off the wall since 2017.
The Power Improvement Project has worked through the class ship by ship, with Dauntless completing the same work before her. The intention is to hold the destroyers in service into the 2030s, and a study is now running on whether their out of service dates can be pushed further right.

SBU secures 15-year sentence for Russian agent who prepared car bombing of UAF soldier, police station in Vinnytsia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:12:30 EEST
16:12:30 KST

An agent of the Russian military intelligence exposed by the SBU in March 2025 while preparing terrorist attacks in Vinnytsia has been sentenced to 15 years in prison with asset confiscation, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) has reported.
"SBU officers detained the perpetrator as a result of a special operation in Vinnytsia when she was preparing to blow up a Ukrainian Armed Forces vehicle and a police administrative building using homemade bombs," the report states.
According to the SBU, the convicted woman turned out to be an unemployed resident of the Kyiv region who was recruited by Russian special services via Telegram channels while looking for "easy" earnings.
Following her recruitment, the woman arrived in Vinnytsia and rented an apartment. Per instructions from her Russian handler, she retrieved two improvised explosive devices from a cache, which she was supposed to plant under a Ukrainian servicewoman's or serviceman's vehicle and near a district police station.
Additionally, the agent was tasked with installing hidden remote-access video cameras near the planned terrorist attack sites so that Russian military intelligence could monitor the targets and remotely detonate the explosive devices.
SBU officers exposed the agent ahead of time and detained her while she was setting up a concealed camera near a Ukrainian Armed Forces soldier's vehicle. During searches, two improvised explosive devices and a mobile phone containing evidence of cooperation with Russian special services were seized from her.
The court found the woman guilty under Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – high treason committed under martial law.

Live: NRL and NRLW stars arriving for Dally M Awards
Unknown

2026-09-30

Fri, 18 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Tigers 0, Raiders 6
Nathan Cleary wins first Dally M Medal, Tamika Upton claims third on NRL awards night
Injured Penrith superstar Nathan Cleary has accepted his maiden Dally M Medal from his couch, while Brisbane fullback Tamika Upton took out the NRLW award for the third time in four seasons.
After years of being the consensus best player in the men's game, Cleary finally made it official by romping clear in the Dally M count, securing the award with two rounds remaining and ultimately finishing 14 votes clear — 67 to Braydon Trindall's 53.
Trindall made a late push to cause a major upset before injuring his shoulder in round 24, while the rest of the top five — Dylan Edwards, Haumole Olakau'atu and Scott Drinkwater — failed to poll in round 25, when Cleary got a maximum six votes in a 22-14 win over Melbourne.
Having suffered a gruesome compound fracture of his left leg in the Panthers' preliminary final loss on Sunday, Cleary was not at the awards ceremony on Sydney Harbour, instead accepting the award via video message.
"I want to start by saying how grateful I am for everyone's support the past few days," he said from a couch with his injured leg propped up in a cast.
"I can't thank everyone enough for the messages they've sent through."
He thanked his parents, who he has been living with this year while his house has been being renovated.
He credited his Panthers teammates for making him a "10,000 times" better player, while he also paid tribute to girlfriend Mary Fowler, who is currently playing for Manchester City in England.
"It's tough doing the long distance but she always makes me feel supported and loved. That's all I could ever ask for," he said.
The NRLW count was much closer, with 2022 winner Raecene McGregor pushing Upton to the 11th and final round of the season, but the Broncos gun finished with 31 votes to McGregor's 29.
Upton is preparing to play for her sixth NRLW premiership when the Broncos face the Roosters for a second straight year on Sunday, when the league will honour Jai Arrow after his MND diagnosis earlier this year.
The tribute is set to occur in place of traditional pre-game entertainment after negotiations with Tones and I fell apart.
NRL boss Peter V'landys on Monday promised "surprises" and said on Wednesday night that a number of Australian artists would be part of the tribute, although Arrow said earlier in the night that V'landys had told him "nothing yet".

CIA Chief Reportedly Warned Russia Its Economy Could Collapse Like the Soviet Union

CIA Chief Reportedly Warned Russia Its Economy Could Collapse Like the Soviet Union
CIA Director John Ratcliffe warned Russian officials that Russia’s economy could collapse in a Soviet-style crisis if the war continues, German outlet Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reported on September 26.
A senior diplomat familiar with the CIA’s briefing to Western partner services after Ratcliffe’s late-August visit to Moscow told FAZ that the intelligence assessment was the trip’s central purpose. “Russia is losing the war,” the diplomat described the US assessment as concluding.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Earlier reporting had already indicated that Ratcliffe brought Moscow a bleak assessment of Russia’s deteriorating military and economic position, after which the Russian leader Vladimir Putin reportedly canceled a planned meeting with him.
The latest FAZ account provides additional detail on the economic warning delivered during the visit.
According to FAZ, the US assessment distinguished between Russia’s military situation and its longer-term economic position. American intelligence reportedly viewed the battlefield as moving toward a stalemate, while concluding that Russia could not sustain the war economically.
“The economy will collapse, just as the Soviet Union did at the end of the Cold War,” the diplomat told FAZ, describing the assessment presented to Moscow.
The message was also tied directly to US policy toward Ukraine, the report noted. Washington wanted Moscow to understand that the assessment shaped its approach, and that Russia’s position would weaken over time.
Putin therefore should not expect US President Donald Trump eventually to abandon Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, according to FAZ. The resulting American message to Moscow was straightforward: “Negotiate!”
FAZ reported that the assessment also influenced how some European officials interpreted Washington’s recent diplomacy toward Russia, including Trump’s invitation for Putin to attend the G20 summit in Miami in December.
Russia’s economic strain has also been visible in its construction sector, where bankruptcies rose 41% year over year by early September. Housing demand fell sharply across several regions as developers faced high borrowing costs, inflation, and mounting debt.

Skyrora hot fires scaled-down orbital rocket in Scotland
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:09:06 BST
16:09:06 KST

Skyrora has completed a 45-second static hot-fire test of a scaled-down version of its Skyrora XL orbital launch vehicle at Machrihanish on the west coast of Scotland, according to the company.
The test vehicle was built to validate subsystems and components similar to those intended for the full-size rocket, and the firing gathered data on the pressurisation system alongside engine characteristics including propellant flow rate and chamber pressure. According to Skyrora, initial data indicates the subsystems operated successfully throughout, and the engineering team is collating and analysing the results before conducting a second test.
Dr Jack James Marlow, the company’s chief operating officer, said: “You don’t build confidence in an orbital launch vehicle by waiting until the finished rocket is on the launchpad. You build it through thousands of decisions, measurements and tests along the way. This scaled-down XL system lets us test and validate the technology, subsystems and components together, understand how they perform and make improvements before scaling up to the full vehicle. Our approach is simple: test, learn, refine and test again, so that when Skyrora XL reaches the pad, we have confidence grounded in evidence.”
The company describes its method as testing early, testing repeatedly and testing systems together before scaling them up, on the basis that problems found at small scale are cheaper and quicker to fix than problems found late. Work will progress through larger and more demanding trials before anything is integrated into the full vehicle.
Skyrora XL is a three-stage rocket designed to carry small satellites into low Earth orbit. The company is headquartered in Scotland and designs, manufactures and tests its vehicles and engines at Cumbernauld, with a wider programme covering the Skylark L suborbital vehicle, propulsion work and additive manufacturing.
In 2025 Skyrora became the first British launch vehicle manufacturer to receive a launch operator licence from the Civil Aviation Authority, permitting a suborbital launch of Skylark L from SaxaVord Spaceport on Unst in Shetland.
Machrihanish, on the Kintyre peninsula, was a Royal Air Force station and a NATO forward operating base during the Cold War, and its runway remains among the longest in Europe. The site has since been taken into community ownership and hosts a range of engineering and aerospace tenants, Skyrora among them.
Domestic launch has been given weight in defence terms that it did not carry a decade ago. Lord Coaker told the House of Lords this week that British national security depends on freedom of action in space, including the ability to protect British and allied space assets, and that investment is going into resilience through the UK Space Strategy and the Defence Investment Plan. Sovereign launch matters to that argument because a satellite replaced quickly after being lost or degraded is worth considerably more than one that has to wait for a slot on somebody else’s rocket.

Nespresso is phasing out its compostable coffee capsules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:07:13 UTC
16:07:13 KST

Nespresso is phasing out its compostable coffee capsules
Nespresso is discontinuing its range of compostable paper capsules, which was introduced just a few years ago.
A spokesperson for the Nestlé subsidiary confirmed press reports when contacted by the AWP news agency. The paper capsules had been launched as a pilot project to offer customers an additional choice. However, feedback highlighted issues relating to their limited shelf life and the overall “product experience”, the company says. Nespresso therefore states that it is now more convinced than ever that aluminium is the best choice for preserving the coffee’s flavour and aroma.
More
Your favourite coffee was probably made by a Swiss machine
In Switzerland, the paper capsules have not yet completely disappeared. They are expected to remain available in some Nespresso boutiques for around a month, depending on when stocks run out. The product had been tested in 14 European markets.
The compostable capsules with 82% paper packaging were launched in 2023, following three years of development. Once the pack of capsules had been opened, Nespresso recommended using them within four weeks. According to the company, the aluminium wrappers, on the other hand, protect the coffee from light, air and moisture for up to a year.
Nespresso does not, however, view this decision as a step backwards in terms of sustainability. According to a life-cycle analysis commissioned by the group, the carbon footprint is virtually identical: for a small cup of espresso, it is 79 grams of CO₂ equivalent with the paper capsule and 81 grams with the aluminium one.
The company now intends to focus more on aluminium recycling, aiming to dispose of the capsules increasingly via standard recycling schemes. In France, 80% of the population can already recycle Nespresso capsules via standard recycling schemes; in Switzerland, the recycling rate stands at 73% and the aim is to increase this further.

Christa’s final night: Tennessee set to execute first woman in 200 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:06:54 UTC
16:06:54 KST

A Tennessee prison is making final preparations for the execution of Christa Pike, who is scheduled to become the first woman put to death by the state in more than 200 years. Pike, now 50, is due to be executed by lethal injection at 3 a.m. Thursday Israel time, after years of delays and legal challenges. Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee this week rejected her request for clemency, clearing the way for the sentence to be carried out.
Pike was 18 when she murdered 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer on Jan. 12, 1995. The two were enrolled in a vocational training program in Knoxville along with Pike’s boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp. Prosecutors said Pike became convinced Slemmer was interested in Shipp and, driven by jealousy and rage, lured her to a secluded area on the University of Tennessee campus.
There, Pike and Shipp tortured and killed her. Pike cut Slemmer with a box cutter and beat her with a large piece of asphalt, while Shipp carved a pentagram into her body. The crime scene drew particular attention amid the “Satanic panic” of the 1980s and 1990s, when widespread fears in the United States centered on supposed satanic cults abducting and ritually abusing people, including children.
Pike’s death sentence made her one of the youngest women ever sent to death row in the United States. She has never denied responsibility for Slemmer’s killing, but for years her lawyers and supporters have argued that execution is disproportionate given her age at the time, her later-diagnosed mental illnesses and a childhood marked by neglect and severe sexual abuse, including rapes at ages 11 and 17.
Her current attorney, Stephen Ferrell, has also argued that Pike’s trial lawyers failed during the sentencing phase to present jurors with crucial details about her background or to emphasize her youth. Pike was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. She told police that she had initially intended only to confront Slemmer physically but lost control and killed her.
In her clemency petition, Pike’s lawyers argued that her untreated mental illness left her unable to “hit the brakes.” Pike herself expressed remorse in a statement included in the petition.
“I was an 18-year-old kid and mentally unstable,” she said. “It took me many years just to understand the gravity of what I had done, and even longer to understand how many lives I destroyed. I took someone’s daughter, sister and friend. It makes me sick today to think that I was capable of committing such a crime.”
Ferrell has argued that scientific understanding of adolescent brain development has advanced substantially since Pike was sentenced and that imposing the death penalty on someone who had only recently turned 18 is now exceptionally rare. He has also pointed to the different sentence received by Shipp, who was 17 at the time of the murder and was given life imprisonment with the possibility of parole because of his age.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, 275 people have been executed in the United States in the modern death penalty era for crimes committed between the ages of 18 and 20, but death sentences for defendants in that age group have become increasingly uncommon. Robin M. Maher, the center’s executive director, has said she does not believe a jury hearing Pike’s case today, with evidence of the sexual abuse and neglect she endured, would sentence her to death.
Slemmer’s family sees the case very differently. Her mother, May Martinez, has rejected arguments that Pike should be spared because she was so young when she committed the murder, saying her daughter was denied the chance to grow older at all.
“Not a day goes by, not a minute goes by, that I don’t think about Colleen,” Martinez said. “The holidays are the hardest. Colleen’s birthday was last week. She should have been 51.”
Executions of women remain exceedingly rare in the United States. Only 18 women have been executed since 1976, roughly 1% of all executions during that period. Tennessee last executed a woman in 1820. The most recent woman executed anywhere in the United States was Amber McLaughlin, a transgender woman put to death in Missouri in 2023 for a 2003 murder.
In a final attempt to halt Pike’s execution, her lawyers appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, arguing that her post-traumatic stress disorder could cause “severe mental suffering and heightened psychological terror” when she is restrained on a gurney for the lethal injection.
Pike has also asked that only women take part in the execution process, arguing that the presence of men during her final moments could trigger trauma. Tennessee corrections officials said they would try to accommodate at least some of her requests, including having female officers move her from her Nashville prison to a high-security facility during the 24 hours before the execution.
Before Lee rejected her clemency petition, Pike said in a letter to the media that whatever the outcome, she had reached a sense of peace.
“I’m not afraid to die,” she said. “I’m just nervous about the process itself.”

New Shelters, Launchers: Russia Expands Drone Base Used Against Kyiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:06:18 UTC
16:06:18 KST

Russia is continuing to expand the Tsymbulova drone base in Oryol Oblast, a facility used to launch large numbers of jet-powered drones targeting Kyiv.
Satellite imagery reportedly shows that construction at the base has continued uninterrupted for the past four weeks, according to the Strategic Aviation Telegram channel.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A new area has appeared southeast of the existing launchers, featuring eight domed shelters for jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and a new launcher. Paved pads have also been prepared for another eight shelters and two launchers.
Six hangars for strike drones that were still under construction in early September have now been completed. Fourteen additional hangars have appeared along the access road.
Some surface-level shelters at the base have also reportedly been converted into underground structures. Analysts cited by Strategic Aviation estimate that the changes could make the facilities more difficult to destroy.
At the same time, a football field has been built on the site of one of the former drone storage structures.
More launchers, fewer drones left exposed
Separately, satellite imagery has revealed construction near existing Geran-5 launchers, with sites being prepared for six additional launchers.
Towers are also being built nearby. Analysts suggest they could be used to support anti-drone netting and communications.
Strategic Aviation said the expansion is already affecting the composition of Russian attacks on Kyiv.
Latvia’s Russian Speakers Reject Putin’s ‘Russian World’ as Election Looms
“We would like to note that the results of constructing more launchers are already visible: the share of ‘Geran-5’ drones among all UAVs launched at Kyiv is now around 75% (compared to about 10% a month ago),” the statement reads.
According to the channel, construction is expected to continue at the Tsymbulova site. Satellite imagery has detected construction equipment in the northeastern part of the facility, an area that had previously been unused. New storage facilities are reportedly likely to be built there.
At the same time, as the number of storage structures increases, fewer Russian drones are being left in the open. While nearly 100 UAVs were located in open areas at the end of summer, monitoring data now indicates that the number has fallen to around 10.
Russia has sharply increased jet-powered drone use
Russia significantly increased its use of jet-powered drones against Ukraine in September, Yuriy Ihnat, spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, said during a televised news marathon.
As of Sept. 29, Russian forces had launched 3,177 jet-powered drones during the month, according to Ihnat.
“We have already seen more drones this month than in the previous one overall... We recorded 2,850 jet-powered UAVs in August, whereas this month the figure is already 3,177. In other words, we see that the enemy has significantly increased the number of jet-powered UAVs,” Ihnat said.
He added that Russian forces were launching the drones in waves, with Kyiv and the surrounding region remaining primary targets.
Other Ukrainian cities, including Kharkiv, Odesa, Mykolaiv, Sumy, Kherson, and Dnipro, are also facing frequent Russian drone attacks, Ihnat said. He added that Russian aerial assets occasionally reach western Ukraine, with jet-powered drones capable of covering much greater distances.
Ihnat said Ukraine needs additional missiles for Patriot systems and other ground-based air defense systems to counter jet-powered UAVs and Russian ballistic missiles.
He also said the Defense Forces were relying on Ukrainian manufacturers to develop faster solutions to the growing aerial threat.
“The Air Force and the entire Defense Forces expect our manufacturers and the defense industry to deliver solutions as quickly as possible, so they can be rapidly scaled up for the troops – the people defending the skies every day,” he said.
Ukraine currently uses a combination of tactical aviation, including F-16 fighter jets, and ground-based air defense systems to repel Russian attacks, although their effectiveness depends in part on available missile stocks.
Ihnat said international partners were already providing Ukraine with additional air defense missile packages but stressed that continued support was necessary.
He added that man-portable air-defense systems (MANPADS) can be used against jet-powered UAVs once the drones enter their engagement range.
F-16 pilots destroyed more than 3,150 aerial targets since entering combat
Ukrainian F-16 pilots have shot down more than 3,150 aerial targets since the start of their combat operations, including 666 cruise missiles and around 2,500 UAVs of various types, according to Air Force Commander Lt. Gen. Anatolii Kryvonozhko.
“Our pilots are employing the available F-16s with maximum efficiency despite the limited ammunition supply,” Kryvonozhko said.
“Using a diverse range of weaponry, Ukrainian F-16 pilots have already shot down over 3,150 aerial targets – 666 cruise missiles and about 2,500 UAVs of various types – and have carried out more than 650 airstrikes against enemy ground targets,” he added.
Kryvonozhko made the remarks following a meeting between a Ukrainian Air Force delegation and representatives of US defense company Lockheed Martin.
Conor McGuire, who heads F-16 capability development, praised the combat use of the aircraft by Ukrainian pilots and the work of ground crews. He also expressed readiness to help Ukraine enhance the capabilities of its existing F-16 fleet.

Flydubai jet diverts after hijacking code triggers Israeli scramble
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:04:00 UTC
16:04:00 KST

A Flydubai flight carrying more than 170 passengers from Dubai to Tel Aviv diverted to Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after transmitting emergency transponder codes, including one associated with a possible hijacking, triggering an Israeli military response before authorities determined the incident was not believed to involve a hijacking.
Flight FZ1073, operated by a Boeing 737 MAX 8, was traveling toward Ben Gurion Airport when it transmitted the international emergency code 7700 and briefly switched to code 7500, which is used to indicate unlawful interference or a possible hijacking.
The aircraft subsequently changed course, descended sharply and headed toward Saudi Arabia, according to flight-tracking data and Israeli media reports. It eventually landed safely at Tabuk Airport.
The unusual flight path and emergency signals prompted Israeli authorities to treat the situation as a potential security threat.
Israeli media reported that the Air Force scrambled fighter jets after the alert, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz held an urgent security consultation with senior defense officials.
The Israeli military also carried out a situation assessment involving the Air Force and other security agencies as authorities sought to determine what had happened aboard the aircraft.
A security source cited by Ynet said there was no confirmed information that the aircraft had been hijacked and that the pilot had activated a distress signal.
The Prime Minister's Office later said the diversion to Saudi Arabia was not believed to have been the result of a hijacking.
The aircraft departed Dubai International Airport early Wednesday on its scheduled service to Tel Aviv. It was carrying roughly 174 passengers, according to reports, including about 27 children.
During the flight, the aircraft transmitted the 7700 general emergency code before briefly transmitting 7500, the code associated with unlawful interference.
The 7500 signal immediately raised the possibility of a hijacking, particularly because the aircraft was headed toward Israel, where security authorities have remained on high alert amid the wider regional security situation.
Flight-tracking data showed the aircraft changing direction and descending to a much lower altitude than its normal cruising level before continuing toward Saudi Arabia. Reports said the aircraft descended to around 15,000 feet.
The combination of the emergency signals, course reversal, descent and temporary concerns over communications intensified the response.
Israeli media initially reported that contact with the aircraft had been lost, although subsequent reports indicated that it was continuing toward Saudi Arabia and was expected to land at Tabuk.
The aircraft eventually landed safely.
The alert prompted an immediate military response in Israel, with fighter jets scrambled as authorities assessed whether the aircraft posed a security threat.
Netanyahu and Katz convened an emergency consultation, while senior military officials assessed the situation with the Air Force.
Other Israeli security bodies were also reported to have been involved in assessing the incident.
Some Israeli reports said departures from Ben Gurion Airport were temporarily affected while the situation was being evaluated.
The response reflected the seriousness with which aviation authorities treat a 7500 transmission. The code is designed to alert air traffic control and relevant security agencies to a possible unlawful interference situation.
However, the transmission alone does not establish that a hijacking has taken place.
As the situation developed, Israeli reports indicated that the incident was not believed to have been caused by a hijacking or an external security threat.
Reports cited by Israeli media suggested that a physical altercation between the pilots may have prompted the emergency signals and the subsequent diversion.
That account remained subject to further verification, however, and detailed official information from flydubai or UAE aviation authorities was not immediately available in the initial coverage.
The Israeli Prime Minister's Office confirmed the broader assessment that the diversion was not believed to have been a hijacking incident.
The aircraft's safe landing in Tabuk brought the immediate security alert to an end.
The incident nevertheless demonstrated how quickly an aviation emergency can escalate when an aircraft transmits a hijacking-related code, particularly on a route involving Israel.
The flight was ultimately diverted well before reaching its planned destination at Ben Gurion Airport.
Rather than continuing toward Israel, the aircraft headed for Tabuk in northwestern Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely after the emergency.
Israeli authorities subsequently scaled back their response after determining that there was no confirmed hijacking threat.
The exact circumstances inside the cockpit, including what prompted the emergency transmissions and the aircraft's abrupt change in course and altitude, remained under review.
The incident also highlighted the sensitivity of commercial aviation routes between the United Arab Emirates and Israel, which were established following the normalization of relations under the Abraham Accords.

These include China, India and the EU.

Canada and the EU are expected to try and boost trade and investment with others, as a spat between Ottawa and Washington intensifies.
Canada's international trade minister Maninder Sidhu stressed Ottawa's support for "open, predictable and rules-based trade."
He plans to speak with partners to "reinforce a multilateral trading system," as officials try to diversify an economy they see as too reliant on an increasingly protectionist United States.
Others like India could finalise a long-awaited trade deal with the United States. Observers are also monitoring for signs of further pressure on Iran.
Outside the G20, workers and activists are protesting what they see as the Trump administration's broken promises to improve conditions for workers, farmers and smaller businesses.

F-16s get new friend-or-foe system cleared for service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:02:44 UTC
16:02:44 KST

- BAE Systems' AN/APX-127(V)1 identification friend or foe system received AIMS certification for the U.S. Air Force F-16.
- The company expects to begin delivering the first 90-unit production lot this year.
BAE Systems’ new identification friend or foe system for the F-16 has been certified by the U.S. Department of War, clearing it for use on U.S. Air Force fighters, the company said Sept. 29.
The AN/APX-127(V)1 Combined Interrogator Transponder received AIMS certification, the approval that shows an identification system meets U.S. and NATO standards and can work with allied equipment. BAE Systems said it expects to start delivering the first production lot of 90 units this year. The company did not say which F-16 units will receive them first, who ordered the first lot or how much it is worth.
An identification friend or foe system, known as IFF, lets an aircraft send a coded radio question to another aircraft and receive a coded answer, so a pilot or air defense operator can tell whether it is friendly before deciding whether to fire. The new unit combines the interrogator, which asks the question, and the transponder, which answers it, in one box sized for fighter jets.
The system is certified for Mark XIIB IFF with Mode 5, the encrypted military mode used by the United States and NATO, and Mode S, which is used in civilian air traffic control. BAE Systems said it adds extra receive channels so the aircraft can passively pick up other aircraft’s Mode 5 Level 2 signals, which carry position data, and ADS-B broadcasts, the location signals most civilian aircraft send out. That lets a pilot build a picture of nearby traffic without sending out interrogations of their own.
The unit meets the latest cryptography and cybersecurity requirements, and its open architecture allows new features to be added through software instead of hardware changes, the company said. It fits in the same space as three older BAE combined interrogator transponders, the AN/APX-113, AN/APX-125 and AN/APX-126, which are used on several U.S. and international aircraft, so it can be swapped in without redesigning the aircraft.
“This solution provides added security and real-time information pilots need in a variety of threat environments,” said Seth Guanu, Combat Identification Products program area director at BAE Systems.
BAE Systems says it has delivered more than 1,500 interrogators, 6,000 combined interrogator transponders and 16,000 transponders over more than 80 years. The new system is built at the company’s sites in Greenlawn, New York, and Austin, Texas.

Gene therapy: The breakthrough that inspired Spider-Man | Euronews Tech Talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:02:00 UTC
16:02:00 KST

Although an inspiration for science fiction movies, gene therapy is real. Here is how it works and what could be improved about it.
If you are a science nerd and a Marvel fan, you might have noticed that gene therapy, a promising medical approach to treat diseases by targeting their genetic causes, made an appearance in the latest iteration of the arachnid superhero franchise, Spider-Man: Brand New Day.
In this film, Peter Parker or Spider-Man feels weird. His DNA mutates, and his spider side starts taking over, providing him with new and sometimes difficult-to-control powers.
To manage them, Parker resorts to RNA interference, a real-world gene therapy technique that silences specific gene activity.
But how does gene therapy work? And what are its limitations?
To answer these and more questions, Euronews Tech Talks interviewed Alberto Auricchio, director of the Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine in Naples, professor at the University of Naples and president of the European Society of Gene & Cell Therapy.
How does gene therapy work?
Originally used to treat monogenic diseases, gene therapy is now employed and studied to find a treatment for a wide range of illnesses, including cancer and HIV.
“Gene therapy basically targets the root cause of a genetic disease,” Auricchio explained. This medical approach essentially consists in the introduction of nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) into target cells and tissues for therapeutic purposes.
Nucleic acids can be introduced into target cells either in vivo (directly within the body) or ex vivo (in cells extracted from an organism and then transplanted inside the body). In both cases, delivery is achieved using either viral or non-viral vectors.
Types of gene therapy include gene addition and gene editing, with the latter being further divided into gene silencing and gene correction.
As the names suggest, gene addition consists of adding a gene; gene correction is the fixing of a dysfunctional gene; and gene silencing deactivates a gene.
What’s the state of gene therapy in Europe?
Gene therapy is a complex and evolving field, but it is not only material for science-fiction stories. “We are beyond clinical trials now. There are approved [gene therapy] products that are available to patients,” Auricchio told Euronews Next.
The first in vivo gene therapy approved in Europe was Glybera, which received the European Commission marketing authorisation in 2012 and offers a medical treatment for patients with severe or multiple pancreatitis attacks due to lipoprotein lipase deficiency.
The first ex vivo gene therapy approved in Europe was Strimvelis, which received authorisation in 2016. This drug treats severe combined immunodeficiency due to adenosine deaminase deficiency and was developed at the Hospital San Raffaele in Milan.
What makes gene therapy promising?
Among others, gene therapy has a crucial advantage: it is a durable treatment.
“There are approved gene therapy drugs, for which we have decades of follow-up in patients where we know that the therapeutic effect is stable over decades, and in theory for the lifetime of the individual,” Auricchio explained.
As a matter of fact, gene therapy drugs are designed to be a once-in-a-lifetime treatment, meaning that a single administration should last for a long time.
On the other hand, beyond the scientific difficulties, the main limitation of gene therapy is the economic obstacle.
“These are very expensive drugs to be developed, and those that get to the market have very high prices, some of them matching millions of euros,” Auricchio explained.
For instance, the cost of Strimvelis amounts to €594,000 excluding VAT.
“These drugs are developed for rare diseases in many cases, which are not a very attractive market for typical developers like pharmaceutical companies; the high development cost of this drug is a challenge,” Auricchio said.
Spider-Man: Brand New Day does not explore the economic problem behind gene therapy. Peter Parker is lucky to know the brilliant scientist Bruce Banner or Hulk, who helps him develop his therapy.
But real-life science is often more challenging than a superhero movie.
Euronews Tech Talks is a podcast produced, written, presented and published in English.

I heard one thing loud and clear in Andy Burnham’s landmark speech: the left has won the arguments | Owen Jones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:00:14 UTC
16:00:14 KST

As Andy Burnham delivered his conference speech to the Labour faithful yesterday, it was hard not to recall Jeremy Corbyn’s words after the party’s shattering 2019 election defeat. “I am proud that on austerity, on corporate power, on inequality and the climate emergency,” he wrote for this publication, “we have won the arguments and rewritten the terms of political debate.” Given Boris Johnson’s 80-seat majority, widespread mockery ensued.
But when it comes to rhetoric, who can now deny that the left has won the argument? A Labour prime minister has declared that “Britain has been on the wrong path for a long time”, listing five villains: “Deindustrialisation, deregulation, privatisation, austerity, Brexit.” His speech was infused with class politics, as he condemned a society “run for vested interests, not in the public interest, with power held in too few hands”.
When he committed to break with the “flawed thinking of the last 40 years”, he lumped together Conservative and Labour governments. He has already repeatedly labelled the culprit: neoliberalism. This has long been the received wisdom of the left: that as Clement Attlee’s postwar government established a social-democratic consensus that the Tories upheld for a generation, so Margaret Thatcher bequeathed a settlement that New Labour maintained.
These beliefs were condemned to the fringes of Labour, even though Tony Blair himself eventually confessed: “I always thought my job was to build on some of the things she had done rather than reverse them.” Any mention of neoliberalism was a sure way of provoking an eye-roll from a mainstream politician or commentator. We were denied any debate about an economic system based on extraction rather than investment; an economy based on financialisation rather than making things. Corbynism was an insurgency against all of this – until it crashed on the shores of Brexit.
Add to this the new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, telling those who opposed Israel’s genocide and were infuriated by Labour’s position on Gaza: “You were right.” We should add, too, the disastrous past wars backed by Labour: Iraq, Afghanistan and Libya.
The left should feel vindicated by the political shift taking place. We were right – at home and abroad. We were mocked, demonised and marginalised for making these arguments. Now most of the left’s worldview is embraced by the Labour top brass. This happened after Keir Starmer’s faction based their entire project on defining themselves against the left. As the Labour activist Ali Milani – who was part of Burnham’s team – told me, that strategy nearly brought about the party’s destruction.
Burnham only became prime minister because Labour’s leftwing voters rebelled – by defecting en masse to Zack Polanski’s Green party in the Gorton and Denton byelection, then in local elections in England, Scotland and Wales. That is clearly understood by Burnham’s team, or they would not be so confidently doubling down on their new strategy.
But winning the argument on a rhetorical level is not the same as substance. Burnham is clearly shifting towards state intervention. That’s taking the form of Great British Grid, a new publicly owned network body, and he condemned privatised water as “a symbol of what has gone wrong with Britain”.
The shift in this direction actually began under the last Conservative government. Did Liz Truss not commit to a subsidy for energy bills worth tens of billions of pounds? What of Rishi Sunak being forced to bring railways into public ownership? Starmerism expanded the semi-nationalisation of the railway and founded Great British Energy. Neoliberalism has exhausted itself and governments are being forced to abandon its tenets, whether they want to or not.
But full public ownership of water seems far off, with “public control” acting as a rather flexible label. Burnham has committed to a large-scale building of new council homes and preventing them from being flogged off through right to buy. Yet he has already backtracked on a pledge to spend the government’s entire £39bn affordable homes programme on council and social housing.
Crucially, he remains committed to the suffocating fiscal rules that block the investment Britain’s crumbling infrastructure and starved services need, especially given there remains no promise to hike taxes on the well-to-do.
While committing to a national care service is extremely welcome, scrapping the triple lock on pensions is not. Britain still spends significantly less on pensions than other major European countries such as Germany, France and Spain, and about two million pensioners languish in poverty.
Consider, too, that the Labour parliamentary benches were stuffed with candidates deemed loyal to the Starmer project. The rightwing factionalists who ran the party may currently be sulking on the fringes, but do not underestimate their capacity to inflict damage.
A key difference between Burnhamism and what came before may well be expressed by what Miliband told activists attending a Labour fringe event organised by the soft-left pressure group Mainstream. “Too often in the past, we thought that kicking some of our supporters would do us political credit,” he said, “and we were absolutely wrong.” Offending people “in the progressive community”, he admitted, was sometimes done “deliberately”.
Because of pressure from the streets and the ballot box, Labour has shifted its rhetoric. The substance is a bit more complicated. Where Starmerism defined itself against the left, could this new government be pushed in a more progressive direction? That question has not yet been answered. But the left should indeed feel emboldened. The winds are shifting in our direction.
- 
  Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist. His latest book, The Fall of the West: How They Really Lost It, is published on 1 October. Order your copy at the Guardian bookshop

Sixteen English councils spend more than 80% of core funding on social care
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:00:13 UTC
16:00:13 KST

Sixteen English councils spent more than 80% of their core funding on adult and children’s social care last year, highlighting the growing financial pressure on other local services.
Guardian analysis of government figures found that councils responsible for social care spent a net £42.8bn on adult and children’s services in 2025-26, equivalent to a record 71.9% of their combined core spending. Adult social care took 44.5% and children’s services accounted for 27.4%. In 2017-18, care costs made up 62.4% of councils’ core spending.
The overspending, which is driven by an ageing population with increasingly complex care needs, rising inflationary pressures and growing children’s social care demand, is pushing many councils to the brink of bankruptcy.
These challenges have led Andy Burnham to make reform of the care system key to his government’s ambitions.
Speaking at the Labour conference on Tuesday, the prime minister announced that the government would begin laying the groundwork for a National Care Service to be introduced after the next election, paid for in part by changing the earnings element of the triple lock.
He has already accelerated a government-commissioned independent review of adult social care carried out by Louise Casey, which initially was due to be published in 2028 but is now expected next year. That review will now shape the form the new care service takes.
Lady Casey delivered a withering critique of the state of the English social care system earlier this year, describing it as held together by “sticking plasters and glue”. She said the country faced a “moment of reckoning” over its failure to meet growing care needs.
Halton in Cheshire had the highest net spending on social care relative to its spending power at 92.9% in 2025-26. Just over half of its core spending was spent on adult social care and 42% was spent on child social care, which includes fostering services.
An official audit of the council published last month found its finances were unsustainable, despite it making cuts and selling off council assets. Halton received £35m in government-approved exceptional financial support this year.
A spokesperson for the council said the demand for services continued to place pressure on their finances. “The council is making necessary changes to drive down spending and improve its long-term financial sustainability,” the spokesperson said. “This includes introducing new ways of working that reduce costs while continuing to deliver good outcomes for vulnerable residents.”
Many of the 16 councils spending the largest proportions of their budgets on social care were forced to apply to the government this year for permission to borrow money to meet the day-to-day costs of running services and balance their budgets. Some cover among the most deprived areas in England, including Blackpool, Middlesbrough and Hartlepool.
Adult care alone consumed more than half of core spending power at 19 councils. That number has more than tripled since 2017-18, when six authorities crossed the same threshold.
Core spending power is the government’s measure of the money councils can use to provide services, combining locally raised income such as council tax and business rates with central government grants. It is not ringfenced, meaning councils can choose how to use it.
Councils in England overspent their 2025-26 adult social care budgets by £715m, and in response have drawn up plans to save £909m, according to the Association of Directors of Adult Social Services. These will include higher charges for care and cuts to adult care services such as daycentres.
Analysis by the King’s Fund found that the recent rise in spending reflected a rise in the number of people being supported – contrasting with 2015-20 when, during a period of cuts to council budgets, increased social care costs were mainly going on the fees to social care providers. As of March this year, 684,920 adults were in long-term care, up from a low of 613,360 in 2021-22.
The King’s Fund’s senior fellow for social care, Simon Bottery, said demand for social care had risen due to England’s ageing population as well as more adults living longer with complex needs.
He said: “Councils are meeting some of the extra costs faced by care providers, while also supporting more people. Those two factors combined account for the extra expenditure and the rising proportion of council funding going on care.
“A higher proportion of council budgets is being spent on adult social care than a few years ago, which means services such as refuse collection, libraries and roads get squeezed. Only about 2% of the population receives adult social care in any one year, but councils are spending a huge proportion of their budgets providing it.
“We need to move to a national system for funding social care to avoid the variation we’re seeing. At the moment, someone may receive support in one local authority but not in the next.”
Dr Wendy Taylor, the chair of the Local Government Association’s health and wellbeing committee, said: “Overall overspend has decreased slightly this year, but it remains high and is impacting spending on other council services. At the same time, councils’ capacity to spend on planned prevention is shrinking, with knock-on effects elsewhere in health and care services.
“Sustained and predictable funding and infrastructure will be essential for the future of adult social care, if councils are to successfully meet growing demand, deliver on their duties under the Care Act and support people to live the independent lives they want to lead.”
The Guardian excluded six councils that had not submitted their spending data for 2025-26.

Edinburgh joins UK universities heading for strikes as cuts spread through entire sector
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:00:13 UTC
16:00:13 KST

Welcome classes for students at the University of Edinburgh this year did not focus on the lectures, seminars and essays expected. Instead, students were told about how their education was going to fit in around the strikes planned for this year, which for many will in effect wipe out a term of teaching.
“This term I’ve got two courses and my dissertation. Currently, I’ve got no teaching for five weeks,” said Theo Warshaw, 22, in his final year studying geography at Edinburgh, where staff are striking over budget cuts and compulsory redundancies needed to bridge what the university’s leaders have said is a £400m shortfall.
“I think it’s a shame that students are the only bargaining chip they really have. But I understand it. I would obviously rather it didn’t happen but I do get it,” Warshaw said. “No one goes into academia to drive a Ferrari or live in a mansion. They do it because they love it. They don’t want to be striking. They just want a little bit of job security.”
Similar conversations are taking place at universities across the UK as administrators grapple with the erosion of tuition fees by inflation, a drop in international recruitment and changing patterns of demand as students shift away from arts and humanities subjects towards more vocational subjects in science, law and business.
When University and College Union (UCU) members in Edinburgh launched their industrial action, their colleagues at the University of Dundee were embarking on a five-week strike. And this week UCU members at the University of Nottingham announced a further round of strikes starting on Monday 5 October and lasting until the end of the semester in December, a stretch of 10 consecutive weeks.
Strike ballots, marking boycotts and votes of no confidence in leadership punctuated campus life in the spring and summer as universities announced course and department closures and redundancies, leading one UCU officer to note that it was easier to list the universities that had avoided being in dispute with their staff so far.
Lopa Leach, a professor of vascular biology and immediate past president of Nottingham’s UCU branch, said: “The word is carnage, it is carnage what they are doing now – at the local level and also at the national, senior management level in the UK. Why are they thinking about the destruction of higher education?”
Nottingham’s industrial action has been brewing since its management declared that an £85m deficit required dramatic restructuring, including a plan announced in May to cut nearly 10% of its 7,000 effective full-time positions and suspending entry to all modern language and music courses for new students.
Nick Clare, the current branch president, said that while the strikes were frustrating for students, the uncertainty was being caused by the university’s demands for restructuring, which had left hundreds of staff unsure of their future, while watching colleagues take voluntary redundancy and leave.
“I met my new master’s students yesterday and I said: ‘I don’t know if I can teach the rest of this course because my job is at risk and I don’t know if I’ll still be here,’” Clare said. “They are appalled and they understand that many of the things they like about this university are under threat – the small group teaching, getting to know staff, all the things they appreciate are the things that are going to go.
“So students are angry, but they are angry at what’s happening, not at staff. Honestly I’ve never seen more support or solidarity from our students, having been at Nottingham for more than 10 years. Returning students get it, new students get it, it’s amazing in that regard.”
A spokesperson for Nottingham said: “We understand this news is concerning for our students, particularly at the start of the academic year, but experience from previous strike action suggests that many students will experience little or no disruption to their teaching. We want to reassure them we have clear procedures and support in place to minimise any disruption and ensure they get the most from their university experience.
“All Future Nottingham counterproposals have been reviewed and considered to help inform the university’s final business case, which will go to the university council for a decision.”
Clare said the university’s offer of voluntary redundancy had probably been popular enough to wipe out the deficit, leading him to question why the administration was insisting on going ahead with steeper cuts.
Clare warned of a potential “death spiral” hitting the university if its cuts went too far and harmed its standings in international league tables and research income, causing it to shed students and talented staff.
Leach and Clare both warned that the cuts planned at Nottingham were likely to be repeated across the UK because of the nationwide similarities in funding.
“Sadly, higher education doesn’t seem to be a top priority,” Clare said. “It’s going to take something bad to happen, it’s going to take a university to go under, a so-called elite institution where the children of MPs or journalists go, for people to take notice. If a Russell Group university goes bust, people might stand up – we really don’t want that to happen but that’s my fear.”
But for students at Nottingham, Dundee and Edinburgh, the bad news is already very real. One English literature student at Edinburgh, who asked to remain anonymous, said her GCSEs were cancelled because of Covid. Now her classes had been cancelled due to the strikes.
“I think it’s completely understandable. I’m very sympathetic to their situation. They’ve all been very clear with us about why they need to do it and it’s impacting them as well, because obviously they’re not being paid,” she said. “But it’s frustrating for me. It’s nerve-racking. I’m in my fourth year, my final year, which is 100% of the degree, marks-wise. I’m stressed, because I know missing out on teaching is a shame. It’s a key part of the education process, and I was looking forward to it.”
Prof Peter Mathieson, the vice-chancellor of Edinburgh, said: “We are extremely disappointed that, despite ongoing discussions, the UCU has announced five weeks’ strike action, which will unfairly and deliberately target our students’ first semester of the academic year.
“While we recognise the right of staff to take this action, I want to assure our students that we will continue to do everything we can to mitigate the impacts of that action on them. In addition, we remain firmly committed to constructive and transparent engagement with our joint unions.”
