Majorca vs Menorca vs Ibiza: Which of Spain’s Balearic Islands should you visit?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:00:45 UTC
14:00:45 KST

They may be part of the same archipelago, but Majorca, Menorca and Ibiza each have their own distinct character. Here’s what to know before booking.
Planning a holiday to the Balearic Islands? Majorca, Menorca and Ibiza may be three of Spain’s best-known islands – and the largest of the group – but each offers a very different take on a Mediterranean getaway.
All three have beautiful beaches with crystal-clear waters, plenty of sunshine, which lasts well into the autumn shoulder season, and lots to see and do.
Despite these shared assets, your experience on each island can vary considerably.
Majorca has the widest range of landscapes, from dramatic mountains and pretty villages to long sandy beaches and lively resorts. Menorca is more laid-back, with unspoilt coves, walking trails and a slower pace of life and hasn’t suffered from so much overtourism as its larger neighbour.
Meanwhile, Ibiza is best known for its legendary nightlife but also has plenty to offer beyond the clubs, including rural landscapes, beaches and historic villages.
So which Balearic Island is right for you? Whether you’re looking for an action-packed break, a relaxing beach holiday, a taste of local culture or somewhere to party until sunrise – and beyond – here’s what to expect from Majorca, Menorca and Ibiza.
Majorca
If you want plenty of choice, Majorca is difficult to beat. The largest of the three islands, it can feel like several different holiday destinations rolled into one.
The coastline has everything from long sandy beaches backed by resorts to small coves surrounded by pine trees. Cala Mondragó, Cala Varques and Formentor are among the better-known spots, while the north-western coast becomes increasingly dramatic around the Serra de Tramuntana mountain range. The UNESCO-listed range is dotted with stone villages, olive groves and hiking and cycling routes.
Deià and Valldemossa are some of the prettiest villages in all of Spain, while the town of Sóller is home to a historic tram which ferries passengers to the port.
No trip to Majorca is complete without a visit to Palma, the capital. It adds a city-break element to a beach holiday, with its Gothic cathedral, historic old town, restaurants and nightlife.
Palma is perhaps what makes this island the best year-round destination of the three main Balearics, as its cultural offerings, including Fundació Miró Mallorca, where Joan Miró lived and worked, can be explored even in the winter.
If you’re lucky, the winter might still be sunbathing weather – I got burned here in November!
Majorca also has the widest choice of accommodation, from large family resorts to rural fincas and boutique hotels, which means it’s a great destination for everyone from young families to party-loving youngsters.
For families, there are plenty of beaches and activities, while the mountains make the island particularly appealing to hikers and serious cyclists.
At night, the choice ranges from the lively spots of infamous Magaluf to cocktail bars and restaurants in Palma.
Food is another strength, with traditional Mallorcan specialities combined with an increasingly varied restaurant scene.
Be sure to try tumbet, a slow-cooked, baked vegetable stew made with layers of potato, aubergine, red pepper, and tomato sauce and arròs brut – or dirty rice – which is a hearty rice stew mixed with meats and seasonal vegetables.
Majorca is best for: A bit of everything – beaches, mountains, culture, food, nightlife and plenty of choice
Menorca
Menorca has a noticeably slower pace than Majorca to its west, and its appeal lies largely in its beaches, natural landscapes and traditional towns rather than big resorts and nightlife.
There are more than 200 kilometres of coastline here, with dozens of beaches and coves ranging from broad sandy stretches to tiny calas hidden between cliffs and woodland, many of which remain relatively undeveloped.
The island has also been a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve since 1993, awarded to celebrate its unique balance of human activity, traditional rural life, and rich natural heritage.
For active types, the Camí de Cavalls is a real highlight. This historic coastal path circles the island, offering opportunities to walk between beaches, viewpoints and rural landscapes. There are also plenty of opportunities for cycling, kayaking and sailing, too.
Ciutadella and Mahón, Menorca’s two main towns at opposite ends of the island, are both worth exploring for their historic streets, churches, buzzy squares and countless restaurants.
The island also has an important prehistoric heritage and, in fact, it’s effectively an open-air museum with more than 1,500 prehistoric sites – one of the highest densities of ancient monuments worldwide.
Food is focused on fresh ingredients from the land and sea. Local Mahón-Menorca cheese is a must-try, and Caldereta de Langosta is a popular local stew, originating in the fishing village of Fornells.
Nightlife does exist on Menorca, but it’s not really the place to come if staying out until sunrise is a priority. Evenings tend to revolve around dinner, drinks and wandering through old towns.
Menorca is best for: A slower pace of life, with beautiful coves, outdoor activities and natural beauty.
Ibiza
Think of Ibiza, and nightlife is likely to be the first thing that comes to mind.
The island has long been one of Europe's most famous clubbing destinations, with huge venues and internationally known DJs, like David Guetta and Calvin Harris, attracting visitors to venues including Pacha and Amnesia throughout the summer.
That, though, is only one side of Ibiza. I visited in October when the weather is still warm, but the clubs have shuttered for the season. It’s an ideal time to explore the island’s pine-covered hills, rural villages, traditional farmhouses and rugged coastline.
On Ibiza, the beaches range from busy stretches with seasonal beach clubs to small coves where the main attraction is simply the perfectly clear water.
Cala Saladeta is a particular favourite on the west coast, with swathes of fine white sand and crystal-clear turquoise waters.
For a day trip from Ibiza, the smaller island of Formentera is a dream. Taking just 30 minutes on a ferry, it’s home to turquoise waters and long stretches of beaches flanked by dunes and pine trees. Hire a bicycle to see more of this spot, the smallest of all the Balearics.
Ibiza itself is also particularly good for sunsets you won’t forget in a hurry. The western coast faces out towards the Mediterranean, with plenty of places to watch the sun disappear over the sea. Café Mambo in San Antonio is iconic for a reason.
Perhaps surprisingly for those unfamiliar, there’s lots of culture to explore in Ibiza.
The old quarter of Ibiza Town, Dalt Vila, sits within historic fortifications and forms part of the island’s UNESCO World Heritage listing.
Elsewhere, there are archaeological sites, including the Phoenician settlement at Sa Caleta and the Puig des Molins necropolis.
For families, locales including Santa Eulària offer a more relaxed atmosphere than the main clubbing areas, while the island’s north is well-known for its bohemian vibe, which boasts relaxed hotels and villas as well as “hippie” markets.
When it comes to food, don’t miss bullit de peix, a stew made with rockfish and potatoes boiled in a saffron and garlic broth, or ensalada payesa, a salad filled with boiled red potatoes, tomatoes, green peppers, and onions.
Ibiza is best for: A legendary party scene, but plenty of culture if you know where to look.

Chinese researchers reconstruct face of 8,000-year-old man from remains
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:00:34 CST
14:00:34 KST

This photo taken with a mobile phone on Sept. 29, 2026 shows a reconstructed face of a man based on human remains unearthed at the Jiahu archaeological site in central China's Henan Province. (Xinhua/Ren Zhuoru)
ZHENGZHOU, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- A reconstructed face of a man who lived more than 8,000 years ago was unveiled Tuesday in Zhengzhou, capital of central China's Henan Province, providing insight into the region's prehistoric inhabitants.
The sculpture, based on human remains unearthed at the Jiahu archaeological site in Henan, combined physical anthropology with high-precision 3D facial reconstruction technology, according to researchers from the Henan Provincial Institute of Cultural Heritage and Archaeology and Jilin University's bioarchaeology laboratory.
This work represents a significant application of scientific methods in archaeology and gives the public a more direct way to visualize the people of Jiahu, said Wang Wei, head of the institute.
The individual was identified as a man aged between 25 and 30, based on the shape of his pelvis and the wear on his teeth, according to Zhu Hong, a professor at the laboratory.
His skull was regularly oval, with a prominent brow ridge and strong cheekbones, while his face was angular and relatively flat, and his nose was of moderate size, Zhu said. The features reflect physical traits typical of prehistoric people in the Central Plains, he added.
Researchers collected high-resolution 3D data and built a detailed model of the skull of the man. For the facial reconstruction, they used 28 key points on the skull and assessed muscle attachment features to shape the contours. They also added subtle wrinkles and a natural beard, taking the man's age at death into account, Zhu said.
The Jiahu site, located in Jiahu Village in Wuyang County, dates from about 9,000 to 7,500 years ago. It is a large and culturally rich early Neolithic settlement. Archaeologists have unearthed bone flutes, tortoise shells, pottery and stone items there, among other artifacts, which hold great importance in exploring the origins of the Chinese civilization.
Digital tools are increasingly used in archaeology in China. The country's latest five-year plan for the protection and inheritance of cultural heritage calls for using technologies such as artificial intelligence, satellite remote sensing, drones, 3D reality modeling and virtual reality to improve digital protection, and for stronger management of cultural heritage archives and digital assets. ■

Diesel taxes in Europe: Which countries charge the most?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:00:17 UTC
14:00:17 KST

Diesel has overtaken petrol as Europe's most expensive fuel, at a record €2.226 per litre. Yet EU governments still tax it about 12 cents less than petrol.
Diesel is now the most expensive fuel at Europe's pumps.
The EU weighted average price of diesel reached €2.226 per litre on 21 September 2026, according to the European Commission's Weekly Oil Bulletin. That was the highest level since the data began in 2005.
That is 13.4 cents more than a litre of Euro-super 95 petrol.
Filling a 50-litre tank with diesel now costs about €111. Roughly 40% of that amount goes on taxes.
Taxes on diesel averaged €0.861 per litre across the bloc, or 38.6% of the pump price.
On petrol, the tax bill is €0.981 per litre, about 12 cents more.
The war with Iran, which began in February, has disrupted energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, and diesel has been hit harder. Its EU average price has risen by about 40% since late February.
European Central Bank experts estimate that refining margins added €0.41 per litre to diesel in the third week of September, or 19% of what drivers pay.
For prices to fall, ECB experts said, "the key factor would be a cessation of the war in the Middle East, a normalisation of flows through the Strait of Hormuz and a restoration of global refining activity."
Why is diesel taxed less than petrol?
Diesel's lighter treatment is not new.
EU rules set a minimum excise duty of €0.33 per litre on diesel, against €0.359 on petrol.
Most governments also maintain a gap in their own rates, long defended as support for hauliers, farmers and other businesses that use diesel.
In 2015, the Brussels-based campaign group Transport & Environment calculated that Europeans paid an average of 14 cents more tax per litre of petrol than diesel. A decade later, the gap remains.
A 2021 Commission plan to tax fuels by energy content rather than volume would have ended diesel’s advantage. It requires the agreement of all 27 member states, but a compromise text failed to win unanimous support in November 2025.
How the tax bill adds up on diesel
Diesel is taxed in two stages.
First comes excise duty, a fixed amount per litre. Some countries add levies such as a carbon charge.
Then value-added tax (VAT), ranging from 17% in Luxembourg to 27% in Hungary, is applied on top of everything, including the excise. It is a tax on a tax.
Here are the 10 EU countries with the highest taxes on diesel. The ranking compares the amount of tax paid per litre, rather than the percentage of the pump price that goes on tax.
10. Greece: €0.855 per litre
Greece charges €0.41 per litre in excise, unchanged since July 2017, plus 24% VAT. Including other taxes of about €0.014 per litre, taxes make up 38.4% of the €2.224 pump price.
With petrol excise at €0.70, Greek diesel is taxed 28.6 cents less than petrol, the widest gap in the EU.
9. Austria: €0.897 per litre
Austria combines a mineral oil tax of €0.378 per litre with a carbon levy of about €0.145, before applying 20% VAT.
Taxes account for 40.1% of the €2.238 pump price.
8. Lithuania: €0.945 per litre
Lithuania charges a fixed diesel excise duty of €0.50 per litre, higher than the fixed duty on petrol, plus a CO₂ component of €0.0536.
It then applies 21% VAT.
A temporary cut in the fixed component of the excise duty to €0.45 per litre, approved in April in response to the Middle East conflict, ended on 15 June.
Together, taxes account for 41.9% of the €2.258 pump price.
7. France: €1.005 per litre
France levies €0.6075 per litre in excise on diesel, plus 20% VAT.
Taxes represent 42.2% of the €2.383 pump price.
6. The Netherlands: €1.006 per litre
The Netherlands has the EU's most expensive diesel, at €2.579 per litre, yet ranks only sixth for tax.
Its diesel excise is €0.55 per litre, against €0.84 on petrol.
That leaves Dutch diesel taxed 26.7 cents less than petrol.
5. Belgium: €1.014 per litre
Belgium charges exactly the same excise, €0.600 per litre, on diesel and petrol.
Because diesel's pre-tax price is higher, 21% VAT pushes its tax bill 6.9 cents above petrol's.
Taxes are 42.5% of the €2.387 price.
4. Germany: €1.024 per litre
Germany applies an energy tax of €0.4704 per litre, a carbon price of €0.162 and 19% VAT.
Taxes account for 41.7% of the €2.457 pump price.
That is about to change. On 25 September, the Bundestag approved a 14.04-cent cut in energy tax from 1 October to 31 December, worth around 17 cents per litre including VAT.
3. Finland: €1.030 per litre
Finland charges €0.511 per litre in excise and 25.5% VAT, the second-highest rate in the EU.
Taxes make up 40.3% of Finland’s €2.555 pump price.
**2. Italy: €**1.034 per litre
Italian drivers paid €2.281 per litre according to the European Commission’s Weekly Oil Bulletin for 21 September. At the excise rate then in force, €0.5729 per litre, plus 22% VAT, taxes totalled about €0.984 per litre, or 43.1% of the pump price.
However, on 26 September, excise rose to €0.6229 as the government scaled back its temporary tax discount. That rate applies until 5 October. Using the same €2.281 pump price for illustration, the higher excise combined with the standard 22% VAT would bring total tax to about €1.034 per litre, or 45.3%.
1. Denmark: €1.081 per litre
Denmark's excise of 4.261 Danish kroner per litre is worth about €0.571, and 25% VAT adds another €0.511.
Taxes account for 42.3% of the €2.555 pump price.
With diesel and petrol prices at record levels in Europe, these duties and taxes could change quickly, as European governments seek to cushion drivers from rising prices. From 1 October, Germany will cut petrol and diesel taxes by around 17 cents per litre, including VAT, while Czechia’s diesel tax reduction is expected to save drivers about 10 cents per litre. Spain has also extended its fuel tax relief.

SEOUL, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's finance ministry on Wednesday unveiled a revised fiscal outlook for 2026, forecasting a record-high tax revenue amid an unprecedented semiconductor boom.
The total tax revenue was estimated to hit an all-time high of 478.6 trillion won (about 353.1 billion U.S. dollars) in 2026, according to the Ministry of Finance and Economy.
The re-estimation was higher than last year's collection of 373.9 trillion won, surpassing the previous record of 395.9 trillion won set in 2022.
Revenue from corporate income tax was expected to surge 61.2 percent year-on-year to 136.4 trillion won in 2026, fueled by soaring corporate earnings, particularly from the country's top two chipmakers, Samsung Electronics and SK hynix.
The estimate for the combined operating profit of the two tech giants was set at 638 trillion won in 2026, sharply higher than 91 trillion won in 2025.
The collection of individual income tax was projected to increase 16.9 percent to 152.4 trillion won on the back of faster wage growth, driven by performance bonuses in the semiconductor and financial sectors, alongside Samsung's massive special dividend payment plan.
The value-added tax revenue was forecast to grow 12.4 percent to 89.0 trillion won due to private consumption recovery and import expansion.
Revenue from securities transactions and special rural taxes was estimated to spike in triple digits owing to explosive stock trading volumes in the first half. ■

Andy Burnham wants to review the UK’s relationship with the EU. What are the options?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:00:13 UTC
14:00:13 KST

Andy Burnham – pictured here with the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen – told Labour’s party conference that Brexit has ‘done more harm than good’, pledging to launch a big review of the UK’s relationship with the EU. Photograph: Toby Melville/AFP/Getty Images
Andy Burnham – pictured here with the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen – told Labour’s party conference that Brexit has ‘done more harm than good’, pledging to launch a big review of the UK’s relationship with the EU. Photograph: Toby Melville/AFP/Getty Images
Andy Burnham wants to review the UK’s relationship with the EU. What are the options?
The PM said Brexit has ‘done more harm than good’ and wants an assessment before the next UK-EU summit
Andy Burnham has said Brexit has “done more harm than good” and pledged to launch a major review of the UK’s relationship with the EU, opening the door to a potential referendum over rejoining the union.
He said he would “lay out options” around the time of the next EU-UK summit, due to be held at the end of November or soon after.
While he didn’t specify options, he did not explicitly rule out rejoining. Keir Starmer’s red lines of not rejoining the single market or customs union could now also be up for discussion within Labour’s ranks in the coming weeks.
“I would be stunned if Starmer’s red lines are in the next manifesto,” said Joël Reland, senior research fellow at UK in a Changing Europe, a key Brexit thinkthank.
What exactly did Burnham say on the EU?
“Brexit hasn’t given us control,” he said, arguing the UK had not just lost control of immigration – contrary to what Brexiters had promised – but also over the economy.
“I will take the opportunity around the summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe the different options are for Britain’s long term relationship with our European partners,” he said.
“There are different options and I will see if we can find consensus around one, which will give us clarity about our position and the future of the continent that we live in.”
Why is this significant?
Going beyond Starmer’s reset ambitions is a risky move and will test Burnham’s ability to sell any closer relationship with EU to a country still bruised by Brexit.
The stakes are high. In the 10 years since the Brexit referendum, the UK has drifted from its nearest trading bloc.
The UK has seen exports to the EU drop, travel restrictions for British passport holders and even potential new red tape for employers who send staff to the continent on short-term contracts.
A fight is under way to prevent the UK from being further locked out from trade by being included in coming Made in Europe legislation designed to protect European supply chains from cheap Chinese imports. So far it has the backing of the Netherlands, Italy and Germany but not France.
So what are the options?
Long shot – rejoin the EU
Rejoining the EU would require a referendum in the UK and potentially years of de-Brexit negotiations. Plus, Brussels would need some cast iron guarantees that the UK wouldn’t just walk out again.
It would mean a return to freedom of movement allowing EU citizens to live and work in the UK, and vice versa – viewed as unchecked immigration by Brexiters – but would also offer total freedom to trade without checks on standards of goods or customs forms, adding a potential 3-5% to GDP, according to the UKICE’s analysis.
The Swiss-style halfway house?
Switzerland is not a member of the EU but it struck a deal last year cementing its “frictionless access” to the single market, access to the EU’s electricity market, space programmes, Erasmus and the Digital Europe research programme, and participation in the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control.
In exchange, Switzerland agreed to free movement of people and to pay €375m (£322m) a year into the EU’s economic and cohesion funds.
The EU has previously offered the UK a Swiss-style deal but it was rejected by Boris Johnson because it required regulatory alignment and free movement.
Join the European Economic Area
Joining Norway and Liechtenstein in the EEA could add 2-3% to growth but would mean joining the single market, one of Starmer’s red lines, and accepting immigration of EU citizens again.
The single market brings with it four freedoms of movement – labour (people), capital (money), services and trade (goods).
Associate membership
Although many have reported that the EU’s offer to Canada was the first time associate membership has come up, it is not.
The EU can work expediently when the political need is there and three years ago mooted associate membership for Ukraine as a shortcut to the long accession process.
This could be an option that allows the UK a closer relationship than it currently has with the EU, with less requirement to cross previously stated red lines.
What is behind Burnham’s promise to redefine the UK’s relationship with Europe?
Labour already sees the relationship with the EU as a point of difference with the staunchly pro-Brexit Reform UK, but has felt nervous of handing Nigel Farage free political capital by suggesting Brexit could be reversed, or at the very least heavily watered down.
But sources say there is now a recognition in the Labour party that the offer to the public has got to be bigger than the current reset.
How long has Burnham got to set out a fresh Brexit review?
Time is short. Burnham has said he wants to have the conversation about the options over the next two months to coincide with the delayed EU-UK summit to be held in Brussels, perhaps at the end of November.

Nandy says children’s social media ban only ‘staging post’ in online safety drive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:00:12 UTC
14:00:12 KST

Lisa Nandy has warned technology firms that the government’s online safety crackdown is not finished, saying that banning under-16s from social media platforms is only a “staging post”.
Earlier this year the government announced that teenagers under the age of 16 would be banned from accessing “high-risk” social media apps, while safer platforms would be subjected to restrictions.
The social media ban will come into effect by March, with further measures targeted at 16- and 17-year-olds – including restrictions on websites that allow infinite scrolling and algorithms promoting harmful content as well as tighter age-verification checks – to follow.
Nandy has now vowed to go further. “We shouldn’t accept that this is the end,” the culture secretary said before her speech at the Labour party conference, which will be introduced by Georgia Harrison, a campaigner against image-based sexual abuse. “This is a staging post to what must be a very active interventionist state, policing and regulating the online space so that people are safe.”
She said the UK would be “pioneers of tech as a force for good” and would promote online spaces that were “genuinely safe, inclusive and empowering”.
She praised the former prime minister Keir Starmer and the former technology secretary Liz Kendall for announcing the ban in June. But she felt there had been a “step change” in the government’s approach since Andy Burnham became prime minister in July and handed her the online safety brief.
Comparing social media to real-world civic spaces, she said: “If we were in a situation where we were saying our town centres are now so unsafe that we’ve decided that every child is going to have to stay in their bedrooms, people would rightly be up in arms.
“How have we got to a point where we’re saying these social media sites are so harmful and dangerous that we cannot conceive of any way of protecting our children except to remove them altogether? This ends now.”
A consultation on the ban, which will apply to apps such as TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube and Instagram, attracted more than 116,000 responses, with 85% of parents thinking the risk of social media outweighed any benefit.
Nandy said she had told families bereaved as a result of teenagers experiencing online harm: “I want you to understand that that era ends today, and we start a new chapter where we have an active and empowering state that shapes those civic spaces so that they work for us.”
The MP for Wigan said the government had already shown a willingness to take on the big tech companies – and risk disapproval from US authorities – with plans to hand established broadcasters and media companies greater prominence on digital platforms such as YouTube and TikTok. “That is a difference of opinion with the US administration, but we do reserve the right to take a different approach,” she said.
While new technologies had always “upended society”, the internet was the only one to have been “entirely outsourced to the private sector” with no role for the state, Nandy said. “It’s not acceptable to outsource this to [the X owner, Elon] Musk or anybody else,” she said.
In one of her first moves on online safety, Nandy ordered technology companies to her office, and she said she was “not surprised, but appalled” that representatives from X failed to attend.
She acknowledged “there really is a problem” with Ofcom’s ability to enforce regulations and make firms adhere to the Online Safety Act. “Laws are only as good as the ability to enforce them,” she said.
Nandy has welcomed a suggestion from the BBC director general, Matt Brittin, that a “public service algorithm” could compete with big tech, which she felt fitted “with [Burnham’s] vision about the UK being a world leader in tech as a force for good”.
“In order to do that, you’ve got to be in the game, investing [and] shaping the technology,” she added. “But I think to win the permission of the public to do that, they’ve got to hear from us loud and clear that we will take action to protect people, particularly children, right now.”

  This article was amended on 30 September 2026. An earlier version said the UK’s upcoming social media ban would include “restrictions for 16- and 17-year-olds on websites that allow infinite scrolling and algorithmic content”; in fact, these restrictions are planned but do not yet have a determined date.

Healthy Babies programme to be expanded across England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:00:11 UTC
14:00:11 KST

The government is rolling out a Healthy Babies programme to every local authority in England, as part of its efforts to expand a Sure Start-type system of help for deprived children and families.
It aims to support parents with infant feeding, their mental health and building strong bonds with their babies, alongside health visits, midwifery care and wider services.
The scheme seeks to follow the principles of Sure Start, a network of centres offering integrated services for the under-fives and their families, launched in 1998 under a Labour government. Sure Start was seen as one of that government’s major successes, with one study saying it generated longer-term savings worth twice the system’s cost.
But much of that scheme was dismantled amid massive spending cuts by the Conservatives. The new policy of family hubs will commit £500m to opening 1,000 centres from April 2027.
Announcing the expansion of the Healthy Babies programme at the Labour conference in Liverpool, Yvette Cooper, the Health and Social Care secretary, is expected to say that the programme will reach up to 1,000 family hubs over the next two years.
Since the election the Labour government has opened new family hubs across England, but more than half of local authorities have hubs without Healthy Babies services.
“Something is missing in half of communities … the Healthy Babies services – mental health support for mums and dad, the feeding and bonding support for your new baby. That changes now,” Cooper will say.
“We will bring back the Sure Start health services into every family centre. One of the Labour party’s greatest achievements, restored to families throughout the land.”
Sure Start and its successor programmes are seen as integral to the narrative of the modern Labour party, with housing secretary Angela Rayner saying her life as a teenage mother and that of her son were turned around by her local centre, which offered her a parenting course.
In an article for the Guardian in July last year, Bridget Phillipson, then the education secretary, recounted working closely with the first Sure Start centre in Washington, Tyne and Wear, where, before entering politics, she ran a refuge for women fleeing domestic violence.
“It was a lifeline for those women who, despite everything, were determined to give their children the very best start in life,” she wrote. “The gap in achievement we see between our poorest and most affluent children at 16 is baked in before they even start school, creating a vicious cycle of lost life chances that’s all too visible in the shameful number of young people not earning or learning.”
In a follow-up announcement to the plan for family hub centres, Phillipson’s department had announced plans to pay qualified early years teachers to work in the most deprived areas, where their work could have the greatest impact.

Inside the Ukrainian military unit training fighters from China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:00:11 UTC
14:00:11 KST

On the makeshift workbench in the cramped front room of a cottage near the frontlines of the Russia-Ukraine war, there are all the accoutrements of a drone workshop. The walls are lined with pliers and rolls of duct tape; the table is cluttered with screwdrivers and piles of wire. Propped up against the wall are two kamikaze drones. Only one item looks out of place in this Ukrainian village house: a pot of Chinese longjing tea, the leaves wilted from repeated top-ups.
Good tea is one of the many things that Tim misses about his life in China. His parents post monthly supplies to Ukraine. “I think about all of it,” the 44-year-old said, of his home country. “It brings back memories and emotions.”
Tim, who asked to be referred to by his English name, is the lead volunteer in a Ukrainian military unit that this year launched an unusual project: to recruit soldiers from the country seen as Russia’s biggest backer, China.
Many Ukrainian military units have their own brands and public presences as they compete with each other for funding and new recruits. But in this case, the commander of the unit, which focuses on reconnaissance, asked that its identity be withheld because of the sensitivity of the Chinese volunteers project.
“It’s for their sake first and foremost,” said the commander, known by the call sign Muse. “For their own safety and that of their families.”
Muse said five Chinese men who had joined his unit had returned to China after completing their training because of pressure from the Chinese authorities. “We’d put our heart and soul into them,” he lamented. He is fearful that more Chinese soldiers – there are about a dozen so far in the unit – could quit if their identity is revealed. He asked that none of his soldiers’ faces be shown in photographs.
Ukraine’s military is facing an acute manpower shortage. Most of those willing to volunteer to fight have done so, and are fatigued, while some civilian men have gone into hiding to avoid being mobilised. That has turned attention to another pool of potential recruits: foreigners.
There are about 16,000 foreign fighters in Ukraine, making up less than 3% of the armed forces. Before being sacked as defence minister in July, Mykhailo Fedorov passed several reforms designed to make foreign recruitment easier. He predicted that 50% of frontline service members or assault troops could be foreign citizens.
But Chinese volunteers present a unique challenge.
On the one hand, they are uniquely vulnerable to pressure from their own government. The Chinese authorities keep close tabs on their citizens. Chinese law does not specifically forbid citizens from joining foreign armies, but several Chinese volunteers in Ukraine said security services had questioned them or their relatives about their work.
A spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry said it had issued multiple security alerts “to ask Chinese nationals to stay away from areas of armed conflict … and, in particular, avoid participation in any party’s military operations”.
On the other hand, the Chinese soldiers hail from a country that has provided overwhelming support for Russia during the war in Ukraine. Although China claims to be neutral, Beijing has increased trade links with Moscow to record levels since 2022 and provided diplomatic support on numerous occasions. There have also been reports, denied by China, of high-level military cooperation between the two countries.
Some people worry that the Chinese soldiers in Ukraine could provide useful military intelligence to Beijing. An officer from another brigade said he would “think twice” before taking someone from China.
Muse, however, is unbothered. “In this situation, for us commanders, for the Ukrainian people, anyone will do. Because there aren’t enough people,” he said.
Plus, he added, the Chinese work hard. Tim’s main job in the unit is repairing drones. In one week he repaired about 10 Mavics and 15 first-person view (FPV) drones. Impressed, Muse joked that “it is better to have one Chinese person than 10 Ukrainians”.
Chinese volunteers find their way to Muse’s unit through social media and word of mouth. Although there are cursory background checks done by central authorities in Kyiv, Muse entrusts Tim to do the main screening, through a series of interviews.
Tim said the main qualities he looked for were a commitment to Ukraine’s democracy and sovereignty and an ability to communicate well. He added: “I am firmly against accepting someone who is driven simply by hatred for his own country.” He said he had already rejected more than 30 Chinese applicants since joining the unit himself in January, and that he attempted to screen out people with criminal records as well.
But in the murky world of foreign fighters, where people come with stories and claims that are often impossible to verify, dissatisfaction with one’s own country is often a factor.
Vanya, a 36-year-old from central China’s Hubei province, joined the unit over the summer.
Sitting under a trellis of grapevines outside a cottage near the frontlines, stalked by Russian FPV drones, he said life in China had become “suffocating”.
Using a VPN to jump over China’s firewall of internet censorship, he had read about the war in Ukraine, and become familiar with “ideas about democracy and freedom”. That awakening coincided with China’s own economic downturn. His own income, working in home renovations, fell by as much as 50% in some months.
He had long been interested in the military, but was too old to enlist in China. The decision to come to Ukraine “didn’t come out of the blue”, Vanya said. “It was the result of a lot of things building up over time: my weariness of my previous life, my longing for democracy and freedom, as well as my views on Ukraine.”
Other members of the unit claim a more fervent ideology. Nero, a 37-year-old from Fujian province, spent years posting online in support of Ukraine, becoming a well-known influencer. Several of his accounts were deleted; Nero thinks this was in response to his pro-Ukraine views.
He said the blowback he got from suspected Russian spam accounts for his support for Ukraine propelled him towards volunteering.
“I thought: the world shouldn’t be like this. Why should I suffer or go through all this just for speaking the truth?”
His move, which he publicised on social media, led to more harassment. As he arrived in Ukraine, a Russian-language “wanted” poster, which included his real name, date of birth, and picture, appeared online. The poster, which appeared to be faked, accused him of “participating in an armed conflict as a mercenary” and “illegally crossing the state border of the Russian federation”. Nero suspected it was produced by a Chinese propaganda agency working on behalf of Russia, and denied making it himself, saying that revealing his identity endangered him.
Until recently a project manager earning a decent salary in China, Nero is now training to be an FPV drone pilot. “I want people to know that not all Chinese people support Russia’s aggression. Many Chinese people, like me, are kind and want to help Ukraine,” Nero said.
All of the volunteers agreed that scrutiny from the Chinese authorities would make it difficult to return home. “If I go back now, it would be hard to leave again,” said Jinmu, a welder by trade, now working as an electrical engineer, specialising in explosives and batteries.
Whatever contribution they may ultimately make towards peace, or to war, as Chinese nationals their decision is likely to have consequences that last beyond the conflict that they are now a part of. On 23 September, one of their Chinese comrades in the unit was killed in a Russian attack. Upon hearing the news, one volunteer, a doctor, decided to leave. The rest, said Nero, insisted on staying.

Autumn sunshine could extend Britain’s bumper year for butterflies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:00:11 UTC
14:00:11 KST

Summer is over, most flowers were frazzled long ago and we might expect to see few butterflies beyond September. But it is not over yet.
The reverberations from one of the best butterfly seasons in Britain this century will continue if there is more autumn sunshine.
Thanks to extended warm seasons, more species are squeezing in an extra generation. Small coppers are on the wing again alongside large and small whites, while red admirals and peacocks pop out of hibernation to feed on late-flowering buddleia.
Britain’s two main migratory species, the painted lady and the clouded yellow, are also still whizzing around, pausing on their flight back to frost-free southern Europe.
The most exciting autumn sighting is a third, much rarer migrant, the Queen of Spain fritillary. It’s almost certainly been the best ever year in Britain for this graceful orange-brown butterfly with dazzling panels of silver on its underside.
Like other migratory butterflies, this species can rapidly produce a new generation of adult butterflies in about eight weeks. If we enjoy more sunshine in October, more offspring of the Queen of Spains spotted around the south and east coast of England in August will emerge as adult butterflies, complementing the ginger, cinnamon and gold of the autumn leaves.

Cullen skink pies, vegetarian haggis and chippy fritters: Ali Stoner’s recipes for twists on Scottish classics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:00:10 UTC
14:00:10 KST

There is a depth and history to Scotland’s food that reaches far beyond deep-fried Mars bars or urban myths about haggis. Kitchens were humble and full of life – recipes passed by word of mouth, scraps of paper shared between friends, generations stitching together simple meals. I’m lucky enough that my mum taught me how a potato, a handful of oatmeal and a bit of salt and butter could make a meal and hold a story, but life changes – new ingredients arrive, we move away, time grows shorter – and, sometimes, those simple, comforting recipes drift out of reach. Today’s dishes began as a keepsake for my children – to save old recipes, to record a feeling of home – but also as an invitation to discover what happens when memory meets invention.
Cullen skink bake (pictured top)
The starting point for these smoked fish pies is basically a cullen skink soup, which I thicken to make the filling. Traditional cullen skink relies on Scottish smoked haddock for its flavour. There is just nothing else like it, though Shetland smoked cod also works really well here. Finish these wee pies with a grating of sharp cheddar. Delicious.
Prep 15 min
Cook 1 hr 20 min, plus cooling time
Makes 4 pies 
15g unsalted butter, plus 1 knob extra for frying
Olive oil, for frying
100g onions, peeled and finely chopped
Salt and black pepper, to taste
250g potatoes (use a good all-rounder such as maris piper or king edward), peeled and cut into 1cm cubes
200ml whole milk
  250g good (ie, undyed) smoked haddock, or smoked cod, cut into bite-sized pieces
15g plain flour
1 tbsp chopped chives
1 tbsp chopped flat-leaf parsley
1 tsp dijon mustard
  1 standard 320g sheet ready-rolled all-butter shortcrust pastry, or puff pastry (27cm × 35cm)
Grated cheddar, to finish
1 egg yolk mixed with a little milk
Melt the knob of butter and a drizzle of oil in a large saucepan on a medium heat. Add the onions and a pinch of salt, and saute on a low to medium heat for about five minutes, to soften. Add the cubed potatoes, keep the heat low, cover and sweat for 10 or so minutes, until the potatoes start to soften but are still a little hard. Stir in the milk, lay the fish on top of the potatoes, then cover again and simmer for 10 minutes more, until you can easily press the point of a knife into the potato: you want them to retain their shape, rather than be mushy. Using a slotted spoon, carefully lift the fish, potatoes and onion out of the hot milk, then pour the liquid into a jug.
Melt the 15g butter in the same pan, then stir in the flour and cook on a low heat for a couple of minutes. Pour in the reserved poaching liquid, stir for about five minutes, until the mixture thickens, then take off the heat and carefully fold in the fish, potatoes and onions. Add the herbs, mustard and black pepper to taste, then leave to cool.
Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas7. Lay out the pastry on a lightly floured work surface and cut it into four strips. Pile the filling on one half of each strip, leaving enough of a border to seal around the edges later. Top the filling with a little grated cheddar, then brush some of the beaten egg yolk mixture all around the edges. Fold the empty half of each pastry strip up and over the filling, press all around the edges to seal, then crimp with the back of a fork.
With a sharp knife, cut a small steam vent in the top of each pie, then transfer them to a lined baking sheet and brush with the remaining egg yolk mixture. Bake the pastries for 30 minutes, until puffed and golden. I like to serve these with a sharply dressed green salad for a crunchy, vinegary contrast. You will probably have a little filling left over, which is perfect for an omelette or toasted sandwich the next day.
Vegetarian haggis
I often make a veggie haggis, mainly for pals who are scared by the real deal, and this one really does replicate the original in flavour, texture and looks. It also makes a brilliant filling for “sausage” rolls. After making so many Scottish dishes over the years, I noticed I was using the same herbs and spices on repeat, so I created a blend that represents the essence of Celtic flavours. It is so adaptable that, if you’re anything like me, you will find yourself using it in so many things, from marinades to roast potatoes and everything in between.
Prep 25 min
Soak 15 min
Cook 1 hr 10 min
Serves 6
For the Scottish seven-spice blend (makes 1 small jar)
25g black peppercorns
  15g coriander seeds
  1 tbsp juniper berries
  1 tbsp allspice berries
  1 tbsp dried thyme
  1 tbsp dried rosemary
  1 tbsp ground nutmeg
For the haggis
15g dried mushrooms (porcini or shiitake), diced
2 tbsp olive oil
  25g butter
  1 brown onion, peeled and finely chopped
2 garlic cloves, peeled and minced
4 portobello mushrooms, diced
2 tsp Scottish seven-spice (see above and method)
1 tsp white pepper
  ½ teaspoon ground mace
  2 sprigs fresh sage, leaves picked and finely chopped
1 sprig fresh rosemary, leaves picked and finely chopped
2 carrots, very finely diced (I use a food processor)
75g black beluga lentils
  1 tbsp yeast extract (Marmite or Vegemite, say)
500ml vegetable stock
  400g can white beans, drained and chopped
Finely grated zest of 1 unwaxed lemon
  Salt
  50g steel-cut or pinhead oats
  Onion jam, to serve, ideally spiked with a little whisky and warmed (optional)
First, make the Scottish seven-spice blend. Toast the peppercorns, coriander seeds, juniper and allspice berries in a dry pan until fragrant, then blitz to a powder in a spice grinder (alternatively, use a pestle and mortar). Add the thyme and rosemary, blend again, then add the ground nutmeg and blend again. Decant into a jar and use freely and creatively whenever you want to add a bit of Celtic flavour.
Now for the haggis. Cover the dried mushrooms in about 100ml boiling water and leave to soak for 15 minutes.
Put the oil and butter in a saucepan on a low to medium heat, then add the onion and garlic, and saute gently until they start to soften. Add the fresh mushrooms, followed by the drained rehydrated dried mushrooms (save their soaking liquor) and, after a couple of minutes, when they have softened, add all the spices, herbs, carrots, lentils, yeast extract, reserved mushroom liquor and 400ml of the stock. Simmer, stirring frequently, for about 30 minutes, until the lentils are almost soft.
Stir the beans and lemon zest into the mix and add a half teaspoon of salt. Test the lentils for “doneness”: they should still have a little bite and most of the liquid should have been absorbed, so if they need more cooking, add the rest of the stock. Add the oats, cook for five to 10 minutes, until they absorb the remaining liquid, then taste and add more salt, if required.
Serve with champit tatties (buttery mash studded with sliced spring onions), mashed neeps (swede) and some warm, whisky-spiked onion jam.
Chippy batter potato fritters
This simple batter gives the most amazing crunch to fish, fritters and even sausages: no fancy ingredients required. The vinegar reacts with the baking powder to produce a light, airy batter, while the cornflour helps with that all-important crunch. You could serve these with tartare sauce, but the pickled onion mayo, inspired by that big jar on the chip-shop counter, works a treat.
Prep 15 min
Cook 30 min
Serves 4–6
For the fritters
2 large unpeeled baking potatoes, cut into 5mm-thick slices (I use a mandoline)
Plain flour, for dusting
Vegetable oil, for deep-frying
Salt
For the chippy batter
75g plain flour
  60g cornflour
  1 tsp baking powder
  ½ tsp salt
  2 tsp malt vinegar
For the pickled onion mayo (optional)
70g pickled onions, roughly chopped, plus 1–2 tbsp of the onion pickling vinegar
20g small capers, finely chopped
1 tbsp finely chopped parsley
  1 tbsp finely chopped chives
  2 tbsp mayonnaise
  1 pinch salt
Rinse and drain the potato slices, then put them in a pan of salted cold water – if possible, use a wide saute pan, so the slices aren’t piled on top of each other. Bring to a boil, simmer for five minutes, then lift out with a fish slice or large slotted spoon, transfer to a rack and leave to steam dry. Chill uncovered while you make the batter and pickled onion mayo.
For the batter, sift the flours, baking powder and salt into a bowl, then gradually whisk in 150ml cold water until incorporated. Add the vinegar and whisk again to combine.
For the pickled onion mayo, simply mix all the ingredients in a bowl.
Take the potato slices out of the fridge. Put a bowl filled with flour next to your frying station and season it with salt. Heat enough oil for deep-frying in a deep, heavy-based pan or a deep-fat fryer to 180C (350F) (or until a drizzle of batter sizzles and browns immediately). Working in small batches, dip the potato slices first in the seasoned flour, then in the batter, and deep-fry, turning as needed, for up to five minutes in total, until golden and crisp. When they are cooked, the oil will almost stop bubbling and be nearly still – that’s when you know they’re ready. Lift out with a slotted spoon (remove any bits that fall off into the oil, too) and drain on kitchen paper. Season immediately with salt, then keep warm while you fry the rest of the fritters.
Get the fritters into buttered rolls, if you like, or serve them just as they are with some pickled onion mayo, and enjoy the crunch.

China’s corporate sector remains considerably weaker than it was before the Covid-19 pandemic, but the country is emerging as a key beneficiary of the global artificial intelligence boom thanks to its ample power capacity, according to a Natixis survey of thousands of firms and a separate research report.
Profit margins at Chinese firms had stabilised at about 4.5 per cent for the first half of 2026, but remained well below the nearly 9 per cent recorded by their global peers, according to the French bank’s latest China corporate monitor presented on Tuesday.
Returns on capital at Chinese firms hovered at around 6 per cent in the same period, compared with more than 11 per cent globally, the report said. The findings were based on a comparison of about 2,300 Chinese firms and 9,000 overseas counterparts.
Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for the Asia-Pacific region at Natixis, highlighted what she described as the “duality of the Chinese economy”, arguing that it extended well beyond macroeconomic data.

Time to get tough on food, booze and tobacco
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Want to receive this newsletter straight to your inbox? Sign up here to receive the reporting and intel from the Gastein Health Forum.
— Don't shy away from regulating food, alcohol and tobacco to tackle Europe's biggest threat to society — chronic diseases — says the head of Austria's food and drugs agency.
— An expert panel in Germany hands down a proposal to reward pharmaceutical companies that invest in Germany through clinical trials or manufacturing.
— One MEP remains unconvinced on a critical patent proposal on the table for the Biotech Act following a roundtable of industry and European officials.
Welcome to Wednesday’s Morning Health Care! Seven coffees, two schnitzels, two paninis, a lemon tart and a heaping of scrambled eggs later, and that’s a wrap on our first 24 hours in Gastein. Another week like this and Claudia and I might need to take a closer look at the Commission’s heart health screening recommendations we’ve written so much about after we get back to Brussels …
Get in touch: [email protected], [email protected]. Follow us on X: @chiappa_claudia,@domgiannini_
RAMPING UP PREVENTION: Governments should focus on regulating key unhealthy ingredients instead of getting caught up in the “complex” debate on ultra-processed foods, according to Johannes Pleiner-Duxneuner, managing director of the Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety.
Prevention: Preventing growing rates of chronic diseases is one of the main areas governments should focus on “because non-communicable diseases, diabetes, obesity are the main threats for our society,” he told Morning Health Care on the sidelines of the European Health Forum in Gastein, Austria.
But but but: discussions on prevention can get complicated, he said, for example when trying to tackle ultra-processed foods. The key is to keep it simple, Pleiner-Duxneuner said. “We should focus on sugar, salt, alcohol, tobacco. I think these are the main killers.”
Zooming out: Brussels is currently a hotspot for the prevention debate, with discussions on how to tackle ill health caused by industries such as food, alcohol and tobacco often heating up. Earlier this week, MEPs clashed over language describing the impact of alcohol on cancer in a parliamentary cancer report. Some lawmakers argued industry profits were being put before people’s health.
But it’s not just alcohol: Lawmakers are struggling to figure out how to nail down the best measures to reduce consumption of ultra-processed foods and tobacco. The debate on UPFs is gaining momentum, with the European Commission recently asking its Scientific Advice Mechanism to assess how UPFs should be defined, their health effects and consumption patterns. And tobacco regulation continues to divide countries as the EU mulls a proposal to raise taxes on cigarettes and set minimum levies for vapes, heated tobacco and nicotine pouches.
The sugar debate: More countries are introducing sugary drink taxes in an attempt to curb consumption amid soaring obesity rates, particularly among children. The measures are backed by the World Health Organization, which says “… taxes are one of the strongest tools we have for promoting health and preventing disease.” The German government is planning to introduce a new tax on sugary drinks starting in 2027, while the U.K., for example, has had one for years. Pleiner-Duxneuner said he’s a “fan” of the U.K.’s sugar tax: “From a scientific clinical point of view, there is no reason not to implement it in other European countries.”
Tricky: Though Austria does not currently have a sugar tax, the topic often enters the public and political debate — though it receives pushback from industry, Pleiner-Duxneuner said. “Definitely no one wants to damage the industry, so that's one of the reasons why it's not a hot topic at the moment,” he said. “But I think it is one of the tools that you can [use] to reduce sugar consumption.”
Don’t forget education: It’s key to pair regulation with educational programs targeting children, starting as early as kindergarten. “Austrian figures show that it's seven times more effective if you do education in kindergarten or early school pupils rather than doing it with teenagers,” he said. And it’s key to meet children where they are: social media. “This is something we're looking at — advertisements also on social media, not only TV commercials.”
WHO’S GOING TO COUGH UP FOR THE BONUS? A proposal to reward pharmaceutical companies that invest in Germany, through clinical trials or manufacturing, has left the hardest question unanswered — how to pay for the industry incentives, our colleague Louis Westendarp writes in.
An expert panel handed over its plan on Tuesday to two state secretaries — one from the German Ministry of Economic Affairs and one from the Ministry of Health. The government promised to deliver the proposal by the end of the month, after concluding sweeping health care reforms in July, including cutting drug prices by more than doubling mandated discounts.
At the same time: Germany is under U.S. pressure to increase its drug prices, and many are watching to see if this proposal will also appease Trump administration officials. Closed-door talks between the two countries are ongoing.
Will it be enough? As our Berlin colleagues reported at the start of the month, the offer is to phase out the scheduled 8.5 percentage points increase in the manufacturer discount from 7 percent to 15.5 percent — with a 2 percentage point cut for adhering to collective bargaining agreements, 3 percentage points for local research and development, and 3.5 for German production.
The cost: The scheme costs approximately €1.3 billion, according to the National Association of Statutory Health Insurance Funds (GKV-Spitzenverband). However, it remains unclear who will cover this expense. The report merely outlined several financing options, also scooped by our Berlin colleagues.
Proposal 1: Pharmaceutical companies that do not meet the bonus criteria should bear the cost of the scheme through a higher price discount. However, the expert panel deemed this proposal "ineffective," according to the report.
Proposal 2: Funds for the bonus could be saved elsewhere within the statutory health insurance system. This would require a further review of the finance commission's report.
Proposals 3 and 4: The regulation could pay for itself through macroeconomic effects, or the bonus could be funded via the federal budget.
No decision reached: The matter has been left for others to decide — specifically, the coalition parties, people close to the panel told Louis. "We will now examine it in greater detail and proceed to implementation as quickly as possible," Frank Wetzel, State Secretary at the economic affairs ministry, said.
Ahem: It’s not the only tricky financial issue Germany is trying to resolve right now, with long-term care, pensions, and the fuel tax rebate also up for debate.
BAND OF BROTHERS: Back at Gastein, Pleiner-Duxneuner revealed that Austria is working on a reimbursement model with Belgium, the Netherlands and other countries with similar pricing systems, as pharma companies were becoming increasingly willing to walk away from talks. Companies were instead opting to maintain higher prices in the U.S. to avoid Trump policies that copy lower prices in Europe, said Pleiner-Duxneuner.
Changing track: “In the past years, the companies were fighting actually to get access in Austria, and what we see more and more is that actually they're leaving the table: ‘No, we are not launching it with that price … otherwise we would have an average price that is ruining also the U.S. market price’,” Pleiner-Duxneuner told Morning Health Care. This has already happened for a handful of medicines including those for orphan diseases and cancer, he said.
** Every weekday afternoon, the Brussels Playbook Capitals newsletter draws on our reporting across national capitals to look ahead at what is shaping the EU agenda next. Sign up here.**
STAYING PUT: A roundtable of industry and European officials to thrash out the pros and cons of extending patents for certain biotech drugs failed to convince one of the MEPs critical of the proposal in the Biotech Act to change his mind.
What’s this about? Leading MEPs on the law hosted the meeting Tuesday to address concerns from some lawmakers that no independent impact assessment had been conducted on the bill. The proposed patent extension — known as a supplementary protection certificate — is one of the main sticking points in negotiations between MEPs. The one-year extension is designed to entice drug developers to test and manufacture in Europe.
No thanks: Socialists and Democrats MEP Tiemo Wölken — who is leading the legal affairs committee opinion on the law — said he didn’t hear anything to change his mind on granting patent extensions. “The Union cannot afford to grant additional patent protection without securing tangible benefits in return,” he told Morning Health Care. His amendments have sought to remove the patent offering.
Conditional: Some in industry have lobbied to remove the clinical trial and manufacturing conditions for the patent. “Multi-country clinical trials and the significant production within the Union are the only real added value in the Commission’s proposal, and we must safeguard them,” Wölken said. “Anyone seeking to weaken or remove these criteria is working against the Union’s interests.” He said it would have been good to hear from patient groups about the impacts as well.
They agree: Several NGOs expressed disappointment to Morning Health Care that they weren’t invited, arguing the panel was too industry-heavy. “We are particularly surprised and concerned that civil society representatives, especially patient representatives, were not invited to this meeting,” the European Patients’ Forum said. “Patients and their representatives have an essential role to play in this debate. We also have important perspectives to contribute on the Biotech Act and the extension of Supplementary Protection Certificates (SPCs), particularly as patients will be directly affected by its consequences.”
Patients first: The European Patients’ Forum wants to scrap the patent extension proposal, “because of its impact on timely patient access to medicines and the sustainability of healthcare systems,” it said. The EPF also doesn’t want clinical trial timelines to be further reduced so that patients’ rights and safety remain the priority.
Moving too fast: The forum also raised concerns about the pace of negotiations, as MEPs are trying to agree on a compromise text by December. “This is particularly important given the exceptionally fast pace of negotiations, which raises concerns that key issues may not receive the in-depth consideration they require, particularly in a broader political context where competitiveness is increasingly being prioritised over public health objectives,” EPF added. You can see all their asks here.
INCREASED SPREAD: Climate change is spurring the spread of diseases like dengue and chikungunya through vectors such as mosquitoes, ticks, and bugs as temperatures warm and new places become at risk, delegates at Gastein were warned Tuesday.
Speedy: One mosquito in Europe moves 60 kilometers farther north each year, and outbreaks and local transmission of dengue and chikungunya are moving even faster, reaching up to 120 kilometers farther north than before, said Jan Semenza, an environmental epidemiologist at Heidelberg University. This is putting tens of millions more people at risk every year, he said.
You can’t say we didn’t know: The world might have been caught off guard by the coronavirus and the ongoing outbreak of the Bundibugyo ebolavirus in the Congo, but it can see the rise of vector-borne diseases, HERA Deputy Head Laurent Muschel told a panel at the European Health Forum in Gastein. This was growing “slowly but surely,” which means Europe shouldn’t be caught out, he said. “We have a bit of time, but not so much, and it's time to invest.”
Underprepared: Gaps in the European system included a lack of medical contingencies for most vector-borne diseases, including insufficient antivirals and vaccines that cover a broad spectrum, Muschel said. Diagnostics also needed to improve, he added.
A 1-year-old baby has been euthanized in the Netherlands, the Telegraph reports.
Novo to pay up to $2.6 billion for the rights to an experimental weight loss pill, reports Reuters.

EU accused of hiding environmental impact of data centers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

According to the European Commission's figures, Europe’s data centers used 20.7 terawatt-hours of electricity and more than 8 million cubic meters of water in 2025. | Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP via Getty Images
The European Union has shielded data centers from public scrutiny about how much energy they use, according to a formal complaint filed Monday against the European Commission.
The complaint lodged this week by Lighthouse Reports, and first reported by POLITICO, accuses the EU executive of setting up rules keeping the public from seeing how much energy and water are used by individual data centers.
This comes as public opposition to power-hungry AI data centers grows across Europe, while energy prices rise.
Advertisement
Lighthouse Reports, a Netherlands-based non-profit conducting cross-border investigations of alleged government and corporate wrongdoing, accuses the Commission of building a "wall of silence" about energy consumption.
EU policymakers are determined "to deny or deter access to, and obfuscate understanding of, how data centers are performing," reads the complaint filed under the Aarhus Convention, a legally binding international treaty that gives the public rights to information and participation in environmental decision-making.
The challenge will face its first test in November, when the Aarhus Convention Compliance Committee meets to decide whether it is admissible. Subsequently, Aarhus could find the EU in breach of its obligations under the convention.
The Commission didn't respond to POLITICO's request for a comment.
Big power
As the boom in artificial intelligence drives rising energy demand, the EU has publicly declared its target of tripling data-center capacity in the coming years in a bid to keep pace with the U.S. and China. Meanwhile, as energy prices rise, public resistance to data centers is expanding around Europe.
To limit the environmental costs, the Commission presented a new transparency label last week to drive investment towards greener facilities, with minimum performance standards expected to follow.
Advertisement
"If we do not make sure that these big power consumers are indeed in line with our overall objectives… then they will risk undermining our ability to live up to our own targets," the EU's energy chief, Dan Jørgensen, said in an interview with POLITICO.
According to the Commission's figures, Europe’s data centers used 20.7 terawatt-hours of electricity — about as much electricity as the entire nation of Croatia consumes — and more than 8 million cubic meters of water in 2025. That's a 26% increase in electricity use and 52% in water use from 2024.
But those numbers do not fully account for the sector's actual use, as the totals are the result of incomplete data collected by the Commission. The data has only been published in aggregate, following a 2024 law that banned Brussels and EU capitals from disclosing "all information and key performance indicators for individual data centers" amid lobbying from tech giants, which cited commercial interests.
Diego Solier, a conservative member of the European Parliament working on the EU's legislative push to boost the bloc's digital capacity, said Europe's data center expansion must be accompanied by reliable information for citizens and policymakers about how much energy and water is being used.
"Transparency should be the starting point," said Solier, who didn't comment on the complaint itself, which wasn't yet public. "At the same time, transparency must be proportionate, and should not require companies to disclose genuinely commercially sensitive information."
Right to know
Lighthouse Reports says the Commission "holds the primary responsibility [of] denying public knowledge of the effects of Europe's massive data center build-out," by allowing operators to keep details of their consumption under wraps and dodge scrutiny in the process — in breach of the Aarhus Convention, which the EU has been a party to since 2005.
Advertisement
After failed efforts to force the Commission and national governments to disclose the data they hold, Lighthouse Reports is accusing them of wrongfully hiding behind secrecy carve-outs.
"The Commission sits at the top of an edifice of non-disclosure encompassing the vast majority of the EU," the report said. "Siding with commercial secrecy over the public's right to know erodes legitimacy and damages trust further."
New efforts towards more transparency, including a rating label heavily criticized by industry groups, fall short of correcting course, the complainant added.
The label will require operators to grade their energy efficiency, water usage and clean power uptake on a scale of A to G, starting from next summer. But Lighthouse Reports argued that the rules still conceal the total energy consumption and other key metrics to properly assess their carbon footprints.
"The choice of ratios over actual consumption figures has no basis in technical constraints, it is a choice that favors the industry over public interest," says the Lighthouse complaint.

As European leaders warn of Russian attacks, Lithuania sees no signs of new escalation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

As European leaders warn of possible Russian attacks and hybrid provocations, experts and officials agree that there are no signs of a new escalation.
“In my view, the situation remains as it was. The point is that the Russians certainly have not stopped, so talk of possible provocations is nothing new,” military expert and Vilnius University Institute of International Relations and Political Science (VU TSPMI) associate professor Deividas Šlekys told the ELTA news wire.
In his assessment, large-scale military operations are less likely than specific provocations aimed at spreading panic among the public and exerting political pressure.
“Nobody is preparing to conquer us at the moment – neither right now nor this year. In this case, some kind of specific, highly precise attacks or provocations are more likely, aimed not so much at causing physical damage as at sowing serious panic in people’s minds,” Šlekys said.
According to him, Russia could use such provocations to divide Lithuanian society and undermine unity among NATO countries.
‘Nothing new’
Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of the National Crisis Management Centre (NKVC), said Russia’s hybrid pressure on Lithuania and other European countries is “not a new phenomenon”.
“Since 2024, Lithuania alone has recorded a number of attacks or provocations involving acts of sabotage, as well as cyber and information operations,” Vitkauskas told ELTA.
He said warnings and preparedness measures by neighbouring and allied countries were a responsible response to the current security environment.
“Early warning, institutional preparedness and informing the public reduce the impact of provocations and strengthen NATO’s overall resilience,” the NKVC head said.
When assessing specific incidents, Vitkauskas urged people to distinguish confirmed facts from speculation and rely on information provided by official institutions.
“Based on the official information published so far, there is no evidence that the drones that entered Lithuanian airspace were targeting sites in Lithuania,” Vitkauskas said.
He noted that Lithuania has strengthened the protection of strategic infrastructure, while the NKVC, together with intelligence and other responsible institutions, has issued recommendations to companies and institutions that may face the risk of sabotage or acts of subversion.
Vitkauskas also urged the public to remain vigilant and not spread unverified information, as kinetic incidents or provocations may be accompanied by information operations aimed at causing fear and undermining trust in institutions.
Martinaitis: threat level remains unchanged
Meanwhile, Tomas Martinaitis, a Social Democrat and member of the parliamentary National Security and Defence Committee (NSDK), says the level of the Russian threat remains unchanged.
Meanwhile, Moscow’s messaging about possible retaliatory actions against NATO and EU countries may be intended to cause anxiety and undermine public confidence.
"If we assess the situation as a whole, I would say that the level of the threat, as intelligence officials have also confirmed, has not changed. Russia's unpredictability remains. The tactics may be changing slightly, with different types of actions emerging, but the essence remains unchanged," Martinaitis told ELTA.
A similar sentiment was repeated by the Lithuanian prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevičius, as well as the secretary-general of NATO, Mark Rutte, in Brussels on Tuesday.
Further reading
In recent weeks, the leaders of several European countries have spoken about the threat of possible Russian provocations.
In early September, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that, based on intelligence assessments, Russia could be preparing hybrid drone and missile attacks against countries supporting Ukraine, and urged the public to be prepared for various scenarios.
Meanwhile, Finnish President Alexander Stubb also urged people to prepare for possible drone attacks and other hybrid attacks.
