09:40:00 KST

OpenAI takes on Meta with dots agent in autonomous AI push
SAN FRANCISCO - OpenAI on Sept 29 unveiled always-on agents called dots that chase user goals across apps on their own, deepening its push into the lucrative enterprise market and pitting it against Meta in the race to sell AI that can work autonomously.
The dots agents aim to capitalise on growing demand for agents that can handle everyday work with little supervision.
The launch marks a new front in the competition among AI companies to move beyond chatbots and sell software that acts on users’ behalf – a shift that could reshape how businesses operate but that has raised safety concerns after a string of incidents in which AI agents acted in ways their makers did not intend.
OpenAI has faced scrutiny after its rogue AI agents hacked Hugging Face and an Australian government health website, fanning fears about its ability to contain technology that some researchers say could kill all humans.
The company on Sept 28 decided not to release a more powerful version of its Astra model because it showed a high willingness to mislead users about its actions.
Its chief executive Sam Altman said dots have been “safety tested” and were powered by OpenAI’s model that most closely follows human directions, GPT-6 Astra.
Interest in AI agents has surged since Meta’s Muse drew millions of downloads earlier this month and jolted shares of companies that investors believe could benefit or be disrupted by autonomous services.
Instinct, the start-up behind the eponymous agent, also quadrupled its valuation to US$10 billion (S$12.8 billion) this week, a little over a month after its previous funding round.
OpenAI’s competitive positioning
OpenAI launched dots at its annual Developer Day in San Francisco on Sept 29 while also touting its growing business and consumer presence, a sign that the reception for the company’s Astra model has allowed it to make up ground in the AI race.
Growing quickly is crucial for OpenAI’s plans to spend tens of billions of dollars on AI data centres and keep pace with rivals such as Anthropic and Meta.
OpenAI, which ignited the AI boom with ChatGPT in late 2022, is also preparing for an IPO that could value it at more than US$1 trillion. Rival Anthropic could be worth US$2 trillion when it goes public.
Dots capabilities and demo glitches
“We believe (the agent) is going to feel like a whole new way to work with AI. This is the real deal version of AI that we’ve always imagined for ourselves,” Altman said at the event, which had around 2,500 in-person attendees.
OpenAI’s live demos to show off the new capabilities, however, hit snags as the agents repeatedly failed to deliver voice updates in response to requests. “We might have some voice difficulties at the moment. Which is pretty unfortunate,” Developer Experience chief Romain Huet said on stage after a command failed.
One OpenAI employee said on X that the glitches stemmed from rolling out all the updates at once, but that OpenAI remained committed to live demos.
Dots can manage projects as they evolve, such as updating a sales proposal when customer needs change, and building a working demo for review. Users can communicate with dots on Slack and Teams, and the agents can draw on OpenAI’s Codex and ChatGPT Work tools to research, analyse data, prepare documents and build software.
Data privacy and safety concerns
On Sept 29, OpenAI highlighted safeguards it has built into dots. It said users could set custom rules that dictate what dots can do and when the agents should seek permission, adding that sensitive tasks such as changing passwords and permanently deleting data require explicit user consent.
The company also said dots run on their own cloud computers, and that it was rolling out private intelligence tools to check for safety risks without retaining business customers’ data.
Several tech executives, including Palantir CEO Alex Karp, have in recent months said that businesses need certainty that AI companies are not retaining their data, especially in regulated industries such as healthcare and finance.
Reuters reported on Sept 25 that OpenAI was still working to understand the full scope of its rogue agent activity, two months after the Hugging Face hack, with the latest example coming when the company said its agents had leaked 53 images from ChatGPT users.
OpenAI reiterated on Sept 29 that it does not use business customers’ data to train its AI by default, and that personal-plan users could opt out of sharing conversations and dots work used for training.
Weekly users of Codex and ChatGPT Work have reached more than 35 million, up from about five million Codex users in June, the company said on Sept 29, while consumer-focused ChatGPT now has more than 1.2 billion weekly users.
The company is rolling out ChatGPT Space, which is a shared workspace for business teams and its AI agents, as well as the cheaper GPT-6.1 Sol model and a US$500 Pro plan offering higher usage and faster performance. Reuters

Source: Ukrinform citing Ihnat
Quote: "The enemy is using high-quality materials in its drones and increasing the resolution of their cameras. In other words, the cameras are becoming increasingly expensive and of higher quality, allowing the enemy to view the situation on the ground in greater detail and use the drones for various purposes."
Details: Ihnat said that in this context, a single UAV could potentially be used for several purposes at once: as a reconnaissance drone, a strike drone and a relay drone that transmits information along a chain.
"That is why they fly one after another… [Russian drones] can be connected through a mesh network, and in this way the information can reach the operator," he explained.
Responding to a question about the operation of repeaters in Belarus and the Russians' use of jet-powered Shaheds for targeting, he said that the Russians had announced that their satellite network was ready.
"And the use of mesh networks is indeed taking place. Of course, this is quite dangerous," Ihnat said.
He noted that there is currently no information on whether the Russians are using telecommunications masts.
Quote: "But we often see along the Ukrainian-Belarusian border that drones cover long distances in a chain, one after another. And therefore nothing can be ruled out. At this point, we need to ask our intelligence service whether there is any evidence of this or not."
Details: Responding to a question about Russia's preparations for a new ballistic strike and Ukraine's readiness for it in the near future, Ihnat said that intelligence will provide information on the situation and warn people when particular vigilance is necessary.
Background: Ihnat said that Russia had launched around 350 jet-powered UAVs in June, 1,500 in July and more than 2,800 in August.

According to them, ten members of the UN Security Council supported Grynspan, three voted against, and two abstained. Kyiv came under a fresh Russian missile-and-drone attack early on Wednesday, with multiple ballistic missiles targeting the Ukrainian capital as explosions echoed across the city and air defenses engaged incoming threats.
Ukraine’s Air Force warned of an incoming ballistic threat before reporting “ballistic missiles on Kyiv.” Two minutes later came another urgent alert: “More ballistic missiles on Kyiv.”

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A Kyiv Post journalist in the capital described the assault as it unfolded.
“Kyiv is currently under a ballistic attack. I’ve heard a few loud explosions and several thuds so far. I just saw flashes from the active air defense operations outside my window,” she reported.
Initially, Kyiv authorities reported that at least one woman was wounded in the attack as fires broke out at multiple impact sites across three districts of the capital.
In the Sviatoshynskyi district, private residential buildings caught fire following a Russian strike. A warehouse building was burning in Holosiivskyi, while a shop caught fire in Obolonskyi, according to the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) and Mayor Vitali Klitschko.
According to the latest data from the KMVA, two women were killed in the Russian attack.
“We extend our condolences to their families and loved ones. Four people were also injured, one of whom has been hospitalized,” the report said.
Russian Air Strikes Target Major Ukrainian Drugs Manufacturer Darnytsia, Ice-Cream Maker
Klitschko later clarified that the number of injured had risen to five, with two of them hospitalized.
According to the State Emergency Service (DSNS), Russian strikes caused fires and damage across four districts of Kyiv between Tuesday evening and Wednesday morning.
In the Sviatoshynskyi district, a private house caught fire, while around 10 others were damaged.
In the Podilskyi district, Russian forces struck a non-residential building, sparking a fire that spread to the roof and construction materials on the sixth floor.
A warehouse was also damaged and caught fire before firefighters extinguished the blaze. A two-story private house at another location also caught fire.
In the Holosiivskyi district, a bathhouse, utility cabin, and concrete mixer caught fire. The blaze was subsequently extinguished.
In the Solomianskyi district, grass caught fire in an open area.
Emergency crews were dispatched to the affected areas as air defenses continued operating over Kyiv.
As of 8:50 a.m., dense fog was observed across Kyiv. The DSNS said the haze was caused by residual smoke and soot from the recent Russian strikes.
“Residual smoke and soot rose into the upper atmosphere, but an anticyclone is temporarily pressing them down toward the ground. There is almost no wind right now, so the air is not circulating. Once the wind picks up and the sun comes out, the haze will gradually dissipate,” the message read.
Emergency responders advised Kyiv residents, particularly those in Podil, Lukianivka, the Shevchenkivskyi district, and Borshchahivka, to keep their windows and vents closed and avoid airing out their homes.
An air raid alert due to the threat of drones has been in effect in the city since 4:42 a.m. Kyiv Post correspondents have periodically heard explosions and the sound of air defenses engaging.
In an update at 10:02 a.m., the mayor reported that debris had been found on the grounds of one of the Western embassies in the Shevchenkivskyi district of central Kyiv.
“Emergency services are heading to the scene,” he wrote, without providing further details.
Child killed as Russian attack hits wider Kyiv region
The Russian assault also caused deadly destruction across the wider Kyiv region, where authorities confirmed that a child was killed.
In Vyshhorod, rescuers pulled three people from the rubble of a destroyed private home. A child suffered an acute stress reaction, a man sustained shrapnel wounds to the head, and a woman suffered leg injuries.
Rescuers later found the body of another child beneath the rubble.
Elsewhere in the Vyshhorod district, private homes were damaged or destroyed, while fires broke out in a residential building and garages.
In the Bucha district, three private homes, 11 vehicles and two warehouses were damaged, and another fire broke out.
Authorities also reported damage to infrastructure facilities in the Bucha, Vyshhorod and Obukhiv districts.
188 drones, ballistic missiles used in overnight barrage
According to the Air Force’s morning report on Wednesday, Russia launched an overnight attack beginning at 6 p.m. on Tuesday, using Zircon/Onyx anti-ship missiles, Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles, 188 Shahed-type strike drones – 86 of them jet-powered – as well as Gerbera and “Parodiya” decoy drones.
The Kyiv region was the primary target of the attack.
As of 8 a.m., Ukrainian air defense forces had shot down or neutralized 160 targets, including five ballistic missiles (Iskander-M/S-400/Zircon/Onyx) and 155 Russian drones of various types.
“Enemy aerial assets were recorded striking 18 locations,” the report adds.
Zelensky: energy infrastructure was primary target
President Volodymyr Zelensky has responded to the latest massive attack, writing on Telegram that emergency services and repair crews have been working since the night to address the aftermath of the Russian strike.
“It was a difficult barrage: nearly 190 attack drones, as well as ballistic missiles. The primary target was the energy infrastructure of the capital and the Kyiv region. Residential buildings have been damaged. Work is underway to restore electricity and water supplies wherever they have been cut off,” he wrote.
Zelensky also said that in the morning, Russian forces struck a grocery supermarket in Ivankovychi with a drone. Rescue workers are currently extinguishing the fire there.
Russia is also continuing its drone attacks on Kyiv, with its forces striking a warehouse building and causing one fatality.
Zelensky said strikes had hit critical infrastructure in the Zhytomyr, Mykolaiv, Kirovohrad, and Rivne regions, while damage was reported in the Odesa, Sumy, Kharkiv, Kherson, and Cherkasy regions.
As of his update, 14 people across the country had been injured in the attacks, while five people, including a child, had been killed. Zelenskyy expressed his condolences to the victims’ families and loved ones.
He emphasized that while Ukrainian forces managed to shoot down some of the ballistic missiles, there were also impacts.
According to Zelensky, new air defense support packages have been announced in recent days.
“I thank our partners for the missiles, and everyone who is honoring our agreements and strengthening the defense of our skies. This is exactly how we must continue to work. Every interceptor missile truly saves lives,” Zelensky wrote.
The president added that the closer winter approaches, the more such protection is needed.
“We must do everything to ensure that Russia’s gamble on ballistic and drone terror fails. Thank you to everyone who stands with Ukraine.”
A rapidly escalating aerial blitz
The new assault came only hours after President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had launched more than 100 drones against Ukraine during Tuesday alone.
Twenty-nine were high-speed jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), with Ukrainian forces intercepting 18 of them, according to Zelensky.
Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yuriy Ihnat said Russia used more than 2,800 jet-powered drones during August, compared with far lower numbers earlier in the summer. Their interception rate has been only slightly above 60%, compared with roughly 90-95% for slower piston-engine UAVs.
Capital under relentless attack
Kyiv has endured repeated Russian attacks over the preceding 48 hours.
Overnight into Tuesday, Moscow had launched a Zircon/Oniks missile, two Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles and 152 drones against Ukraine, including 82 jet-powered UAVs.
Ukraine’s Air Force said it shot down or suppressed all three missiles and 106 drones – 109 targets in total.
Russian weapons nevertheless struck 24 locations across Ukraine, while debris from intercepted targets fell at another 16 locations.
In Kyiv, the attack damaged residential and non-residential buildings and an educational facility. Fires broke out in several districts, while a drone strike on a six-story residential building injured at least one person.
That barrage followed a deadly daytime attack on Monday, when a high-speed Russian drone slammed into the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine in central Kyiv during working hours.
The strike on one of Ukraine’s leading scientific institutions came as Russia increasingly targets Kyiv during daylight hours with faster jet-powered drones, creating an almost continuous air threat for civilians in the capital.
Devastation across Ukraine
Russia’s escalating aerial campaign has inflicted casualties far beyond Kyiv.
Earlier on Tuesday, Russian forces struck Sumy with four guided aerial bombs. One bomb hit a school while children were inside. Students and teachers had taken shelter and escaped injury, according to Zelensky.
A separate strike hit a residential building. Local authorities later reported two people killed and nine wounded.
In Zaporizhzhia and the surrounding region, Russian attacks wounded 34 people over the previous day. Thirty-three of them were injured when Russian forces struck an industrial facility.
Russian strikes in Odesa also damaged civilian infrastructure, housing, a school, and an animal shelter. Six people were reported wounded in the overnight attack.
Patriot supplies under growing pressure
The sustained multi-axis attacks are placing enormous pressure on Ukraine’s air-defense network.
The Patriot remains Ukraine’s principal system capable of reliably intercepting Russian ballistic missiles, but supplies of the advanced interceptors are under severe strain.
US Patriot missile stocks in Europe have reached what American and NATO officials described to the Associated Press as a “beyond critical” level, amid competing global requirements for the weapons.
Zelensky said on Tuesday that Kyiv continues pressing its partners for additional Patriot missiles.
Ukraine has meanwhile received a new package of missiles for its NASAMS systems, while Belgium will provide three additional F-16 fighter jets before the end of the year. Ukrainian combat aircraft are already being used to destroy Russian attack drones.
Kyiv is also racing to develop its own high-speed interceptor drones capable of hunting Russia’s newer jet-powered UAVs.
Zelensky said Ukrainian interceptors are already being tested and used in combat.
Ukraine has set new production targets for October as developers, manufacturers and the military work to increase interception rates and expand deployment.
Systematic strikes on civilians condemned as war crimes
The deliberate and systematic targeting of civilian infrastructure – including schools, research institutions, residential blocks, and shelters – has drawn renewed condemnation from international legal bodies and human rights organizations, who reiterate that such actions constitute war crimes under international law.
As emergency crews continue clearing wreckage and treating casualties, Kyiv maintains that protecting civilians requires not only intercepting incoming weapons but reducing Russia’s capacity to launch them in the first place.

US Senate blocks measure demanding report on rights violations in West Bank

US Senate blocks measure demanding report on rights violations in West Bank
WASHINGTON – US Senate Republicans on Sept 29 blocked a bid to require US President Donald Trump’s administration to report to Congress on increasing violence in the occupied West Bank, including the deaths of American citizens.
The procedural vote was the latest sign of friction between US Democrats and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government over Israel’s treatment of Palestinians and of Republicans’ continuing strong support for his coalition.
The Senate voted 47 to 51 to block the resolution. The vote was largely along party lines, with every Republican voting no except for Rand Paul of Kentucky and every Democrat except John Fetterman of Pennsylvania in favour.
The resolution would have required the State Department to report to Congress on the killing of US citizens by Israeli settlers or Israeli security forces in the West Bank and to assess the human rights situation.
Violence by Jewish settlers against Palestinians in the territory has risen sharply in 2026.
While the resolution would not have cut aid to Israel, the largest cumulative recipient of US foreign assistance since World War Two, a failure by the administration to deliver the report could have triggered restrictions on aid.
Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, the measure’s lead sponsor, had argued that it was “long past time” to examine human rights in the West Bank, including the deaths of nine Americans since 2022.
“It is our responsibility to ensure recipients of US taxpayer dollars act in line with our laws and our values,” he said in a statement, referring to Israel.
Republicans accused Democrats of seeking to score political points as Israel is under threat, seven months after US and Israeli forces launched airstrikes that began an ongoing conflict with Iran.
“I urge my colleagues to vote no on this resolution so we can stand with our ally Israel as they beat back the scourge of Iranian-backed terrorism,” Montana Republican Senator Steve Daines said in a speech.
Elections loom
The vote took place weeks before US midterm elections on Nov 3, in which polls show Trump’s Republicans could lose their congressional majorities, signalling a potential shift in Israel policy in the new Congress.
Polls show the war with Iran is not popular with Americans, who are frustrated with higher energy prices resulting from the conflict.
Netanyahu, who has long aligned himself with US Republicans, faces an election in Israel on Oct 27, which public opinion polls show his right-wing coalition could lose.
Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967. The UN and most countries consider settlements there illegal under international law governing military occupation. Israel rejects this, viewing the territory as disputed rather than occupied.
Some Democrats – and a few Republicans – also have called for curbs on military aid to Israel over its conduct of the war in Gaza, with tens of thousands of Palestinians killed and much of the enclave in ruins. REUTERS

Trump and US tech giants sign pact to stop AI from going rogue (VIDEOS)

Trump and US tech giants sign pact to stop AI from going rogue (VIDEOS)
The heads of six top US-based AI companies signed a pledge at the White House on Tuesday to introduce stronger controls to ensure that their technology does not go rogue.
The document, titled the White House Accord on Super Intelligence – Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities, was signed by US President Donald Trump, as well as Google’s Sundar Pichai, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, xAI’s Elon Musk and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang.
The signatories agreed that every company developing advanced artificial intelligence models should have “robust internal processes and controls to ensure that their technology behaves as intended and that any issues are promptly identified and resolved.”
The companies pledged to ensure that their models “do not hack or access technical systems in unintended ways” and said they would “empower an internal team to ensure all of the controls, monitoring, and detection are operating as intended, and that any issues are remediated.”
They also pledged to allow independent external audits of their safeguards and designate “an independent committee of the board of directors” to evaluate compliance.

The deal is aimed at addressing concerns among developers and the general public about AI models’ ability to self-improve much faster than expected and a growing number of cases in which they have hacked into external systems without authorization.
“The basic idea is that we want to give the American people and our customers confidence that the technology works in a way that we intend,” Zuckerberg told reporters on the White House lawn.
“The idea isn’t that this is the only thing that we will ever do. This is a start and an accord that the whole industry can come to,” he added.

During the same meeting, Trump signed an executive order directing the federal government to use the terms “super intelligence” and “SI” instead of “artificial intelligence” and “AI.”
“The name Super Intelligence conveys the true capabilities of the technologies being developed today, unlocking new forms of human creativity and empowering Americans to achieve what was previously impossible – not simply imitating or automating human intelligence as is implied by the term ‘Artificial Intelligence,’” the White House said.
Debate over AI safeguards was reignited this month when Amodei called for a slowing of the development of AI models to find “a balanced rate” that would give researchers time to develop the necessary controls. Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman quickly backed his appeal.
Over the summer, OpenAI agents escaped their testing environment and hacked into the servers of Hugging Face, an online repository for AI models and datasets. Since then, AI agents have gained unauthorized access to or attempted to breach websites belonging to US federal agencies, the Australian government and the UN.
Trump has ruled out slowing AI development under his watch, dismissing fears of the technology going rogue as “a hoax.”
“We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry,” the president wrote on Truth Social earlier this month.
Huang has supported calls for stronger safeguards but voiced skepticism about slowing AI development. “We should go as fast as we can, irrespective of anyone else. But we would never ever, and never should, ship products before they’re ready and deliver products that are unsafe,” he told CBS.
The US and China agreed to set up a hotline for AI incidents following Chinese President Xi Jinping’s meeting with Trump at the White House last week.
China has similarly called for stronger safeguards but stopped short of supporting a slowdown in AI development. Beijing said this month that regulation and governance should keep pace with rapidly advancing models to prevent AI from “getting out of control,” while criticizing what it described as “fearmongering” and technological competition between countries.

CST: Antisemitism on campuses still higher than pre October 7, despite reduction from last year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
00:25:06 UTC
09:25:06 KST

Campus antisemitism in Britain remained significantly higher than pre-October 7 levels in 2025-2026, despite numbers falling since 2023-2024, a Community Security Trust (CST) report detailing antisemitic incidents on or tied to college campuses revealed on Wednesday.
The report recorded 178 university-related antisemitic incidents over the two years, with 83 in 2024-2025 and 95 in 2025-2026.
In comparison, in the final academic year before the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack, 53 antisemitic attacks tied to college campuses were reported to have occurred.
Among the incidents, the majority (149 out of 178) were categorized as abusive behavior, including verbal abuse and antisemitic comments as well as graffiti and written abuse.
There were also two incidents classified as "extreme violence," six assaults, eight incidents of damage and desecration to Jewish property (including five that took place within student accommodations), 10 direct threats, and three instances of "mass-produced antisemitic literature."
These incidents took place both in person and online, with the most common platform used to commit university-related antisemitic incidents being Instagram.
Sixteen of the antisemitic incidents had been done by university staff and faculty, the CST report described, while 61 were committed by students. Another 28 instances were committed by student societies or their representatives.
Antisemitic attacks done with political motive tied to Gaza, Israel
The majority of the antisemitic attacks and incidents had been done with some political motive, with many of them tied to Israel, Gaza, or October 7.
According to CST, 62% of the incidents had some reference to Israel, Gaza, Hamas, October 7, or the ensuing war. Another 26% referenced Hitler, Nazis, or the Holocaust.
"These figures show that Jews are still facing a very serious campus antisemitism problem," said CST Chief Executive Mark Gardner.
"Universities have a duty to ensure that Jewish students and staff can study, work, and participate on campus the same as anyone else. Sympathy is not enough; it needs action against those who abuse, threaten, or target Jews, whether they are students, staff or external activists.”
Education secretary stands against antisemitism
UK Education Secretary Lucy Powell emphasized in response to the report that the English education system had "no place" for antisemitism.
"No student should have to choose between expressing their identity and feeling safe on campus, yet for too many Jewish students that remains a reality," she said. "We expect universities to take a zero-tolerance approach to antisemitism, and are providing training to help university staff identify and respond to incidents swiftly."
UK government advisor on antisemitism Lord John Mann said that "Those incapable of civility need to be challenged by their university."
"Those who target abuse and threats need to be disciplined, and in extreme examples they should forfeit the privileges afforded to those who work or study in our centers of learning,” Mann added.

Former Argentine President Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner requested the United Nations (UN) on Tuesday to review her corruption conviction, which currently bars her from seeking the presidency in next year's elections.
Fernandez's defense team filed an addendum with the Geneva-based UN Human Rights Committee requesting the suspension of her political ban, alleging that her fundamental rights were violated during the trial.
The 18-member body of independent experts monitors compliance with the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. While its rulings are not legally binding, they hold substantial political weight and can be cited in domestic judicial proceedings.
The former leader is under house arrest in Buenos Aires following a 2025 sentence of six years in prison and a lifetime disqualification from public office for fraud against the state.
Throughout her political career, Fernandez has remained one of Argentina's most polarizing figures. Her presidency was marked by heavy state intervention, currency controls and fierce clashes with the media, the judiciary and the agricultural sector.
Supporters praise her expansion of social welfare programs and nationalist economic policies, while critics accuse her administration of institutional erosion and systemic corruption, pointing to multiple high-profile legal cases involving public works contracts, money laundering and illicit enrichment that have dogged her for over a decade.
Despite remaining a deeply polarizing figure, polls show Fernandez maintains voter support levels comparable to those of current President Javier Milei.
This standing positions her as a strong contender for the October 2027 presidential race. If cleared to run, the former two-term president (2007–2015) and former vice president (2019–2023) would first need to secure the Peronist nomination before facing Milei at the ballot box.

The Future of Shipbuilding in Southeast Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
00:19:00 UTC
09:19:00 KST

Global shipbuilding demand is likely to remain resilient for the long-term, with increasing geopolitical conflict and uncertainty one of the primary drivers. The 2026 war between Iran, the United States and Israel has caused a spike in demand for alternative suppliers and routes, leading Fitch Rating to revise sectoral outlook to “neutral” from “deteriorating.” According to the non-profit Container Trades Statistics, global container volumes reached 16.2 million 20-foot-equivalent units (mTEUs) in April — the first full month of data since the Strait of Hormuz closures triggered by February’s Persian Gulf crisis — marking a 4 percent year-over-year increase and a 1.6 percent rise over March. Year-to-date volumes are also running 5 percent ahead of 2025 levels.
Shipping sector analysts also predicted that the market had become oversaturated with vessel capacity and fewer orders would be placed to shipbuilders in 2026 and 2027. However, geopolitical disruptions are one major reason why orders have remained strong. Shocks such as Red Sea attacks, the Russia-Ukraine war, the Panama Canal drought, the Baltimore bridge collapse, and now the Iran-Israel-US conflict have demonstrated the importance of excess capacity. Carriers can more easily navigate these conflicts with a large and diverse fleet, resulting in expansive orderbooks that are now treated as insurance rather than oversupply.
These trends are good news to the world’s leading shipbuilding nations, which are highly concentrated in East Asia, particularly China. However, in the current geopolitical climate, there are significant opportunities for Southeast Asian nations to scale up their shipbuilding industries and take advantage of the sustained demand for global trade.
Southeast Asian nations are taking the initiative to capture greater shipbuilding market share through structured international partnerships. At the OECD-Southeast Asia Policy Roundtable on Shipbuilding, Steel, and AI held in Tokyo in February 2026, Indonesia, Vietnam, and Thailand agreed to a regional peer review of their shipbuilding sectors with the OECD, covering priorities such as workforce skills, technical capabilities, supply chain dependencies, energy-efficient ships, and leveling the competitive playing field. The Philippines separately agreed to follow up on implementation pathways for OECD peer review recommendations, while all four countries were invited to join the OECD’s shipbuilding committee meeting in Paris in April.

Finnish-founded smart ring maker Oura has postponed its planned Nasdaq listing, citing uncertainty in the US initial public offering market despite strong demand from investors.
The company announced the decision on Tuesday as rising bond yields and interest rates put pressure on the US market for new listings.
Oura said its business had strengthened since it began the IPO process.
The company expects revenue to increase 90 per cent year on year in the 2026 financial year, while the number of paid members has reached 5.7 million following the launch of Oura Ring 5.
Oura had reached the final stages of the listing process. Helsingin Sanomat reported that the company had expected to set the final IPO price on Monday, with trading scheduled to begin on Wednesday.
Bloomberg reported last week that orders for the offering had reached about four times the number of shares available.
Oura had sought proceeds of up to $2.2 billion from the offering, with an indicated share price range of $40 to $44, HS reported.
The listing was intended mainly to provide an exit for some existing shareholders rather than raise new capital for the company’s expansion, according to the newspaper. Finnish venture capital firm Lifeline Ventures planned to sell between one-third and one-half of its Oura holding as part of the transaction.
Oura has not announced a new timetable for the IPO.
“Our mission is to empower people to live healthier, longer, and an IPO is just one step in our journey,” chief executive Tom Hale said in the company’s statement.
“We aim to deliver an extraordinary IPO for our employees and investors and we have the luxury of choosing our moment,” he said.
Oura joins other companies that have delayed US listings in September. Reuters said a growing number of prospective issuers have pulled back as higher interest rates and bond yields affect financial markets.
According to Bloomberg data, only nine of more than 20 companies that had filed public listing documents since the start of July had completed their IPOs.
Oura said it remains profitable and continues to grow. The company has filed its registration statement with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, but the filing has not yet become effective.
Founded in Finland in 2013, Oura produces a wearable ring that tracks sleep, activity and other health measurements. The company has its headquarters in San Francisco and its European headquarters in Oulu.

US tightens Cuba travel rules, restricts private sector banking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
00:08:00 UTC
09:08:00 KST

US tightens Cuba travel rules, restricts private sector banking
- The US has banned banks from working with Cuba's private sector and tightened travel rules, aiming to pressure Cuba's one-party government.
- US restrictions block accounts for Cuban private entrepreneurs and close travel loopholes for professional and educational visits.
- Despite trade growth aiding Cuba's economy, US sanctions and fuel blockades continue, complicating reforms and increasing tensions between Washington and Havana.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The US is barring banks from working with Cuba’s nascent private sector and is further restricting travel to the island, as President Donald Trump’s administration presses to end nearly seven decades of one-party rule in the country.
Under updated guidance from the Treasury Department published on Sept 29, US banks are no longer permitted to open and maintain accounts for Cuban nationals “who are independent private sector entrepreneurs,” the Office of Foreign Assets Control said.
“U-turn” transactions, in which US banks could process Cuba-related transactions that “originated and terminated outside the United States,” have also been disallowed.
Loopholes that allowed people from the US to travel to Cuba for professional meetings and academic activities are also being closed, OFAC said.
In addition, “people-to-people” educational travel, which was previously authorised, is no longer permitted.
Educational trips under the auspices of an accredited organisation are still allowed.
And there are no new restrictions on commercial flights to the island, as some Florida Republicans had been calling for.
But it’s the private-sector measures that could have the most impact, given small businesses have become a lifeline for the island as entrepreneurs import badly needed goods from abroad.
Bloomberg News reported last week that US cargo ships have made more than 200 trips to Cuba in 2026, loaded with goods including fuel, solar panels, food, vehicles and auto parts.
That trade boom contrasts sharply with Trump’s aggressive push for political change.
“The administration does not have a clear message at all when it comes to how they see the private sector and its role in this,” Michael Bustamante, director of Cuban studies at the University of Miami, said in an audio message.
Expanding the use of trade loopholes – including authorising private fuel sales – has helped stave off “a complete economic or social collapse” and reinforced “a message to Cuba that their only way out is through their connections with the United States,” he said.
“And yet the administration is not taking any proactive measures to make life easier for the private sector.”
Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have been hammering Cuba’s economy with ever-tighter sanctions and a de-facto fuel blockade for months in hopes of forcing the Communist Party to relinquish its grip on power.
Amid reports that planning for a military intervention was in the works, Trump said this week that Washington and Havana would likely “make a deal.”
Cuba has said it’s willing to make economic changes but that its system of government is not up for debate.
Intense US pressure, however, is getting in the way of market-friendly reforms, Deputy Foreign Minister Carlos Fernandez de Cossío told Bloomberg Television on Sept 25.
His boss in Havana also shot back on Sept 29 at Trump and Rubio’s latest salvo.
“Less than 24 hours ago, the Secretary of State said that ‘Cuba has already fallen.’ Now it turns out that additional measures are needed,” Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez said in a post on X.
“They openly attack both the public sector and the private sector, the one that some US officials say they want to help develop.” BLOOMBERG

BAGHDAD – US forces withdrew from their remaining bases in Iraq on Sept 30, raising fears of a security vacuum that would embolden Iranian-backed Shi’ite militias and allow ISIS to regroup.
The withdrawal of the final troops, mainly from an airbase in Erbil in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region, was celebrated as a victory by Tehran and its allies, although many Iraqis were concerned that their own security forces were unprepared.
The pullout was agreed in 2024 under then US President Joe Biden and carried out by Donald Trump’s administration even as it wages war against Iran next door.
It comes 23 years after US-led forces toppled dictator Saddam Hussein, triggering years of upheaval and chaos.
US troops initially left at the end of 2011 but returned less than three years later after ISIS fighters seized a third of Iraq.
More than 4,500 US troops died in America’s biggest war of this century, around twice as many as in the parallel war in Afghanistan.
The Iraq Body Count project says more than 200,000 Iraqi civilians were killed.
The Pentagon said the United States and its coalition partners had formally concluded Operation Inherent Resolve, adding that the US would continue to provide targeted training and intelligence support to Iraqi partners.
The Iraqis are expected to lead the effort to secure the country, an ally of both Washington and Tehran, and keep the remnants of ISIS suppressed.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi said in a statement: “The end of the international coalition’s mission does not mean the end of our battle against terrorism, but rather Iraq’s transition to a phase in which it assumes full responsibility for its security and stability.”
Tehran has steadily entrenched itself through proxies in Iraq since the fall of Saddam.
While the departure of US forces is broadly popular among Iraqis, some worry that security forces trained and funded by the United States still cannot protect the country.
“The lesson from the past two decades is that security vacuums can be extremely dangerous,” said Jassim al-Bahadli, an Iraqi analyst who advises the security forces.
Adil Salman, 45, a high school English teacher, said Iraqis “should not rush to celebrate” the withdrawal. “Militias still operate outside the state’s control and (Islamic State) still has not disappeared,” he said. “I’m concerned that the US departure could lead to a new period of instability. In the end, people will judge this decision by one thing: whether security remains stable in the coming years.”
The presence of both US troops and armed groups allied to Iran in the region has pulled Iraq into the expanding Middle East conflict.
Of the 18 US service members listed as killed since Trump launched “Operation Epic Fury” alongside Israel against Iran in February, seven died in Iraq.
The last was an army sergeant who died during the controlled detonation of a drone at a base near Erbil in July.
Iran, allies are the winners
Iran, which says its ultimate aim is to force American forces to leave the entire Middle East, casts the US withdrawal from Iraq as a triumph for its “axis of resistance” of allied armed groups across the region.
The withdrawal raises “the possibility that Iran’s proxies will feel increasingly empowered in the absence of a Western military presence”, said Baghdad-based political analyst Ahmed Younis.
“These groups may attempt to expand their role in shaping state policies and consolidating their presence within key institutions.”
Some Iraqi security officials, both in the federal government and the semi-autonomous northern Kurdish region, say the US pullout also risks giving new life to Islamic State fighters who, despite the defeat of their self-proclaimed caliphate nearly a decade ago, retain a sleeper cell network.
The last time the US withdrew, the Iraqi army proved no match for ISIS. Soldiers took off their uniforms and fled when the group captured Mosul, Iraq’s second-largest city, in 2014.
Since ISIS’ self-proclaimed caliphate was defeated in 2017, US troops have been providing Iraqi security forces with critical intelligence on the group’s movements, aerial surveillance and reconnaissance.
Retired Iraqi Army General Mohammed al-Jubouri, who led a brigade in the war against ISIS, said: “The most important question now is whether Iraq’s security institutions have prepared a viable Plan B for the post-coalition phase.
“One of the worst-case scenarios would be Islamic State obtaining armed drones or improvised explosive drones at a time when Iraq still lacks sufficient air defence capabilities to counter such threats effectively.”

Finance presenter Alan Kohler retiring after three decades at ABC
After a brilliant 31-year career as the ABC's finance guru, Alan Kohler has decided to hang up his boots at the end of the year.
With a successful career in print before moving to television, Kohler has been one of the most influential journalists Australia has ever produced, as a former editor of The Australian Financial Review (AFR) and The Age and as an incisive columnist on all affairs financial.
"I love the ABC, always have, even more so after I joined it," he told ABC staff in a statement.
"I find it very hard to imagine this wonderful place not being part of my life, but I'm 74 and it's time to spend more time with my family, including the six grandchildren."
Kohler joined the public broadcaster in 1995 as business and economics correspondent for the 7.30 Report and went on to host Inside Business.
For the past 24 years, he has been the lead 7pm News finance presenter, unravelling the mysteries of financial markets for the audience with a format all his own that has often begun with: "Now, here's an interesting graph."
ABC managing director Hugh Marks said Kohler had made an extraordinary contribution to the organisation and the nation.
"For decades, he has helped Australians make sense of complex issues with insight, clarity and a uniquely engaging style, always delivered with warmth, humour and that trademark cheeky grin.
"I can't thank Alan enough for everything he has given to the ABC and our audiences. While this marks the end of an incredible chapter, it is certainly not the end of Alan's contribution, just the beginning of a new one."
Kohler hosted Inside Business for many years. He currently writes a weekly column and hosts a podcast, That's Business, every Friday.
While he is a distinguished editor, Kohler's biggest impact on the nation has been as a communicator.
After several stints as the chanticleer columnist for the AFR, he joined The Sydney Morning Herald (SMH) and The Age as senior business columnist, working with your correspondent during my time as SMH business editor.
A canny entrepreneur, he had by that stage already launched The Eureka Report and later left Fairfax Media when he added online news service Business Spectator to the mix.
Throughout his various incarnations, he has remained steadfastly loyal to the ABC and to his audience and is expected to continue his association with one-off specials.

Hong Kong’s executives are ‘ill prepared’ for AI era, report finds
The city’s firms have a severe lack of AI and cybersecurity expertise at the board level, leaving them ‘ill prepared’ for the coming era, report finds
Executives at Hong Kong’s largest listed companies have a severe lack of technological expertise, with fewer than 1 per cent of directors possessing dedicated artificial intelligence or cybersecurity skills, according to a new report by Grant Thornton Hong Kong.
The firm’s 15th annual Corporate Governance Review – which surveyed 100 major listed firms on Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Composite Index – found that 59 per cent of companies view cybersecurity or AI as principal business risks. Yet only 11 per cent had established specialised board committees to oversee digital threats and technology integration.
These gaps have persisted despite the introduction of updated Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) Corporate Governance Code standards last year, which introduced mandatory director training, board skills matrices and stricter overboarding limits.
“While overall disclosure quality on HKEX has improved, there remains a disconnect between acknowledged risks and technical expertise at the top,” said Barry Tong, head of advisory at Grant Thornton Hong Kong.

Why Daniel Tupou is a Sydney Roosters grand final specialist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
23:58:52 UTC
08:58:52 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
analysis
Why Daniel Tupou is a Sydney Roosters living legend and grand final specialist
The Roosters boast a galaxy of stars for Sunday's NRL decider against Newcastle, but veteran winger Daniel Tupou might be the only one who can call himself a grand final specialist.
Not that he ever would. The 35-year-old has for many years now been a firm believer that actions speak louder than words, and those actions demand his automatic inclusion in any discussion about an all-time Roosters XVII.
A win over the Knights will make Tupou, already the club's highest-ever tryscorer and only a few games shy of being their most capped player, the first Rooster to win four premierships with the club since the 1940s.
He's the only player to have appeared in all three grand final wins under coach Trent Robinson, although calling what Tupou has done merely "appearing" sells him short.
Back in 2013, in just his second year of first grade, Tupou went skywalking to score a spectacular try in the Tricolours' win over a Manly side containing future teammate Daly Cherry-Evans.
Back then, Tupou was like so many of his teammates are now — young and hungry in his first grand final, with everything to prove.
"I can't remember much, to be honest it's a bit of a blur, it was such a long time ago. Most of these boys are where I was in 2013 — I was the same age then as Rob Toia is now," said Tupou.
"He's (Cherry-Evans) has never brought it up. I might not bring it up this week, not until after the game on Sunday at least."
That try was just the 17th of Tupou's career, and his 199th in the preliminary final win over the Dolphins is proof he can still fly.
But that and his calm demeanour are about the only things that are still the same after all this time, with Tupou himself having become one of the best wingers of the modern era in the years since.
His performances in the club's back-to-back premiership wins in 2018-19 are living proof of that transformation from skinny aerial specialist to a truly complete flanker.
In the first victory, a comprehensive win over Melbourne, he scored the opening try and worked like a dog from the backfield, running for the second-most metres of any Roosters player.
In the second, a 14-8 war with Canberra, he was unlucky not to become the first winger to win the Clive Churchill Medal as man of the match.
Tupou ran for a team-high 185 metres from 17 carries and saved several tries with perfect defensive decision-making before making the break and throwing the final pass for James Tedesco's premiership-winning score.
It's as good a game as a winger has ever played in a grand final, but when Tupou explains how he finds his best form on the season's biggest day, he makes it sound maddeningly simple.
"You have to stay calm and collected. Enjoy the week and the hype around it, enjoy the atmosphere once we hit the field but embrace the vibe, embrace the energy," said Tupou.
"There's a lot of stuff to tick off, but you have to enjoy every bit of it.
"Just stay present. Don't overthink, be where your feet are."
It's the advice he'll give the grand final rookies on Sunday, even though the Roosters have plenty of premiership experience on hand.
Victor Radley and James Tedesco both played in 2018-19, Nat Butcher and Angus Crichton were both there for the latter and Spencer Leniu won three titles with Penrith.
But given 15 of the 22 players named on Tuesday have yet to play in a grand final, they have a fair share of first-timers.
None could ask for a better example of how to make the most of it than Tupou, whose deeds under the brightest of lights have made him a stone-cold living legend of the club he'll once again try to bring to glory on Sunday.
"It's in the preparation. We've worked so hard during the year to earn this moment," said Tupou.
"It's nothing less than what we've already done, we just have to stay consistent."

Hegseth to Slash 20 Percent of Generals and Flag Officers, Deepening Cuts to Top Ranks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
23:58:46 UTC
08:58:46 KST

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth plans to announce Sept. 30 a directive to slash the number of general and flag officers across the U.S. military by 20 percent, Pentagon officials told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Hegseth is doubling down on the 10 percent cut to general and flag officers he ordered last year, which he dubbed the “less generals, more GIs” policy.
Hegseth’s announcement will come during a “State for the Force” address. The cuts will reduce the number of general and flag officer billets, meaning some moves may play out over time, rather than swiftly removing 20 percent of generals and admirals.
Fox News first reported the new cuts and details of the planned announcement. Pentagon officials later confirmed that account.
The “State of the Force” speech comes a year after Hegseth convened senior U.S. military leaders from commands around the globe to outline his philosophy for running the Pentagon—an extraordinarily rare gathering.
The services are expected to make the cuts by Jan. 1, 2027. How reductions will be apportioned among the services is, so far, unclear.
Generals and admirals make up less than 1 percent of the military. According to the Congressional Research Service data, there were about 850 general officer positions in 2023. Some of those positions were unfilled at the time, as is the case today.
The maximum number of general officers allowed per service is set by law, though those caps do not apply to joint positions. The law also sets a minimum number of general officers in joint jobs.
The Air Force has roughly 250 generals. The Space Force about 30 generals, with plans to continue to grow that number.
In Hegseth’s Quantico address a year ago, he told the ranking military officers and senior enlisted advisers in the audience that “more leadership changes will be made” and asserted that “fat generals and admirals” were roaming the halls of the Pentagon.
A top Democratic lawmaker complained the cuts were arbitrary and Congress had not been consulted, and noted that Hegseth has removed senior officers from their roles with little explanation.
“Efficiency and streamlining in the military are worthy goals, but the size and structure of our military’s senior officer corps are matters in which Congress has a fundamental role,” said Sen. Jack Reed (D-R.I.), the ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee. “Article I of the Constitution assigns Congress the power to raise and support the armed forces and to make rules for their government. Reshaping the senior leadership of the world’s most powerful military is precisely the kind of decision that requires consultation with and justification to Congress.”
The new cuts are not the only step Hegseth is taking this week to reshape the military establishment. In a Sept. 29 memo released by the Pentagon, Hegseth directed military service academies to drop tenured positions for civilian professors. Hegseth said the move was needed because “civilian academic norms … dilute our focus on lethality.”
Critics have said the Pentagon’s efforts to reform the institutions could compromise the academic independence and the quality of education at the service academies, which include the U.S. Air Force Academy, the U.S. Naval Academy, and the U.S. Military Academy at West Point.
USAFA only recently began offering tenure to civilian faculty.
Hegseth served on and off in the Army National Guard, reaching the rank of major. He has cast himself as a Pentagon chief who relates to rank-and-file troops.
His previous directive to reduce general officers mandated a 20 percent reduction in Active four-stars, a 20 percent cut in National Guard generals, and a 10 percent cut in overall general and flag officers. Hegseth has said that cuts were needed to reduce bureaucracy.

helvetus uses FKM rubber to rethink integrated luxury watch strap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
23:55:34 UTC
08:55:34 KST

helvetus uses FKM rubber to rethink integrated luxury watch strap
helvetus develops reference-specific FKM rubber straps for rolex watches, combining precise case-fitting geometry with the material’s durability and resistance to everyday wear.
How Vulcanised Rubber Became a Luxury Material on the Wrist
Helvetus develops reference-specific FKM rubber straps for Rolex watches, combining precise case-fitting geometry with the material’s durability and resistance to everyday wear.
From industrial seals and aerospace applications to luxury timepieces, vulcanized FKM rubber has taken on a new role in contemporary watch design. Its chemical resistance, dimensional stability, and ability to hold a precise molded shape make it suited to straps that function as engineered components rather than simple accessories.
When the strap became part of the watch case
For much of the 20th century, a watch strap was essentially a strip of leather fitted between two lugs, with its design largely independent of the watch. Integrated cases changed that relationship. When Gérald Genta designed the Royal Oak in 1972 and the Nautilus in 1976, the bracelet became a continuation of the case, carrying its geometry from the bezel to the clasp.
Cartier had explored a similar approach much earlier with the Santos, designed in 1904 for pilot Alberto Santos-Dumont. Its exposed bezel screws and case geometry extended into the strap. The 2018 redesign made this connection more functional, introducing QuickSwitch for tool-free strap changes and SmartLink for bracelet adjustment.
The result is a category of straps designed around specific watch references. Once a strap must follow a particular case curve and interface, its geometry, thickness, and end pieces have to be developed for that model. Helvetus, for example, produces Cartier Santos straps for Medium and Large cases with curved ends that meet the lugs without a visible gap, while retaining the original buckle.
Why Helvetus chooses FKM instead of silicone
Silicone is common in watch straps, but it can attract dust and lint because of its electrostatic properties and may develop a tacky surface over time. FKM, a fluoroelastomer originally developed in the 1950s for seals and O-rings exposed to jet fuel, heat, and solvents, offers greater chemical resistance and dimensional stability across a wide temperature range.
FKM also retains its molded form instead of gradually relaxing into a curl. However, the material is more difficult to process. It must be vulcanized and is less receptive to color than silicone, contributing to the restrained palettes and higher prices of FKM straps.
Rolex’s own approach, the Oysterflex introduced in 2015, combines a titanium and nickel alloy blade with an elastomer overmold, functioning more like a bracelet with an elastomer exterior than a conventional rubber strap.
Aftermarket straps as a design discipline
Aftermarket components are often treated as secondary to the original, but their development involves a specific set of design constraints. The strap must fit a case it did not originally accompany, work with an existing buckle, and maintain the proportions and geometry of the watch.
Details such as end pieces machined to match a specific case curvature, flush-fitting keepers, and carefully controlled thicknesses help maintain the continuity of the original design. The FKM rubber range for Rolex follows this reference-specific approach, with straps organized around the Submariner, Daytona, GMT-Master II, Datejust, Day-Date, and Sky-Dweller rather than simply by lug width.
A replaceable layer of wear within the life of the watch
The use of a replaceable strap also changes how wear is distributed across the watch. A factory bracelet accumulates wear directly on the original component, while a replaceable strap concentrates everyday wear in a part that can be exchanged independently.
Keeping the original bracelet stored while using a replaceable strap therefore provides a way to reduce wear on the original components while preserving the watch’s factory configuration. In this sense, the strap becomes both a functional interface and a replaceable layer within the life of the watch.
project info:
name: The FKM Rubber Range For Rolex
 designer: Helvetus

United States President Donald Trump has announced that he will spend 32 days travelling and campaigning for the midterm elections in November, which will decide which party controls Congress.
The upcoming race is widely seen as a referendum on Trump’s second term in office, and it could decide whether his political agenda faces legislative hurdles for the next two years.

Still, on Tuesday, Trump expressed optimism as he spoke to reporters. He also denied that Republican candidates are seeking to distance themselves from his administration ahead of the vote.
“You love me, and I love them,” Trump said, as he outlined his plans for a multi-state tour to support Republican midterm contenders.

Recent polls suggest that Trump’s approval has fallen to new lows as voters express frustration over the rising cost of living, caused in part by Trump’s decision to launch a war against Iran that has roiled global energy markets.

Democratic and Republican lawmakers have slammed those efforts as an inappropriate use of taxpayer funds that could violate anti-propaganda laws.
“We should not have to remind you that using government funding to create or air political ads like the ones that have been running over the last few days is illegal and a shockingly corrupt misuse of taxpayer dollars,” Democratic Senator Patty Murray wrote to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in a letter on Tuesday.

Brazil’s patron saint pulled into latest election scrap
- Brazil’s patron saint Our Lady of Aparecida has become a political issue in the presidential race, with Lula accusing Bolsonaro of plans to demote her status.
- Lula uses the controversy to rally Catholic voters, while Bolsonaro denies the claims and accuses the government of spreading fake news.
- The debate highlights tensions between Brazil’s Catholic majority and growing evangelical population, influencing voter preferences and political strategies.
AI generated
RIO DE JANEIRO - Brazil’s patron saint has become a political flashpoint as the predominantly Catholic country’s leading presidential candidates make a last-ditch effort to court religious voters.
Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has lashed out at President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva for apparently feeding rumours about his right-wing rival, with the saga exposing tensions between Brazil’s Catholic majority and its expanding evangelical population.
In recent days, the leftist incumbent has referred to claims that Bolsonaro plans to strip Our Lady of Aparecida of her patron saint status if elected.
Evangelicals, a booming denomination in Brazil with growing political power and an important right-wing voter base, do not recognise the saint as an object of worship.
“As long as I am president... no one is going to disrespect Our Lady of Aparecida,” Lula, who is seeking a fourth nonconsecutive term, said at a rally on Sept 28.
Bolsonaro, 45, has frequently invoked religion on the campaign trail, and denies the accusations.
“Everyone knows that I respect religions. All of them!” he said, accusing the government of spreading “fake news.”
‘Oxygen to rumours’
The quarrel erupted after media reports that figures in the Catholic Church were concerned about the future status of the beloved saint, who is depicted in Brazil as a black woman.
The unearthing of an abandoned 2007 Bill, initially proposed by a Bolsonaro-aligned lawmaker, to demote the patron saint subsequently unleashed rampant speculation online.
The president’s decision to “give oxygen to rumours” signals a sea change in how he engages with religious voters, said Victor Araujo, a comparative politics professor at the Britain’s University of Reading.
“By actively engaging with religious controversies and bringing them into the mainstream campaign, Lula is trying to neutralise Bolsonaro’s moral appeal and force his rival onto the defensive on religious grounds,” Araujo told AFP.
Lula currently has 48 per cent of Catholic voting intentions on Sept 27 compared with 29 per cent for Bolsonaro, according to a Quaest survey.
Evangelical voting intentions go in the opposite direction, with 46 per cent for Bolsonaro and 27 per cent for Lula.
Janaina, 51, a Catholic art teacher working in Rio de Janeiro, firmly believes that the right-wing camp has the saint in its sights.
“Religion has nothing to do with politics,” she said, voicing concern that Evangelicals “want this other religion to grow…and attack the Catholic Church.”
Andre Paschoal, a worshipper at the same church, is less convinced.
“Lula took advantage of this and he will certainly lose many votes because of it,” the civil servant, 58, told AFP.
“Instead of being sincere, he is making use of an artificial lie to sway Catholics or Evangelicals in his favour,” Paschoal believes.
‘Pure politics’
“It’s pure politics,” echoed Tereza Helael as she made her way to an evangelical service in the city centre.
“It’s meant to target a certain area, a certain group… just to get votes,” the 70-year-old artist said.
Brazil, known for its Christ the Redeemer statue looming over Rio de Janeiro, hosts the world’s second-largest Christian population after the United States, according to the Pew Research Centre.
Catholics have historically dominated that cohort, but rapid demographic changes in recent years have seen the country’s evangelical population shoot up.
Ultra-conservative actors from this community have provided crucial political backing to Flavio Bolsonaro’s father, ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, who was convicted of plotting a coup.
“This controversy is a reaction to these churches’ political activity becoming ever more aggressive in recent years,” said Rodrigo Nunes, a philosophy professor at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro.
However, he said, most Catholics are perturbed by the rumour “because it challenges their tacit, unspoken position as the dominant religion in Brazil.” AFP

Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani has condemned Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, saying whoever is responsible for the devastation in the besieged Palestinian territory is a “war criminal”.
Sheikh Mohammed, who is also Qatar’s foreign minister, made the remark on Tuesday on “Piers Morgan Uncensored” when asked about the nature of Israel’s actions in the Gaza Strip.

He described the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, as “a massacre” that “should be condemned”. He called for accountability for the perpetrators of that attack, but said the Israeli response was unjustified.
“Hospitals have been targeted, schools have been targeted. Whatever the justifications and the arguments, nothing is justifying this,” he added.
Sheikh Mohammed also criticised Israel’s near-daily violations of the “ceasefire” that took effect in October 2025, saying more than 1,400 Palestinians in the Gaza Strip had been killed since.
“There is more occupied territory – almost 70 percent of the Strip has been occupied and not allowed by the Israeli forces. They are not fulfilling their commitments of this agreement,” he said. “This is just showing that they have different intentions.”
He said Qatar’s efforts to broker a ceasefire had been repeatedly “undermined” by Israel “from day one of the war”.
He also condemned Israel’s strike on the Qatari capital, Doha, in 2025, which targeted senior Hamas officials who had gathered for negotiations. The attack, which caused a deadly explosion, was an unprecedented violation of Qatar’s sovereignty.

It’s setting a precedent of attacking the mediator that has never happened throughout the wars in history.”
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin “Netanyahu has crossed the line”, he added, “like he has crossed other lines before that”.
Sheikh Mohammed said that serving as a mediator had not been easy, but that he believed quiet diplomacy was the most effective way to make progress.
Qatar has also been playing a mediatory role, along with Pakistan, between Washington and Tehran following the launch of the US-Israel war on Iran in February.
“We are trying to do our best to give the best advice to the US government on how to reach a solution, as well as to the Iranians,” he said.
Sheikh Mohammed said that three matters needed to be resolved to end the war.
These are: an agreement on Tehran’s right to “peaceful nuclear power” and the removal of sanctions; agreement on freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz according to international law; and reform of regional security arrangements, including the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries and Iran.
The last, he said, “wouldn’t happen without dialogue between Iran and GCC and setting the principles of what a good neighbourhood relationship should be”.
That should include, he said, “non-interference in each other’s affairs” and “non-aggression” against each other.
He added that if the region were to “build an area of common interest where we work together in areas of energy and economy, and trade and business”, it would “allow the chance for this region to unleash its potential”.

Bucking the downward trend, utilities and communication services led the gainers, advancing 1.14 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.

The document revealed that the company is seeking a valuation of up to 2 trillion U.S. dollars while explicitly cautioning that advanced AI systems could pose existential risks to humanity. Concurrently, rival research lab OpenAI reportedly shelved the release of its latest frontier model following safety concerns identified during internal evaluation.
The broader market for public listings showed signs of strain amid surging government bond yields. Health technology firm Oura abruptly halted its planned market debut on Tuesday, citing heightened market uncertainty.
In commodity markets, crude oil benchmarks retreated as fears of supply disruption eased. Saudi Arabia resumed crude transport via its key East-West pipeline, while U.S. and Iranian representatives engaged through intermediary channels to restart diplomatic talks. Upon settlement, Brent crude for November delivery hovered near 102.6 dollars per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate crude traded at 89.38 dollars per barrel.
On the macroeconomic front, the Conference Board reported that U.S. consumer confidence dropped to its lowest level since 2014. In the labor market, the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey showed available positions fell to 7.097 million in August, down from a revised 7.335 million in July and trailing market forecasts of 7.228 million.
Meanwhile, borrowing costs continued to climb alongside elevated U.S. Treasury yields. The average rate on a benchmark 30-year fixed-rate mortgage jumped eight basis points to 7.58 percent on Tuesday, touching its highest level since November 2023 and adding further pressure to housing affordability ahead of Friday's monthly nonfarm payrolls report. ■

US Supreme Court allows Trump to continue deportation policy after judge labels it unlawful
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
23:46:52 UTC
08:46:52 KST

The US Supreme Court on Tuesday let US President Donald Trump's administration resume deporting migrants to countries other than their own without offering them the chance to show the harms they may face, bolstering a tool his administration has used for rapid expulsions as part of his immigration crackdown.
The court granted the Justice Department's emergency request to put on hold Boston-based US District Judge Brian Murphy's ruling that the Department of Homeland Security's policy to remove migrants to so-called third countries is unlawful. The court also agreed to hear arguments in the dispute in December, with a formal ruling on the policy to follow.
The court has a 6-3 conservative majority. Its three liberal justices dissented from the decision to let the deportations immediately resume pending the final outcome of the litigation.
Murphy's ruling came in a class-action lawsuit filed by immigrant rights groups on behalf of migrants seeking to prevent the US government from sending them to third countries without notice and a chance to assert the harms they could face.
More than 25,000 migrants have been deported to 29 countries under the policy implemented last year, according to a tally by human rights groups, with the vast majority going to Mexico.
The policy is one of a number of measures the administration has taken in its pursuit of Trump's goal of mass deportation. The Republican president has enforced a sweeping crackdown on immigration - among his top priorities - since returning to office last year.
The administration has carried out third-country deportations to politically unstable South Sudan, which the US State Department urges Americans to avoid due to the risks of crime, kidnapping, and armed conflict, as well as Uganda, Equatorial Guinea, Liberia, the Central African Republic, and other nations.
Department of Homeland Security General Counsel James Percival welcomed the court's decision.
"A bad day for criminal illegals and open-borders activists alike," Percival wrote on social media.
Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the plaintiffs at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, said the court has "allowed the administration to resume sending people to third countries where they face persecution or torture. That is a devastating result for people who may be put on a plane before they ever have notice or an opportunity to raise a fear claim."
Judge rules US immigration policy against immigration law, due process protections
In February, Murphy ruled that the policy violates immigration law procedures and due process protections under the US Constitution's Fifth Amendment. Due process generally requires the government to provide notice and an opportunity for a hearing before taking certain adverse actions.
The Supreme Court, which has allowed a number of Trump's hardline immigration policies, previously sided with the administration in the legal challenge, suspending a preliminary order that Murphy issued earlier in the case halting the removals. In another win for the administration, the Supreme Court subsequently lifted limits the judge had imposed to protect a group of men from being sent to South Sudan.
The case began in 2025 after the Department of Homeland Security moved to step up deportations of migrants who cannot be returned to any country listed on their deportation orders.
The policy provided that migrants could be swiftly removed without notice to third countries that have provided credible diplomatic assurance that they will not persecute or torture the individuals. For countries that have not provided such assurance, deportees would be notified of their destination and US authorities would assess the likelihood of persecution or torture only if the individual raises such fear on their own.
In its emergency filing to the Supreme Court, the Justice Department said third-country deportations are "an essential tool to remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens."
But both Murphy and critics of the administration said the policy is also targeting migrants who had been granted legal protection from being sent back to their home countries.
Deportees see sexual assault, unlawful transference, plaintiffs say
The policy has resulted in deportees being unlawfully transferred by third countries back to their home countries from which the US had already granted them protection, while others have been beaten, sexually assaulted, detained, or have disappeared, the plaintiffs said in a court filing.
The administration is ignoring "the significant harm resulting from deporting thousands of longtime US residents, many with no criminal history, to third countries without regard to the persecution or torture they face there," the plaintiffs said.
The Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld most of the judge's ruling on September 18.
The case has been hotly contested since it began, and included findings by Murphy that the administration "repeatedly violated, or attempted to violate" his orders. Murphy in 2025 found that the administration had violated another order he issued requiring additional steps before attempting to send a group of migrants to South Sudan.

European countries should have shown more solidarity and offered more support to Spain after the mass arrival in Ceuta of tens of thousands of migrants, Spanish King Felipe VI said on Tuesday during a gala dinner to mark a visit by French President Emmanuel Macron.
In an unusually outspoken address reflecting the depth of the crisis facing Spain following the Ceuta border rush that took place two months ago on Wednesday, the king said what happened in the enclave on the North African coast was "unacceptable" and generated an enormous security, public order and humanitarian challenge.
"It's a situation that ought to have as a consequence a reinforcement of collaboration between member states in resources and cooperation," he said. "The European countries that suffer the most pressure from being on the external borders of the European Union cannot alone bear a responsibility that also belongs to everyone."
The king spoke during a dinner at the Royal Palace in Madrid, also attended by Spain's Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, a rare European proponent of the benefits of migration who launched a mass regularisation of irregular migrants that concluded in the summer. Sanchez, however, has proposed possible changes to asylum rules to return arrivals more quickly, which NGOs and lawyers say would violate human rights conventions.
Asked in a news conference about the plans, territorial policy minister Angel Victor Torres said the government was "analysing the possibility" of a legislative amendment but that it was "not easy" due to questions of international law.
72,000 migrants crossed into Ceuta
Following the mass crossing of 72,000 migrants into Ceuta on July 30, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen commended Spain's swift action in returning most arrivals to Morocco. Other leaders were less understanding, however, with Italy suspending the European Union's border-free Schengen arrangements with Spain for one month.
European Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner unveiled a plan on Tuesday to strengthen EU border controls in the wake of Ceuta.
The plan, which requires the approval of member states, would strengthen the mandate of Frontex, the EU border protection agency, and give it a standing corps ready for immediate deployment.
