Trump, tech leaders sign accord on 'Super Intelligence' safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
22:12:00 UTC
07:12:00 KST

Diyar Güldoğan
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
US President Donald Trump shared a copy of an accord on his Truth Social platform on artificial intelligence (AI) safety that he said was signed with several of the technology industry's leading executives outlining a joint commitment to strengthen safeguards around the development and deployment of advanced AI systems.
The White House Accord on "Super Intelligence," described as a “Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities,” calls on companies developing and deploying frontier models to establish robust internal processes and controls designed to ensure their systems operate as intended and that potential problems are identified and addressed quickly.
According to the accord, each participating company should implement four layers of controls and audits covering model development and deployment.
The first layer calls for companies to establish internal controls to monitor model capabilities and alignment, including potential risks involving cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats. The controls would also be designed to prevent models from hacking or accessing technical systems in unintended ways.
The second layer would involve an internal team responsible for verifying that controls, monitoring and detection systems are working properly and ensuring identified problems are addressed.
Under the third layer, companies would also work with independent external auditors or evaluators to assess whether their controls and monitoring systems are operating as intended.
The fourth layer would establish an independent board committee to oversee the process, receive reports from internal teams and outside evaluators, and ensure that identified issues are resolved.
According to the accord, the measures are intended to give companies, customers and the public greater confidence that advanced AI systems are operating as intended.
Under the agreement, participating companies will meet regularly to establish standards and best practices aimed at improving the safety of their systems.
The document also leaves open the possibility of government regulation in the future, saying the measures could eventually be incorporated into laws or regulations.
Regardless of whether such requirements become mandatory, the signatories state that implementing the controls and audits is critical to developing the technology safely and commit their companies to adopting the framework.
The agreement lists Trump and executives from several of the world's largest technology companies as signatories.
Those named are Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman, XAI CEO Elon Musk and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Tuesday called for efforts to forge a new path toward a world free of nuclear weapons.
Nuclear disarmament is not a favor, it is a binding legal obligation under the Non-Proliferation Treaty, he said at a high-level meeting to mark the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons. "As we mark this important day, it's time to forge a new path," he said.
States possessing nuclear weapons must return to dialogue to prevent any use of a nuclear weapon. Maintaining the decades-old reduction in global arsenals is essential to prevent another nuclear arms race. All nuclear-weapon states must reduce the role of nuclear weapons in their security policies, said the UN chief.
"These devices of death must never decide the fate of humanity. A divided world cannot be an excuse for inaction. We know the danger and we know the consequences. We know that we have to do everything to change course: replace threats with dialogue, replace arms racing with arms control, replace paralysis with concrete action," said Guterres.
Nuclear arsenals are being expanded and modernized. The rattling of nuclear sabers is growing louder. Advances in technology are increasing the odds of mistake and miscalculation. And just when they are most needed, the safeguards built over decades to contain these dangers are breaking down, he noted.
"Humanity has lived under the nuclear shadow for more than eight decades. We must ensure that future generations do not. Let's choose a future free from nuclear weapons," said Guterres. ■

FAO chief calls for reducing food loss, waste to ease pressure on forests
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:09:14 CST
07:09:14 KST

ROME, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Reducing food loss and waste can help transform agrifood systems, conserve natural resources and ease pressure on forests, Director-General of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) Qu Dongyu said Tuesday.
Qu made the remarks at a joint FAO-UN Environment Programme (UNEP) event at FAO headquarters in Rome marking the seventh International Day of Awareness of Food Loss and Waste.
According to FAO, 13.4 percent of food produced globally is lost after harvest and before reaching retail, while 19 percent of food available to consumers is wasted at the retail, food service and household levels.
Food loss and waste also means a waste of the land, water and other resources used to produce food. FAO estimates that about 1.4 billion hectares of land are used to produce food that is ultimately never consumed.
As agricultural expansion remains the leading driver of deforestation globally, reducing food loss and waste could help make better use of existing agricultural land and reduce pressure on forests, FAO said.
"To protect forests, we must transform agrifood systems; to transform agrifood systems, we must reduce food loss and waste, and by reducing food loss and waste, we help safeguard forests," Qu said.
Food loss and waste account for around 10 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions. When discarded food decomposes, particularly in landfills under anaerobic conditions, it also produces methane, a potent greenhouse gas.
Despite international commitments, the world has made no apparent progress in reducing food losses since 2015 and remains off track to meet Sustainable Development Goal target 12.3, which aims to halve per capita food waste at retail and consumer levels and reduce food losses along production and supply chains by 2030.
At the event, FAO also released an interactive Food Loss Index data map, presenting food loss estimates for 2024 at the subregional and regional levels.
FAO said the tool will improve access to food loss data and support evidence-based policies and efforts to reduce losses across agrifood systems. ■

Israel's public broadcaster Kan reported that Netanyahu also met during the visit with senior representatives of at least two Gulf countries that do not currently have diplomatic relations with Israel. If confirmed, analysts suggest that the contacts could extend beyond Israel-UAE ties to broader regional security coordination.
WHY A LOW-PROFILE VISIT NOW?
Analysts say the Israeli prime minister's visit to the UAE, which came amid continued tensions between Israel and Arab countries over the Gaza conflict, was shaped by both regional security considerations and Israel's upcoming parliamentary election.
Since the United States and Israel launched surprise strikes on Iran in February, tensions have remained high across the Middle East, particularly in the Gulf, with several Gulf states, including the UAE, coming under drone and missile attacks.
Meanwhile, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has compounded the fallout from the Israeli-U.S.-Iranian conflict, dealing a blow to the economies of Gulf countries.
As one of the few Arab states that maintain diplomatic ties with Israel, the UAE has repeatedly called for regional de-escalation through political solutions while maintaining diplomatic and security communication with Israel.
Analysts say the country is likely wary of over-publicizing top-level interactions with Israel as it's walking a fine line between security cooperation and its diplomatic stance towards Israel.
The timing also carries domestic political weight for Netanyahu, with Israel's parliamentary election less than a month away and Israeli media focused on whether he had received warnings before Hamas' surprise attack on Oct. 7, 2023.
Earlier this month, Israel's Haaretz newspaper reported that the UAE president had warned Netanyahu about 10 days before the attack that Hamas could be planning a major operation.
Netanyahu denied the report while the UAE Foreign Ministry noted on Sept. 8 that relevant Israeli and UAE authorities maintained open and direct communication channels and exchanged intelligence when necessary.
After Sunday's visit was exposed, Channel 12, citing sources, reported that Netanyahu asked the UAE leader to deny personally warning him before the attack. Neither Israel nor the UAE has confirmed the claim.
Citing sources, the Jerusalem Post said that Israel had pressed for the meeting to take place before the election.
WHAT DOES IT SIGNAL?
The visit indicates that despite disagreements over the Palestinian issue and ongoing regional conflicts, high-level communication between Israel and the UAE remains intact, with security cooperation continuing to serve as a common ground between the two sides.
Since normalizing diplomatic relations in 2020, the two countries have expanded cooperation in trade, technology and security. Though the UAE has criticized some Israeli policies toward the Palestinians since the new round of Gaza conflict erupted, it has maintained government contacts with Israel.
Analysts say pressure from Iran and the Houthis could further encourage Israel and some Gulf states to maintain contacts on intelligence sharing, missile warning and air defense.
The Jerusalem Post noted that Gulf states' growing demand for stronger air defense and early-warning capabilities, coupled with Israel's expertise in radar, intelligence and missile interception, creates the possibility of discreet security cooperation.
Israel and some Gulf countries, analysts add, share security interests amid rising regional tensions, but their cooperation remains constrained by the Palestinian issue, regional political considerations and differing diplomatic priorities. ■

News Analysis: Jobs, housing shape when young Europeans leave home
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:08:52 CST
07:08:52 KST

WARSAW, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Job prospects, housing affordability and family traditions help explain why young Europeans leave the parental home at widely varying ages, according to the latest Eurostat data.
In Finland, young people left home at an average age of 21.4 in 2025, compared with 31.5 in Croatia -- a gap of about a decade within the European Union (EU).
Employment data reveal a clear divide across the bloc.
In 2025, 65.5 percent of people aged 20 to 29 in the EU were employed. Eurostat data showed that in most countries where young people left the parental home earlier than the EU average, the employment rate among 20- to 29-year-olds was above the bloc's average.
The Netherlands, Denmark, Germany and Sweden were among those countries, while Greece, Croatia, Spain and Italy combined later home-leaving with lower youth employment rates.
Poland, however, shows that favorable labor-market figures do not necessarily translate into earlier home-leaving. The country's overall unemployment rate stood at 3.1 percent in 2025, the second-lowest in the EU alongside Malta and behind only the Czech Republic's 2.8 percent, according to separate Eurostat data.
Despite the relatively strong labor market, young people in Poland left the parental home at an average age of 26.8 in 2025, slightly above the EU average of 26.3.
Housing data reveal another constraint. According to Eurostat, young people bear a heavier housing burden than the population as a whole.
A 2025 report by Eurofound, the EU agency for improving living and working conditions, said young adults were disproportionately affected by Europe's housing affordability crisis.
Young adults often have lower incomes or less secure jobs while seeking homes in major cities, where demand and prices are typically highest.
Since 2010, average house prices in the EU have risen by 55.4 percent and rents by 26.7 percent.
In many areas of Bulgaria, Ireland, Poland, Portugal and Spain, rent for a standard two-room apartment could absorb more than 80 percent of the median wage, according to Eurofound.
In 2025, 9.1 percent of EU residents aged 15 to 29 lived in households that spent at least 40 percent of their disposable income on housing, compared with 7.7 percent of the overall population. Young people were also more likely to live in overcrowded homes, with the rate reaching 26.9 percent, 10.1 percentage points above the overall figure.
Eurofound said unaffordable housing was forcing some young people into living arrangements they would not otherwise choose, affecting their education, employment opportunities, well-being and family formation.
Employment and housing costs, however, do not fully explain the divide.
Eurofound research also suggests that cultural context plays a role, with more individualized family systems in Nordic and some Central European countries and stronger intergenerational ties across much of Southern Europe.
Nearly half of EU residents aged 18 to 34 -- 49.8 percent -- lived with at least one parent or contributed to or benefited from the parental household income in 2025, according to Eurostat.
The share ranged from under 26 percent in Nordic EU countries to 75.3 percent in Croatia.
The figures reveal a deeply uneven pattern across the EU, with young people in some countries leaving home about a decade earlier than in others, as housing constraints and job opportunities shape evolving trends. ■

Displaced Syrians returning home face new challenges: UN

06:08:30 CST
07:08:30 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- The flow of Syrians routed by violence from their homes into displacement camps has reversed, creating new challenges, UN humanitarians said Tuesday.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said nearly 39,000 people have left displacement sites in July and August alone.
"These returns are a positive sign, but needs are increasingly shifting from camps to communities of return, where damaged homes, limited basic services and a lack of jobs are making it difficult for families to rebuild their lives," OCHA said.
The office said that the United Nations, working with partners, is helping restore essential services in the communities, including water and electricity networks, hospitals, schools, bakeries, roads and homes.
OCHA cited Aleppo and Idlib as examples, where more than 120,000 people have better access to bread, with additional facilities expected to benefit another 320,000 people.
Humanitarian assistance also continues across the country.
The office said that between January and July, an average of 2.5 million people a month received support, including food, health care, shelter, clean water, and education, while some 120 million U.S. dollars in cash and vouchers were provided to families.
However, OCHA said that more than 15 million people still require humanitarian assistance in Syria, and the 2.9-billion-dollar humanitarian response plan is less than one-third funded.
"Sustained and flexible funding is essential both to keep life-saving assistance going and to help people returning home rebuild their lives," the office said. ■

F-47 Maker Boeing Tapped for Navy’s F/A-XX Sixth-Gen Fighter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
22:08:23 UTC
07:08:23 KST

The Navy has awarded Boeing a contract worth more than $20 billion to build its new carrier-based sixth-generation fighter, the F/A-XX. Boeing is also building the Air Force’s sixth-gen F-47.
“The F/A-XX is a critical pillar in our commitment to maintaining peace through strength,” Michael P. Duffey, the undersecretary of defense for acquisition and sustainment, said in a Sept. 29 release from the Pentagon “F/A-XX will dominate contested airspace, extend operational reach, and deliver a decisive combat advantage for the warfighter. The F/A-XX platform represents a crucial, non-negotiable investment in America’s national security and long-term air combat capabilities.”
The Pentagon release states that the F/A-XX will first augment, and eventually replace, older F/A-18E/F Super Hornets and EA-18G Growlers beginning in the 2030s. It will operate alongside the carrier-based F-35C Joint Strike Fighters, which the Navy and Marine Corps both fly.
The selection ensures Boeing will make two of the three sixth-generation aircraft in development for the U.S. military—the firm won the contract for the Air Force’s sixth-gen fighter program in March 2025 with the F-47. It also represents a loss for Northrop Grumman, the only other company that remained in the running for the Navy’s Next-Generation Air Dominance fighter, and the maker of the Air Force’s B-21 Raider.
“We are joining forces with Boeing to field these capabilities rapidly, ensuring our warfighters possess the lethal and highly networked systems required to deter aggression, project undisputed power, and secure absolute air superiority,” Duffey said.
The Pentagon release said F/A-XX will be able to fly alongside and control semi-autonomous Navy drones known as Collaborative Combat Aircraft.
“This achievement marks a new era for the U.S. Navy,” acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said. “The sixth-generation fighter is a generational leap in air superiority and will provide the world’s best aviators with unparalleled capabilities to fight, win, and come home safe. We are excited to partner with Boeing, and for our warfighters to continue to dominate the skies and defeat our nation’s enemies.”
Advanced stealth is also considered to be a key attribute of sixth-generation aircraft.
Now-retired Rear Adm. Michael Donnelly, the former director of the Navy’s air warfare division, said at an April 2025 conference that F/A-XX could be the Navy’s last manned fighter.
“It could be our last tactical manned fighter that we operate out of the Navy,” Donnelly said at the Navy League’s Sea Air Space conference in National Harbor, Md. “It will actually be at a point where we are more man-on-the-loop than man-in-the-loop, and be the bridge to fully integrating towards the hybrid air wing [combining piloted aircraft and unmanned platforms] in the future, in the 2040s.”
Donnelly told reporters at that conference that F/A-XX would likely be able to fly more than 25 percent farther than current Navy fighters before needing refueling. The F/A-18 Super Hornet has a roughly 1,275-nautical mile combat range, which is slightly more than the F-35C Joint Strike Fighter’s combat range of more than 1,200 nautical miles.
“That’s a core attribute of the F/A-XX,” Donnelly said in 2025. “It will definitely have longer inherent range, and then with refueling, you could say that’s indefinite, as long as refueling is available.”
Boeing said in a statement that F/A-XX “will revolutionize advancements in open mission systems architecture, advanced mission systems, and operational reach and capacity.”
“It’s an honor to be selected to produce the Navy’s first sixth-generation platform,” Steve Parker, president and chief executive officer of Boeing Defense, Space and Security, said in the company’s own statement. “Backed by decades of work, bolstered by game-changing innovations and solidified by the investments we’ve made in new facilities uniquely suited to build multiple products with next-generation capabilities, our dedicated and talented team is ready to execute this critical program.”
Boeing said technical and program details on the F/A-XX are classified and could not be released.
Longtime defense analyst J.J. Gertler said the Navy’s choice of Boeing could leverage work Boeing is now doing with its F-47 sixth-generation fighter for the Air Force. That connection could accelerate the F/A-XX process and get it into production faster.
“If it’s based on the F-47 or was codeveloped with the F-47, they might be able to put an aircraft in the air very quickly,” Gertler told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Boeing has invested heavily in building more facilities for advanced aircraft production in St. Louis, Mo., where the F-47 is now in the works, Gertler said.
Boeing is also building F-15EX Eagle II fighters and T-7 Red Hawk trainer jets for the Air Force in St. Louis. Indeed, also on Sept. 29, the Pentagon awarded Boeing a $2.38 billion contract for 22 more F-15EX fighters.
Boeing said construction is still ongoing for its secure manufacturing facility in St. Louis, which will “be part of the world’s most advanced, all-digital aerospace design and manufacturing system.”
“Delivering two advanced fighters in parallel was always our plan, and we invested accordingly,” Parker said. “We are ready and able to build multiple concurrent future combat aircraft franchise programs.”
Gertler said it remains to be seen whether Boeing will be able to follow through on commitments for many critical military aircraft.
“We don’t know how much of [Boeing’s new advanced aircraft facility] is taken up by F-47,” Gertler said. “They’ve got F-15EX numbers expanding. They’ve got T-7 there. Do they have the people to be able to produce this [F/A-XX] aircraft quickly?”

US Supreme Court allows Trump to continue third-country deportations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
22:06:43 UTC
07:06:43 KST

US Supreme Court allows Trump to continue third-country deportations
The high court grants an emergency petition ahead of expected arguments in the case, slated for December.
The United States Supreme Court has allowed President Donald Trump’s administration to continue third-country deportations, halting a lower-court ruling that paused such removals over questions of due process.
On Tuesday, the high court granted the administration’s emergency request to resume the deportations, which involve sending immigrants to countries they may have no connection to.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘Not a small issue’: People deported by US to Liberia face uncertain future
- list 2 of 3‘Wrong’: Trump administration completes deportations to South Sudan
- list 3 of 3US court blocks Trump plan to deport migrants to third countries
The court’s order was unsigned, as is typical for an emergency petition. It also does not include an explanation or a list of how the justices voted.
But at the bottom of Tuesday’s order, the court’s three left-leaning justices – Sonia Sotomayor, Ketanji Brown Jackson and Elena Kagan – indicated they would have denied the Trump administration’s petition.
The Supreme Court’s decision to pause the lower court ruling is temporary. The order calls for arguments to be heard in December.
That hearing comes as Trump administration continues its appeal against the lower court’s ruling, handed down by Judge Brian Murphy in Boston, Massachusetts.
Murphy had ruled that immigrants must be given a “meaningful” chance to raise safety concerns before their removal to third-party countries.
In pausing such deportations, Murphy indicated that some immigrants may have been denied the opportunity to challenge their deportations as part of their due process rights.
Tuesday, however, is not the first time the Supreme Court justices have weighed in on the practice of forcibly sending people to third countries, which Trump dramatically stepped up since his return to office in 2025.
Trump campaigned on a pledge to implement the “largest deportation operation in American history”, and his officials have argued that third-country deportations are a means of removing individuals whose home countries may not accept them.
In June 2025, the Supreme Court also issued an unsigned order allowing such removals to proceed.
That cleared the way for eight men, including nationals of Cuba, Myanmar and Vietnam, to be deported to South Sudan, a country the US State Department advises against visiting because of “crime, kidnapping, and armed conflict”.
The Department of Homeland Security at the time called the removals “a win”, while rights groups said the move flouted basic legal protections.
Critics have expressed concern that many of the governments receiving third-country deportations have a record of human rights abuses.
Third-country deportations have been used to bypass court protection orders that prevent immigrants from being sent back to their home countries due to fears of persecution.
But advocates say that some of those third-party countries have ultimately sent deportees, including asylum seekers, back to the places where they feared they would be at risk of torture or other harms.
At least 35 countries have signed agreements with the Trump administration to take in the third-country nationals, according to a tally by the nonprofits Refugees International and Human Rights First.
The groups estimate that more than 25,000 people have been subject to third-country deportations so far.
On Monday, human rights experts at the United Nations wrote to the US government urging a halt to such removals, warning they were putting deportees at heightened risk of abuse.
“At gravest risk are children, women, persons with disabilities, victims of trafficking, LGBT persons, human rights defenders, stateless persons and other people in extremely vulnerable situations,” the experts said.
On Tuesday, Burundi became the latest country to enter an agreement with the US to take non-citizen deportations.
Officials said the country would only take in people who were not facing prosecution and had no links to “terrorism”.

‘Godzilla’ of weight-loss drugs could provide other important health benefits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
22:01:02 UTC
07:01:02 KST

The ‘Godzilla’ of weight-loss drugs could help improve blood sugar levels, reduce inflammation and cut a person’s body weight by a quarter, according to the largest study of its kind.
Retatrutide mimics three key gut hormones that help control appetite, blood sugar and metabolism: GLP-1, GIP and glucagon. Unlike other drugs such as Wegovy, which primarily targets the GLP-1 pathway to suppress appetite, or Mounjaro, which contains GLP-1 plus GIP to control blood sugar levels, retatrutide also engages the glucagon receptor, which helps increase energy expenditure.
The drug has not yet been approved by any regulatory agency. But the results of the global trial in people living with obesity and type 2 diabetes suggest it could help them shift enormous amounts of excess weight while also providing other important health benefits.
“Retatrutide demonstrated substantial reduction in body weight alongside glycaemic control and cardiometabolic risk factors, with a safety profile generally similar to other molecules with GLP-1 receptor agonist activity,” the researchers said.
The findings from the study, funded by retatrutide maker Eli Lilly, were published in the Lancet medical journal and presented at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes in Milan, Italy.
The randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 2,047 adults in eight countries: Argentina, Australia, Brazil, India, Mexico, Romania, Spain and the US.
Participants had a body mass index (BMI) of 27 or above and type 2 diabetes. 48% were women and 52% were men. Their average age was 55.
In the 80-week phase 3 trial, 1,152 were randomly assigned to receive a weekly injection of placebo (289), or retatrutide 4 mg (292), 9 mg (284) or 12 mg (287), alongside dietary counselling and guidance on physical activity.
By the end of the study, those on 4mg of retatrutide lost 11.9% of their body weight on average, increasing to 16.8% with 9mg and 18.8% on 12mg. Those in the placebo group lost 5.1%.
Among those on the 12 mg dose, almost half (47%) shed at least 20% of their starting weight and almost a third (31%) lost at least 25%. That compared with 6% and 3%, respectively, with placebo.
Additionally, 72% achieved an HbA1c (measuring average blood sugar levels for the last two to three months) of 6.5% or lower, a standard threshold used to diagnose type 2 diabetes, compared with 29% in the placebo group.
Retatrutide also significantly improved cardiometabolic risk factors, including blood pressure and lipid profiles, and reduced high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP), a marker of inflammation, according to the researchers.
The most frequently reported adverse events were gastrointestinal. Diarrhoea occurred in 27-34% of participants in the retatrutide groups, compared with 13% in the placebo group, and nausea occurred in 14-28% of participants on retatrutide, compared with 8% receiving the placebo.
Seven deaths occurred during the trial: two in the retatrutide 4 mg group, three in the 9 mg group, one in the 12 mg group and one in the placebo group, and were deemed unrelated to the study intervention by the investigator.
Meanwhile, separate research presented at the conference in Milan and published in the Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology & Women’s Health medical journal showed that in most cases, weight-loss drugs are not associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes in women living with type 2 diabetes.
But researchers stressed that more research was urgently needed to address the large evidence gaps and to keep pace with the huge and accelerating rise in women of reproductive age using the drugs.

Market services inflation worries CBA economists
A note on the monthly Consumer Price Index from one of the big bank economics teams.
Trent Saunders, a former RBA and Queensland Treasury economist, notes that the increase in prices for market services remains stubbornly high, indicating ongoing domestic price pressures.
"Market services inflation increased by 0.4%/mth in August, with the annual rate remaining unchanged at 4.1%," he writes.
"The result suggests that market services inflation was a bit stickier than we had expected, with more of July's start‑of‑financial‑year step‑up in services prices persisting into August.
"Within the detail, restaurant meals slowed to around 0.3%/mth after rising 1.2% in July. Takeaway meals also slowed to 0.2% in the month, while hairdressing slowed from 0.6% in July to 0.4%.
"The slowdown in these categories was partly offset by a pick‑up in price growth in motor vehicle maintenance, insurance, and veterinary services.
"Overall, the market services detail was mixed in August but continues to point to an aggregate inflation rate that will make it difficult for the RBA to hit its target in a timely manner."
Given that, Saunders thinks there is a substantial risk of a follow-up rate rise in November, even though it's not CBA's 'base case'.
"The RBA's November Board meeting remains live given the ongoing strength in underlying inflation, but yesterday's press conference suggests the hurdle for another rate increase is now higher," he explains.
"Governor Bullock emphasised the need to assess the broader flow of data and appeared to push back against the idea that a single strong inflation outcome would necessarily be sufficient to prompt another increase.
"For now, we continue to expect the RBA to leave the cash rate unchanged in November. For the first time in history, younger generations are worse off than their parents, a Greens-led senate inquiry into intergenerational housing inequity has found.
The committee has published its final report today after spending six months hearing evidence from across the country about Australia’s growing housing divide.
The report noted that over the past 30 years, housing in Australia has become a vehicle for private wealth accumulation.
Meanwhile, the report said the big winners of the housing crisis—banks, the real estate industry, big developers, and multiple property investors—have seen their profits and wealth grow exponentially.

"This Senate inquiry revealed a housing system stacked against younger generations who have lost the intergenerational housing lottery," Ms Pocock said.
"Millennials are the first Australian generation to be worse off than their parents.
"Young people have been ripped off, locked out of the growing housing divide, forced into insecure housing and as a result are delaying major life decisions."

High salt diets disrupt the gut microbiome and impair memory in mice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
22:00:09 UTC
07:00:09 KST

A new study demonstrates that both abnormally high and abnormally low dietary salt intake can induce cognitive impairment in mice, though through distinctly different biological pathways. The research reveals that while excessive salt triggers systemic inflammation, severe salt restriction starves the gut microbiome of metabolic byproducts needed for optimal brain function. The findings were published in the journal Food Research International.
The human digestive tract is home to trillions of microorganisms, collectively known as the gut microbiome. These microbes engage in constant communication with the central nervous system through a biochemical pathway called the gut-brain axis.
Health professionals routinely recommend reducing dietary sodium to protect cardiovascular health. Diets heavily loaded with salt are already known to disrupt the gut microbiome and impair memory. A high-salt environment can promote inflammation and harm the hippocampus, a brain region central to learning and memory formation.
The neurological effects of eating extremely small amounts of salt remain much less understood. Clinical observations occasionally link severe sodium deficiency with cognitive difficulties, but the direct biological mechanisms connecting extreme salt restriction to brain function have not been systematically mapped out.
Researchers from Zhejiang University in China, led by Anji Chen, designed a study to compare the neurological and metabolic effects of high-salt and low-salt diets. To make their animal model more relevant to human biology, they utilized a technique called microbiome humanization.
The researchers designed a small study using 32 male mice. They first treated the majority of the animals with antibiotics to deplete their natural gut bacteria. They then fed the mice a solution containing human fecal matter, allowing human-derived bacteria to colonize the animals’ digestive tracts.
Following this colonization period, the humanized mice were divided into three groups and fed distinct diets for 14 weeks. One group received a normal-salt diet, another received a heavily restricted low-salt diet, and the third group consumed a high-salt diet. A fourth control group of standard mice maintained their natural gut bacteria and ate a normal-salt diet.
After the 14-week feeding period, the researchers tested the animals’ memory and anxiety levels using a series of behavioral tests. They used a Y-shaped maze to evaluate short-term spatial working memory by tracking how well the mice remembered which arms of the maze they had already explored. They also used a novel object recognition test, which measures long-term memory by seeing if the mice spend more time investigating a new item compared to a familiar one.
Both the low-salt and high-salt groups exhibited substantial impairments in short-term spatial working memory and long-term recognition memory compared to the normal-salt group. The high-salt diet produced the most severe cognitive deficits. These mice also displayed elevated anxiety-like behavior in an open arena test and drank substantially more water. The low-salt group experienced memory deficits without the added symptoms of anxiety or excessive thirst.
To understand why these behavioral changes occurred, the researchers examined the animals’ brain tissue. They specifically focused on the hippocampus, a brain region highly sensitive to metabolic disruptions. The scientists measured the levels of specific proteins that help build synapses, which are the physical communication junctions between neurons.
Both extreme diets reduced the abundance of key synaptic proteins and essential growth factors. One suppressed protein was brain-derived neurotrophic factor, a molecule that supports neuronal survival and helps the brain adapt to new information.
The high-salt diet caused a widespread reduction in proteins that structure both the sending and receiving ends of a synapse. The low-salt diet primarily affected the proteins involved in structural stability and synaptic adaptability, leaving the physical abundance of neuronal vesicles relatively intact.
The team then sequenced the genetic material of the bacteria living in the animals’ colons to see how the diets altered the microbiome. The high-salt diet prompted an expansion of bacteria associated with inflammation. The low-salt diet caused a different shift, slightly increasing certain specialized bacteria but reducing the overall population of beneficial microbes like those in the Lactobacillus genus.
Next, the researchers measured the metabolic byproducts produced by these gut bacteria. When microbes digest food, they produce compounds called short-chain fatty acids that help regulate immune responses and nourish the brain.
Both extreme diets reduced the levels of two helpful short-chain fatty acids called propionate and butyrate. The low-salt diet, however, also caused a sharp drop in two additional compounds, acetate and isobutyrate. Acetate is a primary metabolic signal that can travel from the gut to the brain, and its depletion suggests a broad suppression of microbial metabolism under severe salt restriction.
The researchers also analyzed lipids in the animals’ intestinal tracts. The high-salt group showed signs of severe oxidative stress, a condition where reactive oxygen molecules damage cells, and an increase in pro-inflammatory fats. The low-salt group experienced a drop in certain lipids that support neuronal membranes, but they did not exhibit the oxidative stress seen in the high-salt group.
Finally, blood tests were conducted to measure circulating cytokines, which are signaling proteins that trigger immune responses. The high-salt diet elevated multiple inflammatory cytokines, indicating a state of systemic inflammation. The low-salt diet did not produce any observable increase in these inflammatory markers.
The study suggests that severe salt restriction is not biologically neutral and might represent a distinct risk factor for cognitive decline. Extreme low-salt intake appears to impair memory by starving the gut microbiome of its ability to produce essential metabolic signals, rather than by triggering the aggressive inflammation seen with high-salt consumption.
Several caveats should be kept in mind when interpreting these results. This was a small study conducted entirely on male mice. While the humanized microbiome technique makes the findings more relevant to humans, the biological responses of a mouse may not perfectly mirror human physiology.
The study highlights statistical correlations between specific bacteria, metabolic byproducts, and memory scores, but it does not definitively prove that the missing short-chain fatty acids directly caused the memory loss. The experimental diets represented extreme ends of the sodium spectrum, which were necessary to isolate biological mechanisms but do not necessarily reflect typical human eating habits.
Future research will need to establish the exact lower limits for healthy human salt consumption. Scientists also need to determine whether supplementing specific missing metabolites could prevent the cognitive decline associated with imbalanced sodium intake.
This research provides a foundational step in understanding how dietary minerals influence neurological health. The study, “Long-term low-salt and high-salt diets differentially disrupt the gut – metabolite – brain axis and induce cognitive impairment,” was authored by Anji Chen, Shilong Hu, Fansen Zeng, Chengfeng Yu, Danying Chen, Xingqian Ye, Zengliang Jiang, and Shiguo Chen.

Eli Lilly’s Experimental Weight-Loss Drug Shows Promising Results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
22:00:04 UTC
07:00:04 KST

Two new studies published in separate journals show that an experimental drug developed by Eli Lilly leads to meaningful weight loss.
One study, published in the Lancet and presented at the European Association for the Study of Diabetes, tested the drug retatrutide in people who were overweight or obese and had Type 2 diabetes: a population in which weight-loss medications have historically been less effective. People who took the highest dose lost about 18.8% of their starting body weight, while people who took a placebo lost 5.1%. About a third of the people in the study who took the highest dose of retatrutide lost at least 25% of their body weight, compared to 3% of those on placebo over the study period of 1.5 years.
“This is the most potent drug, showing the greatest percent weight loss in people with Type 2 diabetes with a pharmacological agent, shown to date,” says Dr. Juan Pablo Frias, medical director at the Los Angeles Institute for Metabolic Research and one of the Lancet study authors.
People in the study also showed improvement in their diabetes control. Of those who took the highest dose, 63% lowered their A1C to less than 6.5%—the threshold for diabetes—and lost at least 10% of their body weight.
In another study published in the New England Journal of Medicine, researchers reported similar weight-loss benefits in people who were overweight or obese but who did not have diabetes. In that study, people who took the highest dose of retatrutide lost about 25% of their starting body weight, while just 3.9% of people who took a placebo did the same. People taking the drug were also studied for other benefits; those with osteoarthritis in the knee reported lower pain scores than those on placebo, while people with obstructive sleep apnea also reported fewer apnea episodes than those taking placebo.
Retatrutide targets three weight-related hormones: GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon. Since each has specific receptors in the body and brain, targeting all three may be contributing to the more potent effects on weight for people with diabetes than drugs that target GLP-1 alone, like Ozempic and Wegovy (semaglutide), or GLP-1 and GIP together, as Mounjaro and Zepbound (tirzepatide) do. Zepbound is approved to not only control weight but to also treat obstructive sleep apnea, and Wegovy and Ozempic are approved to reduce the risk of heart disease.
In both studies, the side effects among people taking retatrutide were similar to those that have been reported with other GLP-1 medications, including GI issues such as abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
Eli Lilly says it plans to submit a request in early 2027 to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to approve retatrutide based on these results.

Pentagon Hands Out $20.7B Contract for AMRAAM Missiles to RTX
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:52:36 UTC
06:52:36 KST

The Pentagon on Sept. 28 announced a contract potentially worth $20.7 billion for RTX to build Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missiles used by Navy and Air Force aircraft and for ground-based interceptors.
The announcement of the Sept. 25 award noted that the contract is for five years, with two optional years, and is meant to ramp up production of the munition, used for air-to-air combat and missile defense.
The Pentagon release highlights both roles of the AIM-120 AMRAAM as “a proven air-to-air capability” and a “critical air defense capability for U.S. and allied forces.”
In its own release, RTX said the money would “accelerate production of AMRAAM missiles to record-setting levels” but did not specify the quantities.
However, RTX’s Raytheon division previously announced in February it had reached “framework” agreements to boost annual production of the AMRAAM to at least 1,900 missiles annually, along with increased production of the Tomahawk, SM-3 Block IB, SM-3 Block IIA, and SM-6 missiles, all of which are Raytheon products.
The latest contract award does not make clear whether the $20.7 billion is funding for the framework agreement or a separate deal. Neither the Pentagon nor RTX immediately responded to a request for comment.
The Air Force’s fiscal 2026 spending plan included $680 million for 423 AMRAAMs, split between regular appropriations and reconciliation funding.
Munitions Options
The new $20.7 billion contract aims to supply the USAF, Navy, and potentially foreign military sales, according to the release.
The AIM-120 is a radar-guided, supersonic missile. According to RTX, 11 currently operational platforms across 40 nations use it, including:
- F-15 Eagle / F-15E Strike Eagle / F-15EX Eagle II
- F-16 Fighting Falcon
- F/A-18 Hornet & F/A-18E/F Super Hornet
- F-22A Raptor
- F-35 Lightning II
- AV-8B Harrier II
- Eurofighter Typhoon
- JAS 39 Gripen
- FA-50 / T-50 Golden Eagle
- NASAMS (National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System)
- SL-AMRAAM / CLAWS Ground Launchers
There are three variants: the “B” model, which offers reprogrammable aspects not on the initial AMRAAM; the “C” model, which has smaller control surfaces so the F-22 and F-35 can carry it and high-angle off-boresight launch capability; and the “D” model with GPS-assisted guidance, improved range, updated data links, and jam resistance.
The latest version, with System Improvement Program update III, was fielded in March 2024.
The Pentagon plans SIP IV and SIP V upgrades, which will increase the munition’s computing power to four times its current level and expand its engagement envelope.
USAF has announced plans to use the AMRAAM alongside its still-under-development AIM-260 Joint Air Tactical Missile.
Air & Space Forces Magazine reported on Sept. 17 that Lockheed Martin announced a deal to expand JATM production through a separate multiyear agreement. Beyond production, the Air Force also faces operational availability problems with another air-to-air missile, the AIM-9X Sidewinder, as Air & Space Forces Magazine recently reported.
Both the AIM-9X and AIM-120 are key for tactical aircraft operations. The Sidewinder is a within-visual-range, dogfighting missile, while the 12.7-foot-long AMRAAM is a “fire-and-forget” missile used for beyond-visual-range interception.
The 9.8-foot-long AIM-9X uses imaging infrared focal plane array seeking technology, while the AMRAAM uses active radar and conducts mid-course updates for terminal strikes. The Sidewinder can strike targets up to 22 miles away, while the AMRAAM can travel more than 100 miles.
President Donald Trump’s administration has been vocal and adamant about increasing munitions stockpiles for everything from interceptors to air-to-air and air-to-ground missiles.
Separately from the AMRAAM and JATM work, the Air Force is ramping up production under its Family of Affordable Mass Missiles program, which saw a July announcement naming Anduril, CoAspire and Zone Five Technologies as builders of thousands of cruise missiles for air-to-ground engagements.
The companies are expected to produce as many as 5,300 missiles annually starting in 2028 and reach nearly 8,000 missiles a year by 2032.
Many Uses
Not only is the AMRAAM used for air-to-air combat, it is also part of the National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System, a midrange air defense system built jointly by Raytheon and Kongsberg Defense & Aerospace.
NASAMS reached operational capability in 1994 and was then deployed by the Royal Norwegian Air Force, according to a 2022 Congressional Research Service report. It can engage 72 targets in both active and passive modes using active-seeker missiles such as the AMRAAM. It has three launchers, each carrying six missiles.
The system uses an AN/MPQ-64 Sentinel Radar, a Fire Distribution Center, and the AMRAAM. The missiles have about a 25-mile range, according to the CRS report.
In 2022, President Joe Biden announced an $820 million aid package to Ukraine, which included funding for two NASAMS. That was followed by six more systems committed later that year and a finalized $1.3 billion contract with Raytheon to build a total of a dozen NASAMs for Ukraine.
Later, the State Department approved an FMS sale of one additional NASAMS to Ukraine in 2023 for $285 million.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said that his nation has more than 10 NASAMS in operation.
In 2024, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported that Japan would begin to co-produce AMRAAMs.
Mitsubishi Heavy Industries is the missile manufacturer under a license agreement. However, as of April 2026, the company was still in discussions “regarding the scope of Japan’s participation in the AIM-120 AMRAAM” program, according to a company release. Separately, the Pacific nation signed a deal in 2023 to acquire 120 AMRAAMs for its own stockpile.

Mavic vs Slavic: Ukrainian developers adapt reconnaissance drones to the modern battlefield. “The drone was developed as a Ukrainian alternative to Chinese commercial quadcopters,” Vyriy Industries said.
A Ukrainian firm now rents out drone jammers by the day—but the deposit is the device’s full price. The daily fee comes off a deposit worth the whole device—rent long enough and the jammer becomes yours.
Ukraine just caught a Geran-5 at 425 km/h—the jet drone that has often outrun Ukrainian interceptor drones since January. Ukrainian crews now stop just over half of Russia's jet-powered drones, against more than 90% of the older Shaheds, even as Moscow builds them by the thousand.
Russia is stepping up fake Ukrainian government pages as bait for recruiting agents, Ukraine’s security service says. Russian intelligence uses the counterfeits to spread disinformation and to harvest data on the Ukrainians who subscribe.
Russia is launching a faster Geran-5 at Ukraine that satellite jamming may no longer knock off course, a monitoring channel says. The drone can steer by images of the terrain below, and its extra speed makes it harder for interceptors to catch, though Ukrainian officials have not confirmed the system.
International
Russia ordered arson attack on Estonian military robot-maker supplying Ukraine, Estonia confirms. Estonia says its intelligence service established that Russia’s special services ordered the August fire at Milrem Robotics, as Russian sabotage operations spreads across Europe.
Belgium rushes three F-16s to Ukraine as Russia expands its drone and missile assault. Zelenskyy says the aircraft will arrive by the end of 2026, strengthening Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian air targets and conduct combat missions.
Russian jet-powered drone hits near Yahodyn, just 1.5 km from Poland, as Warsaw changes air defense rules. Poland plans to allow decisions to engage aerial targets based on radar data.
Lithuania gets its US tank battalion back while the Pentagon weighs pulling up to 40,000 troops from Europe. The Lithuanian leader calls the decision an encouragement and says fewer American soldiers will remain on the continent overall.
Humanitarian and social impact
Russian troops enter homes and threaten starving Oleshky residents for food and alcohol, officials say. Residents who escaped the occupied Kherson Oblast city describe threats and abuse by Russian troops amid severe shortages of food, water, and medicine.
Russian mercenaries blew off African prisoners’ legs to practice battlefield medicine, Wagner fighter says. A Russian mercenary captured by Ukraine describes alleged Wagner training sessions where prisoners were deliberately maimed and killed so recruits could practice battlefield medicine and killing techniques.
Russia hits a Kharkiv high-rise overnight, injuring 43 people, then kills four in daylight strikes on central Kyiv and Dnipro. A pre-dawn strike on Ukraine's second city gave way to drone attacks on a business center and then a national science institution during working hours.
Political and legal developments
Russia raises its war budget by 27% and expands the army again – both to new records – even as its budget deficit widens and oil revenues fall. Moscow plans to spend a record 17.1 trillion rubles on defense in 2027 as it raises taxes and borrowing to cover a widening deficit.
The Kremlin calls mobilization talk “nonsense”—Zelenskyy says it has already begun, with North Korean reinforcements. The claim comes from Ukraine's military intelligence, which has tracked Russian preparations for a larger call-up for months.
War is costing Ukraine $155 billion per year. With Western aid running late, Kyiv is freezing everything but army, pensions, and public wages. Kyiv froze parks, fountains, and road repairs to pay its army and pensioners first.
After Russia hits Kyiv’s Academy of Sciences with jet-powered drone, the Kremlin says Ukraine must “pay a price”. Peskov calls Russia's intensified strikes part of that price.

‘as a spectator, you also have a responsibility’: fabio cherstich on the boundaries of art and theater
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:47:42 UTC
06:47:42 KST

‘as a spectator, you also have a responsibility’: fabio cherstich on the boundaries of art and theater
the italian director's unique approach to performance has taken him to new york archives, miu miu performances in shanghai, and even the countryside home of the late painter, lucia di luciano.
Cherstich, a theater director among other things
Fabio Cherstich is a theater director. Not the theaters of days of yore, but the type of theater where a face may flash onto a screen that backgrounds the stage, glowering down on its audience. The kinds of productions that slink into the piazzas of Rome, carrying actors, pomp, and circumstance by means of long-haul semi-trucks. Or a spectacle that forms around vintage cars racing from Venice, Italy, through the Dolomites, for Louis Vuitton’s Classic Run. Chatting with designboom in his home-studio in Milan, Cherstich speaks about art on and off the stage, his collection of Alessi moka pots, and how difficult it has been for him to condense all this into a website.
on the woes of making a website
As the list of his projects, which seem to leap and saunter between the worlds of painting, film, and the performing arts, grows, the container that is ‘theater director’ starts to bulge at the seams. Perhaps it’s best remarked on by the man himself on his website, a work in progress, blank page with just a sans serif font that starts with ‘a note instead of a website.’ At the end of the list of all the things he has done – opera, theater, contemporary art, film, books – he adds, ‘and other territories that are not always easy to name.’
In his kitchen on a Sunday morning, in an apartment that looks out onto a historic Milanese palazzo fitted with a church’s bell tower that chimes on the hour, he expands more on his difficulty in creating this website, a journey that extends well beyond HTML and CSS. ‘But the problem for me is how I define myself,’ he says of trying to form his experience into a zippy portfolio. ‘This was a very important topic with my psychotherapist for two years. I have to say, ‘I am a director,’ but it’s not true. I work as a director, but this is the definition of my job, it’s not the definition of myself.’
design, a coffee maker, and aldo rossi
He pontificates on this while making coffee in La cupola, a moka pot designed by Aldo Rossi for Alessi. ‘Since I was very young, I liked stories. I always ask myself, how could I tell an audience this story? Maybe the most important thing that I learned from theater is always speaking about an audience. Storytelling, for me, has been crucial.’
Behind a conical silver pot for olive oil bordering his stove, two more coffee makers by Rossi perch nearby. He mentions La cupola was a gift from a friend. It soon becomes clear that most of the things in his home studio are materializations of his life, his friendships, or his career. And often, the boundaries between even these three are understood to be quite porous. ‘You see? Design! Alessi is always with us,’ he says as he puts a second pot on the stove. For the first one, he had forgotten to add water, but was delightfully unbothered by the mistake. In his kitchen, there is a large work next to the window made by friends who had staged a performance in that very home.
things you can Learn from design, art, and beyond
As the conversation moves into his living room, a lamp made by Formafantasma frames a monumental, pink, upside-down triangle, a work by Jade Guanaro Kuriki-Olivo, also known as Puppies Puppies. ‘I learned something about theater through the point of view of Simone Farresin from Formafantasma, who comes from the world of design. This is why I love doing collaborations, especially with people who didn’t study theater.’ Cherstich had worked with the Milan-based design studio back in 2024 on Staging Modernity, a scenography in Teatro Lirico Giorgio Gaber on the occasion of Cassina’s 60th anniversary of industrially production of pieces by Le Corbusier, Charlotte Perriand, and Pierre Jeanneret. In that 2025 show during Milan Design Week, visitors could walk among the seats, amble onto the stage, and peer over the mezzanine – the scene blurred the line between spectator and the show itself.
This fluidity, between viewer, performer, and stage, is a hallmark of Cherstich’s work. In 2016, Operacamion, which was conceived for Teatro dell’opera di Roma, brought operas into the streets of the city, performed in an open container on a truck bed. ‘I am particularly proud that it has become a Harvard case study in culture and has even been cited recently by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani as an example of how opera can reach new audiences and move beyond traditional theatre spaces,’ he says of the work that is still continuing today, nearly 10 years later, although under different direction.
‘as a spectator, you also have a responsibility’
Although theater is something of an ancient craft, Cherstich touches on how it may be even more imperative today to practice it. ‘I do think that today working in the fields of theater and performance is quite necessary because things are happening live between real bodies. Everything is becoming more and more digital, flat, transformable,’ he says of the current media ecosystem. ‘So you need to assume responsibility, both if you are on stage and in the audience. On stage, you have a responsibility because what you are telling to people comes from a very vulnerable but also powerful place. But as a spectator, you also have a responsibility. You are in front of real bodies. You need to own your point of view. You need to invest time. And I do think that today, this dynamic is quite incredible because it’s the opposite of what is happening outside the theater.’
in 2019, Cherstich directed the opera Turandot with graphics created by the art collective, AES+F
his projects and their ever expanding boundaries
He takes these lessons beyond the stage. Currently, Cherstich is the curator of The Estate of Larry Stanton, in line with his interest in the queer scene of New York in the 80s and 90s, which he explores in his performance, A Visual Diary. He’s gone on to create art books and even films on the likes of artist Lucia di Luciano and Annina Nosei, Basquiat’s first gallerist, both of whom were close friends of his. Thinking back on Cherstich’s website woes, it’s perhaps not because the artist struggles to define himself, but more because he pointedly defies the confines of the medium, the temporality, and the contexts presented in each of the projects he pursues.
project info:
name: Fabio Cherstich | @fabio_cherstich
This interview is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, presented in partnership with SolidNature, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away. Discover more stories that turn onlookers into participants, alter perception and disrupt the everyday here.

Turkish sides Anadolu Efes and Fenerbahce Tarfin secured victories in the second week of the EuroLeague on Tuesday, with Anadolu Efes beating Real Madrid 94-84 and Fenerbahce cruising past Bayern Munich 100-76.
Anadolu Efes secured its first win of the season in the competition, while Real Madrid suffered its second defeat.
Real Madrid led 29-27 after a closely contested opening quarter in which both teams shot at a high percentage.
Anadolu Efes took control late in the second quarter, scoring several consecutive 3-pointers in the final 3 minutes and 40 seconds to build a double-digit lead. The hosts went into halftime ahead 53-41.

The Spanish side reduced the gap to four points at 82-78 with three minutes remaining after finding success from inside the paint.
Anadolu Efes, however, made no mistakes in the closing minutes and pulled away to seal the 94-84 victory.
Fenerbahce Tarfin meanwhile maintained its perfect start to the EuroLeague season with a 100-76 win over Bayern Munich at home.
The Istanbul club improved to 2-0, while Bayern Munich suffered its first defeat.
Fenerbahce took control early, leading 16-9 after the opening five minutes before extending its advantage to 18 points at 31-13 late in the first quarter.
Despite a basket by Oscar da Silva with two seconds remaining, Fenerbahce finished the opening period 31-15 ahead.
The hosts continued their effective play in the second quarter and went into halftime with a 50-31 lead.
Fenerbahce maintained its tempo after the break, staying effective at both ends of the court and extending its advantage to 27 points at 70-43.
The Turkish side entered the final quarter with a 75-51 lead and did not allow Bayern Munich to close the gap, securing a 100-76 victory.
Before the game, former Fenerbahce and Turkish national team goalkeeper Sukru Ersoy, who died Tuesday, was commemorated.

Six Flags Closes Its X2 Roller Coaster After Brain-Injury Lawsuits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:39:01 UTC
06:39:01 KST

The Six Flags theme park company announced on Tuesday that it would permanently close the X2 roller coaster at its Magic Mountain park in Valencia, Calif., following allegations of serious brain injuries linked to the ride.
The closure has renewed questions about how the intense forces generated by extreme roller coasters can affect the brain. Experts told TIME that abrupt acceleration, twisting, and changes in direction can stretch brain tissue and blood vessels, potentially increasing the risk of concussions and bleeding.
Three lawsuits filed in late September allege that riders suffered brain injuries after riding X2, and attorneys told CNN that more than 100 people have contacted them with similar allegations. The suits came in the wake of a CNN investigation published in August about the ride's long history of incidents, including at least two deaths.
"After almost 20 years, we have decided to permanently retire X2," wrote Magic Mountain president Brian Oerding in a blog post. "While X2 consistently passed a multitude of safety tests, we have decided to close the ride because we believe it’s the right thing to do. Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously."
X2 was a two-minute thrill ride that reached a top speed of 76 miles per hour and opened in 2002, according to a Six Flags webpage about X2, which is no longer online. In July 2026, two women—six days apart—were hospitalized after riding X2, CNN reported. Both suffered from a subdural hematoma, or bleeding on the brain.
The first woman, who was 40, had emergency surgery and was unconscious for two weeks. Upon awakening, she had to relearn how to walk and talk. She is “very lucky to be alive,” one of her surgeons told CNN in August. The second woman, 26, underwent similar surgery and is still in a coma, the news outlet reports. On July 12, Six Flags closed X2 indefinitely—a closure made permanent at the end of September.
Billed by Six Flags as a “fifth-dimension wing roller coaster,” X2 ran along 3,610 feet of track. Its seats did not sit directly on the track. Rather they were mounted on wings on either side of the track—essentially suspending riders in space—and rotated 360 degrees. “Your body will be flipping around the entire time,” the now-removed Six Flags website says. “Quite simply, you will be spun into another dimension.” (Earlier this month, in response to a request from TIME for more details about the ride, a spokesperson for Six Flags said only that “the ride remains closed at this time.”)
The troubled history of roller coasters
“You are supposed to have a good time,” says Brian Avery, a faculty member at the University of Florida who teaches legal and risk management in the attractions, sport, and entertainment industries. (He does not have ties to Six Flags.) “You are supposed to walk away with enjoyment and a great experience. You aren’t supposed to leave in an ambulance or potentially dead. This is a serious problem that the industry needs to contend with.”
X2 is not the only American roller coaster that has caused concern—and alleged injury. In 1895, developers opened what was named the Flip Flap Railway—a short, single stretch of wooden track notable for a tight, tear-shaped loop in the middle—at Captain Paul Boyton’s Sea Lion Park in New York. Given the narrowness of the loop, the ride has historically been said to have produced a crushing amount of G-forces—or the pressure a rider feels relative to Earth's gravity.
Designers of early roller coasters like this “didn't know from a ride’s dynamics perspective and the tolerances on a person's body,” says Avery, “and unfortunately, a lot of people were injured as a result.” By 1902, the ride had closed.
Wooden roller coasters don’t have anywhere near the flexibility of steel roller coasters. First introduced in 1959, and throughout the second half of the 20th century, a “roller coaster arms race” took off, Avery says, with designers building tracks “taller, faster, more extreme.”
X2 was part of this boom, going into operation in 2002 and undergoing an upgrade in 2008, during which the rotating seats were introduced. Brain-injury allegations linked to the roller coaster date back to at least 2009 when, according to the CNN investigation, a 62-year-old man alleged he suffered a brain bleed as a result of the ride, recovering after surgery. The next year, a 28-year-old woman died on X2 when a congenital vascular abnormality in her brain ruptured after the ride, medical experts suspected.
What roller coasters can do to the brain
The shearing, tearing, and torquing forces at work on extreme roller coasters affect the brain, experts say.
“Brain tissue has very low rigidity (similar to jello), so it is prone to shearing and twisting during head motion,” wrote Lyndia Wu, an associate professor in the department of mechanical engineering at the University of British Columbia who studies the mechanics of brain injuries, in an email to TIME. “The tissue shearing and twisting can be amplified when the head rapidly accelerates or decelerates, such as when it moves in one direction and then abruptly whips in another during a roller-coaster turn, or when it strikes a headrest or another object. Blood vessels can also be experiencing stretching and twisting, posing risks of rupture and bleeding.”
The high levels of acceleration the coasters generate are a complicating factor. The head, which moves and swivels throughout a ride, may take more of a pounding than, say, the relatively stationary torso. G-force calculations, Wu says, only apply to “whole body accelerations that can be measured [or] estimated at the seat level when the roller coaster is designed. The head can be experiencing different acceleration profiles during a ride, which bring about additional brain injury risk considerations.”
While these forces can be damaging when an adult is in the coaster seat, they can do even more harm when the rider is a child. “Roller coasters are inherently higher risk in children than adults,” says Dr. Michael McDowell, associate professor of neurosurgery at Penn State Hershey Medical Center and Penn State Children's Hospital, and a co-author of a 2025 paper in the American Journal of Emergency Medicine on roller coaster injuries in minors. “Children are simply physically smaller on average and the forces they are subjected to are higher relative to their body mass. [In addition], the head is disproportionately larger in a child than an adult. The head and neck are functionally a bowling ball on a toothpick. A high energy turn on a roller coaster can snap the head in a direction which stretches the neck beyond the normal limits.”
Dr. James Mooney, assistant clinical professor of neurosurgery at Virginia Commonwealth University and another author of the 2025 paper, adds that “concussions have been documented in children after roller coaster rides, including in our study.”
Even if it were possible to model and correct for all of these factors perfectly when a roller coaster is being designed, not every set of metrics applies to every rider equally. “It could be just how you sit in a seat, how you're striking your head on the back of the seat,” says Avery. “It could be the height that you are in relation to a piece of the seat.”
The question of how to make roller coasters safer
What this means for the safety of roller coasters is uncertain. Wu suggests that research being conducted on brain injury in sports such as football may offer some “transferrable considerations” that can help in making roller coaster rides safer. “More research needs to be done to investigate possible head accelerations during rides beyond the seat acceleration levels, and the effect of factors such as neck strength [and] control to stabilize the head during rides, as well as possible impact of the head with the headrest.”
At the very least, operators of other roller coasters around the world can—and should—see the X2 as a cautionary tale. Even before Six Flags shuttered the ride, Avery thinks the damage had already been done. “I would have a complete review before this thing is reopened to see if they can isolate the cause,” he said at the time. “If they can, and it can be corrected, fine, correct it and move forward. [But] usually, when you've gotten to a point where a ride has made this much noise…the ride could be tainted in the sense that the public perception of it is deemed, ‘Hey, this is not for me.’”

US supreme court allows Trump officials to resume deportations to third countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:38:19 UTC
06:38:19 KST

The Trump administration can resume quickly deporting immigrants to “third countries”, or countries other than those immigrants’ homeland, without giving them any opportunity to contest their removals, the supreme court ruled on Tuesday.
The six-justice conservative majority of the high court temporarily lifted a lower-court decision that required the administration to provide immigrants sufficient notice and the opportunity to claim fear of torture or persecution in the countries where they are being sent. The Trump administration had claimed this stipulation had prevented it from “efficiently removing aliens” from the US.
As is typical in emergency orders, the justices did not explain why it granted the administration’s request.
The three liberal justices of the court, Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson, dissented from the order.
Tuesday’s ruling will take effect while the supreme court considers the larger question in the case. Justices said they would hear oral arguments in December.
It is the second time the supreme court has sided with the Trump administration over “third-country” deportations.
Todd Blanche, the attorney general, called the administration’s policies “entirely lawful and a critical tool for immigration enforcement” in a social media post following the supreme court’s order.
“Unlike the lower court, SCOTUS waited to hear from both sides before making the decision,” Blanche wrote.
The supreme court’s intervention comes days after the administration filed an emergency request to the justices, hoping to continue deporting immigrants to third countries – including those that the US state department considers dangerous.
The Trump administration has entered into a series of agreements with other countries that have allowed it to deport more than 25,000 immigrants to at least 29 countries, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a project run by Refugees International and Human Rights First.
Countries that have received US deportees include the Central African Republic, which is grappling with unrest and terrorism due to political and militia instability, and South Sudan, where a humanitarian crisis has been unfolding because of political and economic collapse.
On Monday, two dozen UN human rights experts warned that the deportation of thousands of migrants from the US to third countries has set off a “cascade of human rights violations” that could have “deadly” consequences.
Many third-country deportees have faced dire conditions and violence after they ended up in countries without any legal status. Earlier this month, two men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US deportees, according to witnesses and human rights lawyers. Detainees said the men were facing retaliation for speaking to journalists and human rights experts about the poor conditions they faced.
“This cruel and inhumane policy is a black eye on Lady Liberty,” said Adelita Grijalva, a Democratic representative from Arizona. “We are a nation that promises to welcome the ‘poor’ and ‘huddled masses’ yearning for freedom. Instead, we are sending vulnerable people into harm’s way – and, in some cases, potentially to their deaths.”
One of the men who was beaten in Equatorial Guinea was her constituent, Ahmed Soliman – a gay man from Egypt who had fled discrimination in his home country and spent most of his life in Phoenix.
Lawyers for the immigrants have challenged the “third country” deportation policy, arguing that they had not been given “notice and a meaningful opportunity to present fear-based claims”.
Lawyers for the administration have said there’s no need for individual fear-based claims because countries willing to accept immigrants have already agreed not to persecute or torture anyone. Solicitor general D John Sauer, the government’s attorney, wrote to the supreme court that the lower-court orders “created substantial logistical problems with ongoing removal operations – including the cancellation of flights – and led to added expense, potential diplomatic issues, and the inability to remove dangerous criminals”.
Prior to the supreme court’s order on Tuesday, two lower courts had separately sided with the immigrants.

Ceuta mass migrant crossing handling 'responsibility of all EU,' Spanish king says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:37:52 UTC
06:37:52 KST

Ceuta mass migrant crossing handling 'responsibility of all EU,' Spanish king says
MADRID, Sept 29 - European countries should have shown more solidarity and offered more support to Spain after the mass arrival in Ceuta of tens of thousands of migrants, Spanish King Felipe VI said on Tuesday during a gala dinner to mark a visit by French President Emmanuel Macron.
In an unusually outspoken address reflecting the depth of the crisis facing Spain following the Ceuta border rush that took place two months ago on Wednesday, the king said what happened in the enclave on the North African coast was "unacceptable" and generated an enormous security, public order and humanitarian challenge.
"It's a situation that ought to have as a consequence a reinforcement of collaboration between member states in resources and cooperation," he said. "The European countries that suffer the most pressure from being on the external borders of the European Union cannot alone bear a responsibility that also belongs to everyone."
The king spoke during a dinner at the Royal Palace in Madrid also attended by Spain's Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, a rare European proponent of the benefits of migration who launched a mass regularisation of irregular migrants that concluded in the summer. Sanchez, however, has proposed possible changes to asylum rules to return arrivals more quickly, which NGOs and lawyers say would violate human rights conventions.
Asked in a news conference about the plans, territorial policy minister Angel Victor Torres said the government was "analysing the possibility" of a legislative amendment but that it was "not easy" due to questions of international law.
Following the mass crossing of 72,000 migrants into Ceuta on July 30, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen commended Spain's swift action in returning most arrivals to Morocco. Other leaders were less understanding, however, with Italy suspending the European Union's border-free Schengen arrangements with Spain for one month.
European Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner unveiled a plan on Tuesday to strengthen EU border controls in the wake of Ceuta.
The plan, which requires the approval of member states, would strengthen the mandate of Frontex, the EU border protection agency, and give it a standing corps ready for immediate deployment. REUTERS

America’s foreign policy of coercion must end
Trump’s routine use of threats and ultimatums in place of diplomacy may yield immediate gains, but it inflicts lasting damage to America’s global standing
3-MIN READ3-MIN
3
 Listen
Zhou Xiaoming is a senior fellow at the Centre for China and Globalisation in Beijing and a former deputy representative of China’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office in Geneva. 
If you want to understand how Washington exercises power in the world, watch what it does when its closest allies try to deepen ties with each other.
When EU chief Ursula von der Leyen proposed making Canada the European Union’s first-ever “associate member”, US President Donald Trump’s response was swift and blunt: “If they do that, if I think it’s at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe, on many things.” He called the idea “laughable” and Canada – America’s neighbour and closest ally – a “terrible trade partner”.
In place of diplomacy, the US uses threats and ultimatums as an instrument of statecraft. Trump has threatened to seize Greenland by force, never mind that Denmark is a Nato ally. He has threatened tariffs on Brics nations if they try to create an alternative currency to the US dollar. More recently, the US State Department reportedly drafted a letter warning its partners against joining a China-led AI framework.
The examples are too many to list.
