Has Netanyahu's postponement of a state commission of inquiry into October 7 backfired? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:48:21 UTC
02:48:21 KST

For Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, postponing a state commission of inquiry into October 7 may have looked like the sound political move.
Netanyahu’s stated argument in the aftermath of the massacre was that the time for a national inquiry would come after the war. That argument had a certain practical appeal. A country fighting on several fronts has urgent demands on its political and military leaders’ attention. An inquiry into the greatest security failure in Israel’s history would be long, difficult, and divisive.
It was also politically convenient. Why open the door to testimony, documents, and potentially damaging findings while trying to hold a coalition together through a war? Why allow an independent commission to establish a public record that might place at least part of the responsibility for October 7 at your doorstep? What politician with an eye on reelection would welcome that?
And, somewhat counterintuitively considering the anger in the country following the attack, Netanyahu appeared to have his eye not only on remaining in power but on running again. A commission of inquiry that produced damaging findings before an election could only hurt his chances.
Netanyahu, against considerable odds, has now made it to the end of his term. The election is less than a month away, and no state commission of inquiry has been established to examine the decisions that preceded the Hamas attack. If part of the calculation was to prevent its findings from shaping the next election, that part worked.
Or did it?
Postponing inquiry does not end questions
The difficulty with postponing an inquiry is that postponement does not put an end to the questions. It leaves them hanging, waiting for someone else to answer them. And that is what is happening now, in the final weeks of the campaign.
Reports that leaders in Egypt and the United Arab Emirates warned Netanyahu of danger from Gaza before October 7 have thrust the days and weeks before the attack back into the limelight. Netanyahu has denied receiving such warnings. The accounts remain contested, as do crucial questions about what, precisely, was said, how specific the warnings were, and whether any information reached Israel’s security agencies through other channels.
Meanwhile, a public confrontation has erupted between Netanyahu and former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar. Netanyahu has accused Bar of knowing of warning signs during the night before the attack and failing to inform him. Bar denies that accusation. He says he warned Netanyahu of danger before October 7 and has called for the release of documents that he says would establish what the prime minister knew. The two are making claims about different points in the period leading up to the attack, and each is challenging the other’s account.
What is taking place now is not a commission weighing all the evidence, examining the documents, and questioning witnesses. It is a political argument conducted through statements, selected documents, media reports, and threats of lawsuits. The public is left to judge sharply conflicting claims without access to anything near a full record.
And that is the potential boomerang in Netanyahu’s strategy. An independent inquiry before an election could have damaged him. Without it, the campaign is full of speculation about what did and did not transpire before the attack.
Every new disclosure opens another question that triggers a response. Instead of containing October 7 as an issue, the failure to establish what happened has allowed it to return repeatedly, each time with a new set of allegations. And this is now dominating the agenda.
The timing could hardly be worse for the prime minister. Netanyahu wants to shift the election from who failed to protect the country on October 7 to who fundamentally changed the Mideast since then and who can protect Israel now: who stood up to Iran, who prosecuted the wars against Hamas and Hezbollah, and who can navigate a hostile international environment. His argument rests on his experience, his resolve, and the threats still facing the country.
Netanyahu’s remark at Tel Nof Airbase on Tuesday – that Israel’s adversaries may attempt an attack before the election – has stirred controversy. The warning may well reflect a genuine threat. It also reinforced the argument he wants voters to consider: that the danger is not over, and that his experience makes him the leader best equipped to confront it.
The reports about the period before October 7 pull the discussion in the opposite direction. They ask what the country’s most experienced prime minister understood about the threat that materialized on his watch, and what exactly he did with the information available to him.
That question does not absolve the IDF, the Shin Bet, or anyone else of responsibility. Their failures were profound, and a serious inquiry would have to deal with them as well.
No one account is widely accepted
But the prime minister cannot make questions about his actions before October 7 go away by pointing to failures elsewhere. He has ultimate political responsibility for the security policy his government pursued. The issue now is not whether he personally knew the date and hour of Hamas’s attack. It is what warnings reached him, what they conveyed, what decisions followed, and whether the government’s view of Hamas made it less willing to recognize a growing danger.
There is an irony here. A state commission might have given Netanyahu a forum to challenge the claims against him. It could have demanded relevant documents, questioned witnesses, and established whether the accounts emerging now are accurate, exaggerated, or wrong. It might also have found much that supported his argument about failures in the security agencies.
Instead, no account is widely accepted across the political divide. Netanyahu didn’t want a state commission and advanced a different mechanism, one whose composition and mandate would be shaped by politicians. His supporters argue that a commission appointed through the usual process would itself lack public trust.
None of this means that the latest reports will change the election result. Many voters formed their views of Netanyahu long ago; others will judge him on the wars that followed October 7, the economy, military service, or the available coalition alternatives. And an earlier commission, had one been established, might have produced headlines still more difficult for him than those appearing now.
But if politics played a part in the decision to delay, the apparent advantage was clear: get to election day without the findings of a state commission hanging over him. Netanyahu has done that. What he could not do was ensure that the questions themselves would fade.
He now faces the election with the facts of what preceded October 7 still bitterly contested – and with those arguments playing out in public, weeks before the vote. Whether that proves more politically costly than the inquiry he resisted is something voters will decide on October 27.

WATCH: Strock says Israel will establish settlements across West Bank Areas A, B as sanctions mount

02:48:15 KST

National Missions Minister Orit Strock said that Israel will establish settlements "with God's help" across the West Bank, during a speech at the Israeli settlement of Karmei Tzur near Hebron on Tuesday.
"We are planning to build four towns," said Strock, noting that the state is restricting the construction of two of them due to their planned location in Area B.
Her comments come after the foreign ministers of 12 countries confirmed on September 8 their intention to impose national restrictions on trade in goods from Israeli settlements.
"With your help, towns will be built in Area B, and also in Area A, because both A and B are the Land of Israel," she said. "We won't forget about them."
Areas A, B, and C are administrative categories of the West Bank established under the 1993 Oslo Accords.
Strock, a member of the far-right Religious Zionist Party (RZP) led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, noted that the movement to fix "all of Oslo's problems" had begun, referring to the policies set by the accords regarding Israel's presence in the West Bank.
"We started, and we succeeded a lot, a lot, beyond the Holocaust," she emphasized. "But we didn't finish. We, with God's help, are going to build towns in every corner of the Land of Israel."
Ben-Gvir: 'No difference' between Areas A, B, C if appointed defense minister
Also on Tuesday, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir said that he would make no distinction between Areas A, B, and C if he is appointed as defense minister.
“Areas A and B will be treated exactly like Area C," said Ben-Gvir during a tour of farms and settlement sites in the West Bank. "There will be no difference.”
Mathilda Heller and Anna Barsky contributed to this report.

Ra’am, Joint List appeal election bans as petitions target Otzma Yehudit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:47:44 UTC
02:47:44 KST

Ra’am and the Joint List have appealed their exclusion from the October 27 election, while separate High Court petitions filed Tuesday seek to overturn the Central Elections Committee (CEC) decision to allow Otzma Yehudit to run.
Together with the mandatory Supreme Court review of the committee’s decisions to disqualify MK Ofer Cassif and Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh, the filings placed the major election-disqualification disputes before the High Court.
The cases have reached the court through several legally distinct routes. Ra’am and the Joint List are appealing decisions against entire lists. The decisions against Cassif and Abu Shehadeh were transferred automatically because a committee vote barring an individual candidate cannot take effect without Supreme Court approval.
The Democrats and the Zulat Institute, meanwhile, filed High Court petitions challenging Otzma Yehudit’s approval. The Democrats are also contesting the rejection of their attempt to disqualify National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and MK Tali Gottlieb.
Tuesday was the statutory deadline for election appeals. The Supreme Court must deliver its rulings in the ordinary election proceedings by Sunday. The Otzma petitioners are seeking intervention within the same compressed timetable, although their cases were filed as High Court petitions rather than statutory appeals.
Democrats, Zulat pushed for court intervention following disqualification vote
The Democrats and Zulat asked the High Court to intervene after the committee voted 19-10, with one abstention, against disqualifying Otzma Yehudit.
Both petitions face an immediate procedural obstacle. Under the law, only the attorney-general, the committee chairman, or at least one-quarter of the committee’s members may appeal the approval of a list. Neither petitioner secured the required support.
Zulat argues that the High Court should nevertheless exercise its broader constitutional authority to review the committee’s decision.
The Democrats’ petition challenges two separate decisions. It asks the court to require the committee to explain why Otzma Yehudit should not be barred or, alternatively, why Ben-Gvir and Gottlieb should not be individually disqualified.
Sohlberg did not consider the allegations against Ben-Gvir and Gottlieb, ruling that the request could not proceed because it had not obtained the signatures of one-third of the committee’s members as required for an application to disqualify an individual candidate.
The petition acknowledges that The Democrats lack both the signatures required to initiate the individual cases and the one-quarter support required to appeal the approval of a list. It argues that the High Court should make an exception because the case against the list was heard by the committee, the party is represented on the committee, and the allegations rely partly on court decisions and formal positions issued by the attorney-general.
The petition’s central argument is that senior Otzma candidates have used government authority and parliamentary immunity in ways that undermine the rule of law, civil rights, and the separation of powers.
Regarding Ben-Gvir, it cites court decisions and attorney-general opinions concerning alleged political interference in police operations, investigations, and appointments.
Regarding Gottlieb, it cites her assertion in civil proceedings that court orders did not apply to her because of parliamentary immunity; her call for demonstrators to go to the Beit Lid military base on the day protesters breached its outer barrier; and her refusal to report for questioning over the publication of a Shin Bet (Israel Security Service) employee’s identity. Gottlieb was subsequently indicted over that publication. The charge has not been decided.
The petition’s racism argument cites support by several Otzma candidates for Amiram Ben-Uliel, who was convicted of murdering three members of the Dawabshe family, and alleged identification with the outlawed Kach movement.
It also relies on Otzma’s “Disengagement Plan 710,” which calls for a government ministry to facilitate what the party describes as voluntary migration from Gaza. The petition argues that its numerical targets make it a plan to remove a population defined by nationality and residence.
Otzma Yehudit disqualification opposed by Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara
Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara opposed disqualifying Otzma before the committee. She described the evidence as deeply troubling and said it brought the list dangerously close to the prohibited territory, but she concluded that it did not amount to the “critical mass” required for disqualification.
Ben-Gvir and Gottlieb have rejected the applications as politically motivated.
Ra’am’s appeal argues that the three applications against it – filed by Otzma Yehudit, Likud, and the Choosing Life Forum – relied largely on allegations and evidence considered in previous unsuccessful disqualification proceedings.
The applications sought to link Ra’am with the southern branch of the Islamic Movement, Aid 48, and other associations accused of transferring assistance to entities connected to Hamas. Ra’am argues that these are indirect organizational links and that the applicants did not produce clear evidence that the list itself supports armed struggle.
It also argues that much of the material consisted of media reports and internet publications rather than evidence concerning the current list, its platform, or its candidates. Ra’am cited its participation in the Bennett-Lapid coalition and the addition of former police major-general Yoav Segalovich to its slate as evidence of its present political course.
Baharav-Miara opposed Ra’am’s disqualification, saying the evidence did not meet the Supreme Court’s stringent standard. Eighteen committee members nevertheless voted to bar the list, with one abstention.
The Joint List has also appealed after the committee voted 18-5, with one abstention, to disqualify it. The list has called the decision political persecution directed at Arab representation.
The committee voted 19-5, with two abstentions, to bar Cassif on the grounds that he rejects Israel as a Jewish and democratic state and supports armed struggle against it.
Cassif argues that the statements and political activity cited against him, including support for international proceedings and sanctions against Israel, cannot be equated with support for armed violence.
He also alleges a procedural defect, saying Likud improperly combined its request against him with its request against the Joint List. He argues that the committee’s decision to separate the hearings prevented him from answering claims directed at the list rather than at him personally. Baharav-Miara opposed his disqualification.
The court will also review Abu Shehadeh’s disqualification on Thursday. Baharav-Miara and State Attorney Amit Aisman urged the justices on Tuesday to approve it on the ground of support for armed struggle, focusing primarily on an article he wrote on October 8, 2023, while the Hamas attack was still unfolding.
Abu Shehadeh maintains that the article did not endorse the attack and was written before its full scale was known. The committee voted 30-4 to disqualify him, with Sohlberg also supporting the decision, bringing the result to 31-4.
The court will hold two hearings before the same nine-justice panel on Thursday, first reviewing Abu Shehadeh’s disqualification and then considering Cassif’s case, together with the Joint List’s appeal. Ra’am’s appeal was not included in the Thursday schedule previously announced.
All the cases arise under Section 7A of Basic Law: The Knesset, which permits a candidate or list to be barred for rejecting Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, inciting racism, or supporting armed struggle by an enemy state or terrorist organization.
Supreme Court precedent treats disqualification as an exceptional measure requiring clear, convincing, and unequivocal evidence of a dominant and sustained objective. The court has not yet decided whether that standard has been met in any of the current cases.

Israeli opposition forms joint teams in bid to oust Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:47:00 UTC
02:47:00 KST

Israeli opposition parties formed three joint working teams Tuesday to coordinate their campaign to remove Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from power in the Oct. 27 election and prepare a common platform for a new government.
The five-party opposition alliance notably excluded Arab parties from the joint initiative ahead of next month’s general election, seen as crucial for both Netanyahu’s government and the opposition.
On Saturday, opposition leaders Yair Lapid, Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Avigdor Lieberman, and Yair Golan agreed to form a "change bloc” to coordinate their election efforts.
Opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition bloc would secure the 61 seats needed to form a government in the 120-member Knesset.
The opposition could potentially form a government with Arab parties, but most Jewish party leaders reject such an alliance, while the government has also sought to exclude Arab parties.
In a statement Tuesday, the opposition said it had decided to "establish joint working teams to ensure victory in the election and form a stable Zionist government that works for the state.”
The term "Zionist government” is generally used for a coalition made up of parties that embrace Zionist ideology, whether from the right, center or left, and focus on what they regard as the national interests of the Jewish people, effectively excluding Arab parties from such governments.
"In 28 days, Israeli citizens will go to the polls to participate in the upcoming decisive election and determine the path Israel will take in the coming years,” the statement said.
Netanyahu has led the current government since late 2022. It has been described as the most right-wing government in Israel’s history.
Criticizing Netanyahu, the opposition said the election comes "after years of internal polarization, lies, failures and loss of trust.”
"It is our responsibility to form a Zionist government that works for the state, puts Israel back on the right track and unites the country,” it added.
The opposition said that following Saturday’s meeting of party leaders, "three joint working teams were formed to strengthen cooperation, coordinate preparations to win the election and lay the groundwork for forming a Zionist government that works for the state.”
The first team is tasked with increasing voter turnout, while the second will be responsible for drafting the guiding principles of the next government and an action plan for its first 100 days.
Among the issues it will address are "equality in sharing the burden” of military service and universal enlistment, establishing an official commission of inquiry, limiting the number of terms a prime minister may serve and advancing the adoption of a constitution for Israel.
Israel has no formal constitution despite its establishment in 1948. Instead, it relies on a series of Basic Laws amid longstanding disagreements over the state’s identity and whether it should be defined primarily as "the state of the Jewish people” or "a state of all its citizens.”
Israel rejects the establishment of a Palestinian state along the June 4, 1967 borders with East Jerusalem as its capital, as stipulated in relevant UN resolutions under the two-state solution.
"The third team will be responsible for media coordination and combating disinformation and smear campaigns,” the statement said.
The opposition party leaders have not agreed on who would head a future government if they are able to form one after the election.

NATO sets out plan to make allied forces quantum ready
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
18:45:40 BST
02:45:40 KST

NATO has published a public summary of a quantum technology roadmap intended to speed up the adoption of quantum computing, communication and sensing across the alliance and allied armed forces, and to guard against the disruption those technologies could cause in the hands of others, according to NATO.
Allies approved the roadmap on 30 July, with the summary released on Tuesday. It builds on the alliance’s Quantum Strategy of 2023 and concentrates on the three branches of the field, alongside how each interacts with other dual-use technologies including artificial intelligence, space and next generation communication networks.
Delivery runs through the Transatlantic Quantum Community and its industry network, working with industry and academia. That body met in Washington on 24 and 25 September, where according to NATO the discussion covered how advances in quantum computing could affect secure communications, critical infrastructure, intelligence, strategic stability and decision making in a crisis, along with what the convergence of artificial intelligence and quantum means for defence.
The same meeting looked at positioning, navigation and timing, and at sensing, in light of the Questor 26 experimentation campaign run earlier this month at La Spezia by the NATO Centre for Maritime Research and Experimentation together with the industry network.
A sufficiently capable quantum computer would break the public key cryptography that protects most military and civil communications, which is why encrypted traffic intercepted today is worth storing against the day it can be read, and why allied governments have been migrating towards post-quantum algorithms. Quantum sensing runs the other way, offering navigation that does not depend on satellite signals at all, which matters a great deal to forces operating where those signals are jammed or spoofed as a matter of routine, as they now are across the Baltic and the Black Sea.
The Transatlantic Quantum Community welcomed Belgium and Bulgaria at the Washington meeting, bringing it to 24 allies alongside six partner nations. The Netherlands took the chair in May for a year with Canada as vice-chair, and the body, established in 2024, is an informal and non-binding grouping of experts drawn from national governments, industry, academia, funding bodies and research institutions rather than a decision-making forum.
Britain has been working the same ground nationally for some years, and the Ministry of Defence and the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory have run quantum navigation trials at sea and in the air over recent years, and the National Quantum Strategy commits public funding across the decade with defence as one of the intended beneficiaries. The Royal Navy’s experimentation vessel XV Patrick Blackett has been used for trials of this kind.
The full roadmap summary is published on the NATO site alongside the announcement, and the alliance gives no figures for what the work will cost or timescales for when any of the capability is expected to reach the field.

25,000 crash victims treated under PM-RAHAT; hospitals reimbursed in 13,000 cases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:44:23 UTC
02:44:23 KST

PM-RAHAT provides care to 25,000 crash victims (PTI file photo)
NEW DELHI: In the past eight months, nearly 25,000 road crash victims have been treated under PM-RAHAT, govt’s cashless scheme, and in nearly 13,000 cases, hospitals have been reimbursed for cost of treatment, a top road transport ministry official said Tuesday.Speaking at a roundtable on “Rethinking Urban Speed” organised by Road Safety Network, additional secretary in road transport ministry Mahmood Ahmed said that the scheme has helped save lives. The scheme under Motor Vehicles Act makes it mandatory for hospitals to treat road crash victims for free treatment up to Rs 1.5 lakh per victim, subject to a cap of seven days from the date of crash. Different studies suggest that 50% of lives can be saved by providing quick medical care to road crash victims.Mahmood highlighted the need to strengthen electronic enforcement of traffic rules considering that there is a tendency to break rules and deployment of manpower to detect this can never be sufficient. “Unless there is a certainty of punishment, the deterrence will never come,” he said. The official said the system would work only if violations were detected and followed through.Experts and govt officials at the workshop observed that India’s growing vehicle-safety capabilities cannot substitute for controlling speeds on urban roads, where pedestrians, two-wheeler riders and cyclists remain exposed to crash and their severity is directly linked to speedChairman of newly set up National Road Safety Board (NSRB), Nitin Gokarn, said the nature of Indian urban roads compounds the problem as different users, including pedestrians, two-wheelers, cars, trucks, and others use the same space.
It’s worse in congested areas where pedestrians have no option left than walking on the main road because pedestrian facilities are absent. What adds to their risk are wrong-side driving, inadequate medians and poorly lit road infrastructure.
Gokarn said at times when segregation of vulnerable road users is not possible, there are cars and bikes on roads that can reach speeds of 240 kmph and 100 kmph. This makes them vulnerable and more so when the speed is higher, he said.Experts, at the meet, shared examples such as Paris which has a maximum speed of 30 kmph or less on 89% of its urban road network; Brussels-Capital Region has 86%. They added that speed management in Indian cities needs to move beyond the setting of speed limits and focus on the interaction between road design, enforcement, local conditions and the behaviour of road users.
Prof Bhargab Maitra of IIT, Kharagpur said that speed management provides an immediate opportunity to improve road safety. “Speed management is doable, implementable and workable in the short term. It is not merely about reducing speed limits; it requires the right combination of engineering, enforcement and context-based speed regulation. Aligning road design, speed limits and operating speeds, while prioritising pedestrians, cyclists and two-wheeler users, can help make our urban roads safer and more inclusive,” he said.

U.S. consumer confidence drops sharply in September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
01:38:12 CST
02:38:12 KST

NEW YORK, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- U.S. consumer confidence index deteriorated sharply in September, driven down by surging energy costs and persistent price pressures, according to survey results issued by The Conference Board on Tuesday.
The Conference Board Consumer Confidence Index fell 6.7 points to 81.9 in September, down from 88.6 in August, marking the lowest level since April 2014. This also marks a notable acceleration in household pessimism after two consecutive months of softening sentiment.
Both components of the index declined. The Present Situation Index, which tracks consumers' assessments of current business and labor market conditions, retreated 7.9 points to 109.3.
The Expectations Index, which measures consumers' short-term outlook for income, business and labor market conditions, dropped by 5.9 points to 63.6, marking its third consecutive monthly decline.
"The Consumer Confidence Index deteriorated notably in September, following two prior months of softening," said Dana M. Peterson, chief economist at the board.
Peterson said consumers' views of current business conditions turned negative for the first time since September 2024, while perceptions of the labor market also worsened. Looking ahead, consumers expected both business conditions and the labor market to weaken over the next six months.
Consumers also expressed growing concern about prices. References to the high cost of goods and services, particularly oil and gas, rose to new highs in September amid a surge in fuel costs, according to The Conference Board.
U.S. diesel prices hit a record average of about 6.53 U.S. dollars a gallon on Sept. 22 and remained above 6.40 dollars on Tuesday, compared with about 3.68 dollars a year earlier, according to the American Automobile Association.
On Friday, the University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers found that its Consumer Sentiment Index fell to 48.1 in September from 51.7 in August, down 7 percent month-on-month and 15 percent from January. ■

BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China on Tuesday said a reported tool being pushed by some European Union (EU) member states is a typical example of protectionism and unilateralism that would disrupt China-EU trade as well as the stability of global industrial and supply chains.
A spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce made the remarks in response to a media inquiry regarding reports that some EU member states are preparing a joint document calling on the European Commission to accelerate the development of a so-called European "301" tool and take tougher measures against China.
The tool referenced in the reports would not resolve any issues and could even backfire, the spokesperson said, noting that the EU itself was once a victim of such measures.
As an important member of the World Trade Organization (WTO), the EU has long presented itself as a defender of multilateralism. If it fails to set an example and instead takes the lead in violating WTO rules, it would seriously undermine the rules-based multilateral trading system, the spokesperson said.
China and the EU are currently engaged in dialogue under their trade and investment consultation mechanism and exploring methods to address each other's concerns, according to the spokesperson.
If the EU engages in dialogue and consultation with China while at the same time stepping up pressure against China, it would seriously damage mutual trust, disrupt the overall consultation process and affect broader China-EU economic and trade cooperation, the spokesperson said.
China called on the EU to stay on the right track of managing differences through dialogue.
China will closely follow the EU's subsequent moves, the spokesperson said, adding that if the EU insists on introducing discriminatory restrictive measures targeting Chinese companies or products, China will respond firmly to safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese industries. ■

China Focus: China to implement mortgage interest subsidies to unlock housing demand
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
01:38:04 CST
02:38:04 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China will implement interest subsidies for housing loans starting Oct. 1, 2026, as part of efforts to help reduce home-buying costs and better unlock the housing demand of residents.
With a tentative implementation period of one year, the fiscal authorities will provide an annualized subsidy of 1 percentage point for eligible first-time homebuyers, according to a notice jointly issued by the Ministry of Finance, the People's Bank of China and the National Financial Regulatory Administration on Tuesday.
This is the first time the central government has offered interest subsidies on commercial housing loans.
This interest subsidy policy is focused on first-time homebuyers. The floor area of each purchased unit must not exceed 120 square meters, and the purchase price must not surpass 1.5 million yuan (about 222,516 U.S. dollars).
Under this policy, the maximum amount of interest-subsidized loans can reach 1 million yuan, and the subsidy period can extend up to five years.
According to estimates, for a long-term 1-million-yuan commercial personal mortgage, the subsidies could help borrowers reduce cumulative interest payments by nearly 50,000 yuan.
By defining housing price, floor area and loan category, the policy aims to precisely benefit target groups and help lower-income families reduce their monthly mortgage burdens, the departments said.
The policy focuses on first-time buyers with essential needs, supporting families in purchasing small and medium-sized, and relatively low-priced homes, according to the departments.
The policy is expected to reduce the mortgage burden for new urban residents, newly employed college graduates, and urban wage-earning families, said Luo Zhiheng, chief economist at Yuekai Securities.
In recent years, China has introduced supply-side measures to support the development of the real estate market, including supporting the issuance of new special-purpose bonds for land reserves and supporting local governments in purchasing existing commercial housing for use as affordable housing. This time, the focus has shifted to the demand side, further expanding policy efforts through fiscal-financial coordination.
Industry insiders believe that interest subsidies can reduce home-buying costs, accelerate the destocking of new homes, and ease the funding pressure on real estate developers.
The policy clearly demonstrates strong support for rigid home-buying demand, or first-home demand, and will in turn influence subsequent replacement and upgrading demand, said Yan Yuejin, deputy director at E-house China R&D Institute.
Li Yujia, chief researcher at the Guangdong Housing Policy Research Center, said the interest subsidy policy will reduce the cost of residents' mortgage loans and improve their willingness to take on leverage, thereby restoring the financial accelerator effect of the real estate sector.
Data released by the National Bureau of Statistics earlier this month showed narrower year-on-year declines in home prices across major Chinese cities in August, pointing to further signs of stabilization.
In August, Chinese authorities deepened reforms to the housing provident fund system, and refined regulations on commercial housing sales and property financing.
The package of policies is working in a coordinated manner from both the supply and demand sides, aiming to improve market expectations, restore residents' willingness to buy homes, and promote the steady and healthy development of the real estate market, experts said. ■

WFP warns of critical funding shortfalls as climate risks surge in Somalia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
01:38:01 CST
02:38:01 KST

MOGADISHU, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- The World Food Program (WFP) warned Tuesday of severe funding shortfalls that are drastically reducing its reach in Somalia amid a humanitarian crisis driven by drought and climate risks.
The WFP warned that current funding constraints will force it to assist fewer than 5 percent of Somalis facing emergency hunger starting in October, down from more than four million people per month during the 2022-2023 drought response, while funding for nutrition treatment will be completely depleted by the end of September.
"Malnutrition remains alarmingly high, with nearly 2 million children projected to suffer acute malnutrition in 2026, including 433,000 children facing severe acute malnutrition and requiring urgent treatment," it said in its latest report.
According to the WFP, Somalia is entering the October-December Deyr rainy season under a high-risk climate scenario.
El Nino conditions are expected to bring above-normal rainfall across parts of central and southern Somalia, with climate signals mirroring the severe flood events of 1997 and 2023, WFP said.
It said areas along the Juba and Shabelle river basins face the highest risk, raising grave concerns over widespread displacement, loss of livelihoods, and severe disruptions to humanitarian access.
Last week, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned that projected El Nino rains and severe flooding could affect up to 3.4 million people in Somalia across 16 regions between October and December.
OCHA warned that the combination of flooding, displacement, and inadequate sanitation risks triggering widespread waterborne disease outbreaks, occurring just as at least 380 health facilities have closed or scaled back operations due to critical funding shortages.
"The potential flooding might match or surpass the severe 2023 and 1997 seasons -- Somalia's two worst flood benchmarks -- and arrive before communities recover from the prolonged drought this year," OCHA said on Sept. 22.
According to the WFP, one-third of Somalia's population, or 5.4 million people, is acutely food insecure, with nearly 1.5 million facing emergency-level hunger between October and December. ■

ACCRA, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Thousands of residents in the Hohoe Municipality of Ghana's Volta Region, in the southeast of the country, have been displaced after River Dayi burst its banks, affecting more than 400 houses, local media reported on Monday.
According to Thomas Worlanyo Tsekpo, member of parliament (MP) for Hohoe, rainfall in parts of neighboring Togo is contributing to rising floodwaters in the municipality, despite a break in the rain in the area.
Several communities along the river have been hit by the flooding, with the Zongo community reported to be underwater, leaving residents displaced as floodwaters spread through homes and surrounding areas.
"The major cause is the torrential rains in Togo. It has been raining in Hohoe for months now, but not to this magnitude. It has rained continuously, so the load from Togo that joined the Hohoe rains led the river to overflow, causing what we are seeing," Tsekpo told local media.
Some of those affected are reported to have been temporarily accommodated in nearby classrooms while authorities work to find more suitable shelter.
"The flooding has displaced more than 3,000 residents, and over 700 affected people are now sheltering in classrooms," according to the MP.
He added that the situation remained unstable, as water levels continued to rise despite the end of heavy rainfall. He called for sustained emergency support as authorities work to provide shelter and protect residents in the affected communities. ■

UN Security Council extends mandate of Haiti Gang Suppression Force
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
01:37:48 CST
02:37:48 KST

Representatives vote on a draft resolution during a Security Council meeting at the UN headquarters in New York, Sept. 29, 2026. The Security Council on Tuesday adopted a resolution to extend the mandate of the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) in Haiti for six months. (Rick Bajornas/UN Photo/Handout via Xinhua)
UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- The Security Council on Tuesday adopted a resolution to extend the mandate of the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) in Haiti for six months.
Resolution 2829 was adopted with 12 votes in favor and three abstentions cast by China, Russia and Pakistan among the 15-member council.
The resolution decides to extend the mandate of the GSF until March 31, 2027, and requests the UN secretary-general to continue to provide logistical and operational support through the UN Support Office in Haiti.
The resolution notes the agreement between the Haitian government and the GSF, signed in July 2026, confirming the legal personality of the GSF, as well as other arrangements extending to the GSF and its personnel the status and protections necessary for the continued independent exercise of their functions.
It says the Security Council encourages UN member states to take measures, as appropriate, to acknowledge the legal status of the GSF and accord to the GSF and its personnel the privileges and immunities necessary for the continued independent exercise of their functions.
In September 2025, the Security Council adopted a resolution to transition the then Multinational Security Support mission in Haiti to the GSF, authorizing the GSF to adopt urgent temporary measures on an exceptional basis to assist the Haitian National Police in maintaining basic law and order and public safety, including through arrest and detention. ■

South Africa's formal sector sheds 123,000 jobs in H1 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
01:37:46 CST
02:37:46 KST

JOHANNESBURG, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- South Africa's formal sector lost 123,000 jobs in the first half of 2026 while real worker earnings continued to decline, official data showed Tuesday, underscoring persistent economic headwinds.
According to Statistics South Africa's (Stats SA) Quarterly Employment Statistics, formal non-agricultural employment decreased by 14,000 quarter on quarter to about 10.42 million in the second quarter (Q2), following an upwardly revised loss of 109,000 jobs in Q1. Year on year, the sector shrank by 95,000 positions.
Manufacturing recorded the steepest contraction in Q2, shedding 20,000 jobs, or 1.6 percent, with cuts spanning food and beverages, textiles, chemicals, metals, and transport equipment. Business services lost 13,000 jobs, trade dropped by 8,000, and transport contracted by 5,000.
Conversely, community services added 29,000 jobs, primarily driven by recruitment in local government, universities, and educational institutions. Mining, electricity, and construction each added 1,000 jobs.
The small net drop in Q2 masked a shift toward lower-quality employment. Full-time positions fell by 40,000 to 9.33 million, while part-time jobs rose by 26,000 to 1.095 million.
Average monthly earnings reached 30,611 rand (about 1,860 U.S. dollars) in May, up 4.1 percent year on year in nominal terms. However, adjusted for inflation, real average earnings fell by 0.4 percent.
Gross employee remuneration dropped 0.5 percent quarter on quarter to 1.025 trillion rand in Q2, driven by a 26.9 percent plunge in bonus payments, primarily in the financial and business service sectors.
The labor market weakness aligns with a broader economic downturn. Stats SA previously reported that South Africa's gross domestic product contracted by 0.2 percent in Q2, while the overall unemployment rate climbed to 33.6 percent, leaving 5 million youth out of work. ■

Africa's first World Academic Summit opens in Cape Town with focus on AI
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
01:37:46 CST
02:37:46 KST

CAPE TOWN, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- The World Academic Summit 2026 opened in Cape Town, South Africa, on Tuesday, focusing on the future of higher education in the age of artificial intelligence (AI).
Held in Africa for the first time, the summit is organized by Times Higher Education (THE) and jointly hosted by the University of Cape Town (UCT) and the University of Bristol.
It runs from Tuesday to Thursday, gathering 500 delegates and 100 speakers from universities, governments, research organizations, businesses and civil society organizations around the world.
Under the theme "Knowledge, justice and futures: Universities in the age of intelligence," discussions on the opening day centered on how universities can respond to the rapid development of AI and its growing use by students and academics.
UCT Vice-Chancellor Mosa Moshabela said that the university had moved away from using AI detection tools to penalize students and was instead focusing on helping them develop the skills to use AI appropriately.
"Initially, our academics were penalizing students for using AI in their assignments and so forth and we ended up using tools that would detect AI and then would penalize students for this," Moshabela said. "After we developed our own framework for AI, we decided that we are going to turn off those AI detection tools. And the idea is to allow students to use AI, not penalize them but rather focus on supporting them on how to use AI."
University of Bristol President and Vice-Chancellor Evelyn Welch said attitudes toward AI varied across cultural contexts, while universities also faced a need to establish shared standards.
"There is quite a different set of anxieties that we can see depending on the cultural contexts. But that doesn't mean that we don't all have to come up with some common standards," she said.
THE World University Rankings 2027 will be released on Wednesday, with the latest edition covering higher education institutions in 118 countries and territories. ■

EV charging costs less than half of diesel fuel costs in Europe: analysis
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
01:37:43 CST
02:37:43 KST

BRUSSELS, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Electric vehicle (EV) drivers in Europe pay, on average, less than half as much per kilometer to charge as diesel drivers pay to refuel, according to the Brussels-based environmental group Transport & Environment (T&E).
An analysis released Tuesday by T&E called on Europe to accelerate its transition to EVs and opposed across-the-board cuts in fuel duties. It recommended targeted support for low-income households, together with windfall taxes on energy firms to fund public transport and vehicle scrappage schemes.
"We are at a critical moment in the diesel crisis. Prices are already sky high for citizens and businesses and if the U.S. blocks exports of diesel, there is a real risk of a genuine shortage of supply," said Antony Froggatt, senior director at T&E.
"Electrification is the only way to ensure this is the last oil crisis. But we need short-term measures as well," he said.
The analysis showed that diesel drivers now pay 32 euros (36.4 U.S. dollars) more to fill a 50-liter tank than at the start of the year, with about 16 euros of the increase due to higher refinery margins.
Estimates by the European Central Bank (ECB) show that the margin rose from about 0.10 euro per liter in February to 0.41 euro per liter around Sept. 14.
The comparison covers refueling and recharging costs only. It is based on average consumption of 6.9 liters per 100 km for diesel vehicles and 20.2 kilowatt-hours per 100 km for battery electric vehicles, with electricity priced at 0.343 euro (0.39 U.S. dollar) per kilowatt-hour.
T&E said its charging-cost estimate, which takes into account the correlation between electricity and gas prices and the delayed pass-through to household electricity prices, is likely an upper bound.
An earlier T&E analysis showed that six of the eight major oil companies it studied, including BP and Shell, more than doubled their profits in the European Union (EU) in the second quarter of 2026 from a year earlier.
A T&E study published Monday found that battery-electric heavy trucks have a lower total cost of ownership than diesel ones in six of nine major EU markets. These six markets account for 46 percent of new heavy truck sales in the bloc.
EU Commissioner for Energy and Housing Dan Jorgensen wrote to member states asking them to consider implementing energy-saving measures in response to potentially high gas prices.
T&E said the European Commission should not focus on gas alone, arguing that oil and diesel are at the sharp end of the energy crisis. ■

China's zero-tariff scheme boosts South African commodity exports via Port of Ngqura: official
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
01:37:38 CST
02:37:38 KST

GQEBERHA, South Africa, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China's zero-tariff policy for qualifying South African exports has significantly driven demand for dry bulk commodities moving through South Africa's deep-water Port of Ngqura, including chrome, magnetite, iron ore, and corn, a port official said Tuesday.
Xola Mkontwana, business strategy manager at the Port of Ngqura, said the port has recorded "exponential growth" in commodity throughput destined for the Chinese market since the implementation of the trade policy.
"There was an exponential market in terms of demand from China," Mkontwana told journalists during a media tour of the adjacent Coega Special Economic Zone (SEZ) in South Africa's Eastern Cape Province.
He highlighted that the tariff preferences have significantly enhanced bulk operational volumes across the regional logistics hub. "The zero-tariff has assisted the throughput for bulk across the port system because there's chrome and magnetite, iron ore, and also corn," Mkontwana added.
The zero-tariff treatment for qualifying exports from South Africa and 19 other non-least developed African countries officially took effect on May 1, 2026. Running through April 30, 2028, the two-year non-reciprocal framework expands duty-free access for African goods to the Chinese market, provided exporters comply with rules of origin and standard customs regulations.
The initiative fulfills commitments made under the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation framework to promote balanced bilateral trade and support industrialization across the African continent.
Addressing the drivers behind the surge in Chinese orders, Mkontwana pointed to expanding industrial and infrastructure activity in China alongside favorable price realizations for South African mining and agricultural enterprises.
"It's the companies that they're actually developing on that side. It's the market that is there and the price that is good for the miners and owners," he noted.
Located approximately 20 km northeast of Gqeberha, the Port of Ngqura is South Africa's newest deep-water commercial port and serves as a critical maritime gateway connecting Eastern Cape minerals, agricultural produce, and automotive manufacturing to global shipping lines.
South Africa remains China's largest trading partner in Africa, with bilateral trade dominated by mineral products, raw materials, and agricultural goods. As South African producers seek to expand export destinations, China's preferential tariff framework provides key momentum for economic diversification, job creation, and increased logistics activity across South Africa's supply chains. ■

China Focus: China outlines sci-tech priorities for 2026-2030 to underpin high-quality development
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
01:37:31 CST
02:37:31 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China will strengthen basic research, tackle core technologies and speed up the industrial application of research results during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) to better support high-quality development, officials of the Ministry of Science and Technology said on Tuesday.
At a press conference held by the State Council Information Office, Minister of Science and Technology Yin Hejun said China's total R&D spending exceeded 3.92 trillion yuan (about 582 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, or 2.8 percent of GDP. This amount exceeded the average among the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) members for the first time.
China has ranked first in the world for many consecutive years in international patent applications under the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) and in papers published in high-level international journals, Yin said.
China ranks ninth among 60 countries in overall national innovation capability, according to the National Innovation Index Report 2025 released by the Chinese Academy of Science and Technology for Development.
Looking ahead, basic research will be organized in areas such as mathematical theory and applications, control of states of matter, synthetic biology, the materials genome, controlled nuclear fusion and intelligent scientist systems, Yin said.
He also called for faster application of artificial intelligence (AI) in scientific research to lead a shift in how research is carried out.
Paramount core technologies are another important priority, Yin said. China will push for progress along the entire innovation chain in key fields such as integrated circuits, machine tools and high-end instruments, and step up R&D in frontier technologies including AI, quantum technology, biotechnology and brain-computer interfaces.
Sci-tech innovation should also deliver more quality products and services that improve people's well-being, he said, with tasks laid out in areas including environmental pollution control, resource recycling, agricultural biological breeding, innovative drug development, high-end medical equipment and responses to population aging.
On turning research results into real-world productivity, Zhang Guangjun, vice minister of science and technology, said China will break the stereotype of producing results first and considering their application later on. Policies will instead direct research to where demand lies and ensure that results, once achieved, can be put to use, so that scientific and industrial innovation are planned in tandem and support one another, he said.
Zhang also called for stronger enterprise-led collaboration among industry, universities and research institutes, with innovation resources such as projects, platforms, data, talent and funding channeled to enterprises. Proof-of-concept and pilot-scale testing platforms will be built to help technologies mature and upgrade faster, he said.
Venture capital has played a vital role, with investors increasingly backing early-stage and small companies, taking a long-term view and focusing on hard technology, said Qiu Yong, vice minister of science and technology. New funds raised in the equity investment market exceeded 1 trillion yuan in the first half of 2026, up 49 percent year on year, he said, citing statistics from relevant institutions.
Universities are adjusting their disciplines to meet urgent national needs, he said.
China will continue to build Beijing and the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region, Shanghai and the wider Yangtze River Delta, and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area into international sci-tech innovation centers, Yin said. The three centers account for 58.8 percent of the country's R&D spending and 81.1 percent of its PCT international patent applications, and are helping drive innovation in surrounding provinces and municipalities and across the country.
R&D spending in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region has reached 4.48 percent of regional GDP, with major sci-tech achievements emerging in fields such as AI and biomanufacturing, Yin said.
The Yangtze River Delta accounts for nearly 30 percent of the country's basic research spending, with corporate spending on basic research up 38.3 percent year on year in 2025. It has witnessed key breakthroughs in areas such as integrated circuits and quantum technology, he said.
The Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area draws on Guangdong's industrial innovation strengths and the science and education resources of Hong Kong and Macao, Yin said. Guangdong, Hong Kong and Macao have jointly built 35 laboratories, and produced 14,000 papers under international collaboration. ■

Eiffel Tower chief to step down over removal of women staff for Hindu group visit
Decision to accommodate religious group’s request regarding female employees sparked walkout and closure of landmark
The operating company that runs the Eiffel Tower said on Tuesday its chief would step down at the end of this year in the wake of a controversy over the removal of women staff during a visit by a Hindu religious group.
Patrick Branco Ruivo, who has been director general of the Paris landmark since 2018, would leave his job at the end of the year after an internal probe revealed that “operational flaws and shortcomings” in organising the visit led to the “unacceptable” removal of women staff, the company SETE said in a statement.
The removal of women staff during a visit by the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement on September 5 prompted a staff walkout and the closure of the monument for a day, as well as an outcry across the political spectrum in France which prizes secularism and gender equality.
At the time, SETE acknowledged the Hindu delegation had requested the visit be organised so as to limit “interactions with women” and said that “these conditions should not have been accepted”.

IISc team uses blue light to switch on cell division; may aid cancer research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:31:58 UTC
02:31:58 KST

BENGALURU: Scientists from IISc’s Department of Microbiology and Cell Biology (MCB) have found a way to use blue light to switch on a key part of the machinery that helps cells divide, and have used it to restore cell division in cells from which a crucial structure had been removed.The finding could help scientists understand how cells divide and, eventually, identify new targets for drugs against diseases such as cancer. The study has been published in EMBO Reports. And their new technique may also help further cancer researchCell division is a tightly controlled process. Before a cell splits into two, its genetic material has to be copied and then pulled apart accurately. This is done by the mitotic spindle, a network of thread-like structures that attaches to the genetic material and separates it.The centrosome, a small structure inside the cell, helps organise this spindle. It’s made up of more than 200 components, but which are essential has remained unclear..The IISc team has developed a technique called Light-Induced Spindle Activation (LISA), which allows them to switch on Aurora A, an enzyme involved in building the spindle, by shining blue light on it.Aurora A normally becomes active at the centrosome, where it gathers into clusters.
Scientists had believed that a protein called Cep192 was needed to help activate it. LISA showed that Aurora A can instead be artificially clustered and activated using light, without Cep192.Researchers adapted an existing technique called LARIAT, which uses light to make proteins cluster together. They attached Aurora A to a light-sensitive plant protein called CRY2 and introduced it into human cells.When blue light was shone on the cells, CRY2 interacted with another protein, CIB1, causing Aurora A molecules to cluster. This, in turn, triggered the formation of microtubules, the tiny structures that make up much of the spindle.“This provides a novel way to trigger and activate an artificial Aurora A kinase complex – Aurora A fused to light-sensitive plant proteins, which is sufficient to induce microtubule nucleation,” Vignesh Olakkal, a PhD student in Sachin Kotak’s lab and first author of the study, said.Researchers then asked whether the technique could actually compensate for a missing centrosome. They chemically removed centrosomes from human cells, which normally causes problems during cell division. They then introduced the light-controlled Aurora A system.When blue light was applied during cell division, Aurora A clustered and triggered the formation of microtubules. The cells were able to rebuild their spindles, effectively rescuing the division defects caused by the loss of centrosomes.
The technique may also help in cancer research. Aurora A is overexpressed in many solid tumours and is already targeted by some drugs. But because the enzyme acts on several different proteins, it can be difficult to determine exactly which of its functions should be blocked.“In many solid tumours, Aurora A kinase is overexpressed, and that’s why there are drugs targeting it. But Aurora A kinase has multiple targets. Now, with our strategy, we can find out what the Aurora A kinase-specific targets are, independent of the centrosome, as far as microtubule nucleation is concerned. Then we will hopefully be able to find other targets of Aurora A kinase and design drugs,” Kotak said.
Chethan Kumar is a Senior Assistant Editor with the Times of India. Aside from specialising in Space & Science, he has reported extensively on varied topics, with special focus on defence, policy and data stories. He has covered multiple elections, too. As a young democracy grows out of adolescence, Chethan feels, there are reels of tales emerging which need to be captured. To do this, he alternates between the mundane goings-on of the Common Man and the wonder-filled worlds of scientists and scamsters, politicians and soldiers. In a career spanning nearly 18 years, he has reported from multiple datelines — Houston, Florida, Kochi, Hyderabad, Chennai, Sriharikota (AP), NH-1 (J&K Highway), New Delhi, Ahmedabad, Raichur, Bhatkal, Mysuru, Chamarajanagar, to name a few — but is based out of Bengaluru, India’s science capital that also hosts the ISRO HQ.

Ukraine runs first supply mission with amphibious robot
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
18:30:39 BST
02:30:39 KST

Ukrainian troops have carried out what is described as the first logistics mission using a domestically developed amphibious uncrewed ground vehicle, covering more than 40km over land and water to deliver rations and ammunition to positions, according to the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence.
The mission was flown, or rather driven and swum, by personnel from one of the separate mechanised brigades of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. The department said the vehicle retained the cross-country mobility of a conventional ground robot on land and could transition to water within seconds before continuing.
Water is the reason the capability exists in the first place, and according to the ministry, rivers, canals and marshy ground along the front complicate or entirely block routes for ordinary uncrewed ground vehicles, while resupply from the air is not always the better answer. Putting both modes on one platform removes the need to plan around obstacles or to hand a load between systems partway along a route.
The vehicle was refined over several months in cooperation with the units that would use it, drawing on real missions, operational experience and the particular characteristics of front-line terrain. Development was supported through grant funding from Brave1, the Ukrainian defence innovation cluster, which introduced a dedicated amphibious uncrewed ground vehicle track within its grant programme in June.
The ministry stated: “We are expanding the capabilities of robotic systems so that Ukrainian service members have more technological tools to carry out combat missions.”
Ground robots have moved quickly from novelty to routine in Ukrainian service. The department has previously reported that its forces more than tripled their use of uncrewed ground vehicles for logistics and casualty evacuation, work driven by the same pressure that has reshaped so much of the war, namely that the last few kilometres into a position are watched continuously by drones and that anything moving along them in daylight is liable to be struck.

British Commandos called in air strikes alongside Navy SEALs
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
18:26:13 BST
02:26:13 KST

Royal Marines from the UK Commando Force guided in attacks by American fast jets and seized a ship at sea during three weeks of maritime special operations training with United States Navy SEALs in Virginia, the Royal Navy stated.
The exercise, codenamed Resolute Strike, was intended to get the two forces operating together as one and to keep the British teams ready for NATO tasking. It ran through close-quarter combat scenarios by day and night, taking in vessel boarding and compound clearance, and finished with a validation exercise mounted from the San Antonio-class amphibious transport dock USS Arlington.
Major George Eatwell, Officer in Command of M Company, 42 Commando, said: “Resolute Strike was not only an exceptional Maritime Special Operations training opportunity, but it also proved vital integration with our US partners, testing interchangeability of tactics, equipment, and processes. Whenever, or wherever we may fight alongside the US in the future, we are now better aligned at the operator level having built those lasting foundational relationships.”
Twenty-seven commandos from M Company travelled to Virginia Beach alongside specialists from 148 Battery, who handle multi-domain fires and targeting, after a month of riverine and jungle raiding in southern Mississippi.
The 148 Battery party worked with SEAL teams at the Navy Dare Bombing Range in North Carolina, a remote facility of 72 square miles, which the Royal Navy compares to the size of Wigan, where American aircrew practise air to surface attack. There the British teams talked in strikes by F-18 Super Hornets against area denial systems including surface-to-air missiles, work that falls under the suppression of enemy air defences. Completing it leaves the battery fully certified to support operations at very high readiness.
M Company forms Special Operations Maritime Task Unit 9 and concentrated on maritime interdiction. According to the Royal Navy, task units of this kind are built to deploy worldwide from hubs ashore or from ships, working alone or folded into a partner force, and each can field one force protection team and two boarding teams, with scout snipers, uncrewed systems, dive teams, explosive ordnance disposal and electronic warfare added as required.
The training began with the two sides exchanging tactics before moving on to close-quarters battle objectives, with teams inserted by helicopter in darkness to take compounds, and more than twenty missions were run across various scenarios.
Attention then turned to the water, where an assault team conducted a vessel takedown at night covering explosive and mechanical methods of entry alongside close quarters marksmanship. In the final week the commandos embarked on USS Arlington for a last mission against an American target vessel, with two Black Hawk helicopters putting a combined British and American team onto the ship to seize it.
Both forces hold Arctic responsibilities for their respective countries, and the Royal Navy says the integration work moves to colder conditions this winter.
42 Commando is based at Bickleigh outside Plymouth and is the Royal Marines unit specialising in maritime operations, including boarding and interdiction work. 148 Battery, part of 29 Commando Regiment Royal Artillery, provides forward observation and joint fires support to the commando force and its members qualify as joint terminal attack controllers, which is what allows them to direct strikes by other nations’ aircraft.
The Commando Force has been the subject of considerable investment, with Wes Streeting restating from the Labour Party conference platform this week that half a billion pounds is going into the force and its drone equipment as it helps defend NATO’s High North.

Ethiopia blames regional rivals as risk of conflict spillover rises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:25:09 UTC
02:25:09 KST

Ethiopia blames regional rivals as risk of conflict spillover rises
Addis Ababa’s accusations against neighbours raise fears that its conflict could spill over into the region.
As renewed fighting spreads across northern Ethiopia, the government has accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of backing armed opposition groups, raising fears that the conflict could draw in regional powers.
Over the weekend, Ethiopian army chief Birhanu Jula attributed his country’s unrest to those he called Ethiopia’s “historical and contemporary adversaries”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Ethiopia’s army promises restraint amid fears of new civil war
- list 2 of 3Ethiopia accuses Sudan, Egypt of backing Tigray rebels as fighting rages
- list 3 of 3Fighting in Ethiopia intensifies: What’s the latest?
Birhanu accused Eritrea of being the go-between linking these external powers – including Sudan and Egypt, which he explicitly named – with armed groups inside Ethiopia.
Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt have all rejected the accusations. Speaking to Al Jazeera, Egyptian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Nader Zaki said that Egypt’s foreign policy was founded on “full respect for the sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity of states, and noninterference in the internal affairs of other countries”.
Zaki added that Egypt “is fully committed to the rules of international law and the Charter of the United Nations, and rejects any practices that would undermine regional security and stability”.
Major-General Samir Farag, the former head of the Egyptian Armed Forces’ Morale Affairs Department, also told Al Jazeera that the accusations against Egypt were false. “It has not been Egypt’s policy to interfere in the internal affairs of any state in the region,” he said.
Sudan’s military also dismissed the accusations as “baseless” and levelled its own charge of destabilising behaviour at Ethiopia, accusing it of supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been fighting the Sudanese Armed Forces since 2023. Ethiopia has denied those allegations.
Troubled relations
Ethiopia’s relations with the countries it has accused have already been strained by other disputes that predate the latest fighting.
Relations between Cairo and Addis Ababa have remained tense as a longstanding dispute over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) remains unresolved. Competition between the two has increasingly extended to regional security, the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa.
Sudan’s relations with Ethiopia are similarly troubled. Since the outbreak of the Sudanese civil war, Khartoum has accused Addis Ababa of providing training, supplies and the use of Ethiopian territory to the RSF.
Eritrea had fought alongside Ethiopia against rebel groups in the latter’s Tigray region during a war between 2020 and 2022, but relations between the two neighbours have since soured, with Eritrea alarmed by Ethiopia’s attempts to gain access to the Red Sea.
Against that background, some analysts and Ethiopian opposition figures say that Addis Ababa is pointing the finger at foreign conspiracies in a bid to rally support behind its national army.
Mohamed Selim, deputy chair of the Egyptian parliament’s African Affairs Committee, told Al Jazeera that he believes the accusations were an attempt to shift attention from Ethiopia’s domestic problems by creating an external enemy and seeking to unify the internal front.
Amani al-Tawil, director of the Africa Programme at the Al-Ahram Centre for Political and Strategic Studies, similarly described the accusations as “an understandable attempt to escape from internal crises”.
She questioned why Egypt would choose this moment to intervene militarily in Ethiopia, given the two have been in dispute over GERD since 2011.
Al-Tawil said the breadth of the new opposition alliance in Ethiopia – seven groups representing disparate ethnic groups and regions announced the coalition last week – presented a challenge to Addis Ababa.
Spillover concerns
The renewed fighting in Ethiopia has spread across Tigray and into neighbouring Amhara and Afar.
Mohammed Hussein, the chairman of the Prosperity Party Afar Region Branch Office – the ruling party in Ethiopia’s Afar region – told Al Jazeera that the three regions together have a population of more than 38 million, according to his estimate, and include areas near the borders with Djibouti and Eritrea, raising fears of a regional war.
Ammar Arki, a writer focusing on Horn of Africa affairs, told Al Jazeera that Ethiopia had, at various stages, blamed Sudan, Egypt and Eritrea for contributing to instability inside Ethiopia.
He said the latest accusations could be interpreted as an attempt to redirect some domestic attention towards an external threat and build support around the federal government.
But Arki warned that the longer Addis Ababa continued to explain its internal crisis in terms of an “external conspiracy”, particularly if neighbouring states responded in the same way, the greater the risk that Ethiopia’s conflict could move beyond Ethiopia’s borders and become regional.

Morocco's king appoints first woman prime minister following election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:22:38 UTC
02:22:38 KST

Morocco names Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri first woman PM
- Morocco appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as the first woman prime minister after her party won 97 seats in recent elections marked by low turnout.
- El Mansouri will form a coalition government and aims to address unemployment, living costs, and social disparities affecting youth.
- Her party pledges 5% annual growth, 2% inflation, and one million new jobs over five years, amid political challenges and opposition claims of fraud.
AI generated
RABAT - The king of Morocco on Sept 29 named Marrakesh mayor Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri the country’s first woman prime minister, the royal Cabinet announced, after her party won last week’s parliamentary elections.
Her centre-right Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) had dominated the vote, winning 97 out of 395 seats in the House of Representatives – 31 more than the next closest competitor, although the poll was marked by the lowest turnout in two decades.
The royal Cabinet said King Mohammed VI has now tasked the 50-year-old, who also served as housing minister, with “forming the new government”.
Speaking shortly after, El Mansouri said in a televised address her appointment was “truly historic”.
“For the first time in our country’s history, a woman is taking on the responsibility of leading the government,” she said. “This is a source of pride not only for me but for all Moroccan women.”
Without an outright majority, the PAM will have to form a coalition with other parties, though the monarch retains broad powers over major policies.
For the new premier, “the work starts today”, she said.
“We will first initiate internal consultations within our party before holding discussions with all political groups.”
El Mansouri joined the PAM in 2008, the year it was founded by current royal adviser Fouad Ali El Himma as a counterweight to the country’s Islamist movement.
She was also the first woman to serve as mayor of Marrakesh, winning the office in 2009 before losing it six years later, then retaking it again in 2021.
El Mansouri’s Cabinet will have to tackle several pressing issues including unemployment and living costs, as well as persistent social disparities particularly weighing on young people.
The parliamentary vote came just weeks after tens of thousands of mainly young Moroccan migrants rushed into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, a crisis that highlighted socio-economic frustrations among the youth.
It also came a year after a Gen-Z protest movement took to the streets to demand better health and education.
“We are fully aware that this period will be significant and marked by high expectations from Moroccans, particularly young people,” El Mansouri said. “That is why we will have a programme offering concrete and realistic solutions to citizens’ concerns.”
Her party has pledged average annual economic growth of five per cent, inflation of two per cent and the creation of at least one million new jobs over its five-year term.
The PAM was followed in the polls by the National Rally of Independents (RNI), which heads the outgoing coalition and won 66 seats.
The right-wing Istiqlal party came third with 65 seats, while the Islamist opposition’s Justice and Development Party (PJD) took 54 seats.
The PJD made significant gains after winning just 13 seats in 2021, having focused its campaign in part on fighting corruption.
Its chief, former prime minister Abdelilah Benkirane, hailed a “victory” but ruled out joining a coalition led by the PAM, which he said was “tainted by fraud”, without providing details. AFP

No explosive devices found in vehicles near Fairford just petrol
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
18:19:30 BST
02:19:30 KST

No improvised explosive devices were found in the three vehicles examined after five men were arrested close to RAF Fairford at the weekend, although a quantity of petrol was recovered, according to Counter Terrorism Policing.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing, gave the update on Tuesday evening. “Those vehicles have been subject to extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts, and we can confirm that no improvised explosive devices were found. However, a quantity of petrol was recovered,” he said.
He also set out what prompted the response in the first place. “A police response was activated in the early hours of Sunday morning due to a range of information received, including a call from a member of the public about several vehicles acting suspiciously close to RAF Fairford,” he said, thanking those who had contacted police with information and saying the events of recent days had reaffirmed the part the public plays.
The investigation has extended well beyond Gloucestershire in the days since. “As part of the investigation, we have searched properties in London which I can confirm have concluded,” Taylor said. The scenes around the airfield are being reduced and the assistant commissioner said he anticipated closing them down completely by Wednesday, which he described as an important step towards restoring normality for the local community.
The five men were released on police bail on Monday, a development Taylor acknowledged had not been universally expected. “They remain under investigation and must adhere to strict conditions while we continue our work. The safety of the public is at the forefront of our investigative decision making, and this was certainly the case yesterday,” he said. “I understand why this development will have come as a surprise to many, but I’d like to reiterate that it was investigative decision, and one which is grounded in experience and careful consideration of policing powers.”
Counter Terrorism Policing has released only limited details of those arrested, all five of whom are British nationals resident in London, one aged 25 and the others aged between 23 and 24, with four living in the borough of Westminster and one in Camden, and none of them has been named.
The men were arrested on Sunday morning on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act and later of preparation of a terrorist act under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act, after Gloucestershire Constabulary declared a major incident and evacuated properties in the village of Whelford next to the airfield. Taylor said on Monday that investigators were keeping an open mind on whether the current international situation had any bearing on the case, and that they were considering the possibility of activity by proxies or by individuals knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state, as we reported.
He thanked the community near the airfield, Gloucestershire Police, and what he called many partners in Britain and the United States supporting the investigation.
Fairford is a United States Air Force forward operating location whose long runway has made it the standing European base for American strategic bombers, and B-1B Lancers have been operating from the airfield. The base moved to its highest force protection condition before the arrests were made.
The investigation continues, and anyone with information has been asked to contact the police.
