China’s AI strategy ‘paradox’ really isn’t one
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:14:51 UTC
02:14:51 KST

China’s AI strategy ‘paradox’ really isn’t one
Artificial intelligence is becoming a defining force in economic development, international competition, and national security. While striving to develop more powerful AI systems, China also seeks to determine how they should be governed, shared, and secured in a rapidly changing world.
A technology shaping China – and the world
By June 2026, the number of users of AI products in China had exceeded 500 million, underscoring the technology’s growing reach in one of the world’s largest digital economies. Together with the US, China is a key engine of AI development and innovation. Its domestic choices and international initiatives have consequences well beyond its borders.
At the BRICS summit in New Delhi, Chinese President Xi Jinping advanced proposals for more inclusive AI cooperation, industrial development, and technological exchange. At the same time, State Security Minister Chen Yixin set out a national security perspective that places AI at the center of strategic competition and calls for stronger safeguards.
China’s AI policy combines the pursuit of international openness with domestic security governance. Understanding how Beijing seeks to reconcile these objectives is essential to understanding its ambitions for AI – and the emerging global order around it.
Xi’s BRICS vision: AI as a shared opportunity
Xi’s proposals at the New Delhi summit place AI cooperation within a broader effort to connect technological development with economic growth and international inclusion. The emphasis is on widening access to the capabilities, skills, and industrial networks that make AI economically useful.
China has proposed taking a pioneering role in establishing a BRICS AI open-source community, supporting cooperation on the development and application of large language models, and organizing specialized seminars and training courses. The stated objective is to build an open ecosystem in which countries can exchange knowledge and expand their capacity to develop and use AI.
This approach is particularly relevant for emerging economies. Access to AI requires not only the availability of software, but also computing infrastructure, technical expertise, investment, and the ability to adapt technologies to local needs. Open-source collaboration and skills development can help accessibility, although they cannot by themselves eliminate disparities in resources or technological capabilities.
Xi’s digital industry cooperation initiative extends the same idea into the infrastructure and skills underpinning the digital economy. China has proposed a BRICS digital ecosystem cloud platform, alongside digital skills training, technological exchange, and industrial alignment.
A third proposal focuses on AI-enabled new industrialization. Here, the objective is to deepen cooperation in research and development, practical applications, and industrial and supply chains.
Taken together, these initiatives present AI as a means of expanding productive capacity. For BRICS members, the proposals raise practical questions about how to share expertise, develop compatible infrastructure, and translate technological cooperation into tangible industrial outcomes.
Chen Yixin’s warning
Xi’s international cooperation agenda coincides with a more security-focused assessment from Chen Yixin, China’s minister of state security. In an article published during the summit, Chen described AI as a central arena of global scientific and technological competition and a new front in strategic rivalry among major powers.
Chen’s argument begins with a dual imperative: innovation must be the primary driving force, while security must remain a bottom-line requirement. In this framing, AI is simultaneously an engine of economic and social transformation and a technology capable of changing the conditions of national security.
His assessment identifies several interconnected risks. AI-generated content, including deepfakes and automated online activity, could affect political security by enabling the rapid production and dissemination of misleading information. Chen also warns that AI may transform cyber operations, making it easier to identify vulnerabilities, develop malicious software, and automate elements of complex attacks.
Another concern is the potential for AI-assisted data collection and analysis to amplify espionage and information-security risks. Chen points to the possibility of sensitive government data, commercial secrets, and personal information being gathered or exposed through intelligent crawling, data mining, and profiling.
He also identifies structural challenges: concentration of technological capabilities could deepen inequalities between countries, while AI-driven decision-making could strain existing systems of social governance. In the military sphere, he argues that AI is helping move warfare toward an increasingly intelligent era, with implications for sensing, decision-making, and targeting.
These concerns are not confined to China. Cybersecurity, data protection, misinformation, military applications, and the concentration of technological power are subjects of international debate. What distinguishes Chen’s article is the way it brings them together under a comprehensive national security framework.
From principles to institutions
Chen calls for AI security to be integrated into other key areas of national security, supported by stronger cross-sector cooperation and improved capacity to identify and anticipate emerging risks. He also calls for an AI safety supervision platform, expanded risk assessment and monitoring, and greater investment in fundamental research and core technologies, including computing chips, development frameworks, and application software. His article advocates strengthening AI infrastructure while reducing vulnerabilities associated with dependence on critical technologies.
Chen advocates the implementation of China’s Cybersecurity Law and Counter-Espionage Law, alongside further development of rules addressing AI research, applications, data protection, algorithmic security, and accountability. He also emphasizes public communication and national security awareness.
These measures reflect Beijing’s view that AI governance cannot be separated from overarching questions of technological self-reliance, data control, and national security, and that when it comes to AI, innovation has to be inseparable from oversight.
A global governance agenda
China’s domestic security priorities sit alongside an international agenda that predates the New Delhi summit. Its 2023 Global AI Governance Initiative calls for people-centered development, international cooperation, respect for national sovereignty, and broader access to AI technologies. It also advocates risk-based governance, privacy and data protection, human oversight, and greater representation for developing countries.
The initiative supports discussions within the United Nations framework on establishing an international institution for AI governance. Chen’s article echoes several of these themes, describing AI as an international public good and calling for cooperation that helps Global South countries strengthen their technological capabilities and bridge the global intelligence gap.
China recently released its AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0, following earlier versions issued in 2024 and 2025. The updated framework revises risk classifications and adjusts technical and governance measures in response to emerging challenges.
Making openness and security compatible
China’s international and domestic AI agendas may seem to be contradictory, but a country can support international technology exchange while seeking to protect sensitive data, strengthen infrastructure, and manage risks. The challenge is determining where legitimate safeguards end and restrictions on cooperation begin.
For China, the task is to demonstrate that its security framework can support innovation and international engagement without unnecessarily constraining them. For its partners, the task is to assess how cooperation will work in practice: what technologies will be accessible, how data will be protected, and how shared initiatives will be governed.
BRICS member countries have different development priorities, regulatory systems, and strategic interests. A common AI ecosystem will require practical arrangements that accommodate those differences while delivering measurable benefits.
A defining question for the AI era
Xi Jinping’s BRICS proposals and Chen Yixin’s national security assessment capture two dimensions of China’s AI strategy: expanding the technology’s reach internationally while strengthening its governance at home.
AI cooperation could widen access to technological capabilities and support industrial development. Security governance could help address genuine risks involving cyber operations, sensitive data, and increasingly autonomous systems. Yet both agendas also raise questions about implementation, institutional accountability, and the balance between openness and control.
China’s approach will be judged by the practical outcomes it delivers: whether cooperation is genuinely inclusive, whether safeguards are effective and proportionate, and whether international partners can participate on mutually understood terms.
The underlying proposition is that artificial intelligence need not be treated as a domain of zero-sum competition. When innovation is prioritized and security requirements are treated as non-negotiable, the technology can be steered toward benefit for all.

He was arrested in a dramatic police raid amid escalating concern over ShinyHunters, a hacking group known for large-scale data breaches and extortion, and its recent theft of what it said was terabytes of sensitive personnel data from US FBI servers.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:11:10 UTC
02:11:10 KST

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Tuesday unveiled what he described as the first municipal strategy of its kind in the United States to combat antisemitism, announcing investments in hate-crime prevention, security coordination and Jewish cultural institutions.
The announcement comes nearly nine months after Mamdani took office and revoked several executive orders issued by his predecessor, Eric Adams, including measures concerning antisemitism and boycotts of Israel.
"Over the last year, I've met with Jewish New Yorkers across the five boroughs," Mamdani said. "Time and again, I've heard the same thing: antisemitism is real, and it is growing."
According to figures cited by the mayor, Jewish residents account for approximately 12% of the city's population, while antisemitic incidents represent more than half of its confirmed hate crimes. Police recorded 229 antisemitic incidents between January and August, an 8% increase over the corresponding period last year.
Mamdani increases NYC hate crime prevention budget by $26 million
Mamdani said his administration had increased hate crime prevention funding by $26 million, or more than 800%, compared with last year. The strategy includes $6.4 million for community organizations working to prevent hate-motivated violence.
The city will also revive an interagency security working group disbanded in 2024, bringing together agencies including the NYPD and Department of Transportation to identify threats before attacks occur.
Cultural investments include $2 million for the Queens Holocaust Memorial Garden and $2.5 million for the Brooklyn Center for New Jewish Culture.
"Jewish New Yorkers should feel cherished and celebrated in the most Jewish city in America," Mamdani said.
On his first day in office, Mamdani revoked an Adams executive order adopting the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance's working definition of antisemitism. The definition includes examples addressing certain forms of anti-Zionist rhetoric, including denial of Jewish self-determination.
He also rescinded an order restricting city agencies from participating in boycotts or divestment targeting Israel, along with a directive requiring police to examine regulations governing protests outside houses of worship. Mamdani retained the Mayor's Office to Combat Antisemitism.
Seven major New York-area Jewish organizations criticized the reversal of the IHRA and boycott orders. Mamdani defended the decision, arguing that some Jewish organizations had concerns about the definition and pledging to fight antisemitism through prevention and community engagement.
The newly announced strategy does not adopt a replacement definition of antisemitism. The administration maintains that existing hate-crime and anti-discrimination laws provide a basis for enforcement without a single codified definition.
Mamdani concluded his announcement by appealing to New Yorkers to protect their Jewish neighbors.
"Our safety is bound up together," he said. "That is the work we are undertaking at City Hall, and I am asking every New Yorker to join us."
Ofir Akunis, Israel's consul general in New York, criticized Mamdani in a Tuesday X post, saying that "money can't buy values," and calling on the NYC mayor to readopt the IHRA definition of antisemitism.
"Until you recognize that your language against the Jewish State, which you don’t recognize as the homeland of the Jewish people, is the fundamental reason for the rise of antisemitism in New York City, it will continue to increase."
"Truly combating antisemitism requires readopting the IHRA Working Definition of Antisemitism, which you overturned as the first decision of your administration on day one," he said. "To truly fight antisemitism would be to call for your supporters to stop shouting “from the river to the sea” and “globalize the intifada,” have them condemn the October 7th massacre, and instead of supporting Hamas, declare that they are a terrorist organization."

Lindsay Clancy returned to court on Tuesday, as her lawyers sought to head off a retrial by having a judge find the Massachusetts woman not guilty of murder for the killing of her three young children in 2023.
Judge William Sullivan in Plymouth, Massachusetts, took up the issue after declaring a mistrial on September 4, which occurred after a single juror prevented the 12-member jury from reaching a unanimous verdict on whether to convict Clancy or find her not guilty by reason of insanity.
Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz's office has in the weeks since been silent on whether it plans to retry Clancy, 36, on first-degree murder charges, which carry a life sentence.
No one at Clancy's trial disputed that she strangled her three children with exercise bands on January 24, 2023, in the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury. She then cut herself with a knife and jumped from a second-story window in an attempt to end her own life, leaving her paralyzed.
Defense lawyer Kevin Reddington during her first trial sought to convince jurors that she did not understand what she was doing was wrong and that she had been in the throes of postpartum psychosis when she killed Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old Callan.
Total, complete lack of evidence
During Tuesday's hearing, Reddington told Sullivan that there was a "total and complete lack of evidence" at the trial to prove she killed the children and knew what she was doing was wrong.
He said non-lawyers had trouble understanding the idea that someone could admit culpability while maintaining a lack of criminal responsibility. That was leading many members of the public to call Clancy a "demon" and call for her execution, he said.
"This is coming from politicians, from President Trump all the way down," Reddington said.
Several jurors have in televised interviews stated that but for the one holdout juror, they had been prepared to find her not guilty by reason of insanity, known in Massachusetts as lack of criminal responsibility.
If found not guilty on those grounds, she would be committed to a state psychiatric hospital for evaluation. Her commitment would then be subject to regular review by the court.
Prosecutors have several options before them, including trying to reach a plea deal or retrying Clancy on lesser second-degree murder charges, which would give her the option to waive a jury trial and proceed before a judge.
Clancy's lawyers file series of motions to head off retrial possibility
Clancy's lawyers have filed a series of motions seeking to head off the possibility of a retrial by urging Sullivan to declare her not guilty and bar a retrial on the grounds that there was no reason to declare a mistrial and that it would as a result violate her right to avoid being tried twice for the same crime, known as double jeopardy.
They say jurors had been clear in notes delivered to the judge that the holdout had been refusing to apply the court's instructions on how to determine if prosecutors proved their case beyond a reasonable doubt, and that the juror should have been dismissed rather than allowing the case to be retried.
Her attorneys have also asked Sullivan to allow them to review normally confidential records about the jury and the holdout and question him about his truthfulness during the jury selection process and his cellphone use.
Sullivan said he would take up that issue and several other motions during a November 2 hearing. The holdout's lawyer, Edward Paltzik, told Fox News in an interview that aired on Monday that his client, Michael Desronvil, "had zero doubt" and "rigidly applied the reasonable doubt standard."

West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee and Abhishek Banerjee are also expected to join. RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav, Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Omar Abdullah and PDP chief Mehbooba Mufti are among the other leaders likely to participate.The Left parties are also expected to be represented, with CPM Rajya Sabha floor leader John Brittas likely to attend. Leaders of the CPI, CPI(ML), RSP and other Left parties are expected to join as well.Shiv Sena (UBT) chief Uddhav Thackeray is likely to participate virtually due to prior engagements in Mumbai, including a campaign against the Election Commission.NCP (SP) leader Supriya Sule and leaders of smaller opposition parties, including the JMM, IUML, VCK, MDMK, Kerala Congress factions, RLP, BAP, Lok Dal and Forward Bloc, are also expected to attend.Independent Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal is likely to participate in the deliberations.
Who is skipping
Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav is unlikely to attend in person. The party is expected to send senior leaders instead. Reports said Akhilesh cited commitments linked to the upcoming Rajya Sabha elections in Uttar Pradesh and other prior engagements.The absence comes amid differences between the SP and Congress over seat-sharing discussions for the Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections.The Aam Aadmi Party, DMK and Biju Janata Dal are among the parties that will not attend the meeting.The AAP was part of the INDIA bloc's 2024 Lok Sabha alliance but has since distanced itself from the grouping.The DMK, a Congress ally in Tamil Nadu, has also decided to stay away. DMK spokesperson TKS Elangovan said the party remained aligned with the opposition on several issues but was no longer part of the INDIA bloc. He said the party would support a removal motion against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar if one is brought in Parliament.BJD will also skip the meeting.
EC under fire
The meeting comes amid the opposition's campaign against the Election Commission over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.This comes after a report revealed that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised objections on record at least 14 times in the past 10 months over SIR-related decisions and orders they said were issued without their knowledge or recommendation.
The EC has rejected suggestions of institutional dysfunction, saying differing views are a normal part of deliberations and that its orders have full legal sanction and follow established statutory procedures.The opposition has sought to use the SIR controversy to press its demands against the poll panel and the government, while attempting to bring different opposition parties together.
The previous INDIA bloc meeting was held on June 8. The parties had then decided to demand the resignation of then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET-CBSE row and write to the Chief Justice of India over the SIR exercise and allegations of "vote loot".

Russian daily casualties highest since war began
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
18:04:48 BST
02:04:48 KST

The Ukrainian General Staff recorded 2,090 Russian casualties, killed and wounded, in the twenty-four hours to 28 September, the highest daily total it has reported since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022, according to British Defence Intelligence.
In its daily update on the war, the Ministry of Defence organisation set the figure against the rest of the record. Three previous daily totals above 2,000 were recorded during 2024, and the fourth-highest, of 1,960, came earlier this month on 16 September.
British Defence Intelligence stated: “The casualty rate has remained high since the summer, highly likely as Russia maintains its intensity in the fortress belt region, particularly in the vicinity of the Ukrainian stronghold of Dobropillia.”
The fortress belt is the line of fortified towns in Donetsk oblast running through Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka and Kostiantynivka, built up since 2014 and the principal obstacle to any Russian advance across the remainder of the region. Dobropillia sits to the west of that line, north of Pokrovsk, and became a focus of fighting after Russian forces pushed a narrow salient towards it, which Ukrainian units then worked to cut off.
Casualty figures in this war have to be handled with care whichever direction they come from. The Ukrainian daily total counts killed and wounded together without separating them, covers the whole front rather than any one sector, and is compiled by one of the belligerents. Western estimates of total Russian losses have generally been produced separately and with wide margins, and the British assessment has for some time been that Russia continues to accept losses at a rate it can sustain in manpower terms while taking ground at a pace measured in fields rather than towns.
What the figure does indicate, if the trend holds, is the cost of the tempo Russia has chosen to maintain through the autumn rather than pausing to reconstitute, with the highest and fourth-highest daily totals of the entire war now both falling within the past fortnight.
British Defence Intelligence has published updates on the war since shortly after the invasion began, releasing them through the Ministry of Defence account most days, and the format has settled into a short set of observations drawing on open sources alongside its own material. The updates carry the probability language deliberately so that readers can distinguish between what the organisation knows, what it assesses and how confident it is in the assessment.

Netanyahu is embracing Israel’s isolation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

Benjamin Netanyahu’s address to the United Nations General Assembly last week sounded more like a speech marking the end of an era than one opening a new chapter. Perhaps behind it was an awareness that this could be the last time he stands on that podium as Israel’s Prime Minister.
With the approach of Israel’s elections, set for October 27, Netanyahu’s political future has become inseparable from the way he addresses Israelis and the world. Yet his speech appeared directed primarily at his electoral audience at home, with little regard for the international community.
Netanyahu did not come to New York to offer a new political vision, propose a way out of the war, or present a vision for the region’s future. He came above all to defend his standing in Israel and his conduct of the war, while recasting Israel from a state facing growing international criticism into a purported victim confronting a hostile world. The question was thus turned on its head: instead of asking what Israel was doing to Palestinians and to the region, the focus became what the world was doing to Israel.
The sight of dozens of delegations walking out of the hall as he entered provided a striking image of the very predicament Netanyahu sought to deny. Rather than treating it as a sign of growing political isolation, however, he incorporated it into a narrative of “heroism”. The more others walked out, the more steadfast he appeared in his own telling. And the louder the criticism became, the more determined he was to present himself as the leader who stands alone but refuses to bend.
Israelis united against the world
When political options narrow, military force and confrontational rhetoric can serve as substitutes for a political way forward. The aim was less to convince the world that Netanyahu had a plan to end the conflict than to demonstrate that he could still defy the world and reject its demands — and ultimately settle the conflict by force.
At the same time, the speech was clearly directed at Israelis. Netanyahu spoke of unity, resilience, and courage, of Israel standing against its enemies, invoking the image of a leader who protects his people and knows how to confront the world. This is what led some analysts to describe it as an electoral speech rather than a diplomatic one.
Netanyahu was not trying to convince the world that Israel had changed; he was trying to convince Israelis that Israel did not need to change. The speech sought to move the narrative from accusation to victimhood, from isolation to heroism, and from accountability to persecution.
But the image of a united Israel he presented sits uneasily with the country’s internal reality. Israel’s divisions did not begin on October 7. The war was preceded by a profound crisis over the nature of the state, democracy, the judiciary, religion, society, and identity. These divisions have deepened around Netanyahu’s project and that of his allies. Presenting himself as the leader who unites Israelis against the world, therefore, overlooks the fact that his own policies have been part of the internal struggle that has divided Israeli society.
This is the deeper political meaning of the false heroism in the speech: an attempt to turn isolation into evidence of strength, the absence of a political solution into proof of steadfastness, and the world’s rejection of Israeli policies into evidence that those policies are justified.
What should Palestinians take from this?
Simply, that force may impose new realities, but it cannot by itself turn them into lasting legitimacy. Palestinians should not compete with Israel over power, but consolidate their existence and national rights as a political and legal reality grounded in self-determination, freedom, and equality. That requires moving beyond reaction, strengthening unified national institutions and resilience, and speaking to Israelis and the world in a language aimed at ending the conflict rather than denying the other side.
Between the end of Netanyahu and a new image of Israel
Perhaps the absence of a meeting between Netanyahu and Donald Trump during this visit was more than a matter of protocol. The meeting was not on the U.S. president’s schedule at a time when Netanyahu is fighting an electoral battle and facing growing international isolation. It would be an exaggeration to turn that absence alone into a judgment about his political future. But the question remains legitimate: did it reinforce Netanyahu’s sense that his political era is approaching its end, and that Israel itself is paying the price for conflating the state with his government and its policies?
Netanyahu has increasingly blurred, in both his rhetoric and political practice, the distinction between the Israel he claims to represent and himself as the person who represents it. At this moment, the new Israel exposed by war and international isolation appears more starkly before the world: a state attempting to protect its old image through force, even as the gap widens between that image and what the world sees in its policies — occupation, settlement expansion, genocidal war, ethnic cleansing, and the denial of Palestinian rights. The construction of ever more “iron walls” may not be enough to conceal this image forever.
If this was indeed Netanyahu’s final address to the General Assembly as prime minister, he wanted to leave the podium with the image he had chosen for himself: a leader standing alone but refusing to bend, confronting the world while insisting that his people stand united behind him.
Yet his speech revealed another image: a leader trying to turn isolation into heroism, force into a substitute for politics, and the denial of the Palestinian people’s rights into a reality imposed through brute power. Perhaps this is the clearest irony of all: he sought to present himself as the leader whom the world could not isolate, yet, unwillingly, he may have contributed to deepening Israel’s isolation.

Malchevsky concentrated on his wife, two adult children and seven grandchildren. His fear of heights did not get in the way as he clambered onto a ledge outside the window to avoid the smoke and fierce flames.
Images of Malchevsky and a colleague trapped in the burning Tsarist-era building fuelled fresh anger at Russia’s escalating strikes on Ukraine’s capital Kyiv and other cities.

California recognises Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha as state holidays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:56:56 UTC
01:56:56 KST

Breadcrumb
California formally recognises Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha as state holidays
California has formally recognised the Islamic Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha festivals as state holidays, making it the second state of the United States to do so.
Authored by Assembly member Matt Haney, Assembly Bill 2017 (AB 2017) now allows state and school employees to observe both Eids by using existing personal holiday credits or available leave.
The legislation also permits K-12 schools and community colleges to close for Eid, provided such closures are established through locally negotiated arrangements.
Many states, cities and school districts recognise Eid locally, but not as statewide holidays. Washington state was the first one to officially recognise the two festivals as state holidays in 2025.
Eid al-Fitr marks the end of the holy fasting month of Ramadan, and Eid al-Adha honours Prophet Ibrahim's (Abraham's) willingness to obey God by sacrificing his son.
Eid al-Adha, the most important event in the Muslim calendar, coincides with and marks the culmination of the annual Hajj pilgrimage in Mecca, home to Islam’s holiest mosque and site, the Kaaba.
The California chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR-CA) welcomed Governor Gavin Newsom’s signing of AB 2017, saying it addresses a longstanding challenge for the state’s more than one million Muslim residents who are often forced to choose between practicing their faith and showing up to school or work.
"For far too long, Muslim students and employees in California have had to make the difficult choice between participating in observances essential to their faith or falling behind on their academic or professional obligations. AB 2017 removes these structural barriers and aligns state policy with the values of inclusion, equity, and respect for cultural diversity that define our state," it said in a statement shared on its website.
CAIR, the United States' largest Muslim organisation, said the passage comes at a time of increased Islamophobia in the country, saying it recently documented a 183% increase in incidents targeting mosques and Islamic centres from May to July compared to the same three-month period last year.
"Officially recognising these holidays sends the necessary and powerful message that California values and protects its Muslim community in the face of growing hostility".
In May, a shooting at the Islamic Centre of San Diego by two gunmen killed a security guard and two community members outside the mosque.

Brazil’s cellphone crime a security nightmare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:39 UTC
01:49:39 KST

Eduardo Metzker, 29, was riding his motorcycle in Rio de Janeiro when he was suddenly boxed in by two other bikes. One of the riders put a gun to his head and demanded his phone and passcode.
The software developer watched with horror as the robbers drained up to 80,000 reais (about US$15,000) from his banking apps, mostly in credit, while he scrambled to block his accounts.
“You know you go out every day, earning a living, saving money, building a life and then someone sticks a gun in your face and takes everything you have. My credit rating was ruined,” Metzker said.
Photo: AP
Cellphone crime, which can involve violence, financial fraud and even murder, has become a potent symbol of the security crisis gripping Brazilian cities like Rio de Janeiro ahead of a first round presidential election on Sunday.
“The cellphone appears to encapsulate a growing panic over urban violence,” the Brazilian Public Security Forum (FBSP) said in its annual report.
An FBSP survey published in May estimated that about 14 million people had been a victim of the crime in the 12 previous months.
However, only about 830,000 cellphones were reported stolen or robbed last year, according to the annual report, which draws on police data.
“We walk around completely afraid, constantly on alert,” said Caroline Lo Bianco, 36, a dentist who had her phone ripped from her hands through the window of an Uber when she was seven months pregnant.
Ahead of a closely contested election, both leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his right-wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro have vowed to crack down on the crime.
Bolsonaro promises to quadruple jail sentences for cellphone crimes, while Lula has said “our goal is zero phone theft.”
Polls show security is the major concern of Brazilians this election, but Metzker said he does not believe any candidate would make a difference.
“Honestly, they can say whatever they want, I have no faith in them,” he said.
Fear of cellphone crime has pushed an estimated 30 percent of Brazilians — about 65 million people — to keep a cheap second phone, nicknamed a “robber’s phone,” the FBSP said.
Metzker said that after the robbery, he now carries one phone that he takes out on the street, and one that he keeps at home with all his banking applications on it.
Leonardo Silva, a coordinator for state and organized crime issues at the FBSP, said that cellphone crime was growing more sophisticated.
Criminal “interest has shifted away from the phone itself, its physical value, to the data contained in those devices,” he said.
After being robbed, Lo Bianco blocked her bank cards, but the thieves managed to transfer almost US$700 from a digital bank account. They also bought an Xbox on her Amazon app, which she managed to block before delivery.
The thieves even used her food delivery applications to send beer, meat and McDonalds to different addresses across Rio de Janeiro.
Luiz Fernando Bugiga, a prosecutor with the Special Action Group for Combating Organized Crime, said a major police operation in Sao Paulo this month revealed an organized scheme behind cellphone crime with four distinct criminal cells.
Those who steal the phones hand them off to a specialized cell whose members “initiate bank transfers and data theft.”
A third group make technical modifications to “legitimize” the phone, allowing it to re-enter the market. The final group is charged with selling parts and devices.
“Cellphone theft creates multiple forms of loss for the victim and therefore multiple sources of profit for the criminal,” he said.
For many, just replacing the phone is a major financial blow.
Joel da Silva, 42, who works as a doorman in Ipanema, “went a month without a phone,” before being able to buy one over four installments, after being robbed at gunpoint.
He said that in his seven months at his job, he has witnessed four phone robberies from the building where he works.
Lo Bianco, who is originally from the capital, Brasilia, and was a victim of an armed carjacking in Rio a few years ago, dreams of leaving.
“I tell my husband that if he asked me to move to the Amazon, my bags would be packed the next day,” she said.

Major canals in Bangkok filled with accumulated rainfall exceeding 20cm, officials said yesterday. Floodwaters spread across the city, particularly in the central and eastern parts, blocking roads and stopping traffic. The Thai Meteorological Department warned that the heavy rain would continue in most parts of the country through today, citing a strong low-pressure system over the central region and strengthening southwest monsoon conditions. Eight food products fail inspections at border, FDA says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:39 UTC
01:49:39 KST

Japanese cantaloupes, fresh black truffles from Bulgaria and Thai bird’s nest drinks were among eight imported food products found to contain excessive pesticide residues, heavy metals or sweeteners, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said yesterday.
The list also included celery from Vietnam and sesame products from Tanzania.
Part of a shipment of Japanese cantaloupes imported by Kaohsiung-based fruit importer Yang Jhen International Co contained 0.07 parts per million (ppm) of the pesticide isofetamid, exceeding the 0.01 ppm limit, the FDA said.
Photo courtesy of the Food and Drug Administration
Taiwan does not permit the use of isofetamid on cantaloupes, FDA Northern Center for Regional Administration Director Liu Fang-ming (劉芳銘) said.
The 320kg shipment must be returned or destroyed, Liu said, adding that all future shipments from Yang Jhen would be subject to border inspections.
In the past six months, 11 of 111 shipments of fresh melons imported from Japan failed inspections, with excessive pesticide residues the main reason for noncompliance, FDA data showed.
The FDA would inspect all batches of fresh melons imported from Japan through Oct. 28, Liu said.
Fresh black truffles imported from Bulgaria by European Arcade Food Ltd contained 5 milligrams per kilogram (mg/kg) of cadmium per kilogram, exceeding the 2mg/kg limit, the agency said, adding that the 4.5kg shipment must be returned or destroyed.
Although the batch was the company’s only noncompliant shipment in the past six months, it had contravened regulation in September last year, and so all future shipments would be inspected, Liu said.
Three of 17 shipments of truffles from Bulgaria inspected over the past six months failed inspections, FDA data showed.
A shipment of Thai bird’s nest drink imported by Hsiang Yen Trading Co contained 0.06g/kg of saccharin, which is not permitted in the product category. The 4,991kg shipment must be returned or destroyed.
Separately, a Consumers’ Foundation survey found that 80 percent of basil samples and 20 percent of scallion samples bought in traditional markets, supermarkets and big-box stores in Taiwan’s six special municipalities contained pesticide residues exceeding legal limits.
The foundation bought 10 samples each of garlic, scallions and basil in May and June and tested them for 410 pesticides and dithiocarbamate pesticides.
Of the 30 samples, eight basil and two scallion samples failed. The 10 noncompliant samples contained 16 types of pesticides, while the risk coefficient for basil ranged from two to 141.9.
The tests detected chlorpyrifos, an organophosphate insecticide that can affect the nervous system after prolonged or excessive exposure, the foundation said.
Taiwan removed chlorpyrifos from its permitted pesticide-residue standards in April 2024 and has been phasing out its use.
The foundation advised people to soak garlic, scallions and basil in water for 10 to 15 minutes and thoroughly rinse them under running water before using them.

Free flu and COVID-19 vaccines start tomorrow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:38 UTC
01:49:38 KST

The first phase of government-funded seasonal influenza and COVID-19 vaccination begins tomorrow, amid heightened flu activity, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said yesterday.
There were 138,654 outpatient and emergency medical visits for flu-like illnesses last week, about 3.2 percent fewer than the previous week, but that number might be affected by many clinics being closed over the long holiday weekend, CDC Epidemic Intelligence Center Deputy Director Lee Chia-lin (李佳琳) said.
As 12.2 percent of those visits were to emergency rooms, the seasonal flu is still considered to be in its epidemic period, she said.
Photo: CNA
Thirty flu-related deaths and 87 severe flu cases were confirmed last week, Lee said, adding that it was the most weekly flu-related deaths since October last year.
Flu activity is also rising in China, South Korea, Japan and Singapore, as well as in the US, she said.
The centers estimated that weekly medical visits would vary slightly this week and in the coming weeks, due to long weekends, but would remain high as people gather on holidays, CDC Deputy Director-General Lin Min-cheng (林明誠) said.
The number of weekly medical visits might begin to drop from the middle of next month, but whether the weekly number would reach a peak of 150,000 to 160,000 as previously predicted is not certain, he added.
Meanwhile, 10,502 medical visits for COVID-19 were reported last week, Lee said.
Weekly numbers for the disease have been gradually falling in the past few weeks, but it is still at epidemic levels, she said, adding that there were 33 severe cases and 14 deaths confirmed last week.
Eligible recipients should get the flu and COVID-19 vaccines as soon as possible, as vaccination remains the most effective way to protect against the diseases, Lin said.
The enhanced flu vaccine first introduced to the program this year provides stronger protection, and the updated COVID-19 vaccine from Moderna uses a lower dose while providing greater protection, he said.
Eligible groups in the first phase for both vaccines include people aged 65 and older, medical and disease-prevention workers, indigenous people aged 55 to 64, nursing home residents and workers, pregnant women, caregivers of children younger than six months, and employees at preschools, childcare centers and at-home childcare providers.
They also include people with high-risk, chronic, rare or catastrophic illnesses, while flu-vaccine eligibility additionally includes students at elementary schools, junior and senior-high schools, vocational schools and the first to third years of five-year junior colleges, or people working with poultry or livestock, and animal epidemic prevention workers.
Children aged six months to preschool age are also eligible for the free flu vaccine, while the eligibility for the free COVID-19 vaccine has been revised to children aged six months to younger than six years who have never received a COVID-19 vaccine.
The second phase is to begin on Nov. 2, when the eligibility of the vaccines would be expanded to include people aged 50 to 64, the CDC said.
In addition, the government’s “health token” program launches tomorrow, meaning that people aged 18 and older who receive an eligible vaccine, either government-funded or paid for out of pocket, can earn health tokens, Lin said.
They can earn 450 health tokens for a flu vaccine, 900 for a COVID-19 vaccine and 600 for a pneumococcus vaccine, he said.
The tokens can be exchanged for health-related products and services starting from Dec. 1, he added.

Stop waiting for US to save Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:37 UTC
01:49:37 KST

The most important lesson for Taiwan from last week’s summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping (習近平) is not found in any formal agreement. It is in the way Taiwan was treated — as an issue to be managed between Washington and Beijing.
Xi pressed Trump to adhere to what China called the “correct position” of opposing Taiwan independence — a stronger formulation than Washington’s traditional position that it does not support Taiwanese independence.
For six months, China has been watching the US fight Iran. Beijing is not simply observing the battlefield. According to Taiwan’s own 2026 defense assessment, China is studying the lessons of that war: the US’ rapid ammunition consumption, pressure on air-defense systems, the demands of industrial mobilization and what the Ministry of National Defense called the “fragility of allied cooperation.”
The Iran conflict, launched with US and Israeli strikes in February, was initially presented by Trump as a war that could be won quickly. Instead, it has hardened into a costly stalemate. Iran, vastly weaker militarily than China, has nevertheless threatened US bases, disrupted energy flows, forced the US to expend expensive defensive missiles and used regional partners to widen the conflict.
Trump has repeatedly threatened escalation while also leaving the door open to negotiations. Meanwhile, most European and Asian allies have refused his demands to join a war they say was launched without adequate consultation.
We cannot know precisely what conclusions Xi has drawn, but Taiwan would be reckless to assume he has drawn none.
China does not need to believe it can defeat the US everywhere. It needs only to believe it can make intervention in the Taiwan Strait so militarily costly, economically disruptive and politically divisive that a US president ultimately chooses negotiation over escalation.
China would be a far more formidable adversary than Iran: a much larger and more sophisticated military, an enormous industrial base, nuclear weapons and the advantage of fighting close to its own shores.
That gives new significance to Xi’s decision to press Trump on Taiwan.
Trump’s response should concern Taipei. A roughly US$14 billion US arms package for Taiwan remains on hold, and Trump has previously described it as a “very good negotiating chip.”
The US remains Taiwan’s most important security partner and weapons supplier, and congressional support remains substantial, but Taiwan must distinguish between US support and a US guarantee.
There is no treaty obligating the US to send its forces into a war with China. Strategic ambiguity might have helped preserve peace, but ambiguity is a dangerous foundation on which to stake the survival of 23 million people.
The lesson from Iran is diplomatic as well as military. The war has shown that even Washington cannot automatically assemble an international coalition behind its military actions. Trump has struggled to persuade longstanding allies to follow him, while also searching for a negotiated way out of a conflict in which US military power has not ended.
Taiwan’s response must not be anti-Americanism. It must be diversification.
Taiwan should undertake a sustained diplomatic, economic and security campaign across Europe — particularly in the UK, France, Germany, Poland, the Czech Republic, Lithuania and other democracies willing to resist coercion. It should deepen semiconductor partnerships, cybersecurity cooperation, intelligence relationships, parliamentary ties and critical-infrastructure collaboration.
Europe does not need to recognize Taiwan diplomatically tomorrow or promise troops. The objective should be to create relationships so extensive that any Chinese blockade or attack would immediately carry political, technological and economic consequences across Europe.
The same strategy should reach farther: Japan, Australia, India, Canada, the Philippines and other democracies.
Taiwan is not merely a small nation asking larger countries for protection, it is a successful democracy at the center of the global technology economy. Its semiconductor industry is essential to economies worldwide. Taiwan must convert that importance into durable international relationships before a crisis begins.
The central question after the Trump-Xi summit is whether Taiwan can safely assume that, when the decisive moment comes, a US president would risk direct war with nuclear-armed China to save it. Iran should have taught Taiwan that it cannot afford to make that assumption.
Hope is not a defense policy. Friendship is not a treaty. No democracy should entrust its survival to the decisions of one president in one capital.
Taiwan still needs the US, but the time has come for Taipei to build a world in which it no longer needs the US alone.

The legislature began the confirmation vote at 10am, with most nominees receiving 50 votes in favor and 60 against.
Photo: Chen Yi-kuan, Taipei Times
Under Article 29 of the Act Governing the Legislative Yuan’s Power (立法院職權行使法), nominations require approval from more than half of all legislators, or 57 votes, to pass.
Ahead of the vote, Democratic Progressive Party caucus chief executive Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) said the caucus unanimously supported Lai’s nominees for the government watchdog.
Chinese Nationalist party (KMT) caucus deputy secretary-general Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) said that the party would not allow any unsuitable candidates to serve as Control Yuan members.
The KMT had raised numerous concerns about the Control Yuan’s performance over the past few years, she said, adding that critics had long accused the government watchdog of applying uneven standards of oversight to different political parties and cases.
The Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) unanimously voted against the nominees, TPP Legislator Hung Yu-hsiang (洪毓祥) said, citing what he described as failures in oversight, protection of the powerful and a lack of exemplary conduct among Control Yuan members.
The Control Yuan’s previous members completed their six-year term on July 31. Under the law, newly appointed members should have assumed office on Aug. 1.
Lai announced his list of candidates in June.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) urged the ruling and opposition parties to work together to restore constitutional order and uphold their constitutional responsibility by reviewing the budget according to the law and within the statutory time frame.

16:49:36 UTC
01:49:36 KST

Japanese volleyball player Rui Takahashi yesterday came out as gay, saying that he wanted to help others struggling with their sexuality in a country where openly LGBTQ athletes are extremely rare.
The 26-year-old Takahashi, who plays in the top division of Japan’s professional volleyball league, posted a statement on social media accompanied by a black-and-white photo of himself.
In it, he said he had been “afraid to face a certain side of myself” since he was young.
Photo: AFP
“I struggled with it and ended up denying who I was,” he wrote. “That is the fact that I am gay and that I am one of the sexual minorities.”
Takahashi said his brother, Ran, who is a hugely popular star with Japan’s national volleyball team, helped him come to terms with his sexuality.
“Talking with Ran became the trigger that finally allowed me to accept myself for the first time,” he wrote.
“By putting my feelings into words, I was able to sort out my thoughts, and little by little I started to feel that it was OK to be just the way I am,” he added.
Takahashi became one of a very small group of openly LGBTQ professional athletes in Japan.
Women’s soccer player Shiho Shimoyamada was the first to come out as gay in 2019.
Kumi Yokoyama, who played for Japan at the FIFA Women’s World Cup, later came out as a transgender man.
In June 2021, the Japanese Olympic Committee appointed transgender former fencer Fumino Suhiyama to its board of directors, just weeks before the Tokyo Olympics.
Takahashi said he hoped him coming out would help others in a similar situation.
“I would be happy if my decision to face myself and speak in my own words could, even in a small way, become a catalyst for them,” he wrote.

KMT moots payout with future money
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:35 UTC
01:49:35 KST

The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) caucus yesterday said it plans to propose a bill that would issue a NT$20,000 cash handout to every citizen with the aim of “sharing economic gains and stabilizing livelihoods.”
The government collected NT$528.3 billion (US$16.57 billion) more in taxes than expected last year, and about 40 percent, or NT$230 billion, was allocated for universal cash handouts, KMT caucus whip Fu Kun-chi (傅?萁) told reporters as the new legislative session began yesterday.
This year’s tax revenue surplus is expected to exceed NT$1 trillion, and if the government allocated 40 percent of it, it would be enough to provide each citizen with a NT$20,000 cash payment, he said.
Economic growth is expected to reach almost 12 percent this year, so the government should report its largest tax revenue surplus yet next year, possibly exceeding NT$2 trillion, meaning next year’s cash handout could be even more than NT$20,000, he said, without citing any government data.
The government should have a clear plan for surplus tax revenue, prioritizing debt repayment and improved benefits for older peoeple before determining how much can be distributed as cash handouts, Taiwan People’s Party caucus chief executive Hung Yu-hsiang (洪毓祥) said.
Any proposal involving a large increase in government spending must identify its funding source and first be discussed with the Executive Yuan according to the Budget Act (預算法), Democratic Progressive Party caucus chief executive Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) said.
Ahead of the meeting, Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said in an interview: “We can decide how to allocate the resources generated by our own efforts, but the debt incurred by our generation must never be left for the next generation.”
Executive Yuan spokeswoman Michelle Lee (李慧芝) said recently that any plan to disburse cash payments to the public must be based on three principles: it must not result in any increase in actual government borrowing, it must not crowd out other government programs such as social welfare, national defense, healthcare and education, and the process must comply with the law and the Constitution.
The Constitution mandates that the Legislative Yuan cannot propose increases in spending when reviewing a budget submitted by the Executive Yuan, Chuang said.
Policies should consider the government’s overall fiscal capacity and spending needs, including national defense, social welfare and economic development, he said.
Measures taken during energy crises to limit or freeze increases in electricity and fuel prices should be considered, he added.
Once the government has comprehensively addressed national needs, any remaining surplus funds should be shared with the public, but the issue should not turn into a bidding war between political parties, he said.

The White House’s arms dealer diplomacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:32 UTC
01:49:32 KST

US Ambassador to China David Perdue on Sunday told Fox News that US President Donald Trump had asked Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) if he would like to buy US weapons. Perdue offered no further detail and no word on Xi’s answer, which is itself instructive: Apparently even the ambassador telling the story thought better of dwelling on it.
Asked to confirm the story, the US Department of State said US law forbids arms sales to China and that no such offer exists. Both can be true. The department’s formal denial can be several steps removed from whatever Trump says to Xi over dinner in Beijing or Washington.
Set aside for a moment the legality of such sales. That a US president floated it to the leader of a country the Pentagon has spent two decades identifying as the pacing threat, the one building the world’s fastest-growing military and the one most US officials across party lines expect to eventually collide with US forces somewhere over Taiwan, tells you what Trump actually thinks a defense relationship is.
It is a transaction, available to whoever is in the room.
That China’s defense companies are arming Iran and Russia with dual-use equipment and satellite imagery, some of it linked to strikes that killed US troops, did not apparently register as disqualifying.
The more damning context sits one paragraph over. While Trump was reportedly pitching Xi on US weapons, his administration has spent the better part of a year sitting on a US$14 billion arms package for Taiwan, a package State Department officials assembled and congressional leaders approved, and which the US has been legally obligated to provide since the Taiwan Relations Act of 1979.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s excuse, that the sale is under review for its effect on the US’ own industrial base, might carry some weight if the same administration were not simultaneously offering weapons to the country Taiwan needs the arms to deter. You cannot claim a shortage of rifles while asking the other side of the fight if it wants to buy some.
Trump has been candid about what Taiwan is in his calculus. In May he called the withheld arms package a good negotiating chip with Beijing. Asked about a 1982 commitment barring Washington from consulting China on Taiwan arms sales, a commitment his own conversations with Xi appear to violate, he waved it off as ancient history, a “big, far distance.”
Four Republican senators led by Mitch McConnell last week wrote to Rubio and US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth begging them to release funds Congress had already approved. Representative to the US Alexander Yui (俞大?) still managed to sound hopeful on CBS on Sunday, saying he trusted nothing had changed in Washington’s position, which is either admirable discipline or the diplomatic version of whistling past a graveyard.
Ryan Hass, director of the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center, put it plainly: This disclosure should end any lingering doubt about whether Trump treats China as a genuine security threat. It should also end any illusion that Taipei occupies a fixed place in US strategy rather than a rotating one, useful as leverage when Trump needs something from Xi and inconvenient when he wants a smooth summit.
A superpower that offers its rival first pick of the arsenal while stalling delivery to the ally that rival is threatening has not miscalculated. It has simply told you, plainly, what it values and in what order, and Taiwan should take the hint.
Clive Hazell is a Kaohsiung-based writer and educator. A 30-year-resident of Taiwan and Japan, he writes on geopolitics, culture and East Asia.
If Taiwan falls, the true battle moves from the beaches into the concrete streets. Western analysts fixate on the invasion phase. They end wargames when missiles stop flying and submit policy papers after the fate of a beachhead is decided. This narrow focus ignores the grim reality of “the day after.” To address this blind spot, the Irregular Warfare Center (IWC) published a seminal study on March 5, 2026, titled China’s Way of Occupation: Implications for Taiwan. Authored by Jan K. Gleiman and others, the report analyzes Beijing’s actions in Tibet, Xinjiang (East Turkestan), and Hong Kong to expose a chilling playbook
Beijing has for decades insisted that Taiwan is a matter to be settled between China and the US — or, preferably, by China alone. The strategic environment around Taiwan is making that increasingly difficult. The clearest evidence this week came not from Washington or Beijing, but from Tokyo. The delusion of increased AI productivity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:32 UTC
01:49:32 KST

Is AI a bubble? We are told that it depends on whether massive investments in the technology can massively boost productivity. Optimists are convinced that future productivity gains could be colossal, even if a market correction is necessary to draw some hot air out of the current boom. Pessimists, from Goldman Sachs’ Jim Covello to MIT’s Daron Acemoglu, have their doubts. Optimists and pessimists alike are in the grip of what could be called AI productivity delusion.
What both sides miss is that AI could devastate capitalism even if it boosts productivity beyond our imaginations — and regardless of whether it delivers the promised economy-wide automation of everyday corporate workflows. The reason why we tend to miss this point is that we look at today’s world through the lens of another world that cloud capital, especially now that it is AI-enhanced, has rendered obsolete.
Until recently, it was a foregone conclusion that every technological revolution represents a moment of creative destruction. Whole sectors, professions, and skill sets were destroyed by innovations which ushered in new sectors, new professions, and new skill sets. Automobiles ruined saddlers, farriers and knackers but begat auto workers, road builders, mechanics and service-station personnel. The transition from coal to oil condemned whole mining communities and trade unions to oblivion. In net terms, more was created than was destroyed. Creative destruction became synonymous with economic growth.
Faced with the AI juggernaut, it is natural to focus on the technology’s net effects. Could it create more than it destroys? The real question is, “More of what?” To avoid the AI productivity delusion, we must rethink how we define productivity.
If by productivity we mean tasks accomplished per unit of human labor, there is no doubt that AI could prove an immense success — in fact, it already has. If we continue to measure productivity in terms of monetary value produced per unit of labor, the chances are that AI is going to prove an unmitigated disaster.
Earlier technological revolutions, from the steam engine and the automobile to the personal computer and the smartphone, expanded the domain of capitalist markets. Despite the wreckage of whole professions and communities they left in their wake, they resulted in simultaneously more material output and a higher aggregate monetary value of that output.
Can AI do likewise? Maybe in China, where AI is coupled with robotics, material production could rise and, at least in the short run, so would net revenues. In the West, AI agents are deployed in the service sector — from Amazon.com to back offices, law firms, hospitals and more. In those domains, AI-enhanced cloud capital could shrink markets in two distinct ways.
The first way, the one everyone worries about, is that AI is going to kill off entire professions: paralegals, coders, translators, accountants, even architects, mathematicians and school teachers, while creating far fewer new jobs filled by the prompters, overseers, engineers and operators of the new machinery. The second way is far less visible but perhaps even more worrying: the conversion of markets into cloud fiefs and of profits into rents.
As I argued long ago, Amazon might look like a market, with countless buyers and sellers within its digital walls, but it lacks the central feature of a market: decentralization. It is more centralized than the Soviet planned economy ever was, with an inscrutable algorithm deciding which consumer is matched to which vendor on the basis of a probabilistic model optimized to maximize the likelihood that Jeff Bezos collects 40 percent of the maximum price every customer is willing to pay.
As AI becomes more deeply embedded in Bezos’ algorithm, interfaces like Alexa would communicate with us not as mere shopping assistants but as an all-knowing friend, companion and even therapist. Soon, capitalist vendors’ profits would end up in some tech lord’s account in the form of cloud rent, which he would most certainly invest in more AI-enhanced cloud capital that produces more power to extract more cloud rents.
So, as Apple’s Siri, Google’s Gemini and an army of such agentic assistants develop the same capacities for their tech lords as Amazon has for Bezos, the capitalist market domain is going to continue to shrink. While AI might have proven exceedingly productive in terms of economic activities performed per unit of human labor, the profit rates of capitalist enterprises would collapse, following society’s aggregate wages to the bottom. At that point, none of the tools of the liberal state — no amount of quantitative easing, no politically feasible levels of universal basic income, no wealth tax that the tech lords might find hard to evade — would be able to prevent a systemic collapse.
The question of whether AI is going to generate massive productivity gains is easy to answer: Yes. AI is already proving capable of exponentially increasing the amount of work that is being done per human worker. However, as long as it is used to eliminate wage labor while siphoning off profits from actual markets into our tech lords’ cloud rents, the economic value produced per worker is going to tank.
Unless this distinction is made, the AI productivity delusion is going to persist. And as long as it does, we are unable to hope for a post-capitalist future of abundance where we, along with our AI helpers, produce according to ability and distribute according to need.
Yanis Varoufakis, a former finance minister of Greece, is leader of the MeRA25 party, professor of economics at the University of Athens, and a senior research fellow at Fudan University.

Environmental Impact Assessment: How eDNA can revolutionize Taiwan’s biodiversity research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:31 UTC
01:49:31 KST

Last year, a Taiwanese-Japanese team of scientists described a new species: the Yuchi music frog (Nidirana shyhhuangi), an amphibian previously thought to be an isolated population of the Ryukyu music frog (Nidirana okinavana).
Careful comparison of body sizes, patterning, and vocalizations convinced the researchers they were looking at different species, meaning that Nidirana shyhhuangi — found at only two locations in Nantou County — is a critically endangered Taiwan endemic. According to a press release issued by NTNU’s Center of Public Affairs, this discovery “shows that even on an island as small as Taiwan, the richness and complexity of biodiversity are still widely underestimated.”
In the last two decades, various technological leaps have made the detection and identification of species easier than ever. Among them, environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding is one of the most transformative.
Photo courtesy of the National Institutes of Applied Research
Every plant and animal within an environment sheds genetic material in forms such as feces, urine, feathers, spores or pollen. Some of these traces last just a few hours, but viable DNA fragments have been extracted from the teeth or bones of creatures that died over 1,000 years ago.
So far, most eDNA studies have focused on what can be learned by analyzing a location’s soil or water. But an article in June last year on the University of Florida’s online news hub quoted David Duffy, a professor of wildlife disease genomics at the university, as saying that a great deal of informative DNA can be found in the air.
“That means you can study species without directly having to disturb them, without ever having to see them. It opens up huge possibilities to study all the species in an area simultaneously, from microbes and viruses all the way up to vertebrates like bobcats and humans, and everything in between,” Duffy said.
Photo: Steven Crook
TECHNOLOGICAL PROGRESS
Filters fine enough to catch all but the very smallest bacteria — which are less than 1/200th of the width of a human hair — have been around since the 1960s. Only recently, however, have scientists gained access to sufficient computational power to process the enormous amounts of data a single study can generate. Computers are now able to compare eDNA sequences against vast reference databases such as GenBank (maintained by the US National Institutes of Health). In addition to producing a list of the species found at a particular place, bioinformatics software suites can estimate species abundance and biomass.
Even though the Yuchi music frog was identified using more traditional methods, Taiwanese researchers have embraced the potential of eDNA metabarcoding.
Photo courtesy of the National Academy of Marine Research
Lin Yen-ting (林晏廷), an expert on invasive fish species (see “Taiwan’s freshwater invaders” in the Aug. 26, 2026 Taipei Times), has applied the technology to the piscine population of New Taipei City’s Feitsui Reservoir (翡翠水庫).
According to a paper authored by Lin, an assistant professor in the Master’s Program in Biodiversity at National Taiwan University, and seven other specialists, eDNA demonstrated “superior sensitivity” compared to traditional survey methods such as gillnetting (Environmental and Sustainability Indicators, September 2025).
Damming a waterway to create a reservoir — in the case of Feitsui, the Beishi Creek (北勢溪) was impounded — changes it from a lotic (flowing) to a lentic (still) system. This leads to “profound alterations in aquatic environments and shifts in species composition [which] often favor species adapted to stagnant waters…The result is often species replacement, altered community structures, and declines in ecological stability and native biodiversity,” Lin and his coauthors point out.
Traditional sampling at Feitsui had previously documented 23 fish species, while eDNA analysis not only matched this count but detected 13 additional species. Capture methods appear to be biased toward “large-bodied, invasive taxa” while metabarcoding favors “native and small-bodied species,” the paper states. At the same time, the authors express concern that among the species detected exclusively through eDNA were the Florida or largemouth bass (Micropterus salmoides) and the blue tilapia (Oreochromis aureus). Both are “high-risk invasive species.”
While there can be no doubt as to “the dominance of invasive species and the evident shift in community structure,” the authors take heart from the fact that native fish haven’t entirely disappeared from the reservoir. The evidence they present indicates “these species continue to exist — albeit potentially in lower abundance or occupying less-sampled habitats — suggesting that invasive species, while impactful, have not entirely displaced native fauna.” Feitsui Reservoir’s native fish populations may, they speculate, benefit from ecological connectivity between the reservoir and upstream tributaries of the Beishi Creek.
Metabarcoding demonstrates “both time and cost efficiency” compared to older sampling methods, Lin’s team writes, but it’s not without its drawbacks. Depending on their life stages, activity levels and stress levels, individual organisms shed varying amounts of DNA. Temperature, UV radiation and microbial activity influence the rate at which DNA degrades, while running water can move it far from the source fish. This makes it “difficult to infer community structure solely based on eDNA data [and] accurately estimating abundance remains a major challenge in fish surveys using eDNA methods.”
BLUE OCEANS, GREEN FIELDS
Even in the open ocean, metabarcoding produces useful data. Scientists at National Sun Yat-sen University’s Department of Marine Biotechnology and Resources recently used it to better understand the boundary between tropical and subtropical marine communities.
They took samples of seawater from 10 coastal locations, including Taiwan’s north and northeast coasts, the Penghu archipelago, Siaoliouciou (小琉球) and Green Island (綠島). In July paper in Marine Environmental Research, they explain that hard corals and benthic organisms (those that dwell on or close to the seabed) were more evident in southern waters, whereas the richness of copepods (small crustaceans) was highest in the north.
Rice fields cover a major part of Taiwan’s lowlands, and rice is a crop of great importance. It’s hardly surprising, then, that local researchers have been conducting eDNA biodiversity surveys to assess the presence of native and non-native pests across cultivation phases.
Rice fields are “ephemeral wetlands particularly vulnerable to invasive species,” according to an April paper in Ecology and Evolution. To study these habitats, the authors collected water and soil samples from eight rice fields in Chiayi County, generating 1.01 million usable DNA sequencing reads. After excluding unclassifiable results, 93 percent of the reads were matched to arthropods (a group that includes agricultural pests such as stem borers and planthoppers) and nearly 6 percent to annelids (segmented worms). Rotifers — microscopic swimming organisms — and mollusks made up most of the remainder.
The paper concludes that, despite the limited number of samples, the study provided “valuable insights into the pest community.” The detection of the Asiatic rice borer (Chilo suppressalis), the Formosan termite (Coptotermes formosanus) and the golden apple snail (Pomacea canaliculata) “are highly concerning.” Humans who live near paddy fields may be alarmed to know the scholars also found “high abundances of Culex tritaeniorhynchus, a vector of Japanese encephalitis virus.”
Metabarcoding offers distinct advantages over conventional biomonitoring, which in rice fields relies on dip nets, funnel traps and taxonomic expertise. As the technology advances, analyzing water, soil or leaf swabs will become increasingly accessible to ordinary farmers. By providing a real-time picture of field biodiversity, metabarcoding could make it possible to target pests more precisely — and reduce farmers’ reliance on broad-spectrum pesticides.
Steven Crook, the author or co-author of four books about Taiwan, has been following environmental issues since he arrived in the country in 1991. He drives a hybrid and carries his own chopsticks. The views expressed here are his own.
