Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:06:50 UTC
23:06:50 KST

MOSCOW, September 30. /TASS/. A new version of Russia’s high-speed Supercam S180 reconnaissance unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) is capable of promptly transmitting a digital map of the terrain to the command post while conducting reconnaissance deep behind enemy lines, Unmanned Systems Group Spokeswoman Yekaterina Zgirovskaya told TASS ahead of the ADEX-2026 International Defense Exhibition in Baku.
"Developers at the Unmanned Systems Group have created a new version of the high-speed Supercam S180 reconnaissance drone, capable of promptly providing the military command with a detailed map of the terrain while the drone is still in the air. Such digital terrain map can be used for various purposes, such as in-depth reconnaissance behind enemy lines, detecting camouflaged objects, assessing roads and bridges, and identifying new trenches, fortifications, and warehouses," Zgirovskaya stated.
According to her, the data generated by the S180 system can serve as a faster alternative to visual reconnaissance data from satellite constellations, support strike planning, and track changes in the situation, including retrospectively.
The Unmanned Systems representative added that using the S180 system with a camera payload reduces the human factor. "During 'here and now' video monitoring, an operator might fail to notice something, overlook it, or simply not attach importance to it due to other aerial reconnaissance objectives. But the aerial photographs can be reviewed at any time and examined in detail," Zgirovskaya noted.
The company added that the Supercam S180 automatically adjusts its shooting speed based on the aircraft’s speed and transmits high-quality images in real time to the ground control station.

‘Terrorist attack’ by Israeli settlers on Palestinian family in West Bank condemned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:05:42 UTC
23:05:42 KST

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has said Israeli settler violence in the West Bank has made everyday life for Palestinians “untenable”, as a mob attack on Palestinians trying to return home prompted one of Benjamin Netanyahu’s main rivals to warn of a campaign of settler terror.
More than 100 militant settlers overwhelmed Israeli security forces early on Tuesday to attack a Palestinian family as they attempted to reclaim their homes which had been seized by settlers in the West Bank village of Jalud. Three Israeli security officials were injured and houses were set on fire.
The impotence of the Israeli military, the scale of the assault and the injuries inflicted on Israeli security officers by settlers prompted unusually harsh condemnation from Israeli politicians and commenters.
Israel is facing unprecedented international pressure over surging violence in the occupied West Bank, where settler militants backed by cabinet ministers have accelerated a campaign of ethnic cleansing ahead of Israel’s elections next month.
Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, condemned the attacks in Jalud as a “moral stain”. Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief and Netanyahu’s leading challenger in the upcoming elections, called for action to halt a “campaign of terror and violence”.
Deadlier attacks by Israeli settlers, including ones targeting Palestinian children, have drawn less attention inside Israel.
“Palestinian rights or safety are not the concern, even for people who are in the opposition,” said Mairav Zonszein, a senior analyst on Israel-Palestine with International Crisis Group. “The settler violence is an issue [for them] because it’s making Israel look bad, and also the idea that the military is losing control.”
The ICRC said attacks, settlement expansion and severe restrictions on movement were making everyday life untenable for Palestinian civilians and violated Israel’s obligations under international law.
“The frequent and severe violence must be brought to an end,” said Julien Lerisson, the head of the ICRC’s delegation for Israel and Palestine. “What international humanitarian law says on the protection of private and public property, and on the population’s access to essential services, must be respected.”
A bar on imports of settlement goods came into force in the Netherlands last week, the UK has announced plans for even broader controls on trade and financing of settlements, and a similar bill will be introduced in the US legislature on Thursday.
On Tuesday, a Senate bill demanding a human rights report on Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was narrowly defeated after winning backing from all but one Democrat.
“Tonight a disaster was averted, but the barrier has been broken,” the Israeli analyst Roy Sharon wrote on social media after the vote, warning that “anarchy in the West Bank” may cost Israel military aid from the US and its international legitimacy.
A cartoon in Israel’s largest-circulation newspaper, Yedioth Ahronoth, on Wednesday showed two soldiers watching an arson attack on a Palestinian home. “They’re going to ruin my trip to Amsterdam,” one says to the other.
More than 60 Palestinian communities in the occupied West Bank have been wiped off the map since October 2023 and 18 others have been partly displaced, according to the Israeli rights group B’Tselem. Nearly 5,000 people have been forced from their homes, almost half of them children.
The Tubasi family, whose homes were burned in Jalud, had been forced out this summer after a weeks-long siege by settler militants. Last week they secured a high court ruling ordering the Israeli state to evict settlers and secure their return.
Late on Monday the Israeli military told the family that about 15 military police officers would escort them home immediately, Israel’s Haaretz newspaper reported. That was a small number given that Israel is celebrating the Sukkot holiday. The number of violent extremists in illegal settlements usually rises during festivals, and the force was outnumbered by a violent crowd within minutes of arriving.
“To carry out an operation such as this, and during the holiday of Sukkot when the [settler] outposts are packed, is madness,” a security source said. The military had not informed national police and the Shin Bet domestic intelligence service of their plans, so they had no security backup.
Settlers attacked a house when the Tubasi family arrived, forcing them to the roof, before the military decided to evacuate them in armoured military vehicles. The crowd then set the homes on fire, blocked roads and threw stones at Israeli security forces, injuring three personnel.
The two houses “were damaged beyond description”, said Wael Tubasi. “They damaged everything – the doors, the tiles were removed, the stairs were removed. They smashed the bathrooms, doors and windows. They left nothing, everything was broken,” he told Reuters.
Earlier this year the former prime minister Ehud Olmert called for the international criminal court to intervene to stop settler violence because the state had failed.
Netanyahu condemned the “violent riots” and called for prosecution of the attackers, but defended the illegal settler movement. “The handful of rioters are not representative of the law-abiding settler public in Judea and Samaria,” the prime minister said, using an Israeli term for the occupied West Bank.
A landmark 2024 ruling from the UN’s international court of justice found that the occupation violated international law, a position the British government has endorsed.
An Israeli military spokesperson said two suspects had been detained, and called for action to tackle settler militants who targeted Israeli security forces.
“The violence directed at soldiers while they were carrying out their duties crosses a clear red line and is unacceptable,” the spokesperson said. “There is no place for such incidents in the state of Israel, and they must not be allowed to become the norm. Such phenomena must be addressed at their root.”
On Wednesday, some in Israel questioned whether the army and the state had the capacity to do that. “We have to look reality squarely in the eye: this was a terrorist attack and a failure by the Israeli defence establishment in its entirety,” Avi Ashkenazi wrote in the Maariv newspaper. “It is clear at this point that the real sovereign in Judea and Samaria are the extreme rightwing terrorist activists.”

France, UK discuss scrapping 2025 accord on migrant Channel crossings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:05:40 UTC
23:05:40 KST

France is in discussions with the UK on ending a 2025 accord which aimed to reduce the number of migrants irregularly crossing the Channel to England on small boats, the French interior ministry said on Wednesday.
Talks are under way on "the terms for withdrawing from the agreement", the French ministry told AFP, confirming a report in Le Monde newspaper. London had been keen to extend the deal, under which Britain takes in the same number of migrants returned to France, but Paris was less enthusiastic.
The deal was agreed in 2025 by former British prime minister Keir Starmer in a bid to help a post-Brexit reset in Paris-London ties by easing what had become a major source of tension between the neighbours.
The pilot scheme was initially agreed to last for a year but had been extended until October 1, meaning it was due for renewal.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said in June that he had "clearly announced" to Britain that this "pilot agreement... was not intended to be renewed beyond October 1, 2026."
The deal enabled Britain to deport some of the arrivals deemed not to have a right to stay.
Targeting smuggling networks
In return, London was to accept an equal number of irregular refugees from France who are likely to have their asylum claim granted, giving priority to nationalities most vulnerable to smugglers and those with ties in Britain.
The agreement aimed to smash the business model of smugglers who charge migrants huge amounts to make the perilous and sometimes deadly journey.
The deal, which was criticised by rights groups who said it was treating humans as commodities, initially targeted 2,600 exchanges.
But by early August, only 1,087 irregular refugees who had reached Britain had been returned to France under the agreement. In exchange, as of the end of June, London had legally admitted 1,117 other asylum seekers who had applied in France, according to UK data.
On Monday, three migrants, including a 10-year-old boy, died off the French coast while trying to cross the Channel to Britain, French authorities said.
At least 22 people have died this year trying to cross the Channel, according to an AFP tally based on official French and British sources. As of Sunday, some 19,135 people had crossed the Channel from France so far in 2026, down 42 percent year-on-year.

Africa's richest man Aliko Dangote broke ground on a $16 billion oil refinery in Kenya's coastal Lamu County on Wednesday, launching a major energy project intended to supply fuel to the wider East African market.
The Dangote East Africa Refinery is designed to process 700,000 barrels of crude oil a day and supply gasoline, diesel and jet fuel to Kenya and neighboring countries, potentially reducing the region’s reliance on imported refined fuel.
"I want to promise you that we will come back and commission this refinery 40 months from today," Dangote said at the groundbreaking ceremony.
Kenyan President William Ruto, who attended the ceremony, said the government planned to acquire a stake through its National Infrastructure Fund and open investment opportunities to the public.
"Kenyans from all walks of life have an opportunity to invest in this refinery. Government is going to have a stake in the refinery, and we are going to deploy assets. We do not want anything for free," Ruto said.
Earlier Wednesday, Ruto inspected construction equipment assembled at the site, saying “the magnitude of the machinery” reflected ambitions to make Lamu a major energy and industrial hub for East Africa and beyond.
Dangote also highlighted the pace of preparations, saying more than 110 pieces of equipment were already on site, with another 400 expected within 60 days.
“This is the second-fastest project we have launched, after the fertilizer factory in Ethiopia. I don’t know what magic you used on me, President Ruto,” he said.
He also argued that African economies needed to expand refining and other processing industries to reduce their reliance on exporting raw materials and importing finished products.
"Africa cannot build lasting prosperity by exporting what we have and importing what we need," Dangote said.
Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, Benin President Romuald Wadagni, Togo President Jean-Lucien Savi de Tové and Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed attended the ceremony, alongside former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo and representatives of other African governments.
Project faces legal challenge
The project is, however, facing a legal challenge over land earmarked for the development.
A group of 133 residents has gone to court claiming ancestral rights to the disputed land and raising concerns about compensation and environmental safeguards.
Dangote said the company was prepared to face legal challenges.
"We're not scared of people taking us to court. Anybody who wants to cause trouble, we're ready for his trouble, and we'll give him a headache," he said.
The Environment and Land Court in Malindi has ordered the parties to maintain the status quo on the disputed land pending further proceedings scheduled for Oct. 14.

Rare bronze statuette of Priapus discovered at Novae near Svishtov
Wednesday 30 September 2026 15:48
Wednesday, 30 September 2026, 15:48
PHOTO uw.edu.pl
Font size
A rare bronze statuette of the ancient Greek god Priapus has been discovered during archaeological excavations at the Roman city of Novae near Svishtov. Only five similar finds are known from the Lower Danube region, the University of Warsaw said.
Novae has been continuously studied by a Polish-Bulgarian archaeological team since 1960. Prof. Piotr Dyczek, Director of the University of Warsaw’s Antiquity of Southeastern Europe Research Centre, said the latest finds also include “a fragment of a gold ring and two inscribed altars, one of them almost completely preserved”.
“Each of these finds is another piece of the puzzle that allows us to better understand the lives of the inhabitants of Novae and the history of this exceptionally important Roman centre on the Danube,” the professor said.
The bronze statuette was discovered by archaeologists from the University of Warsaw while excavating a monumental residential complex covering more than 3,000 square metres, Petya Andreeva, Chief Assistant Professor at the National Archaeological Institute with Museum at the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences, told 24 Chasa. Other finds include painted plasterwork and an exquisitely crafted multicoloured floor.

Voice of America cuts undermine US national interests, inspector general says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:03:55 UTC
23:03:55 KST

Yasin Gungor
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Sweeping cuts to the agency overseeing Voice of America weakened US broadcasting during international crises and damaged US interests, a State Department watchdog said.
The Office of Inspector General said the US Agency for Global Media (USAGM) rushed to slash operations without adequate planning or cost analysis after President Donald Trump ordered it to scale back in March 2025.
The cuts reduced the agency’s ability to inform audiences worldwide and counter disinformation in countries with restricted access to independent news, according to the evaluation, which was published last week and publicized Tuesday.
“The reduction in operations diminished USAGM's capacity to fulfill its core statutory mission of informing, engaging, and connecting people worldwide in support of freedom and democracy,” the report said.
The watchdog said leadership bypassed established procedures for managing organizational changes and acted within 24 hours of Trump’s executive order, without sufficiently considering the reforms or using “reliable data or evidence to inform its decision making.”
The consequences became apparent during the June 2025 strikes on Iran. When Voice of America sought to restart its Persian-language service, only two employees remained, including one who did not speak Persian, according to the report.
Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, which receives core federal funding from USAGM, likewise suspended transmissions across 27 languages in 2025 due to funding cutoffs, halting Ukrainian and Russian programming.
“Decreasing the number of broadcasting languages may lessen USAGM’s impact on advancing U.S. national interests, supporting democratic values and countering disinformation in closed societies,” it added.
The evaluation said that protracted legal challenges left 420 employees on paid administrative leave as of July 2026, costing taxpayers $82.8 million annually.
Federal courts ruled the mass dismissals unlawful and ordered staff reinstated, but operations had not been fully restored, the report added.
Trump’s March 14, 2025 executive order directed USAGM to eliminate functions not required by law and reduce its remaining activities and staffing to the legal minimum.

He owns 49% of USM, a Russian investment group that controls Metalloinvest, the country’s largest iron ore producer, as well as telecoms giant Megafon.
- Usmanov was able to wield influence in Paris thanks to his connections across other ex-Soviet countries — specifically a longstanding friendship with Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev. In exchange for French support to remove sanctions on Usmanov, Aliyev promised to release two French businessmen jailed in Baku — Martin Ryan, sentenced to 10 years on espionage charges in March 2026, and Anass Derraz, jailed for 12 years in a bribery case. A former aide to Emmanuel Macron was implicated in the Derraz case. In the end, only Ryan was released.
- When it emerged that Usmanov might escape sanctions, Luxembourg followed the French lead and announced that it would demand an end to sanctions on Mikhail Fridman, who had similarly been pressing for years to be taken off the list and filed a €16-billion lawsuit against the government.
- Fridman is a Russian business veteran who also made his riches in the chaotic 1990s. His Alfa Group included leading Russian bank Alfa Bank, the country’s top retailer X5 and the prominent Vimpelcom mobile phone operator. In 2010, Alfa Group made more than $8 billion from the sale of 25% of oil company TNK-ВР to state-owned Rosneft. Fridman and his partners used that money to buy up international assets, consolidating them under the LetterOne holding. The billionaire himself moved to London but fell under British and European sanctions in 2022.
- For now, the removal of sanctions on Usmanov and Fridman is the exception, not the rule. The European Council extended sanctions against 3,000 other Russian individuals and businesses for a previously unimaginable three years (before, there was debate inside the EU about whether to extend sanctions for six or 12 months).
- Now both Russian oligarchs can travel freely in Europe, manage their unblocked assets, including bank accounts, villas, yachts and aircraft, and do business inside the EU. Fridman, for example, can reclaim his stake in Luxembourg-registered LetterOne, which controls the portfolio of international assets acquired with his partners over the decades. Both men remain under American and British sanctions.
Why the world should care
Blacklisting oligarchs has arguably been the most pointless of the West's sanctions initiatives in practical terms. If anything, it has helped Vladimir Putin's regime by rallying the oligarchs around the Kremlin and trapping their capital inside Russia. It might have made sense to offer the oligarchs a way out of sanctions in exchange for doing something useful, such as condemning the aggression or helping Ukraine. But Usmanov and Fridman have now been delisted for nothing, and for the rest, that window has closed, at least until 2029.
France’s willingness to undermine the EU’s agreed sanctions policy in favor of its own specific interests risks further dividing European sanctions policy — something the Kremlin has long hoped for, bet on and tried to engineer. Other EU states will now be far less willing to vote for sanctions that run counter to their own national interests. For instance, Greece and Malta do not like sanctions targeting the maritime transport of Russian oil, and central European countries have interests in Russian gas.

Everything Netanyahu does is to stay out of jail: The Bibi Files’ director
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:58:14 UTC
22:58:14 KST

- ‘It’s sort of almost like a monkey on his back, and people forget that he’s motivated to stay out of jail, and everything he does comes back to that,’ Alexis Bloom tells Anadolu
- Bloom says film struggled to secure mainstream US distribution despite Academy Award shortlist, international screenings
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s every political move is shaped by his ongoing corruption trial and his desire to avoid jail, according to Alexis Bloom, director of the documentary The Bibi Files.
“The main message of the documentary is that this man who is leading Israel to the bottom of the sea has a very serious legal case,” Bloom told Anadolu ahead of a screening of the film at the European Parliament in Brussels.
“It’s sort of almost like a monkey on his back, and people forget that he’s motivated to stay out of jail, and everything he does comes back to that,” she said.
Netanyahu was indicted in 2019 on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate cases. He has denied wrongdoing and pleaded not guilty. His trial, which began in 2020, remains ongoing.
Bloom said she wants audiences to look beyond the rapidly changing daily news cycle and consider Netanyahu’s legal troubles as part of the broader context surrounding his political decisions.
“I would just say, in the daily reporting of deaths and riots and settlements and all the very intense news that happens day to day, take a breath and step back and remember the big picture,” she said.
The Bibi Files is built around leaked footage of police interrogations of Netanyahu, his wife Sara, his son Yair and people in their political and personal circles.
Producer Alex Gibney received more than 1,000 hours of leaked interrogation material before approaching Bloom to direct the documentary, which also involved interviews with insiders willing to speak about Netanyahu.
For Bloom, the film, which premiered in 2024, is an example of how cinema can turn complex political and legal issues into a story that audiences can experience on a more immediate and personal level.
Difficult journey to audiences
The film itself has faced obstacles reaching audiences.
The day before its screening at the Toronto International Film Festival, lawyers representing Netanyahu sought an injunction from an Israeli court to prevent publication of the interrogation footage.
The court rejected the request and the screening went ahead.
The film has also faced restrictions in Israel because of privacy laws, while it has been distributed and screened internationally.
However, Bloom said the difficulties continued beyond Israel, particularly in the United States.
"It was very difficult to release this film in America, and some newspapers didn't even want to review it," she explained.
"We did not get mainstream distribution, even though we were shortlisted for an Academy Award, and it broadcast all over Europe. An American mainstream streamer didn't want to take us on, so it was difficult to get it out there," the director added.
The film has received strong critical attention internationally. Rotten Tomatoes currently lists it with a 95% critics’ score.
‘People are moved by art’
For Bloom, the documentary also illustrates the ability of art to engage audiences with political and social questions in ways conventional political discourse often cannot.
“I think that people are moved by art, and it’s very important for art to engage them,” Bloom said.
“I think art is political. That’s my instinct.”
Political issues, she said, are frequently presented through legal documents, official statements, speeches and daily news reports, but cinema can create a different form of engagement.
The ability of art to move audiences is not separate from its political significance, she added.
"If we want to make political changes, we have to engage people not just with dry old literature, or slogans or kind of bureaucratic means. It has to be through art. It has to be through music. It has to be through everything," she said.
'You cannot stop thousands of cinemas'
Despite distribution hurdles, the film is finding another route to audiences through cinemas.
The documentary is preparing for a major theatrical release in Italy, with screenings planned in around 130 cinemas, accompanied by a live event.
"People want to see what's happening in Israel and want to know what are the corruption allegations against Netanyahu," Italian distributor and journalist Giulia Innocenzi told Anadolu.
She said some screenings had already sold out and expressed hope that the response would encourage more cinemas to show the documentary.
"But not all of them want to screen this movie because, of course, Netanyahu is very powerful, and it's a political issue," Innocenzi said.
She also recalled attempts to block the film’s screening.
"Bibi Files was not screened in Israel because of violation of privacy policy, but also Netanyahu tried to block this movie before the Toronto Film Festival," Innocenzi noted.
She argued that cinema can offer political expression more room than traditional media because attempts to restrict one outlet do not necessarily prevent audiences from accessing a film elsewhere.
“You can try to stop one media stream. You can try to stop a TV channel, but you cannot stop thousands of cinemas,” she said.

Spain orders probe after rights group alleges troops abused migrants in Ceuta

Spain orders probe after rights group alleges troops abused migrants in Ceuta
MADRID, Sept 29 - Spain's Defence Ministry said on Wednesday it had alerted prosecutors to an Amnesty International report alleging the military tortured or mistreated migrants in Ceuta, and ordered an internal probe into whether any personnel were to blame.
The rights group accused members of Spain's armed forces of torture and other cruel, inhumane or degrading treatment of migrants stranded in the North African enclave after over 72,000 crossed the border from Morocco in late July.
Though most of the migrants later went back, at least 10,000 remain in the tiny Spanish enclave in North Africa, straining local resources and fuelling tensions.
Amnesty International Spain Director Esteban Beltran told Reuters the group had documented 22 cases of torture and abuse by military personnel. In what he said appeared to be a pattern, troops had pursued, beaten and humiliated migrants, including women and unaccompanied children, in nighttime operations.
Amnesty said photographs and videos it reviewed were consistent with allegations of excessive force, including images of hooded personnel striking migrants and spraying their faces with irritants before pushing them across the border.
"In view of the report made public by Amnesty International, it has been agreed to send the report to the prosecutor's office and the duty court in Ceuta, and to instruct the Operations Command to investigate and clarify any possible individual responsibilities," the Defence Ministry said.
Amnesty's Beltran welcomed the move but said it should have come sooner, calling for an exhaustive investigation and the suspension of any military personnel implicated.
"These individuals cannot remain in their duties for a single minute longer, at least as a precautionary measure, until responsibilities are determined," he said.
Amnesty also called for improved humanitarian assistance for migrants still sleeping rough in Ceuta.
"This situation has worried us greatly. They are living in deplorable conditions," Beltran said. REUTERS

Sweden should apologise for injustices against Sami people, commission says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:57:48 UTC
22:57:48 KST

Sweden should apologise for injustices against Sami people, commission says
STOCKHOLM, Sept 30 - The Swedish government should apologise to the indigenous Sami people for past injustices and Sami interests should be given stronger consideration against mining and wind power projects, a government-appointed commission said on Wednesday.
An estimated 80,000 to 100,000 Sami live in the northern lands of Sweden, Finland, Norway and Russia, where reindeer herding over vast areas has been the cornerstone of their culture and livelihood.
The government-appointed Truth Commission said that the Swedish state had unilaterally taken ownership of large parts of Sami land, especially during the 18th and 19th centuries.
"The indigenous Sami people today face major challenges in preserving and developing their culture as a direct consequence of the Swedish state's past and present policies," the Truth Commission wrote in the report published on the government webpage.
The commission's findings add Sweden to a list of Nordic countries confronting their treatment of the Sami. Norway, which is home to around 50,000 Sami people, officially apologised in 2024, and a Finnish commission called for redress in 2025.
The report said Sami communities had been forcibly displaced as far back as the 17th century. The commission urged the government to "acknowledge the historical wrongs, abuses, and violations ... and the harm this has caused the Sami people".
The Swedish parliament recognised the Sami as an indigenous people in 1977, but relations with the state have often been contentious. In recent years, they have clashed with authorities over mining and wind power projects the Sami feel impact their reindeer herding.
The commission said the government should strengthen the land use rights status for reindeer herding. The Sami reindeer herding areas cover around a third of Sweden, bigger than the total area of England. REUTERS

Farage spoils for a Brexit brawl with Burnham
Unknown

2026-09-30
13:55:45 UTC

Nigel Farage speaks at a press conference during the Reform UK party conference in Birmingham, England on Sept. 4, 2026. | Oli Scarff/AFP via Getty Images
LIVERPOOL, England — Nigel Farage will use a speech in a Brexit-backing Labour heartland to start the fightback after Andy Burnham reignited Britain’s EU debate.
The Reform UK leader — a key architect of Brexit — will make a “major speech” in Doncaster on Thursday to rail against the Labour prime minister opening the door to a possible return to the bloc, a senior Reform official told POLITICO.
Burnham used his first Labour conference as leader, in Liverpool on Tuesday, to snip three political livewires in British politics, including proposing a change to the “triple lock” protecting the state pension and electoral reform.
Advertisement
Farage is spoiling to address all these fault-lines on Thursday.
“He will talk about Burnham wanting to take us into the Euro, return us to freedom of movement with 500 million people and losing the ability to nationalize key industries,” said the Reform official, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss the pending speech in Doncaster.
The Yorkshire city voted 69% in favor of leaving the EU in the 2016 referendum, making it one of the most pro-Brexit areas in the U.K. One of its MPs is Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.
Burnham has reopened the debate in Labour and beyond by saying he will canvass opinion on several options for Britain’s future arrangement with Brussels and set them out around the time of a EU-U.K. summit later this year.
Those options, he has said, could include rejoining the single market, the customs union, or “go all the way,” which Reform is interpreting as scrapping the Pound in favor of the Euro. Burnham has not made that specific pledge, and Labour resisted Britain joining the single currency when it was introduced.
Farage is meanwhile planning to argue that EU re-entry would curb the ability of British governments to nationalize key industries — a play by the Reform leader that upends the traditional left-right debate in British politics. Burnham has put emphasis on bringing back “public control” of privatized utilities rather than public ownership, but Farage has changed tack from his Thatcherite credentials to express support for nationalization in some sectors.
Advertisement
So far most of Farage’s criticism of Burnham’s speech has centered on accusing Labour of “going after pensioners” on the triple lock.
But his stance on the PM announcing a commission to investigate overhauling Britain’s first-past-the-post electoral system will be one to watch.
The current voting system makes it incredibly hard for insurgent parties, like Reform, to get a foothold in Parliament. But after a certain polling threshold is crossed it rewards parties with vast numbers of seats on proportionally little of the vote.
Farage has long been in favor of changing this system — but his party has recently attacked Labour’s reversion to a more proportional voting system in mayoral races as being an “establishment stitch-up.”

A commercial plane travelling from Dubai in the United Arab Emirates to Israel has been forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, after an apparent brawl between its pilots prompted distress signals that briefly raised fears of an attempted hijacking. The flydubai flight was over Jordan when it diverted to Saudi Arabia, transmitting three emergency signals, one of which indicated a possible unlawful interference.
The plane dipped dramatically during the reported fight, descending about 16,000ft in just two minutes. Israeli officials scrambled fighter jets, fearful of a possible hijacking attempt on a plane containing dozens of Israelis, and the plane landed at Tabuk airport in north-western Saudi Arabia.
Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu said one of the flydubai pilots stabbed his fellow pilot and intended to crash the plane. He added that one of the passengers on the flight managed to break into the cockpit with one of the crew members, and together they “neutralised” the attacking pilot.

Netanyahu thanked the passengers and crew who helped to stop the attack, saying they “showed exceptional resourcefulness and courage”.

The Boeing 737 plane, which Israeli officials said had between 160 and 180 passengers on board, transmitted a general emergency signal about two and a half hours after departing from Dubai, according to flight-tracking website Flightradar24.
Passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon said the plane was “pretty much out of control” when the alleged stabbing took place over Jordan on the flight’s path from Dubai to Tel Aviv. “The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane,” she told reporters by speakerphone held up by her mother who was waiting at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv.
The plane again transmitted the initial general emergency signal before later landing at Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk airport. Tabuk airport said the plane landed at 9.45am local time and that both pilots were taken to hospital after sustaining injuries.

A key piece of information from the FlyDubai flight is that someone in the cockpit transmitted emergency codes.
Pilots use four-digit ‘squawk codes’ to broadcast their position for air traffic control. These are used for routine flight but also in emergency situations.
Aircraft trackers at Flight Radar say the FlyDubai plane transmitted both emergency and hijack signals.
The plane transmitted a 7700 squawk code that means emergency. It also transmitted a 7500 squawk code, which can mean a hijacking.
These codes have to be manually entered from the cockpit.

“TEKNOFEST is a confidence revolution. It is a rebellion against the mentality that says, ‘We cannot do it.’ It is an objection to imitation and learned helplessness,” Bayraktar said in his opening address.
Türkiye’s premier aviation, space and technology festival TEKNOFEST opened its doors to visitors Wednesday in the southeastern province of Sanliurfa.
TEKNOFEST Southeast, a leg of the event held in southeastern Türkiye, brings together tech enthusiasts, young investors and thousands of visitors for various shows, exhibitions and the finals of technology competitions across 14 categories from Wednesday through Oct. 4.
Describing Sanliurfa as “the zero point of history,” Bayraktar said it was among the lands where humanity transitioned to settled life, developed agriculture and laid the foundations of civilization.
‘More than 1.6 million young people applied’
Holding its 15th festival since its launch in 2018, Bayraktar said the TEKNOFEST “seedling we planted in 2018 has today turned into a major technology movement.”
He said young people from all 81 provinces of Türkiye and 97 countries were participating in the festival, adding that more than 730,000 teams and over 1.6 million young people had applied to technology competitions in 62 categories.
“These are not just numbers. They are Türkiye’s changing story,” Bayraktar said.
He highlighted the participation of young people from southeastern Türkiye, saying children in the region were learning artificial intelligence and robotics at DENEYAP Technology Workshops.
Referring to the region’s hot climate, Bayraktar said: “When we came to Urfa, we understood something else. If a system works smoothly at noon in the Urfa heat, it will work anywhere in the world, and even in space.”
‘National Technology Initiative is not only in the sky’
Bayraktar said confidence strengthens production, production strengthens technology, and technology creates the foundation for independence.
“That is why the National Technology Initiative exists,” he said.
“The National Technology Initiative is not only in the sky. It is in the fields, factories, laboratories, hospitals, workshops and universities.”
He said the initiative aims to turn ideas into economic value, dreams into production, projects into employment and technology into prosperity for Türkiye.
“Our goal is high technology, domestic production and value-added exports,” Bayraktar said.
“We want to build an entrepreneurship ecosystem that will strengthen our country’s full independence, led by the TEKNOFEST generation.”
- Agricultural technologies in focus
Bayraktar also highlighted the strategic importance of agricultural production, saying food had become a more critical issue than ever.
“We can no longer view agriculture simply as a traditional sector. Agriculture must become one of the high-technology fields of the future,” he said.
He pointed to next-generation national agricultural technologies, AI-supported solutions, genetic science, efficiency and sustainable production as areas of focus.
“As the solutions developed by young people meet these fertile lands, our future will become stronger and more prosperous,” he said.
- Bringing science together with conscience
Bayraktar also addressed the rapid transformation driven by artificial intelligence, saying the technology could accelerate learning and research but should be viewed as a tool that expands human potential rather than a guide that replaces human judgment.
“Technology is a tool. It is the human who determines its direction and must make the final decision,” he said.
“Our aim is not merely to develop technology, but to determine what kind of spirit and direction we will give it,” Bayraktar said.
“We want to use technology for the benefit of humanity. We want to bring science together with conscience, intelligence with morality, and power with justice.”

An Israeli passenger who helped subdue the suspected attacker aboard Flydubai Flight FZ1073 said Wednesday that passengers restrained him using cables from the headphones distributed during the flight, offering new details of the struggle inside the aircraft.
Zvika Manes, CEO of Bank Leumi underwriting company Barak Capital Underwriting and one of the passengers who helped overpower the suspect, told Kan 11 that three passengers restrained the pilot using the cables from the aircraft’s multimedia headphones.
According to Manes, passengers first realized something was wrong when his wife went toward the restroom with their daughter and heard a confrontation coming from the cockpit.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also provided new details Wednesday after speaking with one of the Israeli passengers involved in the incident.
“During the flight, as they approached Israel, one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot and apparently tried to crash the plane with everyone aboard,” Netanyahu said.
He said the passenger described the aircraft entering a spin and beginning to plunge.
“He told me that, somehow, he managed to break into the cockpit with one of the crew members, and together they subdued the stabbing pilot while he was trying to sabotage the aircraft’s systems,” Netanyahu said.
Netanyahu said another member of the flight crew then entered the cockpit and managed to stabilize the aircraft.
“I salute these heroes, who showed extraordinary resourcefulness and courage,” he said. “They saved many lives. They prevented a major disaster.”
The incident occurred aboard Flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv. Israeli security officials have increasingly been investigating the episode as a suspected terrorist attack after the aircraft plunged sharply, transmitted emergency and hijacking codes and diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
Passenger testimony from aboard the aircraft has described Israelis entering the cockpit during the violent confrontation and helping overpower the suspected attacker.
Manes previously told ynet’s sister publication Calcalist that his wife was near the cockpit when she heard screams and called for help. He said a relief pilot and several passengers then entered the cockpit and subdued the suspect.
Netanyahu said Wednesday that the suspected attacker had been arrested and was being questioned by Saudi authorities.
“The stabbing pilot has been arrested and is currently being interrogated by the Saudi authorities,” he said. “We are maintaining continuous contact with the relevant authorities to ensure the passengers remain safe and are returned home securely.”

====================================================================================================

China to accelerate modern water network development during 2026-2030
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:42:54 CST
22:42:54 KST

The State Council Information Office (SCIO) holds a press conference on accelerating the construction of a modernized water network in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Jin Liwang)
BEIJING, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- China will step up efforts to build a modern water network during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), with the national water network expected to cover 82 percent of the country's territory by 2030, Minister of Water Resources Li Guoying said Wednesday.
As part of this effort, China will strengthen flood control by improving a system comprising reservoirs, rivers, levees and flood storage and detention areas, and by upgrading monitoring and forecasting based on satellites, radar, rainfall stations and hydrological stations, Li told a press conference.
By the end of 2030, the country aims to add 15 billion cubic meters of reservoir storage capacity and bring 91 percent of key levees up to standard, he said.
China will accelerate efforts to build a system for the optimal allocation of water resources and water supply, and coordinate the development of the national backbone water network with provincial, municipal and county-level water networks.
It will speed up the modernization and upgrading of irrigation districts and promote standardized rural water supply and management. By 2030, the country aims to add 40 million mu (about 2.67 million hectares) of irrigated farmland and raise the rural tap water coverage rate to 98 percent.
The country will strengthen the protection and restoration of aquatic ecosystems, including restoring rivers and lakes and tackling groundwater over-extraction and soil erosion. By the end of 2030, it aims to treat an additional 310,000 square km of land that has been affected by soil erosion.
The country aims to establish a national water network dispatch center, a big data center and basin-level sub-centers, enabling comprehensive monitoring and sensing, intelligent analysis and forecasting, and forward-looking decision support to improve the coordinated management of flood control, water supply and ecological protection, said Li.
Building a modern water network is of particular importance for China, where water resources are unevenly distributed across regions and seasons and floods and droughts occur frequently, with intensifying impacts of global climate change and frequent extreme flood and drought events.
The water network is one of the "six networks" prioritized during China's 15th Five-Year Plan period, alongside new-type power grids, computing power networks, next-generation communication networks, urban underground pipeline networks and logistics networks.
During the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), China completed 5.68 trillion yuan (about 843 billion U.S. dollars) in water conservancy investment, started construction of 181 major water conservancy projects and put 94 major projects into operation, with the national water network covering 80.3 percent of the country's territory by the end of 2025. ■

Italy's main opposition PD boycotts antisemitism bill vote amid split on left
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:42:52 UTC
22:42:52 KST

Italy's main opposition PD boycotts antisemitism bill vote amid split on left
ROME, Sept 30 - Italy's Democratic Party did not take part in a parliamentary committee vote on Wednesday on a highly contested bill against antisemitism, highlighting divisions on the left over a law seen as potentially curbing criticism of Israel.
A PD source said the party considered the definition of antisemitism included in the bill was "divisive" and urged the right-wing ruling coalition backing it to change its formulation, but this call is likely to fall on deaf ears.
The bill would write into law the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition of antisemitism, which lists certain criticisms of Israel as examples of antisemitism.
Critics say this definition could restrict freedom of expression, censoring legitimate activism for Palestinian rights and contributing to conflating Jews with the state of Israel.
The dispute reflects broader differences on the Italian left over the war in Gaza. The PD has condemned the violence, but has adopted a more cautious tone than its allies, the Five Star Movement and the Green Left Alliance (AVS), which have accused Israel of genocide, which Israel denies.
APPEAL TO CHANGE
Most PD lawmakers abstained when the bill passed the Senate earlier this year, but a small group voted in favour, exposing divisions within the party. The bill is now due to obtain final approval at the lower house Chamber.
"We call on the majority to heed our appeal to change that divisive definition and make it clear that those who criticise the actions of the Israeli government cannot be accused of antisemitism," PD lower house leader Chiara Braga said last week.
Party member Emanuele Fiano, the son of an Auschwitz survivor who supports the bill, criticised the PD's decision not to back it, saying: "I will not accept the fight against antisemitism being portrayed as an obstacle to criticism of (Benjamin) Netanyahu's government, the Israeli military or violence by settlers."
The AVS and Five Star voted against the proposal.
"There is no doubt that on an issue such as antisemitism it would be desirable to have a unanimous vote, but there is equally no doubt that this bill needs to be changed because it is fundamentally flawed," AVS co-leader Nicola Fratoianni said.
Supporters of the bill say stronger safeguards are needed following a rise in antisemitic incidents after Hamas-led attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, and the ensuing Gaza war. Italy's Antisemitism Observatory recorded 963 cases in 2025, more than double the number reported in 2022. REUTERS

Chinese icebreakers Xuelong, Xuelong 2 return after fruitful Arctic expedition
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:42:37 CST
22:42:37 KST

SHANGHAI, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- China's research icebreakers Xuelong, or "Snow Dragon," and Xuelong 2 returned to Shanghai in east China on Wednesday after nearly three months of the country's 16th Arctic Ocean expedition.
The expedition successfully completed key tasks, including comprehensive investigation and monitoring, cutting-edge scientific research, and international cooperation. According to the expedition team, both the scale of the expedition and the total number of tasks reached new highs.
It achieved fruitful results in new scientific discoveries, theoretical breakthroughs, technological tests, and equipment applications, providing strong support for a deeper understanding of and effective response to global climate change and promoting sustainable development in the Arctic, said Wang Jinhui, the leader of the expedition team.
A series of new discoveries and breakthroughs made during the expedition have refreshed China's understanding of the marine environment and geophysics of the Arctic Ocean. For example, researchers found that the subsurface water in some areas of the Arctic Ocean exhibited a warming phenomenon.
During the expedition, Chinese researchers also captured some juvenile polar cod in a densely ice-covered area in the high Arctic, a discovery that may deepen scientists' understanding of the species and its habitat's ecosystem.
Through the dual-vessel operation of the Xuelong and Xuelong 2, 19 ice station operations and 95 sets of ice-based buoy deployment tasks were completed in the high-latitude waters of the Arctic Ocean in a coordinated manner, establishing a local unmanned observation array. Both the number of stations and the number of ice-based buoys deployed reached a record high, according to He Jianfeng, the chief scientist of the expedition team.
"The relevant work can not only deepen China's understanding of the rapid changes in the Arctic Ocean, improve the accuracy and level of our prediction of sea ice and ocean changes in the Arctic Ocean, but also provide valuable cross-seasonal first-hand observational data for the international governance of the Arctic Ocean's ecology," He added.
Significant breakthroughs have been achieved in the application of high-latitude communication technology. During ice station operations, the Xuelong icebreaker achieved video call and data transmission with the Qinling Station in Antarctica via its shipborne satellite internet communication equipment.
The expedition team has carried out various forms of scientific research cooperation, with seven scientists from Russia, Germany, Thailand and China's Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.
Organized by the Ministry of Natural Resources, the 16th Arctic Ocean expedition was carried out by four vessels: Xuelong, Xuelong 2, Jidi and Tansuo-3.
Jidi and Tansuo-3 are still on their research missions and are expected to return in mid-October. ■

ATHENS, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis on Wednesday announced a new package of measures aimed at easing pressure on households and businesses from rising fuel and operating costs.
Speaking at a Cabinet meeting, Mitsotakis said the government would raise the diesel subsidy from 10 euro cents (11 U.S. cents) to 15 euro cents (17 U.S. cents) per liter for the first 15 days of October. Combined with discounts offered by refiners, the total reduction will be 20 euro cents (23 U.S. cents) per liter.

“We have taken supportive measures to improve service infrastructure, upgrade streets and create suitable conditions for construction and strengthening buildings,” Golpayegani said, adding that the broader objective is to improve the urban environment and create conditions conducive to the restoration and revival of historical houses.
Regarding the historical bazaars, he said the ongoing projects include paving, organizing roofs and improving the façades of around 20 bazaars in cooperation with municipalities and shopkeepers.
“When a historical bazaar is restored and brought into suitable condition, it naturally creates the basis for revitalizing construction and restoring houses in the surrounding area,” he said.
Golpayegani also highlighted efforts to restore historical houses, some of which had fallen into poor condition over the years. Among the projects, he cited the restoration of the Badie al-Sanae’ House in Isfahan and the Salehan House in Hamedan.
He said restoring a historical house and converting it into a suitable, high-quality service facility can have a positive impact beyond the building itself, encouraging the improvement, renovation and strengthening of neighboring properties.
The former official also referred to the restoration of historical bathhouses in several cities, saying the projects are being carried out with the assistance of municipalities and funding allocated by the Urban Regeneration Company of Iran.
Following restoration, the bathhouses can be converted into service facilities, he added.
Golpayegani said several medium-sized and small cities across the country have also taken effective steps toward reviving historical buildings with support from the Urban Regeneration Company.
“There is still considerable potential and much work to be done in this field, and we hope this process will continue,” he said.
He stressed that revitalizing historical districts should not be limited to restoring individual buildings. Instead, a comprehensive approach involving street improvements, provision of services, the revival of bazaars and historical buildings, and the creation of appropriate new uses for them is needed to gradually stimulate the regeneration of entire historical areas.

CIA's Ratcliffe Reportedly Warned Kremlin of Soviet-Style Collapse in Moscow Visit

13:29:45 UTC
22:29:45 KST

CIA Director John Ratcliffe reportedly warned the Kremlin during his Moscow visit against a collapse similar to that of the Soviet Union in the 1990s should it continue the war in Ukraine, a new German report claimed.
Ratcliffe visited Moscow unannounced in late August, with details of the visit undisclosed.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
But German outlet Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ), citing “a high-ranking diplomat familiar with the CIA’s briefings to Western partner agencies,” claimed on Saturday that Ratcliffe cautioned Moscow of a potential collapse similar to that of the USSR.
According to the outlet, Ratcliffe conveyed Washington’s assessment that Russia has struggled to make military gains while its economy risks buckling under war-related pressure, reinforcing the call for Moscow to negotiate and not count on Washington to abandon Kyiv.
Recent reports note that the Kremlin expects its 2026 budget deficit to reach 3.2% of gross domestic product (GDP) – up from an earlier estimate of 1.6% – while optimistically lowering that forecast in 2027 to 2%, mainly by borrowing.
For context, a World Bank assessment from March 1992 estimated the budget deficit to the gross national product (GNP) to be 20% by 1991, the year of its collapse, after rising from the average of 2% in the early 1980s – though the ratio itself is not a sure-fire indicator of economic collapse.
But the FAZ’s claim is broadly in line with those reported by the New York Times (NYT) in the wake of the visit, with the outlet – citing current and former US officials – claiming that Ratcliffe delivered a similar assessment to Aleksandr Bortnikov, head of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB).
While Russia Pounds Kyiv, Most Russians Support ‘Global Cooperation’
US officials reportedly hoped Putin, himself a former Soviet intelligence officer, would take a message from the CIA director more seriously than one delivered through traditional diplomatic channels.
Other outlets speculated the visit might have been to caution Moscow against aiding Iran or escalating against NATO.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin signed three undisclosed decrees following Ratcliffe’s visit – though their connections with the visit remain unclear – while President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv was subsequently briefed on the visit without disclosing details.
Zelensky also reportedly met Ratcliffe during a stop in Ireland en route to New York’s UN General Assembly in September, following earlier rumors that Ratcliffe might be taking over the negotiator role from US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner due to the lack of progress.
Little signs of de-escalation
While it’s unclear whether Ratcliffe delivered his warning against a Soviet-style collapse, Moscow has braced for major escalation.
Days after mid-September’s State Duma elections, Putin has signed a new decree expanding the military to 2.4 million personnel, including 1.5 million active-duty troops, while Kyiv warned that Moscow is also expanding North Korean contingents deployed to the country.
Financially, Moscow is also eyeing a historic hike in defense spending in its 2027 budget, bringing the sum to a record 17.1 trillion rubles ($203 billion) – or roughly 35% of Russia’s total federal expenditures that year.
The measures also coincide with European warnings of a potential armed confrontation with Moscow in the coming months, with the Kremlin also raising its nuclear posture in its exclave of Kaliningrad.
With Russia’s winter campaign against Ukraine beginning in earnest on Wednesday, Sept. 30, according to Kyiv, and the Kremlin ruling out peace talks for now, FAZ suggested the winter could be Putin’s last bid to consolidate his position before negotiations begin.

S. Korean ambassador highlights Iran’s ecotourism potential

S. Korean ambassador highlights Iran’s ecotourism potential
TEHRAN – South Korean Ambassador to Iran Kim Junpyo has highlighted the potential of Iran’s ecotourism sector to support local economies and offer visitors authentic experiences of local culture and daily life.
What is taking shape in Iran’s ecotourism sector today is not merely the provision of accommodation services, but the creation of experiences rooted in local communities and people’s real lives, Kim said, according to a report published by the Iranian Ministry of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts and carried by IRNA on Wednesday.
The ambassador made the remarks during a meeting with Yavar Abiri, head of the Iranian Ecolodge Association, at the Sangan Ecolodge in Tehran, held during the National Tourism Week.
Kim said tourism was changing globally, with travelers increasingly seeking opportunities to interact with local people, explore indigenous cultures and experience the lifestyles of destination communities rather than simply visit tourist attractions.
Reflecting on his approximately two and a half years in Iran, the ambassador said the country had considerable tourism potential because of its history, culture and civilization. He added that Iran could introduce its distinctive cultural characteristics to international visitors.
“Iran has considerable potential for tourism rooted in culture and local life,” he said, referring to the diverse cultures and lifestyles he had encountered during his stay.
Drawing on South Korea’s experience in developing cultural tourism, the ambassador said tourism experiences with stronger local and authentic characteristics had greater potential for international promotion.
He noted that preserving traditional architecture, historic houses, clothing, cuisine and handicrafts in some parts of South Korea had become an integral part of the visitor experience.
Abiri said the meeting aimed to introduce Iran’s ecotourism potential to South Korean travelers and create opportunities to expand tourism cooperation between the two countries.
He said ecotourism lodges offer visitors more than accommodation, allowing them to discover local culture, cuisine, handicrafts, nature and the lifestyles of communities in different regions.
Given Iran’s climatic and cultural diversity, the country could host tourists throughout the year, Abiri said, adding that ecotourism lodges could help attract international visitors by offering distinctive local experiences at affordable prices.
Participants also stressed the importance of strengthening links between Iranian ecotourism operators and specialized tourism organizations in South Korea, as well as exchanging experience in rural tourism, traditional accommodation and community development.

AI becomes matter of global power as White House pushes for techno-feudal era
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:29:31 UTC
22:29:31 KST

Mertkan Oruc and Emir Yildirim
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
 Artificial intelligence (AI) has been positioned as a central element of the global power struggle, with the White House under US President Donald Trump gathering AI leaders and reigniting debates over techno-feudalism, the head of the Turkish AI policy association AIPA told Anadolu.
 
Zafer Kucuksabanoglu stated that the world’s most powerful tech figures took part in the meeting, which he said showed a snapshot of how the new world order is taking shape, with figures like Elon Musk, Jensen Huang, Mark Zuckerberg, Sundar Pichai, Satya Nadella and Jeff Bezos seated alongside senior government officials.
He noted that these tech billionaires were also prominently placed during Trump’s January 2025 inauguration, which served as a harbinger of this new era.
“This concentration of power is precisely at the heart of the ongoing techno-feudalism debate — for instance, Trump’s push to redefine AI as ‘superintelligence’ is not just a terminological shift but a claim to global leadership in this advanced technology as a political and strategic narrative,” he said. “Trump asserted that the AI competition is essentially between the US and China, while stressing that development must not slow down.”
Kucuksabanoglu stated that industry leaders recently called for slowing the pace of AI development for safety reasons, but Washington is arguing that slowing down will only benefit China.
“The US approach can be summarized as controlling the technology but not slowing down and enhancing security but not losing the pace of innovation — I think the central AI debate will be shaped by these balances in the coming period,” he said.
He emphasized that Türkiye must be a part of this global transformation, urging local decision-makers to prioritize AI and assess what these global developments could mean for the country.
“The assessment of potentials must take place not only within tech circles but on a platform gathering the public and private sectors, universities and civil society,” he said. “Decision-makers and developers must sit down much more frequently and listen to one another as this is a field where significant changes come to the fore within a matter of months, so annual meetings are no longer sufficient.”
Kucuksabanoglu stated that AIPA launched monthly dialogue meetings to bridge the gap between the Turkish public sector’s policy perspective and the private sector’s hands-on experience.
“It’s not realistic for Türkiye to compete with the US and China on the same scale when it comes to every area of AI, so Türkiye should identify a few strategic areas and allocate resources there — we’ve built a strong industrial base and a culture of production through our defense sector, while other sectors like finance, healthcare, logistics, tourism and public services are areas where AI could generate significant added value,” he said. “I would add agriculture to these areas as AI can help in a range of activities, from improving efficiency and water use to early disease detection and crop planning.”
“We see the US innovation- and competition-related approach, while Europe has its own more regulatory approach, and China has a whole other model, but Türkiye does not have to copy any of these approaches — we must establish our own balance, one that ensures security without stifling innovation and accelerates AI transformation. Türkiye may not become an AI leader in every field, but it must determine where it will stand in this new world order, as what we’re discussing today deals with the future of the economy, production, agriculture, companies, the workforce and global power balances,” he added.

Finland pledges millions of euros for Gaza reconstruction
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:29:16 EEST
22:29:16 KST

Finland will grant four million euros to the UN's Horizon Fund and three million euros to develop Palestinian hospitals in East Jerusalem, the Finnish Ministry for Foreign Affairs has announced in a press release.
The Horizon Fund — officially known as the UN Palestine Recovery Horizon Trust Fund — aims to bridge the gap between immediate humanitarian relief and long-term reconstruction in Gaza.
According to the ministry's press release, the fund also helps support the implementation of the Gaza peace plan, as it seeks to bolster job creation as well as the restoration of basic services in the region.
"The Horizon Fund creates opportunities for the large-scale reconstruction of Gaza. Through the fund, it will be possible to respond to the extensive needs of the population of Gaza, for example in education, housing, health, and the revival of jobs," Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Ville Tavio (Finns) stated in the press release.
The three million euros in support granted to the Palestinian Authority will be provided through the EU's PEGASE support mechanism, and it is intended for the funding of healthcare services in East Jerusalem. Finland's pledge is allocated for the years 2027–2029.
According to the ministry, PEGASE is a long-term support mechanism through which around 20,000 Palestinians gain access to specialised medical care in East Jerusalem hospitals each year.

Russia’s Dan-T munition blurs line between UAVs, cruise missiles — Rostec
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:28:15 UTC
22:28:15 KST

MOSCOW, September 30. /TASS/. Russia’s newest loitering munition, the Dan-T, combines the firepower of a cruise missile with the maneuvarability of a drone, the state corporation Rostec reported.
"In fact, a classic cruise missile is already a fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV). However, not every fixed-wing UAV is a cruise missile. Nevertheless, in the new S-71M, S-71K, and Dan-T models, this distinction is blurred. These systems are specially designed to perform the functions of cruise missiles and possess the corresponding precision, maneuverability, and range. "At the same time, they are significantly cheaper than conventional missiles," Rostec told the Krasnaya Zvezda newspaper.
The state corporation specified that as drone production technologies continue to mature, the difference between such drones and cruise missiles themselves will become increasingly less noticeable.
Rostec told TASS that the effectiveness of the Dan-T system has been confirmed by hundreds of successful launches against enemy targets in the special military operation zone. The system is designed for use from aircraft and helicopters, including foreign ones, and as a result, strong interest in this munition from foreign countries is expected.
The latest unmanned platforms, the S-71M and S-71K, are designed to be launched from fifth-generation fighter jets, including the Su-57.

Russia will lose gas revenues: citizens will pay for the war — intelligence
Kyiv • UNN
Russia has downgraded its forecast for gas production and exports for 2026–2029. The Kremlin plans to offset the losses by raising taxes and tariffs.
Russia’s Ministry of Economic Development has downgraded its forecast for gas production and exports for 2026–2029. The Kremlin will force Russians themselves to pay for the consequences of the war: this is happening through higher taxes and utility tariffs. This was reported by the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine, according to UNN.
Details
According to intelligence reports, Moscow has realized that it will not be possible to quickly replace the lost European market. In 2025, pipeline exports to Europe fell by 44% to 18 billion cubic meters. The forecast for LNG exports in 2026 was lowered from 40.3 million to 35 million tonnes. Even according to official estimates, a return to previous supply volumes is not expected.
The Kremlin will plug budget holes at the expense of the population. Russia’s Finance Ministry proposes raising taxes on dividends, bank deposits, and property sales to 22%. From July 1, 2027, utility tariffs are planned to rise by an average of 11%, instead of the previously projected 8.7%. The Russian authorities are already factoring deteriorating gas indicators into their budget calculations. Lost export revenues are not returning, dependence on China is growing, and the Kremlin is shifting the financial bill for the war against Ukraine onto citizens

Christa Pike seeks firing squad, not lethal injection: Inside US executions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:14:39 UTC
22:14:39 KST

Christa Pike seeks firing squad, not lethal injection: Inside US executions
Set to be Tennessee’s first female execution in 200 years, before it was stayed at the 11th hour on Wednesday, Pike made an unusual request about how she should die.
A Tennessee appeals court has stayed the execution of Christa Gail Pike, the only woman on the state’s “death row”, US media reported on Wednesday.
Tennessee had been set to execute the first woman in more than 200 years on Wednesday, after the United States Supreme Court rejected a bid to halt it. However, the US Court of Appeals Sixth Circuit intervened at the last minute.
Christa Pike, 50, who was convicted of torturing and killing a classmate when she was 18, was due to die by lethal injection at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, but according to a report by The New York Post, she has asked to be shot by an all-female firing squad instead.
Human rights experts have condemned the decision to continue with the execution at all, but say the Supreme Court can still overturn the stay of execution.
Lawyer Clive Stafford Smith, who has represented many death row inmates in the past, told Al Jazeera: “Very few women are executed, but fewer still in Tennessee – it has been 200 years. So this is a step back to about 1820.
So why does Pike hope to avoid lethal injection in preference for the firing squad, and how does the US put people to death? Here’s what you need to know:
What was Christa Pike convicted of?
Pike was found guilty of the murder of another young woman she viewed as a romantic rival more than 30 years ago.
In January 1995, Pike, her 17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp and 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson lured Colleen Slemmer, 19, into a wooded area and tortured and killed her. All four were students at a Job Corps vocational centre in Knoxville.
The case attracted huge public interest, especially after it was revealed that the attackers had carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest, which Shipp later admitted to carving. Pike kept a piece of Slemmer’s skull.
Pike and Shipp confessed and were convicted of first-degree murder in 1996. Pike was sentenced to death; Shipp received life with the possibility of parole.
“Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions,” her lawyers wrote.
Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, has spoken in support of the execution.
What do her lawyers argue?
That she should not be executed at all.
On Wednesday, just hours before Pike’s execution was due to be carried out, the Tennessee appeals court issued an order stating: “The United States District Court for the Eastern District of Tennessee determined that it did not have jurisdiction over Christa Pike’s Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b)(6) motion to reopen the judgment denying habeas relief. Therefore, it is ORDERED that execution of the sentence of death upon the movant is STAYED until further order of this court.”
However, the Supreme Court can still overturn this order, Stafford Smith told Al Jazeera. “The Supreme Court has been overturning stays recently,” he added.
Pike’s legal team previously petitioned the governor to commute her sentence to life without parole. It pointed to evidence that her mother drank heavily during pregnancy, impairing Pike’s brain development and her impulse control.
“The 18-year-old girl suffering from severe mental illness and near-debilitating trauma no longer exists,” her lawyers wrote.
She would be the only person to be executed in modern-era Tennessee for a crime committed as a teenager.
Her lawyer, Stephen Ferrell, said scientists now understand far more about adolescent brain development and that her sentence was an outlier.
Stafford Smith said:,”Christa was just a teenager, and had undergone horrendous abuse as a child. Now she is 50, a totally different person. It is so pointless – will this really make the world a more civilised place?”
Governor Bill Lee has denied clemency, however. A group of United Nations human rights experts has called for her sentence to be commuted.
Why is this case so rare?
The US almost never executes women.
Women account for 18 of the 1,683 people executed since the Supreme Court allowed capital punishment to resume in 1976 – just more than 1 percent.
Tennessee has executed just 17 people in that time before Wednesday, with Pike the only woman on its death row.
If the execution goes ahead, it will be the state’s first execution of a woman since 1820, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Why does Pike not want a lethal injection?
Her legal team and trauma experts say it could force her to relive abuse she suffered in childhood.
Her clemency petition documents childhood violence, neglect and sexual abuse, including rapes when she was aged 11 and 17. It also cites her diagnoses of bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.
Sexual violence and trauma experts argue that the procedures around lethal injection would likely trigger severe flashbacks of that abuse.
Her legal team also argues that she has small veins and a blood condition that could make it difficult to place an IV line, a claim the state disputes.
In May, Tennessee prison officials abandoned the execution of another prisoner, Tony Carruthers, after failing to find a suitable vein.
According to The New York Post, Pike’s lawyers said she also fears a painful death by lethal injection.
The paper reported that she wants to be shot by an all-female firing squad, with members of Slemmer’s family among the witnesses.
Tennessee is not among the five states that authorise the firing squad.
In court in August, her lawyers proposed hanging instead, noting it was the method Tennessee last used to execute a woman.
The state opposed that, saying Tennessee has neither the equipment nor the legal authority to carry it out. The judge sided with the state but allowed for the possibility of an all-female execution team.
Tennessee also allows prisoners whose crimes predate January 1999 to choose the electric chair; Pike’s crime took place in 1995.
What rules do different states have?
There are 27 states with the death penalty, although four have placed its use on hold.
Lethal injection is authorised in every state with the death penalty; electrocution in nine states; gas in nine; and the firing squad in five. In Idaho, the firing squad became the primary method in July 2026.
Tennessee authorises lethal injection and electrocution. If both are found unconstitutional, its law allows any constitutional method.
Since 2008, the Supreme Court has required prisoners challenging an execution method to identify a feasible alternative that significantly reduces the risk of severe pain.
In June, a federal judge permanently barred Alabama from executing Jeffery Lee with nitrogen gas, ruling that it violated the Eighth Amendment’s ban on cruel and unusual punishment.
She found his proposed alternative, the firing squad, feasible.
What are the different methods?
The US has used five: lethal injection, electrocution, gas, the firing squad and hanging.
Lethal injection accounts for 1,491 executions since 1976, while electrocution has been used 163 times. Gas has been used 19 times, with Alabama and Louisiana the only states to have used it.
In nitrogen executions, a mask is placed over the prisoner’s face, and the air they breathe is replaced with pure nitrogen.
The firing squad, the method Pike reportedly wants, has been used just six times since 1976.
Hanging, once a primary method, is not currently authorised in any state.
Why are execution methods so controversial?
Because none of them reliably work as intended, many experts say.
The Eighth Amendment to the US Constitution bars “cruel and unusual punishments”. But the Supreme Court has made challenges to the death penalty harder to win. It has ruled that proving a method risks severe pain is not enough; prisoners must also identify a feasible alternative that significantly reduces that risk.
Lethal injection depends on finding a usable vein. If the drugs go into a muscle instead, or the needle clogs, the prisoner can suffer extreme pain.
In 2017, legal challenges in Arkansas cited botched lethal injections in Oklahoma and Arizona.
Meanwhile, the electric chair does not always kill with the first jolt. If the prisoner’s heart is still beating, another jolt must be applied.
An autopsy of Mikal Mahdi, executed by firing squad in South Carolina in 2025, found that only two of three bullets hit him, and neither struck his heart.
A miscalculated hanging can mean death by slow strangulation.
Witnesses said Kenneth Smith, the first person executed with nitrogen gas, appeared conscious and writhed for several minutes.
