Protesters camped out across Spain demand passage of housing measures
MADRID, Sept 30 - Thousands of protesters camped out on Madrid's main square and in other Spanish cities demanded on Wednesday that parliament swiftly approve new measures to protect tenants and curb the country's acute housing crisis.
The demonstrations were ignited last week by the dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her Madrid home of more than seven decades. Her case highlighted mounting pressure on long-term tenants in major cities and tourist hotspots, where soaring rents, gentrification and a shortage of affordable housing have fuelled social and political unrest.
Spain's leftist minority government passed two decrees on Tuesday with a host of measures, including a ban on evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, but their full implementation hinges on approval by the fragmented lower house, which is due to hold a vote on Friday.
Many activists said even those measures fell short of tackling the crisis.
"It's not enough — it might be a starting point or a stopgap," 32-year-old pharmaceutical worker Julio Gomez told Reuters, adding that he was willing to stay with his tent in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square for "as long as it takes".
Others criticised the government's decision to split the measures into two separate bills with the expectation that one, which automatically extends leases to prevent abusive rent hikes, would be rejected by a slim right-wing majority.
"They've done it so that one gets approved and the stronger one gets rejected, just to sneak one through by the skin of its teeth," said veterinarian Gonzalo Sanchez, 26.
ACTIVISTS FIGHT EVICTIONS
Madrid's Tenants' Union, which organised the initial protests, described some of the measures as "crumbs", although it also called the government's move a "historic victory" for the social movement.
Meanwhile, dozens gathered on Wednesday in Burjassot, near Valencia, to block the eviction of Daniel Gonzalez, a university professor who has lived at his home since 2009. Faced with the protest, court officials agreed to postpone his eviction for at least 10 days.
Gonzalez said he has paid rent on time for more than 17 years, despite the property changing hands among investment funds, but after a legal dispute lasting nearly a decade the courts ultimately backed the owner.
The public outcry over last week's eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal in Madrid led to a deal with her landlord, property firm Urbagestion, to let her stay in the apartment with unchanged rent. She remains in hospital following the eviction but is expected to return home in the coming days.
Urbagestion's co-owner, Ricardo Alonso, told newspaper El Economista he and his partner had faced a pressure campaign over the eviction, citing the delivery of a box containing live cockroaches. REUTERS

U.S. Air Force plans missile warning upgrade for F-15EX
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:13:35 UTC
22:13:35 KST

- The U.S. Air Force issued a sources sought notice on Sept. 29, 2026, for a missile warning system to integrate into the F-15EX Eagle II.
- The system must use the jet's six existing sensor locations and wiring, with industry responses due Nov. 12.
The U.S. Air Force is looking for a system that warns F-15EX Eagle II crews when a missile has been fired at them, and it wants one that is already proven on other military aircraft so it can be fitted to the new fighter quickly.
The F-15 program office at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, posted a sources sought notice on Sept. 29 asking companies to describe an operationally qualified missile launch and approach warning system for rapid integration into the F-15EX fleet. A sources sought notice is market research, not a request for bids, and the U.S. Air Force says it has made no commitment to buy anything. Responses are due Nov. 12.
A missile warning system uses sensors around the aircraft to spot the launch or approach of a missile, typically by detecting the heat or light of its rocket motor, and alerts the crew so they can maneuver or release flares. The U.S. Air Force says the new system must warn F-15EX crews of missile threats without distracting them with too many false alarms.
The notice shows the F-15EX was built with room for such a system. Any candidate must use six existing sensor locations on the aircraft that are set aside for missile warning, along with the jet’s existing data cables, power cables and cooling. Maintainers must be able to install and remove it in the field without changing the aircraft beyond fitting the sensor units into those six spots.
When the first F-15EX flew in 2021, The Aviationist noted that it had mounting points like those used for missile approach warning sensors on Qatar’s F-15QA, but appeared not to carry the sensors themselves.
The F-15EX’s current self-protection comes from BAE Systems’ Eagle Passive/Active Warning Survivability System, known as EPAWSS, an electronic warfare suite that provides radar warning, jamming and control of chaff and flares. Radar warning tells a pilot when enemy radars are tracking the jet, but a dedicated missile warning system is designed to catch missiles, including heat-seeking ones, that may not give off radar signals.
The U.S. Air Force’s questions point toward an existing product. It asks which U.S. military aircraft the system is already cleared to fly on, including approval for airworthiness and cybersecurity, whether it is in production today, and how many months after a contract award it could be delivered. It also asks for contacts at the offices that bought the system for other aircraft.
Several questions deal with fitting the system into Boeing’s jet. The U.S. Air Force wants to know whether it can connect to the aircraft’s standard MIL-STD-1553 data bus and on what terms a company would share its interface specification with Boeing, so the system can exchange data with the F-15EX’s mission computer. It also asks about each unit’s size, weight, power and cooling needs, and whether a vendor plans to adapt its system to a new government reference design for aircraft mission systems.
To avoid handling classified material, the notice does not ask how well each system detects missiles. The program office said it may follow up for that information with companies whose systems look like they would fit the F-15EX.

Brazil briefed French, German officials on alleged US, Russian election interference
PARIS, Sept 30 - A French and German delegation travelled this month to Brasilia, where intelligence officials briefed them on alleged US and Russian interference before Brazil's election, according to sources and documents seen by Reuters.
Officials from Abin, Brazil's spy agency, "confirmed the existence of interference from the United States as well as Russia," according to a report of the meetings compiled by an attendee.
The alleged US interference ranged "from lawfare to interference that is openly acknowledged," the Abin officials said, according to the report. They gave no details of the alleged Russian interference.
The previously unreported visit underlines growing concern on both sides of the Atlantic over US President Donald Trump's efforts to support MAGA-aligned candidates. It also shows how potential targets of US meddling are now comparing notes.
The first round of Brazil's election takes place on Sunday, with leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a tight contest against right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro whose father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a prison term under house arrest for plotting a coup after the 2022 election.
The spectre of US interference to support Flavio Bolsonaro has loomed over the vote, with Lula saying he had warned Trump not to meddle.
The US State Department did not respond to a request for comment. It has previously denied seeking to interfere in Brazil's elections. Abin and Russia's embassy in Brazil also did not respond to requests for comment. Moscow has previously denied interfering in other countries' elections.
TRUMP'S SUPPORT FOR RIGHT-WINGERS TESTS OLD NORMS
The Trump administration's overt support for right-wing candidates around the world represents a break with longstanding US policies, and poses a challenge for incumbent governments over whether such support counts as foreign interference.
Washington has openly supported ideologically aligned candidates across Europe and Latin America in recent months.
The United States offered a bailout potentially worth $40 billion to boost Argentine President Javier Milei before his difficult midterm elections, while US Vice President JD Vance travelled to Hungary to support former Prime Minister Viktor Orban in his failed reelection bid.
Officials in France, where far-right candidate Marine Le Pen leads in opinion polls, have been vocal about rejecting any US meddling in their domestic affairs. Privately, they say they view Brazil's election as a potential early warning sign for France's own presidential election next year.
In Germany, where the far-right Alternative for Germany party came first in elections in two states last month, officials have regularly criticised the Trump administration's support for the AfD.
EU DELEGATION
The French and German officials visited Brazil from September 9 to 11 as part of a European Union delegation to discuss implementation of the bloc's Digital Services Act (DSA), which requires online platforms to do more to tackle illegal and harmful content. Washington has been critical of the DSA, which it says unfairly targets US tech giants.
The delegation's aims in Brazil also included "preparing coordinated responses ahead of the 2026 elections," according to a document seen by Reuters.
The French officials came from Viginum, a foreign disinformation detection agency, and media and communications regulator Arcom.
The German officials were from the Federal Network Agency, which regulates telecoms, energy, rail and postal services.
Arcom confirmed one of its officials participated in the visit, as did Viginum. Germany's Federal Network Agency said "possible US meddling in the elections in Germany was not discussed" at the meeting.
A senior Brazilian cyber official who was present at the meeting, and who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the number of cyberattacks in Brazil had nearly doubled compared with 2025, while there had also been a sharp rise in hacks and phishing attempts of the president's office, which the official said was clearly "election-related." Russia’s newest minesweeper Semyon Agafonov put afloat in St. Petersburg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:11:38 UTC
22:11:38 KST

MOSCOW, September 30. /TASS/. The launching ceremony for the newest Project 12700 Alexandrit minesweeper, the Semyon Agafonov, took place in St. Petersburg at the Sredne-Nevsky Shipyard (part of the United Shipbuilding Corporation, USC), the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"The newest naval minesweeper Semyon Agafonov has been launched for the Russian Navy. The ceremonial launch of the 12th ship in the series was attended by Navy Deputy Commander-in-Chief for Armaments Vice Admiral Igor Mukhametshin, USC Deputy CEO for Military Shipbuilding and Special Programs Andrey Bogomolov, representatives of the St. Petersburg government, CEO of the Sredne-Nevsky Shipyard Sergey Karachkov, Chief Engineer of USC’s Almaz Design Bureau Mikhail Alyoshin, and other distinguished guests," the ministry stated.
As Mukhametshin noted, ships of this class are currently successfully carrying out missions in all of Russia’s seas. "Today is a remarkable event that demonstrates the correctness of the decisions made at the time by the leadership of the Russian Navy, the Defense Ministry, and our shipbuilding industry regarding the organization of the construction of series-production ships of this class at the Sredne-Nevsky Shipyard. We have mastered the most complex technology," Mukhametshin noted in his speech.
A ship-blessing ritual was performed, followed by the traditional breaking of a bottle of champagne against the hull as part of the ceremony. Marina Liberova, deputy head of the Sredne-Nevsky Shipyard’s production and dispatch department, became the ship’s godmother. She has worked at the company for 20 years and oversees the mechanical engineering division.
Outfitting work will start at the ship immediately after the launch.
Ship’s history
By order of the Russian Navy’s commander-in-chief, the ship was named after Hero of the Soviet Union Semyon Agafonov, who served in the 181st Special Reconnaissance Detachment of the Northern Fleet during WWII. He carried out 50 missions and participated in raids behind enemy lines. In October 1944, Agafonov took part in the Petsamo-Kirkenes Operation and the battle for the German battery at Cape Krestovy, which controlled the entrance to Pechenga Bay. On November 5, 1944, Semyon Agafonov was awarded the title of Hero of the Soviet Union.
The Project 12700 naval minesweeper Semyon Agafonov was laid down in a ceremony on January 18, 2024. Project 12700 was developed by the Almaz Design Bureau. The keel-laying took place at the Sredne-Nevsky Shipyard. The Alexandrit class is designed to search for and destroy sea mines and provide mine countermeasures. One of the project’s key features is a monolithic fiberglass hull formed using the vacuum infusion method.

Putin’s Secret Mountain Bunker Is Key Node in Russia’s “Dead Hand” Nuclear System
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:11:19 UTC
22:11:19 KST

- Category
- World
Putin’s Secret Mountain Bunker Is Key Node in Russia’s “Dead Hand” Nuclear System
A joint investigation published on September 26 identified a secret bunker inside Mount Kosvinsky Kamen in Russia’s Sverdlovsk region as a key node in the modernized Perimetr nuclear command system.
The system, known in the West as Dead Hand, is designed to enable automated nuclear retaliation if the country's leadership is destroyed. This was reported by The Moscow Times on the same day.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The outlet cited research by the Dossier Center, Danwatch, and The Sunday Times, whose teams studied construction and equipment documents, open-source data, and accounts from people connected to the facility.
The site, code-named Grot and designated Object 1335, is hidden inside a mountain whose rock allows radio waves of specific frequencies needed for communication to pass through, the report noted.
It contains underground chambers and tunnels, radio centers, communication and life-support systems, and the equipment that controls strategic nuclear forces.
Retired Major General Viktor Khalin took part in the creation of Perimeter in the 1970s and led its modernization from 2005 to 2010. He stated that the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, signed a secret decree in May 2005 to build a new control element for the system.
By 2010, the new system had been tested and delivered to Grot, the report added, and a military town called Kytlym was built near the mountain by 2020.
Khalin explained that Object 1335 gave Russian leaders a tool for "implementation of retribution in both an automated and an automatic mode." The report clarified that this means a final decision without human participation.
In the Soviet Perimeter, by comparison, duty officers rather than a machine retained the final press of the button. The examined documents, however, provide no evidence that the current system has operated in fully automatic mode.
Public procurement documents show that 22,000 tons of steel and 56,000 tons of cement were supplied to the facility, where construction began in 1982, the investigators indicated.
By their calculations, that volume of materials could yield enough concrete to build two large modern Moscow Metro stations along with adjacent tunnels.
Jeffrey Lewis, a Stanford University professor and US nuclear nonproliferation expert, argued that the Kremlin regards Grot as a "stabilizing element" that gives Russian leaders "more confidence and time."
"They do this not because they are some cartoonish villains," he declared. "They do it because deep down they feel insecure. That the US could do to Putin what it did to Iran's leader."
The Grot upgrade is part of a broader overhaul of Russia's nuclear command infrastructure.
Earlier reports indicated that a large-scale work at Object 1335 began in 2018, with procurement orders covering roughly 600 kilometers of electrical cables, ventilation systems, and filtration equipment designed to protect against chemical, biological, and radioactive contamination.
Procurement records also refer to at least 24 underground chambers, and the distance between the main and emergency exits is about 2.5 kilometers.
The facility is believed to have been placed on combat duty in 2023. Moscow has meanwhile continued to exercise other components of its strategic forces: on April 2, crews of mobile RS-24 Yars intercontinental ballistic missile systems practiced dispersal, combat duty, and operations under radioactive contamination in Siberia.

Foxconn rose 0.4% to NT$251.5. Delta Electronics gained 3% to NT$1,890, and ASE rose 2.33% to NT$703, according to Anue.
Market reports said Nvidia is developing glass substrate technology and working with equipment suppliers, with related supply chains in Taiwan, Japan and South Korea expected to complete development within two years. The technology could enter production as early as 2028, with related stocks gaining on the reports, according to FTNN.
Major panel makers AUO and Innolux both hit their daily price limits, with trading volume for each exceeding 400,000 lots, or 400 million shares. Glass processing firms G-Tech Optoelectronics and Onano Industrial also hit limit-ups.
E&R Engineering and Laser Tek Taiwan, which focus on through-glass via (TGV) technology, also reached their daily price limits. TGV is a key process in glass substrate development that involves creating microscopic vertical holes through glass layers to allow electrical signals to pass between different parts of advanced semiconductor packages, according to Sinotrade.
Silicon wafer stocks were also active, with industry leader GlobalWafers reaching the daily price limit at NT$1,035. Wafer Works and Sino-American Silicon Products also hit limit-ups.
Silicon wafers are high-purity silicon substrates used as the base material for manufacturing semiconductor chips. Major global suppliers are planning price increases for products as a structural supply gap persists due to AI demand, according to FTNN and Pocket Securities.
Plastic and petrochemical stocks also remained strong as companies in the sector expand into semiconductor electronic chemicals. Formosa Plastics gained 5.42%, while Nan Ya Plastics, Formosa Chemicals & Fiber, and Formosa Petrochemical all rose more than 3%.
Looking ahead to October, Taishin Securities Investment Advisory General Manager Huang Wen-ching (黃文清) said investor conferences held by TSMC, Largan Precision, and Nanya Technology will be closely watched by investors. Their outlooks could influence market sentiment for the technology sector.
Huang sees the TAIEX maintaining a gradual upward trend next month. He expects AI to remain the main market theme, with funds rotating into sectors that have lagged in gains.
For the fourth quarter, Huang said the market could remain volatile due to factors including higher dividend yields and pressure on liquidity. However, he said fundamentals and AI-related themes continue to support the market.
During the period, electronics and traditional industries are expected to see gradual gains and continued sector rotation, while technology and electronics are likely to remain the market’s main focus. Huang said the market is nearing the end of the interest rate hike cycle, with financial stocks potentially benefiting from higher rates.

British firm set to clear space junk passes security audit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:01:20 UTC
22:01:20 KST

- Astroscale UK has achieved ISO/IEC 27001:2022 information security certification after a 20-month company-wide program and an independent audit.
- The company is preparing ELSA-M, a planned debris removal mission launching on an ISAR Aerospace Spectrum rocket, and the UK Ministry of Defence's Orpheus program.
Astroscale UK, the British arm of the Japanese company building spacecraft to clear junk from orbit, has earned an international information security certification as it prepares a planned debris removal mission and a defense program for the UK Ministry of Defence.
The company said on Sept. 30 that it achieved ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification after an independent audit and a 20-month, company-wide effort to put new security policies, processes and oversight in place. The standard sets out how an organization identifies and manages risks to its information, and Astroscale UK says its version also covers newer risks tied to artificial intelligence and outside suppliers.
Astroscale UK says the certification is meant to give customers, government partners and suppliers confidence in how it handles sensitive information on ELSA-M, which the company says will be the world’s first active debris removal mission, meaning a spacecraft sent to capture and remove a dead object from orbit. ELSA-M is set to launch on a Spectrum rocket from German launch company ISAR Aerospace, though Astroscale has not given a date.
The company is also working on Orpheus, a UK Ministry of Defence program that Astroscale says is developing a sovereign British defense capability for servicing satellites in orbit. It gave no further details on what Orpheus will do or when.
“Our missions combine frontier robotics and autonomous rendezvous with exacting operational discipline,” said Nick Shave, managing director of Astroscale UK.
Both programs rely on rendezvous and proximity operations: flying one spacecraft close to another, inspecting it and working with it without a collision. The same skills that let a spacecraft grab a piece of debris could let it inspect or service another satellite, which is why the work draws interest from militaries as well as satellite operators.
Astroscale first tested those skills on ELSA-d, launched in 2021, which demonstrated long- and short-range rendezvous and the magnetic capture of a client spacecraft. In 2024, the company’s ADRAS-J mission approached a discarded Japanese upper-stage rocket body to within 15 meters (49 feet) and inspected it, even though the rocket body was not built to be approached. Astroscale UK built the ground systems for that mission and led its flight dynamics, including planning the close approach maneuvers and handling collision warnings.
Astroscale, founded in 2013 and headquartered in Japan, has also won work with Japan’s space agency JAXA, the U.S. Space Force, the European Space Agency, the UK Space Agency and satellite operator Eutelsat.
“Achieving ISO 27001 is tangible evidence that we are building the secure, resilient organisation needed to deliver complex space missions in the UK,” Shave said.

China fails to create US and Taiwanese skepticism despite best efforts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:01:05 UTC
22:01:05 KST

The recent summit in Washington between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping concluded with a heavily publicized trade truce that saw Beijing walk away with a reprieve on electric vehicle tariffs, while Washington secured expanded purchase agreements for US coal.
Yet, beneath the veneer of transactional diplomacy, the summit exposed a sophisticated, multi-layered arena of geopolitical posturing, psychological warfare and state-sponsored disinformation centered entirely on the future of Taiwan.
A primary point of public friction leading up to the summit was the temporary hold on a NT$450 billion (US$14 billion) arms sale package to Taipei, which includes critical air-defense assets and anti-drone systems. While immediate commentary characterized the delay as a symptom of a transactional foreign policy, seasoned analysts recognized it as standard Washington posturing.
Historically, modern US administrations — including those of George W Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden — have paused or delayed arms packages to Taiwan at least four times to evaluate domestic defense supply chains, balance regional allocations and maximize diplomatic leverage during high-level bilateral encounters.
Trump’s historical record supports this strategic interpretation. During his first administration, he authorized the largest cumulative arms sales for Taiwan in history, greenlighting paradigm-shifting capabilities such as F-16V fighter jets, M1A2 tanks and critical technology for Taiwan’s domestic submarine program.
This trajectory continued into his second term with a NT$350 billion single-year defense package in December 2025. Once the pending NT$450 billion package is signed, Trump’s aggregate arms approvals will approach NT$1.28 trillion, effectively doubling the totals approved during the entire eight years of the Obama administration.
Strategic hesitation
By withholding final approval until after the summit, Washington effectively retained a major geopolitical counterweight, keeping Beijing off-balance. This strategic hesitation successfully neutralized behind-the-doors lobbying by the Chinese delegation.
Xi reportedly pressed Trump to shift traditional US terminology from “does not support” Taiwan independence to an explicit commitment to “oppose” it. The White House successfully resisted this rhetorical upgrade, scrubbing all mentions of Taiwan from the official readout to preserve long-standing strategic ambiguity.
When questioned, Trump deflected, noting only that “Xi understands very much how I feel,” leaving Beijing to calculate the exact boundaries of US resolve.
Failing to secure concrete policy concessions in the meeting rooms, the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) propaganda apparatus and the United Front Work Department launched a coordinated cognitive warfare campaign. This information operation relied on manufacturing domestic panic and manipulating public skepticism on both sides of the Pacific.
The campaign received an artificial boost just days before the summit when an article by analyst Jennifer Kavanagh went viral. Published by Defense Priorities, a Washington think tank funded significantly by the Charles Koch foundation, the piece advocated for the complete retrenchment of US forces in Asia to the Second Island Chain, effectively suggesting the abandonment of Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines in favor of a consolidated footprint in Guam.
While the article represented a fringe academic viewpoint within Washington, CCP state media and covert influence networks weaponized it instantly. In the US, United Front-linked accounts signal-boosted the piece to exploit isolationist, “America First” skepticism, framing security support for a fellow democracy as an unnecessary economic and military liability.
Economic tripwire
Concurrently, in Taipei, the same text was used to validate the narrative of “US skepticism.” Coordinated online networks circulated rumors that the White House was actively preparing a retreat strategy, trying to break Taiwanese public morale by painting Washington as an unreliable ally ready to discard its partners for commercial concessions.
The US countered this psychological pressure with explicit displays of military capability and symbolic pageantry. As Xi arrived at Joint Base Andrews, the conclusion of the US National Anthem was synchronized with a low-altitude flyover of two nuclear-capable B-1B Lancer supersonic bombers. The display served as an unambiguous, physical reminder of the US military-industrial complex.
Furthermore, Taiwan’s modern “silicon shield” — the global economy’s absolute reliance on TSMC’s advanced semiconductor fabrication — ensures that any contemporary attempt by Beijing to establish a blockade or force cross-strait aggression would instantly collapse global markets, including China’s own economy. It remains a high-tech economic tripwire that makes unilateral aggression a self-defeating trap, reinforcing why the strategic alliance remains bulletproof despite Beijing’s digital rumor mill.
Despite the choreographed optics, the post-summit fallout exposed significant rhetorical friction. The most glaring gaffe emerged when US Ambassador to China David Perdue revealed on Fox News on Sunday that Trump had casually asked Xi if China would like to purchase US weapons.
Though the State Department and a visibly defensive Trump scrambled to walk back the comments by claiming Perdue had likely confused “China with Taiwan,” the leak exposed a hilarious subversion of expectations. Xi spent years demanding an end to US arms sales, only to enter Washington and receive an impromptu sales pitch for American military hardware.
History lesson
Simultaneously, a battle over historical memory erupted. During a state dinner toast, Xi lauded how the US and China “fought side by side as allies to win World War II.” The White House subsequently repeated this framing in its official fact sheet.
Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council immediately issued a sharp rebuke, noting that the current ruling regime in Beijing did not exist during World War II, having only seized power in 1949. The heroic ally that fought alongside the US against militarism was the Republic of China — modern-day Taiwan. Taiwan’s officials directly called out Beijing for attempting to plagiarize Taiwan’s military history to gain favor in Washington.
The summit’s peak of diplomatic theater occurred during that very same White House state dinner. As US and Chinese dignitaries entered the dining room, a harpist performed “The Moon Represents My Heart,” a classic timed to honor the Mid-Autumn Festival.
While Western observers viewed it as a polite nod to Chinese culture, the track choice operated as a biting, high-level diplomatic subtweet. The song was popularized globally by the late, legendary Taiwanese singer Teresa Teng (鄧麗君).
Teng was an unyielding cultural icon of democratic resistance who famously refused to ever perform in China while it remained under CCP rule. At the height of the Cold War, her broadcast concerts were played through massive military loudspeakers across the Taiwan Strait to counter communist programming.
By utilizing Teng’s signature melody to welcome the Chinese delegation, the event served as a subtle but unmistakable assertion of Taiwanese cultural primacy and democratic endurance, directly undercutting Beijing’s attempts to erase Taiwan’s identity from the international stage.
Ultimately, the summit demonstrated that while great powers continue to negotiate over raw commodities like coal and electric vehicles, the strategic autonomy of Taiwan remains protected by a robust blend of US defense commitments, historical military resilience, deep global economic integration and a cultural legacy that continues to outmaneuver Beijing’s finest propaganda efforts.

EU-backed scheme helps rural Swedish households on lower incomes go electric

22:00:58 KST

A Swedish government scheme, part-funded by the EU's Social Climate Fund, is offering rural, lower-income drivers financial support to switch from petrol and diesel to electric vehicles.
"I couldn't understand why people bought electric cars, because it didn't look like it was trustworthy," says project manager Olivia Almquist, who replaced her unreliable 30-year-old petrol car with an electric one. "And now I can't understand why not everyone is buying an electric car."
Sweden's electric car premium gives eligible drivers up to 120 euros a month towards leasing costs, plus a one-off 1,600 euro bonus for the lowest earners. To qualify, applicants must earn under 80% of the national average wage, live in a rural area, and buy a car costing between 6,000 and 40,000 euros.
For social worker Daniel Caldeman, who drives 65,000 kilometres a year, the savings have been dramatic: his monthly fuel bill has dropped from around 800 euros to just 150 euros for charging. "I like being eco-friendly and I think about not polluting the environment," he says, "so yeah, it was a factor, but I think that the main factor was economics for me."
Backed by 400 million euros from the EU's Social Climate Fund, itself financed by carbon taxes raised through Europe's Emissions Trading System, the scheme has drawn over 20,000 applicants since it launched in March. According to the Swedish Environmental Protection Agency, nearly 90% of purchases are second-hand vehicles, with officials aiming to eventually help 115,000 households move away from fossil fuels.

Common diseases decline in Helsinki as health gaps persist
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:00:57 EEST
22:00:57 KST

The prevalence of common diseases in Helsinki fell by 10 per cent between 2019 and 2025, with residents recording lower levels of illness than Finland as a whole, according to data published by the City of Helsinki. Differences between parts of the capital remain substantial despite the overall decline.
The reduction was driven in particular by declines in hypertension and coronary heart disease, the city said in a research review based on data from the Social Insurance Institution of Finland, Kela, and Statistics Finland.
In 2025, the prevalence of the most common diseases in Helsinki stood 21 per cent below the national level.
Researchers examined seven common diseases. Psychotic disorders were the only category with a slightly higher prevalence in Helsinki than across Finland. Coronary heart disease and hypertension showed the largest relative differences in Helsinki’s favour.
A separate morbidity index also recorded a decline. The measure combines data on disability, mortality and eligibility for medicine reimbursements. Disability recorded the largest decrease among those three components.
Helsinki scored 84 on the age-standardised morbidity index in 2025, compared with a national reference value of 100. Age standardisation allows comparisons between areas with different age profiles.
The city-level figures mask differences between Helsinki neighbourhoods.
Morbidity remained below the Helsinki average in the inner city and the northernmost parts of the capital. Nine of the city’s basic districts recorded levels substantially above the city average, even after researchers accounted for differences in residents’ ages.
The gap between areas also increased slightly. Changes in disability between 2023 and 2025 played a central role in the widening geographical differences, according to the review.
The City of Helsinki linked much of the variation to differences in the demographic and socioeconomic composition of neighbourhoods. Disease prevalence tends to be higher in areas where residents have lower incomes, connecting geographical health differences with disparities between population groups.
The findings point to differences in demand for health and social services across the capital. The city said services should be directed towards areas with greater needs alongside measures addressing health differences between population groups.

====================================================================================================

BNN IN FOCUS | Political party review: United List – is the “Kulbergs effect” working?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:00:42 UTC
22:00:42 KST

Author: Ilona Bērziņa
Just a few months ago, the United List (AS) was one of the opposition forces in the 14th Saeima, associated more with heated parliamentary disputes, the Rail Baltica parliamentary inquiry and criticism of Evika Siliņa’s government. Now the situation is completely different. AS representative Andris Kulbergs heads the Cabinet, while the United List is the clear leader in the polls.
In the latest SKDS poll, conducted from the 4th to the 16th of September among 2,035 Latvian citizens, 14.4% of all respondents said they were ready to vote for the United List. This was the highest result among the parties. Sovereign Power/Young Latvians ranked second with 9.4%, while Latvia First was third with 9.2%.
Compared with August, support for AS has declined slightly, but the party has retained first place. The September poll by Latvijas Fakti paints a similar picture. AS received the support of 15.9% of all respondents, compared with 15.6% in August. Among voters who had already made their choice, support for AS reached 23.8%.
This strongly resembles the position New Unity found itself in before the 14th Saeima election. In the final SKDS poll before that election, New Unity had around 20–23% support among respondents who had named a specific choice. The Factum Interactive poll conducted from the 15th to the 20th of September showed a very similar level of support – around 21–24%.
There is another similarity:
both political alliances largely have their prime ministers to thank for their strong voter support.
In New Unity’s case, it was Krišjānis Kariņš, who took on the task of forming his first government under highly complicated circumstances and successfully steered it through the waves of the pandemic. In the case of AS, it is Andris Kulbergs, who was not afraid to take the helm of the government for a very short period – just four months – and whose sharp rhetoric appears to resonate with voters.
SKDS polls showed a sharp increase in support for the United List following the formation of Kulbergs’ government: from 6.8% in April and May to 9.8% in June. In the pre-election period, this makes it possible to speak of a clearly visible “Kulbergs effect”. Whether this story will end in a similar way to the “Kariņš effect” remains to be seen.
A look at the alliance’s history
Officially, the political alliance consists of the Latvian Green Party, the Latvian Association of Regions and the Liepāja Party.
The alliance was also formed with the participation of non-partisan professionals brought together by Uldis Pīlēns in the United List of Latvia association, which was later renamed Latvia’s Restart and is now headed by Andris Kulbergs.
One of AS’s distinctive features is that it brings together people and organisations with very different political backgrounds: the Green Party, which left ZZS because of its cooperation with Aivars Lembergs’ For Latvia and Ventspils, representatives of regional politics, members of Liepāja’s political elite, people from the business community and non-partisan professionals.
In the 2022 election to the 14th Saeima, AS received 11.01% of the vote and 15 seats, becoming the third most popular electoral list. Its strongest support came from Liepāja and South Kurzeme. The parliamentary group later shrank to 12 MPs.
Uldis Pīlēns, without whom AS would most likely not be what it is today, has been both the alliance’s candidate for prime minister and its candidate for President of Latvia. He now publicly acknowledges that he has relatively little involvement with the United List, while stressing that he has not severed ties with the alliance and believes AS is a political force capable of surviving in the long term.
Pīlēns, however, is not among the candidates on the AS electoral lists.
Electoral list leaders and their track records
AS is running under number seven, and each of the five electoral districts is headed by a politician already well known to the public.
In Riga, the list is headed by Andris Kulbergs, the current Prime Minister and AS candidate for the post after the election. Before entering politics, he was known as a representative of the automotive industry. In the Saeima, he became particularly prominent as chairman of the parliamentary inquiry into the problems surrounding Rail Baltica and later a commission investigating costs at Rīgas siltums.
In Vidzeme, the list is headed by Edvards Smiltēns, chairman of the Latvian Association of Regions, former Speaker of the Saeima, current Justice Minister and one of the two co-chairmen of the AS board.
In Latgale, the number one candidate is Juris Viļums, an MP in the 11th, 12th and 14th Saeima and head of the AS parliamentary group, with longstanding ties to Latgale. He founded Latgolys Saeima and is a member and one of the founders of the Latgolys Studentu centrs association, now known as Volūda. Former President Raimonds Vējonis is number two on the Latgale list.
In Kurzeme, the list is headed by Māris Kučinskis, a former Prime Minister who also served as Interior Minister during the 14th Saeima and is one of AS’s most experienced politicians.
In Zemgale, the number one candidate is Edgars Tavars, chairman of the Latvian Green Party, co-chairman of the AS board and current Minister for Smart Administration and Regional Development.
The second and third positions on the electoral lists also include a number of familiar names, among them Raimonds Bergmanis, Ingmārs Līdaka, Linda Matisone, Inga Priede, Edgars Putra, Aiva Vīksna and doctor Andris Skride.
What does AS promise?
The United List’s election programme is relatively broad, but economic policy, security and public administration clearly dominate.
On security, the alliance promises to expand the State Defence Service, strengthen the capabilities of the National Guard, complete the eastern border defence line, develop drone and counter-drone technologies, establish a network of shelters, and strengthen the police, Border Guard and State Fire and Rescue Service.
In public finances, the goal is to achieve a balanced base budget within four years. AS also promises to establish a Latvian Development Fund to manage state assets and to review the Rail Baltica project, reducing it to the “minimum viable” scope.
On the economy, AS promises a more stable tax system, a 10% micro-enterprise tax rate for individuals, a reduction in personal income tax on capital gains to 17%, retention of the current corporate income tax regime, less bureaucracy and a state-guaranteed housing construction programme in the regions.
In healthcare, the alliance proposes a state health insurance model under which funding would follow the patient even if they chose a certified private healthcare provider. It also proposes a unified appointment system, transforming the National Health Service into a fund and gradually reducing co-payments for children, seniors and patients with chronic illnesses.
For the regions, AS promises a new municipal financing model, road funding from vehicle taxes, development of ports and special economic zones, and equal EU area-based payments for farmers. Families would be offered housing grants and guarantees, while returning emigrants would receive a special tax regime for four years.
On energy, AS wants to review the implementation of the European Green Deal, examine the use of small modular nuclear reactors and simultaneously develop renewable energy. In foreign policy, the programme declares clear support for NATO, the EU and Ukraine.
Four months at the helm of government
Kulbergs formed his government as a short-term “government of action”. Even while the coalition was being formed, its partners stressed that they would focus primarily on tasks that could still be completed during the remaining term of the 14th Saeima.
AS also secured a highly influential set of positions: the prime minister’s office, the Finance Ministry under Māris Kučinskis, the Justice Ministry under Edvards Smiltēns and the Ministry of Smart Administration and Regional Development under Edgars Tavars.
One of the most visible changes in governance was an attempt to divide ministers’ work into specific tasks that could be reviewed on a regular basis.
However, creating a “short list” did not go particularly smoothly, and it eventually evolved into a government action plan containing 150 measures, with another 35 tasks to be implemented if additional funding could be found without negatively affecting the budget.
Of the 150 measures, 37 relate to budget stabilisation and spending efficiency, 34 to security and foreign affairs, and 21 to reducing bureaucracy and improving the efficiency of public administration.
By mid-August, seven of the ministers’ priority tasks had been fully completed, while results had been achieved on 26 priority measures overall. The remaining measures had been launched and were still being implemented.
A government with a short “shelf life”
Kulbergs’ government was formed only a few months before the 15th Saeima election, and during the debate on approving his Cabinet, Kulbergs himself said that the election result would provide the true assessment of the government’s performance. Judging by the polling figures at the end of September, voters appear satisfied so far.
Unlike Krišjānis Kariņš’ second government or Evika Siliņa’s government, the Kulbergs Cabinet has not had several years before the election to build up a record of achievements.
Four months is enough to demonstrate a leadership style, priorities and initial decisions, as well as to appeal to the public with sharp rhetoric and tough criticism, but it is too short a period to reliably assess the long-term results of many reforms.
What could strengthen AS’s pre-election position…
The first factor is the prime minister’s office. Following the formation of the Kulbergs government, the party’s polling numbers rose significantly. His advantage in pre-election communication is that he can speak not only about what AS would like to do, but also about what the government is currently doing.
The second factor is the alliance’s regional infrastructure. AS is not simply a project of Riga-based politicians. The Latvian Association of Regions, the Green Party and the Liepāja Party have municipal politicians across many regions, while a large proportion of the candidates are connected with municipalities, regional institutions, agriculture and local businesses.
The third factor is the concentration of experienced politicians. Kučinskis is a former prime minister, Vējonis a former President and defence minister, Smiltēns a former Speaker of the Saeima, and Bergmanis a former defence minister.
This allows AS to project an image of experienced professionals with considerable experience in government. In other words, here is the new “adult in the room”.
…and what could make things more difficult
AS is not a single ideologically homogeneous party, but rather a combination of three parties and non-partisan figures. The Latvian Green Party, the Latvian Association of Regions, the Liepāja Party and the Latvia’s Restart group of professionals all have different political histories and their own regional interests.
During the current Saeima term, the alliance has also lost several MPs, with its parliamentary group shrinking from its original 15 seats to 12. Putting together a joint electoral list is one thing; keeping a unified political organisation together for four years is another.
Another factor is the short lifespan of the Kulbergs government. As AS itself stresses in its programme, four months is not enough to resolve problems that have accumulated over many years.
The party therefore has the prime minister’s office, but still has relatively few results of its own government work on which to base a longer-term assessment.
Who is the AS voter?
The latest publicly available September polling data do not provide a full socio-demographic breakdown that would make it possible to say precisely that the typical AS voter belongs to a particular age, income or education group. However, previous election results, the party’s structure, its candidates and its programme point to several potential segments of the AS electorate.
The first is regional voters. AS already enjoyed particularly strong support in Liepāja and South Kurzeme in 2022, while the municipal networks of the Latvian Association of Regions and the Green Party provide the alliance with recognisable figures in Vidzeme and Zemgale as well.
The second group consists of centrist or moderately conservative voters who want neither distinctly left-wing nor radically populist politics and who prioritise security, business, efficient public administration and regional interests.
The third group is interested in improving the business and economic environment. Since the days of Pīlēns, AS rhetoric has prominently featured the language of “professionals”, “crisis management”, productivity, investment, reducing bureaucracy and making public administration more efficient. The economic proposals are also among the most detailed sections of the party’s programme for the 15th Saeima election.
A fourth potential group consists of people who previously voted for ZZS, New Unity or regional lists but who, for one reason or another, are now looking for an economically pragmatic and simultaneously Euro-Atlantic alternative.

MI5 issues spy alert to UK universities over Chinese front company stealing research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:00:41 UTC
22:00:41 KST

China’s intelligence service used a front company to pay grants to British universities and steal crucial research about technology projects, MI5 said on Wednesday in a rare public espionage warning.
Britain’s domestic security service said researchers and academics should cease work with the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI), sometimes also known as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT). MI5 believes it poses a “significant threat”.
The Chinese organisation has given money to 100 or more academics at a string of universities across the UK, in return getting access to the research, which it is alleged found its way back to China’s intelligence service.
MI5 is now prepared to say publicly that the CGTRI is a front for Chinese intelligence, namely the Chinese ministry of state security (MSS). It said continued collaboration could be prosecuted under the National Security Act 2023.
Areas of research targeted include AI, cybersecurity, covert communications, and the embedding of data in pictures online called steganography. MI5 believes it has clear evidence of sensitive information being passed back to Chinese intelligence. The Guardian understands that as well as research money, some British-based academics were given awards, as in honours, by the Chinese.
Successive British governments have courted Chinese investment and encouraged cooperation.
In the alert issued on Wednesday, the Security Service said: “MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage.”
It said that the CGTRI had “very strong ties to the … MSS, China’s civilian intelligence and security service”.
It added: “Many academic institutions and individuals will to date have engaged with CGTRI in good faith given CGTRI’s obfuscated links to MSS.
“UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions. Further, academics are advised to establish the ultimate funding source when conducting any research collaboration with Chinese institutions, to ensure CGTRI is not involved.”
The alert warns of “potential criminal consequences”, in a section issued after consultation with the Crown Prosecution Service, which authorises criminal prosecutions in England and Wales.
“Through this espionage alert, MI5 has placed the fact that CGTRI has very strong ties to MSS in the public domain,” it states. “Going forward, academic institutions, staff and researchers should ensure they are aware of the National Security Act 2023, particularly offences under section 3 (assisting a foreign intelligence service) and section 17 (obtaining a material benefit from a foreign intelligence service).
“Under section 3, an offence is committed if the person a) engages in conduct that is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out UK-related activities, and b) knows, or having regard to other matters known to them ought reasonably to know, that their conduct is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out UK-related activities.”
Such is the scale of Chinese state espionage targeting the UK that MI5 has decided on a deterrence strategy via a public alert such as this, rather than pursuing every single case. It hopes universities will heed the warning and immediately cease their work with the CGTRI.
The Guardian understands MI5 believes Chinese intelligence gained access to cutting-edge British research on scraping social media (searching and retaining useful information from social media sites).
The National Security and Investment Act 2021 could prevent a state such as China, assessed as having hostile intent towards the UK, from buying access to the technology on a commercial basis.
The security minister, Dan Jarvis, demanded universities end ties to the CGTRI. He said: “This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security and that of our allies.
“I have written to all university vice-chancellors to ensure they support their staff to end all arrangements with this company, preventing further benefit to the Chinese intelligence services and ensuring compliance with the National Security Act.”
He added: “International partnerships are vital to ensure our universities and research institutes continue to thrive, but we will take robust action to defend against the threats we face. That means supporting our police and intelligence services to expose and disrupt harmful activity, using the full force of the law.”
Responding to the MI5 alert, Vivienne Stern, the chief executive of Universities UK, which represents 142 institutions across the UK, said universities took their responsibilities around research security and national security extremely seriously.
“The sector has made significant investments in recent years to strengthen due diligence, risk assessment and research security processes, while continuing to support the international collaboration that is essential to world-leading research and innovation,” she said.
“Close engagement between government and the higher education sector is vital to ensuring that universities and the country continue to benefit from international collaboration while effectively managing national security risks.”
Libby Hackett, the chief executive of the Russell Group of research-intensive universities, said: “All our universities take national security responsibilities very seriously. Working closely with government departments and the security services enables universities to take swift action to protect UK interests – and we will continue to do so in the face of new and emerging threats”.
The Chinese embassy has been approached for comment.

Weight-loss drug semaglutide alters reward-seeking behavior in healthy mice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:00:33 UTC
22:00:33 KST

A new small study in healthy mice reveals that the popular weight-loss drug semaglutide alters behavior and brain activity related to reward and stress. Researchers found that daily doses of the drug changed how animals pursued natural rewards and reacted to stressful situations, while also shifting electrical patterns in a central reward circuit. The findings were published in the journal Molecular Brain.
Semaglutide is a medication widely used to treat diabetes and obesity. The medication is frequently recognized by brand names such as Ozempic and Wegovy. It mimics a naturally occurring hormone called GLP-1, which regulates appetite and blood sugar. Recently, scientists have begun exploring whether the drug might also treat addiction by dampening the brain’s response to cravings.
Most prior research has focused on animal models with obesity or diabetes. To understand the drug’s baseline effects on a typical nervous system, researchers Alejo Mosqueira, Sanaz Ansarifar, and their colleagues at Aarhus University investigated how semaglutide impacts the behavior and brain waves of healthy mice. The research team specifically looked at the nucleus accumbens, a region deep in the brain that plays a primary role in processing motivation, pleasure, and reward.
The researchers first designed a behavioral experiment using healthy adult male mice. They divided the animals into two main treatment groups to test different dosing schedules. One group received a weekly injection of semaglutide for eight weeks, which mirrors how the drug is prescribed to human patients. The second group received daily injections to account for the faster metabolism of mice and to observe any short-term behavioral changes.
Following the injection periods, the researchers ran the mice through a battery of tests designed to measure movement, anxiety, and reward-seeking habits. They monitored the animals’ food intake, water consumption, and body weight throughout the process to track general physiological health. Both the daily and weekly groups experienced substantial weight loss, alongside noticeable reductions in eating and drinking. The researchers ran statistical analyses to confirm that the weight loss itself was not responsible for the altered behavior.
When assessing behavior, the researchers found changes exclusively in the daily injection group. In an open field test used to measure general movement and anxiety, the daily-dosed mice displayed an increase in jumping against the walls of the testing box. The researchers interpret this as an increased attempt to escape the enclosure. In a separate marble burying test used to measure repetitive actions, the differences between the treated and untreated mice were not statistically significant.
The team also used a nestlet shredding test, providing the mice with a cotton nesting material to see how much they would tear it apart. Mice given daily semaglutide shredded far less of the material than the control group. This reduction suggests a shift in how the animals explore their environment or a potential increase in underlying anxiety.
To evaluate reward-seeking behavior without relying on food, the researchers used a scent-based test. Healthy male mice naturally seek out the smell of female mouse urine, which acts as a rewarding social cue. The semaglutide-treated mice spent much less time sniffing the female urine than the untreated mice. This drop in interest indicates a suppression of natural reward-seeking drives.
Finally, the researchers placed the mice in small containers of water for a forced swimming test, which is commonly used to measure stress coping and depressive-like states. Mice treated with daily semaglutide spent less time floating motionless and more time actively swimming compared to the control group. This behavior often suggests improved stress resilience or an antidepressant-like effect.
In a separate experiment, Mosqueira and Ansarifar’s team examined how a single dose of semaglutide affects neural activity. They anesthetized a small group of healthy mice and inserted microscopic electrodes into the nucleus accumbens. The researchers recorded the animals’ baseline brain waves for 30 minutes, injected the drug, and then recorded for another hour.
The researchers focused on local field potentials, which are the collective electrical signals generated by large groups of neurons firing together. They analyzed different speeds of brain waves, breaking the signals down into slower rhythms known as delta, theta, and alpha waves. These specific wave patterns are heavily involved in how the brain anticipates and responds to rewards, making them a useful target for understanding motivation.
Following the semaglutide injection, the rhythmic electrical activity in the nucleus accumbens shifted. The dominant frequencies of the delta, theta, and alpha waves became slightly faster. At the same time, the physical strength or amplitude of these slow waves decreased. The researchers note that a reduction in delta and theta wave strength aligns with a dampened reward anticipation system.
The study relies on a relatively small number of animals, and the behavioral changes only appeared under the daily dosing schedule. The weekly injection group lost weight but did not exhibit the same behavioral shifts. This discrepancy suggests that the frequency of the dose heavily influences the behavioral outcomes in healthy animals.
The brain wave recordings took place while the mice were under anesthesia, which fundamentally alters normal electrical activity in the brain. The behavioral tests, conversely, involved awake animals taking the drug over multiple days. Because of these differing conditions, the electrical changes cannot be directly linked to the behavioral shifts.
Future research will need to record brain activity in awake, freely moving animals over longer periods. Measuring these electrical signals while mice are actively making choices could clarify exactly how semaglutide changes motivation. Testing different dosages may also help determine whether these effects apply broadly across different treatment regimens.
The study, “Semaglutide alters behaviour and nucleus accumbens oscillatory activity in healthy mice,” was authored by Alejo Mosqueira, Sanaz Ansarifar, Sadegh Nabavi, and Andrea Moreno.

The incident also had an immediate economic impact. Shares in Israeli airlines El Al and Israir jumped about 7% and more than 9%, respectively, on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange.

Cannabis users were twice as likely to commit violence, review finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:49:01 UTC
21:49:01 KST

Cannabis users were twice as likely to commit violence, review finds
- Date:
- September 30, 2026
- Source:
- King's College London
- Summary:
- A review of more than 265,000 people found that cannabis use was associated with higher rates of both committing violence and becoming a victim of it. The researchers say the link is significant but does not prove cannabis itself is the cause.
- Share:
A large review led by researchers at King's College London has found that people who use cannabis are more likely both to commit violent acts and to experience violence themselves.
Researchers from the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience (IoPPN) combined data from 63 studies involving more than 265,000 people. They analyzed the general population separately from people receiving psychiatric care.
What the Review Examined
The researchers used the World Health Organization's broad definition of violence, which includes physical, sexual and psychological violence toward another person, both inside and outside intimate relationships.
They also separated self-reported violence from cases that resulted in criminal convictions. When individual studies measured several forms of violence, the researchers focused on the most serious type reported. The findings were published in Psychological Medicine.
Dr. Marta Di Forti, co-author of the study from the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience (IoPPN) at King's College London, and South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust, said:
"As a clinician, I've seen how heavy cannabis use can be a factor in violence. We've been cautious for a long time about how far we could go in describing this link, but a review of this size lets us speak with more confidence about the risks, while being careful not to stigmatize people who use cannabis more broadly."
Cannabis Use and Victimization
The review also found that people who used cannabis were about one and a half times as likely to become victims of violence. This association was stronger among women than among men.
Professor Sir Robin Murray, senior author of the study from the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience at King's College London, said:
"In the general population, people who used cannabis were around twice as likely to have committed a violent act as those who didn't; for those in psychiatric care, cannabis users were around two and a half times as likely to be violent as other psychiatric patients who didn't use cannabis. The link held in studies that followed people over time, though it was smaller than in studies that looked at a single point in time. For violence that led to a criminal conviction, people who used cannabis were three to four times as likely to have been convicted.
"As cannabis becomes more commercialized and legalized around the world, the conversation about its risks has focused mostly on the person using it. This review shows that violence, both committing it and experiencing it, needs to be part of that conversation too."
Implications for Mental Health and Public Health
Based on the findings, the researchers say mental health services should routinely ask about cannabis use when evaluating a person's risk of violence. They also argue that public health information about cannabis should include the possible connection with violence.
However, the researchers emphasize that the review identifies an association and does not prove that cannabis directly causes violence. Cannabis use often occurs alongside other factors that can also increase the risk of violent behavior or victimization, including alcohol use, other drug use and difficult social circumstances.
Important Limitations
Only a small number of the studies measured how much cannabis people used or how often they used it. The findings involving criminal convictions were also based on a relatively limited number of studies.
Most of the research was conducted before high potency cannabis became common. The researchers suggest that daily use of today's more potent cannabis products could potentially be associated with stronger effects.
The study was supported by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Biomedical Research Centre: Maudsley and the Medical Research Council (MR/T007818/1). The views expressed are those of the authors and not necessarily those of the NIHR or the Department of Health and Social Care.
Story Source:
Materials provided by King's College London. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Giulia Trotta, Victoria Rodriguez, Paolo Marino, Meklit Gurmesa, Edoardo Spinazzola, Zhikun Li, Luis Alameda, Marta Di Forti, Robin Murray, Evangelos Vassos. Cannabis use is associated with increased risk of violence: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Psychological Medicine, 2026; 56 DOI: 10.1017/S0033291726105856

Against the backdrop of setbacks in the Chinese market, BMW is preparing steps to improve profitability — what it will do
Kyiv • UNN
BMW plans to invest €2 billion in production in Germany and revise its strategy. By 2028, profitability is expected to rise to 3–5%.
German premium carmaker BMW will unveil plans to expand local production as it seeks to restore profitability following a series of profit warnings caused by weak performance in the Chinese market. Analysts at Bernstein said this on Wednesday, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
BMW is due to present an updated strategy later on Wednesday at a Capital Markets Day event for investors, but Bernstein analysts outlined the key elements of the plan in an analytical note following a meeting with the company’s management.
BMW’s reputation as a resilient company took a hit in June when it unexpectedly announced a cut to its profit forecast — the third such reduction in just over three years due to problems in the Chinese market. The setback highlighted the challenges facing European automakers amid falling sales in China and the imposition of tariffs in the United States.
In response, the Munich-based automaker launched a workforce-reduction program that is estimated to affect around 8,000 jobs in Germany, thereby joining Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz (MBGn.DE) in cost-optimization measures.
BMW, whose shares have fallen by more than a third over the past year, reaching their lowest level in more than six years, is presenting its recovery plan during a two-day event in Munich and at the company’s country estate, "Gut Schwaerzenbach," in Bavaria.
According to Bernstein, BMW will set a medium-term profitability target for its automotive division of 3–5% by 2028.
By the early 2030s, the company plans to restore profitability to 8–10%, which would represent a significant improvement compared with the latest figure of 2.3%.
"At BMW, they understand that the solution is not only about cutting costs. The company is also seeking to drive growth through innovative products," said Bernstein analyst Stephen Reitman, adding that the Neue Klasse lineup, led by the iX3 electric crossover, plays a key role in the recovery plan. According to Bernstein analysts, BMW will confirm plans to launch a luxury SUV positioned above the X7 in the lineup, as well as expand the M and Alpina ranges starting in 2027, with the aim of strengthening its position in the premium segment.
A BMW representative said details of the strategy would be disclosed later on Wednesday.
Separately, the company said it intends to invest around 2 billion euros ($2.3 billion) in producing the next-generation 3 Series sports sedan in Germany.
According to Bernstein estimates, BMW’s production facilities in Europe and the United States are operating at full capacity, while China is the "main region requiring production adjustments and capacity flexibility."

China claims 100th Asian Games diving gold
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:48:06 CST
21:48:06 KST

Gold medalist Lian Junjie (L) and bronze medalist Zhao Renjie of China pose after the awarding ceremony for the men's 10m platform final of diving at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Tokyo, Japan, Sept. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Zhizun)
TOKYO, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Olympic champion Lian Junjie won the men's 10m platform gold medal at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Wednesday, delivering China's 100th Asian Games diving gold medal and completing the Chinese team's sweep of all 10 diving titles at the Games.
Lian scored 501.25 points at the Tokyo Aquatics Center to take the title. Japan's Rikuto Tamai finished second with 497.20 points, while China's 15-year-old Zhao Renjie took bronze with 427.50.
"First of all, I'm very happy," Lian said. "To win the 10th gold medal for the Chinese diving team at these Games, and the 100th Asian Games diving gold in the team's history, on the final day of the competition, was really hard-earned. I'm very happy that we managed to hold on to it."
Lian built his advantage in the fourth and fifth dives, scoring 91.80 points on both his reverse 3 1/2 somersaults and back 3 1/2 somersaults. He finished with 501.25 points. Tamai, also the Paris Olympic silver medalist, scored 93.60 points on his final dive but finished 4.05 points behind Lian.
"It was another silver medal, but more than anything, I feel a great sense of relief," Tamai said. "Of course, I was aiming for gold, but there was also a part of me that realistically thought I might finish with bronze. So I'm really happy that I was able to move up a place and win a medal here at home."
China's Zhao, making his Asian Games debut, meanwhile made an eye-catching start. He scored 86.40 and 91.80 points on his opening two dives before producing 96.90 points on his stunning third dive, a reverse 3 1/2 somersaults. The first three dives also saw judges award several perfect 10s.
"I felt pretty much the same as I did in training," Zhao said of his opening rounds. "I was able to bring out what I normally do in training."
The 15-year-old then suffered two costly mistakes on his fourth and fifth dives, earning only 27.00 and 44.40 respectively, but recovered to finish with bronze.
"There was a little fluctuation in my emotions, but I adjusted afterward," Zhao said. "My coach told me not to be nervous and not to think about the previous dive. Every dive is a new beginning."
Tamai also spoke about Zhao, "I see him as a strong rival," he said. "He's a lovely kid and is well-liked by everyone around him. But I try not to be pulled into that and instead compete with him as an equal athlete." The Japanese diver said the two were similar in some ways and described Zhao as being "like a younger brother."
For Lian, the gold also carried a deeply personal meaning. When he first arrived at the Tokyo Aquatics Center, he said he was quite emotional because the venue reminded him of the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, when he missed out on selection and could only watch his teammates compete on television.
"Being able to come here and compete individually was already very difficult for me," said Lian, now 25. "To be able to come here, win the gold medal and complete what I wanted to do, I feel it is something really worth remembering. In a way, it is also a form of closure for me."
Lian, who has already won the men's synchronized 10m platform title with Yang Hao at these Games, said the men's platform remains one of the most competitive events in diving.
"There is never such a thing as being assured of victory on the 10m platform," he said. "It is about who can withstand the pressure and who can adjust their mindset better."
Earlier in the day, Olympic champion Chen Yiwen scored 358.05 to win the women's 3m springboard title, also China's 99th diving gold in Asiad. Teammate Chen Jia finished second with 347.45 points, while Japan's Sayaka Mikami took bronze with 332.35.
The victory gave Chen her second gold medal at the Games, after she teamed up with Chen Jia to win the women's synchronized 3m springboard title on Sunday. Chen said she had arrived in Aichi-Nagoya aiming for two gold medals, but admitted the road to completing the target had not been easy.
"I was aiming for two gold medals, so the result was in line with my expectations, but the process could definitely have been better," Chen said. "I've had some ups and downs in form over the past two years, so I put some pressure on myself."
Beyond the medals, Chinese divers also pointed to the hard work and values passed down from one generation to the next as key to the team's sustained success.
"First of all, it all comes down to hard training," Lian said. "Without hard training, there would be no solid fundamentals, physical reserves or the ability to adjust mentally."
But training alone is not the whole story. Lian, who once learned from senior divers, now sees himself as part of the generation responsible for passing that experience on.
"I hope the younger athletes can see the spirit of our predecessors, never giving up and continuing to work hard," he said. "I also hope I can set a good example for them."
The younger diver Zhao has already identified Lian as someone he looks up to. "Lian Junjie is particularly strong, and he is also my idol," Zhao said. And for him, the path ahead is already clear.
"I hope to learn from the older brothers, make it to the Olympic stage and become an Olympic champion," he added. ■
