Economic Watch: China's September PMIs return to expansion amid firming recovery
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:47:57 CST
21:47:57 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- China's manufacturing activity was back in expansion territory in September while non-manufacturing activity rebounded markedly, with both above the boom-bust line, official data showed on Wednesday, adding to signs of a firming recovery in the world's second-largest economy.
The purchasing managers' index (PMI) for China's manufacturing sector stood at 50.1 in September 2026, up 0.3 percentage points from August and returning to the expansion zone, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
A reading above 50 indicates expansion, while a reading below 50 signifies contraction.
The manufacturing sector's business climate improved further in September, with the PMI rising for a second consecutive month, said Huo Lihui, a chief statistician with the NBS.
Among the 21 industries surveyed, 12 reported a PMI above the expansion threshold, four more than the previous month, Huo noted.
The sector saw expansion in both manufacturing output and market demand in September. The production sub-index climbed to 51.7, up 1.3 percentage points from August, while the new orders index was at 50.5, still above the threshold.
Driven by the acceleration in production, enterprises' willingness to purchase strengthened, with the procurement volume index reaching 51.0, an increase of 0.5 percentage points from the previous month, said Huo.
PMIs for the equipment manufacturing industry, the high-tech manufacturing industry and the consumer goods industry stood at 51, 52.5 and 50.7, respectively, all remaining in the expansion zone.
Affected by rising international commodity prices and growing demand in some industries, the purchasing price index for major raw materials and the ex-factory price index for manufacturing stood at 60.8 and 54, respectively, up 4.2 percentage points and 3.6 percentage points from the previous month.
PMIs for medium-sized and small manufacturing enterprises came in at 49.7 and 48.9, respectively, increases of 0.3 percentage points and 1 percentage point from the previous month, as business activity picked up.
Non-manufacturing activity also increased. The business activity index for the non-manufacturing sector reached 50.2 in September, a rise of 1.2 percentage points from August. The construction sector index rose 3.4 percentage points to 50.3, the highest level this year, while the services sector index increased by 0.9 percentage points to 50.2, with both returning to expansion.
"The traditional peak season and the upcoming National Day holiday have driven up demand in transportation, tourism and related consumer services," said Wu Wei, an analyst with the China Logistics Information Center.
The improvement came as a package of pro-growth measures was rolled out at a faster pace. The National Development and Reform Commission on Wednesday said it, together with the Ministry of Finance, had allocated the fourth and final batch of 62.5 billion yuan (around 9.28 billion U.S. dollars) in ultra-long special treasury bonds for consumer goods trade-in programs, bringing this year's total to 250 billion yuan.
Starting Oct. 1, China will implement interest subsidies for housing loans for eligible first-home buyers, offering an annualized subsidy of 1 percentage point on loans of up to 1 million yuan for up to five years, the Ministry of Finance and other departments said.
The People's Bank of China, China's central bank, announced a raft of strengthened support measures on Tuesday, including cutting the one-year interest rate of the pledged supplementary lending (PSL) facility from 1.75 percent to 1.5 percent, to better incentivize policy banks to support the real economy and serve national strategies.
It has also decided to increase the quota of the relending facility for sci-tech innovation and technological upgrades by 200 billion yuan and for agriculture and small and micro businesses by 500 billion yuan, out of which 300 billion yuan is dedicated to financial support for private firms.
"The recent policy mix is characterized by stepped-up counter-cyclical adjustments and the concentrated rollout of incremental tools," said Wen Bin, chief economist with China Minsheng Bank.
"With existing policies becoming more effective and incremental policies continuing to be introduced, economic momentum is expected to pick up further in the fourth quarter," he noted.
Looking ahead, China's manufacturing sector is expected to maintain steady and moderate expansion in the fourth quarter, said Wen Tao, an analyst with the China Logistics Information Center, citing accelerated implementation of major projects, including about 2 trillion yuan of planned investment by central state-owned enterprises in six major infrastructure networks this year. ■

Fijian minister warns of possible power rationing amid prolonged dry conditions
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:47:55 CST
21:47:55 KST

SUVA, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Fiji could face electricity rationing if prolonged dry weather pushes water levels at major hydropower facilities to critical levels, Infrastructure Minister Ro Filipe Tuisawau said on Wednesday.
Tuisawau said the water level at Monasavu Dam, Fiji's largest hydroelectric facility, stood at 732.2 meters as of Monday, which was 17.2 meters above the safe operating level and 12.8 meters below the dam's spill level.
He said Fiji's Energy Fiji Limited (EFL) is conserving water at its hydropower dams and increasing thermal power generation to help safeguard electricity supplies amid concerns over below-average rainfall.
EFL currently has 295.07 megawatts of available generating capacity, according to the minister.
However, Tuisawau warned that continued declines in dam water levels could force the government to introduce power rationing, with essential services such as hospitals prioritized.
Fiji is experiencing El Nino conditions, which the minister said could bring below-average rainfall through the end of 2026 and into early 2027.
The government is also investing in renewable energy as part of efforts to reduce the country's dependence on hydropower and fossil fuels. ■

Asian Games | China's forward Wang Yudong keen to step into European football
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:47:48 CST
21:47:48 KST

by sportswriter Xiao Shiyao and Wang Haizhou
OSAKA, Japan, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- China's young forward Wang Yudong said Wednesday that he hopes to take the next step in his career by playing in Europe after testing himself against South Korea's European-based players in the men's football semifinal at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games.
China lost 2-1 to South Korea in the semifinal despite taking an early lead through Wang.
"I feel the gap between us and the top Asian teams is narrowing," the 20-year-old said after the match. "Physically, I believe we are comparable to South Korea. Tactically, we performed well in this game and did not give them many clear chances."
Wang also highlighted South Korea's Eom Ji-sung, who plays for Swansea City in the English second-tier Championship and operates in a similar position.
"South Korea's No. 7 plays in the same position as me and has a similar style," Wang said. "His movement and decision-making on the ball are really impressive. After all, he is playing in the English Championship, and there is still a lot I can learn from him."
The experience has strengthened Wang's desire to try in European football.
"I think the first thing is to take that step and give it a try," Wang said when asked about his future. "No matter what, I want to experience life and the rhythm of football outside China. Once you go abroad, you have to rely on your own."
Asked whether this year would be the right time for him to move overseas, Wang said there were many factors to consider.
"There are many things that need to be taken into consideration, so we have to look at everything as a whole," he said. "If there is an opportunity, I will definitely take that step. Once you take that step, I think things will become much better."
Reflecting on the semifinal, Wang said China had performed well and believed South Korea's high press was not as intense as expected.
"I personally think we played a very good game," he said. "We found that South Korea's high press was not that aggressive, so we were able to keep possession and move the ball around better."
"Football requires both ability and a bit of luck, and it's a shame that we couldn't win," he added.
South Korea scored the winning goal in the 82nd minute. Wang said China's late push for an equalizer was their only option.
"Their second goal came quite late, so all we could do was throw everything forward," he said. "As for Zhang Yuning's final shot, I think it should have been a penalty."
China will play the loser of the other semifinal between Japan and Uzbekistan in the bronze-medal match on Saturday. Wang remains confident that the team can finish the tournament with a medal.
"Our overall goal is definitely to take a medal home," he said. ■

U.S. Army taps five firms for 1,000 km HIMARS missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:42:25 UTC
21:42:25 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded five Other Transaction Authority agreements on Sept. 29, 2026, to develop Precision Strike Missile Increment 4 prototypes.
- Anduril, Castelion, Lockheed Martin, Mach Industries and RTX will develop HIMARS-launched missiles to hit moving ships and relocatable land targets at least 1,000 km away.
The U.S. Army has picked five companies to build competing prototypes of a new Precision Strike Missile that can be fired from a HIMARS truck and hit moving ships and relocatable land targets 1,000 km (620 miles) or more away.
Anduril, Castelion, Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control, Mach Industries and RTX each received a separate Other Transaction Authority agreement on Sept. 29 for PrSM Increment 4, the U.S. Army said. Other Transaction agreements are a faster contracting route used for prototypes outside standard procurement rules. The service did not disclose the value of any of the five awards.
The companies will now race each other in two rounds. In fiscal 2027, which begins on Oct. 1, initial prototype work will end in a competitive fly-off, after which the U.S. Army will cut the field. Vendors whose designs prove mature enough will be eligible for follow-on agreements and a final fly-off in fiscal 2028.
The requirement is demanding. The U.S. Army told industry in March that the fly-offs would focus on three things: a range of at least 1,000 km, compatibility with the M142 HIMARS launcher with room to move to other launchers later, and the ability to strike moving targets at sea as well as mobile targets on land, such as missile launchers and air defense systems.
That range would roughly double the reach of today’s PrSM. The first version of the missile, Increment 1, entered service in 2023 as a replacement for the older Army Tactical Missile System, which flies up to 300 km (186 miles). Lockheed Martin designed Increment 1 for about 500 km (310 miles), and the U.S. Army has said it has been tested against targets more than 400 km away. The missile was used in combat for the first time in March against targets in Iran.
The PrSM family is being upgraded in steps. Increment 2 adds a seeker that lets the missile hit moving ships, and the U.S. Army awarded Lockheed Martin a contract worth up to $1.2 billion for its production earlier this month. Increment 3 is meant to add new warhead and payload options, while Increment 4 is the long-range version.
Two of the five winners have been working on the long-range missile for years. In 2023, the U.S. Army gave Lockheed Martin and a team of Raytheon and Northrop Grumman contracts to develop new propulsion and airframe designs for what was then called the Long Range Maneuverable Fires missile, with Lockheed receiving $33.3 million and the Raytheon team nearly $100 million, Breaking Defense reported at the time.
Lockheed Martin has said its Increment 4 design pairs a rocket booster with an air-breathing ramjet engine to double the range of the current missile while keeping it the same size, so it can still fit existing HIMARS and M270 launchers. In June, the company and L3Harris completed a ground test of the handoff from booster to ramjet, which Lockheed described as the main technical hurdle before flight testing.
The other three awards bring newer defense firms into a program that Lockheed Martin has so far dominated. Castelion is developing the Blackbeard hypersonic missile, which the U.S. Navy selected earlier this year for its Multi-mission Affordable Capacity Effector program. Anduril and Mach Industries have not publicly described their Increment 4 designs.

Ranulph Fiennes’s stepson says he is in contact with police about explorer’s wellbeing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:39:25 UTC
21:39:25 KST

The stepson of Sir Ranulph Fiennes has been contacted by police and says he intends to speak to them this week over his concerns about the explorer’’s wellbeing.
Alexander Millington-Cotes – who is estranged from his mother, Louise, Fiennes’s second and current wife – said an officer from Cheshire police had called him in recent days.
The call, he said, had given him hope that the concerns of Fiennes’s friends and family were being taken seriously, adding that the officer appeared interested in what he had observed. “That’s the one bit of hope,” Millington-Cotes told the Guardian.
Questions have been raised in recent months about the welfare of Fiennes, who has Parkinson’s and is in the care of his wife, who has power of attorney. Among those who have raised issues is his relative Joseph Fiennes, the actor, who wrote in January to the Office of the Public Guardian, setting out concerns about Ranulph being cut off from friends and family. He has not been seen in public for two years.
Millington-Cotes, 31, said he had been disappointed by the response of the authorities so far.
Cheshire police issued a statement on Monday in which they said they did not have “safeguarding concerns” regarding the 82-year-old. It said officers were “satisfied that Sir Ranulph Fiennes is living in an appropriate setting with suitable care and professional oversight”.
Millington-Cotes said a wide group of friends were concerned the police did not have the full picture. It is claimed that the explorer has spent more than a year living under assumed names in a succession of care homes and that even attempts by the king to check on him had been rebuffed by Fiennes’s wife.
Millington-Cotes said: “I might have possibly one more avenue with the police. I just got a call the other day from a detective who wanted to speak to me, which was interesting and encouraging. They kind of wanted to get my perspective on things and the sort of things that I’ve observed and things like that, and what I believe to be the truth.”
Cheshire police said: “Yes, we’re in touch with him. Our original statement still stands.”
Millington-Cotes, an aerospace engineer, described the initial police statement as “slapdash” and “really disappointing”. He is crowdfunding a legal application in an attempt to wrest power of attorney over Fiennes away from his mother.
Among the last people to see Fiennes was Arabella Pepper, the younger sister of Ranulph’s late first wife, Ginny, who claimed visitors were asked to sign non-disclosure agreements. She claimed Fiennes appeared “incredibly relieved” to see her and that he had spoken of “longing” to see friends.
Michael Kobold, a friend who has been among those questioning Fiennes’s treatment, said he was concerned the explorer’s isolation had since become “even more draconian”, including during his time in a care home in Wales, where staff were given strict instructions on his day to day activities.
When the arrangements at that home were raised as an issue of concern by the owner with the regulator, the Care Inspectorate Wales confirmed in an email that the correct protocols were not in place.
They wrote: “Currently [Sir Ranulph] is being deprived of his liberty unlawfully as there is no authorised deprivation in place which reflects the current residence and restrictions in place.”
Kobold said: “This was reported to me by the owner of the care home in Wales, from where Louise moved Ran after the owner raised concerns with the relevant authorities.”
Fiennes’s current whereabouts is not known. Louise Millington-Cotes was contacted for comment.

Ukraine's finances: everything we don't know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:39:17 UTC
21:39:17 KST

BRUSSELS, Belgium — Ukraine, the EU, the IMF, and G7 partners were all in Brussels on Sept. 29 to discuss the state of Ukraine's finances until the end of 2027, but a sense of who will pay what, and how much money is even needed, remains elusive.
"Our idea is to secure some possible solutions in a way which helps us to meet our needs in 2027," Finance Minister Serhii Marchenko said at an event organized the day before by the European Policy Center (EPC) think tank.
And there is a common understanding that Ukraine has significant financial needs.
When the EU finalized its 90 billion-euro ($102 billion) loan to Ukraine in April 2026, it was explicitly clear that it was intended to cover only two-thirds of Kyiv's total budgetary needs until the end of 2027.
Contributions from third countries were expected to fill in the remaining third, but aside from a $9 billion pledge for 2027 from Norway, this has not happened.
"We need to shoulder the financing challenge ahead together," the EU's Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos told attendees of the Sept. 29 Ukraine Donor Platform meeting, according to excerpts of the closed-door speech provided to the Kyiv Independent.
"The European Union will be doing its part. But we need sufficiently ambitious commitments from everyone," Kos said.
But even understanding how much everyone needs to contribute is getting complicated. The calculation of 45 billion euros ($51 billion) remaining outstanding, minus the Norwegian contribution, should leave Ukraine short of around 37 billion euros ($42 billion) until the end of 2027.
read also
Nailing jelly to a ceiling
On Aug. 24, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv had a $27 billion budget shortfall for 2026 and publicly called on the EU to frontload payments earmarked for 2027 already in 2026.
However, Ukraine never formally requested that the EU carry out that maneuver, then or since.
Never entirely explained: the gap itself. Marchenko mentioned that it was part salaries for troops, and part drone procurements, during the EPC event.
But he also said "we can manage the budget this year, and we have some scenarios for how we can react in this year's budget," suggesting the hole has been resolved.
"Unfortunately, we still have an uncovered gap for 2027," Marchenko said.
But Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said that only around $7 billion could be clawed back from the $27 billion shortfall for 2026 via cost-cutting measures, during a press briefing with journalists on Sept. 28.
“The remaining $20 billion is the subject of negotiations with partners," Koretskyi said.
Marchenko also pointed to several budgetary surprises during his panel event, which illuminate how difficult it can be to predict finances in a country at war.
"For the first time since 2022, we realize that we have underperformance in our tax and customs administrations," Marchenko said, noting a 400 million euro ($454 million) projected shortfall for September.
He also mentioned the ongoing blockage of agricultural exports via the Black Sea.
"We are capable of exporting only 40% of our grain … it's a challenge because we can't receive sufficient money from exports to help our budget."
And the evolving needs of Ukraine's defense also play a role. Marchenko listed the costs of the Operation Vivaldi counteroffensive and the need to rapidly develop interceptor technology to take out Russia's jet-powered Shahed drones, as examples.
The European Commission's reaction to this ever-shifting situation remains fairly consistent, with spokesperson Balazs Ujvari telling the Kyiv Independent that there are "three key messages."
"First, Ukraine needs to continue to reform. Second, our international partners need to step up to the plate with concrete pledges, and third, we have to start gearing up for 2027."
And to address the looming budget gap of 2027, Ujvari notes that Kyiv and Brussels need to agree on the financial strategy for that year.
"The sooner we have this document, the final version from Ukraine, the better it is. We can go ahead and adopt it, and that will give predictability as regards next year," Ujvari said.
Marchenko met with the EU's Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis later that day to discuss reforms and the 2027 financing strategy.
Few seem serious about filling the hole
Regardless of how large Ukraine's budgetary gap ends up being, there is no dispute that one will exist.
Even so, repeated requests from the EU and Ukraine for other countries to step up their contributions have failed to bear fruit, and no new pledges came out of the Sept. 29 Donor Platform meeting, even though G7 countries were in attendance.
In terms of EU support, there are ongoing conversations around frontloading 2027 payments of the 90 billion loan earlier in the year, but this does not increase the amount of funding available, it merely provides short-term relief at the expense of the second-half of next year.
And discussions about various mechanisms for using Russia's more than 200 billion euros ($227 billion) in assets immobilized in Europe to help Ukraine have likewise failed to make headway so far.
Closer to home, lawmakers also don't all seem particularly serious about solving the challenge.
Marchenko all but ruled out raising taxes, saying, "I am not sure that this is the right time,"and expressing fear of the pressure it would add to businesses.
"We should find a way … how to combat our shadow economy," Marchenko suggested, but without providing details on how.
Two weeks before, Kos and Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis co-signed a letter to the parliament in Kyiv, reminding of 21 previously agreed reforms that Ukraine could pass by the end of the year, and in doing so unlock over 20 billion euros ($22.7 billion) in financial support.
Kos also reminded of the importance of carrying out reforms in her Sept. 29 speech.
"Substantial EU financing remains available still this year, if reforms are delivered. This will require unity inside Ukraine," she said.
Koretskyi told journalists that there is $29.5 billion "we risk not receiving to the budget from international partners if we do not fulfill the obligations we have undertaken."
At a press conference on Sept. 23, Zelensky defended the parliament, telling journalists that "it's impossible to calculate that the parliament will work the way it works in a normal country in a normal non-military time."
"It's a fact. The parliament does not work in an unconditional format 24 hours a day. That's it," Zelensky said.
"Let's be flexible, because we have a war," he added.
But the parliament's sense of urgency falls far short of what Zelensky's comments suggest, with its next meeting scheduled only for Oct. 12, a month after the last one.
"Of course we know it's a very difficult situation there," Ujvari told journalists.
"There's a war of aggression and it's very difficult to operate in … but at the same time there is a jointly agreed reform agenda … these need to be pursued," Ujvari said.
Koretskyi said the government is working to "fulfill all its obligations by Oct. 15," but that the parliament needs to pass laws.
"We are working with the Verkhovna Rada to make Oct. 12 also a session day to vote on the bills needed to receive these funds," Koretskyi said.
"For Ukraine, time is very short now," he added.

Gazan who called for Jews to be killed, then moved to UK, now disavows Hamas: ‘They forced me’ | Watch

21:38:44 KST

Gazan migrant Mosab Abdulkarim Al-Gassas, 34, known as Abu Wadi, entered Britain by boat illegally last year and was jailed for nine months for entering the country without authorization or a valid visa. He was later granted permission to stay. After taking part in Hamas activity in Gaza and calling for Jews to be killed, he was tracked down by a local newspaper reporter at an apartment in the town of Corby and confronted about his past. Local Labour MP Lee Barron said he was appalled by the discovery and would contact the home secretary to demand Al-Gassas’ immediate deportation.
Abu Wadi was found this week by a Northamptonshire Telegraph reporter at an apartment he shares with three other migrants. During the interview, conducted through a translation app, he acknowledged that he had previously been a member of a Hamas tire-burning unit and had called for Jews to be killed, but said that was eight years ago and claimed Hamas had forced him to do it.
He denied that he still supports the terror group. “Everyone knows Hamas is a terrorist organization that would have killed us if we didn’t speak against the Jews while we lived there,” he said. He also said he now has Jewish friends and enjoys his life in Corby. Asked whether he wanted to remain in Britain, he replied: “I love Corby.” When asked whether he wanted to return to Gaza, he said: “No talk Gaza, no talk Israel, no talk news, no nothing.” He later added: “I need to live here.”
Those statements stand in contrast to material he posted in the past. Abu Wadi, who runs a TikTok account with around 20,000 followers and continues to upload videos from central Corby, previously posted photos and videos showing himself carrying a rifle and confronting IDF forces.
In a video posted to his Facebook account in September 2024, before he arrived in Britain, he said: “Allah, deal with the Jews and those loyal to them. Allah, kill them one by one and leave none of them. Allah, destroy them completely, scatter them entirely and bring the ground down beneath their feet.”
Abu Wadi in a photo he posted. ‘Allah, destroy them completely, scatter them entirely and bring the ground down beneath their feet,’ he wrote.
The discovery that Abu Wadi was living in Corby, about 75 kilometers east of Birmingham, prompted sharp reactions from local officials. Barron said he had previously worked to have migrants removed from Corby and intended to do so again. Local council member Mark Pengelly backed the demand, calling the migrant’s presence in the town a “ridiculous situation” and stressing that residents’ safety was his top priority.
Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp said it was a joke that taxpayers were being forced to cover Abu Wadi’s expenses while he receives a weekly subsistence allowance of 49.18 pounds, about 200 shekels, for what he described as the “lifestyle of a Hamas-supporting, gun-carrying extremist who broke into our country illegally.”
The senior Conservative politician called for the 34-year-old migrant to be deported, adding: “Given that he supports Hamas and Hamas-controlled Gaza, I see no reason why he cannot go back there. He will fit in there perfectly.”
The Home Office is seeking to deport him, but cannot currently do so because of “the dangers in the area and the absence of safe and lawful routes back to Gaza.” A spokesman for the Campaign Against Antisemitism responded angrily: “What is the point of imprisoning someone for being in the country illegally, and then, once he finishes his sentence, allowing him to walk free?”

Qatar PM tells Piers Morgan: Netanyahu is a war criminal

Qatar PM tells Piers Morgan: Netanyahu is a war criminal, nothing justifies what happened in Gaza
Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed Bin Abdulrahman Al Thani described Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as a "war criminal", stressing that what is being committed in the Gaza Strip constitutes "war crimes", during an interview with British broadcaster Piers Morgan on on Tuesday, 29 September.
During the interview, Sheikh Al Thani remarked: "What is being committed in Gaza is war crimes, and everyone responsible for that is a war criminal," and responded with a "yes" when Morgan directly asked whether the description applied to Netanyahu.
He further pointed out that media reports revealed that the Israeli government was organising an official campaign against Qatar, including funding institutions, academic circles, media outlets and content creators, to pressure Doha and undermine its role as a mediator to end the US-Israeli war on Iran.
He added that Netanyahu and "the extremists in his government" had worked throughout the past two years of the war on Gaza to undermine every Qatari effort to mediate and end the war.
Regarding Qatar's relationship with Palestinian resistance group Hamas, he stressed that Doha's engagement and communication with the group came at the request of the United States.
He said the relocation of its political office from Damascus had been fully coordinated to prevent its involvement in the war in Syria during the 2010's and ensure that Syrian territory would not be used as a platform for the group.
He noted that Qatar had mediated during repeated wars over the years between Hamas and Israel and that the office had also proved beneficial to Israel's security.
He stressed that Qatar had been in contact with Israeli officials from the first day after what he described as a "difficult" meeting with Hamas leaders to secure the release of civilian captives from the Gaza Strip.
He also explained that the group's message was a request for a ceasefire period to allow for their release, followed by discussion and negotiations on the remaining issues.
But Israeli officials showed no interest in discussing the idea, the Qatari prime minister said.
In response to a question about accusations that Israel had committed genocide, Al Thani said, "There is no doubt that what happened on 7 October was a massacre, and it must be condemned, and everyone responsible for it must be held accountable."
"But when we look at the response to 7 October, the killing of more than 70,000 people, the wiping out of an entire city, targeting hospitals, targeting schools. Whatever the justifications and arguments, nothing justifies that," he added.
He noted that since the signing of the ceasefire agreement, which was sponsored and facilitated by US President Donald Trump in October 2025, more than 1,400 Palestinians in Gaza had been killed by Israel.
He also pointed out that nearly 70% of the territory had become occupied and Israeli forces had barred access to it.
"They are not fulfilling their obligations under this agreement, and this simply shows that they have different intentions," he added.
On the US-Israeli war with Iran, the Qatari prime minister revealed that he had received a call from the White House half an hour before the military campaign began.
"I was actually asleep in my bed, and I woke up a few minutes or half an hour before the war began and was told that a military campaign was about to begin," he recalled, and Qatar received an early warning, "it would have done everything in its power to prevent the war".
The Qatari prime minister highlighted that Qatar came under attack on its territory about 45 minutes to an hour after the US-Israeli campaign began, paralysing its movement and leaving it unable to engage in diplomacy during the war's initial stage.
On mediation efforts between Washington and Tehran, Al Thani argued that back-channel diplomacy was the most effective way to make progress, but public statements issued by various parties do impact efforts.
"It is much better for everyone to stop making statements, engage seriously in the diplomatic process and give it a real chance," he added.
The Qatari prime minister ended the interview by identifying three issues that any potential agreement to end the Iran war should focus on:
First, solving the nuclear issue via an agreement that satisfies the United States and the International Atomic Energy Agency, while granting Iran the right to the peaceful use of nuclear energy and lifting sanctions; second, restoring the Strait of Hormuz condition to what it was before the war, under international law and backed by a regional agreement; and thirdly, reforming security arrangements between the Gulf Cooperation Council states and Iran via frank and direct dialogue based on the principles of good neighbourliness, non-interference in internal affairs and mutual non-aggression.

Türkiye's Emine Erdogan leads first ladies’ call for UN framework to protect children online
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:35:54 UTC
21:35:54 KST

As technology companies expand their influence over children's lives, first ladies and spouses of world leaders have called for a common international framework to protect young users, with Türkiye's Emine Erdogan urging the United Nations to establish shared standards for digital safety.
Speaking at a high-level meeting at UN headquarters in New York on September 21, Erdogan said national regulations alone could not adequately address the challenges posed by global technology companies and called instead for coordinated international action.
The event, titled “The Invisible Architecture: Building Safe Digital Systems for Children”, was held on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly high-level week under Erdogan's auspices, in cooperation with UNICEF and the Office of the UN Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence against Children.
The discussion brought together first ladies and spouses of heads of state and government from 13 countries, who highlighted the growing risks children face online and the need to make their safety a shared international responsibility.
From national restrictions to global standards
Erdogan cautioned against treating technology as an outright threat, but argued that digital platforms had evolved far beyond communication tools into systems that can direct societies and reshape everyday life.
“We cannot be a mere onlooker to technology, which we have invented ourselves, inventing a new human type that will serve its purposes in front of our own eyes,” she said.
She criticised business models that prioritise profit and engagement over children's well-being, arguing that the pressure exerted by such systems on young users must be addressed.
“Ensuring children's safety is not solely the responsibility of parents; it is all of our responsibility. We must build a healthy digital ecosystem and ensure that safety is not an additional feature added to digital systems later, but the starting point of their design,” she said.
Türkiye, she noted, introduced legal and technical measures on children's social media use early on. However, individual national regulations can make standardisation difficult when companies operate globally.
“Therefore, we should unite our common efforts,” Erdogan said, calling for common global standards under the UN, supported by regular monitoring and reporting mechanisms.
Her proposal found support among other speakers, who similarly argued that the cross-border nature of digital platforms requires a response beyond national legislation.
Lebanese Prime Minister's spouse Sahar Salam backed a common international framework to establish minimum standards for child safety, clear responsibilities for technology companies, and effective cross-border cooperation.
“No country can protect its children in the digital world alone. Technology crosses borders instantly. Our protection systems do not,” she said.
Romanian First Lady Mirabela Gradinaru also compared it to road safety, noting that countries have their own rules and enforcement mechanisms, while the internet has no equivalent boundaries.
“The problem is no longer local; therefore, the solution can no longer be only local,” she said.
Chilean First Lady María Pía Adriasola Barroilhet, meanwhile, urged adults to lead by example, saying parents must be willing to disconnect from their own screens if they expect children to do the same.
The risks children face behind the screen
Beyond regulation, the speeches highlighted how digital environments expose children to exploitation, manipulation, cyberbullying, harmful content and violations of privacy.
Queen Mathilde of Belgium centred her remarks on children’s rights, arguing that children cannot be treated as a variable in technology companies’ business models.
“We have a collective responsibility to act to safeguard children's rights, safety and wellbeing,” she said.
Burundian First Lady Angeline Ndayishimiye acknowledged the opportunities digital technologies offer young people, particularly across Africa, while warning that these benefits come with growing risks to children's safety and dignity.
Kenyan First Lady Rachel Ruto described the internet as a shared digital space in which threats do not respect national borders.
“A child's data, image, location, and online behaviour are not commodities to be harvested; they are part of that child's dignity, rights, and future,” she said.
The discussion also extended beyond social media to artificial intelligence, with Canadian Prime Minister's spouse Diana Fox Carney warning that AI represents the next frontier in child protection.
“Our children should not have to surrender their childhood to the technologies that we create,” she said.
Serbian First Lady Tamara Vucic called for children to be equipped with the knowledge to understand AI, alongside safe standards for its use in education and stronger international cooperation.
Lithuanian First Lady Diana Nausediene, meanwhile, urged countries to explore technological solutions that could enable effective age verification while protecting personal data against leaks, tracking and profiling.
Making child safety a shared responsibility
Several speakers stressed that international standards must be accompanied by clear obligations for technology companies and practical support for families, schools and communities.
Guatemalan First Lady Lucrecia Eugenia Peinado Villanueva called on companies to put children's rights and safety at the centre of their operations, while urging governments to establish and enforce clear standards.
She also emphasised that children themselves must have a voice in decisions affecting their digital lives.
Gambian First Lady Fatoumatta Bah Barrow argued that technological progress should be measured not simply by innovation, but by whether children can benefit from it safely.
“Years from now, the most important question will not be how clever our technology becomes. It will be whether our children were able to experience its promises safely,” she said.
Senegalese First Lady Marie Khone Faye also called on spouses of world leaders to use their public platforms to mobilise support and translate commitments into action.
For Sierra Leonean First Lady Fatima Maada Bio, the guiding principle should be that technological advancement strengthens rather than diminishes children's rights and well-being.
The speeches converged on a central message: protecting children in an increasingly connected world requires more than regulating their access to technology.
It demands accountability from the companies designing digital environments, cooperation between governments and recognition of children as rights holders whose safety must take precedence over commercial interests.

EU to extend Mediterranean mission to counter Russia's shadow fleet by 2 years

EU to extend Mediterranean mission to counter Russia's shadow fleet by 2 years
The EU intends to expand its naval mission in the Mediterranean Sea to counter Russia's shadow fleet and protect subsea infrastructure. According to a draft document, the operational timeline of the mission EUNAVFOR MED IRINI will be extended until 31 March 2029.
Source: European Pravda, citing a draft document from the Council of the EU, as quoted by Euronews
Details: Originally established in 2020 to enforce the UN arms embargo on Libya, the mission was initially scheduled to conclude in March 2027. However, the European Commission plans to extend it for an additional two years with a budget allocation of €16.88 million, while significantly broadening its operational scope.
In June, Kaja Kallas, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, announced that the operation had modified its rules of engagement and begun conducting inspections of vessels suspected of belonging to Russia's shadow fleet.
In the updated mandate, curbing the operations of Russia's shadow fleet is explicitly defined as a key task of the operation. The document also places greater emphasis on maritime domain awareness, particularly identifying and monitoring illegal activities and threats to the EU's security and economic interests.
EU ambassadors approved the mission's updated mandate on Wednesday 30 September. Formal adoption is anticipated during the meeting of Economics and Finance Ministers on 9 October, after which it will be officially published.
Background:
- In early August, EUNAVFOR MED IRINI conducted an inspection of the tanker Toa Payoh – a vessel belonging to Russia's so-called shadow fleet – to verify its nationality and flag registration status.
- Earlier, France imposed a €1 million fine on the Russian shadow fleet tanker Tagor, which was detained in May. An investigation into another similar vessel is ongoing.

Sloped ceilings and narrow halls don’t have to waste space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:21:01 UTC
21:21:01 KST

Partner content
Sloped ceilings and narrow halls don’t have to waste space
Dutch homes are famously charming – and famously awkward to furnish – for cabinetmakers at Cabinetheroes, that is the whole point. Narrow facades, steep staircases, and rooms that seem to defy right angles: these aren’t quirks, they’re history.
Property taxes in many Dutch cities were once linked to the width of a building’s frontage, and the result can still be seen today: narrow hallways, steep staircases and rooms where standard furniture is difficult to place.
The familiar hooks above many gabled windows are another reminder of these challenging layouts – they were traditionally used to hoist furniture through the windows because getting large pieces up the stairs was often impossible.
Converted attics bring their own challenges. In a typical “zolder”, sloped ceilings and unusual angles can leave large parts of the room unused. Standard wardrobes are made for straight walls and predictable dimensions, and simply can’t use that kind of space. A made-to-measure cabinet, by contrast, can follow the exact shape of the room and turn overlooked corners into valuable storage. The result: rooms that look bigger on paper than they feel in practice, with corners and slopes often written off as wasted.
“You often have more space than you think – you just aren’t using it yet,” says Sven, managing director of the Cabinetheroes franchise network and an experienced carpenter himself.
Planning around the room, not against it
 This is where made-to-measure solutions like those from Cabinetheroes come in. With the Cabinetheroes, creating a cabinet built around a room rather than the other way around is straightforward. Instead of adapting a home to fit off-the-shelf furniture, a personal Cabinethero visits, discusses your ideas, measures the room and plans a solution around the space and the way you live.
As an experienced cabinetmaker, he understands both the design and the craftsmanship behind it, and once the cabinet has been individually manufactured, he also takes care of the professional installation. From the first measurements to the finished cabinet, you have one personal point of contact – and every important step is handled by a skilled professional. Two recent projects show us what this all means in practice.
The hallway that finally feels welcoming
 Christian’s hallway was more of a narrow passage than an inviting entrance. A conventional cabinet would have made the space feel even tighter, yet leaving it empty meant coats, shoes and everyday items had nowhere to go.
After measuring the hallway personally, Sven planned a fitted cloakroom cabinet that uses the available space down to the millimetre, with an integrated LED strip adding light and a warmer atmosphere.
“Tidy, I’d say,” is how Christian describes the practical result. But the emotional difference mattered just as much: “You feel welcome.” His verdict on the process was equally clear: “It was really professional. I’d recommend it to anyone.” Every step along the way was handled by one point of contact.
An open dressing area beneath a sloped roof
 For Jennifer, a sloped ceiling appeared to rule out a spacious dressing area. Standard wardrobes would have left gaps beneath the roof and wasted valuable space in the lowest parts of the room. The made-to-measure design follows the ceiling precisely and uses the space right into the furthest corner.
Instead of doors, the open layout keeps clothing and accessories visible and easy to reach, with socks, belts and other smaller items each getting their own place, helping the room stay organised in everyday life.
“We’d never had such a beautiful cabinet,” Jennifer says. Everything was “matched exactly to the room”, while the personal planning took place comfortably in her own home. Her conclusion: “Quality, style and something completely individual.”
Starting with the room, not the shop
 The lesson from both projects: start with the room rather than with the limited dimensions offered by a furniture shop. Slopes, alcoves and awkward corners are not necessarily wasted space – they simply require accurate measurements and thoughtful planning, with lighting, sockets and everyday routines considered from the beginning.
Features such as integrated LEDs are much easier to incorporate during planning than to add afterwards, and even a few centimetres can determine whether standard furniture fits at all.
As Sven puts it: “Your room can do more.”
For anyone facing a similar layout, the Cabinetheroes offer a free, non-binding enquiry: a personal Cabinethero will visit, discuss the possibilities, take precise measurements and guide the process through to individual planning and professional installation.

New Delhi reveals number of Indian sailors in troubled waters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:20:25 UTC
21:20:25 KST

New Delhi reveals number of Indian sailors in troubled waters
More than 4,500 Indian seafarers are aboard commercial vessels operating in the Persian Gulf amid repeated attacks on regional shipping, New Delhi has said. The Indian government is monitoring their safety after one sailor from the country was killed and another went missing this month. 
Six India-flagged commercial ships and six foreign-flagged vessels carrying cargo to India are currently in the Gulf west of the Strait of Hormuz, with around 163 Indian seafarers aboard them. The more than 4,500 Indians are serving on other commercial vessels operating in the area, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said on Tuesday. 
An Indian sailor was killed when the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier MV Cape Dao was attacked in the Gulf of Oman on September 23. Ten days earlier, an Indian crew member went missing after the Panama-flagged tanker El Gaia was struck while passing through the Strait of Hormuz. 
At least 85 shipping incidents had been recorded in and around the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East by September 24, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) confirmed, highlighting the growing risk to commercial vessels operating in the region. 
India has tightened precautions in response. Shipowners and managers have been advised since July to avoid deploying Indian seafarers on voyages through the Strait of Hormuz until further orders. A 24-hour control room and real-time monitoring system are also tracking vessels and crews in coordination with the Indian Navy and other agencies. 
The safety push has also moved to the diplomatic level. India and Liberia launched a new Group of Friends on Safety and Security of Shipping and Seafarers at the United Nations last week, bringing together around two dozen countries with major roles in shipping, vessel registration and supplying crews.
India is now the world’s second-largest supplier of seafarers, with 311,936 maritime professionals accounting for 12.16% of the global workforce, according to the 2026 BIMCO-ICS Seafarer Workforce Report cited by the Shipping Ministry.
The targeting of commercial ships and crews in international waterways is “simply unacceptable,” Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar told the UN General Assembly on Saturday, calling for restraint, de-escalation, and uninterrupted flows of energy and commerce.
Traffic through Hormuz remains well below pre-conflict levels. Ten commodity vessels crossed the strait on September 23, compared with a ten-day average of about 17. Before the US-Israeli war on Iran began in February, around 125 large commercial vessels typically used the route each day.

NEW DELHI: A Meerut court on Wednesday convicted Muskan Rastogi and her lover Sahil Shukla of killing her husband Saurabh Rajput in the infamous blue drum murder case.
Meerut district judge Arvind Kumar Mishra ruled that Muskan , along with her boyfriend Sahil, conspired to murder her husband Saurabh Rajput and hid his body in a industrial drum using concrete and sand.
The ruling came after 126 hearings and 22 witness statements.

Nominees for Rasoul Prize announced, awarding cemony in Dec.
Unknown

The preliminary list of nominees for the second edition of the Rasoul (PBUH) Medal has been anounced, comprising four candidates each in engineering sciences, mathematics, and computer science; eight in biological and medical sciences; and two each in chemistry and physics. It was also decided that the award ceremony honoring the final laureates would be held in the month of Azar (late autumn).
According to the Communications and Promotion Headquarters of the Mustafa (PBUH) Science and Technology Foundation, the final meeting of the scientific working group for the Rasoul (PBUH) Medal—formerly known as the Young Scientist Medal—was held at the Foundation’s headquarters, attended by the heads of the judging panels for each scientific field.
During the meeting, the preliminary list for the Rasoul (PBUH) Medal was announced, encompassing over 100,000 individuals across seven scientific fields. The breakdown of candidates in the preliminary list was as follows: 55,878 in biological and medical sciences; 4,675 in physics; 7,897 in chemistry; 1,965 in mathematics; 5,589 in computer science; and 26,377 in engineering sciences. Additionally, 14 individuals qualified for inclusion in the preliminary list specifically within the field of nanotechnology.
MSTF Media reports:
 
 According to the Scientific Committee of the Rasoul Medal, previously known as the Young Scientist Medal, the initial list of nominees included more than 100,000 candidates across seven categories: 55,878 candidates in Life and Medical Science and Technology; 4,675 in Physics; 7,897 in Chemistry; 1,965 in Mathematics; 5,589 in Computer Science; and 26,377 in Engineering Sciences. The special category of Nanotechnology also involved 14,000 eligible candidates in the initial list. 
 
 After holding several meetings, the Mustafa(pbuh) Prize Scientific Committee finalized the shortlist, which consists of four finalists in Engineering, four in Basic Sciences, four in Mathematics, four in Computer Science, and eight in Life and Medical Sciences and Technology.
The winners of the Medal are expected to be announced in late October, with the award ceremony scheduled to take place in November-December 2026. 
 
 Hossein Naderi-Manesh, the head of the scientific committee of the Rasoul Medal, also stated that, given the international nature of the event, it would be desirable for the award ceremony to be held in various Islamic countries, emphasizing the need to harness the immense capacities available across the Islamic world to host the event. 
The Medal’s secretariat released a call last December for scientists under the age of 40 residing in Islamic countries. Scientific organisations or individuals were invited to nominate candidates by January 20, 2026.
The Rasoul Medal was established through the endowments of several Mustafa(pbuh) Prize laureates. Professors Ugur Sahin, Omid Farrokhzad, and Dr. Vahab Mirrokni dedicated their cash prize to this cause upon receiving their Mustafa(pbuh) Prize in 2019, 2023, and 2025, respectively. The first edition of the Medal was held concurrently with the 6th edition of the Mustafa(pbuh) Prize in 2025.
Rasoul Medal Nomination
The Medal is awarded to impactful works in the fields of Life and Medical Science and Technology, Basic and Engineering Sciences, and Computer Science by young scientists of the Islamic countries. The candidates must be nominated by a third-party scientific or technological body, such as universities and research centers, reputable scientific and technological associations and institutions, academies of sciences, or science and technology parks.
 
 The candidates for the Rasoul Medal must be under 40 years old at the end of the year in which the medal is awarded. This means that candidates for the 2026 Young Scientist Medal must be born in 1987 or later.
The winners are bestowed a medal, a certificate, and a $10,000 cash prize in each category.
The Rasoul Medal promotes scientific and technological breakthroughs by young scientists in the Islamic world and recognizes their influential achievements. Established as a symbol of excellence and scientific merit, the medal honors the contributions of the young generation of scientific talent.

US Uncovers Russian Intel Plot to Assassinate Anti-Kremlin Activists on US Soil
Russian intelligence-linked operatives planned to assassinate chess grandmaster and Kremlin critic Garry Kasparov in the United States this summer, Spanish outlet El Mundo reported on September 30.
US authorities informed Kasparov that he was the target of a Kremlin-linked assassination plot and placed him under special protection. According to El Mundo, preparations to kill former Russian lawmaker Ilya Ponomarev were even further advanced.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“US authorities confirmed to him this summer that he is a target,” a source close to Kasparov told the newspaper.
US prosecutors have identified five alleged members of a network linked to Russian intelligence services that recruited people to surveil and kill Kremlin opponents.
El Mundo reported that two targets were to be killed in the United States, while another potential victim was targeted in Vilnius, Lithuania.
The network, described as the “RIS Network,” has allegedly operated since at least 2024 and previously organized sabotage attacks in Europe using recruited criminals and local operatives. Its alleged preparations for assassinations on US soil marked a significant expansion of such operations, according to El Mundo.
Kasparov has lived outside Russia since 2013 after years of threats linked to his political activity. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow designated him a “foreign agent,” added him to its list of “terrorists and extremists” in 2024, and placed him on an international wanted list in May 2026.
Ponomarev, another alleged target, was the only member of Russia’s State Duma to vote against the annexation of Crimea in 2014. He later joined Ukraine’s territorial defense and has stated that he survived five assassination attempts, El Mundo reported.
A person recruited by Moscow photographed two locations in Washington linked to an individual identified by US prosecutors as “Victim Number 1.” The planned killing carried a $40,000 payment.
The surveillance instructions required videos of at least 30 seconds from several angles, with an agreed hand gesture visible to prove the material was recent. El Mundo reported that the group used coded language, calling surveillance “measuring the land” and the planned killing “construction.”
The assassination was ultimately not carried out after the recruited individual refused to proceed beyond surveillance.
US prosecutors allege that five men formed the Russian intelligence-linked network, including former Russian intelligence colonel Yuri Jrameev and his son Kirill, an FSB officer. Two Cuban nationals and one Venezuelan were also charged, and all five remain in Russia, according to El Mundo.
All five face charges of conspiring to finance acts of terrorism, while three are additionally accused of conspiracy to commit murder for hire. The network also allegedly recruited people to carry out sabotage in countries supporting Ukraine.
El Mundo reported that Russian-linked operatives had also targeted exiled activists in Lithuania, including Free Russia Forum co-founder Ivan Tyutrin and Bashkir activist Ruslan Gabbasov. Gabbasov discovered a tracking device on his car in 2025, after which Lithuanian prosecutors identified an alleged plot to kill him.
The alleged US plots would represent an unusual expansion of Russian intelligence operations. Moscow-linked assassinations and attempted killings have previously been concentrated in Europe, including the 2018 Novichok poisoning of Sergei Skripal in Salisbury and the 2019 killing of Zelimkhan Khangoshvili in Berlin, El Mundo wrote.
Russia has increasingly relied on recruited foreign nationals and local criminals for sabotage and covert operations abroad, allowing its intelligence services to distance themselves from those carrying out attacks.
Days earlier, Ukraine’s Security Service detained an alleged FSB operative in Kyiv who was preparing to assassinate a Russian opposition figure fighting for Ukraine.
Investigators stated that she had received weapons training from the FSB and collected a pistol from a concealed cache before being arrested near the intended target’s workplace.

ISTRA (Moscow Region), September 30. /TASS/. The North Atlantic Alliance, while using Ukraine as a proxy, is soberly assessing the extreme risks and costs of a direct confrontation with Russia, Fyodor Voitolovsky, Corresponding Member of the Russian Academy of Sciences (RAS) and Director of the Primakov National Research Institute of World Economy and International Relations (IMEMO RAS), said during a session at the 23rd annual meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club.
Commenting on the prospects for the future world order, Voitolovsky said that "one should not expect leading powers to develop some sort of shared vision of the future." He recalled that the Soviet Union and the United States "had vastly different visions of the future, yet they soberly assessed the risks associated with a direct military clash and developed a model of peaceful coexistence."
"The conflict in Ukraine has been going on for four years, with Ukraine acting as a proxy for NATO countries in terms of weapons, intelligence, target designation, and so on," Voitolovsky said. "We are all well aware of this. Yet, over these four years, we have not seen a direct military confrontation between Russia and NATO, because the parties soberly assess the extreme risks and costs of such a confrontation."
The 23rd annual meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club, titled "Responsibility for the Future: Limits of the Possible or Possibilities Without Limits?", is being held in the Moscow Region from September 28 to October 1. The club’s flagship conference brings together 120 participants from 40 countries.

Taiwan farmers turn fields into safer habitats for endangered turtles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:07:00 UTC
21:07:00 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Wildlife-friendly farming practices are helping protect two endangered native turtle species in central Taiwan.
The Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency’s Nantou Branch on Wednesday recognized 50 farmers for adopting such practices and helping preserve turtle habitats. The agency’s ecological conservation program encourages farmers to avoid herbicides, rat poison, and other wildlife-unfriendly control methods.
Farmers are also encouraged to retain vegetation and fallen leaves in their fields during winter and take steps to prevent turtles from drowning. These measures help the endangered yellow-margined box turtle and yellow pond turtle — both native to Taiwan — by providing places to forage and shelter in habitats that often overlap with areas where people live and farm.
Ten communities in Nantou and Yunlin counties were also recognized for their efforts to protect habitats for the two species. Their work includes removing traps used to capture wild animals and improving local habitat conditions, helping create safer places for the turtles to live and forage.
The yellow-margined box turtle, Taiwan’s only fully terrestrial native turtle species, lives at elevations below 1,000 meters, mainly in forests, foothills, and plains. Because its habitat overlaps with areas of human activity, the species faces particular challenges from habitat loss and illegal capture, according to the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency and the Academia Sinica.
Population surveys conducted in Yilan and Hualien in 2014-2015 and 2018-2019 found that the species’ range and population had declined rapidly or disappeared entirely in some areas over the previous 15 years. Only scattered individuals were found in some locations, while many remaining populations were too small and had such low densities that natural reproduction was unlikely to sustain them over the long term.
The yellow pond turtle was first recorded in Taiwan in 1908 and is found mainly in aquatic habitats in northern, central, and eastern mountainous areas. The loss and degradation of aquatic environments and terrestrial areas, along with illegal hunting, have caused wild populations to decline rapidly, according to the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency.

KMT pushes amendment to allow referendums to overrule Constitutional Court rulings
Unknown

2026-09-30
12:06:53 UTC
21:06:53 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The KMT legislative caucus announced Tuesday that it would seek to amend the Referendum Act to allow referendums to overturn Constitutional Court rulings.
The KMT caucus announced 40 legislative priorities for the current session, including establishing rules governing the use of surplus tax revenue for cash handouts, increasing maximum fines for major food safety violations, and amending the Referendum Act, per Liberty Times.
The amendment, proposed by KMT Legislator Weng Hsiao-ling (翁曉玲), would allow referendums to overturn Constitutional Court decisions, except rulings involving presidential impeachment, per Newtalk. It would also bar the Central Election Commission from reviewing referendum proposals initiated by the Legislature.
The KMT caucus argued that if the public finds a Constitutional Court ruling unacceptable or believes it violates the law, a referendum could serve as a means of challenging the decision, per Liberty Times. It said Constitutional Court rulings have less legal status than constitutional amendments and can be subject to changes in subsequent rulings.
The caucus argued that because constitutional amendments require approval through referendums to take effect, Constitutional Court rulings should not be excluded from potentially being put to a public vote.
DPP Legislator Chen Pei-yu (陳培瑜) said Weng's amendment would limit the executive and judicial branches while expanding the power of the Legislature, per CNA. Chen cited Soochow University Law School Professor Chang Chia-yin (張嘉尹), who said allowing referendums to overturn Constitutional Court rulings would expand the powers of both referendums and the Legislature beyond the scope permitted by the Constitution while diminishing the core authority of the judiciary.
Asked about the legality of the proposed amendment, Lawyer Fang Yen-hui (房彥輝) said it could violate the separation of powers and the principle of checks and balances, per Business Today. Meanwhile, the Constitutional Court's ability to operate remains a point of political and legal dispute.
During a discussion of the premier's power to countersign presidential orders, DPP Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) said the Constitutional Court is currently paralyzed by the opposition, per CNA.
That view has been echoed by three of the eight Constitutional Court justices who declined to participate in the court's proceedings following a controversial ruling that restored the court's operation. They argued that the court could not function because it had failed to meet the quorum required by law.
The three justices — Tsai Tzung-jen (蔡宗珍), Yang Hui-chin (楊惠欽), and Ju Fu-mei (朱富美) — previously argued that although the Constitution grants the court the authority to interpret laws, it must also follow procedural rules enacted by the legislature. They said ending the previous paralysis would require the nomination of new justices to meet the quorum.
Retired Tunghai University professor Lin Teng-yau (林騰鷂), meanwhile, cited rulings issued by the court since it resumed operations as evidence that it is not paralyzed, per Storm Media. However, Lin suggested that President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) reconsider his strategy for nominating Constitutional Court justices.

Trump campaign ads paid with public money violate federal law, critics say
Robert Tait
Federal regulators have been urged to stop the broadcast of White House advertisements promoting Donald Trump that critics say amounts to government propaganda and violate laws against using public money to promote partisan causes.
Public Citizen, an advocacy group, called on the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to intervene and block further airing of three ads it said were “designed to boost the image and character of Donald Trump” as part of the Republicans’ campaign for November’s midterm elections.
“Federal law explicitly prohibits using appropriated public funds for government propaganda, self-aggrandizement, or partisan political advertising,” the organization wrote. “Yet, that is exactly the nature of Trump’s recent campaign ads.”
Broadcast stations cannot reject ads from legally qualified political candidates – but Trump is not technically a candidate, although he has urged voters to imagine that he is, on the November ballot.
“Public Citizen strongly urges the Federal Communications Commission and Federal Trade Commission to direct broadcasters to stop broadcasting these apparently illegal campaign advertisements and calls on individual broadcasters to cease airing the campaign advertisements,” the group wrote in a letter addressed to both agencies.
The US Senate on Tuesday evening rejected along mostly party lines a Democratic resolution that would have forced the state department to report to Congress on violence in the occupied West Bank, including the killings of nine American citizens by Israeli settlers or security forces over the last few years.
The resolution, led by the Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen, would have given the state department 30 days to report to Congress on those deaths and on wider human rights conditions in the territory, including Israel’s detention of Palestinian children.
The resolution failed to advance by a vote of 47 to 51. Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman, a Democrat, joined Republicans in voting against the resolution, while Kentucky Republican Rand Paul voted in favor.
Van Hollen was able to force the vote under section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act, a law that lets senators demand human rights reports on countries receiving US military aid. The measure drew 24 Democratic and independent sponsors, including Bernie Sanders of Vermont, Tim Kaine of Virginia and Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the foreign relations committee.
“While I was pleased that so many of my Democratic colleagues joined this effort, it’s clear the United States must do more,” Van Hollen said in a statement after the vote. “It is our responsibility to ensure recipients of US taxpayer dollars act in line with our laws and our values – this resolution was an opportunity to shed light on a reality that flies in the face of that principle.”
Experts have expressed skeptism of putting “so much faith in self-policing” in response to Donald Trump’s AI accord.
Robin Jia, an assistant professor of computer science at the University of Southern California, said it’s crucial to ensure the leading labs’ intentions are “well-aligned with the broader interest of the American public”.
He pointed to the recent disclosures of hacking incidents and said:
As the models get better, the consequences of such things are only going to get greater.
Some also took issue with the accord’s vague, broad language.
Alex Pascal, executive director of the Berkman Klein Center for Internet and Society, said:
The only way to reduce the risks and harms of AI to Americans is through robust legal liability, regulation and fundamentally changing the race dynamics that are driving unsafe decision-making by frontier AI developers whose costs are borne by the American people.
Donald Trump announced on Tuesday that the heads of the largest US tech and AI companies had signed on to a “morally binding” agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence. He announced the deal, called the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities, following a White House luncheon with top tech executives.
“It’s almost like a constitution in a way, and the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it really is a form of protection,” Trump said.
Trump also signed an executive order renaming artificial intelligence to “superintelligence”, similar to a declaration he made at the United Nations last week.
“The Order directs all departments and agencies to use the terms ‘Super Intelligence’ and ‘SI’ in official correspondence, public communications, policy documents, and non-statutory documents within the executive branch and to no longer acknowledge the terms ‘Artificial Intelligence’ or ‘AI’,” the order declared.
The agreement, which Trump suggested would allow the companies to perform “tremendous self-policing” of their products and technologies, outlines a vague framework for how AI firms would establish safety standards as they test out new products.
The tech industry has faced increased public scrutiny following a series of incidents where major AI companies inadvertently hacked into outside organizations during safety tests.
While lawmakers, AI researchers and even some AI companies have called for more government oversight of artificial intelligence, Trump has broadly rejected calls for more regulation of the technology – citing competition with China and threats to economic growth.
The joint commitment that Trump posted to his Truth Social account on Tuesday appears to carry no enforcement mechanisms or legal implications and is instead a voluntary commitment.
Democratic lawmakers call for protections over third country deportations after 'indefensible' supreme court ruling
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Democratic lawmakers have called for more formalized steps to prevent the US government from deporting people to countries where their lives would be in danger or they could be subject to torture.
It comes as the US supreme court on Tuesday lifted restrictions on the deportations of immigrants to countries that are not their own, while agreeing to hear the issue on its merits in December.
Rob Menendez, a congressional Democrat, called the supreme court’s decision “indefensible”, adding:
Taxpayers shouldn’t fund tearing people from the only home they’ve ever known, nor should our legal system fast-track these unilateral deportations.
The conservative-dominated high court granted an emergency request by the Trump administration to suspend a lower court ruling that restricted, but did not outright ban, so-called “third-country removals”.
After the ruling, Democratic lawmakers pushed for the tightening of protections to prevent such deportations where lives could be at risk and to uphold due process.
“Congress must step in. No one should be shipped off to a country that is not their own without basic due process and a meaningful opportunity to raise legitimate fears for their safety,” House Democrat Lois Frankel said on X.
The Trump administration has defended third-country deportations as necessary since the home nations of some of those who are targeted for removal sometimes refuse to accept them.
In other developments:
Donald Trump announced that the heads of the largest US tech and AI companies had signed on to a “morally binding” agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence. Trump did not give further details on the controls, but he suggested that the deal would allow the companies to largely “self-police” their products and technology. Later, Trump signed an executive order calling for “artificial intelligence” to be renamed “super intelligence”.
Jack Smith faced Senate lawmakers on the judiciary committee for a contentious hearing that saw a number of Republicans accuse the former special prosecutor of perjury, and conducting a political witch-hunt against Trump when he secured two indictments against the president that were later dismissed when he took office.
A Republican senator blocked a bipartisan bill that would have prevented Donald Trump from demolishing the Kennedy Center without the approval of Congress. Mike Lee, of Utah, objected when the Oregon Democrat Jeff Merkley asked the Senate to pass the Protecting Presidential Memorials Act by unanimous consent.
The US Senate rejected along mostly party lines a Democratic resolution that would have forced the state department to report to Congress on violence in the occupied West Bank, including the killings of nine American citizens by Israeli settlers or security forces over the last few years.
JD Vance and health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr spoke at the conclusion of the Make America Healthy Again summit in Washington. Several reporters were denied entry to the event.
