‘Economic war’: Is Iran losing its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:05:45 UTC
21:05:45 KST

Is Iran losing its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz?
Crude flows through Hormuz have recovered, but tanker insurance costs and geopolitical risks remain barriers to a return to normality.
As Iran and the United States work with mediators to end seven months of hostilities, the reality in the Strait of Hormuz is shifting in ways that could prove to be a game-changer in ongoing negotiations.
According to the latest data from tanker-tracker websites, traffic through the key waterway has been steadily increasing, with some estimates putting oil and petroleum flow through the Strait of Hormuz at nearly 80 percent of what it was before the US-Israeli war on Iran began on February 28.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Iran shifts trade north to Caspian Sea as war impairs Strait of Hormuz
- list 2 of 3‘Iran ready for doomsday war’, FM Araghchi says
- list 3 of 3Why has Trump rejected Iran’s peace proposal?
This could dent Iran’s leverage in reaching a favourable deal for itself in its attempts to end the fighting, which has seriously hampered its already heavily sanctioned economy, amid the US blockade of Iranian ships and ports.
Despite that, experts believe it would be a mistake to think normality in the Strait of Hormuz is imminent, or that Iran will fold easily despite growing economic hardship.
“The fact that oil is getting through the Strait of Hormuz is encouraging, but flows are not yet regarded as completely secure or guaranteed, particularly while the wider conflict remains unresolved,” Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, told Al Jazeera.
Moreover, oil prices remain high globally, including in the US, where President Donald Trump faces a crucial midterm election that could see his party swept away in both houses of Congress.
Tanker insurance costs also remain elevated, and energy flows through Hormuz are still far from secure, suggesting Iran’s leverage may be weakening rather than disappearing.
Oil flows through Hormuz recovering
The latest data from commodity analytics firm Kpler points to a significant recovery in oil exports from the Middle East.
Crude exports reached an estimated 16.328 million barrels per day (bpd) in September – their highest level since the war began in late February, the firm reported this week.
Flows through the Strait of Hormuz itself were expected to reach about 9.719 million bpd during the month. Saudi Arabia has driven much of the increase, with its exports rebounding from 2.446 million bpd in August to about 5.4 million bpd in September.
Kpler said Middle East crude exports have recovered to just less than 80 percent of their pre-war level. But the figures remain about 3.2 million bpd below the 19.513 million bpd exported in February.
The data also does not include ships crossing Hormuz with their tracking systems switched off, meaning actual traffic could be higher.
Prior to the war, an estimated 120-140 vessels crossed through the waterway daily, roughly half of them oil tankers moving approximately 20 million barrels per day. At the height of the fighting, traffic through the waterway collapsed to as few as two tankers a day after Iran effectively closed the strait in retaliation for US-Israeli attacks.
Is Iran losing leverage?
The rebound in oil flow presents a challenge for Tehran. Iran has sought to use its ability to disrupt the Strait of Hormuz – one of the world’s most important energy chokepoints – as leverage against Washington’s military and economic pressure.
But if large volumes of oil can continue moving through the strait while Iran itself remains under a US naval blockade, Tehran’s bargaining power could diminish.
Iran, however, rejects any assessment that its control over the strait is slipping.
Hossein Mohebbi, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesperson, said on Wednesday that there is an ongoing “military conflict” in the Hormuz Strait.
“We have been hitting small ships and preventing them from passing for a long time, but America does not respond,” Mohebbi said in an interview with the semi-official Fars news agency.
Separately on Wednesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre said unknown projectiles struck three ships in the waterway on Tuesday, including a crude oil tanker.
Oil prices are another indication that Iran has not lost all of its leverage.
Brent crude fell 2.6 percent to $102.59 a barrel on Tuesday as traders focused on recovering Middle East exports. But it was still heading for a roughly 13 percent gain in September.
Chris Beauchamp, an analyst at IG, said markets were beginning to incorporate evidence of recovering flows but remained wary about how durable that recovery would be.
“It takes time for evidence to filter through to markets,” Beauchamp said. “Oil prices came off yesterday as the narrative began to take hold, and should continue to fall.”
But he said concerns persisted over whether the US protection system could withstand a renewed barrage of Iranian missiles and drones.
Streeter of Wealth Club said the market still had a geopolitical risk premium built into crude prices, despite the improving flows.
“Insurance costs for tankers also remain elevated because of the perceived risks of operating in the region, adding to the cost of transporting crude even as more ships make it through the waterway,” she said.
Moreover, Streeter warned that crude figures tell only part of the story. Flows of refined fuels, particularly diesel and petrol, remain constrained, while damage to infrastructure has placed additional pressure on energy supply chains, she added.
There is another vulnerability, the investment strategist pointed out. Countries including the US have relied heavily on strategic oil reserves to cushion the impact of the disruption and help contain prices.
“With those stockpiles now significantly depleted, there is a thinner buffer if there is another disruption, which is helping to keep a floor under crude prices,” Streeter added.
‘Economic war’ on Iran
There is little doubt that economic pressure on Iran is intensifying, potentially increasing Tehran’s incentive to reach an agreement.
Official data from the Statistical Center of Iran earlier this month showed gross domestic product (GDP) contracting 10.1 percent year on year between March 21 and June 20, while the crucial oil and gas sector shrank 26.4 percent.
Iran has also been battling high inflation and a plunging currency as the US blockade constrains oil exports and foreign currency earnings.
Twelve-month average inflation reached 69.9 percent earlier in September, while the rial had fallen beyond 2.2 million to the US dollar in early September.
In August, the US announced a new economic pressure campaign against Iran, promising to target Tehran’s financial interests across the world.
Mohammad Eslami, a research fellow at the University of Tehran, told Al Jazeera that Iran was facing an “economic war” alongside the military conflict.
“There is a US blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, which affects Iran’s revenues from oil exports and other products such as petrochemicals, which are important to Iran’s economy,” Eslami said. “As a result, Iran’s dollar revenues have been affected by the blockade.”
But he cautioned against judging Iran’s economy solely through the value of its currency.
“The exchange rate is a very important indicator, but it is not the only measure for explaining what is happening or the difficulties and challenges facing Iran’s economy,” Eslami said, adding that Iran has faced US economic pressure for “five decades”.
Negar Mortazavi, political analyst, and the host of The Iran Podcast, echoed Eslami’s opinion that the economic blockade is imposing “enormous pressure on Iran”, but that does not mean it will fold, she told Al Jazeera.
“Tehran has shown that it is prepared to tolerate considerable economic pain rather than negotiate entirely on Washington’s terms.”
The war is hurting the US economy too
Iran is not alone in facing economic pressure. US diesel prices hit a record $6.53 a gallon ($1.73 per litre) this month, more than 70 percent higher than the price before the US waged its war on Iran. The Trump administration is discussing restrictions on diesel exports to ease prices before November’s midterm elections.
Higher energy costs have also fuelled inflation, experts say, contributing to the Federal Reserve’s decision to raise interest rates by 25 basis points this month – its first increase in three years.
Additionally, the cost-of-living crisis in the country is also weighing on Trump politically. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll put his approval at a career-low 32 percent, with just 17 percent approving of his handling of living costs.
From time to time, Iran has seized on this pressure, often mocking Trump for prematurely declaring victory in the war despite the apparent economic downturn in the US.
Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf this month used a math equation to suggest that Tehran’s ability to disrupt energy supplies is influencing US monetary policy. Analysts say while the claim is exaggerated, it does highlight Iran’s own economic leverage over Washington.
Can a deal be reached?
Despite the military and economic pressure, negotiations have not collapsed.
At the United Nations General Assembly last week, Tehran and Washington engaged in three hours of indirect talks, as US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
President Trump later described the encounter as “very good” and “very productive”.
Iran also proposed a seven-day roadmap under which the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened and normal maritime traffic restored if Washington meets Tehran’s conditions, a plan Trump categorically rejected.
Those conditions included ending the naval blockade on Iran, easing sanctions and releasing frozen Iranian funds.
However, on Wednesday, the Reuters news agency reported that Araghchi had received US feedback on the proposal through Qatari mediators.
An official briefed on the talks said the main disagreement now centred on the sequencing of measures rather than the components of the plan.
Mortazavi said Iran’s latest proposal shows Tehran is willing to be flexible because it wants to bring the war to an end.
The proposal builds on the June memorandum of understanding between Iran and the US but offers a much faster timeline, including an immediate end to the war, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz within a week and a rapid return to nuclear negotiations.
“Iran is offering compromise in order to stop the war, not capitulation under pressure,” Mortazavi said.
But that flexibility is tied to reciprocal concessions from Washington, she added. “There has to be something in return from the US.”
Mortazavi said there was a “danger” if Trump misreads Iran’s willingness to compromise as weakness. “That could instead prolong the war,” she warned.

Germany is buying every missile it can get. What is Berlin preparing for?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:04:33 UTC
21:04:33 KST

Germany is buying every missile it can get. What is Berlin preparing for?
Over the past few months, there’s been a noticeable surge in reports regarding Germany’s interest in missiles – ranging from ballistic and cruise missiles to land- and sea-based systems. Various partners are involved in the initiative, including the US, Ukraine, Türkiye, and Israel. It looks like Germany intends to spend its entire budget on missiles, aiming to become the leading missile power in Western Europe.
Berlin’s financial commitment to advancing military programs has reached unprecedented levels. The country is significantly ramping up defense spending. Between 2024 and 2025, approximately 200 new defense industry companies emerged in Germany, and another 100 have appeared since November 2025. A notable example is Rheinmetall, which has dramatically increased its artillery ammunition production from about 70,000 units to 1.5 million shells per year. Over the next six years, the company plans to invest around €30 billion ($34 billion) into arms and munitions manufacturing. Moreover, Germany is actively seeking to procure ready-made missile systems and is interested in establishing joint production facilities.
Aligned with these initiatives, Germany is establishing new ground forces capable of striking military targets deep within potential enemy territory, essentially creating missile troops within the Bundeswehr. On the one hand, this expansion enhances NATO’s strike capabilities and allows for flexible responses to any external threats over distances of thousands of kilometers. On the other hand, such offensive capabilities could easily inspire ideas of military dominance and hegemony. Historically, we’ve already seen this in Germany.
At the forefront of this new German strategy will be American Typhon MRC (Mid-Range Capability) missile systems, equipped with Tomahawk cruise missiles with a range of up to 1,600 km. The Bundeswehr plans to allocate nearly €3.4 billion for the procurement of these missiles. They will provide the German military with a strategic edge, enabling strikes against command centers, airbases, missile units, logistical hubs, and other critical targets far beyond the potential front lines.
Germany’s main argument in favor of this military buildup is, of course, the need to deter the “threat from the East” – a classic case of history repeating itself. The fact that Russia has no intention of attacking NATO doesn’t seem to matter; it serves as a convenient excuse and a rallying cry to ramp up militarism. Technically, from German territory, Tomahawk missiles can only reach parts of European Russia, but Berlin’s ambitions extend well beyond this missile system.
Germany’s interest in missiles has grown to such an extent that the Bundeswehr is exploring even some rather unconventional projects, such as Ukraine’s Flamingo and Bars cruise missiles, as well as the Anthem missile project. In fact, the Ukrainian Flamingo missile was considered a potential alternative to the US Tomahawk. With a range of 3,000 km, the Flamingo surpasses the Tomahawk in terms of range. Additionally, it boasts an impressive warhead weighing 1,150 kg – a record in its class. The only real question is whether the 10-meter-long missile can successfully hit targets. So far, experience has shown that most of the Flamingos launched by Ukrainian forces are intercepted by air defense systems.
Germany is also ready to produce Bars missiles on its soil, but primarily for export purposes. It remains unclear whether this initiative leans more toward a business venture or a strategic investment in domestic armaments. Bars missiles might not be of much interest to German military officials since they essentially function as a cheap and simple alternative to more costly missiles.
Another notable project is the Anthem long-range cruise missile developed by the US-Israeli startup Covenant. Recently, Reuters reported that Germany is interested in a missile with a range exceeding 1,500 km and a warhead weighing over 200 kg. What’s more, Covenant is willing to establish production of Anthem missiles in Germany. This likely piqued the interest of Bundeswehr officials, especially considering the impressive promised production output of 1,000 units per year. So many missiles can be produced by relying on a simplified design and fairly modest performance specifications. Naturally, there’s no talk of stealth technology here; it’s essentially an alternative to inexpensive long-range kamikaze drones. If this contract goes through, Germany would acquire its own surface-to-surface missile system.
But that’s not all. The Bundeswehr is considering other missile projects as well. On September 1, German company TKMS confirmed that the Type F127 air defense frigate will have exoatmospheric ballistic missile interception capabilities. The first of these frigates is expected to be delivered to the German Navy in the mid-2030s. It will be equipped with SM-2 Block IIIC and SM-6 Block I interceptors. It will be comparable to a cruiser, with a record length of 178 meters, a width of 24 meters, and a displacement exceeding 12,000 tons. Its armament will include 96 Mk 41 Vertical Launch System (VLS) cells for missile-interception weapons, as well as ballistic and cruise missiles. The construction of at least five such ships is planned. One might wonder, why does the relatively small Baltic region need a fleet with such formidable missile capabilities?
At the beginning of September, the German Navy conducted its first test launches of Israeli LORA (Long Range Attack) ballistic missiles from an F125-class frigate. These launches were primarily demonstrative, with missile containers temporarily mounted on the stern of the Sachsen-Anhalt frigate. Two missiles were fired during the tests. The sight of Israeli ballistic missiles similar to American ATACMS aboard a German frigate is quite unusual. This notable experiment illustrates that the Bundeswehr is open to exploring alternatives to US weapons systems. Furthermore, Israeli missiles are modern and highly accurate, boasting ranges from 90 to 430 km and a circular error probable (CEP) of under 10 meters. It’s also quite possible that such missiles could soon be integrated into the Bundeswehr’s land forces.
Simultaneously, Germany is preparing to begin production of ATACMS ballistic missiles in collaboration with US company Lockheed Martin. Rheinmetall expects to receive its first order by late 2026 or early 2027, with a memorandum already signed to establish production at its facility in Unterluess, Germany. This will mark the first production of ATACMS missiles outside the US. Production is anticipated to start between 2028 and 2029. European demand is estimated at 600-800 units.
Additionally, Berlin is showing interest in Türkiye’s missile programs. Reports indicate that Germany is interested in Turkish hypersonic projects and specifically the Yildirimhan long-range ballistic missile with a range of up to 6,000 km. For Türkiye, having Germany as a customer is a compelling prospect, and President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Turkish companies would be eager to secure such an order.
But why is Germany showing such interest in missiles? And behind the facade of nuclear cooperation with the UK, does a part of the Berlin establishment harbor nuclear ambitions? Ideas to replace the American nuclear umbrella amid a perceived “threat from the East” are still popular; and defense companies and war hawks certainly welcome these initiatives. But what will happen if the funding runs dry? Or worse – if this ‘Chekhov’s gun’ goes off in the ‘next act’?

“According to our intelligence, Russia is preparing to stage dozens of videos in occupied Oleshky, forcing local residents to say on camera that they are happy, well-fed, and grateful to the Russian occupiers,” Sybiha wrote on X, calling it another example of what he described as Russian cynicism.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Oleshky, on the left bank of the Dnipro River in southern Ukraine’s Kherson region, has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
According to earlier reports, around 2,000 residents, including nearly 50 children, are facing dire conditions in the town, with limited access to food, drinking water and electricity, while Russian forces block attempts to leave.
“First, they occupy a town, cut off civilians’ escape routes, and block humanitarian aid. Then they force local residents to act in staged propaganda videos,” Sybiha wrote.
He called the alleged recordings part of a “disgusting Russian propaganda campaign” aimed at denying the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky.
Sybiha urged the international community and humanitarian organizations to increase pressure on Moscow and demand immediate access to the town. He said Ukrainian forces were also working to save civilians, including by delivering humanitarian aid with heavy-lift drones.
Medical Center in Central Kyiv on Fire After Russian Jet-Powered Drone Attack
“Every day counts in saving people who are starving and dying there. We urge our international partners to act now and demand immediate humanitarian access to end this disaster,” he said.
Ukrainian forces have already used drones to deliver about 4,000 kilograms of food to Oleshky, according to Kherson Regional Military Administration (OVA) head Oleksandr Prokudin.
Prokudin said the deliveries have been carried out since March in cooperation with units of the Ukrainian National Guard, Marines and Border Guard Service.
“We recently managed to carry out one of the largest operations of this kind,” Prokudin said, describing a coordinated delivery of around 4,000 kilograms of food to 100 designated locations across the city.
Addditionally, Russian forces have attempted to intercept the supply drones and, according to Ukrainian officials, have stolen or resold food intended for children and elderly residents.
Ukrainian authorities also accuse Russian forces of detaining and abusing civilians who accept humanitarian aid, including holding them in basements and subjecting them to physical violence.
In mid-September, Russian authorities failed to honor previously agreed arrangements for a humanitarian mission to evacuate civilians from occupied Oleshky.
The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) was prepared to participate within its mandate, while Ukrainian security and defense forces had made arrangements for a ceasefire during the proposed operation.
“These people must be saved,” Ukrainian Verkhovna Rada Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets said on Sept. 16, warning that “the city has been turned into a death trap.”
Lubinets said his office had received 176 appeals about the humanitarian situation and verified at least 358 people who urgently need to leave.
He estimated that more than 6,000 people, including around 200 children, could remain in Oleshky and the surrounding district. The figures could not be independently verified because Russian occupation authorities severely restrict access to information.
Some residents have reportedly attempted to flee independently through mined areas, despite the risk of artillery shelling and near-daily drone attacks.
The town has also been cut off from basic supplies. Residents have reportedly gone months without food or medicine deliveries, while some have resorted to bartering.
Tetiana Hasanenko, head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, said on July 10 that no vehicles had entered or left the town since May 26.
The hospital’s only pharmacy reportedly ran out of essential medicines months ago. Power cuts and fuel shortages have further disrupted medical care.
Hasanenko also said the hospital morgue was destroyed by shelling, forcing bodies to be stored in a basement, while Russian occupation authorities allegedly prevent the burial of some drone-strike victims pending forensic examinations elsewhere.
Residents also cannot access their bank accounts because cash withdrawals require leaving the town.
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said international humanitarian law requires occupying powers to ensure access to food and medical supplies and facilitate humanitarian relief when local resources are insufficient.
According to the same report, at least 29 civilians were killed and 54 wounded in Oleshky and nearby occupied Hola Prystan in 2026, with many casualties independently verified by the UN Human Rights Office.

New Lebanon-Israel talks set for 20 Oct as Golani Brigade leaves

Breadcrumb
Lebanon told Israel talks to resume in October as Golani Brigade withdraws from south
Talks between Lebanon and Israel are expected to resume in late October, Lebanese media reported on Wednesday, as the Israeli military announced the end of a seven-month deployment by its Golani Brigade in southern Lebanon.
Lebanon has been informed that US-mediated negotiations with Israel will take place on 20 October in Tampa, Florida, a week before Israel’s general elections, according to Lebanese broadcaster MTV.
The direct talks, which began in April, have stalled for months, with little progress on the implementation of a trilateral agreement amid continued Israeli attacks.
The US-sponsored framework signed between Lebanon and Israel in late June calls for the gradual Israeli withdrawal from designated pilot zones, followed by the redeployment of the Lebanese army in those areas. Under the agreement, the Lebanese military is to ensure that the zones have been cleared of Hezbollah weapons and infrastructure.
The first three pilot zones were announced in July, but no further areas have been designated.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam have said the diplomatic track is the only viable option for Beirut to try to end the conflict, and have called on Washington to exert greater pressure on Israel.
US officials reportedly told Salam in New York this week that Israel would continue to occupy parts of southern Lebanon and expand its operations if the Lebanese government failed to bring Hezbollah’s weapons under state control.
Israel currently occupies large parts of southern Lebanon and has expanded its so-called security zone in recent months, with dozens of towns and villages razed or heavily damaged.
Israel says it will not withdraw from Lebanon until Hezbollah is fully disarmed, while the Iran-backed group has rejected disarmament as long as Israeli forces remain in Lebanese territory.
Golani Brigade ends mission
Separately on Wednesday, the Israeli military said forces from one of its elite infantry brigades had withdrawn from southern Lebanon after seven months of operational activity.
Israeli army spokesperson Ella Waweya posted footage on X showing troops from the Golani Brigade’s combat team leaving the area.
She said the forces, operating under the army’s 36th Division, had been deployed in the security zone in southern Lebanon to remove what she called threats to northern Israel.
In recent months, the troops operated in the Shqif Heights area around Beaufort Castle and had recently completed a "focused military operation" to destroy infrastructure in the vicinity of the Litani River, Waweya said.
She added that Israeli forces had destroyed more than 900 structures allegedly used by Hezbollah and found weapons depots containing RPG rounds, explosive devices, booby-trapped drones and Kalashnikov rifles.
Earlier this month, Israeli forces demolished an underground Hezbollah complex beneath the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge, raising fears that Israel could storm the nearby city of Nabatiyeh next as it eyes other strategic heights in the south.
Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed close to 9,000 people since the conflict with Hezbollah began in October 2023, while more than 30,000 others have been wounded, with many civilians among the casualties.

Chinese business chamber voices concern over reported EU "301" trade instrument
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:58:24 CST
20:58:24 KST

BRUSSELS, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- The China Chamber of Commerce to the EU (CCCEU) on Wednesday voiced concern over reports that some European Union (EU) member states are pushing for a new EU "301" trade instrument, warning that such a unilateral measure could raise questions over its compatibility with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules.
In a statement, the chamber said the proposed instrument, if introduced, could risk "weaponizing trade policy" and disrupt China-EU and global trade, while adding uncertainty to global industrial and supply chains.
The CCCEU said unilateral trade measures will not address structural challenges facing European industry, including high energy costs, insufficient investment and the need to strengthen innovation.
European industry has also experienced the negative impact of similar unilateral trade measures. International trade instruments should not become subject to a "race to the bottom," nor should unilateral measures replace multilateral rules, the chamber said, calling for the WTO-based multilateral trading system to be upheld.
The CCCEU said China and the EU are maintaining intensive communication under their Trade and Investment Consultation mechanism and called on European stakeholders to use existing dialogue channels to address differences and concerns.
It also urged the EU and its member states to maintain a fair, equitable, transparent and predictable business environment and safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of companies, including Chinese firms.
The chamber said it stands ready to strengthen communication and cooperation with European stakeholders and contribute to an open and stable business environment and China-EU economic and trade cooperation.
The statement came amid reports that some EU member states are urging the European Commission to accelerate work on an instrument modeled on Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act, which allows Washington to investigate and respond to what it considers unfair foreign trade practices. ■

China loses to South Korea in Asian Games men's football semifinals
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:58:16 CST
20:58:16 KST

Goalkeeper Li Hao (3rd L) of China makes a save during the men's semifinals of football between China and South Korea at 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Osaka, Japan, Sept. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Lui Siu Wai)
OSAKA, Japan, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- China took an early lead but lost 2-1 to South Korea in the men's football semifinals at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Wednesday, missing out on a place in the final.
China reached the Asian Games men's football semifinals for the first time in 28 years. Under head coach Antonio Puche, the Chinese side advanced from the "group of death" with one win and two draws before beating Thailand 3-0 in the quarterfinals.
Defending champion South Korea reached the semifinals after winning all three matches.
China started with its familiar 5-3-2 formation and looked to threaten on the counter-attack, while South Korea sought to create chances from the flanks and set pieces.
China broke the deadlock in the 22nd minute when Mao Weijie sent a lofted through ball to Wang Yudong, who controlled it with his chest before calmly finishing one-on-one.
South Korea equalized in the 33rd minute after a corner reached Lee Young-jun at the far post. His header hit the post and bounced into the net despite Li Hao's attempt to save it.
After the break, China pushed higher and created several opportunities, but South Korea remained dangerous on the counter-attack. Mao was forced off with an injury in the 66th minute.
South Korea completed the comeback in the 82nd minute when Eom Ji-sung broke forward and crossed to the far post, where Bae Jun-ho headed home to make it 2-1.
In the closing minutes, Zhang Yuning's shot inside the box was blocked by a South Korean defender, prompting China's players to appeal for a handball. The referee waved play on, while Puche was booked for protesting the decision.
China had seven shots, three on target, and 55 percent possession, compared with South Korea's eight shots, six on target and 45 percent possession.
"We played an excellent game. Against a South Korean team with many outstanding players playing at a European level, the whole team showed a very high level," said Puche. "I'm naturally disappointed and saddened by the result. But I'm extremely proud and happy with this team."
China will play the loser of the other semifinal between Japan and Uzbekistan in the men's football bronze-medal match on Saturday. ■

Brown bears kill 162 head of livestock in northern Mongolia

20:58:13 KST

ULAN BATOR, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- At least 86 brown bear sightings have been reported in residential areas of Selenge province in northern Mongolia since the beginning of spring, with the animals killing and eating 162 head of livestock, the provincial department of environment said Wednesday.
"These figures are based on reports submitted by nomadic herders. We cannot rule out the possibility that there have been additional incidents that have not been reported or registered," the department said.
In recent months, there have been multiple reports of bears being spotted in or near residential areas in several provinces across Mongolia. In particular, several bear sightings have been reported in the capital, Ulan Bator, in recent days, prompting authorities to urge the public to remain vigilant and take precautions to protect themselves and others from potential risks.
Experts said encounters between bears and livestock, as well as bear sightings in residential areas, have increased in recent years. They cited several contributing factors, including climate change, food shortages in bears' natural habitats, the overexploitation of natural resources, and forest fires. ■

Norwegian ministers grilled in parliament over Epstein ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:58:12 UTC
20:58:12 KST

Breadcrumb
Norwegian ministers, including 1993 Oslo Accords creators, grilled in parliament over Epstein ties
Norway's prime minister denied Wednesday an "unhealthy culture" among the country's diplomats, as current and former ministers addressed a hearing over ties between late US convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and senior Norwegian officials.
The hearings come against the backdrop of the foreign ministry's payment of more than 130 million kroner ($13.5 million at the current exchange rate) to the International Peace Institute (IPI) between 1997 and 2018, a think tank headed by Norway's Terje Rod-Larsen from 2005 to 2020.
"There is no reason to speak of an unhealthy culture at a large organisation just because of what one or several people may have done," Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store told the Storting's standing committee on scrutiny and constitutional affairs.
"You can't tar everyone with the same brush," said the Labour leader, who was called to address the committee about his years as foreign minister from 2005-2012.
The Epstein files have shed light on ties between the US financier and Rod-Larsen and his diplomat wife Mona Juul, the architects of the 1993 Oslo Accords who are now under investigation in Norway—she for "aggravated corruption" and he for "complicity in aggravated corruption".
The couple denies any wrongdoing.
In total, 11 officials who have held the positions of foreign minister or development aid minister since 2005, will address the committee Wednesday and Thursday.
'Accountability failures'
In addition to Rod-Larsen and Juul, the Epstein documents have highlighted ties between the sex offender, who died in prison in 2019, and Thorbjorn Jagland, a former prime minister, foreign minister, secretary general of the Council of Europe and chair of the Nobel Peace Prize Committee.
Epstein also had ties with former foreign minister Borge Brende.
Jagland is also under investigation on suspicion of "aggravated corruption", but is not among the officials summoned by parliament because he was foreign minister prior to 2005 and because parliament wants to avoid interfering with the police investigation.
Brende, who resigned in February as president of the World Economic Forum, was to be heard on Wednesday.
"The Epstein documents raise serious questions about abuse of office, a culture of accountability failures, and poor management of development aid funds," said Jonas Andersen Sayed, a member of the committee.
"The issue concerns public trust in the entire system. It is essential that all the facts are brought to light, that accountability is established, and that the necessary reforms are implemented," he said.
The hearings themselves will not result in any sanctions.
Parliament has also set up an independent inquiry tasked with a much broader examination of the case, which is due to submit its final report by 31 January 2028.

Asian Games | China pockets 3 golds in track cycling, breaking two Asian records
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:58:08 CST
20:58:08 KST

Gold medalists team China celebrate during the awarding ceremony for the women's team pursuit final of cycling track at 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Izu of Shizuoka Prefecture, Japan, Sept. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Cen Yunpeng)
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- China swept all three gold medals on offer in track cycling at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Wednesday, winning the women's, men's team pursuits and women's keirin, with Asian records set in both team pursuit events.
In the women's team pursuit final, China quickly established a lead and extended its advantage to more than two seconds midway through the race. The Chinese quartet crossed the finish line in 4:08.818 to win gold in an Asian record time.
Host Japan took silver in 4:10.424, while South Korea claimed bronze after catching Uzbekistan in the bronze medal race.
"We were very united and rode steadily. Everyone gave their all and pushed beyond their limits, delivering our best performance," said Chinese rider Chen Ning.
Teammate Wang Xiaoyue said the team had set a clear goal of breaking the record and winning gold before the race.
"Now that we have achieved our goal, it not only validates the results of our training but also gives us confidence and motivation for the competitions ahead," Wang said.
The men's team pursuit final also saw a showdown between China and defending champion Japan. China clocked 3:47.621 to break the Asian record and beat Japan to the gold medal.
South Korea came from behind to beat Kazakhstan in the bronze medal race.
"We had originally planned to go for first place in the qualifying round, but a mistake left us slightly behind Japan and we failed to meet our expectations," said Pei Zhengyu, who is making his Asian Games debut.
"But we adjusted our mindset in time and successfully broke the Games record in the first round, steadily improving our times. By crossing the finish line first in today's final, we also achieved our goal of breaking the Asian record," Pei said.
In the women's keirin final, Yuan Liying produced a powerful late surge to overtake her rivals and claim gold. Her Chinese teammate Wang Lijuan took silver, while Malaysia's Nurul Izzah Izzati Mohd Asri won bronze.
"This gold medal is an affirmation of my individual ability," Yuan said. "The keirin is a rapidly changing event, and there is no fixed tactic. All I can do is give my best, maintain my rhythm and respond positively to every change in the race."
"I feel very honored to stand on the podium alongside my teammate," she added.
The women's Madison, men's omnium and men's sprint finals will take place on Thursday. ■

Iran shakes with 379 earthquakes in a month

Iran shakes with 379 earthquakes in a month
TEHRAN – A total of 379 earthquakes have been recorded across the country in a month from August 23 to September 22, according to the seismological networks of the Institute of Geophysics of the University of Tehran.
Statistically, 348 earthquakes with magnitudes smaller than 3, 26 earthquakes with a magnitude between 3 and 4, and five earthquakes with a magnitude greater than 4 on the Richter scale have occurred in the country, IRNA reported.
Of the total quakes, two had a magnitude of 4.3 on the Richter scale; the first occurred on September 7 in Kordestan province, and the other one hit Khorasan Razavi province on September 9 in.
Among the provinces of the country, Khorasan Razavi experienced the highest number of earthquakes with 59, followed by Semnan with 35, and Kerman with 31 earthquakes.
During the same period, 11 earthquakes were recorded in Tehran; the biggest had a magnitude of 3.6 on the Richter scale.
A total of 2,380 earthquakes with a magnitude of more than 2.5 on the Richter scale were recorded across the country over the past calendar year (March 2025–March 2026), according to the Seismological networks of the Institute of Geophysics of the University of Tehran, Mehr news agency reported.
Out of recorded earthquakes, 910 had a magnitude greater than 3, 130 had a magnitude greater than 4, and 15 had a magnitude greater than 5 on the Richter scale.
The Iranian plateau is located in a very seismically active region of the world and is known not only for its major catastrophic earthquakes but also for the disasters relating to natural hazards, especially earthquakes.
 
 About 2 percent of the earthquakes in the world occur in Iran, but more than 6 percent of the victims of the world’s earthquakes during the 20th century are reported from Iranian earthquakes.

Israel systematically burns Palestinian homes in West Bank, assaults holy sites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:43:58 UTC
20:43:58 KST

Israel systematically burns Palestinian homes in West Bank, assaults holy sites
Settler attacks have reached the highest rate in more than two decades
TEHRAN — The return of the Tubasi family to their home in Jalud lasted less than a single day. Forced from their village south of Nablus two months ago by armed Israeli settlers, the family obtained a court order guaranteeing their safe return under military protection.
They arrived on Monday night to find their property vandalized. Hours later, a mob of more than 100 masked settlers descended on the property, set fire to two residential structures, and destroyed what remained.
When Palestinian villagers assembled to defend the family, incoming Israeli troops fired tear gas, shielded the arsonists, and forced the Tubasis to evacuate their land again at gunpoint.
The incident encapsulates a systematic campaign designed to cleanse native Palestinians from the occupied West Bank.
Supported by the U.S., Israel is utilizing coordinated settler terror, military raids, and infrastructure strangulation to annex Palestinian territory and advance its broader regional war against the Resistance Front.
A coordinated campaign of arson and village raids
The arson attack in Jalud formed part of a synchronized wave of violence across northern and central West Bank communities. In al-Mughayyir, northeast of Ramallah, settler gangs operating alongside invading army units attacked civilian properties.
Assailants burned a home belonging to a Palestinian detainee and torched six vehicles, leaving three completely destroyed, while Israeli soldiers raided nearby residences and arrested a local youth.
In Qaryut, settlers smashed through the door of a home and physically battered an elderly Palestinian woman, leaving her with head and hand injuries.
Elsewhere, settlers targeted agricultural life, stealing olive harvests in Beita right before the picking season and launching violent raids in Halhul, Jinba, Ras Karkar, and Deir Abu Mash'al.
During a military raid on Qabatiya, south of Jenin, Israeli soldiers shot a Palestinian man in the abdomen and thigh. Troops then cornered the wounded victim, preventing medical crews from reaching him while he bled on the ground.
This violence is deliberate and coordinated. United Nations monitoring indicates that settler attacks have reached an average of nearly seven incidents per day in 2026, marking the highest rate in more than two decades.
Over 275 distinct Palestinian communities have suffered direct attacks this year. Armed settler militias, operating as unofficial military auxiliaries, routinely destroy water infrastructure, burn livestock shelters, uproot ancient olive groves, and sever power lines.
The structural goal is clear: by rendering rural existence unlivable through constant terror, the regime forces communities to abandon their lands without needing formal eviction orders.
Storming sacred sanctuaries
Alongside physical assaults on rural villages, the regime has intensified its ideological assault on Islamic holy sites, leveraging state power to enforce control during Jewish religious holidays.
In occupied Hebron, extremist National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir led hundreds of illegal occupiers into the Ibrahimi Mosque.
Israeli military authorities completely closed the sanctuary to Muslim worshippers, banning daily prayers and suppressing the Islamic call to prayer.
Speaking inside the mosque during a televised interview, Ben-Gvir openly celebrated the intrusion while hundreds of armed occupiers cheered behind him.
The site has been subjected to forced division since 1994, when an Israeli terrorist murdered 29 Palestinian worshippers inside the sanctuary.
Simultaneously, in occupied East Jerusalem, nearly one thousand settlers under heavy military guard stormed the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound on Tuesday morning.
Over four thousand settlers forced their way into the site across a three-day period during Sukkot, performing prohibited Talmudic rituals, singing, and dancing in the eastern quarter of the compound.
Israeli forces locked down surrounding Palestinian neighborhoods, forcing local merchants to close their shops and confining Palestinian residents to their homes.
The systematic desecration of Islamic sanctuaries drew immediate condemnation from the Palestinian Resistance.
Senior Hamas official Abdul Rahman Shadid issued an urgent call for general mobilization, urging Palestinians across the West Bank, occupied al-Quds (Jerusalem), and the broader Islamic world to march to the Ibrahimi and Al-Aqsa mosques.
Shadid stated that turning Hebron into an open-air military barracks and besieging its population will never break the steadfastness of the Palestinian people.
He emphasized that these growing violations are fueling widespread public anger, reiterating that the Resistance remains fully committed to defending holy sites and confronting Israeli aggression across every operational front.
Checkpoint strangulation and the fatal cost of closures
The physical violence directed at Palestinian communities is reinforced by a suffocating network of physical barriers engineered to fragment the West Bank into disconnected cantons.
According to the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, Israeli forces maintain 942 active checkpoints, iron gates, military roadblocks, and earth mounds across the West Bank.
Spanning over 107 kilometers, this infrastructure grants military commanders total authority to sever entire towns at a moment's notice.
While illegal settlers move freely along modern bypass highways, native Palestinians are forced to wait for hours at militarized crossings or navigate dangerous unpaved detours.
This closure regime carries a devastating human cost. In Deir Istiya, near Salfit, 66-year-old Zahriya Abu Hijleh collapsed during a family gathering.
She required urgent care at a government hospital located just eight minutes away. However, Israeli troops had locked the heavy iron gate at the town entrance, blocking the entry of an incoming ambulance.
Family members were forced to transport Zahriya to the gate, lift her off the stretcher, carry her across the barrier on foot, and load her into a second ambulance waiting on the other side.
She suffered a pulmonary embolism and died before reaching the hospital. Her son, Mohammed, confirmed that the critical delay caused by the locked gate proved fatal.
Similar collective punishment is inflicted on thousands of families daily.
During recent holiday closures, families traveling between Ramallah and Nablus found themselves trapped inside their vehicles for over 14 hours due to military road blockades and roving settler gangs.
At a checkpoint near al-Lubban Asharqiya, an Israeli soldier physically assaulted an 11-year-old Palestinian boy, punching him in the head because the exhausted child did not wake up instantly during a vehicle search.
To support thousands of stranded commuters, local Palestinian municipalities and mosques have converted community halls into emergency shelters, providing food and basic supplies to those trapped on the roads.
American patronage and the resilience of the Palestinian people
The continuous expansion of Israeli war crimes in the West Bank is made possible through direct political, military, and financial backing from Washington.
While American officials occasionally issue performative statements expressing concern over settler violence, the United States continues to pump billions of dollars in advanced weaponry to Tel Aviv.
Washington consistently uses its veto power at the United Nations Security Council to shield the Israeli regime from international sanctions and legal accountability.
High-ranking regime officials, including Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, have openly demanded the complete destruction of West Bank communities and advocated copying the Gaza genocide across the occupied territory.
Since October 2023, Israeli forces and armed settlers have killed at least 1,206 Palestinians in the West Bank, including 254 children. Over 13,350 people have been injured, and more than 24,600 Palestinians have been detained.
Meanwhile, the illegal settler population has surpassed 750,000 individuals spread across 194 settlements and 400 outposts. United Nations leaders have warned that these policies raise the immediate specter of ethnic cleansing.
Yet, despite decades of military occupation, American weapons, and institutionalized terror, Israel has failed to suppress Palestinian steadfastness. The resistance in the West Bank continues to grow in coordination with the broader regional front.
Every burned home, blocked road, and desecrated sanctuary only reinforces the conviction among Palestinians that liberation cannot be achieved through compromise with a genocidal occupying entity. The Palestinian people remain rooted in their land.

The Ministry of Finance expects proposals from the aviation industry to develop a unified approach to the taxation of aircraft leasing
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:42:07 EEST
20:42:07 KST

The Ministry of Finance expects proposals from the aviation industry to develop a unified approach to the taxation of aircraft leasing
Kyiv • UNN
The Ministry of Finance is asking the aviation industry to provide examples of leasing transactions in order to prepare tax guidance. The Economic Security Bureau of Ukraine interprets aircraft rentals as royalties.
The Ministry of Finance of Ukraine continues to work on the application of the provisions of the Tax Code and international agreements on the avoidance of double taxation to lease payments made by Ukrainian airlines to non-residents. The ministry expects industry representatives to provide examples of the incorrect interpretation of these transactions and their positions on resolving the problem in order to prepare a generalized tax consultation. This is stated in the Ministry of Finance’s response to a request from UNN.
Details
The Ministry of Finance is working on an issue that concerns not the regulation of the leasing market in general, but the application of the provisions of the Tax Code of Ukraine and international treaties of Ukraine on the avoidance of double taxation to income received by non-residents in the form of lease or rental payments for the use of aircraft
What is the problem with the taxation of aircraft leasing?
As UNN previously reported, since 2024 the Bureau of Economic Security has begun interpreting transactions involving the leasing of air transport from non-residents of Ukraine as the use of equipment. According to investigators, Ukrainian air carriers were supposed to pay royalties for the rental of aircraft and helicopters. Based on this approach, the BES opened criminal proceedings against at least five air carriers, including MAU, "Constanta Airline," "Wind Rose," N3Operations, and "Skyline Express." According to UNN, another airline, "Urga," may also be involved in a similar case.
The criminal cases were opened despite the fact that almost all air carriers had successfully passed tax audits, and the tax authorities’ comments concerning leasing applied to only one company.
Representatives of the aviation industry insist that the problem arose because of an ambiguous interpretation of the legislation and requires the formation of a unified state approach.
Earlier, in response to a request from UNN, the Ministry of Finance said that the taxation of aircraft leasing transactions is carried out in accordance with the Tax Code and international treaties of Ukraine. At the same time, the Tax Code of Ukraine does not provide for the possibility of taxing aircraft leasing as royalties.
Therefore, representatives of the aviation industry describe the Bureau’s approach to interpreting aircraft leasing without amending the tax legislation as pressure that could destroy the entire passenger and cargo transportation sector. According to the State Register of Civil Aircraft of Ukraine, 86% of the aircraft fleet of Ukrainian companies is leased.
To resolve the situation, the issue of aircraft leasing was submitted for consideration to the Committee on Tax Policy, Accounting and Auditing of the Public Council under the Ministry of Finance. Following the first meeting, it was decided to initiate the establishment of a working group under the Ministry of Finance, which is to develop a draft generalized tax consultation on the taxation of lease payments made to non-residents.
The Ministry of Finance expects proposals from the aviation industry
The Ministry of Finance said that, following the meeting, the participants also agreed to provide the ministry with practical examples of leasing transactions for further analysis.
Following the discussion, an agreement was reached for interested participants to provide, for further consideration, practical examples of the relevant transactions, including taking into account the specifics of agreements concluded by airlines with companies that are residents of different states, as well as proposals and positions regarding the application of the provisions of the Tax Code of Ukraine and international treaties of Ukraine on the avoidance of double taxation to such transactions
The ministry plans to summarize and process the specified materials and, on their basis, prepare a draft generalized tax consultation.
The work will be coordinated by two specialized departments of the Ministry of Finance. In particular, the application of international treaties of Ukraine on the avoidance of double taxation to the income of non-residents is handled by the International Taxation Department, while the application of the provisions of the Tax Code is handled by the Tax Policy Department of the Ministry of Finance.

EU commercial flights rise despite higher jet fuel prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:39:25 UTC
20:39:25 KST

The number of commercial flights across the EU increased in every summer month compared with last year, although traffic fell in several member states.
More than two million commercial flights took place across the EU between June and August 2026, according to Eurostat, even as European jet fuel prices rose during the final month of the summer.
August recorded 708,980 flights, 2.3% more than in August 2025 and 5.7% more than in August 2024. July was slightly busier, with 709,931 flights, while June recorded 662,480.
All three months were busier than the same periods last year. Flights rose by 2.1% year on year in June and 2.8% in July, according to Eurostat.
Growth varied across the EU
The increase in August was not shared by every member state, however.
Commercial flight numbers rose in 19 EU countries compared with a year earlier, but fell in eight.
Slovakia recorded the largest annual increase, at 37%, followed by Malta at 12.4% and Estonia at 8.3%.
Spain added the most flights in absolute terms: 9,600 more than in August 2025. Italy recorded 8,128 more, while Slovakia’s 37% rise amounted to 1,325 additional flights.
Austria saw the steepest decline, at 4.7%. Flights were also down by 3% in Cyprus and 2.4% in Germany.
Jet fuel prices rise
This rise comes during a costly year for airlines. EUROCONTROL, the pan-European organisation that helps manage and coordinate air traffic, says European jet fuel prices climbed again in August after falling in the spring.
In a June forecast, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) expected European airlines' combined net profit to fall from an estimated $13 billion (€11.5 billion) in 2025 to $9.6 billion in 2026, citing fuel costs as a significant pressure.
EUROCONTROL put the European average jet fuel price in August at $3.86 per gallon, 71% above its level before the Middle East crisis, attributing the renewed rise to geopolitical tensions and pressure on fuel supplies.
IATA estimated that European airlines had hedged about 70% of their fuel needs before the current crisis, but warned that higher costs would eventually feed through as Europe faces significant fuel cost pressure partly due to its reliance on imports from the Gulf.

The prime minister of Germany’s North Rhine-Westphalia state on Wednesday vowed to build on longstanding economic ties with Türkiye and further strengthen cooperation.
Hendrik Wust made the remarks at the Türkiye-North Rhine-Westphalia Business Forum in Istanbul.
The event was jointly organized by Türkiye’s Foreign Economic Relations Board (DEIK) and Germany’s trade agency NRW.Global Business.
“For decades now, people, ideas, and investment have moved in both directions. Especially now, as international trade barriers increase and supply chains are under pressure, reliable connections are more valuable than ever.
“Our aim is to build on these strong ties and strengthen our cooperation even further.”
He said the state government had agreed on a fast-track visa process for Turkish businesspeople to overcome lengthy processing times that hinder essential face-to-face cooperation.
Wust backed efforts to modernize the 30-year-old European Customs Union and update EU industrial policy to reflect the current structure of global supply chains.
He described the Turkish economy as an indispensable part of the European value chain.
He noted that Türkiye stood out as a top player in foreign direct investment and ranked as the state’s third-largest trading partner.
More than one in three Turkish-owned companies in Germany are based in North Rhine-Westphalia, totaling about 1,300 businesses, he said.
Wust also highlighted Türkiye’s large onshore wind market and investment in power generation and transmission infrastructure, saying energy prices and security were crucial to North Rhine-Westphalia’s heavy and energy-intensive industry.
“We see that Türkiye has one of Europe’s largest onshore wind markets,” he said.
He said new memorandums of understanding signed at the forum could create future partnerships and further strengthen economic and geopolitical ties.
 
Focus on implementing agreements
Serap Guler, a state minister at the German Federal Foreign Office, reaffirmed Berlin’s commitment to expanding economic cooperation with Türkiye and integrating Turkish industry into European supply chains.
Guler highlighted that around 8,600 German companies currently operate in Türkiye, creating more than 100,000 direct jobs.
She noted that geopolitical tensions and supply chain risks threaten competitiveness, emphasizing that both nations must focus on implementing agreements reached during the German-Turkish Foreign Ministers’ Strategic Dialogue held in May.
Unlocking the full economic potential of nearly 540 million people across the EU and Türkiye requires modernizing the Customs Union, the minister said.
She stressed the need to remove tariff and non-tariff trade barriers, rely on rule-of-law instruments, and ensure Türkiye applies the agreement to all EU member states.
Guler stated that Germany strongly advocates in Brussels for a “Made with Europe” approach under the EU Industrial Accelerator Act to include key partners like Türkiye.

EU accused of concealing resource consumption information for data centers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:38:30 UTC
20:38:30 KST

According to a complaint filed against the European Commission on the 28th of September, the European Union has shielded large data centers from public scrutiny regarding the amount of energy they consume, reports Politico.
The complaint was filed by the organization Lighthouse Reports and accuses the European Commission of implementing rules that prevent the public from learning how much energy and water is required for the operation of individual data centers. Public opposition to the construction of energy-intensive data centers in Europe is currently growing, as are energy prices. The Dutch non-profit Lighthouse Reports – which conducts cross-border investigations into misconduct by governments and large corporations – has stated that the Commission is creating a “wall of silence” regarding actual energy consumption. EU policymakers are allegedly intent on denying or restricting access to information and obscuring understanding of how data centers operate.
The complaint will face its first test in November, when the Aarhus Convention Compliance Committee decides whether to accept it. If the complaint is accepted, the Aarhus Convention body will determine whether the EU has violated its obligations under the convention. The European Commission did not respond to a request for comment from Politico.
As the rapid development of artificial intelligence drives up demand for energy,
the EU has announced a goal to triple data center capacity in the coming years
to keep pace with the US and China. At the same time, rising energy prices have fueled growing public opposition to data centers across Europe. To curb environmental costs and promote greener construction, the Commission unveiled a new transparency label last week. EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen told Politico that unless major energy consumers align with the bloc’s overarching goals, the EU risks failing to meet its own targets.
According to Commission data, European data centers consumed 20.7 terawatt-hours of electricity—equivalent to the annual consumption of the entire country of Croatia—and more than eight million cubic meters of water in 2025. This represents a 26% increase in electricity consumption and a 52% increase in water usage compared to 2024. However, these figures do not present the full picture, as the Commission does not provide comprehensive data. They were released in aggregate form after a 2024 law barred Brussels and EU national capitals from disclosing full information and key metrics regarding individual data centers. The law was adopted under pressure from tech giants, who justified the measure by citing “commercial interests.”
Diego Solier, a representative of the European Parliament’s conservative wing, stated that the expansion of European data centers must go hand in hand with providing citizens and policymakers with reliable information on energy and water consumption. While he did not comment on the specific complaint, he noted that transparency is the starting point; at the same time, he emphasized the need for proportionality, noting that companies should not be forced to disclose commercially sensitive information.
The complaint filed by Lighthouse Reports alleges that the EC is responsible for withholding information from the public
regarding Europe’s massive data centers—by allowing operators to keep energy consumption data private—and that this constitutes a violation of the Aarhus Convention.
After failing to persuade the Commission and national governments to release the data they hold, the organization has accused the Commission of unjustifiably hiding behind confidentiality exemptions. The organization also believes that the new compliance labels (criticized by industry representatives) fail to address the issue of concealed information. These labels require operators, starting next summer, to rate their energy efficiency, water consumption, and share of green energy on a scale from A to G. “Lighthouse Reports” pointed out that the new rules still obscure total energy consumption and other metrics needed to assess the carbon footprint of data centers.

30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
French President Emmanuel Macron called Wednesday for stronger European trade defenses and greater investment, warning that dependence on China and fossil fuels threatens the continent’s competitiveness.
Speaking in Spain, Macron urged Europe to boost innovation, simplify regulations, increase financing and protect industrial producers from unfair competition.
“China has completely flooded the European market. For decades, we told ourselves: ‘Wonderful, China is a huge market for us Europeans. We need China.’ That is true. We transferred a great deal of technology, we sold a great deal, and we still do to some extent.”
He accused China of heavily subsidizing companies and engaging in dumping to eliminate competitors.
“Today, as we speak, we Europeans run a trade deficit with China of €1 billion every day.”
Macron called for faster European Commission investigations, stronger trade defense instruments and requirements ensuring imports meet the same standards imposed on European producers.
On energy, he warned that decarbonization had not eliminated Europe’s vulnerabilities.
“Today, we remain heavily dependent on fossil fuels. We can clearly see this with what is happening in the Strait of Hormuz, which poses a problem for our economic models. Even countries that have made substantial progress in decarbonisation, such as Spain and France, each following its own path, still have these dependencies.”
He called for stronger electricity interconnections and greater investment in artificial intelligence, quantum technology and defense.
“We Europeans have more savings than the Americans. Those savings go into our banks and insurance companies. Because we introduced extremely restrictive rules following a financial crisis that originated with American market participants, we overregulated our banks and insurers.”
Macron urged easing financial rules to channel savings into investment, alongside a stronger EU budget and deeper integration of the single market.

Meta shields billions in taxes by classifying AI data centers as experimental models: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:27:57 UTC
20:27:57 KST

Yasin Gungor
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
US tech company Meta exploited a federal research tax credit to shield billions of dollars from corporate taxes by classifying its artificial intelligence data centers as experimental pilot models, The New York Times reported Tuesday.
Meta told the Internal Revenue Service that its AI data centers were a “giant experiment that could fail,” the newspaper reported, citing four people familiar with the company’s operations. The maneuver trimmed nearly $4 billion from Meta’s 2025 tax bill, making it the largest beneficiary among publicly traded companies, according to IRS filings.
The strategy relies on a provision dating to the 1980s that was intended to spur innovation by allowing tax credits for supplies used in research rather than standard business operations. People familiar with the matter said Meta began classifying commercially proven processors, including chips bought from Nvidia, as experimental supplies when they were used in artificial intelligence facilities.
Meta defended the practice, saying it invested $200 billion in research over five years, including $57 billion last year.
“Like other companies that invest at this scale, we use the tax incentives Congress established decades ago to encourage this type of domestic investment,” the company said.

Russia Expands Drone Launch Hub as Geran-5 Drones Dominate Attacks on Kyiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:27:18 UTC
20:27:18 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Expands Drone Launch Hub as Geran-5 Drones Dominate Attacks on Kyiv
Russia has continued expanding the Tsymbulova drone base in the Oryol region, adding new launch infrastructure, shelters, and storage facilities over the past four weeks, an OSINT channel Strategic Aviation reported on September 29.
Satellite imagery shows a new area southeast of the existing launch positions with eight dome-shaped shelters for jet-powered drones and an additional launcher. Strategic Aviation reported that paved areas have also been prepared for eight more shelters and two additional launchers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russia’s Geran drones are domestically produced derivatives of Iran’s Shahed attack drones, while newer variants increasingly use jet propulsion.
The Geran-3 was developed from the jet-powered Shahed-238, while the newer Geran-5 is linked to Iran’s Karrar design and can reach far higher speeds than propeller-driven Shaheds. UNITED24 Media recently detailed how these jet-powered variants are becoming harder for Ukrainian air defenses to intercept.
Six garages for strike drones that were still under construction in early September have now been completed. Another 14 garages have appeared along the access road, the OSINT channel noted.
The facility’s protective infrastructure has also been reinforced. Strategic Aviation reported that several above-ground shelters were converted into underground structures, while additional defensive measures are being installed around launch areas.
Construction has also expanded near existing Geran-5 launchers, with space prepared for six additional launch positions. Towers under construction nearby could be used for anti-drone netting or communications, the channel said.
Strategic Aviation assessed that the expansion is already affecting the composition of Russian drone attacks on Kyiv. The channel estimated that Geran-5 drones now account for roughly 75% of the drones launched toward the Ukrainian capital, compared with about 10% a month earlier.
Further construction is visible in the northeastern section of the site, where heavy equipment is operating on previously unused land. The channel assessed that new storage facilities may be under construction there.
The expansion has also reduced the number of drones left outdoors. Strategic Aviation reported that nearly 100 drones were visible outdoors at the end of summer, while the latest imagery shows fewer than a dozen.
Recently, Russian drones struck civilian sites in Ukraine’s Odesa region, including an animal shelter in Velykodolynske, where three dogs and 10 cats were killed. The attack also damaged residential buildings, warehouses, a gymnasium, a dormitory, and vehicles.

Fire Point Says Its 850-Km FP-9 Ballistic Missile Is Entering the Final Stretch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:27:11 UTC
20:27:11 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Fire Point Says Its 850-Km FP-9 Ballistic Missile Is Entering the Final Stretch
Ukrainian defense company Fire Point plans to complete development of its FP-9 ballistic missile, designed for a range of up to 850 kilometers, by the end of fall 2026, while its shorter-range FP-7 has already entered the codification process.
Fire Point CEO and CTO Iryna Terekh outlined the company’s progress in an interview with entrepreneur and blogger Andrii Fedoriv published on September 25.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Terekh said Fire Point has been working on its ballistic missile program for less than two years—a timeline she contrasted with traditional development cycles that can stretch for decades.
“Similar developments have never taken less than 15 years,” she said.
Fire Point is developing two ballistic missiles simultaneously, with both projects now approaching their final stages.
“The short-range ballistic missile is, you could say, already ready. That is, it is going through the codification process,” Terekh said.
She confirmed that the weapon in question is the FP-7, with a range of up to 300 kilometers, or roughly 185 miles.
The second missile is significantly more ambitious.
“The long-range one is 850 kilometers. You could also say that it is in the final stage. But the final stage still means a series of tests,” Terekh said.
Asked when a Ukrainian ballistic missile could reach Moscow, Terekh said Fire Point already has a target timeline.
“We plan to do this by the end of autumn. Specifically, the long-range ballistic missile that should be able to reach Moscow,” she said.
Terekh stressed that Fire Point does not select targets for the weapon. Operational targeting decisions belong exclusively to Ukraine’s Armed Forces. She added, however, that personally she would “very much like it to be Moscow.”
The pace of development has come with an enormous price tag. According to Terekh, Fire Point has invested approximately $200 million in the FP-7 program alone.
“Development of our first ballistic missile, the FP-7, is approximately $200 million that we spent on R&D and preparation for initial production,” she said.
The larger FP-9 will require even greater investment. Terekh attributed the costs to highly specialized engineering teams, repeated testing, expensive materials and the need to develop critical technologies and components internally.
Many of those components cannot simply be purchased internationally because their export is tightly restricted—or because, in some cases, commercially available equivalents do not exist.
“Ballistic missiles mean hundreds of millions of dollars in R&D,” Terekh said.
Only a relatively small group of countries possesses indigenous ballistic missile capabilities, she added.
Earlier, Terekh revealed that Ukraine’s FP-7 ballistic missile completed about 15 test launches and is now undergoing Defense Ministry certification, putting it on track for its first combat use as early as this fall.

Russia Loses 2,090 Troops in 24 Hours, Highest Reported Daily Toll of Full-Scale War
Unknown

2026-09-30
11:27:05 UTC
20:27:05 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Loses 2,090 Troops in 24 Hours, Highest Reported Daily Toll of Full-Scale War
Russian forces recorded their highest reported daily casualty total since the start of the full-scale invasion, with 2,090 troops killed or wounded over a 24-hour period, according to UK Defence Intelligence on September 29.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Citing figures from Ukraine’s General Staff for September 28, UK intelligence said the reported losses marked the highest single-day total since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Three previous daily totals exceeding 2,000 Russian casualties were recorded in 2024. The fourth-highest figure, 1,960 troops killed or wounded, was recorded on September 16, 2026.
“The casualty rate has remained high since the summer, highly likely as Russia maintains its intensity in the fortress belt region, particularly in the vicinity of the Ukrainian stronghold of Dobropillia,” the intelligence added.
The latest figures add to Russia’s mounting personnel losses throughout the war. Ukraine’s General Staff has separately estimated total Russian military losses at approximately 1.5 million personnel, describing the figure as the country’s highest losses in a single war since World War II.
According to the General Staff, the total exceeds the combined losses sustained by Soviet and Russian forces in wars and armed conflicts since the second half of the 20th century. It estimated that Russia’s losses in Ukraine are roughly 100 times those suffered by the Soviet Union during the war in Afghanistan and 125 times Russia’s officially acknowledged losses in the First and Second Chechen wars.
Separate reports have also pointed to internal problems within Russian military units. Documents obtained by Cyber-ATESH detail combat losses, widespread unauthorized absences, suicides, and serious disciplinary issues within Russia’s 127th Motor Rifle Division.
When assessed alongside battlefield reports and independent Russian investigations, the documents suggest that the division’s official casualty records may significantly lag behind losses documented at the front, while some of its units appear to be facing broader problems with morale and command.

Russian Forces Seize Ukrainian Food Aid From Civilians in Temporarily Occupied Oleshky
Russian forces in temporarily occupied Oleshky are confiscating food dropped by Ukrainian drones for residents, according to Tetiana Hasanenko, chief of the Oleshky Municipal Military Administration, in an interview with Ukrinform published September 30.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian forces have conducted multiple drone deliveries of humanitarian supplies to the trapped civilian population. The most recent operation delivered approximately four tons of food to residents across the city before Russian forces began seizing the aid.
"If you receive food supplies from the Ukrainian Armed Forces, it means you are collaborating with them," Hasanenko stated, describing the confiscation tactic.
Russian occupation authorities treat the town as Russian territory and characterize residents receiving non-Russian food as having violated Russian law and engaged in support for Ukraine's military.
Beyond confiscations, Russian forces continue to detain and abduct residents.
Hasanenko described the practice as ongoing: "People are taken, families disappear without a trace. We don't know where they are—they take them to the basement, and that's it. Whether they're alive or not, we don't know."
Russian forces have systematized the blockade of Oleshky since early 2024, with civilians facing severe shortages of food, water, medicine, electricity, and gas.
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine reported in June that no official food deliveries had reached the city since late May.
Ukrainian drone operations represent one of the few channels through which humanitarian aid now reaches the roughly 2,000 remaining residents, down from a pre-war population exceeding 24,000.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard spokesman Gen. Hossein Mohebbi speaks during a news conference in Tehran, Iran, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. (AP Photo)

The message was laid out on Sept. 29 in a 25-page open letter to the American public, calling on U.S. voters to oppose Washington’s support for Israel and its involvement in overseas conflicts.
The letter also argued that Iran and the United States could coexist if Washington were to fundamentally alter its foreign policy toward Tehran.

IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi said he did not expect the letter to prompt any change in the U.S. administration’s conduct just weeks before the elections, but suggested that its message could nevertheless reach American voters.
Mohebbi said that the only way for the war in Iran to end is for Washington to admit defeat and leave.
Later, in remarks to The Associated Press, Mohebbi urged Americans to reconsider their leadership and take to the streets and protest Trump’s policies to denounce what he called the U.S. government’s warmongering policies.
He accused the United States of using Iran’s nuclear program as a ruse to “plunder Iran’s wealth” and to turn the country “back into a colony.”
Meanwhile, Iranian authorities said on Sept. 29 they received the official U.S. response to their proposal to end the Middle East war, days after rejected the plan.

Rasul Medal announces shortlist of nominees for second edition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
