Qalqilya main entrance
Wadi an Nar
Yassin follows a protocol for crossing. Windows down before the soldiers ask. Then the script, which she can recite: "Hand over your ID. Where are you going, where are you coming from, what do you do?" Sometimes the soldier holds his phone up close and takes photos of her face with her ID and license plate. One time, she said, a soldier leaned in through the window: "You're beautiful," he said.
She often saw men pressed face-down against the hoods of their cars, hands behind their backs, the soldiers shouting. Sometimes, on her way back, the same men are still detained.
When asked, nearly two-thirds of people say humiliation or fear most characterize their feeling about checkpoints. Of people stopped at a checkpoint in the last six months, nearly 40 percent said their vehicle was searched by a soldier, and more than 20 percent said they were physically searched. About one in seven said a soldier had pointed a gun toward them.
Eventually, even dropping her daughter off in the morning stopped making sense. Yassin began staying at her parents' house near Nablus most nights. Her husband Montasir stayed in Ramallah and visited on some weekends. He usually left them Saturday morning, before the settler traffic on Route 60 picked up and checkpoints got worse.
As Yara grew older, she began to ask questions. When she opened her eyes in the morning, she’d ask: "Mama, why didn't you take us to Baba?" Then, because she already knew the answer, she’d say, "Is the road closed?"
In the end, the checkpoints proved too great a barrier for Yassin too. The move to her parents’ wasn’t enough. She was still losing hours at the checkpoint. After her second child was born earlier this year, Yassin decided not to go back to work. She extended her maternity leave and was weighing what comes next: a pause, a position closer to home if she can find one, perhaps something abroad. "I can't do it again," she said. Since then, Yassin has left her job at the hospital.
Deadly Delays
In the summer of July 2024, a young man from Reem Yassin’s village was shot by Israeli forces in the leg. The injury itself was not life threatening. But after soldiers held his ambulance at a checkpoint for almost an hour, he entered severe hemorrhagic shock, Yassin recalled.
Yassin, who was completing part of her medical residency at Rafidia Surgical Hospital in Nablus, was the doctor who received him. Recognized immediately by his family, she worked to stabilize him as his blood pressure plunged.
"We almost lost him," Yassin recalls. "We had to keep pumping blood into him." He survived, luckily, but his situation is far from unique: Nearly two-thirds of people in the West Bank say checkpoints have been a barrier to their access to medical care.
Between October 2023 and August 2026, the Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS) documented 237 access denials and 240 mission delays by Israeli forces. In early 2026, incidents included soldiers detaining a medical crew at the Sarra checkpoint, soldiers throwing an ambulance crew’s keys down a mountainside at Huwwara, and a Palestinian woman in labor being transferred between vehicles across locked gates. (In response to questions on medical delays, the Israeli Military said, “In accordance with international law, the IDF allows freedom of movement for medical vehicles, including ambulances, for the purpose of providing medical treatment and evacuating the wounded.”)
These delays carry fatal consequences. The Red Crescent attributes 25 deaths since 2023 to the obstruction of its medical teams. In July 2026, a Palestinian infant, Ahmad Zaid, died after Israeli soldiers at a checkpoint blocked the vehicle transporting him for more than an hour.
In response, the Red Crescent has begun bringing facilities to the people, building makeshift medical points inside villages since ambulances are now so often delayed and cannot reliably access hospitals. Doctors Without Borders (MSF) also started providing first aid training to medical and nonmedical volunteers so they can respond to urgent medical needs in cases when an ambulance is delayed or stopped at a checkpoint.
Sleeping at the Factory
After October 2023, delay times at checkpoints across Nablus spiked to levels beyond anywhere else in the West Bank. Commuters in Nablus spent an average of nearly an hour and 50 minutes avoiding checkpoints. Ali Haj Ali has worked at Sama Pharmaceuticals, a medicine factory east of Nablus city, for over a decade; now, at 37, he supervises the maintenance of the company’s production lines. When he leaves at the end of his shift at 4:30 pm, he has stopped expecting to reach his home before 8:00 pm, even though it’s only 16 kilometers away.
Some nights, he doesn't get home at all. He sleeps at the factory, in an arrangement Sama built during Covid-19: Two offices hold a bed and a dozen mattresses for whoever can’t make the trip home.
When checkpoints close, Sama’s employees sometimes have to sleep on site.PHOTOGRAPH: Lama Rabah
“My three kids, my wife, my mother, my father, I’d barely see them,” he said. “And forget about seeing friends.” But this is the best job he thinks he can find, so he keeps going.
On a recent afternoon, Ali sat in a room at Sama Pharmaceuticals, along with his colleague, Ohood Khatatbeh. In minutes, they were filling in the details for one another, recounting what they call “Nablus’ checkpoint crisis” in 2024 and 2025. Ali would sometimes reach the checkpoint, sit there for hours, then just turn around and go home.
"Nothing is guaranteed, that's just how it is here. It's like a lottery," Ali said.
Ohood, the factory’s quality assurance manager, is 38 years old, and the mother of three sons. Her town, Beit Furik, is southeast of Nablus. It has a single gate, in or out. Her whole day is dictated by that gate.
The town has had to come up with its own protocol, as Ohood calls it: For every three private cars, one shared taxi gets through. What they cannot control is the pace, interrupted by the soldiers’ change of shifts.
Best case, if the Beit Furik gate is open and traffic is moving freely, the drive home can take 15 minutes. But for a year and a half, it routinely took her more than 5 hours daily. On the worst day, it took 10 hours. In 2024, Ohood's teenage son had finished a final exam in biology at his school in Nablus just before she was finishing her shift. They found each other at the Beit Furik gate at 4:30 pm, in a line that packed the road several cars wide, all heading for the single entrance to a town of almost 16,000.
Ohood and her son waited in line together until 3 am the following morning.
"The regular employee, the one not separated from work by a checkpoint," she said, "would be home, eaten, showered, asleep, and already dreaming, while I'm still at the checkpoint."
Across the West Bank, checkpoints have begun to reshape how businesses like Sama operate. The company has started rejecting highly qualified candidates after assessing the checkpoints they would have to cross to get to work, Ohood said. It’s even started writing it into the job postings, as a requirement: Candidates must live in Nablus. About half of people polled said checkpoints have impacted their or their spouse’s ability to get a job.
In late 2025, Ohood’s one-week-old baby, Aws, came down with jaundice. She and her husband drove him out of town to the hospital. But on the way back, as she remembers it, they they found the soldier already closing the gate.
"Go back," the soldier yelled in Arabic from the other side of the gate in Beit Furik.
"Go back where?" her husband asked. "We have a sick child with us."
The soldier raised his rifle and pointed it toward them. "For God's sake," Ohood told her husband, "let's just go back." He tried once more anyway, offering to turn around himself if the soldier would just let Ohood and the baby cross the gate on foot. The soldier lost his temper. "I'll shoot you," he said.
They turned around, the baby crying in their arms, and waited in line for an hour and a half until the soldier opened the gate again.
A Different World
By 2000, Aref Jaber says every road in and out of the Jaber neighborhood in Hebron, named after his family, was sealed with earth mounds and concrete slabs. By 2010, he says, iron gates were installed and checkpoints were manned by soldiers. Three years ago, new closures were installed on the very entrances to people's homes, and iron fencing was wrapped around the gates so no one could squeeze through.
The neighborhood sits between the Ibrahimi Mosque, the settlement outposts in the old city in Hebron, and the Kiryat Arba settlement, and has only one way in or out: a turnstile, an inspection room with digital scanning, a metal gate, and a military watchtower, called Checkpoint 160. It’s “as if we’re entering another country,” Jaber says of crossing it. Except the country on the other side is his own house.
For months after October 2023, Israeli forces imposed a curfew on the neighborhood every night, from 10 to 7 in the morning. Now it's every weekend, Aref said. From Friday afternoon until Sunday morning, the checkpoint is closed. No one in, no one out. Jaber says the people who die on Sundays are lucky, because you can bury them the same day. Die on a Saturday, and there is nothing to be done until the checkpoint opens again.
The Palestinians in the neighborhood need to wait for Israeli approval for things big and small: whether they want to evacuate a patient, hold a funeral, or bring in a canister of cooking gas. Locals cross the checkpoint on foot and climb the hill, carrying the sick, carrying groceries up to the neighborhood, dragging suitcases down toward the checkpoint. Jaber’s 6-year-old grandson should be able to go to the school 50 meters away. But it now sits behind an earth mound wrapped in barbed wire, and reaching it would mean a three-kilometer detour on foot, along settler-dominated roads. Jaber waves at his cousins, who live behind the same earth mound. "They have a whole different life there," he says. "We're in the closed zone."
Houses belonging to Palestinians who have been forced to leave them or use a different entrance by the Israeli Military and Israeli settlers are seen in the Jaber neighborhood of Hebron.PHOTOGRAPH: SAMAR HAZBOUN
Even amid the unrelenting pressure of apartheid, people can still imagine a different life. On January 6, 2026, at around 3:00 pm, a Palestinian driver approached Wadi an-Nar, the checkpoint controlling the only road linking the north of the occupied West Bank to the south since 2000. He noticed something strange. No soldiers stood in the way. The checkpoint was open. He took out his phone, recorded a twenty-second video, and posted it in a local Telegram channel.
Within the hour, the clip spread through the West Bank. Everyone was confused. Did Israel remove its checkpoints? Was this really happening?
At 5:57, admins of the “Road Conditions” Telegram group were joking about crossing checkpoints off their lists.
At 6:10, the admins posted that the soldiers had returned. At 6:12, they said the gates were shut.
There was never an explanation. Some assumed it was a drill for Israeli forces. Others, simply a change of shifts. But for three hours, people allowed themselves to imagine a West Bank without checkpoints. A West Bank you can drive the full length of, 130 kilometers from north to south, in less than two hours.
And for a moment, they inhabited a world where they could plan the next day, the next hour. Where Amal’s daughters would reach their lecture halls in minutes. Where Reem wouldn't have to give up a job to keep her family together. Where Ali would walk through his front door before his son fell asleep. Where Ohood would take her baby to the hospital without a rifle raised at her. Where, perhaps, you just keep driving: to Haifa, to Gaza, anywhere you want.
And Aref Jaber would walk down his own street, past the ladders he no longer needs. He would open his front door, and be home.

Fewer California Republicans approve of Trump, poll says. That could hurt GOP midterm chances

Fewer California Republicans approve of Trump, poll says. That could hurt GOP midterm chances
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
With gas prices topping $6 a gallon and an unpopular war continuing in Iran, President Trump’s approval has slipped with California Republicans — a falloff that could diminish the party’s chances in the state’s few competitive congressional races.
A new poll by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies, co-sponsored by The Times, found that 76% of Republican voters in the state approve of the president’s performance, down from 83% last year.
The president’s approval has softened even among those who still support his performance. Only 44% of Republicans in California said they strongly support Trump’s performance, down from 57% who said the same in August 2025.
That could translate into lower Republican turnout in the state’s few competitive races, said the poll’s director, Mark DiCamillo.
“Republicans are losing some of their enthusiasm in terms of being motivated to vote,” he said.
In addition, the more Trump tries to make the midterm elections about himself — such as the pro-Trump ads recently sponsored and paid for by the government — the more Democrats might be inclined to show up, said G. Cristina Mora, the UC Berkeley institute’s co-director.
“That might actually have a galvanizing effect on voters,” she said.
Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton are competing in the race for California governor. Here’s what you need to know about the candidates.
Trump’s sinking support in California mirrors a national decline in the president’s approval, even among Republicans.
The congressional map in the state was already challenging for Republicans after voters last year approved a referendum championed by Gov. Gavin Newsom to redraw districts to be more favorable for Democrats — a response to similar efforts by Republicans in Texas and other states.
In the new map, only four of the state’s 52 districts are currently considered safe Republican districts, while three additional districts are seen as competitive, according to the Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan political handicapper.
The remaining 45 districts are seen as either likely or solidly Democratic in a state where Democrats hold a roughly 20% advantage in party registration.
Only one race is considered by Cook to be a true toss-up — California’s 22nd Congressional District in the Central Valley, which is held by Republican Rep. David Valadao.
“We’re looking at the best case scenario for Democrats at this point,” said Erin Covey, Cook’s U.S. House editor.
Valadao, one of only 10 Republicans to vote for Trump’s impeachment in the wake of the Jan. 6, 2021, insurrection, faces progressive Democrat Randy Villegas, a political science professor who has the backing of Bernie Sanders. The Vermont senator is joining Villegas this weekend for a rally in Bakersfield.
Valadao first won a seat in Congress in 2012, but was ousted from office during the Democrats’ “blue wave” election in 2018, in which the party gained 40 seats in the House in the first election after Trump took office in 2016. Valadao was able to win back his seat in 2020 and has held it since.
As Californians prepare to elect a new governor in November, the top concern they want the new leader to prioritize is reducing the state’s entrenched high cost of living, according to a new poll.
There has been scant public polling in the race, but a poll conducted in June by a political committee backing Villegas showed the Democrat holding a 4-point lead over Valadao.
Two other congressional districts in the state are listed by Cook as leaning Democratic: 
- California’s 48th Congressional District in Riverside and San Diego counties, now held by Republican Rep. Darrell Issa, who opted to retire rather than seek reelection in the redrawn district.
- California’s 13th Congressional District in the San Joaquin Valley, where Democratic Rep. Adam Gray is trying to fend off a challenge from Republican Kevin Lincoln, the former mayor of Stockton.
Trump’s approval also dipped among Black and Latino voters in the poll. Both groups were part of Trump’s winning coalition in the 2024 presidential election.
The poll also found broad disapproval of two signature Trump administration policies.
It found that 70% of California voters disapprove of Trump’s decision to go to war in Iran, including 1 in 5 Republicans.
Also, 70% of California voters believe that the president’s immigration policies are hurting California’s economy and local businesses, including 1 in 5 Republicans.
The poll was conducted online in English and Spanish between Sept. 15 and Sept. 20 and included the opinions of 6,989 registered California voters. The margin of error is plus or minus 1.5 percentage points.

Hamas, PIJ and Mohammed Dahlan form electoral coalition despite Hamas pledge to cede Gaza rule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:59:34 UTC
18:59:34 KST

Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad and the exiled leader of Fatah’s Democratic Reform Current, Mohammed Dahlan, have formed an electoral alliance to run in the Palestinian Legislative Council elections in November, PIJ Deputy Secretary General Mohammed al-Hindi confirmed to the Associated Press.
The confirmation comes weeks after Dimitri Dilliani, a spokesperson for Dahlan, told The Jerusalem Post that the UAE-based Palestinian politician was working to unify the factions ahead of the elections.
Al-Hindi claimed the terrorist organization would support “a unified national list” made up of independent figures rather than members of the groups. The PIJ has not historically participated in elections run by the Palestinian Authority, but Al-Hindi claimed the group would “support a national list that is agreed upon.”
Trump’s 20-point plan stipulated that Hamas would have no role in governing Gaza and would disarm. Hamas subsequently agreed to relinquish governance, though implementation of the plan’s disarmament provisions remains contested. Hamas political leader Khalil al-Hayya, however, affirmed to Al Araby TV earlier this week that the group had planned to run in the November elections.
Coalition would allow Hamas to commit to PLO but retain 'resistance ideology'
Prof. Kobi Michael, a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) and the Misgav Institute, previously told the Post that forming a list with Dahlan, and creating a new coalition outside of the official Hamas movement, would allow the group to accept the Palestinian Authority’s terms for running in the election, without giving up the resistance ideology at the core of its belief system.
Candidates are required to commit to the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) as the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people, as well as its political and national program and relevant international resolutions. The PLO recognizes Israel, something Hamas has historically rejected.
Diliani, who repeated his comments to AP to the Post, did not confirm the reported alliance, though he stopped short of denying it, acknowledging that multiple Palestinian factions are creating a unified list.
The reported alliance comes after years of tension between Dahlan and Hamas, and Dahlan and the Palestinian Authority. The first head of the PA’s Preventive Security Service, he spent years battling Hamas and, according to an exclusive report by Vanity Fair, was involved in a Bush administration-backed plot to oust the group from Gaza in 2008.
Dahlan was removed from his position in Khan Yunis, where he was born, following Hamas’s violent takeover of the Gaza Strip. After years of political confrontation, Dahlan also eventually left the West Bank amid allegations from officials within his own Fatah party.
Following a leaked recording in which Dahlan criticized Abbas and his sons, the PA brought a series of allegations against him, including that he had attempted to mount a coup against Abbas, been involved in the circumstances surrounding Yasser Arafat’s death, and embezzled approximately $16 million in public funds.
Despite the apparent years of conflict, Dahlan wrote in a vision statement shared exclusively with the Post last month that “We want our entire relationship to move from an attempt to weaken one another to cooperation in building the homeland and protecting the national project...”

2 tankers hit by unknown projectiles in Strait of Hormuz: Maritime agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:59:12 UTC
18:59:12 KST

Mohammad Sio
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Two oil and liquefied natural gas tankers were struck by unknown projectiles Tuesday while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said Wednesday.
 
In a warning, UKMTO said it had received a delayed report of an incident that occurred within the strategic waterway on Tuesday.
 
“A verified source has reported that a crude oil tanker has been struck on the port side by an unknown projectile,” the agency said.
 
In a separate warning, UKMTO said it received a delayed report that a liquefied natural gas tanker was struck by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday.
 
It classified the incident as an “attack” and urged vessels transiting the area to exercise caution and report any suspicious activity.
 
UKMTO did not identify the vessel or provide details on possible casualties, damage or the origin of the projectile.
 
It also did not identify the destinations, cargoes, owners or flags of either vessel.
 
It said authorities are investigating the incident.
 
No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack, which comes amid tensions between Iran and the US over navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy and commodity supplies.
 
Iran's military said Sunday that it intercepted 19 vessels that attempted to transit the strait outside a navigation route designated by Tehran during a two-day period.
 
The Strait of Hormuz has been a major point of contention in negotiations between Tehran and Washington, with both sides maintaining differing positions over control and management of navigation through the waterway.
 
In February, the US and Israel launched a war against Iran, which responded with attacks on Israel and US targets in the region before a ceasefire agreement was reached in April.
 
Washington and Tehran later signed a memorandum of understanding in June concerning freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, but implementation stalled over disagreements related to security in the strategic waterway.

Hungarian appeals court cuts German activist's jail term to seven years

Hungarian appeals court cuts German activist's jail term to seven years
BUDAPEST, Sept 30 - A Hungarian appeals court on Wednesday reduced the prison sentence of a German citizen convicted for assaulting suspected far-right sympathisers in Budapest in 2023 to seven years from eight.
The defendant, identified only as Maja T., was among a group of anti-fascist activists who travelled to Hungary to counter a far-right rally. Arrested in Berlin in December 2023, Maja T. was later transferred to Hungary to stand trial. A lower court handed Maja T. an eight-year sentence in February.
• According to the indictment, Maja T. was part of a far-left group that planned to take up an "ideological fight with violent attacks against sympathisers of the extremist right" with the aim of assaulting people with "various instruments capable of causing death."
• The appeals court judge said the sentence was being reduced because for one of the two counts on which Maja T. was convicted, the defendant should be considered an accomplice rather than a co-perpetrator and should not be considered part of an organised criminal group.
• The case drew international attention when Germany's Constitutional Court ruled in February 2025 that it had been unlawful to extradite Maja T., who identifies as non-binary, to Hungary, upholding her argument that the decision violated the European Union's Charter of Fundamental Rights.
• Under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who was ousted in an April election, Hungary introduced anti-LGBTQ+ policies, including laws that Brussels says discriminate against people on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity.
• Authorities in Hungary have given assurances that non-binary people are not subject to discrimination or violence in prisons there.
• Maja T., who was one of several individuals to go on trial over the attacks, had told the court earlier that the accusations against them were political.
• The first accused in the trial was Italian teacher Ilaria Salis, who was released from house arrest in June 2024 after she was elected a member of the European Parliament. Prosecutors were seeking an 11-year sentence for her. Salis and her family said she was innocent. REUTERS

Ukraine Finally Has Bipartisan Support in the US. Why Are Ukrainian Consuls Working to Destroy It?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:47:55 UTC
18:47:55 KST

On Sept. 18 US President Donald Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act. Eighty-six senators from both parties voted for it. So did 262 members of the House of Representatives.
When the $60 billion Ukraine aid package passed the House in April 2024, 112 Republicans voted against it. For the Russian Sanction bill this month, seven did.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Seven.
For two years the fear was that a Trump presidency would be a disaster for Ukraine. It hasn’t been. Republicans who once treated Ukraine as a Democratic cause now vote for it. Trump signed the bill into law. Fifty-eight House Democrats defied their own leadership to vote yes.
Four days after the signing, President Zelensky sat down with President Trump in New York and came out saying Trump had made his “final decision”: Ukraine will get licenses to produce Patriot missiles. The missiles that stop Russian ballistic missiles before they hit Ukrainian targets.
It’s been a long time since the news from Washington was this good.
It’s also fragile. Trump promised the Patriot licenses once before, in July, and walked it back. Days after the New York meeting he wouldn’t confirm it to reporters. Nothing is locked in. Every Congressional vote of support has to be protected.
And the biggest threat to it right now isn’t coming from Ukraine’s enemies in Congress. It’s coming from a small group of people who carry the title of Ukrainian consul.
Ukrainian Intel Exposes Russia Helping Iran Target US Forces
Who they are
Ukraine’s honorary consuls in the United States are not diplomats. They are US citizens, though often of Ukrainian background. Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs gives them the title and apparently, very little oversight.
These consuls have been active in meeting with congressmen and speaking to the press to push a policy that Ukraine opposes.
Working against their own government
Ukraine’s official policy toward its citizens abroad fits in two words: come home.
In December 2024 the government created a Ministry of National Unity, and the Prime Minister said its main job would be “the strategy, programs and incentives on how to bring Ukrainians back to live and work in Ukraine.” That work continues today inside the Ministry of Social Policy. Housing help. Jobs. Services for people coming back.
And people are coming back. According to the International Organization for Migration, over 1 million Ukrainians have returned home from abroad since the full-scale invasion. From Poland, from Germany, from the Czech Republic. Under the drones. Because the country needs them.
Meanwhile some of Ukraine’s consuls in the US are lobbying the American government to keep Ukrainians here permanently, and to bring more.
That isn’t Ukraine’s policy. It’s the opposite. So who are they working for?
For the consuls who practice immigration law, the answer isn’t complicated. It’s their business.
What they’re doing with the title
One consul is an immigration lawyer. At a political event for a Republican congressman who had just taken a hard vote to send weapons to Ukraine, she didn’t thank him. She lectured him about immigration and compared the President of the United States to Nazi Germany. Then asked him to review some cases she was working on.
Another consul, a former Republican political operative, asked me to help him reach Senator. Not about air defense. Not about long-range strikes. About one Ukrainian truck driver ICE had picked up. This summer he went to an American newspaper, speaking as Ukraine’s consul, and accused a state highway patrol and ICE of “using deception” to arrest Ukrainian truckers. The highway patrol program belongs to a Republican governor. The Department of Homeland Security is now run by the consul’s own former boss.
Maybe some of those drivers were treated unfairly. Their lawyers can argue that in court. But think about who read that story. A Republican governor and a Republican cabinet secretary opened their home-state paper and found the representative of Ukraine saying their people lie.
What they want
This month the American Coalition for Ukraine sent a policy sheet to Congress titled “Protecting Displaced Ukrainians in the United States.” A group of Ukrainian-American immigration lawyers wrote the document and their organization is co-sponsor of the program. It counts 510,000 Ukrainians living here on temporary status and asks Washington to keep all of them. No exception.
Many Ukrainians were given temporary residency in America in 2022. The lawyers want it extended and made permanent, meaning the temporary refugees never return to Ukraine but become US citizens.
Then it asks for more. Reopen the Uniting for Ukraine program to more new arrivals.
Why this is so dangerous
Ukrainians should understand one thing about American politics. Donald Trump won the presidency twice on one issue above all others: immigration. For a Republican, this is not a policy detail. It is the core of his party.
So when Ukraine’s representatives spend a meeting on green cards, a Republican hears that Ukraine’s priority is not the war. It’s getting its people into America. And when someone speaking for Ukraine compares his President to the Nazis, he stops taking the calls.
This will not win Democrats votes to help Ukraine either. Democrats introduced the Ukrainian Adjustment Act earlier this year. Thirty-two Democrats co-sponsored the bill which was a vote to support Ukrainian refugees as well as political stance against President Trump. Unfortunately, when it came time to vote for the Russian sanctions bill, only 13 of those Democrats were willing to support Ukraine.
Voting against Trump on immigration is an easy vote for a Democrat. Voting for sanctions or weapons is hard. Many representatives are choosing to show their support for Ukraine by supporting refugees. The consuls are helping them do that.
What needs to happen
To the Ministry of Foreign Affairs: An honorary consul speaks in Ukraine’s name. Consuls who use that title to fight against American immigration policy instead of for Ukrainian defense should be removed or silenced. No more meetings with congressmen to talk about their legal cases. No more statements to the press. The lack of an ambassador in Washington is not helping.
To the Government of Ukraine: Say it publicly. Ukraine’s lobbying the United States government to grant Ukrainians refugees permanent residency is a disaster for Ukraine-US relations.
To Ukrainians and Ukrainian-Americans: Write to the American Coalition for Ukraine. Thank them for their work on sanctions. Then ask them to stop lobbying the United States government for more immigration and to take their name off the immigration sheet. One ask. Weapons.
None of this is against the refugees. My family helped resettle more than a dozen Ukrainians in America. The best way to help the refugees is to help Ukraine win the war. Advocating for the refugees is the opposite of advocating for Ukraine. If you want to push for immigration reform, join an immigration advocacy group, not a Ukrainian group.
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act is a symbol of bi-partisan support for Ukraine and stepping stone to stronger American-Ukraine relations. Don’t let Ukraine’s own consuls tear it down.

Dubai-Tel Aviv flight diverts to Saudi Arabia after suspected hijacking attempt
A commercial flight carrying around 180 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday following a suspected hijacking attempt by one of the pilots.
The aircraft, operated by Emirati airline Flydubai, transmitted an emergency alert two hours into the flight when it plummeted 14,000 feet in less than a minute.
The incident occurred over the Jordan-Saudi border after the copilot, an Omani national, stabbed the captain and attempted to crash the plane, according to Hebrew media reports.
Several Israeli passengers helped the Emirati captain subdue the attacker and prevent the aircraft from crashing.
Israeli fighter jets were scrambled to intercept the aircraft, which safely landed in Tabuk.
Israeli officials are reportedly investigating the incident as a potential terror attack, though the motive remains unclear.
"This morning there was an extremely serious security incident," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a video statement from his office.
"The pilot who carried out the stabbing was arrested and is currently being questioned by the Saudi authorities," he said.
Videos of the injured pilot were circulated on social media while passengers described scenes of chaos and panic as the aircraft descended.
"There were screams. Stabbings, stabbings, blood, blood," a passenger named Adam told Israel's Channel 13 News.
"Several Israeli guys took control of the situation, they managed to stabilise the aircraft," he said.
Tabuk Airport said the Emirati captain and the co-pilot were injured and were receiving treatment in hospital.
Another passenger, Miryam Shira Ohayon, said the co-pilot tried to crash the plane and kill everyone on board.
"The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane," AFP quoted her as telling reporters by speakerphone.
Flydubai said the aircraft “experienced an incident while en route”, adding that it landed safely at Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk airport and that all passengers were safe and accounted for.
"The safety and wellbeing of our passengers and crew remain our highest priority," the statement read. "Further updates will be issued as additional confirmed details become available."
A Flydubai plane landed in Tabuk on Wednesday afternoon to take the stranded passengers to Tel Aviv. Some reportedly refused to board the aircraft and demanded rescue by an Israeli airline.
Israeli transport minister Miri Regev demanded the suspension of all Flydubai flights and asked the Civil Aviation Authority to investigate whether the UAE violated its agreement with Israel. Pentagon announces military withdrawal from Iraq complete
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:46:00 UTC
18:46:00 KST

The U.S. military announced Wednesday it has completed its withdrawal from Iraq – ending a 12-year mission to fight the Daesh terrorist group – after The last troops departed a northern air base under an agreement between Baghdad and Washington.
The withdrawal, agreed on two years ago, comes against the backdrop of the ongoing war between the United States and Iran that has also sometimes spilled over into Iraq, with Iran-backed militias firing on U.S. troops and the U.S. striking the groups' strongholds.
Baghdad touted the end of the U.S. mission as a sign of the country's increasing strength and sovereignty.
The withdrawal was also celebrated by Iran-backed groups but raised concerns among some other Iraqis, particularly in the northern semi-autonomous region. Meanwhile, questions loom around the future of the Iraqi militias, which the Baghdad government has sought – with little success so far – to disarm.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement that U.S. troops and equipment had completed an "orderly departure" from the air base in Erbil, in northern Iraq's Kurdish-majority region.
"This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS (Daesh) as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region," he said. "It also marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship."
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi presided over the handover ceremony and described the U.S. withdrawal as the beginning of a "new phase, one defined by Iraq’s sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, the unity of its decision-making and balanced partnerships with its friends."
He said Iraqi security forces will continue the fight against Daesh and the government will ensure that non-state groups no longer hold weapons.
U.S. troops invaded Iraq in 2003 to topple Saddam Hussein. They departed in 2011, but three years later, Iraqi authorities invited a smaller U.S.-led mission to fight Daesh, which had rampaged across Iraq, seizing large swaths of territory.
With the terrorist group reduced to scattered sleeper cells, Washington and Baghdad agreed in 2024 to wind the mission down.
U.S. troops pulled out of bases in most areas of Iraq last year but maintained a small presence of hundreds of troops in the semi-autonomous northern Kurdish region.
Bases there have regularly come under attack since the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran on Feb. 28. Iran-backed Iraqi militias also have coordinated with Yemen’s Houthi rebels to attack Saudi Arabia.
The Iraqi government initially linked the Sept. 30 deadline for U.S. withdrawal to the disarmament of non-state armed groups by that date.
While a handful of less-influential militias have agreed to turn over their weapons, powerful groups close to Iran rejected the prospect or set conditions for disarming that the government would be unlikely to meet.
Al-Zaidi has since walked back the deadline. He told The New York Times earlier this month that the deadline for militia disarmament has been pushed to June 2027.
The effects of the U.S. withdrawal may not be immediately visible, particularly since the U.S. military presence had already been scaled down. But officials in northern Iraq have expressed anxiety about the departure and particularly about the removal of U.S. air defense systems.
The Kurdish authorities said that the region had faced more than 1,000 drone and ballistic-missile attacks during the recent U.S.-Iran conflict.
"The departure of the United States from the ... Region under these complex regional circumstances, without the provision of a defense system, is a matter of concern," the statement said.
Iran-allied groups in Iraq, meanwhile, have celebrated the U.S. withdrawal.
"The expulsion of the occupation forces, defeated, from the land of Iraq is the beginning of full sovereignty," Abu Mujahid al-Assaf, a security official with the powerful Kataib Hezbollah militia, said in a statement.
He added a warning to al-Zaidi and his government not to carry out American plans, threatening that "any government that does not work for the benefit of the people will be overthrown by all means."

The Voice of Armenia: 100 years of public broadcasting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:45:48 UTC
18:45:48 KST

Wednesday 30 September 2026 12:16
Wednesday, 30 September 2026, 12:16
PHOTO Armenian Public Radio
Font size
The Bulgarian National Radio (BNR) and the Public Radio of Armenia are partners within the European Broadcasting Union (EBU). This year, our Armenian colleagues are celebrating the 100th anniversary of their broadcasting service. To mark the occasion, they have sent the foreign-language services of Radio Bulgaria a special presentation on the history of the broadcaster and its relationship with its audience from 1926 to the present day.
Listen!
If you look at a world map or globe today, you will hardly notice Armenia. Among the world's 194 countries, we rank 138th in terms of area, covering just under 30,000 square kilometres. Only when you zoom in does Armenia come into view. Zoom in further and you can make out a country whose outline resembles the profile of a woman's face. Perhaps that is why we Armenians call our country "Mother Armenia".
But today's conversation is not about Armenia or its historical past. We would like to talk about an event that took place exactly 100 years ago, on 1 September 1926. On that day, the Armenian Radio addressed its listeners over the airwaves for the first time. The historic words were: "Listen! Listen! This is the Yerevan Radio Broadcasting Station speaking."
Regular broadcasts eventually began on 15 June 1927.
From 1929 onwards, programmes were presented for the first time by professional radio announcers.
Today, practically anyone with a smartphone and an internet connection can start a live broadcast from virtually anywhere. Decades ago, however, this was an insurmountable technical challenge even for many specialised institutions equipped with dedicated technology, let alone for individuals.
On 1 May 1934, the editorial team responsible for social and political programmes organised the first-ever live radio report from Yerevan's Lenin Square, today's Republic Square. It was presented by radio announcer Yegishe Hovhannisyan.
The first live sports broadcast took place on 15 September 1937 at Yerevan's Republican Stadium, during a football match between Spartak Yerevan and Dynamo Moscow.
The tragic fate of the Armenian people scattered us Armenians across the world. The time came when Armenian Radio decided to produce and broadcast programmes for our compatriots living abroad as well.
In 1947, the Armenian Radio began preparing programmes for the diaspora. The first such programme was broadcast on 10 September 1947 at 7 p.m. And the first words were: "This is Yerevan, this is Yerevan..."
Yerevan, Armenia
PHOTO Reuters
Alongside all this, public broadcasting has another fundamental mission: preserving our audio heritage. Whether it is called an archive, a phonotheque, or a golden collection, the essence remains the same: safeguarding Armenia's national cultural treasures and passing them on to future generations.
Today, the Amernian Radio phonotheque contains 102,422 audio tapes with a total duration of 12,324 hours. Naturally, these recordings have been digitised, so they can no longer be lost, erased, destroyed by fire or simply disappear. They include music recordings, radio dramas, speeches by prominent figures, addresses and broadcasts, and by no means only in Armenian or exclusively related to Armenia. We also preserve recordings in the languages of many other peoples.
The Public Radio of Armenia has a rich heritage and a wealth of wonderful stories born out of collaborations with prominent Armenian writers, composers and artists.
Another distinctive feature of our broadcaster is that we have four resident musical ensembles. The oldest of them, the Aram Merangulian Honoured Ensemble of Folk Instruments, is also celebrating its 100th anniversary this year. They are joined by the Estrada Symphony Orchestra, the Sayat-Nova Ashugh Ensemble and the Arevik Children's Music Ensemble.
It was precisely the Arevik ensemble that represented Armenia at the Junior Eurovision Song Contest for the first time in 2007, finishing in second place. In 2021, Armenia's Junior Eurovision representative, Maléna, won the competition, and as a result, the following year's contest, in 2022, was held in Armenia.
Incidentally, Armenia also hosted the international Eurovision Young Musicians competition this year, in 2026.
Radio today is no longer simply radio. It is a multimedia platform, a major media holding comprising seven radio programmes, dozens of large and small recording studios, a website and video productions. The website of Radio Armenia is available in twelve languages and features both the languages of Armenia's national minorities and those of the countries in the region.
Today, the Public Radio of Armenia is a full member of the European Broadcasting Union. On this occasion, we would also like to congratulate our four partner broadcasters from Ireland, Croatia, Lithuania and Finland, which are likewise celebrating their centenaries this year.
Wherever you live, whoever you may be, if you ever find yourself in Yerevan, come and visit the Public Radio of Armenia. Right here at the entrance, you will be greeted by our singing statue, from which beautiful, sophisticated Armenian music can be heard every day. Our building, constructed in 1956 and still serving radio and the public to this day, is known as "Radiotun", the Radio House. This is our home. The home of our national culture, our music, literature, spirit and spoken word."
PHOTO Armenian Public Radio
On the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Armenian Radio, we wish our colleagues continued success in their dedicated efforts to promote and preserve the cultural wealth of their country!
Edited by R. Petkova

AI firms set sights on data from bankrupt companies

Bahattin Gonultas and Emir Yildirim
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Artificial intelligence (AI) companies are on the lookout for large data sets from bankrupt firms to train their models, resulting in a new commercial market and a data security crisis in the global tech sector.
US tech giant Google and AI startup Micro1 submitted multimillion-dollar bids to buy internal communications and passenger data from Spirit Airlines, which had filed for bankruptcy.
Suppliers and workers are concerned about the potential leak of sensitive information.
Google bid $10 million for the data set, while Micro1 is willing to pay $12.5 million.
Spirit Airlines sold 27 aging Airbus aircraft for $668 million on Sept. 25 amid financial difficulties.
Some 97.5 million passenger records collected since 1992 are on the sales list, according to court documents filed with the New York Bankruptcy Court.
The database contains 13.7 million email addresses, loyalty program information and data from partner firms.
The package also includes personnel files for more than 175,000 workers and 1.5 million internal communications extracted from various channels like email and Microsoft Teams.
The court will approve the sale at a hearing expected to take place on Wednesday.
Companies selling their data while filing for bankruptcy has become a global business model.
Commercial information like financial data is not covered by data protection laws, leaving the entire process to be governed by contractual agreements, legal experts say.

====================================================================================================

No, Macron isn't planning to trigger a war with Russia to stay in power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:34:37 UTC
18:34:37 KST

Allegations are circulating online that Macron will put France at war with Russia to postpone elections and stay in power as his second consecutive term comes to an end. However, the country's constitution makes this unfeasible in many ways.
For months now, European leaders and NATO have been raising alarms over a sharp rise in Russian hybrid threats with increasing urgency, calls that have been echoed by French President Emmanuel Macron.
A slew of social media users, however, are alleging he is not expressing his concerns for security purposes, but for his own benefit.
As French presidents cannot serve more than two consecutive terms, Macron will have to hand over the reins of power to his successor following the 2027 presidential election, set to take place next spring.
For this reason, according to several social media posts, Macron is exaggerating the threat and drawing France further into the war between Ukraine and Russia, as a means to justify a potential war with Moscow. The end goal? To cancel or postpone these elections and so stay in power, they claim.
Such posts have garnered thousands of views, and appear to have been fuelled by a meeting that Macron held with presidential hopefuls and party leaders in mid-September to brief them on the current security challenges facing France.
However, this is an unlikely and complicated strategy to implement. To understand why, The Cube, Euronews' verification team, spoke with French constitutional experts.
President cannot declare war
The main factor that pours cold water on these claims is the fact that the president's powers are limited by the constitution. Specifically, it says that they cannot unilaterally declare war.
"The constitution states that the president is the head of the armed forces," Guillaume Tusseau, constitutional law professor at the Sciences Po Law School, told The Cube. "But in this matter, he has to share his power with the government because the army is placed at the disposal of the government and not of the president of the republic."
"Based on Article 35 of the constitution, only parliament can authorise an armed intervention by French armed forces, and the government has to present that to parliament," he added. "So it's not the decision [that can be] formally [made by] the president."
Should a president decide to launch a war without consultation, this would constitute a violation of the constitution, which in turn could trigger impeachment proceedings.
Even if, for example, a country wages a war against France, the constitution still does not stipulate that this would automatically influence the timing of an election.
"The postponing of elections is not automatic at all [in case of a war], and my hunch is that it will be very difficult to [influence the timing]," Tusseau said.
This is because the timeline for elections to take place is clearly detailed in Article 7 of the constitution, which states that elections must be held "no fewer than 20 days and no more than 35 days before" the current president's term ends.
Tusseau noted that the constitution only allows for a limited postponement if one of the candidates dies or is incapacitated a few days before the first round, or between the first and second round.
Additionally, if France were directly under attack, elections could be postponed to guarantee the safety of voters.
"But if we read the constitution, nothing in it allows the president to postpone the elections [for the reasons claimed on social media]," Tusseau said.
Activating Article 16?
One key argument put forward by proponents of the original theory is that Macron would support being at war, as they claim this would allow him to use Article 16 of the constitution, and supposedly allow him to decide to stay in office as he sees fit.
Article 16 does grant the president exceptional powers if the country's institutions, independence and the integrity of its territory or the fulfilment of its international commitments are threatened "in a serious and immediate manner."
However, this still requires consultation with the prime minister, presidents of the assemblies and the Constitutional Council.
Baptiste Charvin, a constitutional lawyer who wrote his comparative law thesis on combating disinformation, explained that this is not the first time people have alluded to the threat of activating Article 16.
"As far as I can recall, it was invoked just before Macron took to the stage to announce the lockdown in 2020, and in 2022 following the outbreak of war in Ukraine," he said.
"The article in question seems to give rise to several misconceptions, and is mainly used to attack the executive, which is often accused of harbouring dictatorial ambitions," he added. "All the more so given that Macron cannot stand for a third term in 2027."
Charvin stressed that a "very high threshold of public calamity" must be reached for Article 16 to be activated. This condition was added during a constitutional amendment, specifically to limit abuses.
Here, he referred to former President Charles de Gaulle activating Article 16 in 1961 to handle the Algiers putsch, a military coup d'état staged by renegade French generals in Algeria.
Tusseau noted a caveat to activating Article 16: it requires the president to protect constitutional values, not amend the constitution.
"The philosophy of the device is that the president can only take legislative and administrative measures, but not constitutional ones, because the constitution establishes the timeframe for elections," he said. "Saying that the president could amend the constitution based on Article 16 is highly dubious for the vast majority of constitutional scholars."
Tusseau added that, while there is no empirical evidence that Macron might be brooding over plans to launch a war and postpone elections, considerations should be made regarding the strength of institutions to protect against abuse.
"Constitutional scholars and citizens must realise that there are weaknesses in our institutions, and, as we saw in Poland, in Hungary, in several constitutional countries, it's always possible to abuse constitutional devices despite careful drafting," he said.

EU considers opening its single market to candidate countries – Politico
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:34:00 EEST
18:34:00 KST

EU considers opening its single market to candidate countries – Politico
Politico has learned that EU candidate countries will be offered unprecedented "gradual integration" into the EU's single market, including frictionless trade and access to research programmes while their applications are being assessed.
Source: a draft European Commission proposal obtained by Politico, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Under the plan, the EU would open its market to candidate countries provided they agree to stand with the EU against hostile states and industrial competitors.
Quote: "Earlier integration would open opportunities for Union businesses, strengthen European value chains and reduce strategic dependencies. The Commission will identify where verified regulatory alignment and enforcement capacity allow deeper participation in research, innovation and industrial cooperation, and wider market access. Priority should go to opportunities that advance accession preparations and meet shared economic and strategic needs."
Details: The review, prepared under the leadership of Alexandre Adam, chief adviser to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, would radically change the EU's approach to the countries in the region. At present, almost all the economic benefits of closer cooperation are reserved for EU members, but no new country has joined the EU since Croatia in 2013.
As part of the review, Ukraine, Moldova, Albania and Montenegro will be offered "roadmaps" designed to accelerate the accession process in the coming years. In other countries, such as North Macedonia, Kosovo, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia and Türkiye, the process is dragging on. Concerns are growing that they could move away from the EU or closer to Russia or China.
Under the Commission's plan, candidate countries will receive economic benefits in proportion to their support for the EU's foreign policy objectives. Access to the single market will also depend on whether they refrain from transferring key technologies to hostile states and trade competitors.
"As industrial and market integration deepens, participation in sensitive sectors must be accompanied by cooperation on investment screening, export controls, sanctions implementation and the protection of sensitive technologies," the review document says.
It notes that market access should take into account strategic alignment, critical dependencies and the ability to manage risks to infrastructure and supply chains.
According to the review, the ultimate goal for candidate countries should be full EU membership, and this period "should be put to full strategic use to both prepare the Union for a larger membership and deepen gradual integration in areas of mutual interest".
Background:
- The European Commission has postponed until 6 October the presentation of its assessment of how future EU enlargement will affect the EU's key policies and what changes the EU itself may need to accept new member states.
- European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos previously outlined four areas for changes to the EU enlargement process: internal reforms of the EU, strengthened democratic safeguards, gradual integration and transitional measures.

Is US President Donald Trump right to rename AI as 'Super Intelligence'?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:33:00 UTC
18:33:00 KST

'Super Intelligence': Is Trump right to rename AI?
September 30, 2026
What's with Donald Trump and renaming things? First, the Gulf of Mexico became the Gulf of America — in US federal documents, if not globally. Then Lake Ontario became Lake America. Now he wants to rebrand the defining technology of our time: artificial intelligence (AI).
Earlier this month, the US president claimed on his Truth Social platform that the term artificial intelligence is "inaccurate" and "ineloquent." He said "superior," "extreme," or "supreme" intelligence were better alternatives.
In a three-day social media poll, Trump fans chose "Super Intelligence" (SI) by about 65% to 35% (for Superior Intelligence), allowing him to announce at the United Nations General Assembly last week that US federal documents would use his new term going forward.
'AI is not superintelligence'
The tech industry has yet to adopt the phrase, however, while academics warn that superintelligence is a future term for when technology can beat humans across the board. They say the current AI models are years away from that milestone.
"Most AI is not superintelligence — it's just different intelligence," Pedro Domingos, a computer science professor from the University of Washington, told DW. "AI is doing different things from what humans do, so calling it superintelligence is misleading."
Computer scientists and mathematicians coined the name "artificial intelligence" in 1956 at a summer workshop at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire. "Artificial" simply meant made by humans, as opposed to natural human intelligence.
Not all experts agreed with the name. In the book "Machines Who Think," historian Pamela McCorduck cited AI pioneer Arthur Samuel, who said the term "makes you think there's something kind of phony about this."
Despite this, the name artificial intelligence has stuck for 70 years. Critics say changing it now will not quieten the many fears around AI, including job losses, human obsolescence or machines slipping out of our control.
Rebrand won't quell AI fears
"The name change is fostering these kinds of fears: 'Oh, this is superintelligence and it's going to make humans obsolete, turn on us and take our jobs'," warned Domingos. "If you want to maximize the backlash against AI, rename it Superior Intelligence."
Those public fears are growing fast. In a Public First poll for Politico earlier this month, about half of respondents in six countries — the United States, Canada, France, Spain, Germany and the United Kingdom — backed a pause in further AI development to reduce the risk that the new tech could destroy humanity.
A separate CNN/SSRS poll found nearly nine in 10 Americans are more concerned than excited about AI surpassing human intelligence.
Those concerns have already reached the US Congress. Last week, Vermont's independent Senator Bernie Sanders co-introduced a bill to "permanently ban the development of artificial superintelligence" that humans cannot control.
The legislation also calls for a pause on advanced AI development until federal testing and oversight are in place.
A branding gift to help the AI boom?
Trump's new term could, however, suit the major US AI players, who are keen to play up their advanced models. Those systems already outperform humans on many specialized tasks and until recently were far ahead of China.
Yet both Anthropic, the firm behind the Claude model, and OpenAI, which created ChatGPT, have pushed back plans to go public. Some market watchers blamed the delays on recent scares where AI models hacked into computer systems or ran tasks they were not meant to.ran tasks they were not meant to.
With Chinese models closing much of the quality gap with much less computing power, US labs may still appreciate the branding that helps confirm they are still leading the AI race. Global spending on AI is expected to surpass $1 trillion (€880 billion), according to Goldman Sachs research.
"The [US] labs have every interest in calling it super, hyper, superior and whatnot intelligence, because it's playing up their capabilities. It's like just marketing," said Domingos, the author of the 2015 book "The Master Algorithm."
Superintelligence remains a moving target
While the current AI models keep improving and can already run many tasks on their own, the next step that many labs discuss is AI systems that improve themselves. That's called recursive self-improvement or RSI.
On that journey, Elon Musk has predicted that AI learning could be automated, with limited human input, by the end of this year or 2027. OpenAI thinks it could take a year longer. But even then, AI systems won't be fully recursive.
Jürgen Schmidhuber, a German computer scientist based in Switzerland, argued in a blog post earlier this month that "full RSI, however, will require not just self-improving [AI] software but self-improving hardware in the physical world."
In other words, to reach superintelligence or RSI, tech companies would have to produce chips, humanoid robots and even replace entire factories without human input.
While AI is already speeding up chip design, it cannot yet run the foundry alone. Self-improving machines, with no human input, are likely still decades away.
Beyond the science of machine learning, politics will likely play a bigger role in whether Super Intelligence sticks. While Trump claimed Chinese President Xi Jinping liked the name, China has yet to show any signs of changing from AI.
At a tech summit on Tuesday with key industry leaders, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government bodies and agencies to start using the term SI. While some Big Tech leaders have adopted it, experts say the new term is unlikely to catch on.
"Knowing the political orientation of most people in the [AI] field, they're more likely to have the opposite reaction, which is: 'To hell with you. We're going to call it artificial intelligence even more than before'," Domingos said.

On 3 August some residents of Ramallah were holding a small party for a friend’s son who had recently graduated from high school. The younger ones were dancing in the middle of the hall while the older guests tried to chat over the music. Then the news came in that the Hamayel brothers had been arrested by the Israeli army.
The Hamayels live in a village near Ramallah. Its residents and those of other villages nearby are regularly attacked, and settlers from several ‘outposts’ – one only recently established, a few hundred metres from the brothers’ farm – prevent them from accessing ever-growing areas of their olive and almond groves, springs, water cisterns and grazing lands.
‘Outposts’ are small Israeli settlements in the Palestinian territories, occupied since 1967, which have been established on private or public land without formal approval from the Israeli planning authorities, yet receive logistical support – openly, unofficially or covertly – from state bodies as well as private donors. The drive to establish these outposts has gained considerable momentum since the late 1990s, aiming to hinder the transfer of more West Bank territory to the Palestinian civil authority. According to the Peace Now website (peacenow.org) there are now 390 outposts, compared to 146 settlements officially founded since 1967. As many as 249 have been established in the last four years.
The day before the brothers’ arrest, around a hundred sheep were stolen from one of the Hamayel family’s farms. Fearing that there would be more thefts, the brothers, their father and their brother-in-law returned to the farm to collect cans of olive oil and a few essentials. Immediately, some Israeli Jews, perhaps residents of a nearby outpost, appeared, photographed them and called in soldiers, who arrested the brothers, blindfolded and handcuffed them, and took them away.

Some analyses are like self-portraits: their implicit assumptions reveal most about their authors. This is true of many Western interpretations of what China hopes to get out of the war between the US and Iran. Two experts writing in Foreign Affairs expressed the view that Beijing is ‘keen to exploit the war to sap US power, gain intelligence on US military systems, and erode the US-led order’. Academic Phillips O’Brien asked, ‘Is China going in for the kill?’ and in Le Parisien journalist François Lenglet set out why ‘Beijing will win the Iran war’.
Yet there’s nothing to suggest that the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) is obsessed with the supposed ambition of supplanting US hegemony. Despite alarmist talk of a geopolitical ‘great replacement’, all the evidence suggests that Beijing is, in fact, more a victim than a cause of the erosion of the ‘US-led order’, an order from which it has greatly benefited.
A form of Chinese imperialism may well exist, but it’s less immediately recognisable than the kind that alarms Western media and politicians: it’s not a desire to see China prevail, but a belief that US supremacy is preferable to chaos. Such an unusual – and temporary – geopolitical inclination would lead Beijing to favour the US retaining its dominance, provided it does not cause too great an upset to the global balances it long guaranteed, or hamper China’s own development.
It’s highly likely that China is pleased that the US failed to secure its promised lightning victory over Iran. Now, he predicted, ‘the Russians will gradually react quite adversely and it will affect their policies.’ By 1998 Kennan, the first director of policy planning at the State Department and author of an important article in Foreign Affairs recommending that the US confront the Russians with ‘unalterable counterforce at every point where they show signs of encroaching upon the interest of a peaceful and stable world’. had come to believe that the West, having won the cold war, was squandering the possibility of that peaceful and stable world through its aggressive posture.
‘I was particularly bothered by the references to Russia as a country dying to attack Western Europe,’ he told Thomas L Friedman. ‘Don’t people understand? Our differences in the cold war were with the Soviet Communist regime. And now we are turning our backs on the very people who mounted the greatest bloodless revolution in history to remove that Soviet regime’.
Kennan’s warning went unheeded. And, as he had foreseen, the Russians did indeed react ‘quite adversely’ and invaded Ukraine in order, they claimed, to prevent Kyiv from joining NATO. 'Robbery of the century': Turkey freezes ex-minister's assets as fund crisis grows
Turkish prosecutors have moved to freeze the assets of a top governing party official and former minister who resigned at the weekend over allegations she profited from an investment fund crisis.
In a brief statement late Tuesday, prosecutors said they had sent "a letter concerning the freezing of all assets" of Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya and her husband, Ilyas Kaya, to "all the relevant institutions".
Turkey has been wrestling with the fallout from an investment fund scandal that erupted this month with the collapse of what officials have called a "Ponzi-like" scheme.
Following allegations by Turkey's main opposition Yeni Parti that she and her husband made millions trading in such shares, Kaya, the deputy head of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's AKP party, said late Saturday she was resigning.
While admitting nothing, Kaya, who was Turkey's family minister from 2016 to 2018, said she was taking "political responsibility" to ensure that any investigation could be conducted "independently, impartially".
At a news conference earlier Saturday, a Yeni spokesman, Gokhan Gunaydin, said the party was seeking clarification over claims that Kaya invested 63 million lira ($1.3 million) in shares in April and sold them in September, earning a profit of around 1.3 billion lira ($26.5 million).
He also said her husband had allegedly invested 100 million lira and earned back 826 million lira, collectively netting the pair an alleged profit of nearly 2.2 billion lira ($45 million).
Gunaydin said it was "clear" Kaya had received insider information and pledged that the party would unveil more names this week.
'Robbery of the century'
The scandal is expected to dominate the coming agenda in parliament, which formally reopens on Thursday following the summer recess.
"This name is the tip of the iceberg," Yeni leader Ozgur Ozel told a party meeting on Wednesday, describing the scandal as "the robbery of the century".
On Tuesday, Erdogan held a three-hour meeting with economic aides over the fund crisis, after earlier defending his party's record.
"The AK Party is a clean party, just as its name suggests; it is a party true to its name. No one can tarnish this party's purity or stain that cleanliness," he told party cadres.
"Without looking at their own pitch-black records, they even try to give us lessons in morality and political ethics. 'Get lost', I tell them," he said of his political opponents.
The crisis erupted in mid-September when several funds said they were unable to satisfy investor redemption demands, sending Istanbul's main stock exchange tumbling.
A day later, regulators moved to address the crisis by placing into liquidation seven companies that hold 131 investment funds, whose assets are reportedly worth around $17 billion, with the Capital Markets Board (SPK) saying more than 455,000 individual investors were affected.

BUREAU uses color and translucency to reshape 44 sqm lilac apartment in lisbon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30

BUREAU uses color and translucency to reshape 44 sqm lilac apartment in lisbon
the apartment is arranged around movement, light, and everyday rituals.
A continuous circulation loop reorganizes Lilac apartment
Lilac is one of two ‘family’ apartments in Lisbon designed by BUREAU as the first homes of two ‘brothers, sisters,’ Lilac and Blue. At 44 sqm, the apartment explores how a compact floor area can accommodate everyday routines, objects, and different ways of living. The layout places limited emphasis on privacy, allowing multiple activities to coexist while giving each space its own function and flexibility.
The redesign turns circulation into usable space. The former entrance hall becomes a functional kitchen, while the existing interior bedroom at the center of the apartment is converted into wet areas. A continuous passage wraps around this core, connecting the rooms through four symmetrical openings and reopening routes and light paths that had been closed by previous alterations. The existing structural compartmentalization is retained, while the new circulation creates a more fluid connection between the spaces.
Color, reflection, and translucency define the interior design
At the center, a single countertop serves both sides of the core, connecting the kitchen and bathroom and bringing two typically separate domestic functions into closer proximity. The apartment’s new openings use translucent or mirrored materials, adding light, reflection, and visual depth to the compact interior.
The project considers the apartment as a setting for different domestic scenarios, drawing a parallel with the fluidity of space in Jean-Luc Godard’s 1963 film Le Mépris. White and color distinguish spaces and characters, while partitions and openings shape movement and relationships between them.
Within its 44 sqm footprint, Lilac, conceived by architectural studio BUREAU, accommodates the basic elements of domestic life through a layout shaped around movement, light, objects, and everyday rituals. Its compact scale becomes a framework for considering what is essential to a home.

name: Lilac
architect: BUREAU | @bureau_architects
lead architects: Daniel Zamarbide | @daniel_zamarbide, Carine Pimenta, Galliane Zamarbide
location: Lisbon, Portugal
area: 44 sqm
photographer: Francisco Nogueira | @francisconogueira

Moscow issues warning to NATO over Russian exclave
Increased NATO military exercises near Russia’s Kaliningrad Region and aggressive rhetoric from members of the US-led bloc are raising the risk of a direct armed conflict, Moscow has warned.
Russia has sent NATO a warning stressing its determination to protect the Russian exclave in the Baltic region “with its entire available arsenal,” according to a statement published on Monday by the Russian Embassy in Belgium, which hosts the bloc’s headquarters.
The message alluded to remarks made earlier this month by Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, who said there are “hardly any troops” in Kaliningrad Region and urged NATO to increase its military posture near Russia’s borders so that Moscow would be “uncertain of what we will do.”
NATO spokesperson Allison Hart confirmed receiving the Russian message and accused Moscow of irresponsible rhetoric.
”We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric,” she said.
Western officials have frequently described Russian statements invoking its nuclear deterrent as “blackmail,” while presenting NATO’s own nuclear-sharing arrangements as a pillar of collective defense.
France has offered to discuss the possible deployment of its nuclear weapons in other European NATO countries, arguing that this could reduce the bloc’s dependence on the US. Under NATO’s existing nuclear-sharing arrangements, American nuclear bombs are stored in several European countries, while personnel from non-nuclear member states train for missions involving their potential use.
Russia has repeatedly rejected Western claims that it intends to attack NATO before the end of the decade, describing such warnings as warmongering aimed at persuading voters to support sharply higher military spending.
Moscow, in turn, views NATO’s military preparations as potentially paving the way for an attack on Russia. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has repeatedly warned that any such conflict would be extremely brief, implying that Moscow could resort to nuclear weapons.
The Russian Embassy in Ireland used more direct language, saying on Tuesday that Moscow is prepared to use nuclear weapons in response to an attempted NATO blockade of Kaliningrad Region and may consider pre-emptive military action in such a crisis.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday it was “natural for our diplomats to try and remind hotheads in Europe about our doctrinal documents,” in response to the rhetoric coming from Poland and other nations.

Ensuring energy supply is critical as the cold winter months approach. Russian strikes on the sector last year cut light and heating as temperatures plunged to as low as -20C.
Russia hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure in a wave of deadly drone and missile strikes on Wednesday, prompting an urgent call for contingencies as freezing winter approaches.
Kyiv said it was the opening attack in Russia's inevitable campaign to try to knock out heating and electricity supplies in the capital ahead of winter, a tactic Moscow has deployed throughout the four-and-a-half-year war.
At least four people were killed in and around Kyiv, including a young child found under the rubble of a demolished residential building, after another night of continuous air raid red alerts and repeated blasts.
Sirens screamed across the city warning people to take cover in basement shelters and metro stations from ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as high-speed attack drones in the skies above.
In Moscow, Russia's defence ministry said it had conducted "a massive missile and drone strike" on Kyiv and the surrounding region that targeted the power infrastructure.
Ukraine's main energy provider DTEK confirmed that the grid was damaged and supplies were affected to 8,000 households. Engineers got the power back on, it said, but called it "another difficult night for the capital."
Ensuring energy supply in Ukraine is critical as months of bitter cold approach.
Russian strikes on the sector last year cut light and heating as temperatures plunged to as low as -20C.
The prospect of a repeat has left many in the city considering whether to stay and calls for the vulnerable and disabled to relocate.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said water supplies had also been cut and "critical infrastructure" was also hit in attacks across the country.
Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky indicated that the attacks were the start of a new Russian winter campaign against the energy sector.
"Since the summer, there has practically not been a single day when the enemy has not attacked our energy infrastructure," he wrote on Telegram.

Back-up power

"Local authorities must check the readiness of back-up power systems for critical facilities in communities and complete all work on their installation and connection as quickly as possible," Koretsky said.
The International Criminal Court (ICC) in 2024 issued arrest warrants for Russia's then military leaders over attacks on Ukraine's energy grid, saying they constituted a war crime that was causing "excessive harm" to civilians.
Wednesday's strikes hit residential buildings and businesses, sparking fires and widespread damage to property and cars, the authorities said.
Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said a driver at a local utility firm was killed when a warehouse was hit, while two others were killed elsewhere.
The emergency services said a child was found dead under the rubble of a residential building that was destroyed in the wider Kyiv region.
Russia has been deploying newer jet-powered drones that move faster and are harder to intercept than the traditional models, which are based on Iranian Shaheds.
Zelenskyy has repeatedly appealed to Ukraine's allies for more military support, including US-made interceptors to combat Russia's powerful ballistic missiles.
"Every interceptor missile truly saves lives," he wrote on X on Wednesday. "And the closer we get to winter, the more of this protection we need."
UN Secretary-General António Guterres on Tuesday said he was "alarmed" by the scale of the escalating daily attacks in Ukraine and mounting civilian casualties on both sides.
After talks between Germany's foreign minister and his Russian counterpart at the United Nations on Saturday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Russia was "not interested" in meaningful talks to end the conflict.
