MINSK, September 30. /TASS/. United Aircraft Corporation (UAC, part of Rostec) showcased models of the Il-114-300, SJ-100, MC-21-310, and Tu-214 passenger aircraft at the Innoprom. Belarus international industrial exhibition in Minsk, a TASS correspondent reported.
The corporation’s stand features, in particular, a model of the Il-114-300 regional turboprop aircraft, as well as a model of the SJ-100 short-haul airliner. Models of the MC-21-310 medium-haul aircraft and the Tu-214, which belongs to the same class, are also on display.
The MC-21 is a Russian medium-haul passenger aircraft with a capacity of up to 211 passengers that will replace the Tu-154 and Tu-204 family on the Russian market. It will also be able to serve as an alternative to foreign-made aircraft. The aircraft is expected to complete all certification procedures by mid-2027, Federal Air Transport Agency head Dmitry Yadrov said earlier.
The SJ-100 is a short-haul narrow-body aircraft. As part of import substitution efforts, it has been equipped with Russian-made PD-8 engines and domestic systems. Certification of the SJ-100 is expected in the first quarter of 2027, Yadrov said earlier.
The Tu-214 is a Russian twin-engine medium-haul passenger aircraft designed for flights of up to 4,500 kilometers.
The Innnoprom. Belarus international industrial exhibition is being held in Minsk from September 30 through October 2. TASS is the exhibition’s general information agency.

Türkiye’s trade deficit widens 22.3 pct in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:15:11 UTC
18:15:11 KST

(AA Photo)
Türkiye’s foreign trade deficit widened 22.3 percent year-on-year to $5.24 billion in August as imports grew faster than exports, the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) said on Sept. 30.
Exports rose 8.1 percent to $23.47 billion, while imports increased 10.5 percent to $28.71 billion. Exports covered 81.7 percent of imports, down from 83.5 percent a year earlier.
In the first eight months of 2026, exports rose 4 percent from a year earlier to $185 billion, while imports grew 5.3 percent to $250.79 billion. The trade gap widened 9.3 percent to $65.79 billion. Exports covered 73.8 percent of imports, down from 74.7 percent a year earlier.
Excluding energy products and non-monetary gold, the August deficit stood at $1.09 billion. Exports on this basis rose 2.7 percent to $20.83 billion, while imports increased 9.6 percent to $21.92 billion.
Adjusted for seasonal and calendar effects, exports rose 0.6 percent from July, while imports fell 1.1 percent.
Manufacturing accounted for 93.6 percent of August exports, with high-technology products making up 3.6 percent of manufacturing exports.
Intermediate goods represented 70.7 percent of August imports, followed by consumer goods at 15.5 percent and capital goods at 13.5 percent.
Germany was Türkiye’s largest export market in August at $1.76 billion, followed by the United States at $1.73 billion and the United Kingdom at $1.20 billion. Iraq and Switzerland completed the top five, which accounted for 29.2 percent of exports.
China was the largest source of imports at $4.71 billion, followed by Germany at $2.07 billion and Russia at $1.94 billion.

Unemployment rate falls to 7.8 pct in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:15:00 UTC
18:15:00 KST

Türkiye’s seasonally adjusted unemployment rate fell to 7.8 percent in August from 8.1 percent in July, while a broader measure of labor underutilization edged higher, official data showed on Sept. 30.
The number of unemployed people aged 15 and over declined by 106,000 from the previous month to 2.74 million, the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) said.
Employment rose by 136,000 to 32.51 million, lifting the employment rate by 0.1 percentage point to 48.4 percent.
The labor force increased by 29,000 to 35.25 million, while the participation rate remained unchanged at 52.5 percent.
Youth unemployment, covering people aged 15 to 24, fell by 1.1 percentage points to 13 percent. The rate stood at 9.7 percent for young men and 19.4 percent for young women.
Overall unemployment was 6.6 percent among men and 10.1 percent among women.
Despite the decline in the headline rate, the seasonally and calendar-adjusted labor underutilization rate, which includes time-related underemployment and the potential labor force as well as the unemployed, rose by 0.4 percentage points to 31 percent.
The combined rate of time-related underemployment and unemployment was 20.2 percent, while the combined rate of unemployment and the potential labor force was also 20.2 percent.
Average weekly actual working hours increased by 0.5 hours to 42.5 hours in August.

ISS director: We have prevented 'significant' number of Russian attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:04:00 UTC
18:04:00 KST

ISS director: We have prevented 'significant' number of Russian attacks
The Internal Security Service (ISS) has headed off a significant number of Russian-planned hybrid attacks inside Estonia in recent years, the authority's director general said.
Margo Palloson, head of the ISS, known in Estonia as Kapo, noted Russia's focus has shifted to defense industry companies,
The government announced Tuesday it had found the August 15 arson attack on the Milrem Robotics building in Tallinn was sabotage ordered by Russian special services.
Palloson told "Aktuaalne kaamera" this strategy aims to prevent military aid from reaching Ukraine – Milrems' THeMIS unmanned ground vehicle has been deployed to Ukraine – adding that the threat level remains high.
Are we talking about dozens of Russian attack or sabotage attempts that the ISS has managed to prevent in Estonia in one month?
I won't give an exact figure, but there are quite a significant number of them. Some of these attacks are still at preparation phase. Each attack is preceded by mapping and documenting the object. As early as these phases, if we see that individuals are coming to Estonia who are preparing for an attack, we immediately intervene in their activities. There are individuals who we have detained, deported from Estonia, or handed over to Ukraine, for instance. We use those measures that we have to hand.
So Russia's actions are still highly systematic, and not opportunistic?
Russia's actions across Europe are clearly systematic. There has certainly been a change there; while previously Russia tried to carry out more attacks against symbolic objects — we also had 10 previous attacks aimed at symbolic targets — now we are seeing the emphasis is on defense industry companies to prevent military aid from reaching Ukraine.
Did Russia's activities get significantly more active at some point? Has there been a surge?
I would instead say the level has in fact been high all the time, for the last three years. Perhaps the threat level for attacks has changed just because we are seeing more and more incidents where explosives are used. In Leipzig, we already saw a type of model where explosives were deployed from a drone. We hope that this will not get to be a frequent reality in Europe.
You mentioned that defense companies are under special focus. Does this mean that whereas cyberattacks predominated before, now it is acts of sabotage which are more acute?
Absolutely. There are currently defense industry companies in Estonia which are actual targets of attack. We highly recommend that all defense industry companies, especially those that supply anything to Ukraine, boost their cyber defense measures.
The perpetrators and henchmen you have already caught or are under surveillance — who are they? Are they ideological Putinists, or merely people from the bottom stratum in financial difficulty, or are they all of these: Professionals and complete scumbags alike?
The vast majority are purely financially motivated. It seems easy to commit acts of vandalism or set fire to an object, for money. Where they come from, these are very different segments. There are foreigners — for example, people from Latvia, Russia and Moldova have committed attacks in Estonia. We know that Russia has also tried to use people from Africa and Latin America. Essentially, anyone who enters the Schengen area can be a potential perpetrator of an attack.
So the threat level stays high?
The threat level is high and Russia may succeed with some isolated attacks. However, the ISS, the other Estonian security structures, and the Estonian state are strong enough. We can handle it, and Estonia is a safe country.

What happens if pilots clash mid-flight? Emirati law explained after flydubai plane incident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:03:38 UTC
18:03:38 KST

A flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was diverted for an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday amid initial reports of a violent confrontation between members of the flight crew.
International reports confirmed the aircraft's diversion to Saudi Arabia. However, as of Wednesday morning, neither the airline nor aviation authorities in the United Arab Emirates had officially confirmed that an altercation between the pilots was the reason for the landing, with Israeli sources stating the altercation began when a co-pilot stabbed his partner and attempted to hijack the plane.
If authorities confirm that the two pilots engaged in a physical confrontation during the flight, Dubai could treat the incident not only as an internal disciplinary matter but also as a serious aviation safety incident, potentially leading to regulatory or criminal proceedings.
UAE aviation regulations prohibit assaults, threats, or intimidation against crew members when such conduct interferes with or impairs their ability to perform their duties. Physical violence aboard an aircraft can also constitute an offense when it threatens the safety of the aircraft or those on board.
The UAE's Federal Law No. 20 of 1991, which governs civil aviation, contains separate provisions addressing offenses against aircraft.
Under Article 55, a person commits an offense against an aircraft if the person intentionally and unlawfully commits, attempts to commit, or assists in certain acts. These include an act of violence against a person aboard an aircraft in flight when that act is likely to endanger the safety of the aircraft.
The provision therefore does not mean that any physical confrontation between crew members automatically constitutes an offense under Article 55. Its application would depend on whether the circumstances met the statutory requirements, including whether the act of violence was likely to endanger the aircraft's safety.
Article 72 sets out the penalty for offenses covered by Article 55. It provides for life imprisonment or a term of imprisonment for a person who intentionally commits, conspires to commit, or attempts to commit one of the offenses listed in Article 55.
Not so black and white: Pilots will not automatically receive life in prison
Accordingly, life imprisonment is not an automatic penalty for a fight between pilots. However, if authorities determined that an intentional and unlawful act of violence aboard the aircraft met the conditions of Article 55, including that it was likely to endanger the aircraft's safety, Article 72 provides for life imprisonment or a prison term.
If the confrontation between the pilots itself led to an emergency declaration and the diversion from the planned route for a landing in Saudi Arabia, that could become a significant factor in determining whether the incident affected aviation safety.
Investigators could examine, among other factors, whether either pilot stopped performing his duties, whether control of the aircraft was compromised, whether another crew member was required to intervene, and whether the incident created a safety risk for the aircraft or its passengers.
Similar incidents elsewhere have resulted in immediate suspensions. In 2022, two Air France pilots were suspended after a physical altercation in the cockpit during a flight from Geneva to Paris. Crew members were forced to separate them, and one crew member remained in the cockpit until landing.
An even more serious incident occurred in 2009 aboard an Air India flight from Sharjah to Delhi, when pilots and crew members exchanged blows, and the confrontation spilled from the cockpit into the aircraft's galley. Two pilots and two crew members were suspended, and police opened an investigation.
If it is confirmed that Wednesday's emergency landing in Saudi Arabia was caused by a confrontation between the pilots, UAE authorities could examine the incident as both a disciplinary matter and a possible aviation safety offense. Whether Article 55 and its penalties under Article 72 apply would depend on the facts established in an investigation and, in particular, whether the alleged conduct met the law's requirement that the act of violence was likely to endanger the safety of the aircraft.

Lithuania’s Justice Ministry mounts resistance against same-sex partnership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
09:03:00 UTC
18:03:00 KST

A Lithuanian regional court has rejected the Justice Ministry’s appeal against a decision requiring the state to register the partnership of two women who married abroad, marking another legal setback for the government in cases involving same-sex couples.
The Klaipėda Regional Court on Monday upheld a lower court ruling ordering the registration of the women’s partnership. The Justice Ministry has not yet decided whether to appeal the ruling to the Supreme Court.
The case is part of a growing number of legal disputes over the recognition of same-sex partnerships in Lithuania, where the parliament, Seimas, has not adopted legislation establishing a procedure for registering partnerships.
After Lithuania’s Constitutional Court ruled that same-sex couples must have access to legal recognition of their family relationships, couples seeking to register partnerships have increasingly turned to the courts.
The Justice Ministry has appealed such rulings, arguing that people who are already married abroad should not be registered as partners in Lithuania.
Karolis Kurapka, a lawyer representing same-sex couples, said the ministry’s argument was illogical.
“They say, ‘Look, they are married, so there is no basis to recognise a partnership’,” Kurapka said. “That argument is strange, because I would fully support saying that they are married and recognising the marriage in Lithuania. But we know that, as of today, marriage is possible only between a man and a woman.”
Martynas Norbutas, a Lithuanian man who married his male partner in Belgium, has also been seeking recognition of their marriage in Lithuania. He said the couple decided to marry abroad after exhausting opportunities to marry in Lithuania.
Other same-sex couples who married abroad have similarly sought legal recognition in Lithuania.
Justice Vice Minister Kristina Zamarytė-Sakavičienė said the ministry had not yet assessed whether it would appeal the latest ruling.
“We have not assessed the prospects of the case, so there is no final decision,” she said. “But there is indeed a possibility of examining these decisions through cassation proceedings so that we have clarity on how they should be implemented.”
Kurapka said he expected the ministry to continue its legal challenge.
“I think the Justice Ministry will not back down, and we will go to the Supreme Court, which will put a clear and simple end to the matter,” he said.
The ministry previously lost an appeal concerning the registration of a partnership between two women living in Lithuania who were not married. It has appealed about 20 court decisions concerning partnership registration, according to the report.
The ministry says there is still no clear procedure for registering partnerships because the Seimas has not adopted the necessary legislation.
Vice Minister Zamarytė-Sakavičienė stressed that the Constitutional Court’s ruling does not specifically oblige the Justice Ministry to register partnerships, but rather places an obligation on the state.
“There is no statutory procedure for how a partnership should be registered,” she said. “I would just like to clarify that it is not the Justice Ministry that has been ordered to register partnerships, but the state as a whole.”
Dainius Žalimas, a liberal European Parliament member and former president of Lithuania’s Constitutional Court, said the lack of parliamentary legislation should not prevent the partnership system from functioning.
He said the rules governing civil registration are approved by the justice minister and argued that the ministry could establish a functioning procedure without waiting for new legislation.
He described the ministry’s position as “a masking of homophobia and nothing more”.
“While the parliament has no political will – and it clearly does not – people should not have to suffer because of that,” Žalimas said.
Norbutas said meaningful progress would come only when same-sex couples no longer had to go to court to have their relationships recognised.
“Progress will come when no one has to go to court,” he said. “As long as people essentially have to fight over things that are obvious, there is no real breakthrough.”
Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has previously said that other issues are higher on his list of priorities than civil partnership legislation and that neither he nor his party colleagues would be at the forefront of efforts to legalise same-sex relationships.

TIMELINE - US ends military presence in Iraq after 23 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:56:38 UTC
17:56:38 KST

Iraq on Wednesday announced the end of the US-led international coalition’s mission, marking a transition toward bilateral security relations with coalition member states, the prime minister’s security adviser said.
The announcement comes as the US completes its military withdrawal from Iraq ahead of a Sept. 30 deadline, concluding a 12-year deployment launched to support the fight against ISIS (Daesh).
The departure terminates the multinational mission launched in 2014 rather than representing the first American exit from the country. US Central Command (CENTCOM) reaffirmed the broader timeline to Anadolu while declining to elaborate on final movements.
Here is how the US military presence evolved from invasion and occupation to counterterrorism operations and the final withdrawal.
The long-term American military presence started on Oct. 16, 2002, when the US Congress passed the Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq Resolution.
It empowered the executive branch to deploy armed forces against Saddam Hussein's government over allegations of weapons of mass destruction and ties to terrorism.
On March 19, 2003, US President George W. Bush announced Operation Iraqi Freedom to "disarm Iraq, to free its people and to defend the world from grave danger."
Coalition forces entered Baghdad in April 2003, causing the collapse of the government.
US troop levels crossed 145,600 personnel that month and remained above 100,000 for several years, according to Government Accountability Office data.
American troops captured Saddam Hussein near Tikrit on Dec. 13, 2003, leading to his trial by an Iraqi tribunal and execution on Dec. 30, 2006.
Faced with escalating sectarian strife, Bush announced a strategic reinforcement known as the "surge" on Jan. 10, 2007, deploying additional brigades that raised troop levels from 131,500 in late 2006 to a wartime peak of 169,000 personnel by August 2007.
On Nov. 17, 2008, US and Iraq signed a Strategic Framework Agreement alongside a bilateral Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA), establishing a mandate for foreign units to exit.
On Dec. 14, 2008, during a joint press conference, Iraqi Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki praised the ratification, while Bush called the agreement "a major achievement" during a press conference where an Iraqi journalist threw shoes at him.
Operation Iraqi Freedom formally concluded on Aug. 31, 2010, transitioning into Operation New Dawn with a reduced number of troops tasked with advising domestic forces.
On Dec. 12, 2011, US President Barack Obama and Maliki marked the conclusion of the campaign.
US Forces-Iraq cased their organizational colors in Baghdad on Dec. 15, 2011.
While the bilateral security treaty established Dec. 31, 2011, as the legal deadline for departure, the final operational convoy of 500 soldiers and more than 100 vehicles crossed the border into Kuwait nearly two weeks early on Dec. 18, 2011.
The security environment deteriorated rapidly when ISIS swept through northern and western Iraq, seizing the major metropolis of Mosul on June 10, 2014, and capturing approximately one-third of the Iraqi territory.
Following an official request for assistance from Baghdad, Obama deployed initial assessment personnel on June 16, 2014, authorizing targeted airstrikes and humanitarian airdrops on Aug. 7-8 to blunt attacks against Erbil and protect trapped civilians on Mount Sinjar.
On Sept. 10, 2014, Washington established a global coalition that expanded to dozens of member states, formalizing Combined Joint Task Force - Operation Inherent Resolve (CJTF-OIR) on Oct. 17, 2014, to conduct counterterrorism air operations and assist Iraqi ground units.
Following extensive urban fighting, Iraqi forces liberated Mosul in July 2017.
Iraqi Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi formally declared the territorial defeat of ISIS on Dec. 9, 2017, after regaining control along the border with Syria.
Regional tensions escalated sharply on Dec. 27, 2019, when a rocket strike on a Kirkuk military facility killed an American contractor, triggering US airstrikes against five Kata'ib Hezbollah installations.
Protesters breached the outer perimeter of the US Embassy compound in Baghdad on Dec. 31, 2019.
On Jan. 3, 2020, a US strike outside Baghdad International Airport killed Iranian Quds Force Commander Qasem Soleimani and Iraqi militia leader Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis. Two days later, Iraq's Council of Representatives passed a non-binding resolution demanding the expulsion of all foreign military forces.
On July 26, 2021, then-US President Joe Biden and Iraqi Prime Minister Mustafa al-Kadhimi agreed to terminate combat operations by the year's end.
The coalition formally ended its combat role on Dec. 9, 2021, shifting approximately 2,500 remaining American troops exclusively into training, advising, and intelligence-sharing functions.
Bilateral security dialogue restarted in August 2023, establishing the Higher Military Commission in January 2024 to assess the persistent ISIS threat and evaluate domestic defensive capabilities.
On Sept. 17, 2024, Iraqi Prime Minister Mohammed Shia al-Sudani said that the mission's rationale had concluded.
"Today, Iraq in 2024 is not the same as Iraq of 2014…We moved from a period of wars to a period of stability."
On Sept. 27, 2024, Washington and Baghdad finalized a roadmap: Phase 1 concluded the coalition's military tasks across Iraq by September 2025, while Phase 2 permitted foreign personnel to facilitate anti-ISIS missions in Syria from designated Iraqi facilities until September 2026.
On Sept. 30, 2025, the Pentagon announced it, along with coalition partners, would reduce the military mission.
On Jan. 18, 2026, the commission announced that coalition advisers had fully vacated federal military installations, including Ain al-Asad Air Base and the Joint Operations Command headquarters, transferring authority to domestic security personnel.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi visited Washington on July 14, 2026, where he met with US President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Trump affirmed that Washington would no longer require a military garrison inside the country, while Zaidi said that after Sept. 30, “there will be no need for any armed factions, and our security forces are capable of protecting our territory."
Baghdad reaffirmed Sept. 30, 2026, as the "fixed and final date" for the mission's conclusion following discussions on Aug. 12 between Zaidi and CENTCOM Commander Gen. Brad Cooper.
On Sept. 27, 2026, an Iraqi official said that foreign forces had completely evacuated, though the US did not confirm this on their side.
Casualty figures demonstrate the contrasting physical intensity between the original occupation and the subsequent counterterrorism mission.
During the 2003–2011 campaign under Operation Iraqi Freedom, approximately 1.5 million American service members served in theater.
According to the Pentagon's Defense Casualty Analysis System, 4,418 US military personnel were killed and 31,994 were wounded in action.
Financially, the US Congressional Budget Office reported on April 26, 2011, that military operations had cost taxpayers roughly $752 billion.
During the 2014–2026 campaign under Operation Inherent Resolve, Pentagon casualty registries recorded 123 total deaths and 499 service members wounded in action.
Civilian losses during the operations were extensive.
Across both phases from 2003 through 2024, the tracking initiative Iraq Body Count reported more than 200,000 conflict-related civilian deaths.
According to Every Casualty Counts, more than 300,000, including civilians and combatants, were recorded as killed during the period.

Kyiv shrouded in smoke after Russia strikes power plants, kills 4
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:56:00 UTC
17:56:00 KST

At least four people were killed Wednesday when Russian drone and missile attacks targeted Kyiv and surrounding areas that also damaged energy infrastructure and shrouded the capital in smoke, Ukrainian officials said.
Two women and a 14-year-old child died in overnight strikes on the Ukrainian capital and a town on the northern outskirts. Another person was killed in an attack on a Kyiv warehouse Wednesday, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Ukraine is expecting another winter assault on power and heating facilities after last year entire cities were plunged into darkness and cold for days or weeks.
Russia acknowledged the massive overnight assault, saying it had hit a data center in the capital supporting Ukraine's armed forces, various power plants in the Kyiv region, an industrial complex in Odesa region, and port infrastructure in Izmail.
Ukraine's air force said that Moscow had deployed anti-ship and ballistic missiles and 188 drones, with five missiles and 155 drones intercepted.
Power company DTEK did not detail the damage to energy infrastructure in Kyiv but said workers had restored supply to 8,000 households.
On Wednesday morning, Kyiv was shrouded in thick fog from the smoke of attacks. Emergency services asked residents to keep windows closed.
Citing preliminary information, Klitschko said debris had been found at a Western embassy in the center of Kyiv. He did not specify which embassy.
Among neighboring nations, a drone crossed into Moldova's airspace and exploded near the eastern village of Hirbovet, while European Union and NATO members Romania and Poland both scrambled military jets, the countries said.
Flights at Polish airports Lublin and Rzeszow were temporarily suspended.
Ukraine has also increased attacks on Russia, hitting refineries and online retailers to undermine Moscow's war effort.
One person was killed in drone attacks in Russia's Bryansk region, which borders Ukraine, while a Ukrainian drone attack on the oil-producing Samara region damaged private houses, regional governors said.

US completes Iraq withdrawal after 12-year ISIS mission as Iran-backed militias remain armed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:55:13 UTC
17:55:13 KST

The U.S. military announced Wednesday that it had completed the withdrawal of its troops from Iraq, bringing an end to the 12-year mission launched to fight ISIS after the terror group swept across large parts of the country in 2014.
The final U.S. troops and equipment left the last air base where American forces had remained in northern Iraq under an agreement between Baghdad and Washington. The withdrawal also closes a chapter that Iran-backed militias had long cited as justification for retaining their weapons, though the Iraqi government has now postponed their disarmament until at least June 2027.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said U.S. troops and equipment had completed an “orderly departure” from the air base in Irbil, in Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region.
“This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region,” he said. “It also marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship.”
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi presided over the handover ceremony and described the withdrawal as the beginning of “a new phase, one defined by Iraq’s sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, the unity of its decision-making, and balanced partnerships with its friends.”
The withdrawal comes amid the ongoing war between the United States and Iran, which has at times spilled into Iraq. Iran-backed groups welcomed the U.S. departure, while officials in the Kurdish region voiced concern, particularly over the removal of American air defense systems.
U.S. forces first invaded Iraq in 2003 and withdrew in 2011. Three years later, Baghdad invited a smaller U.S.-led force back after ISIS seized large swaths of northern and western Iraq. With the terror group later reduced largely to scattered sleeper cells, Washington and Baghdad agreed in 2024 to wind down the coalition mission.
U.S. troops withdrew from bases across most of Iraq last year, leaving a smaller contingent of several hundred soldiers in the Kurdish region. Those bases have repeatedly come under attack since the U.S.-Iran war began on Feb. 28.
The Sept. 30 withdrawal deadline had initially also been tied to a commitment to disarm armed groups operating outside state control. While several smaller militias agreed to surrender their weapons, powerful Iran-backed factions rejected disarmament or imposed conditions Baghdad was unlikely to meet.
Al-Zaidi has since pushed the deadline for militia disarmament to June 2027.
Qassem al-Araji, national security adviser to the Iraqi prime minister, hailed the end of the coalition mission as a major milestone.
“Following the negotiations and understandings that began on July 22, 2021, we arrive today at an important milestone: the end of the international coalition’s mission and the presence of its forces,” he wrote on X. “We are moving toward bilateral relations with coalition member states, a transition that strengthens sovereignty and serves the national interests and aspirations of the Iraqi people.”
Al-Araji said the end of the coalition mission did not mean the end of security ties with its members. Security and intelligence cooperation, exchanges of expertise and efforts to build Iraqi capabilities would continue through bilateral relationships, he said.
A ‘new political phase’
Iraqi forces said the coalition had completed its withdrawal from the Kurdistan region and that U.S. forces had returned home or moved to bases in neighboring countries.
They also stressed that the end of the coalition mission removed one of the principal arguments used by militias for keeping their weapons.
“It is essential that weapons be concentrated in the hands of the state. There is no justification for weapons remaining outside state institutions,” Iraqi forces said. “We respected the position of the militias that conditioned the surrender of their weapons on the withdrawal of coalition forces.”
The Qatari newspaper Al-Araby Al-Jadeed described Wednesday as the beginning of a “new security and political phase” for Iraq, marking the end of the U.S. combat military presence that began with the 2003 invasion, despite the eight-year interruption between the 2011 withdrawal and the return of American forces in 2014.
An Iraqi military source told the newspaper that the U.S. military had transferred its remaining equipment out of the country, including material used for housing and troop welfare, to Kuwait, Turkey and Jordan.
But the effects of the withdrawal are unlikely to be felt equally across Iraq. Officials in the Kurdish region have expressed particular concern over the removal of U.S. air defense capabilities at a time of heightened regional conflict.
The Kurdish regional government’s Peshmerga Ministry said the region had faced more than 1,000 drone and ballistic missile attacks during the recent U.S.-Iran conflict.
“The departure of the United States from the Kurdistan Region under these complex regional circumstances, without the provision of a defense system, is a matter of concern,” the ministry said.
‘The occupation is not over’
Iran-backed factions, by contrast, celebrated the withdrawal while making clear they do not view it as the end of their confrontation with Washington.
Abu Mujahid al-Assaf, a security official with the powerful Kataib Hezbollah militia, called the departure of U.S. forces “the beginning of full sovereignty.”
“The expulsion of the occupation forces, defeated, from the land of Iraq is the beginning of full sovereignty,” he said.
He also warned al-Zaidi’s government against implementing what he described as American plans.
“Any government that does not work for the benefit of the people will be overthrown by all means,” he said.
Al-Assaf has also threatened action if restrictions on Iranian flights remain in place after Oct. 1, saying Iran-aligned factions could move to close access routes to countries participating in what he called a blockade of Iran. He said the “Islamic Resistance” would monitor Iraqi airspace, issue warnings to aircraft it deemed hostile and then seek to shoot them down.
Other opponents of the United States in Iraq argue that the military withdrawal does not end American influence over the country.
The Hezbollah-affiliated Lebanese newspaper Al-Akhbar highlighted that argument Wednesday under the headline “Iraq: The day of incomplete sovereignty,” quoting an analyst who claimed that Washington still exercised influence over Iraqi political, economic and security decision-making.
Sources close to the militias told the newspaper that their definition of sovereignty goes beyond the departure of American troops and includes ending all foreign military deployments in Iraq, including Turkey’s presence, as well as rejecting outside influence over the country’s economic decisions.

U.S. military declares end of anti-ISIS Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:54:56 UTC
17:54:56 KST

U.S. military declares end of anti-ISIS Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq
The U.S. military declared an end to its Iraq-based anti-ISIS operation Wednesday, saying all U.S.-led coalition forces and equipment had been withdrawn from a key base in the north of the country in line with an agreement reached previously with the Iraqi government.
"The orderly departure of Coalition forces and equipment from Erbil Air Base marks the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated ISIS in Iraq," Department of Defense spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement. "This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region. It also marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship."
The U.S. military launched Operation Inherent Resolve in 2014 to confront ISIS, the terrorist group that grew out of the remnants of al-Qaeda in Iraq and seized vast portions of Iraq and neighboring Syria in the years immediately preceding the U.S.-led operation.
Roughly 2,000 Americans were present in Iraq as of February, officials said at the time. By comparison, more than 160,000 U.S. service members were in the country at the peak of the late 2000s "surge" under Operation Iraqi Freedom — a prior mission to topple Iraqi President Saddam Hussein and grapple with a years-long civil war.
As part of the anti-ISIS mission, U.S. troops have served in both Iraq and Syria. The roughly 1,500 troops that had been in Syria for a number of years withdrew earlier this year.
The end of the mission was agreed upon several years ago between the U.S. and Iraq in a plan that prescribed a transition to a more bilateral relationship between the two countries. In the 2024 joint agreement, Iraq and the U.S. announced the end of the multi-country coalition to defeat ISIS by 2025, and the expected end of the Inherent Resolve mission by the end of 2026.
The mission has pushed ISIS from controlling any significant territory, but it doesn't mean ISIS ceases to exist. In December 2025, two U.S. soldiers and a translator were killed in an ISIS attack, according to the U.S. military's Central Command. The U.S. retaliated with airstrikes.
American troops have been targeted by Iran-backed militias inside Iraq in recent years, a threat that has grown more pronounced since the U.S. and Israel jointly launched the ongoing war against Iran. According to the Pentagon, militias affiliated with Iran launched more than 600 attacks against U.S. citizens and facilities between February and April 2026.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth addressed the attacks in a July meeting at the Pentagon with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, according to a Pentagon readout. They discussed the transition from the Global Coalition to Defeat ISIS to a bilateral relationship, and Hegseth, according to the readout, committed to ending Inherent Resolve by Sept. 30.
Al-Zaidi has promised to disarm the Iran-backed militias in Iraq. He told The New York Times this week the groups are expected to be disbanded by June 2027, after initially setting a September 2026 deadline.
"We expect the Iraqi Security Forces, including the Peshmerga [Kurdish forces] and other security forces in the Iraqi Kurdistan Region, to lead the continuing effort to secure Iraq and keep ISIS remnants suppressed," Parnell said in his Wednesday morning statement, adding that the U.S. military would "continue to provide targeted training and intelligence support to our Iraqi partners."
"The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq's remaining security challenges, including ISIS remnants and Iran-aligned militias that undermine Iraqi sovereignty and regional stability, now rests with the Government of Iraq," he said. "The United States remains committed to counterterrorism and will continue to work with Iraq and our partners to ensure ISIS can never reconstitute from Iraqi territory."
Can Iraq control Iran's proxies?
The formal end of the U.S. military deployment in Iraq that began with the 2003 invasion was celebrated by the government in Baghdad, which declared Sept. 30, "Sovereignty Day." This year, it will begin a three-day national holiday, and the government has called for nationwide celebrations.
Videos circulated widely on social media Wednesday showed military convoys transporting U.S. equipment out of the Erbil base.
Speaking to the national Iraqi News Agency, Sabah al-Numan, a spokesperson for the prime minister, insisted that the nation's security forces were fully capable of maintaining peace and stability across the country.
But the long-planned U.S. withdrawal comes at a highly volatile moment for Iraq and the region. With the U.S.-Iran war at a critical juncture as President Trump warns of possible new strikes despite furtive diplomacy, many Iraqis remain deeply concerned about a potential resurgence of extremist groups in the country, as well as the expanding influence of the Iran-backed militias that have long held significant power in parts of Iraq.
Despite the government's public optimism, several religious and ethnic minority groups harbor serious doubt about the central government's ability to keep those forces in check on its own.
"The majority of Iraqis doubt the ability of the security and military apparatus to maintain security in the country, whether regarding the prevention of external aggressions and attacks or internal movements by armed groups operating outside state control of the government," journalist and regional political analyst Saman Noah told CBS News on Wednesday.
That is "especially true given that experience has proven the government's inability to subject these [Iran-backed] groups to state decision-making, control their behavior or hold their members accountable," he said.
Noah said some of the concern stemmed from the Iraqi government's lack of adequate air defenses "to protect the country's airspace, as well as the reliance on American weaponry — whose maintenance, and consequently operation, could cease in the event of any dispute."
Those concerns have only been heightened by the government's failure to meet its own initial deadline to disarm the Iran-backed factions, and concern that such groups could draw Iraq into the broader regional conflict in support of Tehran.
The Kurds in Iraq and their Peshmerga forces have been close allies of the United States since the first Gulf War in 1991, partnering on numerous occasions over the past 35 years. They joined the U.S.-led international coalition to depose Saddam Hussein's regime in 2003, and more than a decade later they fought with coalition forces to deprive ISIS of its massive foothold in the region.
They have become increasingly concerned about Iraq's future and the prospect of Iran-allied militias seeking to expand their influence.
"We fought side by side with our American allies to bring peace and stability to the region," said Noreldin Waisy, a senior adviser to the Kurdistan Regional Government's prime minister. "To eliminate any doubt among the Kurdish people, we believe the Kurdistan Region must remain an essential part of the bilateral Memorandum of Understanding between the two countries."

Eiffel Tower chief Patrick Branco Ruivo to step down after female staff excluded during Hindu group's visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:54:00 UTC
17:54:00 KST

Eiffel Tower chief to quit over exclusion of female staff
September 30, 2026
The head of the company that operates the Eiffel Tower is set to step down at the end of the year after female staff were excluded during a visit by a Hindu religious group in September.
An independent investigation found a series of failures surrounding the incident, which prompted Eiffel Tower staff to strike and drew criticism from French politicians.
What happened at the Eiffel Tower?
Patrick Branco Ruivo, director general of the Societe d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), will leave the position he has held since late 2018.
The company said an independent investigation into the September 5 visit had uncovered a series of operational failures that resulted in female employees being excluded.
It described the situation as "unacceptable."
Management had instructed female employees not to come into contact with a delegation from Bochasanwasi Shri Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS), a Hindu religious organization.
The company initially acknowledged that withdrawing female staff from the tower's third floor during the group's visit had been a mistake.
What has the Hindu group said?
BAPS denied asking for female employees to be removed or hidden during the visit.
"The religious practices of our monks were explained to the Eiffel Tower's management in advance. These are personal spiritual commitments, which our monks observe without seeking to impose them on others. They do not require women to be excluded from the places they visit," BAPS said.
BAPS is an international religious and civic organization within the Swaminarayan tradition of Hinduism. The delegation was in the region for celebrations connected with the inauguration of a traditional Hindu stone temple.
What happens now?
The incident led Eiffel Tower employees to strike on September 7, forcing the landmark to close for a day.
SETE chair Ariel Weil said the company would introduce measures and training programs aimed at promoting gender equality.
The German account also says a separate protocol department will be established following the investigation.
The 330-meter (1,083-foot) Eiffel Tower attracts around 7 million visitors annually.

Ministries present progress, transformation of flagship barrier-free projects at Council session
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
11:53:46 EEST
17:53:46 KST

Ministries presented the progress and transformation of flagship accessibility projects during a meeting of the National Council on Barrier-Free Access.
Specifically, Minister for Veterans Affairs of Ukraine Vitaliy Kim presented the implementation status of three Ministry of Veterans Affairs flagship projects: Formula for a worthy return to civilian life, focused on building a comprehensive support system for veterans; Development of sports for veterans, aimed at recovery, adaptation, and return to active life; and Barrier-Free veteran spaces, establishing support hubs nationwide.
He also introduced the updated initiative Unified system of barrier-free support for veterans and veteranas, through which the agency is combining and transforming its initiatives into a new generalized flagship project.
According to the report, key tasks for the near future include: conducting community audits to assess actual service accessibility and local veteran policy implementation (which will reinforce the work of 1,300 regional barrier-free commissioners); ensuring the full operation and quality outfitting of the state veteran spaces network; updating the support system model; and developing regulations for improved veteran nutrition in healthcare facilities.
The Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine presented the results and next steps for two flagship projects: STEP: Comprehensive development, education, and career and Education without discrimination, language without barriers.
In particular, STEP project is designed to combine general secondary education with everyday life skills, career guidance, and practical training—including managing money, planning personal tasks, and performing job assignments.
The Ministry plans to establish 100 STEP classes and groups for about 1,500 children and young people in the first phase. Transition to full-time or blended learning is envisaged for 1,000 children, with group piloting slated for 50 vocational education institutions in the 2027/2028 academic year.
"Along with regulatory decisions, institutional preparation will continue: educators need training programs and professional support, while institutions require equipped workshops and partnerships with employers. The Ministry of Education and Science is also finalizing a spending review of the subvention with the Ministry of Finance and independent experts, and is preparing proposals on funding support for children with special educational needs," the ministry noted.
Additionally, over 2,000 educators have already completed the quest-course Education without discrimination, language without barriers, and another 154 participants completed Power of equality program dedicated to non-discriminatory approaches in education. Furthermore, an all-Ukrainian lesson titled Language of dignity: Seeing the person behind the words was created for grades 1 through 12.
The Ministry of Social Policy, Family and Unity presented the flagship project Active longevity, aimed at fostering opportunities for self-realization and support for older persons within communities.
"The project will encompass physical and mental health support, opportunities for continued professional activity and retraining, and access to educational, medical, and social services. Hubs of the Future will operate on the basis of youth centers. A powerful Mediterranean storm brought torrential rainfall to southern France on Wednesday, prompting authorities to place the Herault and Gard departments under the highest-level red alert for rain and flooding, according to BFMTV.
Meteo-France issued the red alerts at 8 am local time (0600GMT), while the Bouches-du-Rhone, Lozere and Ardeche departments were placed under orange alert for severe weather.
The Herault River rose rapidly.
According to water-level readings cited by the broadcaster, the river rose from 27 centimetres at around 2 am local time to 3.34 metres more than five hours later.
Authorities said the river had risen by more than 2 metres in just two hours overnight as heavy rainfall affected the Cevennes region.
Nearly 140 millimetres of rain was recorded in Moules-et-Baucels in the Herault department, equivalent to almost two months of average rainfall.
Other rivers and waterways also rose rapidly following the heavy rainfall early on Wednesday.
The Herault prefecture ordered schools to close for the day in eight sectors, including Montpellier, Mauguio, Lunel, Sommieres, Ganges, Sete, Clermont-l’Herault and Lodeve.
The prefecture also said public transportation was suspended across the department.
Authorities urged residents to remain at home, avoid unnecessary travel and refrain from using their vehicles.

Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir cancels planned visit to the US amid rising IDF alert level
A senior IDF official explained the decision: "You can’t put the army on high alert and fly abroad"
The Chief of Staff, Lieutenant General Eyal Zamir, canceled his planned visit to the United States on Wednesday. This comes against the backdrop of increased alertness in the IDF and a sensitive security situation, as reported by i24NEWS military analyst Yossi Yehoshua.
The decision to cancel the trip was made by the military's top echelon even before Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's statements yesterday regarding threats to Israel. One senior IDF official made it unequivocally clear what prompted the move, saying, "You can't put the military on alert and fly abroad."
As part of the official visit to Washington, Zamir was scheduled to hold a series of strategic meetings with the American Chief of Staff and with the commander of the United States Central Command (CENTCOM).
The talks were intended to deal with joint security coordination and preparations for developments in the region. Nevertheless, the state of high alert declared in the operational units of the IDF, alongside the need for close management of readiness on the ground, determined that at this time the Chief of Staff must remain in Israel.

EU to offer single-market access to candidate countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:39:52 UTC
17:39:52 KST

EU to offer single-market access to candidate countries
Economic benefits would be conditional and can be taken away if non-members backslide on democracy or share sensitive tech with unfriendly governments, the plan says.
BRUSSELS — The European Union will open its vast economy to countries waiting to join its ranks, provided they agree to stand with the bloc against hostile states and industrial rivals, according to a draft European Commission proposal obtained by POLITICO.
Candidate countries — some of which have been waiting decades to become EU members — will be offered unprecedented "gradual integration" into the single market, including frictionless trade and access to research programs, while their applications are being worked on, according to the draft plan.
"The single market is the first priority for economic convergence," reads a review of the "pre-enlargement" benefits to be offered to candidate countries.
Advertisement
"Earlier integration would open opportunities for Union businesses, strengthen European value chains and reduce strategic dependencies. The Commission will identify where verified regulatory alignment and enforcement capacity allow deeper participation in research, innovation and industrial cooperation, and wider market access. Priority should go to opportunities that advance accession preparations and meet shared economic and strategic needs."
The review, overseen by top von der Leyen advisor Alexandre Adam — a former aide to French President Emmanuel Macron — would radically overhaul the EU's approach to countries in its neighborhood. At present, almost all economic benefits of closer cooperation are reserved for members, but no new state has joined since Croatia in 2013.
As part of Adam's package of measures, Ukraine, Moldova, Albania and Montenegro will be offered "road maps" designed to speed up the process of joining in the coming years. Others, like North Macedonia, Kosovo, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia and Turkey, have seen the process drag on — with fears growing that they will become disengaged or gravitate closer to Russia or China.
Under the Commission's plan, economic benefits offered to candidate countries will depend on their support for the EU's foreign policy objectives, with single market access hinging on them not sharing key technologies with hostile states and trade rivals.
"As industrial and market integration deepens, participation in sensitive sectors must be accompanied by cooperation on investment screening, export controls, sanctions implementation and the protection of sensitive technologies," the review document reads.
"Assessments of access should consider strategic alignment, critical dependencies and the capacity to manage risks to infrastructure and supply chains. Where those conditions are not met, the scope of participation should be adjusted under the applicable instrument."
Advertisement
Among the areas being considered for closer cooperation are semiconductors, quantum technologies, biotechnology, artificial intelligence and space.
In the waiting room
Von der Leyen touches down in Albania for talks on Wednesday as part of her tour of the Western Balkans. She'll also visit Kosovo and North Macedonia, which will miss out on an expedited pathway to join the EU under the new plan, and will use her visit to demand economic benefits of closer alignment.
"Gradual integration should be tangible for our citizens and businesses," Kosovo's prime minister, Albin Kurti, told POLITICO. "We want greater access to the EU single market, European funding and financial schemes, and joint programs in areas such as energy, digitalization, research, education and infrastructure."
"We support gradual integration, but it must be a pathway to full EU membership, not a parallel process or a substitute for it. Kosova is ready to do its part," Kurti added.
According to the review, the ultimate goal of candidate countries should be becoming full EU members. "Accession, however, takes time: candidate countries must complete a rigorous, merit-based process and deliver far-reaching and lasting reforms," it reads. "That time should be put to full strategic use to both prepare the Union for a larger membership and deepen gradual integration in areas of mutual interest."
However, the benefits will depend on the countries doing their part: "Where these obligations are not fulfilled, participation must remain reversible. Access should be suspended or withdrawn where warranted," the proposal warns.
Advertisement
Internal changes
Current EU members have expressed concern about the prospect of admitting new countries to the bloc that could then renege on their commitments and upend key policies. Under its former prime minister, Viktor Orbán, Hungary used its veto to block sanctions on Russia and support for Ukraine.
Adam's review — due to be presented to top officials on Oct. 6 when von der Leyen returns from the Western Balkans — will propose new conditions on those that join the bloc to ensure they don't backslide on democracy and the rule of law.
"The accession process must establish more than legal alignment," it reads. "Institutions must work in practice and reforms must endure. Monitoring, incentives and enforcement should therefore form a continuous framework extending beyond accession."
But the EU will also change to accommodate a broader membership, going far beyond the club of wealthy Western European democracies it was initially conceived as. The bloc can change its rules to be less vulnerable to individual members' whims, the review concludes, without having to reopen fundamental articles of EU law and potentially triggering national referendums across the bloc.
"The Commission supports Treaty change where necessary, but it considers that measures already available under the Treaties should be taken forward now," it concludes. Among the options being considered is a move to ensure more decisions can be made with a qualified majority of member countries on board.
"Qualified-majority voting is already the general rule under the Treaties, but unanimity remains in several strategically important areas. As membership grows, the risk of delay or blockage will likely increase," it reads.
Advertisement
So-called passerelle clauses, which allow decisions to be taken by majority vote rather than unanimously, could be used to smooth the passage of sanctions, responses to human rights crises and the deployment of civilian missions to conflict zones, the review says. However, these clauses require unanimous support of member countries to be activated in the first place.
Leaders from across the EU will be asked to weigh in on the discussion about how to bring new members into the bloc — and what to offer those still waiting — at a two-day summit in Brussels from Oct. 15.
Von der Leyen's enlargement commissioner, Marta Kos, has said that the new proposals, combined with support from capitals to accelerate the process, offer the chance for an “autumn of enlargement” in which unprecedented changes can be made.

German Social Democratic Party revives push for AfD ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:39:28 UTC
17:39:28 KST

German coalition party pushes to ban AfD
Germany’s Social Democratic Party (SPD) has called for a formal review that could pave the way for a ban on Alternative for Germany (AfD), as the right-wing party leads national polls following major regional election victories.
The push follows the AfD’s sweeping victories in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania earlier this month, where it secured 43.8% and 38.2%, respectively. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) suffered heavy losses, including failing to clear the 5% threshold in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
On Tuesday, SPD parliamentary leaders from the Bundestag, Germany’s state legislatures and the European Parliament wrapped up a two-day summit in Bremen by again labeling the AfD a “right-wing extremist party.” They accused it of threatening democracy “from within” and “normalizing racism.”
The AfD has rejected accusations of extremism. Responding to a parallel push for a potential ban in Hamburg this week, AfD parliamentary leader Dirk Nockemann called it an “attack on democracy and the will of the voters” and dismissed the proposed working group as “desperate.”
The Eurosceptic party advocates tougher immigration controls and opposes Berlin’s support for Ukraine and sanctions against Russia.
At the federal level, the AfD remains classified by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency as a suspected right-wing extremist organization.
In February, a Cologne court blocked an attempt by the agency to upgrade the AfD to confirmed right-wing extremist status, pending the outcome of the main proceedings. Several AfD state branches carry the stronger classification.
The SPD wants federal and state governments to set up a joint working group by year-end to examine whether legal grounds exist to seek a ban. Launching the review “is a legal necessity” and a “democratic duty,” it said.
Merz himself has expressed skepticism about pursuing a ban. Earlier this month, the chancellor said the legal hurdle was “very high” and argued that outlawing the AfD would not solve the problems its voters believe they face.
Under German law, only the Federal Constitutional Court can outlaw a party. A ban requires more than anti-constitutional views: a party must actively seek to undermine the democratic order and have the potential to achieve its aims.
The push comes as the AfD has opened up a record polling lead over Merz’s CDU/CSU bloc. An INSA survey put the AfD at 29.5%, compared with 19% for the CDU/CSU and just 14.5% for the SPD. The two governing parties together stood at 33.5%, only four points ahead of the AfD alone.
AfD co-leader Alice Weidel reacted to the poll by accusing the CDU of “clinging to the undemocratic firewall,” saying the policy was ultimately “destroying Germany.” The ‘firewall’ refers to the refusal by other major German parties to cooperate with the AfD.

The Delhi government this week unveiled a plan to battle the recurring toxic smog that blankets the Indian capital in the winter months.
The measures are set to be enforced from November, with some curbs to remain in place until February.
Here’s what the plan entails:
- a ban on dust-generating demolition activities and outdoor civil construction work from November 1 to January 31
- construction and demolition activities will see a complete ban in the peak winter phase, from December 10 to January 20
- use of private vehicles will discouraged with parking fees in authorized parking areas being doubled from November 1 to February 28

INDIA bloc plans 'Save Democracy' marches over SIR, starting October 2
The INDIA bloc has announced a "Save Democracy " march as leaders of the opposition alliance met on Wednesday to mull a joint strategy over the issue of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls.
India bloc leaders will hold nationwide protest marches from October 2 to 8 at the district level, while all opposition MPs will march to the Election Commission on October 6, Congress party President Mallikarjun Kharge told a press briefing after the meeting.
The meeting, which lasted over three hours, included Congress' Rahul Gandhi, All India Trinamool Congress party (TMC) chief Mamata Banerjee, Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, among leaders from other opposition parties.

The bloc's leaders also announced a major rally in the Indian capital on November 1, where they would raise issues related to alleged "vote theft".
Gandhi earlier posted on X, accusing Modi of using India's poll body chief Kumar "to steal elections".
The INDIA bloc on Wednesday also demanded that all cases linked to the SIR that are in the Supreme Court should be resolved "as soon as possible".
Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has accused the opposition of "misleading" the public on the SIR and of an "attack" India's constitutional bodies.
Apple pay debuts in India
Apple on Wednesday introduced its payment service in India as it taps into the lucrative digital payments market in the world’s most populous nation.
Apple Pay is now available for Indian users across iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch, a statement from the US multinational corporation said, adding that support for Mac computers was coming soon.
The launch comes in partnership with India's Axis Bank, which is the country's third-largest private lender.
Customers of Axis Bank will be able to store their credit cards on Apple wallets and "use them at thousands of in-store and online merchants across India," Apple said.
Apple Pay has also held talks with the larger HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank but is yet to agree commercial terms, according to news agency Reuters.
In India, over 80% of digital payments are handled through the homegrown United Payments Interface (UPI), which is also the world's largest real-time payments system in terms of volume, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
"India is home to a dynamic and digitally savvy population that continues to embrace a cashless future while expecting the highest standards of security and privacy, and we're so excited to bring Apple Pay to users in India today," Jennifer Bailey, Apple's vice president of Apple Pay and Apple Wallet, said.

Security was tightened Wednesday around the Shahi Masjid in Ujjain, in the central Indian state of Madhya Pradesh, after clashes over the demolition of part of the historic mosque for road-widening work ahead of a 2028 Hindu pilgrimage.

Eiffel Tower chief to quit over exclusion of female staff during Hindu group visit
The head of the company that operates the Eiffel Tower is set to step down at the end of the year after female staff were excluded during a visit by a Hindu religious group in September.
Patrick Branco Ruivo, director general of the Societe d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), will leave the position he has held since late 2018.
The company said an independent investigation into the September 5 visit had uncovered a series of operational failures that resulted in female employees being excluded.

Management had instructed female employees not to come into contact with a delegation from Bochasanwasi Shri Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS), a Hindu religious organization which has its headquarters in Ahmedabad in the Indian state of Gujarat.
BAPS denied asking for female employees to be removed or hidden during the visit.
The incident led Eiffel Tower employees to strike on September 7, forcing the landmark to close for a day.

India opposition leaders push back against voter roll review
A meeting of the INDIA bloc, the Congress-led alliance of opposition parties, is underway at the Constitution Club in New Delhi on Wednesday, where opposition leaders are expected to discuss the Election Commission of India's (ECI) Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists and the furor surrounding India's Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, that has gripped the nation in recent days.
Mallikarjun Kharge, the president of India's main opposition Congress party, called for the roll back of the SIR, a hotly debated exercise to verify hundreds of millions of Indian voters, that began last year.
Kharge said that the "ballot belongs to the people" and the principle of "one, person, one vote, one value" in Indian democracy was under a "serious threat."
"It is shocking that as many as 13.3 Crore (133 million) voters have blatantly been removed from voter list. Their power to take part in a DEMOCRACY has been snatched. It is ordinary voters who should be deciding who comes to power rather than those who are in power," he said.
Why India's poll body chief is under scrutiny
Wednesday's meeting comes after an investigative report by the Indian Express published last week said that there were differences within the Election Commission of India over decisions related to the SIR.
The report stirred a political storm, with protests calling for the resignation of the poll body's chief, Gyanesh Kumar, for allegedly undermining the ECI's credibility.
According to the Indian Express, Kumar's fellow election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months regarding voter registrations, deletions and restorations, as well as control of electoral-roll data, but those concerns were not taken into consideration.
The report said that in one objection, one of the commissioners complained that the ECI acted against the written advice of two commissioners and claimed its action was "unauthorized and illegal."
The ECI has deemed all its decisions lawful, saying that differing views were a routine "part of decision-making."
The three-member commission, comprising Kumar, Sandhu and Joshi, oversees the SIR, which the poll body says removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also prevents the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."
However, opposition parties and critics allege that the exercise has gone beyond that remit and removed millions of eligible voters to the benefit of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Congress demands CEC Kumar's resignation
On Wednesday, Kharge also called for the removal or resignation of Kumar, saying that there could be no credible election without an "independent and impartial" election body.
He said that the ECI head's "very integrity" and "intentions" were under question.
Last week, Congress carried out demonstrations across the country demanding Kumar's resignation.
Pressure group Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), which claims millions of supporters, said that it would launch nationwide protests on October 2 if Kumar does not step down.
Welcome to our coverage
This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi, back with the Wednesday roundup of the biggest headlines capturing India's attention.
Residents of the Indian capital, who have been waking up to cooler mornings, are discussing whether winter will arrive early. But apart from the nip in the air, there is also growing concern about the winter smog that chokes Delhi in the waning months of the year. The city, however, is trying to stay ahead of the smog with a winter action plan that includes construction curbs, vehicle restrictions and work-from-home arrangements.
In political news, opposition leaders from the INDIA bloc are meeting in New Delhi for a key meeting where they will discuss a joint response to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) row surrounding the country's poll body and calls for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.
In sports news, Indian archers have struck gold twice. India's compound mixed team and women's team have both won gold medals.
We will cover these and other stories in this blog.

U.S. consumer confidence slides to 12-year low
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:30:38 CST
17:30:38 KST

WASHINGTON, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- U.S. consumer confidence dropped in September to the lowest level since 2014, according to data released Tuesday from the Conference Board.
The Conference Board's consumer confidence index fell by a substantial 6.7 points to 81.9 in September, down from 88.6 in the month prior.
"The consumer confidence index deteriorated notably in September, following two prior months of softening," said Dana M. Peterson, chief economist at the Conference Board.
"Consumers' write-in responses regarding factors affecting the economy were mostly pessimistic in September. References to prices, the high cost of goods and services, and oil and gas prices in particular, rose to new heights, reflecting September's surge in fuel costs," Peterson said.
"Comments about war (and) conflict eased this month but remained elevated. Consumers also frequently cited politics, trade and employment in their write-in responses, though to a lesser extent," Peterson added.
Some experts noted this is one of the most negative consumer confidence reports they've seen in some time.
Dean Baker, a macroeconomist and co-founder of the Center for Economic and Policy Research, told Xinhua: "This is one of the most negative reports I've seen. Pretty much everything in it is negative, both current conditions and future expectations."
"Also, it is people assessing their own situation, not just saying the economy is bad. The percent saying their situation is good is less than the period coming right out of the pandemic and the percent saying it is bad is higher. People are not feeling good about the world," Baker said.
On a six-month moving average basis, confidence across all age groups and nearly all income groups trended downward.
By generation, confidence for Gen Z, followed by Millennials, remained the highest on a six-month moving average basis, while confidence among the three oldest generations (Generation X, Baby Boomers and the Silent Generation) continued to weaken.
Consumers' average and median 12-month inflation expectations rose 0.3 points in September to 6.1 percent and 5.1 percent respectively. The share of consumers anticipating higher interest rates over the next 12 months jumped by 5.2 points to 68.4 percent. Consumers still largely expected stock prices to rise in the next 12 months, but optimism moderated in September.
Consumers' net views of their family's current financial situation turned negative in September, as the share of consumers who said their finances were "bad" rose to overtake those saying "good" for the second time since the question was introduced four years ago.
Views of people's family's future financial situation over the next six months were somewhat less optimistic. The share of consumers who believed a U.S. recession over the next 12 months is "somewhat likely" rose while those who believe recession is "not likely" declined. ■

====================================================================================================

World's tallest wind turbine reaches final height in Germany's former coal mining region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
08:30:28 UTC
17:30:28 KST

Winds are stronger at higher altitudes, allowing for twice as much energy to be produced.
A region of Germany once dominated by coal mines has achieved a remarkable pivot to clean energy.
After roughly two years of construction, the world's tallest wind turbine now towers over Schipkau, a small town in Brandenburg.
At 365 metres from the foundation slab to the rotor tip, the wind turbine is only three metres shorter than the Berlin TV Tower, making it among the tallest structures in Germany.
At a time when the Iran war is driving up energy prices for Europeans, the project could not be more needed. "This will help us to become independent of oil and gas from other regions of the world," says Germany's Federal Environment Minister Carsten Schneider.
A telescopic device raised the wind turbine up to its full height
At 365 metres high, the completed turbine is equivalent to a 100-storey building.
What's the advantage of such a giant structure? The wind blows more strongly and steadily above 300m, allowing for more wind energy to be produced.
You might be wondering how a structure as narrow and free standing as a turbine can possibly be built this high. Conventional cranes are not up to the job, after all. Instead, a patented telescopic device was used.
The turbine initially reached a height of 150 metres, then the telescopic device raised it up to 300 metres.
The groundbreaking project has not been without its challenges. At the end of 2025, problems were discovered with steel parts meaning work had to be stopped.
"Safety and quality have absolute priority in this globally unique project," said Jochen Großmann, construction company GICON's CEO and founder, at the time.
If all goes to plan, the wind power giant should be connected to the grid in November.
How much energy will the wind turbine produce?
GICON say they hope for an annual electricity yield of 30-33 gigawatt hours and electricity production costs of less than five cents per kilowatt hour. This is 220 per cent more than conventional turbines nearby and could supply approximately 7,500 four-person households with electricity.
High-altitude wind turbines could be a win in less windy European countries
The higher a wind turbine stands, the stronger and more evenly the wind usually blows. GICON, which says it has been working on the technology since 2010, wanted to scientifically validate this assumption.
On behalf of beventum GmbH, a subsidiary of the Federal Agency for Leap Innovations (SPRIND), the company erected a wind-measuring mast in neighbouring Klettwitz. This showed that the wind does in fact blow more steadily and strongly at a height of 300 metres than at the height of conventional wind turbines.
Large parts of Europe, from eastern Poland to the Iberian Peninsula, have trouble benefitting from wind power due to weak ground winds. High-altitude wind towers could be the answer. SPRIND emphasises: "Europe needs a strong position in wind turbine construction in order to guarantee its own energy production."
Where is the world's tallest wind turbine?
Schipkau is located in Lusatia, a region that was characterised by coal for decades before going through remarkable changes. Authorities in the area now incentivise clean energy projects, offering space, infrastructure and political support.
In the long term, the site is to be developed into a hybrid power plant, with two levels of wind power and a solar park on the ground.
This triple use should quintuple the energy yield compared to pure solar use. The combination of different energy sources should also make it possible to generate electricity year round.
Clean energy is wasted all over Europe due to outdated grids
This ambitious project highlights a problem which is becoming more and more obvious all over Europe: outdated grids can not keep up with the booming growth in renewable infrastructure.
In Germany this creates an expensive irony: if more electricity flows into the grid in windy north-east Germany than the lines can transport to the high-consumption south, wind turbines have to be throttled back or switched off. This means fossil gas and other dirty fuels have to fill the gap, driving increases in prices for consumers as well as more carbon emissions.
According to analysis by German media Tagesspiegel, around 9.3 terawatt hours of wind power were lost in 2023 alone. The costs for congestion management amounted to almost €3 billion and these are borne by consumers via the grid fees that are added to their electricity bills.
GICON and its client SPRIND argue that high-altitude wind towers could alleviate this dilemma in the long term: because high-altitude winds blow more evenly and turbines could also be operated economically where ground winds are too weak, expansion could be more decentralised.
Europe favours wind power
At the end of 2025, around 304 gigawatts of wind power were installed onshore and offshore in Europe, according to the German Wind Energy Association.
With around 77.7 gigawatts of installed capacity, Germany was ahead of the UK with 31.6 gigawatts and Spain with 31.2 gigawatts.
With 5,735 megawatts of newly installed capacity, Germany added more than any other European country in 2025.
Germany is pushing for more renewable energy
At the end of March, German Federal Environment Minister Carsten Schneider presented the Climate Protection Programme 2026 in the Bundestag: 67 measures aimed at saving an additional 25 million tonnes of CO₂ by 2030.
2,000 more wind turbines are to be awarded in the upcoming tenders than previously planned. In addition, 12 gigawatts of wind power capacity will be put out to tender to be connected to the grid by 2030.
