‘Dire situation’: Lebanese prisoners on hunger strike for 18 days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:40:07 UTC
16:40:07 KST

‘Dire situation’: Lebanese prisoners on hunger strike for 18 days
The medical condition of dozens of prisoners has deteriorated as inmates protest against suspension of amnesty law.
The medical condition of dozens of inmates on a hunger strike for more than two weeks inside Lebanon’s largest prison has become “dire”, and prisoners are refusing medication, according to a legal campaigner and a detainee.
Jassem Saad el-Din, who has been held in prison for about 10 years, spoke to Al Jazeera from the Roumieh prison about the protest against the suspension of a general Amnesty law that could have allowed the release of prisoners.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Syria and Lebanon make ‘significant progress’ at talks on joint interests
- list 2 of 3Lebanon and Syria reshape ties amid Israeli attacks and regional shifts
- list 3 of 3Lebanon passes long-sought amnesty law, a day after death penalty repeal
“We have been on a hunger strike for 18 days now – no medication, no medical care, nothing,” said Jassem, who is among hundreds of inmates on hunger strike.
“It’s actually been 10 and a half years that I have been detained without … being sentenced,” said Jassem, who was arrested after being accused of smuggling weapons and medicine to Syria during the war. “I mean, there isn’t a single country in the entire world that would keep a prisoner detained for this long without a sentence.”
Mohammed Sablouh, a Lebanese lawyer, earlier told Al Jazeera that about 400 prisoners are on a hunger strike. “Ambulances enter daily to take [dozens of] them away because their condition is dire,” he said.
“The prisoners are refusing medication, food and water,” Sablouh, who is also the director of the Prisoners’ Rights Center at the Tripoli Bar Association, said on Wednesday.
The inmates at Roumieh prison went on a hunger strike on September 12 in protest against the suspension of the amnesty law, which could have benefitted convicted prisoners and undertrials.
Protests have also been staged in Lebanon’s Tripoli, a Sunni-majority city, against the suspension of the law.
‘A political opportunity’
Most of the prisoners on hunger strike are Sunnis who were arrested for their solidarity with the Syrian revolution against President Bashar al-Assad, who was toppled in December 2024 after more than 10 years of bloody war.
The Free Patriotic Movement (FPM), one of the country’s largest parties, filed an appeal before the Constitutional Council over concerns that some of the inmates were charged with “terrorism”, including attacking the Lebanese army and planning bombings.
Hezbollah, one of the most powerful political groups, initially backed the law in the hope of getting amnesty for prisoners from the Shia community. But the group’s political arm did not vote for the bill due to its opposition to the release of Sunni prisoners, many of whom were jailed for their links to the Syrian war.
The Iran-aligned Hezbollah was a backer of al-Assad during the war, and sent thousands of its fighters to Syria to defend the Syrian regime.
The Constitutional Council is expected to issue its verdict next month.
Jassem said Hezbollah and FPM were behind challenging the amnesty law. “They are treating this as a political opportunity; they want to capitalise on this issue – or perhaps gain something from it, though God only knows exactly what,” he said.
“Our support for the Syrian Revolution is a primary reason why some of our young men – indeed, the majority of us – were imprisoned,” he told Al Jazeera.
Overcrowded prisons
Lebanese prisons are notorious for being overcrowded and thousands of inmates spend years behind bars without trial. Lebanon’s current prison population stands at more than 6,200.
The law passed on August 12 aimed to address overcrowded prison conditions in the country.
“Prison overcrowding exceeds 330 percent of the facilities’ actual capacity,” Sablouh said.
“The situation in Lebanon’s prisons is truly tragic, it can no longer withstand any … shock or any overturning of the amnesty law.”
More than 40 prisoners died in 2025. “Some died due to medical neglect, others under torture. Some died by suicide due to prolonged trials and repeated postponements,” Sablouh said.
The Lebanese lawyer blamed judicial delays for the large number of inmates, many of them arrested for petty crimes.
He pointed out the failure of the judiciary “to adhere to Article 108 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which sets a limit for pre-trial detention: two months for misdemeanours, renewable for an equal period, and six months for felonies, renewable for an equal period [up to a maximum of one year].”

US Supreme Court allows Trump administration to resume 3rd-country deportations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:33:27 UTC
16:33:27 KST

Gizem Nisa Demir
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
The US Supreme Court on Tuesday allowed the Trump administration to temporarily resume deporting migrants to third countries not named in their removal orders, allowing the policy to remain in effect while the court considers the case.
News outlet NPR reported that the justices also agreed to hear arguments in the case in December. The court did not explain its decision to block a lower-court ruling, but asked the parties to address whether lower courts had jurisdiction to intervene and whether the policy violates due process or international conventions against torture, according to the outlet.
Solicitor General John Sauer called the policy "an essential tool to remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens." In a Sept. 24 filing, he argued: "While certain aliens may benefit from stalling their removal, the Nation does not."
The administration says it has deported tens of thousands of migrants to Mexico and countries in Africa and Latin America after their home countries refused to accept them.
The ruling marks the third time the Supreme Court has declined to halt such deportations ordered by US District Judge Brian Murphy in Boston. Murphy has argued that migrants are not given adequate notice or a meaningful opportunity to raise fears of torture or abuse.
The National Immigration Litigation Alliance, representing migrants in the case, said those deported without adequate safeguards have faced "prolonged and arbitrary detention, beatings and sexual assault, disappearance, and chain refoulement to countries from which the US had already granted them protection," lawyer Trina Realmuto wrote. "These harms cannot be undone."
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has said Murphy's rulings created logistical problems, including canceled flights, diplomatic tensions and delays in deporting people convicted of assault and drug offenses.
Three liberal justices dissented from Tuesday's decision.

The third-lowest level of sea ice in the history of observations has been recorded in Antarctica
Kyiv • UNN
The winter sea-ice extent in Antarctica is one million square kilometers below average. The past four years have been the worst on record.
The area of winter sea ice in Antarctica has reached one of the lowest levels ever recorded by satellite observations. The figure is approximately one million square kilometers below the long-term average maximum. The Guardian reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
Scientists have confirmed that winter sea ice in Antarctica reached the third-lowest level in the history of observations, one million square kilometers—or nearly 400,000 square miles—below the long-term average.
According to available data, satellites have been monitoring Antarctic sea ice since 1979, but this year's maximum is approximately one million square kilometers below the long-term average
Confirmation of the peak meant that the lowest figures ever recorded for sea ice on the continent were observed over the past four years—sea ice that is a vital component of the planet's climate and critically important for marine life. Dr. Walt Meier, a senior research scientist at the National Snow and Ice Data Center at the University of Colorado, said the center had refrained from declaring the maximum because at this stage of the continent's sea-ice cycle there is "a great deal of potential variability.
At the same time, the area of sea ice in Antarctica varies significantly every year. In summer, it shrinks to less than 2 million square kilometers; in winter, it expands, and in September it can exceed 17 million square kilometers.
Moreover, according to the publication, in recent years scientists have recorded record-low figures both in winter and in summer. Scientists link this to the possible impact of global warming
This is no longer an isolated event. Sea ice no longer covers the same area of the ocean as it did in the past. We are seeing one low winter temperature after another, and this indicates that sea ice is behaving differently because we have warmed our climate. This is not a problem of the future. It is a problem of the present
Recall
The WMO forecasts an 86% probability of a new temperature record by 2030. The warming will be influenced by the El Niño phenomenon and carbon dioxide emissions.

Anti-Zionist Hasidic Jew faces deportation from US after protesting Israeli flag at New York town hall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:33:12 UTC
16:33:12 KST

An Israeli Hasidic Jew who took part in a 2023 protest against an Israeli flag displayed outside a New York town hall is now facing deportation from the United States, The New York Times reported Wednesday.
Yehonatan Ovadia, 35, an Israeli citizen and religious teacher, has been held in federal immigration detention since August after U.S. authorities revoked his legal status over the incident. Ovadia, who has lived in the United States since 2022 on a religious worker visa, says he attended the demonstration but did not tear down the flag.
His lawyers filed a lawsuit in Manhattan federal court seeking his release, arguing that the Trump administration is retaliating against him for protected political and religious speech. They say authorities are conflating his anti-Zionist views with antisemitism.
“He’s against the Israeli government and the existence of the state of Israel for religious reasons, but to claim that he’s an antisemite is the peak of absurdity,” attorney Eric Lee told the Times.
Ovadia was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement after being summoned to immigration court in Manhattan on Aug. 28. He is being held at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn.
The Department of Homeland Security said Ovadia had “overstayed his welcome and refused to depart” after his legal status was revoked. In a statement cited by the Times, the department said the administration had acted within its legal authority and accused Ovadia of conduct including advocating violence, supporting terrorists, harassing Jews and stealing property.
Ovadia is a husband and father of five who lives in Rockland County, north of New York City, home to one of the largest concentrations of ultra-Orthodox Jews in the United States. He belongs to Satmar, a major Hasidic movement that opposes Zionism and the existence of the State of Israel on theological grounds.
According to the Times, Ovadia appears to be part of a smaller group of politically active Satmar Hasidim who have also publicly aligned themselves with the Palestinian cause. He has regularly attended anti-Israel demonstrations, at times carrying a Palestinian flag.
“We demonstrated for Gaza, for the liberation of Gaza, for the rights of the Palestinians and to show to the world that the Jews, real Judaism, want to have peace,” Ovadia told the Times in a phone interview from detention.
The case stems from a protest in Ramapo, New York, following the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel. Five days after the massacre, town supervisor Michael Specht had a large Israeli flag mounted outside the town hall in solidarity with Israelis.
About a month later, residents opposed to the display of a foreign flag on a municipal building organized a demonstration. Ovadia and other Satmar Jews argued that the Israeli flag represented a state whose existence they believe is forbidden under their interpretation of Jewish law.
Ovadia said he drove several people to the Nov. 13 protest, which drew around 20 Jewish demonstrators. Members of the fringe anti-Zionist Neturei Karta movement were also present.
“We wanted to express our opinion legally, peacefully,” Ovadia said.
Surveillance footage reviewed by the Times showed several men in traditional Hasidic dress tearing the flag down before two men cut it apart with scissors. Ovadia said a friend removed the flag and that he objected to the act and tried to leave immediately.
Police later stopped Ovadia after identifying his van in surveillance footage. He acknowledged driving people to the protest but said he did not know where the flag was.
Ovadia was initially charged with criminal mischief, petit larceny and conspiracy, all as hate crimes. The hate crime charges were later dropped. In February 2024, he pleaded guilty to disorderly conduct, which is classified as a violation rather than a crime under New York law, and paid a $200 fine plus an additional $125.
The immigration consequences emerged later. When Ovadia’s congregation sought an extension of his religious worker visa in September 2025, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services requested police and court records connected to the protest.
The agency issued what the Times described as an unusual split decision in May: It found Ovadia qualified to continue working in the United States as a religious worker but declined to allow him to remain in the country to do so.
In its decision, the agency said it had found no “conviction or commission of a crime involving moral turpitude,” but nevertheless used its discretion to deny his continued stay after weighing what it called “adverse factors.” These included the charges that had been dropped, the disorderly conduct violation and police records indicating that Ovadia declined to identify others involved in the protest.
The immigration decision did not cite Ovadia’s political activism or President Donald Trump’s executive order directing federal authorities to scrutinize noncitizens involved in conduct the administration considers antisemitic.
Ovadia’s attorneys argue, however, that his detention fits into the administration’s broader crackdown on foreign nationals involved in pro-Palestinian or anti-Israel activism.
“He’s very, very devoted, and he is strong-minded,” Rabbi Leibish Iliovits, who helped Ovadia settle in the United States, told the Times. “He would stand up for what he believes is right, and he wouldn’t back down, but he would not harm anyone.”
Ovadia’s lawyers were expected to seek his release at a bond hearing in Manhattan on Wednesday morning.

Ukraine names 23 Russian companies manufacturing missiles for Pantsir air defence system
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has released information on 23 Russian companies involved in a manufacturing partnership to produce 95Ya6 surface-to-air guided missiles used in Russian Pantsir surface-to-air missile and anti-aircraft artillery systems.
Source: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine on Telegram; War&Sanctions portal
Details: DIU said 95Ya6 missiles serve as the primary medium-range ammunition for various Pantsir modifications.
Quote from DIU: "A key role in the creation of these missiles is played by the Design Bureau of Instrument Making named after Academician A. G. Shipunov JSC – the main developer and manufacturer of 95Ya6 missiles. The company is known for its involvement in producing armaments for Orion unmanned systems, Krasnopol guided artillery shells and cannons for Sukhoi fighters."
Details: Crucially, about one-third of the companies disclosed by DIU are not currently subject to sanctions by any member of the sanctions coalition. These include:
- Komponent Plant JSC – manufacturer of non-contact target sensors for 95Ya6 missiles
- Saratov Electrical Instrument Manufacturing Plant named after Sergo Ordzhonikidze PJSC – producer and supplier of emitter and power supply units for these missiles
- Tambov Plant Elektropribor PJSC – manufacturer of flight-control actuators for the 95Ya6.
Quote: "DIU emphasises that to effectively weaken the aggressor's military potential, it is vital to impose coordinated restrictions on businesses that produce the full range of Russian weapons, rather than focusing solely on offensive systems."
For reference: Pantsir is a family of Russian self-propelled short-range surface-to-air missile and anti-aircraft artillery systems designed to protect key military and industrial facilities from aerial threats. Russia also uses these systems to reinforce air defence at low and ultra-low altitudes and to counter massed aerial attacks.
Details: DIU noted that Russian forces have been deploying Pantsir systems on rooftops in Moscow since 2023. This year, they were also spotted deploying another variant, the Pantsir-SMD-E. According to DIU, unlike earlier variants, this model is equipped with small TKB-1055 Gvozd anti-drone missiles instead of autocannons.
Background: DIU released an interactive 3D model and information on over 50 companies involved in the production of the Russian Pantsir-S1 air defence gun and missile system.

Violence against train staff is getting out of control, rail union VVMC has said in a call to politicians. The union says conductors and other employees of national rail company NS are increasingly being assaulted, threatened, and spat at by passengers.
In a letter reported by NOS, the union cites NS figures showing that reports of aggression and violence against staff more than doubled from 2,672 in 2023 to 6,442 in 2025. According to those figures, there have been 5,088 reports so far this year, including 1,368 involving physical violence and 105 threats with a weapon.
“These are no longer unpleasant situations,” the union wrote, according to NOS. “These are serious incidents of violence against people carrying out their public duty.”
The letter lists several recent attacks. In February, a conductor at Rotterdam Blaak station was beaten unconscious. The same happened to a conductor at Den Dolder station 6 months later.
On August 6, several NS staff and police officers were injured during the arrest of an aggressive passenger at Almere Centrum station. According to the union, one NS employee lost part of his thumb after being bitten, and a colleague suffered a broken wrist and torn tendons.
Lost powers
 The union also complained that senior conductors lost their enforcement powers in 2022. Since then, they can no longer write up offenders themselves or check personal details in the national population register.
Senior conductors were given bodycams this year, but the union says that does not make up for the powers they lost.
A VVMC spokesperson told news agency ANP that the union wants more NS security and service staff on trains.
“Politicians can no longer make do with stating that aggression is unacceptable. Action is needed now,” the letter says, according to NOS.
Licence register
 The letter follows the cabinet’s announcement on Tuesday that public transport enforcement officers will get access to the driving licence register. From Thursday, employers can apply to vehicle authority RDW for access.
Officers will then be able to use licence photos to identify fare dodgers and troublemakers who carry no ID, instead of waiting for the police.

Social minister butts heads with doctors over doctor-patient confidentiality

Unknown Publisher

Social minister butts heads with doctors over doctor-patient confidentiality
The Estonian Medical Association has sent an open letter to Social Affairs Minister Karmen Joller (Reform), raising concerns that police and other state agencies can access patient records.
Doctors stressed that the doctor-patient relationship is built on trust and that protecting patient confidentiality is a fundamental principle of medical ethics. Patients must be able to share information about their health with a doctor, confident that it will not reach others.
"The current situation, in which police and other state agencies have access to health records, is unacceptable and threatens trust in the entire healthcare system. Patient confidentiality must remain intact even after information is entered into a database," said Neeme Tõnisson, president of the Estonian Medical Association.
The health information system and its administrator, TEHIK, fall under the social affairs minister's authority. The minister is responsible for protecting the data.
The association is calling on Social Affairs Minister Karmen Joller (Reform) to stop access to health records through government information systems without patients' consent. It says access in exceptions clearly defined by law should require a court order.
"The medical association is breaking through an open door here because a legislative amendment is already being drafted with the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs and will soon go before the government. They know this very well," Joller wrote on social media.
Joller said TEHIK had done nothing wrong, as it had acted and continues to act under current law.
"The Police and Border Guard Board, whose employees sometimes requested health records without sufficient justification, has already changed its practices," she added.
Joller also stressed that no matter how good the systems are, people will always be the weak point. "And here I would also expect the doctors' representative organization to contribute."
Joller said she wanted the association to address healthcare workers who share patients' health information on social media.
The minister said the association should remind its members that sharing patient stories at a conference, training session or elsewhere requires the patient's written consent in a reproducible form. That consent must explain where, when and how the person's information will be used.
She also expects the association to stress to its members that they may not even disclose that a particular person is a particular doctor's patient.
Joller noted that the Data Protection Inspectorate (AKI) has also said patient confidentiality covers all information learned about a person during treatment, not just their diagnosis.
"Disclosing the information requires the patient's consent or a clear legal basis. I have asked AKI to assess the conduct of some doctors to determine whether proceedings should be opened. Why doesn't the medical association do that itself?" Joller wrote.

Royal Navy chief: JEF to create new combat units and get UK nuclear deterrence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:18:00 UTC
16:18:00 KST

Royal Navy chief: JEF to create new combat units and get UK nuclear deterrence
The Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), established to strengthen the security of 10 countries in the Nordic and Baltic region, will form new combat units centered on British military capabilities and nuclear deterrence, Royal Navy chief Gwyn Jenkins said.
The Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), a U.K.-led defense cooperation and rapid-response framework for Northern European countries, which also includes the Netherlands, Finland, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Iceland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, will sign an agreement in Oslo in November to establish new combat units, Gen. Gwyn Jenkins of the Royal Marines said in an interview with Finnish newspaper Iltalehti.
According to Jenkins, deploying JEF combat units would not necessarily require NATO's Article 5 to be invoked. The JEF complements NATO and allows its member states to respond rapidly to situations in which a JEF country comes under threat. He said wartime defense plans have already been drawn up for the new units, which should be capable of entering combat immediately if necessary. The plans cover operations by JEF countries' navies, their own national defense requirements and support for NATO's wartime plans.
The navies of JEF countries would form the core of the new units, although their composition and capabilities would depend on the specific mission. Traditional warships and submarines would be supported by military aircraft, helicopters, marines and special forces. Uncrewed systems, including aerial and maritime drones and other autonomous technologies, would also be used extensively. Jenkins described the approach as a hybrid fleet. Britain's state-of-the-art F-35 stealth fighters based aboard its aircraft carriers would be an important part of the JEF's capabilities.
The backbone of the force's military deterrence would be Britain's nuclear weapons, carried aboard British submarines patrolling the Atlantic Ocean. Jenkins said the Royal Navy maintains constant readiness to provide nuclear protection for the Nordic region as well. He stressed that Britain's nuclear deterrent is not only part of NATO's collective defense but also provides the U.K. with a sovereign defense capability.
According to Iltalehti, Britain's nuclear deterrent would in the future also extend through the JEF to all of its member countries, rather than solely through NATO's nuclear defense framework. Jenkins said this should also send a direct message to Moscow.
The Royal Navy chief linked the strengthening of the JEF primarily to Russia's behavior. He said the greatest problem is Moscow's unpredictability, meaning Russia could at some point test European democracies, including by testing NATO's Article 5 in the Baltic or Nordic region.
At the same time, the general stressed that there was no reason to panic. However, that did not mean the JEF or NATO could lapse into complacency; they must also prepare for worst-case scenarios.
Jenkins said the purpose of military preparedness is not to start a war but to prevent one. Deterrence must be sufficiently credible for Moscow to understand that an attack on a JEF or NATO country would be bound to fail. He said this requires maintaining readiness, conducting exercises and sustaining a military presence in the region.
In his interview with Iltalehti, the Royal Navy chief also said the U.K. was prepared to deploy its military capabilities to the Baltic Sea to strengthen Finland's defense. He said keeping sea routes open would be essential. If military support were needed for Finland, the Nordic countries and the Baltic states, functioning links between the Atlantic Ocean and the Baltic Sea would have to be maintained. Jenkins said Britain wants to use its frigates, destroyers and autonomous systems for this purpose and deploy them wherever they are needed in a particular situation.
The agreement to be signed in Oslo in November is expected to give these plans a concrete organizational structure. It should provide further details on how the JEF's collective defense in the Baltic region, the Nordic countries, the North Atlantic and the Arctic will be strengthened.
Finnish expert: This is a big deal
Finnish security expert Henri Vanhanen commented on the announcement that JEF units would be established, saying the move is far more significant for Finland's security than may currently be understood.
"This is not just about new combat units or British nuclear weapons. A framework is now being created in Northern Europe that would allow Britain and a group of Finland's closest partners to take rapid military action in a critical situation, even without NATO. This is a major change," he wrote on social media.
Vanhanen explained that if Russia were ever to seek to test the West, it would benefit from creating as ambiguous a situation as possible — one in which NATO's 32 member states would have to consider exactly what was happening, whether it constituted an attack and how to respond. The JEF, however, makes such a strategy more difficult.
"This would not even require a joint decision by all 10 JEF countries. Britain could, for example, act together with Finland, Sweden and other willing countries. Each country decides for itself how to use its forces," he noted.
With greater military capabilities now set to underpin the framework through the creation of new combat units and the strengthening of capabilities, particularly at sea, this is highly significant for Finland, Vanhanen wrote.
"We depend on the Baltic Sea and connections to the West. Britain, meanwhile, is one of Europe's strongest naval powers, a nuclear-armed state and a country capable of deploying truly significant military force here," the Finnish expert said. "So Britain is not simply promising to support Northern Europe. It is already building, in peacetime, a system through which it could come here to fight if necessary. The more of this that is prepared in advance, the less room there will be for uncertainty when a crisis occurs."
Vanhanen noted that while NATO is the foundation of Finland's defense, it does not make sense to put all its eggs in one basket. The JEF means that, if necessary, the U.K. and other willing countries can also act quickly by reaching agreements among themselves. Russia therefore can no longer count on hesitation within NATO buying it additional time.
"For this reason, I currently consider strengthening the JEF to be one of the most important pillars of Finland's defense," he concluded.
Vanhanen has worked as a researcher at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs, focusing on Finnish security and defense policy and Northern European security. He has also worked at Finland's Ministry for Foreign Affairs, the European Parliament, the U.S. Embassy in Helsinki and the Finnish Parliament. He has worked with the center-right National Coalition Party.

Source: Iltalehti

Fight between pilots reportedly triggers hijacking code on Dubai-Tel Aviv flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:17:35 UTC
16:17:35 KST

Mohammad Sio
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
- Passenger plane later lands in Saudi Arabia instead of Ben Gurion Airport
- Captain, first officer injured, transferred to hospital, says Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport
A fight between the pilots of a passenger plane flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv reportedly triggered a hijacking code before the aircraft landed in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, according to Israeli daily Ynet.
 
“An altercation occurred in the flight deck of flight FZ 1073,” said Flydubai, and said crew members traveling aboard the aircraft managed to secure the plane and divert it safely to Saudi Arabia.
 
The Dubai-based carrier said the flight, which was operating from Dubai International Airport to Ben Gurion International Airport, landed safely at Tabuk Airport and all passengers and crew were safe and accounted for.
 
Flydubai said the reasons and motives behind the altercation remain unknown and are subject to a formal investigation.
 
“We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts,” it cautioned.
 
The flight was carrying 174 passengers and briefly transmitted a distress signal.
 
Ynet said the aircraft had been scheduled to land at Ben Gurion Airport.
 
The aircraft was operated by Dubai-based carrier Flydubai and was en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv when the incident occurred.
 
According to the report, the code indicating a possible hijacking was activated during the cockpit altercation.
 
The aircraft subsequently landed at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia.
 
Around 90 minutes after takeoff, while entering Jordanian airspace, the aircraft transmitted code “7700,” the international code for a general emergency, the newspaper said.
 
It subsequently transmitted code “7500,” which is used to indicate unlawful interference with an aircraft, including a possible hijacking.
 
At around the same time, the plane changed course, returned to Saudi airspace and began flying at a low altitude over the kingdom, according to the report.
 
After initially heading south, the aircraft turned west while remaining inside Saudi airspace before landing in the kingdom.
 
Captain, first officer injured
 
Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Tabuk said in a statement
 
that its Air Traffic Control Center received a distress call from Flydubai flight FZ1073 at 8.44 am for an emergency landing.
 
It said an emergency was declared at the airport and preparations were made to assist the aircraft, which landed safely.
 
The airport said both the aircraft captain and first officer were injured and transferred to a hospital for necessary medical care.
 
There are conflicting reports over the nationalities of the two officers. Channel 12 said the crew consisted of a Russian pilot and a Ukrainian co-pilot, while Ynet reported that the pilot suspected of attempting to crash the aircraft is of Omani origin and that the second pilot is Emirati.
 
Israeli Channel 12 later said the incident appeared not to be security-related and that authorities were checking whether the distress signal had been activated accidentally because of an argument between the pilot and co-pilot.
 
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz have ordered military rescue planes to be sent to Saudi Arabia to bring home Israeli passengers on the Fly Dubai flight.
 
Flydubai later informed Israeli authorities that a replacement aircraft would be dispatched from Dubai to Saudi Arabia to bring back the Israeli passengers who had been on the flight, Ynet reported.
 
The Israel Airports Authority, meanwhile, denied reports that the country’s airspace had been closed during the incident.
 
Senior officials in Israel’s aviation industry said suspicion of a security incident on the Flydubai flight had not yet been ruled out, Ynet reported.
 
According to an initial assessment cited by the officials, one of the pilots allegedly "attempted to cause a crash," while the other pilot managed to thwart the attempt with the help of Israeli passengers.
 
The Israeli Prime Minister’s Office said the situation was “under control” and that “all means are now being deployed to safely return the Israeli passengers to Israel.”

====================================================================================================

Vaccines may counter Alzheimer's disease. New position paper explains how
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:16:20 UTC
16:16:20 KST

Ever since the accusation, long since debunked, that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine was associated with autism, vaccination has been going out of style. Vaccines had some rebound after the COVID pandemic began, but anti-vaxxers continue to promote vaccine hesitancy; meanwhile, as resistance proliferates, the United States has reported the highest numbers of measles cases in 35 years.
No credible research argues the case against vaccines, and evidence accrued over generations demonstrates that they reduce the incidence and severity of disease. Yet in recent years, it has become evident that vaccination can protect not only our bodies against the diseases they are designed to foil, but our minds.
Now a position statement in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease by a panel of experts, the "Vaccines for Dementia Study Group," including Chuck Greenblatt of Hebrew University and Richard Lathe of the University of Edinburgh, highlights the evidence between various infections and the risk of developing Alzheimer's disease, and the corollary – that vaccination against unrelated diseases can diminish the probability of Alzheimer's disease.
"Hallmark" clumps of abnormal proteins found in the brains of Alzheimer's sufferers weren't the cause of the dementia, as was assumed for decades. They are a byproduct of the brain's fight against infection. And, crucially: "Findings that vaccine recipients are at reduced risk of developing Alzheimer's disease have now been replicated around the world," the statement sums up.
Bow wow how?
Vaccine skepticism may stem from more than personal fear of needles, as suggested by the fact that even inoculating Bowser against rabies is becoming passé. A study of 2,200 American adults found that 37 percent think canine vaccines are unsafe and unnecessary; and a fifth assume they're ineffective.
This is terrible for the pets and their vets. The burgeoning skepticism may also augur ill for our future neurodegenerative disease rates, going by the position statement, which strongly supports the theory of a pathogenic origin for Alzheimer's disease, and the pro-vaxx lifestyle for the greater good of our continuing cognizance.
How could vaccines against other problems prevent Alzheimer's? By causing "immunopotentiation" – strengthening the immune system in general. Do all vaccines cause generalized immunopotentiation? Some do more than others; the anti-tuberculosis shot called BCG and the anti-shingles vaccine Shingrix exhibit heightened potential in reducing the probability of Alzheimer's disease.
The statement does not present new research but summarizes decades of research into Alzheimer's. They stress that so far, links between pathogen infection and dementia, and between vaccination and dementia prevention, are correlational.
"Nevertheless, the consistency of findings across vaccine classes, populations and study designs supports investigation of immunopotentiation as a potential strategy for Alzheimer's disease prevention," it concludes.
Could the results be skewed by "healthy vaccinee bias"? No, which they demonstrate through three recent "natural experiments," which exclude the possibility that people who get vaccinated are merely more healthy and less at risk of dementia." (Natural experiments are where a factor is changed by nature or circumstance, rather than by the investigators themselves.)
All three studies exclude this bias and suggest that shingles and influenza vaccines can protect against dementia.
Note that our pets can develop dementia too. Behavioral changes have been observed in aging cats and dogs, who may become more prone to "accidents" in the house. Maybe this would be worse if the authorities didn't force us to vaccinate our pets on a regular basis.
Plaque and perdition
Alzheimer's specifically is estimated to afflict one in 11 percent of people 65 or older, but its cause remains unclear. It can't even be diagnosed in the living. The verdict remains problematic until autopsy, but doubts are arising even about the classic diagnostic method.
Since 1991, diagnosis of Alzheimer's has relied on postmortem findings of abnormal protein buildup in the brain: neurofibrillary tangles (tau protein) and clumps of amyloid-beta protein.
But there are snags to that diagnostic method. Some people with Alzheimer's have no abnormal proteins, and some elderly people with perfect cognition have brains riddled with plaque. Tests of monoclonal antibodies designed to remove amyloid-beta plaques were not a success, and a panel of world experts concluded that the effects of plaque removal on dementia were "absent or trivial." There have been recent protests about corporate fiddling with statistics to try to show that the clumps cause disease.
All this suggests that protein buildup in the brain isn't the disease: It's the hallmark of a fight against inflammation, likely within the brain itself.
It's become clear that our brains are not the sterile environments we once assumed. They do house some bacteria, fungi and viruses, Lathe and colleagues report separately. The microbes identified in brains appear to be a subset of the gut microbiome. Many others have found similar results, Lathe says, notably the group of Louis Carrasco in Madrid.
Lathe and colleagues in the U.S. have compiled a list of individuals where treatment with antimicrobials apparently reversed the trajectory of dementia, and also found an unusual historical report of a 24-year-old with premature Alzheimer's, apparently as a result of scarlet fever.
Is infection of the brain itself necessary? The critical issue is the inflammation the bug causes, which need not be in the brain, Greenblatt says. But clearly the brain can get infected, for example through the nose; respiratory infection, such as community-acquired pneumonia, correlates with higher dementia rates; also, people with dementia and Parkinson's lose the ability to identify smells.
The heartbreak of brain herpes?
One agent singled out as a possible culprit is herpes simplex, or HSV-1, which heavens knows is common enough. Ruth Itzhaki of the University of Oxford has written that there is "overwhelming evidence" that HSV-1 plays a role in the case of people who also have a certain gene involved in fat metabolism, APOE4 – which is also a known risk for Alzheimer's disease.
Recurring herpes outbreaks cause immunological reactions that may lead to the features Alzheimer's disease, she tells Haaretz. So, herpes may not cause Alzheimer's, but may be associated.
While she suspects herpes may play a major role in our species' dementia problem, the evidence points at many agents - bacteria and fungi, she says, and agrees with the thesis of immunopotentiation to diminish dementia risk. "The facts speak for themselves," she says.
Lathe personally doubts that herpes is a major cause. "Our big study [the Pathobiome] found very little herpes," he explains, adding that if Alzheimer's was caused by herpes viruses, it should be treatable by antiherpetics. Those do work against herpetic encephalitis or neurology; they don't work against Alzheimer's disease, he sums up. What the brain biome project has found so far are "the usual pathogens" – staphylococcus aureus bacteria, candida albicans fungus and the like. Hi guys!
A trivial cost
So the cause of Alzheimer's disease remains obscure, nor is there any cure, despite some claims of drugs that "reverse" the trajectory. There is no question that reducing Alzheimer's incidence would be a boon for the world economy. Vaccines are cheap, typically a few dollars a pop, while the cost of treating the symptoms of Alzheimer's is estimated at about $1.3 trillion a year worldwide, the authors say.
"Even a 10 percent reduction in Alzheimer's disease rates would save $38 billion each year in a single country, the USA," they write, and about £4 billion a year in the United Kingdom. So, vaxxing costs peanuts compared with the financial burden of Alzheimer's, the authors point out; and as the world population continues to grow and age, the burden of care will increase.
There are caveats. Studies detecting diminished Alzheimer's rates among the vaccinated are predominantly observational, the authors caution, but the sheer amount of evidence, activity – going back over a century – weighs against a bias. As early as 1908, it was observed that people, especially children, given the tuberculosis vaccine called Bacille Calmette-Guérin exhibited significantly reduced rates of dying from other infectious diseases. Albert Calmette, the co-inventor of BCG, speculated that BCG somehow conferred "a special aptitude" to resist other infections.
This was prophetic. During the COVID pandemic starting in 2019, it proved that inoculation with BCG administered years before the outbreak correlated with improved COVID outcomes. It is true that the efficacy of protection was inconsistent, but that could reflect different vaccine types used, different susceptibilities of the study participants and differences in a host of other parameters.
The bottom line is that some studies, if not all, found correlation between BCG and a reduction in all-cause mortality.
The anti-TB shot also confers protective effects against a range of conditions including eczema, diabetes, and multiple sclerosis.
At what age? "If you received BCG as a kid and were lucky enough to get booster at 14, you have some chance the effects would last 50 years," Greenblatt answers. "Immunity wanes with age. Most childhood vaccines need boosters. That's why Shingrix [against shingles] is so important, as a booster – the bug has been there all the time; the herpes is just waiting to come out."
You again, herpes. Lathe sums up that vaccination in general seems beneficial to Alzheimer's reduction though some are clearly better. BCG and Shingrix are better, for example.
One paper identifies 45 viral exposures that were "significantly associated with increased risk of neurodegenerative disease."
What have we? Increasing indications that our wellness and vaccine uptake influence the risk of developing Alzheimer's. A recent meta-analysis concluded that adult vaccinations, particularly against with shingles, influenza, pneumonia and the "Tdap" vaccines against tetanus, diphtheria, and whooping cough, are associated with a lower risk of dementia.
Why not end back with our best friends. The cost of vaccinating Froofroo against rabies runs $10 to $55 a year in the United States. The cost of suspected rabies is her life – there is no cure – and if a rabies suspect digs her fangs into your ankle, anti-rabies shots will cost you hundreds to thousands of dollars. In other words, protection is vastly cheaper and unlike the disease, it isn't life-threatening. That is the very point that the statement makes in the case of Alzheimer's disease as well.

Ian Bremmer: 'We have passed peak Trump in terms of disruption on the global stage'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:15:18 UTC
16:15:18 KST

Ian Bremmer: 'We have passed peak Trump in terms of disruption on the global stage'
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
François Picard is pleased to welcome Ian Bremmer, the American political scientist, author, and founder and president of Eurasia Group and GZERO Media. According to Bremmer, we may now be entering the autumn of the "Donroe Doctrine" and the MAGA era: an "America First" isolationist approach in which President Donald Trump envisions a return to "greatness" in Gilded Age fashion. But is this the America voters had envisioned?
Yet Bremmer is equally emphatic about something else: "America, of course, is a democracy where the people do express their will." Ultimately, he believes, the political consequences of Trump's second term will be determined by voters. He has argued that Republicans risk losing the House, and possibly the Senate, in the upcoming midterm elections.
For Bremmer, however, the Trump phenomenon is also deeply personal. "President Trump and his administration frequently put themselves above the interests of the country," he says. "And this really has nothing to do with the Republican Party." Trump, he points out, was once a Democrat. In Bremmer's view, this makes the phenomenon distinctly Trumpian, and suggesting that "this pattern will go away after Trump."
Meanwhile, Trump has mastered what Steve Bannon famously called "flooding the zone": overwhelming the political system with a torrent of executive orders, announcements, and initiatives. But Bremmer cautions against assuming that everything the president declares, or orders, automatically becomes American policy.
"Trump says a lot of things, and he even writes a lot of executive orders," Bremmer observes, "but what ends up being executed and implemented turns out to be a fraction of that."
Courts, Congress, foreign governments, economic interests and, at times, members of Trump's own party have all acted as constraints on what the administration can actually implement.
And yet, beyond the domestic political struggle, Trump's foreign policy is reshaping America's relationship with the world. And while "Trump is deeply unpopular in France, across Europe, in Canada and the UK, he's actually quite popular among most of the Latin American countries".
Across much of Latin America, there has been a rightward political shift, and Trump's hardline policies have found greater resonance, particularly where questions of security, borders, drugs and instability are immediate and consequential. Venezuela, meanwhile, has become one of the most consequential and controversial expressions of his foreign policy, and a centerpiece of what has come to be called the "Donroe Doctrine," a Trump-era interpretation of the Monroe Doctrine asserting a more forceful American role throughout the Western Hemisphere.
The stakes became particularly stark after the United States captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, in a military operation in January 2026. Trump subsequently said the United States would oversee Venezuela during the transition.
At the United Nations General Assembly in September, Trump himself invoked the language of conquest and plunder when speaking about Venezuela and the United States' post-Maduro role. After describing a major oil deal between the United States and Venezuela, he declared: "To the victor belong the spoils."
It was precisely this worldview that prompted one of Bremmer's sharpest critiques of Trump, expressed in an interview with Katy Tur on MS NOW during the week of the General Assembly.
"The most consequential thing," Bremmer had argued, "is when President Trump spoke about Venezuela, declaring, 'To the victor goes the spoils,' which is the way he sees Iran. It's the way he sees AI. But it's absolutely antithetical to the reason the United States set up the United Nations after World War II."
He went on to describe Trump's UN speech as "a knife in the creation of that order," arguing that "you couldn't have said something that was more problematic for what the Americans used to stand for on the ashes of the Second World War that we won."
Bremmer contrasts that philosophy with the principle he believes originally shaped the postwar international order: not that victory entitles you to the gains, but that it carries great responsibility: for governance, stability and peace, not only for the United States but for all nations of the world.
So what happens when the country that built the postwar order begins to challenge the principles on which that order rests?

The European Commission has approved the first five European Defence Projects of Common Interest (EDPCI) worth $369 million, with Ukraine included in four of them.
The projects will strengthen Europe’s defense capabilities by developing key military systems together. Following today’s decision, the defense projects can now move towards funding.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
EDPCI is a funding track within the European Defence Industry Programme (EDIP), a $1.7 billion EU-wide initiative to strengthen and modernize Europe’s defense industry. The Commission allocated €325 million ($368.6 million) to support the creation and deployment of EDPCI, a program of large-scale industrial projects that lays the groundwork for member states to collaborate on major defense initiatives.
“The proposal concerns an area of shared competence, in particular the industrial dimension of the Union’s defence readiness. The objectives pursued by the proposal cannot be sufficiently achieved by Member States acting alone”, the European Commission wrote in the document.
The industrial projects focus on five priority areas: drones and counter-drone systems, maritime and seabed defense, space, air and missile defense, and strengthening security along the EU’s Eastern Flank, wrote the European Commission on its website. Ukraine is participating in all areas except space.
Project Details
The industrial projects focus on the following key initiatives:
Russia Hits Kyiv With Ballistic Missiles, Killing 2 Women as Child Dies in Wider Region
- Drone and Counter-Drone European Resolve (DECODER): Aims to enable the coordinated development, scaling, and deployment of European unmanned and counter-unmanned systems to address critical capability gaps across member states. The estimated budget is $3.97 billion to $5.68 billion by 2033.
- Integrated Maritime and Seabed Defence (IMSD): Seeks to establish a federated and interoperable European maritime and seabed defense architecture. It is designed to strengthen the EU’s ability to prevent, detect, deter, and respond to threats across the maritime domain. The estimated budget is $48.9 billion to $81.8 billion by 2045.
- EU Federated Integrated Air and Missile Defence (EU-FIAMD): Designed to provide member states with a collective and effective integrated air and missile defense system, including early warning information and command-and-control capabilities. The estimated budget is $62.5 billion to $90.9 billion by 2040.
- Eastern Flank Watch (EFW): A comprehensive multi-domain effort to enhance the security of the EU’s eastern border, ensuring the protection of the entire union and strengthening its defense readiness. The estimated budget is $68.2 billion to $113.6 billion by 2036.
- Space: While Ukraine will not participate in this specific initiative, the project aims to create new market opportunities and reduce the EU’s structural dependence in the space sector. The estimated budget is up to $27.3 billion by 2034.

A Flydubai flight carrying more than 170 passengers from Dubai to Tel Aviv diverted to Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after transmitting emergency transponder codes, including one associated with a possible hijacking, triggering an Israeli military response before authorities determined the incident was not believed to involve a hijacking.
Flight FZ1073, operated by a Boeing 737 MAX 8, was traveling toward Ben Gurion Airport when it transmitted the international emergency code 7700 and briefly switched to code 7500, which is used to indicate unlawful interference or a possible hijacking.
The aircraft subsequently changed course, descended sharply and headed toward Saudi Arabia, according to flight-tracking data and Israeli media reports. It eventually landed safely at Tabuk Airport.
The unusual flight path and emergency signals prompted Israeli authorities to treat the situation as a potential security threat.
Israeli media reported that the Air Force scrambled fighter jets after the alert, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz held an urgent security consultation with senior defense officials.
The Israeli military also carried out a situation assessment involving the Air Force and other security agencies as authorities sought to determine what had happened aboard the aircraft.
A security source cited by Ynet said there was no confirmed information that the aircraft had been hijacked and that the pilot had activated a distress signal.
The Prime Minister's Office later said the diversion to Saudi Arabia was not believed to have been the result of a hijacking.
The aircraft departed Dubai International Airport early Wednesday on its scheduled service to Tel Aviv. It was carrying roughly 174 passengers, according to reports, including about 27 children.
During the flight, the aircraft transmitted the 7700 general emergency code before briefly transmitting 7500, the code associated with unlawful interference.
The 7500 signal immediately raised the possibility of a hijacking, particularly because the aircraft was headed toward Israel, where security authorities have remained on high alert amid the wider regional security situation.
Flight-tracking data showed the aircraft changing direction and descending to a much lower altitude than its normal cruising level before continuing toward Saudi Arabia. Reports said the aircraft descended to around 15,000 feet.
The combination of the emergency signals, course reversal, descent and temporary concerns over communications intensified the response.
Israeli media initially reported that contact with the aircraft had been lost, although subsequent reports indicated that it was continuing toward Saudi Arabia and was expected to land at Tabuk.
The aircraft eventually landed safely.
The alert prompted an immediate military response in Israel, with fighter jets scrambled as authorities assessed whether the aircraft posed a security threat.
Netanyahu and Katz convened an emergency consultation, while senior military officials assessed the situation with the Air Force.
Other Israeli security bodies were also reported to have been involved in assessing the incident.
Some Israeli reports said departures from Ben Gurion Airport were temporarily affected while the situation was being evaluated.
The response reflected the seriousness with which aviation authorities treat a 7500 transmission. The code is designed to alert air traffic control and relevant security agencies to a possible unlawful interference situation.
However, the transmission alone does not establish that a hijacking has taken place.
As the situation developed, Israeli reports indicated that the incident was not believed to have been caused by a hijacking or an external security threat.
Reports cited by Israeli media suggested that a physical altercation between the pilots may have prompted the emergency signals and the subsequent diversion.
That account remained subject to further verification, however, and detailed official information from flydubai or UAE aviation authorities was not immediately available in the initial coverage.
The Israeli Prime Minister's Office confirmed the broader assessment that the diversion was not believed to have been a hijacking incident.
The aircraft's safe landing in Tabuk brought the immediate security alert to an end.
The incident nevertheless demonstrated how quickly an aviation emergency can escalate when an aircraft transmits a hijacking-related code, particularly on a route involving Israel.
The flight was ultimately diverted well before reaching its planned destination at Ben Gurion Airport.
Rather than continuing toward Israel, the aircraft headed for Tabuk in northwestern Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely after the emergency.
Israeli authorities subsequently scaled back their response after determining that there was no confirmed hijacking threat.
The exact circumstances inside the cockpit, including what prompted the emergency transmissions and the aircraft's abrupt change in course and altitude, remained under review.
The incident also highlighted the sensitivity of commercial aviation routes between the United Arab Emirates and Israel, which were established following the normalization of relations under the Abraham Accords.

But analysts expect the two days of talks to end in a deadlock as Trump's tariffs strain relationships while China rejects concerns about its exports, which critics see as driven by excess industrial capacity.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer defended Washington's approach at a Tuesday roundtable in Milwaukee, saying the administration "is not anti-trade."
He added that countries are facing similar challenges with global overcapacity and "non-market policies."
This week, key US trading partners like Canada and the European Union are also expected to push for deeper trade ties outside the United States.
"Don't expect any breakthroughs in Milwaukee," Josh Lipsky of the Atlantic Council think tank told AFP, noting Trump's preference for bilateral negotiations.
Even as G20 partners will be anxious to find ways to cooperate with the world's biggest economy, "they will also be under pressure to voice their concerns with tariffs," added former US trade official Wendy Cutler, now at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
The United States holds the rotating presidency of the G20, which comprises 19 nations plus the EU and the African Union.
'Unfairly targeted'
Trump has unleashed a barrage of tariffs on trading partners since last year, separately targeting sectors like steel and autos.
Although the Supreme Court struck down Trump's country-specific tariffs in February, Washington has since alleged insufficient action against forced labour to slap new tariffs on 60 economies.
These include China, India and the EU.
The president's sectoral duties remain intact too, straining ties.
And Washington is investigating 16 partners over excess industrial capacity, a complaint commonly levied at China. Critics say this floods markets, unfairly suppressing prices.
But ongoing US probes go beyond the world's number two economy, bringing the threat of more tariffs to the EU and G20 countries like Japan and South Korea.
Cutler expects some countries will "mince no words" regarding the investigation, feeling "they are being unfairly targeted."
China "will continue to deny the issue of exporting overproduction," by trying to convince others that it is doing good by providing high-quality and low-priced goods, she said.
"This will be a hard sell," Cutler told AFP, as countries see employment and commercial fallout from waves of Chinese imports.
"Meanwhile, members are wondering how much they should agree to with the Trump administration, given trade policy could change in the US after 2028," Lipsky said, referring to the next US presidential election.
Diversifying
With Trump's trade wars, all eyes are on G20 members' efforts to deepen trade ties outside the US, or strike deals with his administration.
Canada and the EU are expected to try and boost trade and investment with others, as a spat between Ottawa and Washington intensifies.
Canada's international trade minister Maninder Sidhu stressed Ottawa's support for "open, predictable and rules-based trade."
He plans to speak with partners to "reinforce a multilateral trading system," as officials try to diversify an economy they see as too reliant on an increasingly protectionist United States.
Others like India could finalise a long-awaited trade deal with the United States. Observers are also monitoring for signs of further pressure on Iran.
Outside the G20, workers and activists are protesting what they see as the Trump administration's broken promises to improve conditions for workers, farmers and smaller businesses.
John Drew, who chairs the political arm of the United Auto Workers (UAW) union in Wisconsin, laments the loss of manufacturing jobs in the state.
While the UAW does not rule out using targeted duties to protect jobs, he said, Trump's sweeping "use of tariffs has done nothing to bring back jobs and rebuild manufacturing."

F-16s get new friend-or-foe system cleared for service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:02:44 UTC
16:02:44 KST

- BAE Systems' AN/APX-127(V)1 identification friend or foe system received AIMS certification for the U.S. Air Force F-16.
- The company expects to begin delivering the first 90-unit production lot this year.
BAE Systems’ new identification friend or foe system for the F-16 has been certified by the U.S. Department of War, clearing it for use on U.S. Air Force fighters, the company said Sept. 29.
The AN/APX-127(V)1 Combined Interrogator Transponder received AIMS certification, the approval that shows an identification system meets U.S. and NATO standards and can work with allied equipment. BAE Systems said it expects to start delivering the first production lot of 90 units this year. The company did not say which F-16 units will receive them first, who ordered the first lot or how much it is worth.
An identification friend or foe system, known as IFF, lets an aircraft send a coded radio question to another aircraft and receive a coded answer, so a pilot or air defense operator can tell whether it is friendly before deciding whether to fire. The new unit combines the interrogator, which asks the question, and the transponder, which answers it, in one box sized for fighter jets.
The system is certified for Mark XIIB IFF with Mode 5, the encrypted military mode used by the United States and NATO, and Mode S, which is used in civilian air traffic control. BAE Systems said it adds extra receive channels so the aircraft can passively pick up other aircraft’s Mode 5 Level 2 signals, which carry position data, and ADS-B broadcasts, the location signals most civilian aircraft send out. That lets a pilot build a picture of nearby traffic without sending out interrogations of their own.
The unit meets the latest cryptography and cybersecurity requirements, and its open architecture allows new features to be added through software instead of hardware changes, the company said. It fits in the same space as three older BAE combined interrogator transponders, the AN/APX-113, AN/APX-125 and AN/APX-126, which are used on several U.S. and international aircraft, so it can be swapped in without redesigning the aircraft.
“This solution provides added security and real-time information pilots need in a variety of threat environments,” said Seth Guanu, Combat Identification Products program area director at BAE Systems.
BAE Systems says it has delivered more than 1,500 interrogators, 6,000 combined interrogator transponders and 16,000 transponders over more than 80 years. The new system is built at the company’s sites in Greenlawn, New York, and Austin, Texas.

Gene therapy: The breakthrough that inspired Spider-Man | Euronews Tech Talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:02:00 UTC
16:02:00 KST

Although an inspiration for science fiction movies, gene therapy is real. Here is how it works and what could be improved about it.
If you are a science nerd and a Marvel fan, you might have noticed that gene therapy, a promising medical approach to treat diseases by targeting their genetic causes, made an appearance in the latest iteration of the arachnid superhero franchise, Spider-Man: Brand New Day.
In this film, Peter Parker or Spider-Man feels weird. His DNA mutates, and his spider side starts taking over, providing him with new and sometimes difficult-to-control powers.
To manage them, Parker resorts to RNA interference, a real-world gene therapy technique that silences specific gene activity.
But how does gene therapy work? And what are its limitations?
To answer these and more questions, Euronews Tech Talks interviewed Alberto Auricchio, director of the Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine in Naples, professor at the University of Naples and president of the European Society of Gene & Cell Therapy.
How does gene therapy work?
Originally used to treat monogenic diseases, gene therapy is now employed and studied to find a treatment for a wide range of illnesses, including cancer and HIV.
“Gene therapy basically targets the root cause of a genetic disease,” Auricchio explained. This medical approach essentially consists in the introduction of nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) into target cells and tissues for therapeutic purposes.
Nucleic acids can be introduced into target cells either in vivo (directly within the body) or ex vivo (in cells extracted from an organism and then transplanted inside the body). In both cases, delivery is achieved using either viral or non-viral vectors.
Types of gene therapy include gene addition and gene editing, with the latter being further divided into gene silencing and gene correction.
As the names suggest, gene addition consists of adding a gene; gene correction is the fixing of a dysfunctional gene; and gene silencing deactivates a gene.
What’s the state of gene therapy in Europe?
Gene therapy is a complex and evolving field, but it is not only material for science-fiction stories. “We are beyond clinical trials now. There are approved [gene therapy] products that are available to patients,” Auricchio told Euronews Next.
The first in vivo gene therapy approved in Europe was Glybera, which received the European Commission marketing authorisation in 2012 and offers a medical treatment for patients with severe or multiple pancreatitis attacks due to lipoprotein lipase deficiency.
The first ex vivo gene therapy approved in Europe was Strimvelis, which received authorisation in 2016. This drug treats severe combined immunodeficiency due to adenosine deaminase deficiency and was developed at the Hospital San Raffaele in Milan.
What makes gene therapy promising?
Among others, gene therapy has a crucial advantage: it is a durable treatment.
“There are approved gene therapy drugs, for which we have decades of follow-up in patients where we know that the therapeutic effect is stable over decades, and in theory for the lifetime of the individual,” Auricchio explained.
As a matter of fact, gene therapy drugs are designed to be a once-in-a-lifetime treatment, meaning that a single administration should last for a long time.
On the other hand, beyond the scientific difficulties, the main limitation of gene therapy is the economic obstacle.
“These are very expensive drugs to be developed, and those that get to the market have very high prices, some of them matching millions of euros,” Auricchio explained.
For instance, the cost of Strimvelis amounts to €594,000 excluding VAT.
“These drugs are developed for rare diseases in many cases, which are not a very attractive market for typical developers like pharmaceutical companies; the high development cost of this drug is a challenge,” Auricchio said.
Spider-Man: Brand New Day does not explore the economic problem behind gene therapy. Peter Parker is lucky to know the brilliant scientist Bruce Banner or Hulk, who helps him develop his therapy.
But real-life science is often more challenging than a superhero movie.
Euronews Tech Talks is a podcast produced, written, presented and published in English.

I heard one thing loud and clear in Andy Burnham’s landmark speech: the left has won the arguments | Owen Jones
Unknown

As Andy Burnham delivered his conference speech to the Labour faithful yesterday, it was hard not to recall Jeremy Corbyn’s words after the party’s shattering 2019 election defeat. “I am proud that on austerity, on corporate power, on inequality and the climate emergency,” he wrote for this publication, “we have won the arguments and rewritten the terms of political debate.” Given Boris Johnson’s 80-seat majority, widespread mockery ensued.
But when it comes to rhetoric, who can now deny that the left has won the argument? A Labour prime minister has declared that “Britain has been on the wrong path for a long time”, listing five villains: “Deindustrialisation, deregulation, privatisation, austerity, Brexit.” His speech was infused with class politics, as he condemned a society “run for vested interests, not in the public interest, with power held in too few hands”.
When he committed to break with the “flawed thinking of the last 40 years”, he lumped together Conservative and Labour governments. He has already repeatedly labelled the culprit: neoliberalism. This has long been the received wisdom of the left: that as Clement Attlee’s postwar government established a social-democratic consensus that the Tories upheld for a generation, so Margaret Thatcher bequeathed a settlement that New Labour maintained.
These beliefs were condemned to the fringes of Labour, even though Tony Blair himself eventually confessed: “I always thought my job was to build on some of the things she had done rather than reverse them.” Any mention of neoliberalism was a sure way of provoking an eye-roll from a mainstream politician or commentator. We were denied any debate about an economic system based on extraction rather than investment; an economy based on financialisation rather than making things. Corbynism was an insurgency against all of this – until it crashed on the shores of Brexit.
Add to this the new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, telling those who opposed Israel’s genocide and were infuriated by Labour’s position on Gaza: “You were right.” We should add, too, the disastrous past wars backed by Labour: Iraq, Afghanistan and Libya.
The left should feel vindicated by the political shift taking place. We were right – at home and abroad. We were mocked, demonised and marginalised for making these arguments. Now most of the left’s worldview is embraced by the Labour top brass. This happened after Keir Starmer’s faction based their entire project on defining themselves against the left. As the Labour activist Ali Milani – who was part of Burnham’s team – told me, that strategy nearly brought about the party’s destruction.
Burnham only became prime minister because Labour’s leftwing voters rebelled – by defecting en masse to Zack Polanski’s Green party in the Gorton and Denton byelection, then in local elections in England, Scotland and Wales. That is clearly understood by Burnham’s team, or they would not be so confidently doubling down on their new strategy.
But winning the argument on a rhetorical level is not the same as substance. Burnham is clearly shifting towards state intervention. That’s taking the form of Great British Grid, a new publicly owned network body, and he condemned privatised water as “a symbol of what has gone wrong with Britain”.
The shift in this direction actually began under the last Conservative government. Did Liz Truss not commit to a subsidy for energy bills worth tens of billions of pounds? What of Rishi Sunak being forced to bring railways into public ownership? Starmerism expanded the semi-nationalisation of the railway and founded Great British Energy. Neoliberalism has exhausted itself and governments are being forced to abandon its tenets, whether they want to or not.
But full public ownership of water seems far off, with “public control” acting as a rather flexible label. Burnham has committed to a large-scale building of new council homes and preventing them from being flogged off through right to buy. Yet he has already backtracked on a pledge to spend the government’s entire £39bn affordable homes programme on council and social housing.
Crucially, he remains committed to the suffocating fiscal rules that block the investment Britain’s crumbling infrastructure and starved services need, especially given there remains no promise to hike taxes on the well-to-do.
While committing to a national care service is extremely welcome, scrapping the triple lock on pensions is not. Britain still spends significantly less on pensions than other major European countries such as Germany, France and Spain, and about two million pensioners languish in poverty.
Consider, too, that the Labour parliamentary benches were stuffed with candidates deemed loyal to the Starmer project. The rightwing factionalists who ran the party may currently be sulking on the fringes, but do not underestimate their capacity to inflict damage.
A key difference between Burnhamism and what came before may well be expressed by what Miliband told activists attending a Labour fringe event organised by the soft-left pressure group Mainstream. “Too often in the past, we thought that kicking some of our supporters would do us political credit,” he said, “and we were absolutely wrong.” Offending people “in the progressive community”, he admitted, was sometimes done “deliberately”.
Because of pressure from the streets and the ballot box, Labour has shifted its rhetoric. The substance is a bit more complicated. Where Starmerism defined itself against the left, could this new government be pushed in a more progressive direction? That question has not yet been answered. But the left should indeed feel emboldened. The winds are shifting in our direction.
- 
  Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist. His latest book, The Fall of the West: How They Really Lost It, is published on 1 October. Order your copy at the Guardian bookshop

Iraq announces end of US-led international coalition mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:52:26 UTC
15:52:26 KST

Murat Basoglu and Ikram Kouachi
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Iraq on Wednesday announced the end of the US-led international coalition’s mission, marking a transition to bilateral relations with coalition member states, the prime minister’s security adviser said.
 
In a statement carried by the official Iraqi News Agency, Qasim al-Araji called the move an “important milestone,” saying it followed negotiations and understandings that began in July 2021.
 
US forces completed their withdrawal from their remaining positions in Iraq by the end of this month.
 
He said the new phase would involve “bilateral relations with its countries” aimed at consolidating Iraq’s sovereignty.
 
Araji credited the victory over the ISIS (Daesh) terrorist group to “the sacrifices of Iraqis and the valor of our armed forces in their various branches and formations,” as well as support from the international coalition and brotherly and friendly countries.
 
He stressed that ending the coalition’s mission “does not mean the end of the partnership,” but rather a shift toward bilateral relations with its member states.
 
Security and intelligence cooperation, along with the exchange of information and expertise and capacity-building efforts, will continue “on the basis of mutual respect and shared interests,” he said.
 
The US Department of War said Wednesday that the US and its coalition partners “formally concluded Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq,” while the “orderly departure” of coalition forces and equipment from Erbil Air Base marked the conclusion of the military mission.
 
Pentagon chief spokesman Sean Parnell said the milestone “marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship.”
 
He said the 12-year campaign “defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region.”
 
Parnell said that the US expects the Iraqi Security Forces to “lead the continuing effort to secure Iraq and keep ISIS remnants suppressed,” noting that the US Department of War will continue to provide “targeted training and intelligence support” to its Iraqi partners.
 
“The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq’s remaining security challenges, including ISIS remnants and Iran-aligned militias that undermine Iraqi sovereignty and regional stability, now rests with the Government of Iraq,” Parnell said.
 
Baghdad and Washington agreed in September 2024 to end the coalition’s military mission in Iraq under a timetable extending through the end of September 2026, with a transition to bilateral security relations between Iraq and member states.
 
The coalition was formed under US leadership in 2014 after ISIS seized large areas of Iraq and Syria, providing Iraqi forces with air, intelligence and training support during operations against the group.
 
Iraq announced in December 2017 that it had regained full control of territory seized by ISIS.

Each hour of air-raid warnings costs Ukraine US$45m in business losses – The Guardian
Ukraine
