Each hour of air-raid warnings costs Ukraine US$45m in business losses – The Guardian
Air-raid warnings cost Ukraine US$45 million for every hour businesses are forced to halt operations, according to The Guardian, citing estimates by Oleksandr Kravchenko, Ukraine's Minister for Economy and Environment.
Source: The Guardian
Quote from Kravchenko: "What we had not fully anticipated was how quickly Russia would develop these jet-powered drones and use them to target everything."
Details: These attacks force a significant portion of the economy to stop as workers are sent to bomb shelters, with sirens sounding for up to 10 hours a day.
According to Kravchenko, more than half of businesses continue operating during "yellow" alerts – warnings used for drone threats.
However, a yellow alert provides no guarantee of safety. This danger became evident on 28 September when a Russian jet-powered drone struck the building of the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv during a yellow alert, killing two people who were still working inside.
Kravchenko noted that Russian attacks this year alone have caused roughly US$10 billion in damages to fixed assets. Targets have included steel plants, warehouses, logistics infrastructure and, recently, data centres.
Russia is also effectively blockading Ukraine's Black Sea ports, which handled the bulk of the country's exports prior to the blockade.
According to Kravchenko, Kyiv is currently seeking additional support from the EU, Japan, Canada and the UK, including potential early disbursements of loans scheduled for next year.
Background: Kryvyi Rih is set to make cuts to its municipal budget and suspend a number of development projects due to a sharp drop in tax revenues from local industrial businesses.

The birth of a painting: Artist Merike Estna on creating in public at the Venice Biennale
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:51:49 UTC
15:51:49 KST

Estonia artist Merike Estna did something extremely unusual for the Venice Biennale, even by its own standards. Over the past five months, she created paintings live in front of daily visitors. The result is 22 canvases which explore the themes of motherhood and feminism.
Visitors to the Estonian pavilion at this year's Venice International Art Biennale may have been surprised to see the country's representative Merike Estna in person, creating her latest works.
During the past five months, right before people's eyes, she has methodically made The House of Leaking Sky exhibition which consists of 22 large canvases.
"The pavilion shows three monumental works. The long bench that is 26 metres. Then the floor [25,000 tiles] people walk on, which I think of kind of as a mind map for the project and then the painting behind me which I started with empty canvas," Esta told Euronews Culture earlier this month.
Motherhood and female art history
Motherhood and female art history were the inspiration for creating the space. It has an extra significant meaning knowing that Estna recently gave birth. She was still on maternity leave with her younger child while preparing to come to Venice and work on the biggest project in her career for five full months, live in front of the visiting audience.
As curator, Natalia Sielewicz, emphasizes in her curatorial text, Estna braids together meditations on motherhood and the lineages of women artists who carved paths toward artistic self-determination.
"As a working mother herself, she often folds complex iconographies of care, lineage, and inheritance into her practice," she wrote.
Sielewicz reminds visitors of the existence of pittore senza opera - the painter without works, most often embodied by women whose oeuvres were absorbed into patriarchal workshops or erased from official chronicles.
"Marietta Robusti Tintoretta was one of them: a Venetian painter-poet who dressed as a boy to work beside her father, Jacopo Tintoretto, in the heat of the family atelier. Her paintings circulated without her name, her skill credited upward; she died in childbirth before she had the chance to fully step into the light of her own authorship," she wrote.
Living in Venice with her family throughout the Biennale, Estna brings motherhood into the conceptual structure of the project and found the experience to be extremely useful for both her and her children. "It is a complicated city to live with a family and to live with small children," Estna said. "My older kid lost his scooter on the first morning of his arrival [in] the canal. Our youngest only learned to walk a couple of months ago. So it's been a challenge, but also... I really love challenges, I think it always gives us new ideas and drives us, leads us to different thoughts."
Living space
Estna created her studio and exhibition inside of the former Church of Santa Maria Assunta in Venice’s Castello district, which was later used as a community space and gymnasium. These overlapping sacred, civic and everyday histories form an active backdrop for her evolving work.
"This studio space, what Merike created, is really like a living space. The painting has changed and then evolved so much throughout those past five months. It is really active and happy place, I would say. Many people who are living in Venice they keep returning," said Maria Arusoo, Commissioner of Estonian Pavilion at la Biennale di Venezia.
"People really want to ask questions, reflect, talk, just sit around."
For Merike visitors were crucial and she wanted them always to be taken care of. "They're definitely not intruders at the pavilion and the main idea to show the painting how it is born, it only carries when people actually visit and see and so this is an important part of the pavillion".
At first she was anxious, but later on these conditions reminded her of being back at the art academy where she always shared a studio and tried to focus by wearing headphones while others were chatting.
Politics and protests
The 61st Venice Art Biennale kicked off with enormous controversy as several countries and artists protested against the organiser's decision to invite Russia to open its pavilion in Giardini, one of the two main spaces of the Biennale.
Maria Arusoo, Commissioner of the Estonian Pavilion told Euronews Culture that art can never be separated from politics.
"Merike said this really beautiful and sad thing, that we [Estonia] were 60 years not part of this dialogue and not part of the Biennial because of Russia, because we were occupied and we couldn't be part as an independent country. So we won't step back because they decide to join."
The protest against the Russian pavilion ended in front of the Estonian pavilion on the opening day of the Biennale. Estna signed also an open letter against the Israeli pavilion.
The 61st International Art Exhibition of the Venice Biennale closes on Sunday, 22 November 2026.

Pentagon buys Israeli smart rifle sights to shoot down drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:50:40 UTC
15:50:40 KST

- JIATF-401 awarded Smart Shooter a three-year, sole-supplier contract worth up to $150 million for SMASH counter-drone rifle sights.
- The contract supports the task force's Domestic Shield Program to protect U.S. forces and bases at home and abroad.
The Pentagon’s counter-drone task force has awarded Israeli company Smart Shooter a contract worth up to $150 million for its SMASH rifle sights, which help soldiers shoot down small drones with their regular service weapons.
The U.S. Department of War’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401, known as JIATF-401, announced the three-year award on Sept. 29, and Smart Shooter said the next day that it is the only supplier under the deal. The contract is an indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity agreement, which sets a ceiling and lets the government place individual orders over time. The quantity, pricing and timing of deliveries will be decided in those orders, and neither the company nor the task force said how many systems the first order will cover.
The contract covers SMASH hardware, software and updates, training and support. It supports JIATF-401’s Domestic Shield Program and related missions overseas, focused on protecting troops, bases and other key sites in the United States and abroad from drones.
SMASH is a fire control system that mounts on a rifle like a scope. It uses artificial intelligence and computer vision to lock onto a target, calculate where to aim and release the shot only when the weapon is lined up to hit. That lets an ordinary soldier hit a small, fast-moving drone that would be very hard to shoot down with iron sights or a standard optic. The rifle can still be used normally against ground targets, and the soldier decides whether to fire. The system can also link to outside sensors and battle management networks.
“Domestic Shield is about giving defenders the tools to stop small, fast-moving drones before they can harm forces, bases, and critical assets,” said Michal Mor, CEO and co-founder of Smart Shooter.
JIATF-401 coordinates counter-drone work across the U.S. military and federal agencies. The task force is led by U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross.
“Our approach allows us to identify the right capabilities for specific operational requirements and rapidly deliver those capabilities to the warfighter,” said U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, director of JIATF-401.
The award is Smart Shooter’s second with the task force, following a contract announced in March 2026. The company says thousands of SMASH systems are already in use across the U.S. Army, U.S. Navy, U.S. Air Force and U.S. Marine Corps, and that it has won a series of new and follow-on orders from those services over the past year. SMASH is also used by forces in Israel, the United Kingdom, Germany and other NATO and allied countries.
JIATF-401 has been signing larger counter-drone deals this year. In May, it gave Perennial Autonomy a three-year contract worth up to $500 million for interceptor drones, including the Merops system that U.S. forces have used against Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones, DroneXL reported.
Smart Shooter, founded in Israel, has offices in the United States, Europe and Australia.

Voters back Burnham's plan to cut back triple lock to fund social care reform by 48% to 28%, poll suggests
Sharon Graham, the Unite general secretary, said earlier this week that getting rid of the pensions triple lock to help fund social care reform would be “electoral suicide”.
This morning YouGov has published polling suggesting that she might be wrong. It suggests the voters support Burnham’s plan by 48% to 28%.
When people are asked in isolation if they support setting up a National Care Service, they were overwhelmingly in favour, by 74% to 11%.
YouGov also found that, when asked in isolation if they would back turning the triple lock into a double lock (by removing the earnings link), respondents were also in favour of that too, by 43% to 30%.
(In fact, Burnham’s proposal is more generous than a simply reversion to a double lock – see 8.45am.)
When YouGov put the two proposals together, and described them as Burnham’s plan, getting rid of the triple lock in its current form became more popular.
What people tell pollsters about a policy after it has just been announced may bear little resemblance to how they feel about it by the time it gets implemented. But these findings suggest Burnham is well placed to win the public argument on the merits of his policy.
When Rachel Reeves announced she was cutting the winter fuel payments in 2024, early polling showed that people opposed the move – and it was particularly unpopular with pensioners.
YouGov has published polling that suggests voters back Andy Burnham’s plan to make the pensions triple lock less generous to help fund the establishment of a National Care Service by 48% to 28%. (See 12.04pm.)

The funding will be given to mayors and leaders in 45 local authorities to back community-led food projects like community food shops, mobile greengrocers, lunch clubs, community kitchens, and cooking and nutrition programmes.
Directed at areas facing some of the highest levels of deprivation and childhood obesity, each local authority will receive £222,000 to develop community-led solutions tailored to local needs.

Nandy says for too long government has ceded too much power over internet to private sector
Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, criticised previous governments for giving private companies too much power over the internet revolution in her speech to the conference.
In the face of new technology, and in particular the threat that the internet posed to women, the state had been “far too small and far too timid for too long”, she said.
She went on:
I am on a mission to change it.
Because the World Wide Web – that created by Tim Berners Lee, to share knowledge, not exploitation - has revolutionised the way we live. An extraordinary democratic force, a source of connection, creativity and solace that has unleashed incomprehensible hatred, anger and polarisation - ask yourselves this, while it has undeniably shaped and defined us, have we done anything like enough to shape and define it?
Like the printing press, electricity and television, it has upended society. But what is almost unique to this moment is how absent the state - on behalf of its people - has been for so long. We have outsourced a revolution almost entirely to the private sphere to shape and police.
It is ... an almost violent indifference. To the women whose privacy and dignity is stripped from them. To the children who are preyed upon, their childhoods stolen. To people - how many of you in this room particularly women - hounded from public life. Where anger is monetised and profit put before people’s lives.
So conference, we are calling time on that indifference. Enough is enough.
Nandy said the government was introducing a social media ban for children and legislation to make it impossible for them to take or share nude images on their phones. She also said the government would take action to stop the circulation of non-consensual intimate images online.
Cooper says violence against women and girls public health problem as she announces £50m for support services
Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, also announced almost £50m to support victims of violence against women and girls. This should be seen as a public health problem, she said.

We don’t treat violence against women and girls as the epidemic it really is. So here’s what we will change. For the first time, we will take a public health approach to violence against women and girls. We will work with survivors, charities, local government, and the NHS to set out how to treat this like the disease it is.
And today I am announcing the rollout of almost £50m support for new specialist referral services from GPs for women and men who are victims of domestic abuse.
Because conference when I stood here as home secretary two years ago and said our mission to halve violence against women and girls covered the whole of government, I meant it.
The money will ensure that victims of abuse can be referred to specialist help through GP practices under a new scheme called Steps to Safety. Around £34m will be spent allowing 12 integrated care boards to set up the programme, and £15m will go to victim support services in England.
Cooper is also appointing anational clinical lead for violence against women and girls to bring together clinical and public health expertise and strengthen the health system’s response.
Officials says health services are often the first places where victims of this sort of abuse disclose what has been happening.
Guess the tracks Burnham picked for each of England’s regions
At the Labour conference, Andy Burnham chose region-specific songs for the regional receptions he was attending. Alexis Petridis, the Guardian’s chief rock critic, has been assessing his choices. And he’s turned it into a quizz.
Brexit 'the biggest lie of the last 30 years', Macron says
Jakub Krupa
Jakub Krupa writes the Guardian’s Europe live blog.
Andy Burnham was critical of Brexit yesterday, but not as critical as the French president Emmanuel Macron who – not for the first time – has blasted those who campaigned for it.

Cooper says government setting up collective pension scheme for workers in care sector

We think this is totally the wrong thing, despite the fact under any system of proportional representation, we’d have got more seats than we did in 2024, in that election.

Burnham says he has spent 'a lot of time' working out how to fill £4.7bn funding gap in defence investment plan

El Nino is a 'postcard from the future' — and could cause 451,000 excess heat deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:49:00 UTC
15:49:00 KST

El Nino: A deadly 'postcard from the future'
September 30, 2026
Peruvian fishermen gave El Nino its name — "the little boy" or Christ Child — after noticing unusually warm Pacific waters around Christmas that caused the fish they depended on to suddenly become scarce.
But what those fishermen observed locally can have consequences thousands of kilometers away. El Nino can shift temperature and rainfall patterns around the world, bringing extreme heat and drought to some regions and heavy rain and flooding to others.
Researchers now estimate that the unusually high temperatures linked to the current El Nino could cause around 451,000 excess deaths worldwide from June 2026 to February 2027.
The event is a "postcard from the future," Tamma Carleton, head of research at the University of Chicago's Climate Impact Lab, told DW. Land temperatures over the coming months are forecast to run about 1.2 degrees C (2.1 F) above normal.
"For the average person, that's roughly the warming climate change is projected to bring about 20 years from now, arriving all at once," Carleton said.
How does El Nino affect weather worldwide?
Normally, winds blowing west across the Pacific push warm surface water towards Asia and Australia, allowing colder water to rise near South America. During El Nino, which occurs erratically every two to seven years, those winds weaken. Less cold water then rises, and much more of the Pacific stays unusually warm.
The warmer water heats the air above it and fuels rainfall over the central and eastern Pacific. The rising air spreads high in the atmosphere, sending waves that disrupt weather worldwide.
"It is like throwing a stone into a lake," climate researcher Fred Kucharski told DW. "Initially the surface perturbation is local, but then the energy spreads all over the lake through wave propagation."
Kucharski said the effects can cross the tropics within one week and reach higher latitudes in about two. Where the waves travel determines whether a region becomes hotter, cooler, wetter or drier.
The current El Nino developed in June and has strengthened rapidly since. It is now on course to become an exceptionally strong — sometimes called "super" — El Nino.
The Climate Impact Lab says its estimate covers only the first nine months of El Nino, as far as the current seasonal forecasts allow. The event is expected to continue into Northern Hemisphere spring, and its effect on global temperatures could last longer.
"We expect the final number to be meaningfully higher than what we are currently reporting here," Carleton said.
Why can El Nino be so deadly?
The estimate of 451,000 excess deaths covers deaths linked to the direct health effects of unusually high temperatures associated with El Nino.
Extreme heat strains the heart and kidneys, makes it harder for the body to maintain a safe temperature and can worsen cardiovascular, respiratory and other illnesses. As a result, the underlying condition is often recorded as the cause of death rather than the heat that aggravated it.
"Most heat deaths never show up in official statistics as heat deaths," Carleton said.
El Nino can also alter rainfall, contributing to drought in some regions and heavy rain and flooding in others.
Floods can kill, contaminate drinking water and spread disease. Drought can damage harvests and cause water and food shortages.
Deaths from these other indirect effects are not included in the 451,000 projection.
Where will the toll be greatest?
The Climate Impact Lab expects some of the largest increases in deaths in the Sahel, South and Southeast Asia and parts of Latin America. The highest numbers of fatalities are predicted for Nigeria, Sudan, Niger, Chad, India, Indonesia and Brazil.
Many are projected to occur between December and February, meaning much of the expected toll still lies ahead.
"Heat headlines usually focus on Europe and North America," Carleton said. "This event's toll is overwhelmingly in lower-income, already-hot countries, where people have the fewest ways to adapt and where these deaths are least likely to be counted."
Are these lives being significantly shortened?
Some people who die during extreme heat are already frail. This raises an important question: Is the heat cutting their lives substantially short, or merely bringing forward deaths that would have occurred days or weeks later — an effect known as mortality displacement?
The underlying research uses annual rather than daily death rates, which largely filters out deaths brought forward by only days or weeks.
Ben Armstrong, an emeritus professor at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, said he could not verify the 451,000 figure. But because the estimate is based on annual mortality data, it largely excludes deaths brought forward by only days or weeks. If the figure is correct, he said, most of those counted "would have lived at least six months longer."
Why predict deaths before they happen?
Scientists have long estimated the death toll from extreme temperatures retrospectively. Better seasonal forecasting is increasingly allowing researchers to look ahead instead.
To produce the estimate, researchers used earlier work showing how death rates change during hot weather in different parts of the world. They combined it with seasonal forecasts showing how hot each place is expected to become.
"Putting the two together lets us estimate the human cost of this event while there's still time to do something about it, rather than counting the deaths after the fact," Carleton said.
Heat warnings, cooling centers and hydration stations, home visits to vulnerable people, protections for outdoor workers and additional health care capacity could all reduce mortality.
The researchers believe targeted interventions could save tens of thousands of lives.
For Carleton, the forecast is a warning to prepare now for the heat that climate change could make commonplace.
"This El Nino gives us a look at future weather in the 2040s," Carleton said. "These temperatures will become normal in 20 years, giving us time and reason to begin investing in adaptive capacity now."
Edited: Carla Bleiker

China factory activity returns to growth in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:45:54 UTC
15:45:54 KST

China’s factory activity returned to growth in September after two months of contraction, official data showed on Sept. 30, offering a modest sign of improvement as Beijing steps up support for the world’s second-largest economy.
The official manufacturing purchasing managers’ index (PMI) rose to 50.1 from 49.8 in August, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
A reading above 50 indicates expansion, while one below that level signals contraction. The index stood at 49.2 in July.
Factory production strengthened, with the production sub-index rising to 51.7 from 50.4 in August. New orders remained in expansion territory at 50.5.
The non-manufacturing PMI, covering services and construction, climbed to 50.2 from 49.0 a month earlier. Construction activity returned to expansion at 50.3, while the services index rose to 50.2.
The composite PMI, which covers both manufacturing and non-manufacturing activity, increased to 50.7 from 49.5.
The figures came as Beijing unveiled additional measures to support an economy still facing weak domestic demand and a prolonged property downturn.
The State Council said earlier this week that it would roll out measures aimed at stabilizing the property market, supporting employment and raising incomes.
The People’s Bank of China followed on Sept. 29 by cutting a key policy lending rate and expanding credit support for infrastructure, technology and smaller businesses.
Authorities also announced an interest subsidy for qualifying first-home mortgages, due to take effect on Oct. 1.
Exports and advanced manufacturing have remained important sources of support for the Chinese economy, with demand linked to the global artificial intelligence boom helping parts of the technology sector.

The EU is negotiating a reform in Brussels to better integrate its capital markets. Germany has secured an exemption for major European operator Deutsche Börse’s domestically focused trading venues from centralised supervision, leaving a key part of the system under regional control.

The move could weaken the proposed reform or delay an agreement in Brussels on capital markets integration, a flagship legislative package that the bloc has placed at the centre of its mandate to enhance Europe’s global economic competitiveness.
Overcoming fragmentation is one of the goals of the supervision reform, which would cede supervisory power to the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA).
Some trading venues with limited cross-border operations would remain under national supervision. However, the proposed exclusion of some trading venues belonging to Deutsche Börse — widely considered a player of major importance — from direct ESMA supervision is facing opposition among other member states and risks undermining the goal of reaching an agreement on the law by the end of the year.
EU economic and finance ministers are set to meet on 9 October, and according to the sources, the aim is to discuss the reform and reach an agreement on that occasion.
In response to Euronews’ request for comment, the German government specified that the proposed exemption would apply only to trading venues with a primary domestic focus; those would remain outside centralised supervision, rather than the whole Deutsche Börse Group.
"The compromise is not a carve-out for Deutsche Börse Group. Irrespective of the discussion about trading venues, Deutsche Börse Group will come under direct ESMA supervision from day one with its financial market infrastructure entities (CCPs and CSDs)," a German Ministry of Finance spokesperson told Euronews, referring to Deutsche Börse’s clearing houses (CCPs) and central securities depositories (CSDs).
Central counterparties (CCPs) manage risks between buyers and sellers in financial transactions. Central securities depositories (CSDs) hold securities and help settle trades.
What are capital markets?
Capital markets are marketplaces where individuals, institutions and governments buy and sell long-term financial instruments, such as equities or debt.
They offer businesses a way to raise funds and support their growth. However, scaling up in Europe remains challenging. Cross-border operations can be costly, time-consuming and involve significant administrative burdens. This is because rules differ between member states, and even where they are the same, their implementation may differ.
The reform is part of the EU’s Savings and Investments Union (SIU) strategy, which aims to reduce fragmentation of capital markets while incentivising European citizens to invest part of their savings in the capital market.
A weak European capital market is among the reasons why firms in Europe obtain most of their financing through bank credit.
Without enough diversification, businesses look for other markets where funding is more readily available, such as the US.
That was, for example, the case for Klarna, which chose New York over Europe for its stock market listing: Europe's fastest-growing companies often look across the Atlantic for deeper pools of capital.
According to the European Commission’s 2026 European Macroeconomic Report, every year, around €300 billion of savings flow out of the EU in net terms, funding investment abroad, mainly in the United States.
The integration of capital markets has been called for on several occasions by European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde as a main priority.
The reform of capital markets was also mentioned by former Italian Prime Minister Mario Draghi in his 2024 report on European competitiveness as a major step.
The question now is whether other member states will seek similar exemptions, and how much authority the EU’s supervisor would have if they succeed.

“Russia is raising the stakes, and unfortunately, we cannot rule out civilian casualties,”

Dubai-Tel Aviv flight lands in Saudi Arabia after distress signal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:36:27 UTC
15:36:27 KST

A flydubai flight from the United Arab Emirates to Israel diverted to Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after issuing a distress signal, prompting initial fears of a hijacking and the dispatch of Israeli fighter jets.
An Israeli official told Haaretz that authorities are treating the event as a terror incident and believe that one of the pilots may have purposefully attempted to crash the plane. Other scenarios are being considered. According to an Israeli source, the pilot suspected of the act is of Omani origin – a country with which Israel does not have diplomatic relations – while the co-pilot is reportedly from India.
Flydubai confirmed an incident had occurred on the flight, saying in a statement that the aircraft had landed safely and all passengers were safe. A spokesperson for the flight company said the motives for the altercation are still under investigation.
An additional flydubai aircraft evacuating the Israeli passengers from the UAE has taken off from Tabuk and is expected to land in Ben Gurion Airport in Israel around 6:30 P.M.
According to a source familiar with the matter, Saudi Arabia did not agree to an Israeli military aircraft landing in its territory to carry out the rescue.
At 8:22 A.M., while over Saudi Arabia and about an hour before its scheduled arrival in Israel, the aircraft suddenly began a steep descent. Flight data recorded by several tracking sites showed it dropping from 34,000 feet to 16,000 feet in less than two minutes, a rate of about 5 kilometers (3.1 miles) per minute.
The aircraft then activated a general distress code, followed several minutes later by a hijacking code. It flew toward Jordan and crossed into the country before turning back toward Saudi Arabia.
According to Saudi state television, authorities at the Prince Sultan Bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Tabuk, northwest Saudi Arabia, received a distress call requesting an emergency landing.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz held consultations on the matter.
In a statement, Netanyhau's office said the incident was under control, "and all necessary measures are now being taken to safely return the Israeli passengers to Israel."
Opposition leader Yair Lapid said a security briefing he received from Netanyahu late Tuesday did not mention any warning of a threat like the one involving the flydubai flight. Netanyahu briefed Lapid after saying he had received a warning of an imminent attack on Israel ahead of the election.
In a statement, Lapid said that those claiming otherwise were "trying to play cheap politics at the expense of Israel's security."
Passengers on the flight said the pilots had lost control of the plane before other passengers broke into the cockpit and intervened.
Dalia Shpigel told Haaretz that passengers seated toward the front of the plane broke into the cockpit after realizing something was wrong.
"An hour before landing, we felt that there was no control over the plane, that it was starting to jump," she said. "The guys saw that the plane had begun to dive and broke into the cockpit."
Speaking to Israel's Channel 12 News, two women said they believed one of the pilots had been stabbed. "People started screaming. Then the plane began moving from side to side. We understood that the pilots had lost control because one of them had been stabbed."
Almog, who spoke to Haaretz after deplaning in Saudi Arabia, said Saudi authorities were going "above and beyond" and had provided lunch to passengers. He said passengers had yet to receive an update on how they would return to Israel. "All options are on the table," he said.

Polar oceans transformed as warming melts ice habitats: Research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:35:00 UTC
15:35:00 KST

Polar oceans transformed as warming melts ice habitats: Research
- Polar oceans are rapidly warming, with Arctic sea surface temperatures rising 4.2°C since 1982, much faster than the global average, causing significant ice loss.
- Arctic sea ice has shrunk by nearly half a million square kilometres per decade, exposing coastlines to erosion and threatening coastal communities and infrastructure.
- Antarctic sea ice loss has led to the first large-scale emperor penguin breeding failure, pushing the species to endangered status with over 90% of colonies at risk by 2100.
AI generated
PARIS – Climate change is increasingly reshaping the polar oceans, with Arctic waters warming rapidly, sea ice shrinking and wildlife losing habitat at both ends of the planet, an annual report said on Sept 30.
The Copernicus Ocean State Report depicts profound changes across the world’s seas, from record-breaking heatwaves in the Mediterranean and Black seas to shifts in marine ecosystems and increasingly acidic waters.
“The message is very clear. The ocean is changing rapidly,” said Pierre Bahurel, director general of Mercator Ocean International, which runs the European Union’s Copernicus Marine Service.
Some of the more dramatic effects from global warming are taking place in the poles, which occupy around 20 per cent of the global ocean surface.
The Arctic’s combined sea surface and sea-ice surface temperature rose 4.2 deg C between 1982 and 2024, or around 1 deg C per decade, according to the 10th annual oceans report.
By comparison, global sea surface temperatures have been increasing by 0.12 deg C per decade.
In the Kara Sea north of Siberia, temperatures have climbed by 6.7 deg C since 1982, or 1.68 deg C per decade.
As temperatures rise, Arctic sea ice has shrunk by nearly half a million square kilometres per decade since 1979, equivalent to losing an area the size of Spain every 10 years.
The retreating ice exposes Arctic coastlines to waves, worsening coastal erosion and raising risks for coastal communities and infrastructure, the report warned.
“The Arctic sea ice has been declining since the early 80s, leaving around 60% of coastal infrastructure vulnerable to erosion and sea level rise,” Karina von Schuckmann, director of the oceans report, said in a media briefing.
Ice loss in Antarctica, meanwhile, is threatening penguin populations on the frozen continent.
Record-low Antarctic sea ice in 2022 coincided with the first-ever recorded large-scale breeding failure of emperor penguins, the report said.
Emperor penguins rely on stable sea ice to live, hunt and breed and their chicks can perish if they fall in freezing water before developing waterproof feathers.
In April, emperor penguins were upgraded from “near threatened” to “endangered” by the IUCN, the global authority on threatened wildlife.
More than 90% of emperor penguin colonies could be near-extinct by 2100 if sea ice loss persists at its current rate. AFP

US troops exit Iraq after more than a decade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:22:00 UTC
15:22:00 KST

US troops exit Iraq after more than a decade
September 30, 2026
After more than ten years, US forces are to withdraw from their remaining military bases in Iraq on Wednesday.
"Today, the United States and our Coalition partners formally concluded Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq, consistent with the September 2024 US-Iraq joint statement and US national interests," the Pentagon said in a statement.
The Pentagon added that it will continue to provide targeted training and intelligence support to Iraqi partners.
"This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region,” Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said.
“It also marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship,” he said.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi declared that October 1, the day following the coalition's departure, should be celebrated as Sovereignty Day.
It is "a national occasion that affirms the completion of Iraq's path toward sovereignty and consolidates the presence of the state and its institutions," the heads of the executive, legislative and judicial branches said on Monday.
The troops were deployed in Iraq and Syria in 2014, to tackle the "Islamic State" (IS) terrorist group, which had taken over large swathes of both countries.
The IS was defeated in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria in 2019, but coalition forces stayed on to battle the group's remnants.
The complete departure of US troops from Iraq comes 23 years after US-led forces toppled Saddam Hussein, triggering widespread upheaval and chaos, before the rise of IS.
Iran celebrates US withdrawal from Iraq
Iran and its allies celebrated the withdrawal of US forces, which was agreed upon in 2024 by then-US President Joe Biden. The agreement has now been executed under Donald Trump's term even as US continues to wage a war against Iran.
Iran, which wants a US-free Middle East, sees the US pullout from Iraq as a triumph for its "axis of resistance" of allied armed groups across the region.
The withdrawal of the US troops from Iraq has raised threats of diminished security in the region as Iran-backed Shi'ite militias are vying to gain more control and potentially regroup 'IS'.
US withdrawal leaves Kurds in Iraq anxious
The withdrawal leaves the the federal government and the semi-autonomous northern Kurdish region, where most of remaining US bases operated, vulnerable.
Kurds in Erbil, capital of the Kurdistan region, told AFP news agency they are increasingly anxious about their safety from drones that have repeatedly targeted their autonomous canton, once the US air defense systems are removed.
“The departure of the United States from the Kurdistan Region under these complex regional circumstances, without the provision of a defense system, is a matter of concern,” the Kurdish regional government's Peshmerga Ministry said in a statement.

Taipei's Mume dives into Indigenous cuisine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:18:44 UTC
15:18:44 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Since its founding in 2014, contemporary European restaurant Mume has built a reputation for showcasing local ingredients through modern fine dining.
Marking a major milestone in its 10th year, the restaurant regained its Michelin star this year after a five-year hiatus. The team is now turning its focus toward Indigenous ingredients and Austronesian culinary heritage to define its direction for the next decade.
Culinary Director Kai Ward reflected that after a decade of growth, the team began searching for what makes Taiwanese cuisine truly distinct globally. As an Australian, Ward said his background in a country with a rich Indigenous culture gives him a deep appreciation for Taiwan’s native food traditions.
He said that younger generations are increasingly open to sharing tribal culture, making previously hard-to-find produce more accessible for culinary creation. To understand these elements, Ward and his team frequently visited Indigenous communities in Hualien, Yilan, and Taichung, engaging directly with farmers, fishermen, and scholars.
Ward emphasized that the initiative is about understanding the cultural context and rituals behind each ingredient rather than simply adding new items to the menu.
For instance, traditional fermented pork, known as tmmyan and aged with millet, mountain pepper, and salt, inspired the team’s fermentation techniques, even if legal restrictions and diner preferences prevent serving raw wild game directly.
This cultural exploration extends to table craftsmanship, featuring hand-woven bamboo cups, custom knives, and local ceramics.
In Mume’s latest menu, these native flavors are interpreted through refined techniques. The meal opens with a bite inspired by the traditional tribal millet donut, paired with fermented tofu and maitake mushrooms.
Refreshing seafood courses include Yilan blush prawns with pomelo, and Matsu mussels paired with sweet summer bamboo shoots and lardo. Hot courses showcase leopard coral grouper served with chayote shoots, daylilies and lily bulbs, along with squid sauteed with Penghu XO sauce and water bamboo.
The main course features Wagyu strip loin accompanied by white water snowflake greens and preserved green chili, served alongside rice cooked with Tainan No. 11 rice, prickly ash, chicken fat, celery, and cold-extracted shiitake broth.
For dessert, millet koji is paired with Eureka lemon and bee pollen, highlighting millet’s vital role in Indigenous foodways.
Additionally, Ward creatively reinterpreted Paolyta — a popular local tonic drink — into a nonalcoholic, caffeine-free gummy served to select guests as a playful homage to working-class and tribal culture.
Over the past decade, Mume has used its platform to bridge international dining with Taiwanese terroir. This culinary journey into Indigenous heritage signals a new chapter centered on the nation’s cultural roots.
Mume launches new summer menu. (Taiwan News, Lyla Liu video)

Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to jump by £276 a year from January
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:17:33 UTC
15:17:33 KST

Household energy bills in Great Britain are predicted to reach almost £2,000 a year for the typical household from January as the impact of the Middle East war continues through the coldest months of winter.
The government’s cap on energy prices is poised to jump by 16%, equivalent to adding £276 to the average annual dual-fuel bill to take it to £1,999, according to the leading forecaster Cornwall Insight.
The latest blow to struggling households was published as millions braced for energy charges to rise by 4% from Thursday as the quarterly energy bill cap climbs to its highest level in three years this winter.
The consultancy’s January forecast increase is well above its previous prediction of a 9% rise, with analysts blaming the uptick on the recent rise in gas market prices to three-year highs.
It would be the biggest quarterly jump since January 2023, when the energy crisis that followed the full-scale invasion of Ukraine the year before was at its height.
Craig Lowrey, a principal consultant at Cornwall Insight, said: “These prices are going to hit households hard. January is already a difficult month for many, with cold weather and bank balances still recovering from Christmas, and now they face the biggest price cap rise we’ve seen in four years.”
The chief executive of the supplier EDF Energy, Simone Rossi, said the UK was “walking into a second energy crisis”. Speaking to the BBC, he called for the government to do more to lower domestic bills after its six-month VAT holiday, which will save the typical home about £45 a year from Thursday.
Andy Burnham said he would not call Rossi’s crisis warning an overstatement, telling BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that the rising cost of home energy, as well as pump prices, was “very difficult indeed”.
In response to questions over whether the government would consider abandoning the planned fuel duty rise, the prime minister said “every possible measure” was being considered to ease energy costs, adding: “We’re looking at any measure that can give people breathing space, that can take the pressure off.”
Cornwall’s latest forecast reignited calls for the government to offer targeted support to struggling households this winter. Simon Francis, a coordinator at the Energy Fuel Poverty Coalition, said the number of households in fuel poverty was set to rise again “at the most dangerous time of the year”.
He said: “The chancellor has no choice but to act to provide increased targeted support to vulnerable households and plan to deliver wider universal help for people facing a sixth winter of high energy prices.
“If ministers do nothing, millions will spend this winter in cold, damp homes, unable to cook a hot meal. People will get ill. Some will die. And every one of those avoidable cases will be on this chancellor’s watch.”
Gas prices in Europe have doubled in recent months as the continent prepares to enter the cooler months with gas stores at their lowest level in 13 years after the US-Israel war on Iran triggered an increase in global market prices.
Buyers have delayed refilling storage facilities after a cold end to last winter, and extra gas power generation during the summer heatwaves, depleted stocks while oil and gas exports from the Gulf remain severely disrupted by threats to tankers passing through the Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab straits.
Cornwall Insight said storage levels of EU gas were now at their lowest September level for 15 years.
The energy regulator for Great Britain, Ofgem, sets the government’s price cap. It will base January’s figure on wholesale prices between 19 August and 17 November, so the outlook could still change if market prices drop, but Cornwall Insight said an increase was “all but certain” given the rises so far this month.
From this Thursday the cap rises to the equivalent to £1,723 a year for a typical home’s gas and electricity use. The unit cost of electricity will rise from 26.11p a kilowatt hour to 26.32p, while gas charges will rise from 7.33p to 7.97p. However, actual household bills will depend on how much each consumes.

Menopause supplements costing more than £400 a year ‘no better than cheap multivitamin’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:00:11 UTC
15:00:11 KST

Menopause supplements costing more than £400 a year are no better than a £22-a-year multivitamin, according to analysis by the consumer watchdog Which?.
Which? found that many popular supplements that are aimed at women over 45 going through menopause or perimenopause lack meaningful quantities of key nutrients, yet cost 20 times more than standard multivitamins.
The global menopause supplement market is valued at nearly $17bn and is expected to reach $25bn by 2030, as women look for ways to manage a variety of symptoms associated with menopause such as hot flushes, poor sleep and mood swings.
But research by Which? found that none of the supplements it studied contained the correct nutrients in the right doses to support their use for menopause.
Shefalee Loth, a public health nutritionist at Which? who co-led the research, said: “Which? is concerned that the supplements industry has become a wild west and regulators are not doing enough to get a grip on dubious marketing and unchecked quasi-medical claims from firms apparently seeking to cash in on people’s health anxiety and insecurities.”
Calcium and vitamin D are the most important nutrients during perimenopause and menopause as they support bone health as oestrogen levels decline. Maintaining good levels of iron, magnesium and other vitamins and minerals can also help with symptoms.
Nutritionists from Which? examined the active ingredients in 26 popular supplements sold by retailers such as Holland & Barrett, Boots and Amazon and found that a high-quality multivitamin alongside targeted supplements where needed was often cheaper and potentially more effective than a so-called all-in-one menopause blend.
It found that Asda’s A-Z Multivitamins & Minerals, costing 6p a day (£22 a year), contained all essential vitamins plus 200mg of calcium and 100mg of magnesium. In contrast, the most expensive supplement, Love Mushrooms’ Empower, cost £1.33 a day for a two-tablet dose (£485 a year) yet did not contain menopause-specific nutrients such as magnesium and calcium.
Similarly, Wild Nutrition’s Women’s 45+ Daily Multi Nutrient, costing £1.27 a day (£468 a year), contained just 1.5µg of vitamin D, 60mg of calcium and 30mg of magnesium, significantly under NHS recommended daily amounts, Which? found.
The watchdog also found that many menopause supplements’ key nutrients were in doses too low to be beneficial, or they omitted important vitamins and minerals altogether.
The highest-scoring menopause supplement analysed, Vitabiotics’ Menopace Max, cost 93p a day (£340 a year) – more than 15 times the price of Asda’s 6p multivitamin.
The findings follow research by UCL into 201 supplements sold in the UK that found less than half of products contained vitamin D and calcium and the majority of ingredients were not specifically recommended by major menopause societies.
Responding to Which?’s research, Dr Xand van Tulleken, an honorary associate professor at the UCL Institute for Global Health, said: “Every year our annual spending on menopause supplements is hundreds of times more than our spending on menopause research. There is no persuasive evidence that menopause supplements have a significant effect on women’s symptoms, some of them are dangerous, and the pricing and marketing is exploitative and confusing. They are a massive rip-off for consumers who desperately want to be well.”
Martin Last, the director general of the Health Food Manufacturers’ Association, said: “We encourage industry manufacturers to formulate and recommend supplements as required by the many food regulations that apply to food supplements. Many life stages, including the menopause, may create increased nutritional demands on an individual and these may be met by supplementation as an addition to a healthy diet.”
In a statement provided after publication, Holland & Barrett said its own-brand menopause products were “specifically formulated for the nutritional needs associated with this life stage” and that “they contain meaningful, evidence-based levels of key vitamins and minerals and are not simply standard multivitamins with menopause branding”.

Arrestor gear contract to go to Marshall
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
07:00:02 BST
15:00:02 KST

The Ministry of Defence intends to extend and combine two contracts with Marshall Land Systems covering the aircraft arrestor systems used at British and overseas military airfields, placing the work by direct award on the grounds that no other supplier could do it, the department stated in a transparency notice.
The notice, identifier 2026/S 000-091979, was published on 29 September and gives a contract value of £7.5 million excluding VAT, rising to £9 million with VAT included. The earliest date the contract can be signed is 4 December 2026, with estimated dates running from then to 5 December 2028 and two further one-year options that could carry it to December 2030.
Arrestor gear is what stops a fast jet running off the end of a runway when something goes wrong on landing or during an aborted take-off. According to the notice, the requirement covers a sustained and supported capability delivering a safe, effective and reliable means of preventing runway excursions, supporting the enabling of the Strategic Base, standing commitments and contingent capability in line with Defence Strategic Direction and the RAF Command Plan.
ACCOMM/00087 covers engineering and logistic support to Rotary Hydraulic Arrestor Gear and Portable Hydraulic Arrestor Gear in use in Britain and at overseas bases, while ACCOMM/00035 covers the Arrester Barrier. Both were competitively let, and the department intends to combine them into a single contract as part of a 24-month extension whose value for the extension period alone is put at £5.6 million excluding VAT.
The justification for going direct rests on obsolescence, and according to the notice, the Arrester Barrier System is obsolete and Marshall, as the incumbent, holds the technical understanding of it, the suitably qualified and experienced people, and access to the technical drawings and approved repair instructions from the original equipment manufacturer. A change of supplier, the department states, would deliver services both different from and incompatible with the existing ones, and the age of the equipment means only Marshall holds the necessary know-how and can supply compatible spares, so that going elsewhere would cause disproportionate technical difficulties in operating and maintaining the system.
The extension is being placed under Section 41 of the Procurement Act 2023, relying on the direct award justification at paragraph 7 of Schedule 5, which covers additional services from a single supplier, and the notice is published under the defence and security special regime.
Transparency notices of this type are required before a contracting authority makes a direct award, and exist so that the market can see the intention and the reasoning before the contract is signed rather than afterwards. They can also record a switch from an unsuccessful competitive procedure to a direct award, though nothing in this notice indicates that happened here.
Marshall Land Systems is based at Hangar 22 at Cambridge Airport and is recorded in the notice as not being a small or medium-sized enterprise, which sits oddly with the notice also flagging the requirement as particularly suitable for small and medium-sized enterprises. Options attached to the contract cover spares, repairs and post design services, and the contracting authority is Defence Equipment and Support at Abbey Wood, with the requirement run by the Support Capabilities and Commodities Team within the National Armaments Director Group.

China's non-manufacturing PMI at 50.2 in September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:57:42 CST
14:57:42 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- China's non-manufacturing purchasing managers' index (PMI) came in at 50.2 in September, up 1.2 percentage points from August, official data showed Wednesday.
A reading above 50 indicates expansion, while a reading below 50 indicates contraction.
The business activity index for the construction sector rose 3.4 percentage points month on month to 50.3, and the services sector index rose 0.9 percentage points to 50.2, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
Among services industries, the indices for telecommunications, broadcasting and satellite transmission services, monetary and financial services, and insurance all stood above 55, well above the boom-bust line. The indices for capital market services and real estate remained below the line.
The new orders index stood at 46.5 in September, up 2.4 percentage points from August, indicating a recovery in market demand. The new orders index for construction rose 3.3 percentage points to 45.7, while services rose 2.2 percentage points to 46.7.
The NBS data also indicated that overall input prices for non-manufacturing business activities continued to rise.
The sales price index rose 1 percentage point from August to 50.3, indicating a recovery in overall sales prices.
The employment index rose 0.5 percentage points month on month to 45.9, pointing to improved hiring conditions.
The business activity expectation index reached 55.5, up 0.5 percentage points from August, indicating stronger confidence among non-manufacturing enterprises in market development. The construction business activity expectation index rose 3.6 percentage points to 55.4, while the services business activity expectation index remained unchanged at 55.5.
Huo Lihui, a chief statistician with the NBS, said the non-manufacturing business activity index rebounded noticeably in September and returned to expansion territory.
Huo noted that the services business activity index moved above the boom-bust line, reflecting a recovery in services market activity, while the construction business activity index climbed to its highest level this year, with construction progress accelerating.
Wednesday's NBS data also showed that China's manufacturing PMI stood at 50.1 in September, up 0.3 percentage points from August and back in the expansion zone. ■

Eiffel Tower chief to step down after scandal
Kyiv • UNN
SETE CEO Patrick Branco Ruivo will leave his position at the end of the year following an investigation into an incident involving female employees. The tower was closed due to a strike.
The head of the company that operates the Eiffel Tower will resign at the end of the year. This came after female employees of the iconic Paris landmark were barred from attending a visit by a Hindu religious organization. UNN reports this, citing AP.
Details
Patrick Branco Ruivo, CEO of Société d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), will leave his position after an investigation conducted by an independent firm revealed a number of operational violations related to the September 5 visit.
These violations resulted in "female employees being excluded from the visit that day, which is an unacceptable situation," according to a SETE statement dated September 29. Ruivo was appointed at the end of 2018.
The Eiffel Tower, visited by 7 million people annually, was closed on September 7 due to a staff strike in protest against what a union representative called "unacceptable" management directives.
Anger among employees of the 330-meter landmark intensified after management told staff that female employees should not have contact with a delegation from the Bochasanwasi Shri Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha organization.
The organization, known as BAPS, is a worldwide religious and civic organization within the Swaminarayan sect, a branch of Hinduism, the publication writes. It held celebrations to mark the opening of a traditional Hindu stone temple in Paris.
At the time of the incident, BAPS said in a statement to the Associated Press: "This coordination was undertaken solely for reasons of operational courtesy and logistics, to ensure the smooth visit of a large group of people without inconvenience to tower staff or the public. It was never intended as a gender-based request."
Ariel Weil, head of SETE, said Tuesday that he had requested the implementation of measures and training programs promoting gender equality.
Additional information
This is not the first time the 137-year-old tower has been closed because of a strike. In February 2024, it was closed for six days due to striking employees who demanded improved maintenance of the historic landmark and higher wages.

Eesti 200 and Greens consider merger ahead of 2027 vote
Riigikogu party Eesti 200 and the Estonian Greens (Rohelised) are considering a merger ahead of the March 2027 Riigikogu election, Eesti Ekspress reported.
But the move may not solve either party's central problem: both are polling below the 5-percent threshold needed to win seats, and their combined support would still not be enough. The latest ERR-commissioned Emor poll saw Eesti 200 at 1.9 percent and the Greens at 1.1 percent — a combined 3 percent.
The talks are driven by different needs on each side. Eesti 200, which has 13 Riigikogu seats, has long languished below the threshold and may struggle to find candidates by March. For the Greens, the issue is funding — potential candidates are unable to pay the €946 election deposit themselves, something Eesti 200 may be able to help with.
Party leader and Education Minister Kristina Kallas, according to Eesti Ekspress, "agrees with the statement 'the Greens and Eesti 200 are considering a merger'." Kallas said talks continue and clarity will come by end-October, when the Greens hold a general assembly.
Eesti 200 has met with other parties about potential mergers too. In spring the party met with its former coalition partner, the Social Democrats, though party leader Lauri Läänemets and former minister Piret Hartman soon wrapped up the talks. Eesti 200 also met with the Free Party, which had eight seats at the XIII Riigikogu (2015-2019) but currently has none — those talks drew a blank as well.
More progress has been made with the Greens, who last had Riigikogu seats in 2007-2011, Rasmus Lahtvee, Greens co-chair, and party board chair Marti Soosaar told the paper nothing has been decided, though Soosaar said he likes the merger idea and thought a new party emerging would be viable.
Commercial Register data shows the Greens currently have more members — 705 — than Eesti 200 at 579. The minimum number of members a party can have to remain valid is 500.
The original Eesti Ekspress article is here.
Eesti 200 were founded in 2018, winning their first Riigikogu seats – 14 of them – at the 2023 elections, and finding themselves in office with Reform and, until spring last year, SDE. Eesti 200's rating has tanked since then however, in the wake of donations to Ukraine scandal which engulfed one of its former MPs soon after the election. Another Eesti 200 MP, Züleyxa Izmailova, herself a former Green Party leader, went back to SDE in 2024.

Zakharova said that European countries were directly involved in the conflict through their military support for Ukraine, adding that such activity delayed a resolution to the war.
She was responding to a question about Poland's apparent readiness to host a factory producing Patriot interceptor missiles for Ukraine.
Russian attacks bring Ukraine's steel production to a halt, union says
Ukraine, one of the world's 10 largest steel producers before Russia's full-scale invasion, has halted steel production after Russian attacks shut its remaining operating plants, the country's steel producers' union said.
"Steel is not currently being produced," the union told Reuters.
Ukraine produced 7.4 million metric tons of steel in 2025, down from 21.4 million tons in 2021. In 2021, metal exports generated nearly $14 billion and accounted for about 20 percent of the country's total exports.
Before 2014, Ukraine operated five major steel plants. One was seized after Russia occupied parts of the Donbas region in 2014, while two others were effectively destroyed during fighting for Mariupol in southern Ukraine following Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
Until recently, steel production continued at ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, the country's largest steelworks, at Metinvest-owned Zaporizhstal in the frontline city of Zaporizhzhia, and at several smaller plants.
But intensified Russian attacks in recent weeks have forced the plants to halt production.
ArcelorMittal said last week it had informed the Ukrainian government that "safe and sustainable" operations were no longer possible after four strikes in five weeks caused extensive damage and killed five workers at the southeastern plant.
Death toll from Russian bombing of Ukraine rises to seven, Zelensky says
Russia's attacks across Ukraine killed seven civilians and wounded two dozen more, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said, without providing details.

The jets will contribute to the NATO military alliance's air and missile defence and protect a logistics hub in southeastern Poland that is used for military and civilian support to Ukraine, the Nordic country's government said
Sweden, which joined NATO in 2024, also in 2025 contributed jets to the mission

The fighter jets, which are produced by Swedish defence group Saab, will mainly be based in Sweden while contributing to the mission, the government said

Pentagon: Boeing will produce US Navy's next-generation stealth fighter planes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:33:34 UTC
14:33:34 KST

Boeing has been selected to build the US Navy's next-generation stealth fighter, the Pentagon said on Tuesday, marking the company's second consecutive major win on fighter jets and capping months of delay over a program central to US strategy for countering China in the Pacific.
Boeing beat out rival Northrop Grumman Corp for the development contract, worth $20 billion, to produce test aircraft. The program could grow to hundreds of billions over its lifetime as production ramps up and, potentially, as international customers place orders.
Boeing was also selected in March last year to build the Air Force's new stealthy F-47 fighter, giving it two marquee sixth-generation jet contracts in consecutive years.
Boeing was viewed as a strong contender throughout the competition because of its long history building carrier-based fighters for the Navy, including the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet that the new fighter is designed to replace. That pedigree helped offset questions raised by defense officials about whether Boeing could field enough engineers and suppliers to execute both the F-47 and Navy fighter simultaneously, concerns that appear to have been resolved in the company's favor.
Boeing shares were up 2.25% in extended trading on Tuesday, while Northrop shares were down 3.5%.
St. Louis production boost
The contract is a significant boost for Boeing's fighter production operations in St. Louis, Missouri, which is shutting down the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and EA-18G Growler production lines.
Steve Parker, president and chief executive officer of Boeing Defense, Space & Security, said in a statement the company has made investments "in new facilities uniquely suited to build multiple products with next-generation capabilities, our dedicated and talented team is ready to execute this critical program."
Currently designated the "F/A-XX" program, the new jet will be the centerpiece of the Navy's Next Generation Air Dominance family of systems.
The jet "represents a crucial, non-negotiable investment in America’s national security and long-term air combat capabilities," Michael Duffey, the Pentagon's chief weapons buyer, said in a statement.
Before winning the F-47 and F/A-XX contracts, Boeing had largely exited the fighter business, said Jeremiah Gertler, an aerospace expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
"What we don't know yet is how much F-47 DNA is in the F/A-XX. Are they being developed together or separately?" he said.
Last year, the Pentagon tried to delay the contract due to concerns that the country's defense industry does not have enough engineering capacity to simultaneously develop two sixth-generation fighters.
Democratic and Republican members of Congress from Missouri, which backed President Donald Trump in the last three elections, successfully pushed to continue funding the program.
"With modernized systems and promising new capabilities, F/A-XX and F-47 production will create more opportunities to attract engineering and technology talent to Missouri," Senator Eric Schmitt, a Republican, said in a statement.
The workers who assemble Boeing fighter jets went on strike for 101 days last year, returning to work without winning any concessions from the company.
Delays and congressional intervention
Still, the next-generation fighter jet has been buffeted by delays and funding disputes for years. Some Pentagon officials had sought to delay it by up to three years, citing engineering and supply-chain capacity concerns, before Congress intervened, earmarking $750 million for the program in the 2025 tax-cut and spending law and an additional $1.4 billion in fiscal 2026.
Lockheed Martin Corp was eliminated from the competition in March 2025 after Navy officials determined its design had not met required criteria, leaving Boeing and Northrop as the finalists.
With China rapidly fielding advanced combat aircraft, including designs Beijing describes as sixth-generation, the Navy has faced pressure to move quickly or risk operating without a modern carrier-based fighter in the 2030s and beyond.
The new jet is expected to feature advanced stealth capabilities, improved range and endurance, and the ability to integrate with uncrewed combat aircraft and the Navy's carrier-based air defense systems.
The Navy still plans to buy more than 270 Lockheed Martin F-35C jets for its carrier fleet, which will fly alongside the F/A-XX once it enters service. First production F/A-XX jets are expected in the 2030s, while the Super Hornet fleet, in service since the 1990s, is expected to remain flying into the 2040s.

PHOTO black-sea-maritime-agenda.ec.europa.eu
Font size
Burgas will host the annual Black Sea Stakeholder Conference on 30 September. Entitled Regional Cooperation for a Thriving Black Sea, the event will bring together representatives of institutions, academia and business, as well as investors and experts at the International Congress Centre, according to the European Commission’s EU Blue Economy Observatory.
Participants will discuss progress on the Common Maritime Agenda for the Black Sea, new priorities and projects aimed at building a more sustainable and competitive blue economy – economic activities linked to the sea and coastal areas.
The conference will also recognise projects from Bulgaria, Georgia, Moldova, Romania, Türkiye and Ukraine for their contribution to marine ecosystems, sustainable business and investment in the region.
The event will run from 10 am to 6 pm Bulgarian time and will be held in English.

Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani has called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a “war criminal”, while stressing that Doha would continue its mediation efforts despite heightened regional tensions.

“We are trying to do our best to give the best advice to the US government on how to reach a solution, as well as to the Iranians,” he said.
On the wider regional conflict, he said three issues needed to be addressed to defuse the war: Iran’s nuclear programme and sanctions, freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, and regional security arrangements involving Iran and Gulf Cooperation Council states.

Trump is considering resuming the bombing of Iran - WSJ26.09.26, 09:17 • 5565 views

Ursula von der Leyen proposed an ‘Alliance for the Future’ that could make Canada the EU's first ‘associate member’. But what is an ‘associate member ’, and what does this alliance mean for the EU and Canada? Watch the video!
The 16 September proposal points to a relationship beyond trade, but any associate status would have to be negotiated from scratch. It would not automatically grant EU citizenship, free movement, a commissioner, or a vote in the European Council or European Parliament.
Canada already has building blocks. CETA removes duties on 99% of tariff lines, Horizon Europe lets Canadian teams lead EU-funded research, and since August, Canadian firms can join EU-funded defence procurement.
71.7% of Canada's 2025 goods exports went to the US, while the EU is its second-largest trading partner, worth about $178 billion, according to Ottawa. Brussels wants critical minerals, defence production, and an Arctic partner.
An association agreement needs unanimity among the 27 member states and the European Parliament's consent. Some diplomats say capitals were not consulted, and Germany questions the label. CETA, provisionally applied since 2017, still awaits ratification in ten countries. Donald Trump has threatened tariffs if he sees the arrangement as hostile.

The Luxembourg Pavilion Examines Overconsumption of Living Space Through "Excess!" at the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

A jury of arts and architecture professionals recently announced the selected curatorial proposal for the Luxembourg Pavilion at the Biennale Architettura 2027. The exhibition will be curated by housing expert Céline Zimmer and architects Bùi Quý Sơn and Paul-Antoine Lucas, co-founders of the critical spatial practice Exutoire, one of the winning practices of the ArchDaily 2026 Next Practices Awards. The proposal is titled "Excess! On the Overconsumption of Living Space" and addresses the inequitable distribution of living space as a reflection of "broader habits of excess that contribute to the current housing and ecological crises." The issue will be illustrated through a dialogue between the realities of Luxembourg and Vietnam to reflect on spatial consumption. The Luxembourg Pavilion is located on the first floor of the Sale d'Armi in the Arsenale, which will open to the public for the Biennale on May 8, 2027.
According to the European Housing Coop, Luxembourg's housing supply is structured around a dual system split between a high-cost private market and a strictly regulated, publicly subsidized sector. From a holistic perspective, "Excess!" expands on the implications of demographic and economic growth in a world of finite ecological resources, in light of the country's high per capita housing floor area. The exhibition will share space and resources with Vietnam, bringing into dialogue the realities of Luxembourg, one of Europe's richest countries, a small parliamentary democracy in the form of a constitutional monarchy, with those of Vietnam, one of Southeast Asia's fastest-growing economies and a one-party Communist state. The curatorial team seeks to open up conversations and learn from intersecting perspectives, drawing on professional experience in housing systems and realities, social justice through design, and queer theory in architecture.
Bùi Quý Sơn is a Vietnamese architect and researcher, and co-founder of the Hanoi-based critical spatial practice Exutoire. Exutoire was named one of the 20 winning practices in the ArchDaily 2026 Next Practices Awards, recognized for bringing underrepresented perspectives into architectural discourse and examining established assumptions about how environments are produced and inhabited. Paul-Antoine Lucas is a Hanoi-based architect and researcher interested in housing, social justice through design, and queer theory in architecture. Together with Bùi Quý Sơn, he co-founded the queer critical spatial practice Exutoire in 2019. They published their first book in 2025 with Ruby Press, titled Housing, Micropolitics, and Pedagogies: Designing and Practicing Collectivity. Céline Zimmer is a researcher, housing expert, and activist from Luxembourg. Her research examines housing affordability and the potential of the cooperative housing model, a largely underexplored concept in Luxembourg's housing policy. In 2026, she founded Eist Neit Wunnen Agence, an agency promoting and facilitating the large-scale implementation of housing cooperatives in Luxembourg.
Related Article
"Do Architecture": Wang Shu and Lu Wenyu Announce Theme and Title for 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale
The jury was composed of Valentin Bansac, Mike Fritsch, and Alice Loumeau, curators of the 2025 Luxembourg Pavilion; Maribel Casas, director of LUCA – Luxembourg Center for Architecture; Aslı Çiçek, associate professor at Hasselt University's Faculty of Architecture and Arts and visiting professor at Ghent University's Department of Architecture and Urbanism, and editor of OASE; Sophie Dars, architect, professor, and co-founder of Accattone Magazine; Michelle Friederici, president of the Luxembourg Order of Architects and Consulting Engineers; Claudine Hemmer, advisor for visual arts and architecture at Luxembourg's Ministry of Culture; Pamela Medina Lopez, project manager for biennials, festivals, and fairs; and Eléonore Mialonier, head of architecture, design, and crafts at Kultur | lx – Arts Council Luxembourg.
The upcoming Venice Architecture Biennale will be open to visitors from May 8 to November 21, 2027. The 20th edition is titled "Do Architecture — For the Possibility of Coexistence Facing a Real Reality," curated by Amateur Architecture Studio founders Wang Shu and Lu Wenyu. Other national pavilions responding to the curatorial call include the German Pavilion, examining coexistence and democracy through "CONVIVERE"; the Ukrainian Pavilion, examining displacement and shared space through "Pool of Questions"; and the Türkiye Pavilion, examining reuse and memory through "Spolia Futures."

G20 trade officials meet under shadow of tariffs, overcapacity
