Trump’s tariffs loom over talks as G20 meets in US
Trade ministers of the Group of 20 are meeting in Milwaukee for two days of talks on Wednesday, but US President Donald Trump’s tariffs are expected to hang heavy over the talks. "Don't expect any breakthroughs," an analyst watching the event said.
G20 trade ministers are set to open talks Wednesday in the United States, in meetings strained by President Donald Trump's tariffs as Washington targets partners regarding forced labour and overcapacity.
The gathering of officials from the Group of 20 major economies – which includes China, India, Russia, Japan, Germany and France – takes place in the Midwestern city of Milwaukee.
But analysts expect the two days of talks to be deadlocked as Trump's tariffs weigh on relationships while China rejects concerns about its exports, which critics see as driven by excess industrial capacity.
Read moreTrump announces double digit tariffs on 60 countries over forced labour concerns
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer defended Washington's approach at a Tuesday roundtable in Milwaukee, saying the administration "is not anti-trade".
He added that countries are facing similar challenges with global overcapacity and "non-market policies".
This week, key US trading partners like Canada and the European Union are also expected to push for deeper trade ties outside the United States.
"Don't expect any breakthroughs in Milwaukee," Josh Lipsky of the Atlantic Council think tank told AFP, noting Trump's preference for bilateral negotiations.
Even as G20 partners will be anxious to find ways to cooperate with the world's biggest economy, "they will also be under pressure to voice their concerns with tariffs", added former US trade official Wendy Cutler, now at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
The United States holds the rotating presidency of the G20, which comprises 19 nations plus the EU and the African Union.
'Unfairly targeted'
Trump has unleashed a barrage of tariffs on trading partners since last year, separately targeting sectors like steel and autos.
Although the Supreme Court struck down Trump's country-specific tariffs in February, Washington has since alleged insufficient action against forced labour to slap new tariffs on 60 economies.
These include China, India and the EU.
The president's sectoral duties remain intact too, straining ties.
And Washington is investigating 16 partners over excess industrial capacity, a complaint commonly levied at China. Critics say this floods markets, unfairly suppressing prices.
But ongoing US probes go beyond the world's number two economy, bringing the threat of more tariffs to the EU and G20 countries like Japan and South Korea.
Cutler expects some countries will "mince no words" regarding the investigation, feeling "they are being unfairly targeted".
China "will continue to deny the issue of exporting overproduction", by trying to convince others that it is doing good by providing high-quality and low-priced goods, she said.
"This will be a hard sell," Cutler told AFP, as countries see employment and commercial fallout from waves of Chinese imports.
"Meanwhile, members are wondering how much they should agree to with the Trump administration, given trade policy could change in the US after 2028," Lipsky said, referring to the next US presidential election.
Diversifying
With Trump's trade wars, all eyes are on G20 members' efforts to deepen trade ties outside the US, or strike deals with his administration.
Canada and the EU are expected to try and boost trade and investment with others, as a spat between Ottawa and Washington intensifies.
Canada's international trade minister Maninder Sidhu stressed Ottawa's support for "open, predictable and rules-based trade".
He plans to speak with partners to "reinforce a multilateral trading system", as officials try to diversify an economy they see as too reliant on an increasingly protectionist United States.
Others like India could finalize a long-awaited trade deal with the United States. Observers are also monitoring for signs of further pressure on Iran.
Outside the G20, workers and activists are protesting what they see as the Trump administration's broken promises to improve conditions for workers, farmers and smaller businesses.
John Drew, who chairs the political arm of the United Auto Workers union in Wisconsin, laments the loss of manufacturing jobs in the state.
While the UAW does not rule out using targeted duties to protect jobs, he said, Trump's sweeping "use of tariffs has done nothing to bring back jobs and rebuild manufacturing".
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Billions slashed from NDIS packages as reassessments lead to more cuts

Billions slashed from NDIS packages as reassessments lead to more cuts and less increases
In short:
As NDIS participants brace for cuts to community supports from tomorrow, documents show the agency running the scheme has been slashing packages overall.
They also reveal the average number of eligibility revocations per week from the first three months of this year was more than quadruple the amount from the same period in 2025.
The NDIS is currently undergoing its biggest ever changes, which are expected to remove 240,000 participants over the next four years.
The agency running the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) slashed more than $2.8 billion from participant plans over a 21-month period, documents show, with "ruthless" cuts for whole categories of supports also set to begin from tomorrow.
The figures, from the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) and recently released under Freedom of Information laws, cover participant plans reviewed by the NDIA between July 1, 2024, and March 31, 2026.
The data shows that since mid-2024, the number of plans cut after a reassessment per quarter has been rising, while increases have almost halved.
Of the NDIS plans reassessed between January 1 and March 31 this year, 18,037 were reduced — the most of any quarter since Q1 2024-25.
The 26,998 reassessed plans that increased during the same quarter was by far the lowest return since July 2024.
Briefing documents also show the average number of participant eligibility revocations per week in the first three months of 2026 was 498 — more than quadruple the 116 per week across the same period in 2025.
While $2.83 billion has been cut from reassessed packages since July 2024, $11.11 billion has been paid out across plans that were increased.
The figures align with anecdotal evidence from disability advocates and ABC readers, who have been increasingly reporting sudden cuts to plans, sometimes by staff with little understanding of disability.
Emma Bennison, CEO of Disability Advocacy Network Australia, said it appeared the NDIA was cutting plans long before a generational overhaul of the scheme was passed by the parliament in August.
"This matches what our members have been telling us for some time: plans are being reduced at review, decisions are harder to get changed, and people are coming to advocates when they are already in difficulty," she said.
"It appears the direction was set well before August, and the legislation has locked it in."
Ms Bennison also said increases to reassessed packages did not necessarily indicate the NDIA was being generous to a participant, but that it was correcting an earlier under-assessment.
"Advocates see this every day. People's needs change, informal supports break down, and plans are often written on incomplete information," she said.
In a statement, a NDIA spokesperson said eligibility reassessments have been a normal practice in the NDIS since it began.
"In 2025, the NDIA extended the time-frame from 28 to 90 days to collect information to support a reassessment. As a result, staffing and decision volumes increased," they said.
"It is normal for plans to go up and down as participants' needs change over time. The purpose of many NDIS supports is to build capacity so participants will need less support over time."
The spokesperson said plan changes occurring "through the usual planning process" should "not be confused" with wider government reforms to be introduced gradually over time.
Community supports to be cut
It comes one day before the slashing of a category of funding allowing support workers to take participants to appointments, work and social activities.
From tomorrow, all participants' budgets for social, civic and community participation supports will be cut by 50 per cent.
Budgets for improved daily living skills supports — a category covering allied health therapies and skill training — will also be reduced by 10 per cent.
Those changes will occur as plans are created, renewed or reassessed over a 12-month period, according to the Department of Health.
Ms Bennison said community supports were how many participants stayed connected and safe.
George Taleporos, chair of NDIS advocacy group Every Australian Counts, said the "ruthless" cuts meant participants would be "seen less" and rely more heavily on their families for support.
"The disability royal commission taught us that when isolation increases, the abuse and neglect of people with disability also increases," he said.
The cuts are part of the Albanese government's wider NDIS overhaul, expected to remove 240,000 participants from the scheme over the next four years, saving about $38 billion during that time.
The NDIS was supporting 782,013 participants at the end of June this year and cost more than $50 billion last financial year.
It is currently growing at 10.5 per cent per year, about half the rate it was when Labor took power in 2022, but the federal government wants it down to 2 or 3 per cent.
Tomorrow also marks the first phase of Thriving Kids, a NDIS alternative for children under nine with developmental delay or autism who have "low to moderate" support needs.

Bats may have first evolved in Europe 65 million years ago
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:12:36 UTC
14:12:36 KST

Bats may have first evolved in Europe 65 million years ago
A massive new study traces bats back to ancient Europe and suggests flight and echolocation helped launch their extraordinary evolutionary success.
- Date:
- September 30, 2026
- Source:
- University College Dublin
- Summary:
- A huge genomic and fossil study suggests bats first evolved in Europe around 65 to 60 million years ago before spreading across the globe. The findings also indicate that flight and echolocation emerged near the beginning of bat evolution, potentially helping explain how bats became one of the most successful mammal groups on Earth.
- Share:
New research is reshaping scientists' understanding of bat evolution, with evidence suggesting that bats most likely originated in Europe during the late Paleocene, roughly 65 to 60 million years ago.
For decades, researchers have debated where bats first appeared. Africa, Asia, and North America have all been proposed as possible birthplaces.
Now, an international team of 137 researchers from 64 countries has combined genomic data from every living bat family with evidence from ancient fossils to reconstruct the evolutionary history of the world's only mammals capable of true powered flight. The work was carried out through the Bat1K consortium, a global effort dedicated to sequencing the genomes of all living bat species and co-founded by UCD Professor Emma Teeling.
A New Bat Family Tree
The study, published in Nature, examined 103 bat genomes, including 42 newly generated chromosome-level assemblies, covering all 21 recognized bat families. Researchers also incorporated evidence from 44 fossil bats.
Together, those data gave scientists a much clearer picture of how bats emerged and spread around the planet.
The results suggest that bats first evolved in Europe during the late Paleocene. Their descendants then moved into Africa.
As bats continued to diversify, separate groups expanded into the Americas, Asia, and Australia. Over time, those migrations produced the major bat lineages found around the world today.
Why Bats Are So Unusual
Bats are among the most distinctive mammals on Earth. They are the only mammals capable of sustained powered flight, and most species can navigate and hunt in darkness using sound.
They also represent about one fifth of all living mammals and play important ecological roles around the world.
Many bat species are unusually resistant to disease and can live far longer than other mammals of similar size. Even so, scientists have spent decades trying to resolve basic questions about how bats evolved and how their most unusual traits developed.
"It is extraordinary, after decades of research and conflicting findings, we finally have a robust phylogenetic tree that we can now use to properly understand how and where bats' unique traits evolved," said leading senior author and co-founding Director of Bat1K Professor Emma Teeling, UCD School of Biology and Environmental Science.
"We also have the genomes to uncover the molecular basis of these spectacular mammalian adaptations and know where the fossil bats fall in this tree."
Assistant Professors Graham Hughes and Zixia Huang, both from UCD School of Biology and Environmental Science, also contributed to the project through the international Bat1K consortium.
Flight and Echolocation Appeared Early
The findings also provide new clues about the origins of two of bats' defining features: powered flight and echolocation.
"As bats are the only mammals known to have evolved true powered flight, our findings point to Europe as the most likely place where mammalian powered flight first evolved," added Professor Teeling.
Researchers also analyzed the fossil bat Vielasia, which sits on the oldest branch of the bat family tree. That fossil suggests echolocation had already appeared close to the beginning of bat evolution.
Taken together, the evidence indicates that both powered flight and echolocation emerged before modern bat groups began diversifying. Those abilities may have helped give bats their remarkable evolutionary success.
"The approach we used to model the evolution of fossil and living species together can do what other methods cannot -- identify the oldest group of fossil bats while taking the genomic data into account, and uncover when and where bats originated," said senior author Professor Liliana M. Dávalos, Stony Brook University.
Reconstructing an Ancient Bat Genome
Researchers also computationally reconstructed the genome of the ancient ancestor shared by all living bats.
That reconstruction offers a glimpse into the genetic makeup of one of the earliest flying mammals and creates a new resource for studying how bats developed their exceptional diversity.
Scientists can now use the dataset to investigate the genetic changes associated with flight, echolocation, longevity, and disease resistance. It may also help researchers understand why many bats are unusually resistant to disease and exceptionally long lived for their size.
"We combined state-of-the-art DNA sequencing and computational methods to generate and compare these genomes and identify the genes they contain," said senior author Professor Michael Hiller, Senckenberg Research Institute, Frankfurt.
The genomic resource could eventually contribute to human research involving ageing, immunity, and disease resistance.
"Bats constantly surprise us. They are one of evolution's greatest experiments," said senior author Professor Sonja Vernes, University of St Andrews, and Bat1K co-founding Director.
"This extraordinary genomic resource, the culmination of years of international cooperation of Bat1K, is finally allowing us to understand how their remarkable biology evolved."
"This resource for the community of scientists allows them to investigate the different types of genomic variation, from single base changes to hundreds or thousands of bases missing from one lineage but present in another, that have given rise to the huge variety of bats that we share the planet with, and the origins of their unique characteristics," added senior author Professor David Ray, Texas Tech University.
Decades of Samples From Around the World
The project is the largest study yet to combine bat genomes and fossils. It draws on samples gathered over decades from bats worldwide, including rare species found only in remote regions.
In addition to identifying a likely geographic origin for bats, the analysis also resolves several long-running disagreements about how different bat families are related. Some of the results reveal unexpected evolutionary connections among unusual bat groups.
"This dataset represents decades of work by field researchers from around the world, collecting samples from some of the most remote places, from New Zealand to Madagascar," said Professor Teeling.
"None of this would have been possible without the dedication and collaboration of these researchers, working together through the Bat1K consortium to bring these samples together, allowing us to tell the evolutionary history of these extraordinary flying mammals."
The X Chromosome Helped Resolve a Long Debate
Reconstructing the bat family tree was particularly difficult because different parts of bat genomes can preserve conflicting signals about their evolutionary history.
One likely reason is that early bat lineages exchanged genes with one another. As a result, one section of the genome can suggest one set of evolutionary relationships while another points to a different pattern.
Researchers found, however, that part of the X chromosome preserved an especially clear record of the underlying relationships between bat groups.
That signal helped the team resolve evolutionary trees that had remained disputed for decades.
The study was supported in part by the European Research Council, Science Foundation Ireland and the Irish Research Council, alongside international partners.

Australia's card surcharge ban starts tomorrow. Here's everything you need to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:05:10 UTC
14:05:10 KST

in brief
- The surcharge ban covers eftpos, Visa and Mastercard, including credit, debit and prepaid cards.
- The changes do not affect legitimate booking fees, service fees, delivery charges or hospitality surcharges for weekends and public holidays.
From tomorrow, the familiar sting of a card surcharge will disappear for Australians paying with most major cards.
But the changes come with a few catches — and not every checkout fee is going away.
Here’s what consumers need to know.
What exactly changes from tomorrow?
From 1 October, businesses can no longer add a separate surcharge simply because a customer pays by card on the affected payment networks.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The change comes through new no-surcharge rules introduced by the card networks and follows a Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) review into card payment costs and surcharging that found removing them would support a more efficient and competitive payments system.
"When card surcharging ends, the sticker price will be the price that consumers end up paying," the RBA website explained.
In other words, if an item is advertised at $100, that's the price you'll pay and you should no longer see an extra card-payment fee added when you tap or insert your card.
Which cards and payment methods are covered?
The surcharge ban covers EFTPOS, Visa and Mastercard, including credit, debit and prepaid cards.
American Express and UnionPay are also removing surcharges from 1 October, while PayPal's equivalent change takes effect on 5 October.
The rules generally apply whether the card was issued in Australia or overseas, although individual network rules and exemptions can apply.
Does the ban apply online as well as in-store?
Yes. The change is about the payment method, not whether you are standing at a shop counter or buying from a website.
So an online retailer cannot simply retain a separate Visa, Mastercard or EFTPOS card surcharge because the transaction happens online. The same principle applies to card payments made through apps and other digital checkout systems.
Can businesses still charge booking fees, service fees or weekend surcharges?
Yes, as the RBA site explained: "The changes only apply to surcharges added because a customer pays by card."
The changes do not affect legitimate booking fees, service fees, delivery charges or hospitality surcharges for weekends and public holidays.
Will this make paying cheaper?
The end of surcharges does not necessarily mean lower prices.
Businesses will still have costs associated with processing card payments, but what's changing is they can no longer add them as an extra fee. They may choose to incorporate them into the total price.
The RBA says, "those costs can be reflected in a business’s overall pricing, rather than charged as a separate surcharge".
Could businesses raise prices instead?
Yes. Businesses are generally free to set and change their prices, as long as they do not mislead customers.
That means a cafe, retailer, or professional service could increase its standard price to cover payment-processing costs.
Can businesses set minimum spends or stop accepting cards?
Businesses can choose which payment methods they accept and can set minimum card-payment amounts, subject to applicable rules.
So don't assume every business will have to accept your card simply because surcharges are disappearing.
Can businesses offer discounts for paying by cash or another method?
Yes. Businesses can encourage customers to use another payment method by offering a discount rather than imposing a card surcharge.
For example, a business could offer a discount for paying by cash or PayID.
What should you do if you’re still charged a card surcharge?
The consumer watchdog has advice for customers who suspect they've been hit with a card surcharge.
First, check what the fee actually is. It may be a legitimate booking, service or weekend surcharge rather than a card-payment surcharge.
If it appears to be a card surcharge, raise it with the business and ask them to remove the fee or refund it.
"Businesses shouldn’t try to avoid the 'no surcharge' rules … by describing a card payment surcharge as another type of fee or charge," the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) said on its website.
From 1 October, consumers can also raise concerns with the relevant card network or the business's payment provider and can report potentially misleading pricing to the ACCC or their state or territory consumer protection agency.

In steelmaking, there was a period in September when Ukrainian metallurgy did not produce steel, according to Oleksandr Vodoviz, head of the CEO’s office at Metinvest group said at Forbes Ukraine event. An attempt to restart a furnace at Zaporizhstal lasted 10 hours and cost $50 million, he said.
In agriculture, grain exports have fallen to 40% of what is possible because of blocked seaports and the limited capacity of the Danube route, according to Kernel CEO Yevhen Osypov.
Retail is under similar strain. Intertop Ukraine CEO Serhiy Badritdinov said 2026 is harder for the sector than 2022, the first year of Russia’s full-scale invasion. The business is adjusting its inventory and logistics and expanding e-commerce, he said.

‘Europe is ending its addiction to a toxic, costly drug’: Heat pump sales soar as electricity taxes fall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
05:02:21 UTC
14:02:21 KST

Heat pump sales plummeted in 2024 – but now they’re on the rise again. Here’s why.
Heat pump sales in European homes rose by 11 per cent in the first half of 2026, following a surge in gas prices linked to the Iran war.
The energy shock has added urgency to the EU’s shift away from fossil fuels, with the European Commission encouraging governments to lower electricity tax.
This is a likely driver of the growth in heat pump sales so far this year, according to the European Heat Pump Association (EHPA), which has long argued that their uptake depends strongly on the electricity price.
The new data from the EHPA covers 12 European countries: Austria, Belgium, Switzerland, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, Norway, Portugal and Sweden.
It shows that around 1.16 million heat pumps were sold between January and June – up from 1.04 million in the first half of 2025.
It’s a major shift from 2024, when sales fell by 47 per cent in the first half of the year compared with 2023, after a rush to install them during the 2022 energy crisis slowed.
High gas prices driving heat pump uptake – but electricity taxes remain an obstacle
Heat pumps capture energy from air, water or the ground and turn it into heat or cold air. They run on electricity, making them an appealing alternative to gas-fired boilers, especially in the context of the Iran war.
Iran’s disruption of shipping through the vital Strait of Hormuz, which carries around a fifth of the world’s oil and gas exports, has sent energy prices soaring to record highs.
“Europe is ending its addiction to a toxic, costly drug from dodgy suppliers – gas,” says Paul Kenny, EHPA director general. “The sooner electricity becomes the most affordable solution, the quicker we’ll get clean.”
Although heat pumps are three to five times more energy efficient than boilers, according to EHPA, taxes on electricity are often higher than on gas in Europe, due to complex historical factors. This makes it less financially appealing for households to electrify with things like heat pumps and EVs.
How the EU’s Electrification Action Plan could boost heat pumps
The EU’s Electrification Action Plan, released in July 2026, aims to change that by evening out these taxes. The plan also sets a target of four million annual heat pump installations across Europe by 2030, and aims for electricity to make up almost half of EU energy use by 2040, up from around a quarter today. The Commission estimates that widespread adoption of electric technologies could save roughly €200 billion in fossil fuel imports by 2040.
EHPA points to the Netherlands and Belgium as having successfully shifted taxes on electricity over to fossil fuels. Denmark has separately cut electricity taxes specifically for heat pump households, while countries like France, Germany and Italy offer grants and subsidies for heat pump installation.
Wider EU tax reform would require consensus from all 27 member states, which remains a significant obstacle.

NATO’s only Latin American partner visits Brussels HQ
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
06:00:50 BST
14:00:50 KST

Students from the Colombia War College have visited NATO headquarters in Brussels for briefings on the alliance’s political and military structure and on its partnership with Colombia, the only Latin American country to hold partner status, according to NATO.
The visit on 24 September was hosted by the International Staff Political Affairs and Security Policy Division alongside the International Military Staff Cooperative Security Division. This year’s delegation for the college’s Advanced Military Studies Course brought in students from Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador and Mexico as well as Colombia, and the group was taken through the alliance’s decision making, roles and responsibilities after a tour of the building.
Captain Philippe Vitel, head of the Military Cooperation Branch within the Cooperative Security Division, addressed the students on why the alliance invests in relationships of this kind. “NATO faces challenging times ahead, with a growing global strategic competition and regional challenges,” he said. “Now, more than ever, strengthening cooperation with NATO partners such as Colombia is essential.”
Javier Colomina, the Secretary General’s Special Representative for the Southern Neighbourhood and Deputy Assistant Secretary General for Security Policy and NATO Affairs, gave a keynote on the alliance following the Ankara Summit. According to NATO, he also covered the partnership framework and how working with countries outside alliance territory makes the alliance itself safer, through contributions running from policy development and defence capacity building to interoperability work and crisis management.
The students then attended an expert panel on NATO-Colombia cooperation drawn from both the International Staff and the International Military Staff, concentrating on the Individually Tailored Partnership Programme that governs the relationship and on practical military cooperation within it. The NATO Defense College closed the day with a session on how senior military education connects to strategy and policy.
Colombia became a NATO partner in 2017, and remains the only country in Latin America to hold that status. The main areas of cooperation are cyber security, counter-terrorism and maritime security, the last of those reflecting a Colombian navy with long experience of interdiction work in the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific.
The traffic does not run in only one direction, since Colombia provides demining training to allies and partner countries through a Partnership Training and Exercise Centre at the Colombia International Demining Centre, an expertise built over decades of clearing explosive remnants from its own internal conflict, and one that has obvious application for allies supporting Ukraine with the same problem on a far larger scale.
Partner status carries no security guarantee and no obligation on either side, and sits well short of membership, which under the North Atlantic Treaty is open only to European states. What it provides is a structured route into alliance standards, exercises and education, which is most of what a visit of this kind is for.

As European leaders warn of possible Russian attacks and hybrid provocations, experts and officials agree that there are no signs of a new escalation.

In his assessment, large-scale military operations are less likely than specific provocations aimed at spreading panic among the public and exerting political pressure.
“Nobody is preparing to conquer us at the moment – neither right now nor this year. In this case, some kind of specific, highly precise attacks or provocations are more likely, aimed not so much at causing physical damage as at sowing serious panic in people’s minds,” Šlekys said.
According to him, Russia could use such provocations to divide Lithuanian society and undermine unity among NATO countries.
‘Nothing new’
Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of the National Crisis Management Centre (NKVC), said Russia’s hybrid pressure on Lithuania and other European countries is “not a new phenomenon”.
“Since 2024, Lithuania alone has recorded a number of attacks or provocations involving acts of sabotage, as well as cyber and information operations,” Vitkauskas told ELTA.
He said warnings and preparedness measures by neighbouring and allied countries were a responsible response to the current security environment.
“Early warning, institutional preparedness and informing the public reduce the impact of provocations and strengthen NATO’s overall resilience,” the NKVC head said.
When assessing specific incidents, Vitkauskas urged people to distinguish confirmed facts from speculation and rely on information provided by official institutions.
“Based on the official information published so far, there is no evidence that the drones that entered Lithuanian airspace were targeting sites in Lithuania,” Vitkauskas said.
He noted that Lithuania has strengthened the protection of strategic infrastructure, while the NKVC, together with intelligence and other responsible institutions, has issued recommendations to companies and institutions that may face the risk of sabotage or acts of subversion.
Vitkauskas also urged the public to remain vigilant and not spread unverified information, as kinetic incidents or provocations may be accompanied by information operations aimed at causing fear and undermining trust in institutions.

Meanwhile, Moscow’s messaging about possible retaliatory actions against NATO and EU countries may be intended to cause anxiety and undermine public confidence.
"If we assess the situation as a whole, I would say that the level of the threat, as intelligence officials have also confirmed, has not changed. Russia's unpredictability remains. The tactics may be changing slightly, with different types of actions emerging, but the essence remains unchanged," Martinaitis told ELTA.
A similar sentiment was repeated by the Lithuanian prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevičius, as well as the secretary-general of NATO, Mark Rutte, in Brussels on Tuesday.
Further reading
In recent weeks, the leaders of several European countries have spoken about the threat of possible Russian provocations.
In early September, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that, based on intelligence assessments, Russia could be preparing hybrid drone and missile attacks against countries supporting Ukraine, and urged the public to be prepared for various scenarios.

AI generated

Four other senators from US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party called on his administration last week to release more than US$15 billion (S$19.17 billion) in stalled national security assistance for Taiwan.
The United States does not have formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, but is the island’s most important international backer and weapons supplier.
Washington is bound by the 1979 Taiwan Relations Act to provide Taiwan, which Beijing claims as its own territory, with the means to defend itself.
“As members of Congress, we have a duty to make sure this law is adhered to and that decisions about the defence needs of Taiwan are based on our joint assessment of military necessity,” Wicker said in a statement.
Wicker also said he discussed with Yui what he called the rise of Chinese aggression against the United States’ Indo-Pacific allies.
“In response – and in accordance with the Taiwan Relations Act – Congress has authorised and appropriated a surge in resources to provide Taiwan with enhanced training, security assistance, and arms sales. These authorities must be used for the purposes that Congress intended,” Wicker added.
China has repeatedly called for Taiwan arms sales to end, and in May, following a Beijing trip, Trump said he was keeping a new package worth some US$14 billion in abeyance.
However, after meeting President Xi Jinping in Washington last week, Trump said only that the Chinese leader understood his position on Taiwan.
Wicker urged the US to uphold a precedent when former president Ronald Reagan said Washington would not consult Beijing on arms sales to Taiwan.
Taiwan’s government rejects Beijing’s sovereignty claims and says only the island’s people can decide their future.
Taiwan is in continuous talks with Washington about arms sales and had received reassurances since the summit between Trump and Xi that US policy on Taiwan had not changed, Taiwan Defence Minister Wellington Koo said earlier on Sept 29. REUTERS

Air pollution is slowing down marathon runners, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:49:27 UTC
13:49:27 KST

Higher levels of nitrogen dioxide on race day are linked to slower marathon times, particularly among non-elite runners, new research suggests.
Air pollution added minutes to marathon runners' finishing times across six major races, a new study has found.
Runners in the Berlin, Boston, Chicago, London, New York City and Tokyo marathons have seen their finishing times affected by air pollution levels on race days in recent years.
Researchers at the University of Leicester analysed more than 2.7 million race performances from some of the most popular World Marathon Majors, which host thousands of athletes every year, across editions held between 2010 and 2024.
“From our analysis of more than two million marathon runners, we observed that levels of nitrogen dioxide were strongly associated with their finishing time,” said James Donaldson, the study’s lead author.
For every microgram-per-cubic-metre (µg/m3) increase in nitrogen dioxide, finishing times were 1.43 minutes slower for men and 1.56 minutes slower for women, the researchers found.
On a high-pollution race day when nitrogen dioxide levels reached 10.3 µg/m³ compared with a low-pollution level of 5.2 µg/m³, finishing times were around seven to eight minutes longer.
The researchers also analysed fine particulate matter — PM2.5 — but found no statistically significant association with finishing times.
The highest median race-day concentration of nitrogen dioxide was recorded in London at 10.9 µg/m³, and the lowest in Berlin at 6.1 µg/m³. The good news, that the situation got better in London.
“Despite the known harms of air pollution, it is important to note that levels of nitrogen dioxide and PM2.5 on marathon day in London appear to have fallen substantially since the 2010 event, which is great news for heart health,” said Bryan Williams, chief scientific and medical officer at the British Heart Foundation, which supported the study.
Non-elite runners hit the hardest
The effect was greater among recreational runners, whose finishing times rose by 2.12 minutes per 1 µg/m³ of nitrogen dioxide, compared with 0.34 minutes for elite runners.
Nitrogen dioxide comes primarily from the burning of fossil fuels by human activities, such as cars, trucks and factories, as well as from natural processes and chemical reactions in the air.
It has been linked to impaired lung function, airway inflammation and adverse cardiovascular responses.
The authors identified several potential explanations for these patterns.
As well as spending longer on the course, slower runners are more likely to train in the same urban areas where marathons are held, accumulating chronic pollution exposure, while elite runners typically prepare in cleaner environments and compete internationally, the authors wrote.
Donaldson also noted that “the physiological adaptations that result from the high-intensity training undertaken by elite athletes may offer some protection against the harmful effects of air pollution”.
“As well as this, the fact remains that exercise is still very beneficial for your cardiovascular health - it can reduce the risk of heart and circulatory diseases by up to 35 per cent,” said Williams, adding that the findings should not put people off running.

Power company DTEK did not detail the damage to energy infrastructure in Kyiv but said workers had restored supply to 8,000 households.
Russia acknowledged the massive overnight assault, saying it had hit a data centre in the capital supporting Ukraine's armed forces, various power plants in the Kyiv region, an industrial complex in Odesa region, and port infrastructure in Izmail.
The attacks followed weeks of near-constant barrages of jet drones, which Ukraine struggles to shoot down.
Zelenskiy said Ukraine - which is also short of interceptors to down ballistic missiles - had received new air defence support packages in recent days.
Thanking allies for the deliveries, he called for more protection ahead of the winter.
Ukraine's air force said that five missiles and 155 drones had been intercepted in the overnight attack.
DEBRIS AT WESTERN EMBASSY
On Wednesday morning, Kyiv was shrouded in thick fog from the smoke of attacks. Emergency services asked residents to keep windows closed.
Citing preliminary information, Klitschko said debris had been found at a Western embassy in the centre of Kyiv. He did not specify which embassy.
Among neighbouring nations, a drone crossed into Moldova's airspace and exploded near the eastern village of Hirbovet, while European Union and NATO members Romania and Poland both scrambled military jets, the countries said.
Flights at Polish airports Lublin and Rzeszow were temporarily suspended.
Ukraine has also increased attacks on Russia, hitting refineries and online retailers to undermine Moscow's war effort.
One person was killed in drone attacks in Russia's Bryansk region, which borders Ukraine, while a Ukrainian drone attack on the oil-producing Samara region damaged private houses, regional governors said. REUTERS

Danish People’s Party ready to give its party leader a salary increase
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:27:48 UTC
13:27:48 KST

Eight Danish municipalities did not meet the required staffing ratio in kindergartens in 2025, according to figures published Monday by Statistics Denmark.
The municipalities are Ringsted, Odder, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Struer, Brønderslev, Rebild and Thisted.
Under the political requirement, there must be at least one pedagogical staff member for every six children in kindergartens. In 2024, 14 municipalities failed to meet the requirement.
The trade union BUPL, which represents pedagogues working in Danish children’s institutions, noted that more municipalities now meet the requirement than before.
“Staffing ratios have improved, and that is an important first step to ensure the quality in our daycare institutions,” BUPL chairperson Elisa Rimpler said.
“But we are not at the finish line at all when it comes to giving children the quality they are entitled to.”
Since 2024, there has also been a requirement of at least one employee for every three children in nurseries.
Five municipalities failed to meet that requirement last year: Bornholm, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Thisted and Rebild.
Rimpler said the figures were not good enough and called on municipalities to increase their efforts.
“There is a need to build on top of this, because in many places the staffing ratios on paper are experienced as very far from reality,” she said.
“Both because managers, long-term sick employees, and pedagogues employed to support individual children are counted, and because many of the extra employees do not have the necessary professional qualifications.”
According to BUPL, the law does not require the employees counted in the staffing ratios to have professional training.
The union said the share of pedagogues among staff was 57% in 2019, compared with 50.6% last year.
Children, Elderly and Housing Minister Jacob Mark of the Socialist People’s Party, SF, said it was serious when municipalities failed to meet the legal requirement.
He said the minimum staffing ratios were working because more nurseries and kindergartens were getting more staff around children and nationwide cuts to staffing had stopped.
“But, as I also see, there are eight municipalities that do not meet the minimum staffing ratios. That is completely unacceptable. I am going to intervene against that,” the minister said.
Mark also criticized the practice of counting managers and long-term sick employees in the staffing figures. He said managers are not with children all the time, while long-term sick employees are not with them at all.
According to Mark, municipalities “just” need to hire more pedagogical staff.
The minister said he will send a letter to the eight municipalities that do not meet the requirements. The same municipalities will also face scrutiny from Ankestyrelsen, Denmark’s public authority for supervising municipalities and other public bodies.
Ankestyrelsen can impose a range of sanctions after assessing why a municipality is not complying with the law, including advisory opinions and fines.
“Now they have had four years. Now they must reach the finish line with those minimum staffing ratios,” Mark said.

Tokyo succumbs to ‘rain fatigue’ after a record 35 consecutive days of showers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:23:15 UTC
13:23:15 KST

Residents of Tokyo awoke to a familiar sound on Wednesday: raindrops splashing against windows and balcony floors.
The Japanese capital has seen a record 35 consecutive days of rain that experts blame on a combination of climate change and El Niño, which has created a prolonged front of high pressure in the Pacific Ocean.
The record rainfall has triggered a sharp rise in the price of vegetables, cast a shadow over tourism and left millions of Tokyoites wondering if they will see sunshine again.
Central Tokyo has been drenched by 629mm (24.8 inches) of rain between the start of September through to Monday this week, nearly three times the normal level, according to the agency.
It experienced just 45.8 hours of sunshine over the same period, the second lowest on record, the Mainichi Shimbun said, while on 14 days the sun did not appear at all.
The weather is affecting people’s physical and mental health, according to Hiromichi Ito, a doctor and director of a clinic in the capital, who told the Sankei Shimbun newspaper that prolonged rain, low atmospheric pressure and high humidity can lead to headaches, dizziness and other symptoms.
While the rain had turned to a light drizzle by late Wednesday morning, more could be on the way, as this year’s El Niño warms the Pacific Ocean, intensifying extreme weather patterns triggered by the climate crisis.
“Autumn rain fronts are staying longer than usual,” Masayuki Kyoda, an official at the Japan meteorological agency (JMA), told Agence France-Presse.
Tokyo’s rainy season usually occurs in June, but there have been regular downpours throughout the summer, causing heavy flooding in parts of the region. Earlier this month, Typhoon Dujuan caused flooding and landslides in neighbouring Chiba prefecture, killing eight people and destroying dozens of homes.
This week, meteorological officials said another typhoon, the 26th of the season, was moving in a north-easterly direction and could brush the Kanto region, where Tokyo is located.
While Kyoda said it was difficult to establish a direct link between climate change and the streak of wet weather in Tokyo – the longest since records began in 1886 – the agency said in a recent report that “global warming was affecting Japan’s weather long-term, including through more precipitation”.
The previous longest period of consecutive rain in Tokyo lasted 33 days between 27 June and 29 July 2019.
The prolonged rainfall has triggered a rise in the price of vegetables, particularly leafy greens, as a result of crop damage in agricultural regions near Tokyo, media reports said, with one supermarket worker in the capital quoted as saying that price of a head of lettuce had more than doubled to ¥450 (£2.17).
Residents also complained of not being able to dry their washing, forcing them to make trips to the local launderette.
The news that the city has not enjoyed a single dry day since 27 August prompted many take to social media to complain of “rain fatigue”.
“This endless rain must be to blame for my low mood,” said one X user. “If you’re feeling worn out, it’s not your fault.”
Yojiro Noda, the lead singer of the band Radwimps, posted to his 1.1 million followers: “Tokyo, a lifetime of rain.”
Another wondered if the city would match the 40 days and 40 nights of rain referenced in the Old Testament.

Morocco's King Mohammed VI appoints Fatima Mansouri as the country's first female prime minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
04:21:51 UTC
13:21:51 KST

Mansouri is only the second woman in the Arab world to hold the office of prime minister. Her established political career has seen her serve as mayor of Marrakesh and member of parliament previously.
Morocco's King Mohammed VI named Urban Planning Minister Fatima Zahra Mansouri as the country's prime minister on Tuesday, making the 50-year-old attorney the first woman to hold the office in the Muslim kingdom.
Mansouri, who until her nomination also was the mayor of Marrakech, was tasked with forming a new government, the Royal Palace said in a statement. The announcement came four days after results of parliamentary elections were announced, with Mansouri’s centrist Authenticity and Modernity Party, or PAM, scoring the highest votes.
Mansouri, the second woman to serve as prime minister in the Arab world after Najla Bouden in Tunisia, is expected to build a coalition in the coming days to form a government. Morocco’s electoral system makes it difficult for a single party to win an absolute majority.
Her government is expected to make billions of dollars in investments linked to the 2030 FIFA World Cup, while seeking to deliver on promises to fight inflation, raise wages and create jobs.
The Moroccan Constitution gives the king, who is the country’s highest authority, the power to appoint the prime minister, but he must choose from the party that wins the most seats in parliamentary elections.
That was a change successfully pushed by Arab Spring protesters in 2011. Before that, the king could name the prime minister without any such restriction.
Mansouri joined PAM upon its creation in 2008 by Fouad Ali el-Himma, a childhood friend and close adviser to the king.
A law graduate from the University of Montpellier in France, Mansouri became one of the party’s top leaders in 2024. She twice served as mayor of Marrakech and was a member of parliament.
Mansouri is the daughter of the “pasha of Marrakech” Abderrahmane el-Mansouri, a senior local official who was also Morocco’s ambassador to the United Arab Emirates, headed Marrakech’s bar association and was a major landowner.
She faced accusations of conflict of interest after a group of unidentified hackers claimed she had used her position for personal gain regarding land transactions in Marrakech. Mansouri denied the allegations, called them defamatory and took legal action.
One million of the 15.8 million registered voters in last week’s election voted for the Authenticity and Modernity Party, marking its first win since its creation. The election was the first since the Ceuta migration crisis last July and deadly youth-led protests last year.
After the royal nomination, the focus shifts to the coalition that will form the next government.
PAM has expressed its willingness to work with all parties, but some, including the moderate Islamist Justice and Development party and left-wing Federation of Democratic Left, have announced no plans of such collaboration, insisting they will remain in the opposition.

Sharks can hear nearly 250 feet away and pinpoint the source
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
03:58:33 UTC
12:58:33 KST

Sharks can hear nearly 250 feet away and pinpoint the source
- Date:
- September 29, 2026
- Source:
- Florida Atlantic University
- Summary:
- Wild blacktip sharks can detect low-frequency sounds from nearly 250 feet away, according to experiments conducted off the Florida coast. The sharks not only heard the sounds but sharply changed direction away from them, suggesting they could pinpoint where they were coming from.
- Share:
The ocean is filled with sound, and for sharks, those sounds can reveal what is happening well beyond their field of view. Noise produced by prey, predators, and other animals may provide important information about the surrounding environment. Yet scientists have had little direct evidence showing just how far a shark swimming freely in the ocean can hear, or whether it can tell where a distant sound originated.
A new study from Florida Atlantic University is beginning to answer those questions. Researchers studying blacktip sharks (Carcharhinus limbatus) used an underwater speaker, a drone, and wild sharks swimming naturally in coastal waters. They found that the animals could detect sounds from substantial distances and abruptly turn away from the source, even when it was nearly 250 feet away.
The findings, published in Integrative Organismal Biology, provide the first quantified evidence that free swimming sharks can detect and orient away from sounds in the acoustic far field. The results offer a rare look at a basic shark sense that remains surprisingly poorly understood.
Testing Shark Hearing in the Wild
Blacktip sharks were especially well suited for the experiment because they gather predictably off Southeast Florida. Large numbers congregate along the Palm Beach County coast each winter, while smaller groups can be found there throughout the year. Clear, shallow water also allowed researchers to monitor individual sharks from above while minimizing interference with their natural behavior.
"Their abundance and accessibility made it possible for us to observe them from above without disturbing their natural behavior, while also presenting controlled underwater sounds," said Stephen Kajiura, Ph.D., senior author and a professor of biological sciences in FAU's Charles E. Schmidt College of Science.
Researchers carried out the tests in shallow coastal waters across Palm Beach County. After anchoring a boat, they placed an underwater speaker in the water and allowed it to drift with the current as far as 19 meters from the vessel. This setup helped reduce the possibility that the boat itself would influence the sharks.
The team played three groups of low-frequency sounds, covering 100 to 200 Hertz, 200 to 400 Hertz, and 400 to 800 Hertz. They also used a 10 kiloHertz control sound, which lies beyond the known hearing range of sharks. Rather than attempting to lure the animals toward the speaker, the researchers played the sounds loudly enough to provoke a startle response.
Sharks Responded From 243 Feet Away
Calibrated hydrophones allowed the researchers to measure sound levels at different locations, making it possible to determine what each shark was hearing at the moment it reacted. Meanwhile, a drone flying 40 to 50 meters above the water recorded the movements of free swimming sharks during both the experimental and control sounds.
The researchers then analyzed the footage frame by frame to determine how far each shark was from the speaker and how sharply its swimming direction changed.
The sharks reacted to all three low frequency sound ranges but showed no response to the 10 kiloHertz control. They detected low frequency sounds from distances of up to 74 meters (243 feet), substantially farther than had previously been demonstrated in freely swimming sharks.
Just as importantly, the animals often made rapid turns away from the speaker. That behavior indicates that they were not simply detecting the presence of a sound. They could also determine the direction from which it was coming.
More than 70% of the recorded responses occurred in the acoustic far field. The sharks were also most sensitive to lower frequency sounds, which they detected from greater distances and at lower sound levels.
"What makes this finding particularly interesting is that the sharks were responding to sounds beyond the acoustic near field, where the sound behaves differently than it does close to the source," Kajiura said. "This suggests that they are detecting the particle motion associated with sound even at considerable distances from the source -- something we have not previously been able to demonstrate in free-swimming sharks."
How Sharks Hear Without a Swim Bladder
The result is especially notable because sharks lack the gas filled swim bladder found in many bony fish. In those fish, the organ can contribute to the detection of sound pressure.
Sharks are instead believed to depend largely on their inner ears. These include a specialized sensory structure known as the macula neglecta, which may help them detect motion and vibrations generated as sound travels through water.
The research also demonstrates why studying shark hearing in the ocean can reveal information that is difficult to obtain in laboratory tanks. Inside a tank, sound can reflect repeatedly from the walls, producing complicated acoustic patterns that may make an animal's response harder to interpret.
"Trying to do hearing experiments in a tank results in the sound bouncing off the walls which causes complex and confusing signals -- it is like being in a house of mirrors. This is why it is so important to do these types of experiments in the ocean with wild sharks to get a natural response," said Caroline Sullivan, lead author who conducted this work as part of her master's degree in biological sciences.
Study co-author is Edmund Gerstein, Ph.D., a research director, Charles E. Schmidt College of Science.
A Hidden Sensory World in the Ocean
The findings suggest that sound may provide sharks with useful information about events occurring hundreds of feet away, long before those animals or objects enter view. Researchers now want to understand more precisely how the shark sensory system detects and processes these distant acoustic signals.
"The ocean is an acoustic environment, and sharks are clearly tuned into it in ways we are only beginning to understand," Kajiura said. "Being able to detect and respond to sounds from hundreds of feet away gives these predators an important source of information about their surroundings. The next question is how their sensory system allows them to pick up and interpret these distant sounds."
The work was supported by the Colgan Foundation, awarded to Kajiura, and the National Save the Sea Turtle Foundation, awarded to Sullivan.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Florida Atlantic University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- C L Sullivan, E R Gerstein, S M Kajiura. Orientation of Blacktip Sharks (Carcharhinus limbatus) to Underwater Sound. Integrative Organismal Biology, 2026; 8 (1) DOI: 10.1093/iob/obag033

Spain’s rejection of Russian LNG to boost production costs in other industries — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
03:58:01 UTC
12:58:01 KST

MOSCOW, September 30. /TASS/. Spain’s abandonment of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) could lead to higher fuel prices and increased production costs in a number of energy-intensive industries, like the chemical industry, metallurgy, and fertilizer production, political analyst Ilya Grashchenkov told TASS.
Earlier, Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares said that Madrid intends to comply with the EU restrictions on the supply of Russian LNG despite the existing long-term contracts of Spanish companies. This January the EU Council approved a phased ban on imports of Russian gas. For LNG supplies under long-term contracts, the ban should come into effect from next year.
"The main risk is related precisely to the price. Higher gas prices will affect electricity and production costs. The most vulnerable sectors are the chemical industry, metallurgy, and the production of fertilizers, ceramics, glass, cement, and paper. The scale of costs will depend on the situation in the global LNG market," Grashchenkov said.
According to him, Spain will most likely be able to avoid a direct gas shortage. "Spain is technically ready to replace Russian LNG. It has a well-developed network of terminals, supplies from Algeria, and the ability to increase purchases from the United States, Nigeria, and other countries. This is why the risk of a shortage is low, but gas may become more expensive, especially during a cold winter," the expert noted.
Grashchenkov also drew attention to the possible legal consequences of the cessation of supplies.
"The EU ban gives Spanish companies grounds to claim force majeure, but it does not automatically cancel contracts. This is why the likelihood of compensation claims and lengthy arbitration disputes remains, especially regarding an agreement between Naturgy and Yamal LNG, he explained.
According to the political analyst, Spain’s well·developed LNG infrastructure will not allow it to fully take on the role of the main gas supply channel to other EU countries.
"Spain is capable of receiving large LNG volumes, but its capacity to transfer gas to France and further to Europe is limited. This is why it may become a regional hub, but not the EU’s main gas gateway. At the same time, Europe’s dependence on American LNG will indeed increase," Grashchenkov concluded.

Public workers in France strike over pay as student protests turn violent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
03:53:39 UTC
12:53:39 KST

Public workers in France strike over pay as student protests turn violent
Tens of thousands of workers march nationwide, as police arrest 440 students in clashes at schools.
Tens of thousands of civil servants, including teachers, firefighters and healthcare workers, have marched in cities across France to demand higher pay, as students clashed with the police in separate protests over conditions at their schools.
Unions said some 300,000 people took part in the one-day strike action nationwide, while police on Tuesday estimated a turnout of 30,000 in the capital, Paris. The workers also demanded better working conditions and expressed anger at the government’s planned budget cuts.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Photos: Pope Leo draws hundreds of thousands for open-air Mass in Paris
- list 2 of 3France’s far-right National Rally gains ground in Senate vote
- list 3 of 3Photos: French students protest, public workers strike before budget cuts
Protests also took place at more than 400 schools, about 40 of which were blockaded and 44 of which faced attempted blockades.
Ten people, both students and staff members, were wounded, and at least 440 were detained, officials said.
The strikes and the student unrest came two days before the government is to unveil its draft budget and seven months before the presidential election. According to unions, the government proposes freezing base salaries for state employees in 2027 to save 2 billion euros ($2.3bn).
It would be the fourth consecutive annual freeze and the eighth during President Emmanuel Macron’s tenure. Unions say the freezes have cost workers a double-digit share of their purchasing power, and they are demanding a 6 percent raise.
‘Red alert’
Sophie Binet, general secretary of the General Confederation of Labor, called the protests “a red alert”.
“This anger is not going away. The government must look again at the budget,” she told Al Jazeera. She gave the government 48 hours to reverse the planned cuts before her union decides on further strike action.
The Education Ministry said just more than 11 percent of teachers and other school staff went on strike. French teachers are paid less on average than their counterparts in other European countries.
Fewer than 1 in 10 other civil servants took part, and fewer still in hospitals, with the loss of a day’s pay a likely factor in the turnout. France’s civil aviation regulator had warned of flight disruptions at some airports.
Professional firefighters, who say this summer’s huge wildfires exposed a lack of resources, were among those marching.
The government has already unveiled measures to help households cope with a spike in energy prices driven by the United States and Israel’s war on Iran, but it has failed to quell the discontent with Macron and his administration.
Student unrest
Students, meanwhile, have been protesting outside hundreds of schools over timetables, class sizes, teacher shortages and overheated classrooms during this year’s heatwaves. The demonstrations began in the Ile-de-France region around Paris and spread to other cities.
In addition to the 10 students and staff members who were hurt, 48 law enforcement officials were injured, authorities said, as students in some places set fire to rubbish bins and hurled projectiles, and officers responded with batons and tear gas.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told BFMTV that 440 people had been detained.
“We don’t have the final tally yet, but I’m told two thirds led to police custody,” he said. “Violence is never legitimate. There is nothing that justifies violence.”
Education Minister Edouard Geffray condemned the clashes on social media.
“This violence is unspeakable,” he wrote, adding that legal proceedings had begun. “To legitimize it or… call for an expansion of the blockades is to endanger both our students and public officials. It is irresponsible.”
‘Fewer cops, more money’
In Seine-Saint-Denis, a low-income suburb of Paris, Bally Bagayoko, the district’s mayor and a member of the hard-left France Unbowed party, joined hundreds of students protesting at the Lycee Paul-Eluard.
He led them in singing the national anthem and called the protests “completely legitimate”, saying poorer areas received fewer resources than wealthier ones.
Outside the Arago school in Paris, students, some with their faces covered, sat on dumpsters to block the entrance beneath a placard reading “Macron explosion”. A banner at the Helene-Boucher school read “Fewer cops, more money”.
“We want fewer police because we think there is a huge amount of police repression, both against high school student movements and social movements more generally,” said Mael Breton, a final-year student there. “This is a real problem, especially when there is such a lack of funding… here at our school and in the national education system more broadly.”
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Monday condemned the high school protests as irresponsible but acknowledged that the “difficulties of high schools must be heard and addressed”.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, a hard-left presidential contender, accused the government of steadily dismantling public services as he addressed protesters in Paris and urged his supporters to mobilise against the draft budget.
A Toluna Harris poll on Monday suggested that Melenchon and Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right National Rally, would advance to next year’s presidential run-off, with Le Pen best placed to win.

ChatGPT maker wants to be the App Store for AI as safety concerns grow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
03:50:00 UTC
12:50:00 KST

ChatGPT maker wants to be the app store for AI as safety concerns grow
SAN FRANCISCO – OpenAI on Sept 29 launched a less expensive artificial intelligence model and tools that run continuously, as it aims to reposition ChatGPT as an app store for AI.
Other companies, such as Adobe, will be able to offer their software directly within ChatGPT, which is now used weekly by 1.2 billion people. ChatGPT users will also be able to access their subscriptions in other apps.
“We want to help people discover what you build and connect you with new customers,” OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman told around 2,500 developers from around the world who gathered on the shores of the San Francisco Bay for the company’s annual conference.
During his keynote speech, the 41-year-old executive made no mention of multiple security incidents that forced OpenAI to once again suspend development of some models on Sept 25, after one of its agents gained unauthorised access to the internet.
Altman told reporters that “it is going to take us some time to figure out how to make sure that alignment, monitoring, safety, security stay well ahead of capabilities”.
A new model unveiled on Sept 29, GPT-6.1 Sol, was described as almost as powerful as GPT-6 Astra at one-fifth the price. It comes one day after the company said it scrapped a new version of Astra because it often ignored instructions.
New ‘Renaissance’
Outside the conference, around 30 protesters shouted chants like “put people before profit”, alongside demands that OpenAI drop contracts with the US military and Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Inside, Altman rejected comparisons between the AI era and the Industrial Revolution.
“I think we should learn from the mistakes of the Industrial Revolution, and I think we should be more like the Renaissance,” Altman said.
That new renaissance is now increasingly connected to agentic software – or programs capable of automatically completing tasks like managing calendars, booking reservations and sorting through e-mail.
Attendees cheered the arrival of “dots” – OpenAI’s version of AI agents, which will run continuously and ask users to approve sensitive actions.
Dots will be available only to paid subscribers and are not yet available to individual users in the European Union, Switzerland and Britain because of regulations, though OpenAI hopes to resolve those issues.
It competes with Meta’s Muse and Google’s Spark agents.
Last week, Meta unveiled a small, Tamagotchi-like device powered by Muse that could ship by December. OpenAI is working on its own AI hardware but provided no updates.
However, integrating the new dots onto a device “seems like a very reasonable thing to assume we may do someday”, Altman said.
“Disappoint Wall Street”
As speculation swirls around when OpenAI might go public, Altman told reporters on Sept 29 that the company was “investing more in safety, security, alignment, monitoring, and that will allow us to continue to progress model capability a lot”.
Despite gaining an early lead with ChatGPT, rival Anthropic overtook OpenAI in second-quarter revenue. Anthropic, which has focused more on business customers, generated US$11.6 billion (S$14.8 billion) versus OpenAI’s US$6.7 billion, according to the Wall Street Journal.
Meanwhile, Anthropic’s annual recurring revenue is expected to reach US$100 billion by the end of the year, while OpenAI reached US$70 billion in July, according to various reports.
OpenAI has delayed its own Wall Street debut till 2027 at the earliest, as Anthropic aims for November.
“I want OpenAI to be a public company someday, but I don’t want to put additional pressure right now,” Altman said.
OpenAI is nonetheless seeking to raise at least US$30 billion from private investors in a deal that could increase its valuation to around US$1.4 trillion, up from US$852 billion in March, according to Bloomberg.
On Sept 29, OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman attended an event at the White House where US President Donald Trump said top AI executives agreed to a “morally binding” commitment to build AI with safeguards. AFP

Japan's population falls 2.5 pct from 2020 to 2025
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30

12:13:02 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Japan's total population, including foreign residents, stood at about 122.97 million as of Oct. 1, 2025, down around 3.17 million, or 2.5 percent, from 2020, according to the finalized 2025 census results released by the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications on Tuesday.
The census, which started in 1920, has been conducted every five years. Japan's population has declined in three consecutive surveys since recording its first drop in 2015.
By gender, males numbered about 59.77 million and females about 63.2 million.
People aged 65 and over accounted for a record-high 29.4 percent of the population, underscoring the demographic pressures facing Japan's rapidly aging society.
Among the country's 47 prefectures, Tokyo was the only one to post population growth from the previous census in 2020, with an increase of about 189,000. ■

Creatine may help build muscle even without exercise, researchers find
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
03:12:34 UTC
12:12:34 KST

Creatine may help build muscle even without exercise, researchers find
- Date:
- September 29, 2026
- Source:
- Texas A&M University
- Summary:
- Creatine helped middle-aged adults gain muscle and strength even without a structured workout program in a new 12-week study. When combined with exercise and a calorie-reduced diet, it produced even greater strength gains while helping participants add lean tissue and lose fat. Researchers say the results strengthen the case for creatine as a potentially useful tool for maintaining muscle with age.
- Share:
Creatine is widely known for helping support muscle growth and athletic performance, but researchers are increasingly examining whether its benefits extend well beyond the gym. New findings from Texas A&M University suggest creatine may be particularly useful in middle age, when preserving muscle becomes increasingly important.
In a 12-week study published in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, adults ages 45 to 65 who took creatine increased their lean tissue and strength even if they did not follow a structured exercise program. Participants who combined creatine with regular exercise experienced even larger improvements.
The results add to growing research exploring creatine as more than a supplement for athletes. Scientists are also studying whether it can help support muscle health and healthy aging.
The study was led by Dr. Richard Kreider, professor and director of the Exercise and Sport Nutrition Lab at Texas A&M. Kreider has studied creatine for more than three decades. Creatine occurs naturally in the body and helps restore cellular energy, and decades of research have examined its effects on exercise performance, muscle growth, and strength. Kreider's earlier work has also suggested that creatine may offer health benefits throughout life.
Creatine Benefits Without Structured Exercise
The new study involved 64 healthy adults who completed the full 12-week intervention. Participants decided whether to join a structured exercise and diet-induced weight-loss program or remain in a non-exercise group. Within those groups, they were randomly assigned to consume either 10 grams of creatine monohydrate or a placebo each day.
Among participants who did not join the exercise program, those taking creatine gained roughly 2.4 pounds of lean tissue over the 12 weeks. They also increased their leg press and bench press strength.
Participants in the exercise program performed both resistance and aerobic training three times per week. Those who added creatine experienced greater gains in leg press strength, bench press strength, and time to exhaustion.
Creatine did not appear to improve aerobic capacity beyond the benefits of exercise alone. That result fits with previous evidence showing that creatine primarily supports muscular strength and power rather than aerobic fitness.
Building Muscle While Losing Fat
Researchers also examined another important issue: how to reduce body fat without losing muscle in the process.
Participants in the exercise group followed a diet that created a modest calorie deficit. After 12 weeks, those who took creatine had added nearly three pounds of lean tissue while also losing fat mass. By comparison, participants following the same exercise and diet program while taking a placebo showed little change in lean tissue.
The creatine group also experienced a larger decrease in body fat percentage. According to the researchers, this is the first study to show that adding creatine to an exercise and diet-induced weight-loss program can reduce body fat percentage more than exercise and diet alone.
Creatine and Healthy Aging
The findings add to decades of research investigating creatine for purposes beyond athletic performance.
Kreider has previously emphasized creatine's importance throughout the lifespan, including its potential value for older adults facing age-related declines in muscle mass and cognitive function.
The body makes creatine naturally, and it is also found in foods including meat and fish. However, Kreider says many people do not consume enough through food alone. Reaching a daily intake of 10 grams from diet alone would require eating roughly five to 10 pounds of meat or fish each day, he notes, making supplements a more practical and less costly option.
Creatine is also among the most heavily studied sports and nutritional supplements. In a 2025 analysis, Kreider and his colleagues reviewed 685 clinical trials and found no significant difference in reported side-effect rates between people taking creatine and those receiving a placebo.
The study was funded by the WoodNext Foundation through the Texas A&M Foundation.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Texas A&M University. Original written by Caitlin Clark. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Jisun Chun, Yuhang Liu, Giuliet L. Kibler, Hudson Lee, Khatereh Babakhani, Nathaniel Rhoades, Ian Bivins, Joungbo Ko, Broderick Dickerson, Drew E. Gonzalez, Ryan J. Sowinski, Chris J. Rasmussen, Richard B. Kreider. Effects of creatine supplementation with and without exercise and diet intervention on body composition, cognitive function, and markers of health in middle-aged and older adults. Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, 2026; 23 (sup1) DOI: 10.1080/15502783.2026.2716273
