Canadian Jews considering immigration to US under Trump amid increasing fear of antisemitism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
03:08:10 UTC
12:08:10 KST

Sari Watson was too afraid to attend Yom Kippur services. Concerned by rising levels of antisemitism in Canada, she was safely at home 25 minutes away when a gunman charged at her childhood synagogue.
“My internal alarm has been going off, and you begin to think about escape routes or backup plans,” said Watson, 39, who lives in Quinte West, Ontario, about 15 miles west of Belleville, where the attack during Kol Nidre on September 20 culminated in a shootout that left the gunman dead and one policeman hospitalized. “The only reason I wasn’t at synagogue was because I have been terrified of this exact situation, or worse, happening.”
Florida Sen. Rick Scott, Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt, and US President Donald Trump himself, all Republicans, have alluded to the idea of extending refugee status to Canadian Jews who fear the spike in antisemitism in their country.
“’It’s so amazing to know that the Republicans understand the level of antisemitism we’re dealing with here,” she says. “President Trump gets the climate and the danger.”
Still, Watson has mixed emotions about the thought of leaving her home country. “I want to stay here and fight for our safety in Canada,” she said. “The option to come to the US is really important, but we shouldn’t have to need it.”
The Trump administration has imposed stringent restrictions on immigration, including on asylum seekers, but is inviting South African whites – and, potentially, Canadian Jews – to apply for refugee status. Critics accuse Trump of playing politics with refugee status, but some Canadian Jews see it as a lifeline.
Jewish journalist acquires second passport as antisemitism precaution
Talk of Jews feeling compelled to leave Canada gained momentum last week when a well-known Jewish journalist posted publicly on social media about getting a foreign passport. Neil Herland, a newsreader for the national broadcaster, the CBC, wrote on X/Twitter about his encounter with pro-Palestinian protesters outside Toronto’s Meridian Arts Centre, where Yom Kippur services were being held. Herland said that, concerned about rising antisemitism in Canada, he recently acquired his Austrian passport as a safety precaution. (Independent Press Gallery, a press freedom advocacy group, condemned the CBC for reportedly suspending Herland after pro-Palestinian advocates lodged a complaint about his post.)
Some Jews are past the precaution stage. Sheldon Shugal, 64, and his wife are currently researching how to move to the United States.
“If I were able to claim refugee status to come to the US, I’d do it without hesitation,” said Shugal, who lives in Calgary. “I used to love our country… but it’s just not a place that I want to continue to live in.”
Shugal, a property manager, said he has seen increased antisemitism in Canada in the wake of the deadly Hamas attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, and the war it launched. He said he and his wife have been struggling to overcome the complexity of acquiring an American visa.
“The Jew-hatred is no longer rising in Canada, it’s fully immersed here,” says Shugal. “It’s not the country I grew up in. I don’t feel affinity to Canada anymore.”
Shugal’s concerns are reflected in the findings of B’nai Brith Canada, which recently reported a 9.3% increase in antisemitic incidents from 2024-2025. According to this report, online harassment has surged dramatically, while Ontario saw the greatest total number of antisemitic incidents out of all the Canadian provinces and territories.
Antisemitic attacks have proliferated. In March of this year, Toronto synagogue Temple Emanu-El was shot at following Purim celebrations. The next week, two more Toronto synagogues were hit with gunfire over Shabbat, causing damage to the buildings, though no injuries were reported. In late April, assailants allegedly fired replica guns at “visually-identifiable” members of the city’s Jewish community, with one of the men sustaining minor injuries.
Shugal said reports of antisemitism have rattled him as well as the pro-Palestinian encampment his daughter encountered on her campus. “There hasn’t necessarily been anything I’ve personally experienced. It’s just what I’ve seen throughout the country,” Shugal said.
Antisemitism main motivator for leaving Canada, immigration lawyer says
Lauren Cohen, an immigration lawyer based in Boca Raton, Florida, said that since the October 7 attacks, about half of her Canadian clients cite antisemitism as a primary reason for wanting to leave Canada for the United States.
“In the past three months, I’ve noticed a very significant increase in the number of people between 55-70 who are contacting me,” said Cohen, who is originally from Toronto. “They have grown children or no children, and they have a little bit more money,” she said. “They want freedom.”
Antisemitism is not the only consideration for her clients, Cohen said. “The economy’s struggling. It’s not just antisemitism,” she said. “That might be the straw that broke the camel’s back, but it’s so many other factors as well.”
Cohen founded the Jewish Community Collective, an organization which helps Jewish Canadians and “displaced Jews” find connection in America. Another option for Jewish Canadians looking to make a new home in the States is Lech L’Tulsa, a program cosponsored by the Jewish Federation of Tulsa that helps settle Jewish newcomers, “designed to help Jewish Canadian citizens relocate to Tulsa.”
Some Canadian Jews do not see greener grass south of the 49th parallel, however. They point to Canada’s more expansive social safety net as one of the many reasons life in the Great White North” is better. “Unquestionably, the answer to whether I’d consider moving to the States is emphatically ‘no,’” said Lawrence Stanleigh, a dentist in Calgary.
“I believe our country is a better place to live,” said Stanleigh, 67. “The US doesn’t have a public healthcare system. Why would I want to leave our safety net for the US?”
Stanleigh said the idea that the United States is a safe haven for Canadian Jews is misleading. “As bad as things are in Canada, I think they’re worse in the United States,” he said. “It’s not a better place for education or for healthcare. The whole idea of moving there for our safety is a fantasy that the Republicans believe in.”
Substituting the United States for Canada is shortsighted, Stanleigh said. “There are failures on behalf of Canadian leaders to stand firm in their support of the Jewish community,” he said. “But as bad as things are, I think they’re worse in the States. Our American cousins are blithely unaware of the problems they have at home.”
Jewish parliament member blames right-wing Jews for attacking government
Anthony Housefather, a Jewish Canadian Member of Parliament representing a riding, or electoral district, in Montreal, is skeptical of the notion that the United States would offer Jews better protection.
“I think this idea is inspired by some right-wing Jews who have decided that their mission is to attack the Canadian government, and to make it look like somehow, Donald Trump and the Republicans are the savior of the Jewish people,” Housefather said in an interview.
Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney are at a low point in their relationship, with tensions over trade intensifying – and Trump seeks opportunities to take potshots at Carney.
Housefather also does not believe that leaving for the United States is gaining traction among Canadian Jews. “There are some people who have decided that Florida or Israel is a greener pasture,” he said. “But that does not represent a significant or a predominant view, and the idea that everybody’s leaving Canada is actually not true.”
The increase in antisemitism is universal – and should be treated holistically, he said. “What I do agree with is everywhere there’s a very serious problem with antisemitism,” he said. “Everywhere Jewish communities don’t feel safe, and all levels of government need to keep doing more.”
Housefather encourages his Jewish countrymen to remain proud Canadians. “Antisemitism has grown to an unacceptable level in this country,” he said. “It doesn’t mean that you should have less pride in being Canadian because there’s a loud, angry, small group of Canadians trying to make us scared.”

Israel's peculiar state of affairs: Arab nations friendlier, Europe's relations fall - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
03:07:56 UTC
12:07:56 KST

An Israeli arriving at Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport today could find wine, dates, or other such souvenirs purchased in the West Bank carrying consequences far more serious than excess baggage.
Since September 22, the Netherlands has prohibited goods originating in Israeli communities in the West Bank, east Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights, including items carried in personal luggage. Intentional violations can result in up to six years’ imprisonment; even unintentional violations can carry a sentence of up to one year.
Israeli passengers have reported having their bags searched, although Dutch Customs claims inspections are risk-based and random rather than systematic.
Israel responded by revoking the diplomatic status of Dutch officials working in Ramallah. Relations with a country once considered among Israel’s closest European friends have consequently reached a remarkable low.
Then there is the fall of relations with the UK. Reports emerged this week that passengers arriving at Luton from Tel Aviv were separated from other travelers and had their luggage searched. The Home Office denied racial profiling, saying searches are based on intelligence. Unlike the Netherlands, Britain’s proposed restrictions on settlement goods have not yet taken effect.
Also, at the Labour conference on Monday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband declared that Palestinian suffering was “a stain on the conscience of the world” and addressed those angered by Britain’s previous approach directly: “We hear you. You were right.”
He went further. Britain, he promised, would “call out ethnic cleansing by the settler terrorists,” evidence of war crimes in Gaza and what he called Israel’s “illegal occupation of Palestine.” The government will ban settlement imports and target British financial, construction, and service links to settlements.
Ireland-Israeli relations on all-time low
Ireland almost seems an afterthought. Its relations with Israel have already deteriorated dramatically, with the political hostility now spilling into sport. Ireland’s soccer coach recently declared before the much-disputed match between the two countries, “We are not playing with genocide. We are playing against genocide. We are playing against Israel.”
Yet not all is doom and gloom. Look south and east, and a very different picture emerges.
While European governments erect new barriers, Morocco is preparing to upgrade its relations with Israel to full embassies. They have agreed to expand direct flights, pursue investment and taxation agreements, and arrange reciprocal high-level visits. This has proceeded despite anti-normalization protests across Morocco. More important for Israel is the United Arab Emirates.
On Sunday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu traveled to the UAE at the invitation of President Mohamed bin Zayed. The UAE publicly confirmed the visit, which is noteworthy after years when sensitive contacts were often kept deliberately quiet.
Europe should see irony in situation
Europe should contemplate the irony here. Some Muslim-majority states that live in Israel’s neighborhood increasingly see cooperation with the Jewish state through the prism of shared strategic interests: Iran, Islamism, security, technology, trade, and regional stability.
Their governments certainly disagree with Israel, sometimes sharply, and Morocco’s protests demonstrate that normalization remains contested by some sectors of the population. But in general, their response is engagement.
In parts of Europe, meanwhile, relations with Israel are moving in the opposite direction. Governments face large domestic constituencies demanding increasingly punitive measures against Israel, and Miliband’s appeal to “millions of people in this country” demonstrated how directly domestic politics now intersects with foreign policy. The resulting picture is extraordinary.
In Abu Dhabi, an Israeli prime minister can spend hours discussing common threats with an Arab leader. In Morocco, governments are working toward ambassadors, investment and more flights. In Amsterdam, Israelis wonder whether customs officers will inspect their suitcases for a bottle of Judean wine.
There is something deeply strange about an Israel increasingly able to discuss its future with Arab and Muslim states while its citizens face growing suspicion and restrictions in European countries that once regarded friendship with Israel as essential.
Some in the Middle East have carefully cultivated bridges with Israel. Europe should think very carefully before it starts tearing its own down.

Executives of Iconic American Companies Reflect on How They Stay on Top
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
03:05:32 UTC
12:05:32 KST

A panel of executives spoke on Tuesday at a TIME100 Talk titled "Built to Last: The Enduring Power of Iconic American Brands" about the ways in which their companies have been able to adapt and dominate their industries throughout the years.
Included on the panel were Scott Kirby, chief executive officer of United Airlines; Ruth Porat, president and chief investment officer of Alphabet, the parent company of Google; and Bill Ford, executive chair of automotive company Ford, which sponsored the event.
Each panelist spoke about the unique approaches their companies have taken to remain relevant and an asset to consumers across generations.
Ford said prioritizing his employees and the communities his company impacts is chief among his values.
“We take care of each other. We take care of our communities. We take care of our country,” he said. “Those values are timeless. And it’s different than culture because cultures change and cultures evolve. But I think the values that underlie that culture are what really have sustained us for our whole lifetime.”
Porat stressed “a commitment to long-term investing” and “relentless focus on innovation.” She said that “we should never take innovation for granted.” In this spirit, the founders of her company, she explained, created something called “20% time,” which allows employees to dedicate a fifth of their workload to an idea that is deemed great. “And out of that was born Gmail and our first AI entity, Google Brain,” Porat said. Alongside encouraging innovation, she continued, is setting ambitious goals.
“If we achieve 60% of the objectives we set out in a year, that is success,” she said. “Because if we achieve 100% it just means we have not been audacious enough. We haven’t set the goal high enough.”
Kirby attributed the long-term success of United Airlines to it being what he described as a “brand loyal airline.” This has entailed focusing on four areas of the business: “the reliability, the service, the hard product, and the technology.”
“We need to wow them consistently,” he said. “I wanted them to get on an airplane and be surprised with something new that we have done.”
The United CEO acknowledged that maintaining a high standard in each of these areas has been no easy feat, particularly during the COVID pandemic, which he described as the “most existential financial crisis that ever existed in aviation.” Despite disruptions to his company, his priority is to protect his employees.
After reflecting on how they’ve succeeded in the past, the panelists were also asked about their visions for the future.
“My number one goal, my north star for the company, is actually going to be to set the company up so that there’s never again a furlough at the airline,” Kirby said.
Part of Porat’s vision for the future lies in expanding Alphabet’s business infrastructure into space, where on Thursday the company will launch an AI data center.
“It’s an attempt to continue to ask a question that our technical infrastructure team has been asking for a long time, which is how can we build as efficiently as possible using resources as wisely as possible to deliver the best experiences as possible,” Porat said about the launch. “This is a tiny little step. We still call it research.”
Ford hoped for a lot more of the same, and again stressed the value of his product for customers.
“I think what gets me most excited is the fact that we will still be the most American car company 25 years from now,” he said, “and that we’ll be making our customers' lives better, and hopefully give them back their most precious asset, which is time.”
TIME100 Talks: Built to Last: The Enduring Power of Iconic American Brands was presented by Ford.

Heatwaves, wildfires expose a third of world to extreme ozone pollution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
02:31:15 UTC
11:31:15 KST

Heatwaves, wildfires expose a third of world to extreme ozone pollution
Heatwaves and wildfires helped expose 34 percent of the world’s population to “extremely poor” ozone air quality in the first eight months of 2026, according to a European Union report published Wednesday. Asia recorded the highest exposure, while ozone pollution remained difficult to curb despite decades of progress in reducing other harmful emissions.
Heatwaves and wildfires combined with human-caused emissions this year to expose one third of the world's population to extremely high levels of ozone pollution, a European Union report said on Wednesday.
In a new analysis covering the first eight months of 2026, the European Union's Copernicus Climate Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) highlighted the close relationship between climate change and air pollution.
When heat and sunlight react with airborne emissions from wildfires, vehicles and industry, they create ground-level ozone pollution, which can damage lung tissue, cause breathing problems, trigger asthma attacks and lead to other health issues.
Despite progress in cutting the most harmful air pollutants in recent decades, ozone has proved more difficult to tackle as climate change fuels the conditions that favour its formation.
Read moreFrance puts out massive fire that torched 42,000 hectares and smouldered for 69 days
This year's ozone pollution was driven in part by record-breaking heatwaves and wildfires that seared Europe and North America and sent smoke well beyond their borders.
Indonesia has experienced major wildfires, while the warming El Nino weather pattern, which started in June and is due to peak later this year, could drive more fires in southeast Asia, according to the analysis.
"Air pollution does not stop at borders. It can travel thousands of kilometres, crossing continents and oceans and affecting air quality far from its source," CAMS director Laurence Rouil said in the Atmosphere Watch report.
'Extremely poor' air
CAMS uses satellite data and computer models to track air pollution and wildfires.
The report found that 34 percent of the global population was exposed to "extremely poor" air quality between January 1 and September 15, meaning concentrations of ozone were well above the World Health Organization's exposure guidance.
The WHO's guideline sets 100 micrograms of ozone per cubic metre as the maximum recommended level of exposure, averaged over eight hours.
Read moreWildfires, heatwaves threaten global air quality and health, UN warns
Another 17 percent of the world breathed "very poor" air, while five percent was exposed to "good" levels of ozone.
Asia has the highest rate of exposure to ozone pollution, with 53 percent of its population breathing "extremely poor" air. Another 22 percent was exposed to "very poor" ozone.
The continent's widespread emissions are driven by industrialisation, economic development and transport, as well as wildfires and the burning of agricultural residue.
New Delhi, Dhaka, Chinese megalopolis Chongqing and Pakistan's Lahore were among cities whose ozone levels were "extremely poor".
Two thirds of the population in North America and 45 percent in Europe were exposed to "poor" or "very poor" air quality.
EU regulation has been effective in reducing emissions from air pollutants, except for ozone, the report said.
Read moreFrance recorded 'hottest summer ever' in 2026, environment minister says
Ozone pollution is linked to 60,000 premature deaths per year in Europe, Ian Marnane, an official at the European Environment Agency, told a media briefing.
Ozone levels in North America also remained "relatively unchanged" despite ambitious emissions reduction policies, the report said.
Smoke from forest fires, crop burning and cooking are significant contributors to Africa's air pollution while Saharan dust travels as far as Europe.
Eight percent of Africa's population endured "extremely poor" air quality this year. It was "very poor" or "poor" for 19 percent of the continent.
Ozone levels were very high in the Brazilian city of Sao Paulo and extremely elevated in Rio de Janeiro but the air quality was "good" or "fair" for 81 percent of South America's population.
One bright spot was Oceania, including Australia and New Zealand, where 66 percent of the population enjoyed "good" ozone levels and 34 percent lived under "fair" conditions.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

US Senate blocks resolution seeking report on Americans killed in West Bank
The resolution cites a ‘lack of accountability’ by Israel’s government and an ‘inability to secure justice’ by the US.
The United States Senate has blocked a resolution that would have required President Donald Trump’s administration to report on the killing of nine Americans in the occupied West Bank and on Israel’s treatment of Palestinian children in military detention.
The resolution failed 47-53 on Tuesday, with senators voting largely along party lines.

It was brought to the floor by Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, and cited a “lack of accountability” from the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and an “inability to secure justice” from the US government.
Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania was the only Democrat to vote against advancing the resolution, while Senator Rand Paul, a Republican from Kentucky, joined Democrats in supporting it.
Van Hollen forced the vote under the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, which allows individual members of Congress to demand a formal State Department report on the human rights practices of any country that receives US security assistance.
In a social media post after the vote, Van Hollen pledged to continue to press for justice.
“Tonight, 47 Senators supported my resolution to get accountability for the 9 Americans killed on the West Bank & for Palestinians who face injustices daily. That’s more support than we’ve ever had in this fight,” he wrote on X.
“Republicans blocked us, but we won’t stop until we get justice.”
Nine Americans killed
The resolution called for an unclassified report within 30 days of adoption. It would have detailed investigations into the deaths of the Americans, the treatment of US citizens held in Israeli prisons, and the conditions facing Palestinian children in Israeli military detention.
The measure cited the deaths of nine American citizens in the occupied West Bank since January 2022, including Shireen Abu Akleh, a Palestinian-American journalist and Al Jazeera correspondent who was shot in the head and killed in May 2022 while reporting in the city of Jenin.
It also included Aysenur Ezgi Eygi, who was shot in the head and killed by an Israeli soldier in September 2024, and Sayfollah Kamel Musallet, who was beaten to death by Israeli settlers in July 2025.
The others were Amer Mohammad Saada Rabee, who was 14; Tawfic Abdel Jabbar and Mohamed Ahmad Alkhdour, both 17; Omar Assad; Khamid Ayyad; Nasrallah Abu Siyam; and Khamis Rabee Jabara.
The resolution also noted the arrests of several Palestinian-American children by Israeli forces.
Among them was Mohammed Ibrahim, a 16-year-old from Florida, who was arrested in February 2025 and held in pretrial detention for nine months without contact with his family. It noted that US embassy officials and lawyers who met him told his family that he had lost nearly a quarter of his body weight, contracted scabies, and was beaten and tortured.
Other Palestinian Americans who remain in custody include Adam Wajeh Abdelfattah Karakrah, 16, and Sama Safi, 20, a student detained in June in raids targeting students at Birzeit University.
The resolution cited rights groups that have documented the deaths of at least 44 Palestinians in Israeli military camps since the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023. Those groups, it said, have documented widespread abuses, including beatings, sexual violence, harassment and threats, “pointing to systemic and deliberate mistreatment”.
It also went on to note a sharp escalation in Israeli settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank, and stressed that there have been no convictions for the killings of Palestinian civilians by Israeli settlers since 2020.

Why Nirvana and Midnight Oil made the cut in Songs that Changed the World
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
02:25:40 UTC
11:25:40 KST

Why Nirvana and Midnight Oil made the cut in Songs that Changed the World
In the new book Songs that Changed the World, author Andrew Clarke was aiming for a top 40, but couldn't do away with any two songs.
Here he tells the ABC's pop culture journalist why some songs made the list and others didn't.
You start the book with Strange Fruit. I want to talk about artists paying a personal price for their songs that change the world. You write in the book about Billie Holiday's final moments as well as some of what she went through in life. Tell me about that.
She did become public enemy number one. I mean, a Black woman singing about lynching in the United States was very confrontational, but she was a huge star and she had the power to do it. But the FBI and all the entities didn't really like that. So, she spent a lot of time being interviewed by police.
And you wrote that she didn't receive the medical treatment that she was due when dying in hospital.
Absolutely … the evidence is there to say that she could have got lots of things to help her, but no-one was willing to do that for her, and a lot of it was the pressure from the FBI.
It's pretty obvious why this particular song is on the list, but can you tell me what's going on in this song and why it's so powerful?
It is [written by] Abel Meeropol, who [was] a Jewish poet in New York City, and he saw a photograph of lynchings in Indiana, and he was so taken by that that he wrote this poem, which was later turned into the song Strange Fruit … the fruit is actually the Black people swinging in the trees as they're being lynched and the visual imagery of it is quite confronting.
When you go from that to something like Smells Like Teen Spirit, it seems like quite the jump. Why do both songs belong side by side in this book and tell me why the Nirvana classic made it in there?
I think the beauty of this is that the 42 songs tell different stories in most cases. Smells Like Teen Spirit is really about a disaffected youth finding a voice and finding some power, and maybe just understanding that they are a bit cranky at times … and that's the teen spirit because "you might think I'm just a stoner or lazy, but that's just the way we are and you guys need to understand it because we've got the power".
Would you describe this as a song that doesn't really have political messaging but still has an impact socially?
Oh, absolutely. And there's a couple of songs in this book like that that weren't designed to be political but the message in it was so strong and connected so strongly. Smells Like Teen Spirit [is a] song that connected to a generation in many ways. People I know who don't like that style of music still love that song. And … it gave people [the] feeling that it's OK to feel disaffected. But let's just get people to understand that we can still be productive, useful, and loved.
It appears in a lot of different places in pop culture. I hear the riff every day when I tune into The Breakfast Club — a radio show out of New York on a station that plays mostly hip hop and R&B — but I did go back and listen to the song after reading that part in your book because you mentioned that the lyrics, a lot of them don't even really make sense, and you're absolutely right.
It's pure genius when you think about it. It's just that great abstract way of thinking that older people didn't understand at the time.
Let's jump on to Beds are Burning. Tell me about this song and its impact, as well as the impact of Midnight Oil.
It's an interesting one because Midnight Oil had always been political to a degree, but this ramped it up. It's written specifically around the dispossession of the Pintupi people and it was the first time, I think, in Australia that anybody had really in a public way spoken about Aboriginal land rights, so something that we'd buried and hidden and didn't even want to talk about suddenly became something that we were singing along with … so it really brought that way of thinking into the mainstream.
There's something about having a catchy tune you're singing along to, but then it has this potent message.
It is good, isn't it? That's where some of these songs in the book, not just this one, hook you in without you knowing. You get entrapped by the music or entrapped by the melody, and then underneath it all are these great lyrics that are telling you a story and trying to ask you to think. And subconsciously, whether you like it or not, if you like the sound of that song, you are going to start to take in the lyrics in a way that you don't even understand.
It did make me wonder though why a song like Treaty by Yothu Yindi didn't make the list. Are there songs, Australian songs, that could have made the list but just missed out?
Oh, absolutely. Treaty is one of them, clearly. There's I was Only 19 by Redgum, Khe Sanh by Cold Chisel — they were all on the list that we considered. And hopefully we get to a point where we do a second book and they'll be in there.

The US Senate has rejected a discharge motion to bring forward a resolution introduced by Senator Chris Van Hollen concerning human rights practices in Israel and the occupied West Bank from the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.
The motion to discharge Senate Resolution 852 failed to attain the necessary majority, with 47 senators voting in favour and 51 opposing it.
Cross-party voting emerged during the ballot, with Democratic Senator John Fetterman voting against the motion, whilst Republican Senator Rand Paul voted in favour.
Republican Senators Bill Cassidy and Dan Sullivan did not cast votes.
The measure, titled the "Israel Human Rights Practices" resolution, directs the State Department to furnish Congress with detailed reporting on human rights conditions throughout the occupied West Bank, specifically regarding the circumstances surrounding the deaths and detention of American citizens.
Accountability demands for American deaths
Addressing the floor prior to the roll call, Van Hollen appealed directly to his colleagues to allow the resolution to advance to a full debate.
"I rise today to call up Resolution 852, a resolution to require the State Department to provide Congress with information on the growing violence and human rights abuses taking place in the West Bank, including against American citizens," he said.
Van Hollen pointed out that nine US citizens have been killed in the occupied West Bank over a four-year period by violent illegal Israeli settlers or members of the Israeli security forces.
"The United States government has repeatedly said that our number one priority overseas is to protect American citizens. And yet, as violent Israeli settlers continue to terrorise civilians in the West Bank, American citizens have been killed time and again, in many cases with the complicity of the government of Israel, the Netanyahu government," he said.
The senator challenged whether American authorities have demonstrated sufficient political will to pursue justice for citizens harmed in the occupied territory.
"How many more Americans must die in the West Bank before this administration takes serious, credible steps to secure accountability?" he asked.

Taiwan plans US$850 million ammunition spend to prepare for potential PLA blockade

Taiwan plans US$850 million ammunition spend to prepare for potential PLA blockade
Taiwan should boost conventional ammunition stocks through local production while asking US to speed up weapons deliveries, analyst says
Taiwan’s military plans to spend more than NT$27 billion (US$850 million) to quadruple critical ammunition stocks to 120 days’ supply, strengthening its ability to sustain combat operations during a wartime blockade.
The proposed six-year “urgent ammunition replenishment” programme, running from this year until 2031, comes as Taipei seeks to strengthen its ability to keep fighting if a cross-strait conflict cuts external supply lines.
The spending proposal was revealed on September 26 and still requires legislative approval. The programme is expected to cost NT$27.59 billion, with NT$7.3 billion allocated this year through a supplementary budget. A further NT$7.3 billion is proposed for 2027 to accelerate procurement of various types of critical ammunition.
Lieutenant General Huang Wen-chi, the strategic planning director of Taiwan’s defence ministry, said this month that the military aimed to gradually increase its combat-ready ammunition stocks from the current 30 days to 120 days.
He said more frequent combat-readiness drills and exercises in recent years had also increased ammunition consumption, requiring stocks to be replenished more quickly.

Gordon Brown can’t stop talking to Andy Burnham’s team
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

LIVERPOOL, England — Former U.K. Prime Minister Gordon Brown recently insisted he does not want to become “a backseat driver” telling Andy Burnham’s new government what to do. But it seems he just can’t help himself.
A succession of cabinet ministers and other leading Labour politicians have told POLITICO that Brown, a party elder who was prime minister between 2007 and 2010, contacts them by email — written in capital letters — to offer them advice.
And on Tuesday, Burnham, who has been PM for just 10 weeks, disclosed that he is looking to emulate Brown, heaping praise on his predecessor for showing how Britain could lead the world through a crisis.
Advertisement
“As Gordon Brown has said, we can be the world’s innovation nation, and he’s right, we can,” Burnham told Labour’s conference on Tuesday, saying the U.K. could be “an honest broker” in the debate on regulating AI. “Just as Gordon did in the financial crisis in 2008, so Britain will do it again — step forward, and bring people together around what’s right for the future — securing our prosperity, but also our safety.”
Burnham served in Brown’s government as health secretary until Labour lost power in 2010. He has picked colleagues who served with him in Brown’s ministerial team for key jobs in government — including Ed Miliband, the new foreign secretary, Chancellor John Healey, and Douglas Alexander, the Scotland secretary.
In interviews at the POLITICO Pub during Labour’s conference in Liverpool this week, the extent of Brown’s contacts became clear. Miliband, who was an adviser to Brown during his time in the Treasury, said they had spoken by phone while he was in New York at the U.N. General Assembly earlier this month. “I had a late-night phone call with him actually last week,” Miliband said. “They come thick and fast. It’s a great email to get, honestly.”
Healey, the chancellor, disclosed in an interview with the Sunday Times that he receives emails in bold capitals from Brown, who was Britain’s longest-serving chancellor of modern times, before he became prime ministers in 2007.
Alexander, the Scotland secretary, told POLITICO he, too, was the recipient of messages from Brown, who represented a Scottish constituency during his time in parliament.
“Yes, it took me great restraint when John Healey revealed that he was receiving emails in Bold Helvetica 14, as I remember, from Gordon Brown, not to send him a message saying ‘the first 35 years is the worst, and then you get over it.’”
Advertisement
New Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra also revealed in a POLITICO Pub interview that he’d been in receipt of emailed advice from Brown, “sometimes in caps, sometimes not.” Marra is clearly a fan of the former premier: “He’s a constant force for good, and I feel very privileged every time I get an email from him,” he said.
Healey also told Labour members in Liverpool that he once had to lend Brown a red tie for his speech to the Labour Party conference in 1999. Brown returned it afterwards, and signed it, and Healey said he had kept it safe ever since, until he put it on again on Monday to deliver his own conference speech as chancellor.
Brown, whose office did not immediately respond to a request for comment, does have an official government role: Burnham has kept him on as an adviser on global finance and cooperation, a post he was given by the previous PM, Keir Starmer.
In that role, Brown is due to contribute to developing “new international finance partnerships that can support defence and security-related investment, including measures that underpin the U.K.’s relationship with Europe,” according to the government press release announcing his appointment. Brown’s role is officially “unpaid” and “part time,” although that hasn’t stopped him working late to contact ministers after hours.
Andrew McDonald, John Johnston and Dan Bloom contributed reporting from Liverpool.

Labour picks a side on Gaza — and cheers the party faithful
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Labour picks a side on Gaza — and cheers the party faithful
Sanctions on Israeli settlements buoyed pro-Gaza Labour supporters at the party’s Liverpool conference. But critics fear politics are trumping diplomacy.
LIVERPOOL, England — One of the most stinging criticisms thrown at Andy Burnham is that he is a people-pleaser who hates to pick a side. But on one of the most contentious issues facing Labour, he has done just that.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband made the shift clear in his speech to Labour’s annual conference in Liverpool this week — directly telling internal critics who had accused the governing party of failing to take strong enough action to defend Palestinians: “You were right.”
Many of those internal critics now hope a shift in Labour policy — imposing trade sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank — will go some way to repair electoral damage done to the center-left party in recent years.
Advertisement
But in addressing one of the most difficult fault lines in the party membership, Miliband has also sparked deep anger among some of his colleagues, particularly some Jewish Labour members, and charges of diplomatic recklessness. Miliband’s team has yet to respond to a request for comment on this piece.
Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer, was seen as flat-footed in his support for Gaza as Israel responded with force to the Oct. 7 2023 attacks, and slow in his decision to recognize Palestine. Under his leadership, constituencies with high Muslim populations turned away from the Labour Party in large numbers, either electing independents or preferring the Greens.
But one of Miliband’s first acts as Burnham’s foreign secretary was to announce the sanctions — and accuse Israel’s government of turning a blind eye to the “ethnic cleansing” of Palestinians by settlers. It was a dramatic escalation of the British government’s rhetoric.
Jess Phillips, a Labour former minister who is the MP for Birmingham Yardley, said: “I think it’s a beginning of building back trust with the vast majority.
“I wouldn’t say there is a ticker tape parade or anything but an opportunity for a fair hearing.”
Emily Thornberry, the Labour chair of the cross-party Foreign Affairs Committee, said: “As far as I’m concerned, the only important consideration is that the government has finally done the right thing.” She told at the POLITICO Pub at party conference in Liverpool Tuesday: “If you’re a grown-up politician, you can say sometimes: ‘Well, we were wrong about that. We wished we’d listened to you.'”
Advertisement
Even those on the left of the party who had been the most scathing about Labour’s approach to Gaza appear at least partly satisfied by Miliband’s actions — and think they have a message they can take back to angry voters. Labour MP Rachael Maskell said voters are “really engaging” with a policy shift which “is not about sides but values, and that is what people are latching onto.”
With that in mind, Labour activists are now beginning to feel quietly optimistic about an upcoming by-election in Holborn and St Pancras, Keir Starmer’s former seat, where Labour had expected to face particular pressure from the Green Party over Gaza.
“Because we have moved pretty much as far as we can now on Gaza — short of calling it a genocide — and that issue isn’t as dominating and fraught, we can talk about all sorts of issues and people feel up for listening,” said a Labour staffer.
Green officials dispute that — believing their consistency on the issue will help get candidate (and Green Party Leader) Zack Polanski over the line. “I get the sense that people don’t trust Labour on the issue,” a Green Party councillor involved in by-election campaigning — granted anonymity to speak frankly — said.
“Burnham and Miliband’s words are nice and all, but it’s a little bit too late. Greens have had a position stronger and longer.”
The Miliband factor
Despite earning party plaudits, Miliband has, for some, pushed beyond what is diplomatically wise.
Advertisement
Three people described a meeting with the foreign secretary before the sanctions announcement, in which he was urged to wait until after the Israeli elections because of concern Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would weaponize the move. They said Miliband was intransigent and kept repeating that it was a “moral emergency.”
The same people, who were granted anonymity because of the sensitivity of the discussions, said his refusal to wait forced them to conclude that his decision was partly influenced by the desire to announce the change in policy in time for the Labour conference and the by-election.
Burnham has stood firmly behind the West Bank sanctions since they were announced, but it’s clear that they have been driven to a large extent by Miliband. The prime minister heaped praise on his foreign secretary in his own address to the conference Tuesday, insisting Britain would be “principled in our leadership in securing a two-state solution between Israel and Palestine, as Ed Miliband has shown.”
A one-time Labour leader who carries more political clout than most on the government front-benches, Miliband has indeed chosen to make this fight intensely personal, describing himself as a “proud British Jew,” with the “deepest gratitude” to the state of Israel for giving refuge to his grandmother who lost her husband, Miliband’s grandfather, and 60 other family members at the hands of the Nazis.
Miliband’s sanctions move was followed by allies in fellow middle powers, Canada and France, making similar moves, and one U.K. minister argued Britain had opened international conversations at the United Nations General Assembly that had been impossible before.
For now, the British government is relieved that the feared blowback from Israel has been reasonably restrained. While Israel announced that the British consulate in Jerusalem will be closed as part of a retaliation, ministers were assured that intelligence cooperation will continue. Donald Trump, whose relationship with Netanyahu has wavered during their war in Iran, has appeared uncharacteristically calm about the sanctions.
Advertisement
In Liverpool, some Labour MPs were still to be placated. Left-wing lawmaker Nadia Whittome told a Liverpool fringe event Tuesday night that Israel “needs to face a reckoning” — demanding that Britain impose a complete arms embargo and wider economic sanctions on the state.
But for now, Miliband has at least made parts of the Labour faithful feel better about itself.
MPs and party members making their way to the secure zone of the Labour conference in Liverpool have for years been confronted by demonstrations from pro-Palestinian protestors.
“Ed said we were right,” one placard read on the Tuesday morning after his speech.

GENEVA, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Athletes from over 20 countries and regions competed in the debut of mixed martial arts at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, which the Federation of Mixed Martial Arts (FIMMA) described as a milestone in the sport's pursuit of Olympic recognition.

"Nagoya has shown what MMA can achieve within a major multi-sport environment," FIMMA President Gordon Tang said. "We are extremely proud of the athletes who competed here and of the quality of the competition they delivered."

The prospect of Olympic inclusion was also welcomed by competitors. Tajikistan's Mirzobek Umarov, one of the gold medalists in Nagoya, said, "I hope and wait that MMA will become an Olympic sport. It's not a dangerous sport. There are other sports that are more injury prone than MMA."
FIMMA said the Asian Games debut provided a foundation for the sport's continued international development and its Olympic ambitions.
"The next focus will be on expanding MMA's presence within major multi-sport events worldwide, developing the international competition pathway and preparing for the first FIMMA World Championships," said FIMMA. ■

by Zodidi Mhlana
JOHANNESBURG, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- South African police on Tuesday arrested more than 100 suspects allegedly linked to illegal mining syndicates believed to be connected to a recent deadly tavern shooting in Gauteng province.
The sweeping security operation has intensified scrutiny of the escalating violence, access to heavy weaponry and gang-related criminal activity associated with illegal mining networks operating across the country.
The arrests followed a deadly attack on Saturday night in Wedela, a township near the gold-mining hub of Carletonville, about 80 km southwest of Johannesburg. Eighteen people were killed after heavily armed gunmen stormed a local tavern at around 9:30 p.m. local time (1930 GMT) and opened fire on patrons.
OPERATION FOLLOWING TRAGEDY
Police suspect the incident was a targeted retaliatory attack linked to territorial rivalries between illegal mining syndicates, following a similar shooting at the same tavern last month.
In an immediate response to the security threat, Gauteng police announced on Tuesday that multi-agency security forces arrested 121 suspected illegal miners and seized five firearms, including an AK-47 assault rifle and three handguns, along with gas cylinders, gold-bearing material and specialized extraction equipment during a joint sweep dubbed "Operation Prosper."
Brig. Brenda Muridili, spokesperson for the South African Police Service in Gauteng, told Xinhua that a joint task force comprising police, specialized tactical response teams and the South African National Defense Force has been deployed in high-risk mining districts since March.
"This operation is guided by crime intelligence to target illicit mining hotspots across the West Rand, Johannesburg and Ekurhuleni districts," Muridili said, noting that operations are coordinated at the provincial level.
COMMUNITIES AFFECTED BY MINING-RELATED VIOLENCE
Despite heightened law enforcement efforts, residents living in historic gold-mining towns continue to bear the brunt of syndicate-related violence, including turf wars, armed robberies, kidnappings and extortion.
Locally known as "zama zamas," a Zulu phrase meaning "to try luck," these illegal miners operate in deep, dangerous underground networks, often forming heavily armed ethnic factions to secure territory.
Mapaseka Sethusha, a 24-year-old Wedela resident who narrowly escaped Saturday's attack by leaving the venue early, expressed deep trauma over the recurring violence.
"The people behind the violence are involved in illegal mining, many of them foreign nationals from neighboring countries," Sethusha said. "What scares us most is that ordinary residents have nothing to do with their feuds, yet we are getting caught in the crossfire. We just want them gone and the police to restore safety."
Sethusha's fears are echoed by many in Carletonville, where residents report that gang-related security woes increase dramatically after dark.
UNSEALED SHAFTS
Experts and mining researchers said South Africa's illegal mining crisis is deeply rooted in historical and structural issues, primarily the thousands of unsealed, derelict mine shafts left behind as gold seams were depleted.
Official figures show that South Africa has more than 6,100 abandoned and derelict mines that were never legally decommissioned or environmentally rehabilitated.
David van Wyk, a veteran mining researcher, told Xinhua that some mining corporations failed to fully meet statutory closure obligations, leaving behind unmonitored infrastructure that invited organized crime.
"The root cause is that mining companies abandon these shafts without proper rehabilitation," Van Wyk said. "That initial failure creates the vacuum. Unemployed youth and undocumented migrants from economically struggling neighboring countries are then drawn into these dangerous shafts to eke out a living."
Van Wyk noted that informal syndicates quickly militarize control over these shafts, establishing hit squads and illicit supply chains that sell scrap metal and refined gold to international buyers.
He urged the South African government to enforce strict regulatory accountability on mining companies and compel them to permanently seal abandoned shafts to cut off the illegal mining cycle at its source. ■

Raising Hong Kong’s birth rate is an economic imperative
Economies competing in an AI-driven future will need more highly skilled workers, not fewer. Low fertility is not only a social challenge – it’s an economic threat
But the fertility debate should not be reduced to whether a bonus is large enough to change family decisions. The bigger challenge is whether Hong Kong can remain dynamic and competitive while its younger generation continues to shrink. Demographic trends are often discussed in terms of ageing, labour shortages and pressure on public finances. Yet low fertility has a less discussed consequence: its impact on innovation.
Innovation ultimately depends on people: scientists making discoveries, entrepreneurs building companies and skilled professionals turning ideas into products and services. The stronger the talent pipeline, the greater the likelihood of breakthroughs. This matters even more in the age of artificial intelligence.
AI may offset some labour shortages, but it still depends on capable people to develop, deploy and improve it. Economies competing in an AI-driven future will need more highly skilled workers, not fewer. That is why low fertility should be viewed not only as a social challenge but also as a competitiveness challenge.

Rebeca Grynspan takes the lead in race to become UN chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
00:42:07 UTC
09:42:07 KST

Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan appeared to be pulling ahead in the race to lead the United Nations after the fourth round of informal polling, a diplomat said.
Grynspan, a veteran diplomat who leads the UN trade and development body (UNCTAD) has come top in three of the four straw polls, but a veto from the five permanent members of the 15-member UN Security Council could derail her momentum.
She received 10 favourable votes on Tuesday and three negative votes of "discourage," with two indications of no opinion, according to the diplomat who declined to be named, echoing specialist UN media reports.
A total of seven candidates, four women and three men, are vying to succeed the outgoing secretary-general, Antonio Guterres of Portugal, who ends his second five-year term on December 31, 2026.
Guyanese ex-foreign minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, who narrowly led the second round of the secret process to pick the next UN chief, came second with eight endorsements.
Other candidates include third-placed Argentina's Rafael Grossi, the current head of the UN nuclear watchdog, Macky Sall of Senegal, Ecuador's Ivonne A-Baki, Ecuador's Maria Fernanda Espinosa and Uganda's Olara Otunnu.
Several of the candidates are known to have met with world leaders during the General Assembly, the UN's signature diplomatic event, at the New York headquarters last week.
Rumours have persisted that a compromise candidate could be parachuted into the process at the behest of the five veto-wielding Security Council members: Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States.
Security Council straw poll
Even if a candidate earns the required nine votes from the 15 available in the Security Council, they must also avoid a veto by the five major powers, which are deeply divided.
Once a candidate clears those bars, their name will go to the General Assembly of all UN members for confirmation.
The Security Council straw poll was devised in the early 1980s to break a deadlock between two candidates shut down by vetoes.
The informal mechanism has persisted, in various forms, despite criticism from countries opposed to the opaque process.
Each of the 15 Security Council members must anonymously assign each candidate one of three labels: "encourage," "discourage," or "no opinion."
But after an unspecified number of votes, the ballots of the Council's five permanent members will have a different colour, making it possible to identify potential vetoes, without knowing which country blackballed any given candidate.
Tuesday's vote was held without colour-coded straws, the rotating president of the Security Council, France's UN envoy Jerome Bonnafont, said when confirming that voting had concluded. He did not say when the next round would be held.
It is tradition that the UN's top position should rotate between different regions.
Under that premise, the role should go to a candidate from Latin America this time. There are many candidates from the region, though Sall and Otunnu hail from Africa.

The 18-member body of independent experts monitors compliance with the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. While its rulings are not legally binding, they hold substantial political weight and can be cited in domestic judicial proceedings.

Despite remaining a deeply polarizing figure, polls show Fernandez maintains voter support levels comparable to those of current President Javier Milei.

The Future of Shipbuilding in Southeast Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
00:19:00 UTC
09:19:00 KST

Global shipbuilding demand is likely to remain resilient for the long-term, with increasing geopolitical conflict and uncertainty one of the primary drivers. The 2026 war between Iran, the United States and Israel has caused a spike in demand for alternative suppliers and routes, leading Fitch Rating to revise sectoral outlook to “neutral” from “deteriorating.” According to the non-profit Container Trades Statistics, global container volumes reached 16.2 million 20-foot-equivalent units (mTEUs) in April — the first full month of data since the Strait of Hormuz closures triggered by February’s Persian Gulf crisis — marking a 4 percent year-over-year increase and a 1.6 percent rise over March. Year-to-date volumes are also running 5 percent ahead of 2025 levels.
Shipping sector analysts also predicted that the market had become oversaturated with vessel capacity and fewer orders would be placed to shipbuilders in 2026 and 2027. However, geopolitical disruptions are one major reason why orders have remained strong. Shocks such as Red Sea attacks, the Russia-Ukraine war, the Panama Canal drought, the Baltimore bridge collapse, and now the Iran-Israel-US conflict have demonstrated the importance of excess capacity. Carriers can more easily navigate these conflicts with a large and diverse fleet, resulting in expansive orderbooks that are now treated as insurance rather than oversupply.
These trends are good news to the world’s leading shipbuilding nations, which are highly concentrated in East Asia, particularly China. However, in the current geopolitical climate, there are significant opportunities for Southeast Asian nations to scale up their shipbuilding industries and take advantage of the sustained demand for global trade.
Southeast Asian nations are taking the initiative to capture greater shipbuilding market share through structured international partnerships. At the OECD-Southeast Asia Policy Roundtable on Shipbuilding, Steel, and AI held in Tokyo in February 2026, Indonesia, Vietnam, and Thailand agreed to a regional peer review of their shipbuilding sectors with the OECD, covering priorities such as workforce skills, technical capabilities, supply chain dependencies, energy-efficient ships, and leveling the competitive playing field. The Philippines separately agreed to follow up on implementation pathways for OECD peer review recommendations, while all four countries were invited to join the OECD’s shipbuilding committee meeting in Paris in April.

Oura postpones US IPO amid market uncertainty
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
03:08:20 EEST
09:08:20 KST

Finnish-founded smart ring maker Oura has postponed its planned Nasdaq listing, citing uncertainty in the US initial public offering market despite strong demand from investors.
The company announced the decision on Tuesday as rising bond yields and interest rates put pressure on the US market for new listings.
Oura said its business had strengthened since it began the IPO process.
The company expects revenue to increase 90 per cent year on year in the 2026 financial year, while the number of paid members has reached 5.7 million following the launch of Oura Ring 5.
Oura had reached the final stages of the listing process. Helsingin Sanomat reported that the company had expected to set the final IPO price on Monday, with trading scheduled to begin on Wednesday.
Bloomberg reported last week that orders for the offering had reached about four times the number of shares available.
Oura had sought proceeds of up to $2.2 billion from the offering, with an indicated share price range of $40 to $44, HS reported.
The listing was intended mainly to provide an exit for some existing shareholders rather than raise new capital for the company’s expansion, according to the newspaper. Finnish venture capital firm Lifeline Ventures planned to sell between one-third and one-half of its Oura holding as part of the transaction.
Oura has not announced a new timetable for the IPO.
“Our mission is to empower people to live healthier, longer, and an IPO is just one step in our journey,” chief executive Tom Hale said in the company’s statement.
“We aim to deliver an extraordinary IPO for our employees and investors and we have the luxury of choosing our moment,” he said.
Oura joins other companies that have delayed US listings in September. Reuters said a growing number of prospective issuers have pulled back as higher interest rates and bond yields affect financial markets.
According to Bloomberg data, only nine of more than 20 companies that had filed public listing documents since the start of July had completed their IPOs.
Oura said it remains profitable and continues to grow. The company has filed its registration statement with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, but the filing has not yet become effective.
Founded in Finland in 2013, Oura produces a wearable ring that tracks sleep, activity and other health measurements. The company has its headquarters in San Francisco and its European headquarters in Oulu.

US tightens Cuba travel rules, restricts private sector banking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
00:08:00 UTC
09:08:00 KST

US tightens Cuba travel rules, restricts private sector banking
- The US has banned banks from working with Cuba's private sector and tightened travel rules, aiming to pressure Cuba's one-party government.
- US restrictions block accounts for Cuban private entrepreneurs and close travel loopholes for professional and educational visits.
- Despite trade growth aiding Cuba's economy, US sanctions and fuel blockades continue, complicating reforms and increasing tensions between Washington and Havana.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The US is barring banks from working with Cuba’s nascent private sector and is further restricting travel to the island, as President Donald Trump’s administration presses to end nearly seven decades of one-party rule in the country.
Under updated guidance from the Treasury Department published on Sept 29, US banks are no longer permitted to open and maintain accounts for Cuban nationals “who are independent private sector entrepreneurs,” the Office of Foreign Assets Control said.
“U-turn” transactions, in which US banks could process Cuba-related transactions that “originated and terminated outside the United States,” have also been disallowed.
Loopholes that allowed people from the US to travel to Cuba for professional meetings and academic activities are also being closed, OFAC said.
In addition, “people-to-people” educational travel, which was previously authorised, is no longer permitted.
Educational trips under the auspices of an accredited organisation are still allowed.
And there are no new restrictions on commercial flights to the island, as some Florida Republicans had been calling for.
But it’s the private-sector measures that could have the most impact, given small businesses have become a lifeline for the island as entrepreneurs import badly needed goods from abroad.
Bloomberg News reported last week that US cargo ships have made more than 200 trips to Cuba in 2026, loaded with goods including fuel, solar panels, food, vehicles and auto parts.
That trade boom contrasts sharply with Trump’s aggressive push for political change.
“The administration does not have a clear message at all when it comes to how they see the private sector and its role in this,” Michael Bustamante, director of Cuban studies at the University of Miami, said in an audio message.
Expanding the use of trade loopholes – including authorising private fuel sales – has helped stave off “a complete economic or social collapse” and reinforced “a message to Cuba that their only way out is through their connections with the United States,” he said.
“And yet the administration is not taking any proactive measures to make life easier for the private sector.”
Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have been hammering Cuba’s economy with ever-tighter sanctions and a de-facto fuel blockade for months in hopes of forcing the Communist Party to relinquish its grip on power.
Amid reports that planning for a military intervention was in the works, Trump said this week that Washington and Havana would likely “make a deal.”
Cuba has said it’s willing to make economic changes but that its system of government is not up for debate.
Intense US pressure, however, is getting in the way of market-friendly reforms, Deputy Foreign Minister Carlos Fernandez de Cossío told Bloomberg Television on Sept 25.
His boss in Havana also shot back on Sept 29 at Trump and Rubio’s latest salvo.
“Less than 24 hours ago, the Secretary of State said that ‘Cuba has already fallen.’ Now it turns out that additional measures are needed,” Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez said in a post on X.
“They openly attack both the public sector and the private sector, the one that some US officials say they want to help develop.” BLOOMBERG

====================================================================================================

US Supreme Court allows Trump to continue deportation policy after judge labels it unlawful
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
23:46:52 UTC
08:46:52 KST

The US Supreme Court on Tuesday let US President Donald Trump's administration resume deporting migrants to countries other than their own without offering them the chance to show the harms they may face, bolstering a tool his administration has used for rapid expulsions as part of his immigration crackdown.
The court granted the Justice Department's emergency request to put on hold Boston-based US District Judge Brian Murphy's ruling that the Department of Homeland Security's policy to remove migrants to so-called third countries is unlawful. The court also agreed to hear arguments in the dispute in December, with a formal ruling on the policy to follow.
The court has a 6-3 conservative majority. Its three liberal justices dissented from the decision to let the deportations immediately resume pending the final outcome of the litigation.
Murphy's ruling came in a class-action lawsuit filed by immigrant rights groups on behalf of migrants seeking to prevent the US government from sending them to third countries without notice and a chance to assert the harms they could face.
More than 25,000 migrants have been deported to 29 countries under the policy implemented last year, according to a tally by human rights groups, with the vast majority going to Mexico.
The policy is one of a number of measures the administration has taken in its pursuit of Trump's goal of mass deportation. The Republican president has enforced a sweeping crackdown on immigration - among his top priorities - since returning to office last year.
The administration has carried out third-country deportations to politically unstable South Sudan, which the US State Department urges Americans to avoid due to the risks of crime, kidnapping, and armed conflict, as well as Uganda, Equatorial Guinea, Liberia, the Central African Republic, and other nations.
Department of Homeland Security General Counsel James Percival welcomed the court's decision.
"A bad day for criminal illegals and open-borders activists alike," Percival wrote on social media.
Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the plaintiffs at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, said the court has "allowed the administration to resume sending people to third countries where they face persecution or torture. That is a devastating result for people who may be put on a plane before they ever have notice or an opportunity to raise a fear claim."
Judge rules US immigration policy against immigration law, due process protections
In February, Murphy ruled that the policy violates immigration law procedures and due process protections under the US Constitution's Fifth Amendment. Due process generally requires the government to provide notice and an opportunity for a hearing before taking certain adverse actions.
The Supreme Court, which has allowed a number of Trump's hardline immigration policies, previously sided with the administration in the legal challenge, suspending a preliminary order that Murphy issued earlier in the case halting the removals. In another win for the administration, the Supreme Court subsequently lifted limits the judge had imposed to protect a group of men from being sent to South Sudan.
The case began in 2025 after the Department of Homeland Security moved to step up deportations of migrants who cannot be returned to any country listed on their deportation orders.
The policy provided that migrants could be swiftly removed without notice to third countries that have provided credible diplomatic assurance that they will not persecute or torture the individuals. For countries that have not provided such assurance, deportees would be notified of their destination and US authorities would assess the likelihood of persecution or torture only if the individual raises such fear on their own.
In its emergency filing to the Supreme Court, the Justice Department said third-country deportations are "an essential tool to remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens."
But both Murphy and critics of the administration said the policy is also targeting migrants who had been granted legal protection from being sent back to their home countries.
Deportees see sexual assault, unlawful transference, plaintiffs say
The policy has resulted in deportees being unlawfully transferred by third countries back to their home countries from which the US had already granted them protection, while others have been beaten, sexually assaulted, detained, or have disappeared, the plaintiffs said in a court filing.
The administration is ignoring "the significant harm resulting from deporting thousands of longtime US residents, many with no criminal history, to third countries without regard to the persecution or torture they face there," the plaintiffs said.
The Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld most of the judge's ruling on September 18.
The case has been hotly contested since it began, and included findings by Murphy that the administration "repeatedly violated, or attempted to violate" his orders. Murphy in 2025 found that the administration had violated another order he issued requiring additional steps before attempting to send a group of migrants to South Sudan.

European countries should have shown more solidarity and offered more support to Spain after the mass arrival in Ceuta of tens of thousands of migrants, Spanish King Felipe VI said on Tuesday during a gala dinner to mark a visit by French President Emmanuel Macron.

The pro-Palestinian Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) filed a criminal complaint with Vietnamese authorities against an Israeli reservist who was vacationing in the country, accusing him of involvement in the destruction of civilian property during the war in Gaza, Walla learned on Monday.

As in previous cases, the organization claimed that the reservist incriminated himself by documenting on social media the destruction of homes and civilian infrastructure in the Gaza Strip while operating a military bulldozer. According to the organization, he posted videos and photographs showing the destruction, demolition, and burning of buildings in Gaza City, Khan Yunis, and Rafah.
As of Monday, there was no indication that Vietnamese authorities had taken any action in response to the complaint.
IDF soldier said they 'flatten everything' if nothing suspicious found in Gaza sites
HRF pointed to a post it said was published on November 19, 2023, showing extensive destruction in Gaza. According to the organization's translation, the soldier described his unit's activities as follows: "We look for suspicious things, tunnels, military equipment, suitcases. When we find something, we call the senior commanders, and when there is nothing there, we complete the demolition and flatten everything."
The foundation claimed that H.G. was involved in two incidents. The first was the demolition of the Abbas police station in Gaza City's southern Rimal neighborhood between November 14 and 21, 2023. The second was the demolition of Palestine Square in Shejaia on December 18, 2023.

"This is another link in our systematic pursuit of accountability, wherever the perpetrators are," said the foundation's director-general, Lebanese-Belgian Dyab Abou Jahjah, who is identified with Hezbollah.
"We have already filed a complaint in Vietnam, and we continue to identify soldiers who regularly return there for vacation."
IDF order forbids photos taken from operation areas
A special IDF General Staff order titled "Soldiers' Use of the Online Space" is intended specifically to prevent complaints of this kind against soldiers.
The IDF emphasizes: "Do not photograph or publish pictures in uniform or from operational areas; avoid documentation that could be interpreted as harming the civilian population, and consider the international consequences of every post or photograph."
Despite the directives and what the article describes as a lack of significant enforcement within the IDF, HRF has used information uploaded online to file dozens of complaints in approximately 25 countries since the organization was founded roughly two years ago.
Those countries include Brazil, Argentina, Belgium, the Netherlands, France, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Austria, the Czech Republic, Germany, Denmark, the UK, Cyprus, Greece, Sri Lanka, Thailand, the United Arab Emirates, Canada, the US, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, India, and Vietnam.
A complaint was also filed in Slovenia against Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar. This represents the documented minimum, while the organization says it has also made approaches in additional countries.
Various proceedings were opened in Peru, Brazil, Romania, and Chile, but none resulted in punishment or sanctions.

Trump, tech executives release 'morally binding' accord amid rising fears over AI safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
23:46:31 UTC
08:46:31 KST

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said tech executives agreed to establish standards for AI and reiterated his support for the rapid expansion of data centers, as concerns mount over AI safety and the industry's growing footprint in communities.
Trump made the comments after a meeting with tech executives at the White House. The administration is facing increasing scrutiny over the risks posed by advanced artificial intelligence, after OpenAI and Anthropic reported their AI agents had gone rogue and hacked into other companies' systems.
Data centers, which provide the computing power needed to train and run AI models, have drawn opposition in communities nationwide over concerns about electricity demand, utility costs and other local impacts. The backlash poses a political challenge for Republicans heading into the US midterm elections on November 3.
"It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Trump said, referring to the agreement between the companies. "And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president. And it really is a form of protection."
Trump released the one-page document on his Truth Social platform - which he had earlier described as "morally binding" - and that urged four layers of controls in companies.
First, the document asks companies to partner with an external auditor or evaluator to carry out independent assessments of whether a company's AI control and monitoring systems were operating as intended.
Second, it urges companies to designate an independent committee of the board of directors to oversee and receive reports from internal and external auditors and from teams operating AI controls.
Third, it asks for internal controls to monitor capabilities and alignment of AI models during training and deployment around areas like cybersecurity, biosecurity, and chemical threats to ensure that models "do not hack or access technical systems in unintended ways."
And fourth, it requests that companies have an internal team to ensure "all of the controls, monitoring and detection are operating as intended."
Luncheon spills into public view
What began as a closed-door lunch with technology executives spilled into public view when Trump joined House Speaker Mike Johnson and a lineup of CEOs on the White House driveway, an area rarely used by the president. He took questions for about 30 minutes on AI safety and other topics with the CEOs standing shoulder to shoulder behind him.
The unusual scene came as pressure has mounted on the administration to address the risks and rapid spread of AI, and underscored the alliance Trump has cultivated with leaders of the tech industry. Executives at the meeting included OpenAI's Greg Brockman, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Google's Sundar Pichai and Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
Zuckerberg, pulled forward from the crowd of billionaire executives by Trump to speak, said that the companies agreed to develop "robust internal controls" for their AI systems, adding that auditors would check those procedures and report back to company boards. Trump said he is considering setting up a 10-person board to police the safety of AI tools, without specifying who would make up that group.
The document was signed by Trump and the bosses of Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, social media platform X/Twitter, and NVIDIA.
'Makes sense' to transform steps into laws, White House says
"Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations. Regardless of whether this is required of companies, we believe that implementing these controls and audits is critical to ensuring a safe future for everyone, and each of our companies is committed to doing this," the White House accord said.
"The participating companies will meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems," it added.
Trump doubles down on data centers
Trump separately told reporters at the White House that the tech companies would work to make communities "happy" about the construction of data centers.
Data centers are "going to do things for the community that will be really financially beneficial," he told reporters. "These big, powerful, very rich, very smart companies are going to be making massive contributions to communities."
Trump met with the executives the same day his aides announced a new AI tool that they said will make it easier for the public to use government services.
Silicon Valley executives attended the launch event on Tuesday morning, including Meta's Dina Powell McCormick and Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire. Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia led the design of the new tool. Silicon Valley companies Google, SpaceX, Meta and 8VC were listed in the launch event's program as sponsors.
Trump at the launch event said he does not want to work with Chinese President Xi Jinping on governing AI technology, adding that doing so would make it harder for US companies to build better AI products than their Chinese counterparts.
Trump also said that he discussed AI with Xi when he visited the US last week, adding that the US already works with Xi's government "in so many ways."
