China Focus: China to implement mortgage interest subsidies to unlock housing demand
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
01:38:04 CST
02:38:04 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China will implement interest subsidies for housing loans starting Oct. 1, 2026, as part of efforts to help reduce home-buying costs and better unlock the housing demand of residents.
With a tentative implementation period of one year, the fiscal authorities will provide an annualized subsidy of 1 percentage point for eligible first-time homebuyers, according to a notice jointly issued by the Ministry of Finance, the People's Bank of China and the National Financial Regulatory Administration on Tuesday.
This is the first time the central government has offered interest subsidies on commercial housing loans.
This interest subsidy policy is focused on first-time homebuyers. The floor area of each purchased unit must not exceed 120 square meters, and the purchase price must not surpass 1.5 million yuan (about 222,516 U.S. dollars).
Under this policy, the maximum amount of interest-subsidized loans can reach 1 million yuan, and the subsidy period can extend up to five years.
According to estimates, for a long-term 1-million-yuan commercial personal mortgage, the subsidies could help borrowers reduce cumulative interest payments by nearly 50,000 yuan.
By defining housing price, floor area and loan category, the policy aims to precisely benefit target groups and help lower-income families reduce their monthly mortgage burdens, the departments said.
The policy focuses on first-time buyers with essential needs, supporting families in purchasing small and medium-sized, and relatively low-priced homes, according to the departments.
The policy is expected to reduce the mortgage burden for new urban residents, newly employed college graduates, and urban wage-earning families, said Luo Zhiheng, chief economist at Yuekai Securities.
In recent years, China has introduced supply-side measures to support the development of the real estate market, including supporting the issuance of new special-purpose bonds for land reserves and supporting local governments in purchasing existing commercial housing for use as affordable housing. This time, the focus has shifted to the demand side, further expanding policy efforts through fiscal-financial coordination.
Industry insiders believe that interest subsidies can reduce home-buying costs, accelerate the destocking of new homes, and ease the funding pressure on real estate developers.
The policy clearly demonstrates strong support for rigid home-buying demand, or first-home demand, and will in turn influence subsequent replacement and upgrading demand, said Yan Yuejin, deputy director at E-house China R&D Institute.
Li Yujia, chief researcher at the Guangdong Housing Policy Research Center, said the interest subsidy policy will reduce the cost of residents' mortgage loans and improve their willingness to take on leverage, thereby restoring the financial accelerator effect of the real estate sector.
Data released by the National Bureau of Statistics earlier this month showed narrower year-on-year declines in home prices across major Chinese cities in August, pointing to further signs of stabilization.
In August, Chinese authorities deepened reforms to the housing provident fund system, and refined regulations on commercial housing sales and property financing.
The package of policies is working in a coordinated manner from both the supply and demand sides, aiming to improve market expectations, restore residents' willingness to buy homes, and promote the steady and healthy development of the real estate market, experts said. ■

WFP warns of critical funding shortfalls as climate risks surge in Somalia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
01:38:01 CST
02:38:01 KST

MOGADISHU, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- The World Food Program (WFP) warned Tuesday of severe funding shortfalls that are drastically reducing its reach in Somalia amid a humanitarian crisis driven by drought and climate risks.
The WFP warned that current funding constraints will force it to assist fewer than 5 percent of Somalis facing emergency hunger starting in October, down from more than four million people per month during the 2022-2023 drought response, while funding for nutrition treatment will be completely depleted by the end of September.
"Malnutrition remains alarmingly high, with nearly 2 million children projected to suffer acute malnutrition in 2026, including 433,000 children facing severe acute malnutrition and requiring urgent treatment," it said in its latest report.
According to the WFP, Somalia is entering the October-December Deyr rainy season under a high-risk climate scenario.
El Nino conditions are expected to bring above-normal rainfall across parts of central and southern Somalia, with climate signals mirroring the severe flood events of 1997 and 2023, WFP said.
It said areas along the Juba and Shabelle river basins face the highest risk, raising grave concerns over widespread displacement, loss of livelihoods, and severe disruptions to humanitarian access.
Last week, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned that projected El Nino rains and severe flooding could affect up to 3.4 million people in Somalia across 16 regions between October and December.
OCHA warned that the combination of flooding, displacement, and inadequate sanitation risks triggering widespread waterborne disease outbreaks, occurring just as at least 380 health facilities have closed or scaled back operations due to critical funding shortages.
"The potential flooding might match or surpass the severe 2023 and 1997 seasons -- Somalia's two worst flood benchmarks -- and arrive before communities recover from the prolonged drought this year," OCHA said on Sept. 22.
According to the WFP, one-third of Somalia's population, or 5.4 million people, is acutely food insecure, with nearly 1.5 million facing emergency-level hunger between October and December. ■

Morocco's king appoints first woman prime minister following election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:22:38 UTC
02:22:38 KST

Morocco names Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri first woman PM
- Morocco appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as the first woman prime minister after her party won 97 seats in recent elections marked by low turnout.
- El Mansouri will form a coalition government and aims to address unemployment, living costs, and social disparities affecting youth.
- Her party pledges 5% annual growth, 2% inflation, and one million new jobs over five years, amid political challenges and opposition claims of fraud.
AI generated
RABAT - The king of Morocco on Sept 29 named Marrakesh mayor Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri the country’s first woman prime minister, the royal Cabinet announced, after her party won last week’s parliamentary elections.
Her centre-right Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) had dominated the vote, winning 97 out of 395 seats in the House of Representatives – 31 more than the next closest competitor, although the poll was marked by the lowest turnout in two decades.
The royal Cabinet said King Mohammed VI has now tasked the 50-year-old, who also served as housing minister, with “forming the new government”.
Speaking shortly after, El Mansouri said in a televised address her appointment was “truly historic”.
“For the first time in our country’s history, a woman is taking on the responsibility of leading the government,” she said. “This is a source of pride not only for me but for all Moroccan women.”
Without an outright majority, the PAM will have to form a coalition with other parties, though the monarch retains broad powers over major policies.
For the new premier, “the work starts today”, she said.
“We will first initiate internal consultations within our party before holding discussions with all political groups.”
El Mansouri joined the PAM in 2008, the year it was founded by current royal adviser Fouad Ali El Himma as a counterweight to the country’s Islamist movement.
She was also the first woman to serve as mayor of Marrakesh, winning the office in 2009 before losing it six years later, then retaking it again in 2021.
El Mansouri’s Cabinet will have to tackle several pressing issues including unemployment and living costs, as well as persistent social disparities particularly weighing on young people.
The parliamentary vote came just weeks after tens of thousands of mainly young Moroccan migrants rushed into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, a crisis that highlighted socio-economic frustrations among the youth.
It also came a year after a Gen-Z protest movement took to the streets to demand better health and education.
“We are fully aware that this period will be significant and marked by high expectations from Moroccans, particularly young people,” El Mansouri said. “That is why we will have a programme offering concrete and realistic solutions to citizens’ concerns.”
Her party has pledged average annual economic growth of five per cent, inflation of two per cent and the creation of at least one million new jobs over its five-year term.
The PAM was followed in the polls by the National Rally of Independents (RNI), which heads the outgoing coalition and won 66 seats.
The right-wing Istiqlal party came third with 65 seats, while the Islamist opposition’s Justice and Development Party (PJD) took 54 seats.
The PJD made significant gains after winning just 13 seats in 2021, having focused its campaign in part on fighting corruption.
Its chief, former prime minister Abdelilah Benkirane, hailed a “victory” but ruled out joining a coalition led by the PAM, which he said was “tainted by fraud”, without providing details. AFP

Mystery Deepens Over Alleged U.K. Terror Incident After Suspects Are Freed

====================================================================================================

No explosive devices found in vehicles near Fairford just petrol
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
18:19:30 BST
02:19:30 KST

No improvised explosive devices were found in the three vehicles examined after five men were arrested close to RAF Fairford at the weekend, although a quantity of petrol was recovered, according to Counter Terrorism Policing.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing, gave the update on Tuesday evening. “Those vehicles have been subject to extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts, and we can confirm that no improvised explosive devices were found. However, a quantity of petrol was recovered,” he said.
He also set out what prompted the response in the first place. “A police response was activated in the early hours of Sunday morning due to a range of information received, including a call from a member of the public about several vehicles acting suspiciously close to RAF Fairford,” he said, thanking those who had contacted police with information and saying the events of recent days had reaffirmed the part the public plays.
The investigation has extended well beyond Gloucestershire in the days since. “As part of the investigation, we have searched properties in London which I can confirm have concluded,” Taylor said. The scenes around the airfield are being reduced and the assistant commissioner said he anticipated closing them down completely by Wednesday, which he described as an important step towards restoring normality for the local community.
The five men were released on police bail on Monday, a development Taylor acknowledged had not been universally expected. “They remain under investigation and must adhere to strict conditions while we continue our work. The safety of the public is at the forefront of our investigative decision making, and this was certainly the case yesterday,” he said. “I understand why this development will have come as a surprise to many, but I’d like to reiterate that it was investigative decision, and one which is grounded in experience and careful consideration of policing powers.”
Counter Terrorism Policing has released only limited details of those arrested, all five of whom are British nationals resident in London, one aged 25 and the others aged between 23 and 24, with four living in the borough of Westminster and one in Camden, and none of them has been named.
The men were arrested on Sunday morning on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act and later of preparation of a terrorist act under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act, after Gloucestershire Constabulary declared a major incident and evacuated properties in the village of Whelford next to the airfield. Taylor said on Monday that investigators were keeping an open mind on whether the current international situation had any bearing on the case, and that they were considering the possibility of activity by proxies or by individuals knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state, as we reported.
He thanked the community near the airfield, Gloucestershire Police, and what he called many partners in Britain and the United States supporting the investigation.
Fairford is a United States Air Force forward operating location whose long runway has made it the standing European base for American strategic bombers, and B-1B Lancers have been operating from the airfield. The base moved to its highest force protection condition before the arrests were made.
The investigation continues, and anyone with information has been asked to contact the police.

LONDON - A British probe into a suspected bomb plot at an airbase used by the United States was mired in confusion on Sept 29, as police said no explosives but a “quantity of petrol” was found in vehicles seized nearby.
Police were called to the Royal Air Force Fairford base in south-west England on Sept 27 after a resident saw several vans “acting suspiciously”, triggering an evacuation of the nearby village and the declaration of a “major incident”.
“Those vehicles have been subject to extensive examination ... and we can confirm that no improvised explosive devices were found. However, a quantity of petrol was recovered,” National Counter Terrorism Policing head Laurence Taylor said.

“I understand why this development will have come as a surprise to many, but I’d like to reiterate that it was investigative decision,” Taylor added, after US President Donald Trump said he was “surprised” by the decision.

But the scare forced 85 homes in a nearby village to be evacuated, with many residents having to stay elsewhere for at least one night.

A resident in the neighbouring village of Kempsford, Patricia, 60, told AFP it was “very embarrassing that people around the world thought it was a terrorist attack but in the end no – it’s a lot of noise for nothing”.
The security scare became public after a farmer living in the village of Whelford near the airbase rang police after seeing the three vans blocking a road and a group of masked men fleeing the scene.
Armed officers arrested the five men – all London residents in their mid-20s – on suspicion of explosives offences and, later, “suspicion of preparing a terrorist act” under anti-terror laws.
Police said the men “remain under investigation and must adhere to strict conditions while we continue our work”.
Security at the base had reportedly been heightened recently.
Britain gave Washington permission in March to use Fairford for “specific defensive operations into Iran” to destroy Iranian missiles at source.
US bombers and other planes have since been seen taking off and landing from the base – the only one on Britain’s mainland used for this purpose.
Aerial footage of the vans showed they appeared to contain barrels, and at least one was marked with a fake logo and phone number giving the false impression that it was owned by a legitimate diesel delivery firm.
The legitimate firm said in a statement on its website that “neither the vehicle nor any of the individuals involved has any connection whatsoever with Fuel2U”, adding it was cooperating with the police.
“It’s a bit odd they were here in the middle of the night,” one local told AFP as she did some gardening in the nearby village of Kempsford.
“If they were true terrorists they wouldn’t have released them,” she added, asking not to give her name.
A British military camp was the victim of a “security breach” in 2025 after intruders cut through a fence to steal fuel from a tanker. AFP

Russia uses new domestic-made navigation systems in special military operation — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:21:04 UTC
23:21:04 KST

MOSCOW, September 30. /TASS/. Russian troops are using the new Kometa, Zvezdochet, and Susanin navigation systems for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in the special military operation in Ukraine, an unmanned aviation expert and CEO of the Center for Integrated Unmanned Solutions Dmitry Kuzyakin told TASS.
"The main challenge lies in the navigation of long-range drones. The enemy is relying on Turkish, European, and American solutions. We, on the other hand, are developing our own capabilities, which are bearing fruit in the form of solutions such as Kometa, Susanin, and Zvezdochet. It’s difficult to single out any one of them as the most important. Each of them is not just an out-of-the-box solution, but an entire onboard system with its own analytics, onboard computer, and highly complex software," the expert noted.
According to Kuzyakin, the main advantage of Russian solutions is the software. "It’s not difficult to put together antennas, a controller, and interfaces. What’s difficult is writing software that can do the impossible – navigate a long-range flight through interference, loss of communication, and enemy air defense systems to reach the target, and guide the UAV to it without errors or deviations," the specialist added.
Kuzyakin also highlighted the features of the latest Russian navigation systems for UAVs. "In their operation, these systems do not rely on any single channel of location data. They cross-reference navigation data from various sources, determine the degree of reliability of each, and construct the most plausible navigation picture for the onboard flight computer. Behind this simple explanation lie hundreds of ingenious software solutions developed by the Russian defense-industrial complex. The enemy may find the devices themselves in a pile of metal at destroyed facilities. They may be able to physically dismantle them, but they will never gain access to what matters most – the software," he noted.

The ministry emphasised that human interface in FCRA applications had more or less been eliminated, with all FCRA-related services delivered online through the dedicated FCRA portal. “No intermediary, agent or individual is authorised to facilitate any FCRA service,” said an MHA spokesperson, in a clear message to associations in the process of getting themselves registered under FCRA or seeking prior permission to receive foreign contributions.

Brazil’s cellphone crime a security nightmare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:39 UTC
01:49:39 KST

Eduardo Metzker, 29, was riding his motorcycle in Rio de Janeiro when he was suddenly boxed in by two other bikes. One of the riders put a gun to his head and demanded his phone and passcode.
The software developer watched with horror as the robbers drained up to 80,000 reais (about US$15,000) from his banking apps, mostly in credit, while he scrambled to block his accounts.
“You know you go out every day, earning a living, saving money, building a life and then someone sticks a gun in your face and takes everything you have. My credit rating was ruined,” Metzker said.
Photo: AP
Cellphone crime, which can involve violence, financial fraud and even murder, has become a potent symbol of the security crisis gripping Brazilian cities like Rio de Janeiro ahead of a first round presidential election on Sunday.
“The cellphone appears to encapsulate a growing panic over urban violence,” the Brazilian Public Security Forum (FBSP) said in its annual report.
An FBSP survey published in May estimated that about 14 million people had been a victim of the crime in the 12 previous months.
However, only about 830,000 cellphones were reported stolen or robbed last year, according to the annual report, which draws on police data.
“We walk around completely afraid, constantly on alert,” said Caroline Lo Bianco, 36, a dentist who had her phone ripped from her hands through the window of an Uber when she was seven months pregnant.
Ahead of a closely contested election, both leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his right-wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro have vowed to crack down on the crime.
Bolsonaro promises to quadruple jail sentences for cellphone crimes, while Lula has said “our goal is zero phone theft.”
Polls show security is the major concern of Brazilians this election, but Metzker said he does not believe any candidate would make a difference.
“Honestly, they can say whatever they want, I have no faith in them,” he said.
Fear of cellphone crime has pushed an estimated 30 percent of Brazilians — about 65 million people — to keep a cheap second phone, nicknamed a “robber’s phone,” the FBSP said.
Metzker said that after the robbery, he now carries one phone that he takes out on the street, and one that he keeps at home with all his banking applications on it.
Leonardo Silva, a coordinator for state and organized crime issues at the FBSP, said that cellphone crime was growing more sophisticated.
Criminal “interest has shifted away from the phone itself, its physical value, to the data contained in those devices,” he said.
After being robbed, Lo Bianco blocked her bank cards, but the thieves managed to transfer almost US$700 from a digital bank account. They also bought an Xbox on her Amazon app, which she managed to block before delivery.
The thieves even used her food delivery applications to send beer, meat and McDonalds to different addresses across Rio de Janeiro.
Luiz Fernando Bugiga, a prosecutor with the Special Action Group for Combating Organized Crime, said a major police operation in Sao Paulo this month revealed an organized scheme behind cellphone crime with four distinct criminal cells.
Those who steal the phones hand them off to a specialized cell whose members “initiate bank transfers and data theft.”
A third group make technical modifications to “legitimize” the phone, allowing it to re-enter the market. The final group is charged with selling parts and devices.
“Cellphone theft creates multiple forms of loss for the victim and therefore multiple sources of profit for the criminal,” he said.
For many, just replacing the phone is a major financial blow.
Joel da Silva, 42, who works as a doorman in Ipanema, “went a month without a phone,” before being able to buy one over four installments, after being robbed at gunpoint.
He said that in his seven months at his job, he has witnessed four phone robberies from the building where he works.
Lo Bianco, who is originally from the capital, Brasilia, and was a victim of an armed carjacking in Rio a few years ago, dreams of leaving.
“I tell my husband that if he asked me to move to the Amazon, my bags would be packed the next day,” she said.
Several areas of Thailand’s capital city Bangkok were inundated by continuous rain from Thursday afternoon to yesterday morning that has disrupted traffic and forced some residents to evacuate. Major canals in Bangkok filled with accumulated rainfall exceeding 20cm, officials said yesterday. Floodwaters spread across the city, particularly in the central and eastern parts, blocking roads and stopping traffic. The Thai Meteorological Department warned that the heavy rain would continue in most parts of the country through today, citing a strong low-pressure system over the central region and strengthening southwest monsoon conditions. Eight food products fail inspections at border, FDA says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:39 UTC
01:49:39 KST

Japanese cantaloupes, fresh black truffles from Bulgaria and Thai bird’s nest drinks were among eight imported food products found to contain excessive pesticide residues, heavy metals or sweeteners, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said yesterday.
The list also included celery from Vietnam and sesame products from Tanzania.
Part of a shipment of Japanese cantaloupes imported by Kaohsiung-based fruit importer Yang Jhen International Co contained 0.07 parts per million (ppm) of the pesticide isofetamid, exceeding the 0.01 ppm limit, the FDA said.
Photo courtesy of the Food and Drug Administration
Taiwan does not permit the use of isofetamid on cantaloupes, FDA Northern Center for Regional Administration Director Liu Fang-ming (劉芳銘) said.
The 320kg shipment must be returned or destroyed, Liu said, adding that all future shipments from Yang Jhen would be subject to border inspections.
In the past six months, 11 of 111 shipments of fresh melons imported from Japan failed inspections, with excessive pesticide residues the main reason for noncompliance, FDA data showed.
The FDA would inspect all batches of fresh melons imported from Japan through Oct. 28, Liu said.
Fresh black truffles imported from Bulgaria by European Arcade Food Ltd contained 5 milligrams per kilogram (mg/kg) of cadmium per kilogram, exceeding the 2mg/kg limit, the agency said, adding that the 4.5kg shipment must be returned or destroyed.
Although the batch was the company’s only noncompliant shipment in the past six months, it had contravened regulation in September last year, and so all future shipments would be inspected, Liu said.
Three of 17 shipments of truffles from Bulgaria inspected over the past six months failed inspections, FDA data showed.
A shipment of Thai bird’s nest drink imported by Hsiang Yen Trading Co contained 0.06g/kg of saccharin, which is not permitted in the product category. The 4,991kg shipment must be returned or destroyed.
Separately, a Consumers’ Foundation survey found that 80 percent of basil samples and 20 percent of scallion samples bought in traditional markets, supermarkets and big-box stores in Taiwan’s six special municipalities contained pesticide residues exceeding legal limits.
The foundation bought 10 samples each of garlic, scallions and basil in May and June and tested them for 410 pesticides and dithiocarbamate pesticides.
Of the 30 samples, eight basil and two scallion samples failed. The 10 noncompliant samples contained 16 types of pesticides, while the risk coefficient for basil ranged from two to 141.9.
The tests detected chlorpyrifos, an organophosphate insecticide that can affect the nervous system after prolonged or excessive exposure, the foundation said.
Taiwan removed chlorpyrifos from its permitted pesticide-residue standards in April 2024 and has been phasing out its use.
The foundation advised people to soak garlic, scallions and basil in water for 10 to 15 minutes and thoroughly rinse them under running water before using them.

Free flu and COVID-19 vaccines start tomorrow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:38 UTC
01:49:38 KST

The first phase of government-funded seasonal influenza and COVID-19 vaccination begins tomorrow, amid heightened flu activity, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said yesterday.
There were 138,654 outpatient and emergency medical visits for flu-like illnesses last week, about 3.2 percent fewer than the previous week, but that number might be affected by many clinics being closed over the long holiday weekend, CDC Epidemic Intelligence Center Deputy Director Lee Chia-lin (李佳琳) said.
As 12.2 percent of those visits were to emergency rooms, the seasonal flu is still considered to be in its epidemic period, she said.
Photo: CNA
Thirty flu-related deaths and 87 severe flu cases were confirmed last week, Lee said, adding that it was the most weekly flu-related deaths since October last year.
Flu activity is also rising in China, South Korea, Japan and Singapore, as well as in the US, she said.
The centers estimated that weekly medical visits would vary slightly this week and in the coming weeks, due to long weekends, but would remain high as people gather on holidays, CDC Deputy Director-General Lin Min-cheng (林明誠) said.
The number of weekly medical visits might begin to drop from the middle of next month, but whether the weekly number would reach a peak of 150,000 to 160,000 as previously predicted is not certain, he added.
Meanwhile, 10,502 medical visits for COVID-19 were reported last week, Lee said.
Weekly numbers for the disease have been gradually falling in the past few weeks, but it is still at epidemic levels, she said, adding that there were 33 severe cases and 14 deaths confirmed last week.
Eligible recipients should get the flu and COVID-19 vaccines as soon as possible, as vaccination remains the most effective way to protect against the diseases, Lin said.
The enhanced flu vaccine first introduced to the program this year provides stronger protection, and the updated COVID-19 vaccine from Moderna uses a lower dose while providing greater protection, he said.
Eligible groups in the first phase for both vaccines include people aged 65 and older, medical and disease-prevention workers, indigenous people aged 55 to 64, nursing home residents and workers, pregnant women, caregivers of children younger than six months, and employees at preschools, childcare centers and at-home childcare providers.
They also include people with high-risk, chronic, rare or catastrophic illnesses, while flu-vaccine eligibility additionally includes students at elementary schools, junior and senior-high schools, vocational schools and the first to third years of five-year junior colleges, or people working with poultry or livestock, and animal epidemic prevention workers.
Children aged six months to preschool age are also eligible for the free flu vaccine, while the eligibility for the free COVID-19 vaccine has been revised to children aged six months to younger than six years who have never received a COVID-19 vaccine.
The second phase is to begin on Nov. 2, when the eligibility of the vaccines would be expanded to include people aged 50 to 64, the CDC said.
In addition, the government’s “health token” program launches tomorrow, meaning that people aged 18 and older who receive an eligible vaccine, either government-funded or paid for out of pocket, can earn health tokens, Lin said.
They can earn 450 health tokens for a flu vaccine, 900 for a COVID-19 vaccine and 600 for a pneumococcus vaccine, he said.
The tokens can be exchanged for health-related products and services starting from Dec. 1, he added.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:37 UTC

The opposition-controlled Legislative Yuan yesterday rejected the 27 candidates nominated by President William Lai (賴清德) for the Control Yuan.
The nominees for Control Yuan president Chen Yung-hsing (陳永興) and vice president Wang Jung-chang (王榮璋) were among those who failed to secure enough support in the roll-call vote.
The legislature began the confirmation vote at 10am, with most nominees receiving 50 votes in favor and 60 against.
Photo: Chen Yi-kuan, Taipei Times
Under Article 29 of the Act Governing the Legislative Yuan’s Power (立法院職權行使法), nominations require approval from more than half of all legislators, or 57 votes, to pass.
Ahead of the vote, Democratic Progressive Party caucus chief executive Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) said the caucus unanimously supported Lai’s nominees for the government watchdog.
Chinese Nationalist party (KMT) caucus deputy secretary-general Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) said that the party would not allow any unsuitable candidates to serve as Control Yuan members.
The KMT had raised numerous concerns about the Control Yuan’s performance over the past few years, she said, adding that critics had long accused the government watchdog of applying uneven standards of oversight to different political parties and cases.
The Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) unanimously voted against the nominees, TPP Legislator Hung Yu-hsiang (洪毓祥) said, citing what he described as failures in oversight, protection of the powerful and a lack of exemplary conduct among Control Yuan members.
The Control Yuan’s previous members completed their six-year term on July 31. Under the law, newly appointed members should have assumed office on Aug. 1.
Lai announced his list of candidates in June.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) urged the ruling and opposition parties to work together to restore constitutional order and uphold their constitutional responsibility by reviewing the budget according to the law and within the statutory time frame.
Additional reporting by Lin Hsin-han

Estonian authorities yesterday said they have concluded that an arson attack on Aug. 15 on a defense company that provides military vehicles to Ukraine was an act of sabotage commissioned by Russian security services.
Estonian Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna said that “such actions are absolutely unacceptable” and that Russia’s charge d’affaires in Tallinn was being summoned to his ministry.
A fire broke out overnight on Aug. 15 at a building in the Estonian capital used by Milrem Robotics, but was quickly brought under control, the BNS news agency reported. On Aug. 17, two Latvian suspects were detained in Latvia, and a third followed the next day. The suspects were handed over to Estonia.
Photo: EPA
Milrem has supplied THeMIS uncrewed ground vehicles to Ukraine.
The Estonian Internal Security Service said that it has concluded that the arson attack “was a deliberate and pre-planned act commissioned by Russian security services.”
“The modus operandi of the Milrem attack is consistent with other acts of sabotage carried out in Europe on behalf of Russia,” it said in a statement, adding that it “assesses that the attack is directly attributable to the Russian Federation.”
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that “such statements are unfounded, ill-considered, absolutely not reflecting the reality, not containing any substantiation whatsoever.”
“We cannot take such statements seriously, and we won’t,” Peskov said.
Moscow has been widely accused by Western officials of running a campaign of sabotage and disruption with the aim of undermining support for Ukraine and destabilizing European nations.
The Associated Press has tracked about 200 incidents of sabotage and malign activity across Europe blamed on Russia since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022.
That includes organizing plots to set fire to warehouses, launching drones and trying to kill enemies abroad, as well as stealing defense technology and carrying out cyberattacks on critical European infrastructure.
In a recent case that pointed to an escalation of such activity, Germany blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport early last month using a drone laden with explosives.

Dead ambassador to Nicaragua’s book makes waves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:05 UTC
01:49:05 KST

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs yesterday said Taiwan worked until the last minute before breaking diplomatic ties with Nicaragua in 2021 in response to a former ambassador to Nicaragua’s claim that Taiwan voluntarily gave up diplomatic relations, revealed in a posthumous publication.
On Dec. 9, 2021, Nicaragua severed its diplomatic ties with Taiwan for the second time, switching its recognition to China.
In 1985, Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega’s government first ended 55 years of diplomatic relations with Taiwan and switched recognition to China, but after Ortega was replaced in 1990, ties with Taiwan resumed, which were maintained by Ortega when he returned to office in 2007.
In a posthumous autobiography published this month, former ambassador to Nicaragua Jaime Wu (吳進木) said that “Taiwan chose to stand with the US and voluntarily gave up Nicaragua,” the Chinese-language China Times reported on Monday.
Wu had been ambassador to Nicaragua twice — from June 2007 to June 2011, and again from July 2017 to November 2021 — retiring on Nov. 17, 2021. He was granted Nicaraguan citizenship on Dec. 10, 2021, a day after Nicaragua cut ties with Taiwan. Wu died in April last year.
The China Times cited Wu’s autobiography as saying that Taiwan-Nicaragua relations had been steady when he retired, and that the main reason Nicaragua cut ties with Taiwan the next month was because former president Tsai Ing-wen’s (蔡英文) administration did not congratulate Ortega when he secured his re-election in November that year.
Regarding the report, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Chen Ming-chi (陳明祺) told reporters that the ministry was well-informed about all diplomatic situation, but sometimes when China is engaging in secret diplomacy, the parties involved maintain strict confidentiality.
Regarding Nicaragua severing diplomatic ties with Taiwan, he said the government “worked hard until the last minute” to maintain ties with all of its diplomatic allies, but “sometimes the situation leaves us no choice.”
The ministry is aware of China investing significant resources and effort into poaching Taiwan’s allies, he said, adding that the ministry’s understanding of the situation regarding Nicaragua cutting ties with Taiwan is not the same as Wu’s, and the information has been submitted to the Control Yuan.
Foreign ministry deputy spokeswoman Chen Yi-chun (陳怡君) said when asked for comment that Deputy Minister Chen Ming-chi and the government have a full grasp of the status of all diplomatic allies, and would work hard in their dealings until the last moment.
The Ortega-led Sandinista National Liberation Front (FSLN) had pursued liberation and public welfare, but after Ortega came to power, he established a dictatorship, cracking down on press freedom and civil society groups, she said.
During the 2021 presidential election, Ortega fabricated charges to persecute opposition candidates and potential challengers, violating citizens’ fundamental rights to political participation and betraying his public ideals, as well as the Nicaraguan people’s desire for democratic governance, she said.
“Ortega disregarded the long-standing friendship built on Taiwan’s years of continuous assistance to Nicaragua’s development, and turned to China after the election,” she said, adding that to maintain national dignity, Taiwan severed diplomatic relations with Nicaragua at the time.
The Control Yuan has already issued its findings from an investigation about Wu’s claims in his autobiography, she said.

Malaysia begins repatriation of Burmese nationals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:05 UTC
01:49:05 KST

Malaysia yesterday began repatriating Burmese nationals, including women and children, under a voluntary program, despite warnings from the UN refugee agency and rights groups that conditions in the country remain unsafe.
The 1,476 people being sent back are among 5,000 Burmese nationals who are to be repatriated in stages from Malaysia, where as of Aug. 15, 10,388 Burmese nationals were being held at immigration detention depots nationwide, the Malaysian Ministry of Home Affairs said.
Buses believed to be carrying Burmese returnees arrived at a stadium in Manjung town in Malaysia’s central Perak state early yesterday, amid tight security. Ships believed to be from Myanmar were docked at the nearby Lumut naval base.
Photo: AFP
Home ministry official Makhzan Mahyuddin was quoted by national Bernama news agency as saying the returnees comprised 1,370 men, 79 women, 20 boys and seven girls, aged eight to 60.
The ministry said they would be sent back safely on two Myanmar navy warships and a hospital ship. It is unclear if any of the returnees were minority Muslim Rohingya, who are rejected by the Myanmar government. The ministry did not provide further details of their identities and circumstances, but stressed their return was voluntary.
“This move also sends a clear signal that the government is serious about addressing irregular migration and the issue of undocumented foreign nationals through law enforcement, repatriation and more systematic management and data collection,” the ministry said in a statement.
The UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and rights groups slammed the repatriation, saying the security and humanitarian situation in parts of Myanmar remains volatile and returnees could face serious risks, such as persecution and forced military conscription in an active war zone.
Myanmar is involved in an armed conflict and political instability following the military’s seizure of power in 2021.
Malaysia is home to about 215,600 refugees and asylum seekers registered with the UNHCR, including about 126,000 Rohingya who make up one of Southeast Asia’s largest refugee communities. Despite hosting them, Malaysia is not a party to the UN Refugee Convention and treats refugees as undocumented migrants.
The government recently launched a system to register refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia and to build a biometric database, as it seeks to manage and regulate the population independently from the UNHCR.
Rohingya have faced growing public hostility in Malaysia due to their growing numbers, fueled by concerns over jobs, public services and security.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has defended the repatriation policy as a diplomatic effort to find a long-term solution, saying Malaysia cannot host refugees indefinitely and Myanmar must take responsibility for its citizens.
Anwar said he plans to invite Burmese President Min Aung Hlaing to Malaysia to discuss the long-running refugee and undocumented migrant issue that has dragged on for decades.
“I am inviting him to say that we can be friends and trade, we can accept Myanmar, but Myanmar must accept them back,” he said in a podcast posted online on Sept. 16. “To me, that’s better diplomacy than just shouting angrily at Myanmar.”

Students losing their minds over AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:04 UTC
01:49:04 KST

Taiwanese writer Chu Yu-hsun (朱宥勳) this month spoke out about the difficulties of judging literary competitions when nearly 40 percent of the novel submissions he reviews appear to be generated by artificial intelligence (AI). He said he would refuse to serve as a judge for any literary award that does not explicitly prohibit the use of AI in creative writing.
The use of AI in creative and academic work has become increasingly common. My son, who attends National Chengchi University, says he is exasperated after working to complete assignments on his own, only to receive lower grades than classmates who used AI. Professors might have told students not to use the technology, but they still struggle to identify AI-generated work when grading assignments.
Schools cannot simply allow students to misuse AI to the point that their intellectual and creative abilities stagnate. Concrete measures must be taken to prevent human thinking from being replaced by AI and to preserve education as a process that stimulates creativity.
An important first step should be to encourage more handwriting in schoolwork. Work produced with pen and paper is more likely to be the student’s own, and can help with stimulating thinking and creativity. It could also help foster patience, self-cultivation and emotional regulation as broader life skills.
Schools should also increase the number of written-response questions in assessments. Students would spend more time practicing with pen and paper, developing the fluency and creativity needed to perform well and earn higher marks in examinations.
Reading is, of course, also important. Teachers can take advantage of opportunities to have students read aloud, not only in Chinese-language classes, but also in other subjects. Outside of classes, students could read written materials during morning sessions, class meetings and club activities. Reading can improve students’ comprehension, while reading aloud strengthens their ability to express themselves and helps cultivate literacy.
AI might not be stoppable, but schools still have options to provide students opportunities to develop necessary cognitive skills. Such measures would not only prevent intellectual decline and promote creativity, but also cultivate the kind of self-development needed to navigate the world.
Chen Chi-nung is former principal of Kuohsin Junior High School in Nantou County.

US recognizes Taiwan’s value: analyst
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:49:03 UTC
01:49:03 KST

The US would not abandon Taiwan in exchange for soybeans and Boeing jets, a US analyst said yesterday, as US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) ended their summit in Washington.
The White House understands that Taiwan might be its most important partner and therefore unlikely to take on any course that jeopardizes its relationship with the nation, said Hudson Institute senior fellow Riley Walters, in an interview.
Taiwan makes the semiconductors and artificial intelligence servers that are critical to the US economy and worth more than any amount of soybeans or jets the US could sell to China, he said.
Trump and Xi likely conducted much of their dialogue about Taiwan behind closed doors and any understandings they might have achieved would be kept secret, Walters said.
US officials have said that Trump has made no changes to Washington’s Taiwan policy, he said.
The US government has always considered trade and economics its most important issue, especially Trump, whose attention was focused on getting an agreement to cut tariffs on nonsensitive goods worth US$30 billion, Walters said.
Trump had reasons to attempt to reduce the US economy’s inflation ahead of the midterm elections, although whether slashing tariffs would achieve that goal remained to be seen, he said.
The political motive could explain the communications between the two countries and in the US-China Board of Trade, enabling Washington to make progress on some level, he said.
Washington and Beijing produced different versions of agreements reached during the talks, indicating the two sides need to improve their communication and understanding of each other’s goals, Walters said.
Separately, an academic said the Trump-Xi meeting had no tangible effect on US arms sales to Taiwan.
Tamkang University assistant professor of international affairs and strategic studies professor Ma Chun-wei (馬準威) made the remarks at a conference on the impact of the summits on US-China relations at National Chengchi University.
Ma, recently returned from a visit to the US, said that DC-based think tanks continued to advocate for policies to oppose China and support Taiwan, regardless of their party alignment.
Production capacity shortfalls in the US defense industrial base, managing tensions for Trump and Xi’s many meetings this year, and concerns over Taiwan’s ability to effectively defend itself all played a role in delaying US arms sales, he said.
The policy circle in Washington concurred that China was unlikely to invade Taiwan in the short and intermediate terms, making Taiwan less of a priority in the US’ eyes, he said.
Ma said the Council on Foreign Relations’ Web site has downgraded the risk of a conflict in Taiwan from high to medium.
Although Trump and Xi confirmed to have discussed Taiwan, the US Department of State and US Ambassador to China David Perdue said that no changes had been made to Washington’s stance on Taiwan, he said.
Washington’s Taiwan policy continued to be based on the Shanghai Communique, Taiwan Relations Act and the “Six Assurances,” Ma cited them as saying.
US policy to export arms to Taiwan likely would remain unaltered over the long term, but the nation should stay alert for personal remarks and decisionmaking from Trump that could alter US policy, he said.
Beijing’s strategy in the summits is to shift the narrative of US policy under the guise of conflict management and de-escalation, National Chengchi University associate research fellow of international relations Tzeng Wei-feng (曾偉?) said.
Xi demanded that the US treat China as an equal and oppose Taiwanese independence under Beijing’s definition of the term, while Trump was committed to strategic ambiguity, including arms sales to Taiwan, he said.
However, the risk of Trump’s transactional approach to international relations causing changes to the US policy on Taiwan and China is a risk that the nation should not ignore, he said.

Photo courtesy of Aerospace Industrial Development Corp

The "smart" detection feature allows the operator to identify the make of incoming drones and locate their pilots, AIDC said.

However, the police on Monday released the five on bail, but said the investigation was not over and they were examining whether individuals acting for a foreign state were involved.

====================================================================================================

AI will be wrong more and more without reliable journalism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:48:56 UTC
01:48:56 KST

In her 1967 essay “Truth and Politics,” the philosopher Hannah Arendt said “Freedom of opinion is a farce unless factual information is guaranteed and the facts themselves are not in dispute.” The news supplied by trustworthy journalists has long been a source of that information, without which democratic societies cannot function effectively. However, as people increasingly rely on AI chatbots for news, siphoning traffic and profits from outlets often operating on a shoestring budget, good journalism is at risk of disappearing.
The paradox is that trusted news sources are essential to AI’s credibility. Failure to recognize this dependence might result in AI tools destabilizing the already precarious journalism industry further at a moment of profound upheaval and democratic erosion. Mariya Gabriel, UNESCO’s Assistant Director-General for Communication and Information, said at the World News Media Congress in June: “Support for journalism is not a luxury. It is democratic infrastructure.” Around the same time, UNESCO translated that principle into practice by unveiling its Draft Guidance on Fair Compensation for News, with the final version expected later this year.
AI firms have a responsibility to help sustain the institutions producing the information that their models train on and reproduce, because every AI-generated answer depends on knowledge that someone first had to discover, verify, report, edit and publish. An analysis of more than 680 million individual citations across popular chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini found that journalism accounts for 27 percent of them, rising to 49 percent for queries about recent events. Without verified information from outside sources, AI systems do not just give inaccurate or out-of-date information, but degrade as well.
Supporting journalism could help AI firms win the public’s confidence, as only 20 percent of people worldwide trust chatbot answers. That caution looks justified. A study last year by the European Broadcasting Union and the BBC evaluated more than 3,000 responses from leading AI assistants and found that 45 percent contained at least one significant issue, and that 31 percent had serious sourcing failures.
UNESCO’s proposal seeks to address this problem by establishing a framework rooted in shared responsibility while protecting human rights and media freedom. This approach, which regards journalism not simply as an industry but as a public good whose sustainability underpins access to reliable information, advocates the use of bargaining codes, competition remedies, public and platform-financed funds, and collective licensing. These tools would be paired with transparency and attribution obligations and protections for smaller and local media.
The real strength of UNESCO’s proposal is that it shifts the debate away from copyright toward the public interest in preserving sources of accurate, trusted information. The World Association of News Publishers (WAN-IFRA) endorses that framing of the issue. For two decades, the internet rested on a workable bargain: publishers invested in journalism, and tech platforms helped audiences discover it. The arrival of AI chatbots that answer questions directly instead of sending users to the publishers who invested in finding the answers has broken that bargain.
We must create a new value-exchange model. As the New York Times publisher A.G. Sulzberger told delegates at June’s World News Media Congress, AI companies should “support the healthy, sustainable flow of the information and ideas and creativity” that powers their technology. This is not charity; it is enlightened self-interest. Every AI firm is one misinformation crisis away from discovering the difficulty of rebuilding broken trust. Algorithms cannot replicate independent news publications’ verification process and professional editorial judgment.
Fair compensation should not be viewed as a regulatory burden. It is an investment in trusted information, democratic resilience and the long-term credibility of AI — a technology that, contrary to the popular narrative, news publishers and journalists are embracing. For example, investigative reporters are using AI to analyze thousands of documents and public records, helping them identify patterns, connections and anomalies that would otherwise take weeks or months to uncover. This gives them more time to do what the technology cannot: verify the findings, cultivate sources, ask difficult questions and establish what actually happened.
Building a future in which AI and journalism can thrive is a responsibility that must be shared by publishers, policymakers and tech companies. UNESCO has taken an important step toward making this future a reality, and its guidelines deserve broad global support. The success of the AI ecosystem is going to be determined not only by the sophistication of its algorithms, but by the continued existence of trusted, diverse and economically sustainable news sources.
Stig Orskov is CEO of WAN-IFRA, representing 20,000 publications in more than 120 countries.
Copyright: Project Syndicate

The blasts that wounded three South Korean soldiers last week were apparently caused by North Korean mines, Seoul said yesterday, accusing Pyongyang of an armistice violation and warning of “corresponding measures.”
One soldier lost a foot due to the explosions in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), the heavily mined buffer zone that has divided the two Koreas since their 1953 armistice.
The northern and southern boundaries of the zone are among the world’s most heavily fortified frontiers and landmine incidents have previously heightened tensions between the two Koreas, which remain technically at war.
Photo: EPA
South Korean Minister of National Defense Kang Shin-chul spoke before a parliamentary hearing a day after his ministry said North Korean mines were “highly suspected” of causing the two explosions on Monday last week.
“This is a clear violation of the armistice agreement, and since North Korea bears responsibility, we will take corresponding measures,” he said.
The military “has a range of necessary measures at our disposal, and we will implement them in stages,” he added, without giving details.
The minister said that dense vegetation in the area had hampered the work of mine detectors, and that South Korean forces were in the DMZ to clear the area in advance of an operation with the UN Command.
That operation would assess terrain changes caused by North Korean forces south of the Military Demarcation Line, which marks the nations’ effective border.
Hong Sung-pyo, senior researcher at the Seoul-based Korea Institute for Military Affairs, said it was reasonable to conclude that the mines were North Korean.
“In practical terms, the only forces operating in the DMZ area are the South Korean, US and North Korean militaries,” he said.
“Given the interoperability between South Korean and US forces, there would be little reason for the US military to have laid any mines there,” he said.
Yang Jin-hyeok, director of operations for South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff, told lawmakers that a site investigation yesterday discovered an unexploded North Korean plastic anti-personnel mine.
Since 2024, after North Korean leader Kim Jong-un designated South Korea as his country’s “principal enemy,” Pyongyang’s military has laid mines and built anti-tank barriers along the frontier as part of efforts to permanently seal it off.
During the operation, Pyongyang also blew up the northern parts of inter-Korean roads no longer in use.
Kang said that the North Korean mines linked to last week’s incident were believed to have been laid as part of Pyongyang’s border fortification work.
There was no mention of last week’s blasts on North Korean state media.
In a 2015 incident, two South Korean soldiers were seriously wounded in a landmine blast on the southern side of the DMZ, with one losing both legs.

Yemen mobilisation call signals escalation backed by Saudis

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:35:44 UTC

Breadcrumb
Yemen mobilisation call signals escalation backed by Saudi coordination
A call for military mobilisation by Yemen's government is a sign of growing escalation in the country but has yet to translate into preparations for a new offensive against the Houthis, a leading Yemeni analyst has told The New Arab.
The mobilisation call was issued on Monday by Presidential Leadership Council (PLC) chief Rashad al-Alimi amid heightened tensions with the Houthi movement and signs that Saudi Arabia is taking a more direct role in managing its Yemeni allies.
Al-Alimi called for military forces aligned with the government to increase their readiness and mobilise against the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa and much of northern and western Yemen.
The announcement comes amid renewed speculation over a possible attempt by anti-Houthi forces to alter the military balance after years in which Yemen's main front lines have remained largely frozen.
Maysaa Shuja al-Deen, a senior researcher at the Sana'a Center for Strategic Studies, told The New Arab that there was so far little evidence that the announcement had resulted in mobilisation on the ground.
"I think the call for mobilisation is one of the signals of escalation in Yemen, alongside the fatwa of the Saudi mufti," Shuja al-Deen said.
"I haven't seen anything in practice showing that there is any kind of mobilisation."
"Nothing in practice is happening in response to this call," she added.
Saudi Arabia's Grand Mufti recently issued a religious ruling calling for support for Yemen's internationally recognised government against the Houthis, another indication of increasingly confrontational rhetoric towards the group.
Shuja al-Deen said Al-Alimi's mobilisation call was unlikely to have been issued independently of Riyadh.
"Definitely this call was in coordination with Saudi Arabia," she said.
Saudi Arabia intervened militarily in Yemen in 2015 at the head of a coalition seeking to restore the internationally recognised government after the Houthis seized Sanaa.
Years of fighting failed to dislodge the group from the capital, and Riyadh subsequently sought negotiations with the Houthis as it attempted to extricate itself from the conflict, which has caused one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world.
Recent developments, however, have raised questions over whether Saudi Arabia is again preparing for a more assertive role.
Shuja al-Deen said the most important change was not greater cohesion among Yemen's notoriously divided anti-Houthi factions, but Riyadh's determination to exercise much closer control over them.
"I don't think the government now is more united, but definitely the Saudis are now more determined to manage the situation closely," she said.
She contrasted the current approach with earlier periods of fighting, when she said Riyadh had not followed developments as closely or been as thoroughly prepared.
"I think the preparations of the Saudis are bigger than the last time," she said.
Shuja al-Deen also said Riyadh appeared to be increasingly relying on new Salafi leaders as part of its preparations.
The PLC brings together a collection of factions with often competing political and territorial ambitions, and divisions among anti-Houthi forces have repeatedly complicated attempts to establish a unified military strategy.
Saudi Arabia has traditionally been the internationally recognised government's principal external sponsor, while the UAE has developed close relationships with several other armed factions, particularly in southern Yemen.
Shuja al-Deen said Riyadh's current role went significantly beyond simply providing weapons or financial assistance.
"It's everything under their supervision - definitely close supervision," she said.
"It's not only about military support. It's everything under their supervision."
Whether the mobilisation announcement will develop into a significant military build-up remains unclear.
For now, Shuja al-Deen said there was a gap between increasingly confrontational rhetoric and developments on the ground, suggesting the call should be understood as a warning of possible escalation rather than evidence that a new offensive is already underway.

Russia to cut welfare, education funding in 2027, as spending soars on war in Ukraine
- Russia will cut funding for welfare, education, healthcare, and infrastructure by around 6-7% in 2027 to fund rising military expenses amid the ongoing war in Ukraine.
- Defence spending is set at 17.1 trillion roubles in 2027, a 27% rise from the original budget and the highest since 2022, with increased tax hikes and borrowing planned.
- Debt-servicing costs will increase by 21.6% in 2027, reaching 9.4% of total spending, reflecting high interest rates and growing borrowing, despite cuts in non-military budgets.
AI generated
MOSCOW - Russia will cut funding for welfare, education and health care in 2027’s state budget, in addition to previously announced tax hikes, to help cover soaring military spending, fiscal documents obtained by Reuters showed.
Russia plans to spend 17.1 trillion roubles (S$259 billion) on defence in 2027, around 27% more than the 13.5 trillion roubles originally budgeted and the highest figure since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022.
Funding for social policy, which covers items such as state pensions, payments to war veterans and maternity benefits, will shrink by 7% in 2027.
Funding for education will fall by 6% and healthcare funding by 6.8%, compared with the initial plan.
Spending under the “national economy” section, which includes road construction and other infrastructure projects, as well as subsidies for agriculture and other sectors, will shrink by 7.4% in 2027.
Russia’s budget situation has gradually deteriorated throughout its four and a half years of war in Ukraine, as the country has had to tap its fiscal reserve fund, increase borrowing and raise taxes to keep up with growing military spending.
Russia is drawing up a three-year budget in an attempt to improve long-term planning, but it has had to revise figures sharply upwards each year and has repeatedly missed its annual deficit targets.
The federal budget does not incorporate regional and municipal budgets, which account for a significant share of social spending.
The new tax hikes in the 2027 draft budget, as well as a larger-than-expected increase in utility tariffs planned for 2027 and announced after this month’s parliamentary election, have angered even some Kremlin supporters.
The new State Duma, in which the pro-Kremlin United Russia party will hold a constitutional majority, is expected to approve the new budget, with authorities saying that winning the war in Ukraine takes priority over other needs.
While overall non-military spending is shrinking, the share of debt-servicing costs in the Russian budget is rising due to high interest rates, which the central bank maintains to fight inflation, and increased borrowing plans.
The documents show that debt-servicing costs will rise by 21.6% in 2027 compared with the initial plan, reaching 9.4% of total spending in 2027 and increasing further to 10.6% in 2029. REUTERS

BAE friend or foe system certified for US Air Force F-16
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:30:44 BST
01:30:44 KST

BAE Systems has received AIMS certification for a new Identification Friend or Foe unit fitted to the United States Air Force F-16 Fighting Falcon, clearing the equipment for use on a standard shared across American and NATO forces, according to the company.
The AN/APX-127(V)1 Combined Interrogator Transponder consolidates the interrogator and transponder functions into a single box, an arrangement the company says suits highly manoeuvrable aircraft where space is at a premium. It keeps the same form factor as the units it replaces, making it a drop-in substitute for the AN/APX-113(V), AN/APX-125(V) and AN/APX-126(V), which are in service on a range of American and international platforms.
Seth Guanu, combat identification products program area director at BAE Systems, said: “We are investing in the next generation of our IFF technology to support our customers’ missions for today and tomorrow. Our multi-domain systems are designed for high-performance; easily upgradeable; and meet size, weight, and power objectives for existing and emerging platforms. This solution provides added security and real-time information pilots need in a variety of threat environments.”
According to BAE Systems, the unit is AIMS Mark XIIB certified with Mode S and Mode 5 for secure and encrypted exchange, and carries additional receive channels for passive acquisition of Mode 5 Level 2 and Automatic Dependent Surveillance Broadcast In. The open systems architecture is intended to allow capability to be added through software rather than hardware changes, which the company says reduces the risk and cost of keeping the equipment current.
Identification Friend or Foe is the means by which an aircraft or ship establishes whether a contact is friendly before a weapon is released, and the consequences of getting it wrong are the reason the field attracts the attention it does. Mode 5 is the current encrypted NATO standard, introduced to replace the older Mode 4 across the alliance, and it uses cryptographic keys that have to be loaded and managed rather than a simple coded reply.
Work on the unit is carried out at BAE Systems facilities at Greenlawn in New York and in Austin, Texas, through the company’s American business rather than its British operations. Deliveries against an initial production lot of 90 units are expected to begin this year.

On education, he promised to "rebuild a system of comprehensive education in this country with parity between academic and technical."

Growth and fiscal rules
Burnham said his economic strategy would involve nationalisation and devolution, arguing that greater control over essential services could help create conditions for business growth.
He confirmed that the government would stick to its fiscal rules "to get borrowing and debt down."
The premier said the party would maintain its 2024 general election manifesto commitment not to make changes in the current period, while changes could be considered if Labour remains in power beyond the 2029 election.

Between two chokepoints: Egypt's growing Red Sea dilemma
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:28:23 UTC
01:28:23 KST

Breadcrumb
Between two chokepoints: Egypt's growing Red Sea dilemma
Seven months into the US-Israel war on Iran, Egypt finds itself increasingly exposed to the pressures of a wider regional conflagration.
The Houthis’ recent offensive to consolidate control over Bab al-Mandeb poses serious risks for Cairo, which has already experienced the economic fallout of Houthi attacks on maritime traffic.
In late 2023, when the Houthis targeted commercial shipping in response to Israel’s war on Gaza, the campaign sharply curtailed traffic through the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.
According to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the turmoil reduced Egypt’s Suez Canal revenues by over $6 billion in 2024.
Traffic through the canal has since recovered, with transits exceeding 1,200 in both July and August. August also marked the busiest month since December 2023.
Prolonged disruption could, however, once again constrain one of Egypt’s key sources of foreign currency. A deterioration in Red Sea security would also carry wider economic, political, and security consequences for the broader region.
Houthis seek to maximise Red Sea gains
The Houthis’ expanding offensive along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including their capture of strategically important territory around Mocha and the islands of Mayun (Perim) and Hanish, is aimed at cementing their position around Bab al-Mandeb.
“They know that holding the coast for long may be difficult, which is why they are trying to entrench themselves by securing the highlands overlooking Bab al-Mandeb and cutting the strategic lines connecting Aden and Taiz, which would obstruct the ability to send reinforcements to Mokha,” Yasmeen El Eryani, Executive Director for Knowledge Production at the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies, told The New Arab.
This strategy also reinforces a broader trend in contemporary conflict: the weaponisation of economic interdependence. Recent months have demonstrated the extent of the global economy’s dependence on a limited number of strategic infrastructure networks and maritime chokepoints.
This asymmetry has created opportunities for conventionally weaker actors to generate outsized political gains. Iran’s use of the Strait of Hormuz underscored the strategic leverage that can be derived from weaponising maritime chokepoints.
That logic is particularly relevant to the Red Sea, where the Houthis are closely watching developments around the Strait of Hormuz with a growing awareness that they do not need uncontested control of the entire maritime corridor to impose real costs on global shipping and energy markets. The ability to generate sufficient uncertainty can itself become a major strategic tool.
“The Houthis don’t yet want to strangle all shipping, rather, they seek to leave open the possibility that things could go in that direction if certain demands aren’t met. For now, it serves them better if the threat remains veiled,” Alia Brahimi, Non-resident Senior Fellow at the Atlantic Council, told The New Arab.
Prospects of prolonged disruption weigh heavily on Cairo’s strategic calculations. Consistent with its cautious posture since the US-Israel war on Iran began, Egypt has approached the latest escalation with strategic restraint.
In response to the latest round of Houthi attacks, Cairo established a specialised crisis cell to monitor developments and doubled down on regional diplomacy. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s visit to Cairo in mid-September reflected continued close bilateral coordination.
Multilaterally, the regional quartet (R4), comprising Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan, remains active, convening for the sixth time on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty also met with his Omani counterpart, stressing Egypt’s solidarity with Saudi Arabia and affirming Cairo’s commitment to supporting regional de-escalation.
“Egypt has much to lose from further escalation of regional hostilities, particularly in the Red Sea. This suggests Cairo will likely continue pursuing an intermediary role alongside other regional actors with similar interests, including Oman, Pakistan, Turkey, and Qatar,” Giorgio Cafiero, CEO of Gulf State Analytics, told The New Arab.
The Houthis’ growing confidence, however, cannot be separated from Iran’s broader regional strategy. With Hamas and Hezbollah’s capabilities severely degraded, the Houthis have become a vital lever for Tehran to exert pressure and project power across the region.
Interconnected regional conflict theatres
The Houthis’ increasingly assertive approach to Bab al-Mandeb comes at a strategically significant moment, ahead of the US midterm elections.
With peace negotiations stalled and fears of renewed hostilities mounting, “the Houthis gave themselves a tight timeline to conduct the Bab al-Mandeb operation because, for it to yield optimal results for the Houthis and Iran, it needed to happen ahead of the US midterms, so that it could be used as leverage in Iran-US negotiations,” El Eryani told The New Arab.
These developments illustrate how multiple theatres can be exploited simultaneously, through allied groups, with far-reaching economic and security repercussions.
Previously relatively shielded from the direct effects of the Iran war, Egypt now faces growing challenges from escalating tensions in the Red Sea. Cairo has thus far avoided isolating or antagonising any regional players.
This caution is reinforced by the legacy of Egypt’s 1960s intervention in Yemen, which cost the lives of more than 10,000 Egyptian soldiers and shaped a longstanding preference for diplomatic engagement and close coordination with regional partners over direct military intervention.
Egypt is likely to remain aligned with regional partners, providing political and potentially targeted military support, as it did through naval participation in the 2015 Operation Decisive Storm and through its membership in the Saudi-led Multinational Maritime Defence Alliance, established earlier this year to strengthen maritime security and protect international shipping and energy routes in the Red Sea, Bab al-Mandeb, and Gulf of Aden.
“But the pressure to act is being applied from many directions, and the real risk is that Egypt accidentally becomes entrapped by the escalatory logic of the conflict more generally,” said Brahimi.
The limits of regional alliances
The Houthis’ attacks on Saudi Arabia marked the first real test of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, struck last month between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan. The test revealed the enduring challenges of activating joint regional defence frameworks.
While signatories mobilised rhetorically in response to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, whether that translates into a coordinated joint response remains to be seen.
Egypt remains outside the framework, but this challenging landscape will likely further complicate Cairo’s prospective role in joint defence frameworks, particularly Article 5-style agreements that create commitments to direct intervention.
Any decision to intervene would require caution. Cairo is navigating the Red Sea on two simultaneous fronts, as an economic lifeline and a strategic theatre in which competing regional interests intersect. This creates significant constraints on the scope of direct Egyptian involvement.
These dynamics leave Egypt with a narrow set of options. Further escalation in the Red Sea would expose the Egyptian economy to direct economic and security risks, but the costs of direct intervention remain high.
Cairo is therefore likely to continue relying on its diplomatic channels, intelligence-sharing networks, and naval capabilities while closely monitoring developments.
Ultimately, Egypt’s strategy will be shaped by how far the Houthis and the wider Iran war expand, and how directly the conflict spills over into Egypt’s strategic interests.
Hana Elshehaby is a Senior Research Assistant for the Middle East Council on Global Affairs. She is also a Non-Resident Fellow at the Institute for Middle East Options
